PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractXmlReceiver.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QAbstractXmlReceiver is an abstract base class that provides a callback interface for
receiving an [XQuery
sequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#xquery-sequence),
usually the output of an [QXmlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html),
and transforming that sequence into a structure of your choosing, usually XML. Consider
the example:

```
QXmlQuery query;
query.setQuery("doc('index.html')/html/body/p[1]");

QXmlSerializer serializer(query, myOutputDevice);
query.evaluateTo(&serializer);
```

First it constructs a [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html) that
gets the first paragraph from document `index.html`. Then it constructs an [XML
serializer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlserializer.html) with the
[query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html) and
[myOutputDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) (Note the
[serializer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlserializer.html) is an *XML
receiver*, ie a subclass of QAbstractXmlReceiver). Finally, it
[evaluates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html#evaluateTo) the
[query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html), producing an ordered
sequence of calls to the
[serializer's](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlserializer.html) callback
functions. The sequence of callbacks transforms the query output to XML and writes it to
[myOutputDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

Although the example uses [QXmlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html)
to produce the sequence of callbacks to functions in QAbstractXmlReceiver, you can call
the callback functions directly as long as your sequence of calls represents a valid
[XQuery
sequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#xquery-sequence).

### XQuery Sequences

An [XQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/xmlprocessing.html) *sequence* is an
ordered collection of zero, one, or many *items*. Each *item* is either an *atomic
value* or a *node*. An *atomic value* is a simple data value.

There are six kinds of *nodes*.

- An *Element Node* represents an XML element.
- An *Attribute Node* represents an XML attribute.
- A *Document Node* represents an entire XML document.
- A *Text Node* represents character data (element content).
- A *Processing Instruction Node* represents an XML processing instruction, which is used in an XML document to tell the application reading the document to perform some action. A typical example is to use a processing instruction to tell the application to use a particular XSLT stylesheet to display the document.
- And a *Comment node* represents an XML comment.

The *sequence* of *nodes* and *atomic values* obeys the following rules. Note that
*Namespace Node* refers to a special *Attribute Node* with name *xmlns*.

- Each *node* appears in the *sequence* before its children and their descendants appear.
- A *node*'s descendants appear in the *sequence* before any of its siblings appear.
- A *Document Node* represents an entire document. Zero or more *Document Nodes* can appear in a *sequence*, but they can only be top level items (i.e., a *Document Node* can't be a child of another *node*.
- *Namespace Nodes* immediately follow the *Element Node* with which they are associated.
- *Attribute Nodes* immediately follow the *Namespace Nodes* of the element with which they are associated, or...
- If there are no *Namespace Nodes* following an element, then the *Attribute Nodes* immediately follow the element.
- An *atomic value* can only appear as a top level *item*, i.e., it can't appear as a child of a *node*.
- *Processing Instruction Nodes* do not have children, and their parent is either a *Document Node* or an *Element Node*.
- *Comment Nodes* do not have children, and their parent is either a *Document Node* or an *Element Node*.

The *sequence* of *nodes* and *atomic values* is sent to an QAbstractXmlReceiver
([QXmlSerializer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlserializer.html) in the example
above) as a sequence of calls to the receiver's callback functions. The mapping of
callback functions to sequence items is as follows.

- [startDocument](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#startDocument)() and [endDocument](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#endDocument)() are called for each *Document Node* in the *sequence*. [endDocument](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#endDocument)() is not called until all the *Document Node's* children have appeared in the *sequence*.
- [startElement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#startElement)() and [endElement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#endElement)() are called for each *Element Node*. [endElement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#endElement)() is not called until all the *Element Node's* children have appeared in the *sequence*.
- [attribute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#attribute)() is called for each *Attribute Node*.
- [comment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#comment)() is called for each *Comment Node*.
- [characters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#characters)() is called for each *Text Node*.
- [processingInstruction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#processingInstruction)() is called for each *Processing Instruction Node*.
- [namespaceBinding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#namespaceBinding)() is called for each *Namespace Node*.
- [atomicValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#atomicValue)() is called for each *atomic value*.

For a complete explanation of
[XQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/xmlprocessing.html) sequences, visit [XQuery
Data Model](http://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-datamodel/).

### `[pure virtual]` void QAbstractXmlReceiver::processingInstruction(const [QXmlName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlname.html) \&*target*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*value*)

This callback is called when a processing instruction appears in the
[sequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#xquery-sequence).
A processing instruction is used in an XML document to tell the application reading the
document to perform some action. A typical example is to use a processing instruction to
tell the application to use a particular XSLT stylesheet to process the document.

```
<?xml-stylesheet type="test/xsl" href="formatter.xsl"?>
```

*target* is the [name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlname.html) of the
processing instruction. Its *prefix* and *namespace URI* must both be empty. Its *local
name* is the target. In the above example, the name is *xml-stylesheet*.

The *value* specifies the action to be taken. Note that the *value* must not contain the
string "?\>". In the above example, the *value* is *type\="test/xsl"
href\="formatter.xsl*.

Generally, use of processing instructions should be avoided, because they are not
namespace aware and in many contexts are stripped out anyway. Processing instructions
can often be replaced with elements from a custom namespace.
signatures: processingInstruction(self, target: PySide2.QtXmlPatterns.QXmlName, value: str) -> None

## Detailed Description

This class is used with
[QAccessible::updateAccessibility](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaccessible-obsolete.html#updateAccessibility)().

The event type is one of the values of
[QAccessible::Event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaccessible.html#Event-enum).
There are a number of subclasses that should be used to provide more details about the
event.

For example to notify about a focus change when re-implementing
[QWidget::setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setFocus), the event
could be used as follows:

```
void MyWidget::setFocus(Qt::FocusReason reason)
{
    // handle custom focus setting...
    QAccessibleEvent event(f, QAccessible::Focus);
    QAccessible::updateAccessibility(&event);
}
```

To enable in process screen readers, all events must be sent after the change has
happened.

PythonQt.Qt.QAction.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

In applications many common commands can be invoked via menus, toolbar buttons, and
keyboard shortcuts. Since the user expects each command to be performed in the same way,
regardless of the user interface used, it is useful to represent each command as an
*action*.

Actions can be added to menus and toolbars, and will automatically keep them in sync.
For example, in a word processor, if the user presses a Bold toolbar button, the Bold
menu item will automatically be checked.

Actions can be created as independent objects, but they may also be created during the
construction of menus; the [QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) class
contains convenience functions for creating actions suitable for use as menu items.

A QAction may contain an icon, menu text, a shortcut, status text, "What's This?" text,
and a tooltip. Most of these can be set in the constructor. They can also be set
independently with
[setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#icon-prop)(),
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#text-prop)(),
[setIconText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#iconText-prop)(),
[setShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#shortcut-prop)(),
[setStatusTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#statusTip-prop)(),
[setWhatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#whatsThis-prop)(), and
[setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#toolTip-prop)(). For menu
items, it is possible to set an individual font with
[setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#font-prop)().

Actions are added to widgets using
[QWidget::addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#addAction)() or
[QGraphicsWidget::addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#addAction)().
Note that an action must be added to a widget before it can be used; this is also true
when the shortcut should be global (i.e.,
[Qt::ApplicationShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ShortcutContext-enum)
as
[Qt::ShortcutContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ShortcutContext-enum)).

Once a QAction has been created it should be added to the relevant menu and toolbar,
then connected to the slot which will perform the action. For example:

```
    const QIcon openIcon = QIcon::fromTheme("document-open", QIcon(":/images/open.png"));
    QAction *openAct = new QAction(openIcon, tr("&Open..."), this);
    openAct->setShortcuts(QKeySequence::Open);
    openAct->setStatusTip(tr("Open an existing file"));
    connect(openAct, &QAction::triggered, this, &MainWindow::open);
    fileMenu->addAction(openAct);
    fileToolBar->addAction(openAct);
```

We recommend that actions are created as children of the window they are used in. In
most cases actions will be children of the application's main window.

### checkable : bool

This property holds whether the action is a checkable action

A checkable action is one which has an on/off state. For example, in a word processor, a
Bold toolbar button may be either on or off. An action which is not a toggle action is a
command action; a command action is simply executed, e.g. file save. By default, this
property is `false`.

In some situations, the state of one toggle action should depend on the state of others.
For example, "Left Align", "Center" and "Right Align" toggle actions are mutually
exclusive. To achieve exclusive toggling, add the relevant toggle actions to a
[QActionGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qactiongroup.html) with the
QActionGroup::exclusive property set to true.

### enabled : bool

This property holds whether the action is enabled

Disabled actions cannot be chosen by the user. They do not disappear from menus or
toolbars, but they are displayed in a way which indicates that they are unavailable. For
example, they might be displayed using only shades of gray.

**What's This?** help on disabled actions is still available, provided that the
[QAction::whatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#whatsThis-prop)
property is set.

An action will be disabled when all widgets to which it is added (with
[QWidget::addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#addAction)()) are
disabled or not visible. When an action is disabled, it is not possible to trigger it
through its shortcut.

By default, this property is `true` (actions are enabled).

### iconVisibleInMenu : bool

This property holds whether or not an action should show an icon in a menu

In some applications, it may make sense to have actions with icons in the toolbar, but
not in menus. If true, the icon (if valid) is shown in the menu, when it is false, it is
not shown.

The default is to follow whether the
[Qt::AA\_DontShowIconsInMenus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ApplicationAttribute-enum)
attribute is set for the application. Explicitly settings this property overrides the
presence (or abscence) of the attribute.

For example:

```
QApplication app(argc, argv);
app.setAttribute(Qt::AA_DontShowIconsInMenus);  // Icons are *no longer shown* in menus
// ...
QAction *myAction = new QAction();
// ...
myAction->setIcon(SomeIcon);
myAction->setIconVisibleInMenu(true);   // Icon *will* be shown in menus for *this* action.
```

This property was introduced in Qt 4.4.

PythonQt.Qt.QActionGroup.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

In some situations it is useful to group
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) objects together. For
example, if you have a **Left Align** action, a **Right Align** action, a **Justify**
action, and a **Center** action, only one of these actions should be active at any one
time. One simple way of achieving this is to group the actions together in an action
group.

Here's a example (from the
[Menus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-mainwindows-menus-example.html)
example):

```
    alignmentGroup = new QActionGroup(this);
    alignmentGroup->addAction(leftAlignAct);
    alignmentGroup->addAction(rightAlignAct);
    alignmentGroup->addAction(justifyAct);
    alignmentGroup->addAction(centerAct);
    leftAlignAct->setChecked(true);
```

Here we create a new action group. Since the action group is exclusive by default, only
one of the actions in the group is checked at any one time.

![Alignment options in a
QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qactiongroup-align.png)

A QActionGroup emits an
[triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qactiongroup.html#triggered)() signal
when one of its actions is chosen. Each action in an action group emits its
[triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qactiongroup.html#triggered)() signal as
usual.

As stated above, an action group is exclusive by default; it ensures that at most only
one checkable action is active at any one time. If you want to group checkable actions
without making them exclusive, you can turn off exclusiveness by calling
[setExclusive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qactiongroup.html#setExclusive)(false).

By default the active action of an exclusive group cannot be unchecked. In some cases it
may be useful to allow unchecking all the actions, you can allow this by calling
[setExclusionPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qactiongroup.html#exclusionPolicy-prop)(QActionGroup::ExclusionPolicy::ExclusiveOptional).

Actions can be added to an action group using
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qactiongroup.html#addAction)(), but it is
usually more convenient to specify a group when creating actions; this ensures that
actions are automatically created with a parent. Actions can be visually separated from
each other by adding a separator action to the group; create an action and use
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html)'s
[setSeparator()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#setSeparator) function
to make it considered a separator. Action groups are added to widgets with the
[QWidget::addActions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#addActions)()
function.

### exclusionPolicy : [QActionGroup::ExclusionPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qactiongroup.html#ExclusionPolicy-enum)

This property holds the group exclusive checking policy

If exclusionPolicy is set to Exclusive, only one checkable action in the action group
can ever be active at any time. If the user chooses another checkable action in the
group, the one they chose becomes active and the one that was active becomes inactive.
If exclusionPolicy is set to ExclusionOptional the group is exclusive but the active
checkable action in the group can be unchecked leaving the group with no actions
checked.

This property was introduced in Qt 5.14.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

An animation group is a container for animations (subclasses of
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html)). A
group is usually responsible for managing the
[state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#State-enum) of its
animations, i.e., it decides when to start, stop, resume, and pause them. Currently, Qt
provides two such groups:
[QParallelAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qparallelanimationgroup.html)
and
[QSequentialAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsequentialanimationgroup.html).
Look up their class descriptions for details.

Since QAnimationGroup inherits from
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html), you
can combine groups, and easily construct complex animation graphs. You can query
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html) for the
group it belongs to (using the
[group()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#group) function).

To start a top-level animation group, you simply use the
[start()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#start) function
from [QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html).
By a top-level animation group, we think of a group that itself is not contained within
another group. Starting sub groups directly is not supported, and may lead to unexpected
behavior.

QAnimationGroup provides methods for adding and retrieving animations. Besides that, you
can remove animations by calling
[removeAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html#removeAnimation)(),
and clear the animation group by calling
[clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html#clear)(). You may keep
track of changes in the group's animations by listening to
[QEvent::ChildAdded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[QEvent::ChildRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events.

QAnimationGroup takes ownership of the animations it manages, and ensures that they are
deleted when the animation group is deleted.

PythonQt.Qt.QApplication.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QApplication specializes
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) with some
functionality needed for
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html)-based applications. It
handles widget specific initialization, finalization.

For any GUI application using Qt, there is precisely **one** QApplication object, no
matter whether the application has 0, 1, 2 or more windows at any given time. For
non-[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) based Qt applications,
use [QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) instead,
as it does not depend on the
[QtWidgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-module.html) library.

Some GUI applications provide a special batch mode ie. provide command line arguments
for executing tasks without manual intervention. In such non-GUI mode, it is often
sufficient to instantiate a plain
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) to avoid
unnecessarily initializing resources needed for a graphical user interface. The
following example shows how to dynamically create an appropriate type of application
instance:

```
QCoreApplication* createApplication(int &argc, char *argv[])
{
    for (int i = 1; i < argc; ++i) {
        if (!qstrcmp(argv[i], "-no-gui"))
            return new QCoreApplication(argc, argv);
    }
    return new QApplication(argc, argv);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
    QScopedPointer<QCoreApplication> app(createApplication(argc, argv));

    if (qobject_cast<QApplication *>(app.data())) {
       // start GUI version...
    } else {
       // start non-GUI version...
    }

    return app->exec();
}
```

The QApplication object is accessible through the
[instance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#instance)() function
that returns a pointer equivalent to the global
[qApp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#qApp) pointer.

QApplication's main areas of responsibility are:

- It initializes the application with the user's desktop settings such as [palette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#palette)(), [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#font)() and [doubleClickInterval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#doubleClickInterval-prop)(). It keeps track of these properties in case the user changes the desktop globally, for example through some kind of control panel.
- It performs event handling, meaning that it receives events from the underlying window system and dispatches them to the relevant widgets. By using [sendEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendEvent)() and [postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#postEvent)() you can send your own events to widgets.
- It parses common command line arguments and sets its internal state accordingly. See the [constructor documentation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#QApplication) below for more details.
- It defines the application's look and feel, which is encapsulated in a [QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) object. This can be changed at runtime with [setStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setStyle)().
- It provides localization of strings that are visible to the user via [translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#translate)().
- It provides some magical objects like the desktop() and the [clipboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#clipboard)().
- It knows about the application's windows. You can ask which widget is at a certain position using [widgetAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#widgetAt)(), get a list of [topLevelWidgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#topLevelWidgets)() and [closeAllWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#closeAllWindows)(), etc.
- It manages the application's mouse cursor handling, see [setOverrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#setOverrideCursor)()

Since the QApplication object does so much initialization, it *must* be created before
any other objects related to the user interface are created. QApplication also deals
with common command line arguments. Hence, it is usually a good idea to create it
*before* any interpretation or modification of `argv` is done in the application itself.

A modal widget is a special top-level widget which is a subclass of

parameter of the constructor as true. A modal widget must be closed before the user can
continue with other parts of the program.

Modal widgets are organized in a stack. This function returns the active modal widget at
the top of the stack.

**See also**
[activePopupWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activePopupWidget)()
and
[topLevelWidgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#topLevelWidgets)().

### `[static]` [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \*QApplication::activePopupWidget()

A popup widget is a special top-level widget that sets the `Qt::WType_Popup` widget
flag, e.g. the [QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) widget. When the
application opens a popup widget, all events are sent to the popup. Normal widgets and
modal widgets cannot be accessed before the popup widget is closed.

Only other popup widgets may be opened when a popup widget is shown. The popup widgets

PythonQt.Qt.QApplication.alert.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QApplication::alert([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**widget*, int *msec* \= 0\)

Causes an alert to be shown for *widget* if the window is not the active window. The
alert is shown for *msec* milliseconds. If *msec* is zero (the default), then the alert
is shown indefinitely until the window becomes active again.

Currently this function does nothing on Qt for Embedded Linux.

On macOS, this works more at the application level and will cause the application icon
to bounce in the dock.

On Windows, this causes the window's taskbar entry to flash for a time. If *msec* is
zero, the flashing will stop and the taskbar entry will turn a different color
(currently orange).

On X11, this will cause the window to be marked as "demands attention", the window must
not be hidden (i.e. not have hide() called on it, but be visible in some sort of way) in
order for this to work.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

### `[static slot]` void QApplication::closeAllWindows()

Closes all top-level windows.

This function is particularly useful for applications with many top-level windows. It
could, for example, be connected to a **Exit** entry in the **File** menu:

```
    const QIcon exitIcon = QIcon::fromTheme("application-exit");
    QAction *exitAct = fileMenu->addAction(exitIcon, tr("E&xit"), qApp, &QApplication::closeAllWindows);
    exitAct->setShortcuts(QKeySequence::Quit);
    exitAct->setStatusTip(tr("Exit the application"));
    fileMenu->addAction(exitAct);
```

The windows are closed in random order, until one window does not accept the close
event. The application quits when the last window was successfully closed; this can be
turned off by setting
[quitOnLastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#quitOnLastWindowClosed-prop)
to false.

### cursorFlashTime : int

This property holds the text cursor's flash (blink) time in milliseconds

The flash time is the time required to display, invert and restore the caret display.
Usually the text cursor is displayed for half the cursor flash time, then hidden for the
same amount of time, but this may vary.

The default value on X11 is 1000 milliseconds. On Windows, the **Control Panel** value
is used and setting this property sets the cursor flash time for all applications.

We recommend that widgets do not cache this value as it may change at any time if the
user changes the global desktop settings.

**Note:** This property may hold a negative value, for instance if cursor blinking is
disabled.

PythonQt.Qt.QApplication.exec.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` int QApplication::exec()

Enters the main event loop and waits until
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() is called, then
returns the value that was set to
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() (which is 0 if
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() is called via
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)()).

It is necessary to call this function to start event handling. The main event loop
receives events from the window system and dispatches these to the application widgets.

Generally, no user interaction can take place before calling exec(). As a special case,
modal widgets like [QMessageBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html)
can be used before calling exec(), because modal widgets call exec() to start a local
event loop.

To make your application perform idle processing, i.e., executing a special function
whenever there are no pending events, use a
[QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) with 0 timeout. More advanced
idle processing schemes can be achieved using
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)().

We recommend that you connect clean-up code to the
[aboutToQuit()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#aboutToQuit)
signal, instead of putting it in your application's `main()` function. This is because,
on some platforms the QApplication::exec() call may not return. For example, on the
Windows platform, when the user logs off, the system terminates the process after Qt
closes all top-level windows. Hence, there is *no guarantee* that the application will
have time to exit its event loop and execute code at the end of the `main()` function,
after the QApplication::exec() call.

**See also**
[quitOnLastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#quitOnLastWindowClosed-prop),
[QCoreApplication::quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)(),
[QCoreApplication::exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)(),
[QCoreApplication::processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)(),
and
[QCoreApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)().

### `[static]` void QApplication::setActiveWindow([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**active*)

function is called from the platform specific event handlers.

**Warning:** This function does *not* set the keyboard focus to the active widget. Call
[QWidget::activateWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#activateWindow)()

It sets the
[activeWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activeWindow)() and

[WindowActivate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)/[WindowDeactivate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
and
[FocusIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)/[FocusOut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
events to all appropriate widgets. The window will then be painted in active state (e.g.
cursors in line edits will blink), and it will have tool tips enabled.

**See also**
[activeWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activeWindow)() and
[QWidget::activateWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#activateWindow)().

### `[static]` void QApplication::setFont(const [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) \&*font*, const char \**className* \= nullptr)

Changes the default application font to *font*. If *className* is passed, the change
applies only to classes that inherit *className* (as reported by
[QObject::inherits](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#inherits)()).

On application start-up, the default font depends on the window system. It can vary
depending on both the window system version and the locale. This function lets you
override the default font; but overriding may be a bad idea because, for example, some
locales need extra large fonts to support their special characters.

**Warning:** Do not use this function in conjunction with [Qt Style
Sheets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet.html). The font of an application
can be customized using the "font" style sheet property. To set a bold font for all
QPushButtons, set the application
[styleSheet](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#styleSheet-prop)() as
"[QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html) { font: bold }"

**See also** [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#font)(),
[fontMetrics](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#fontMetrics)(), and
[QWidget::setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop)().

Changes the application palette to *palette*.

If *className* is passed, the change applies only to widgets that inherit *className*
(as reported by
[QObject::inherits](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#inherits)()). If
*className* is left 0, the change affects all widgets, thus overriding any previously
set class specific palettes.

The palette may be changed according to the current GUI style in
[QStyle::polish](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#polish)().

**Warning:** Do not use this function in conjunction with [Qt Style
Sheets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet.html). When using style sheets,
the palette of a widget can be customized using the "color", "background-color",
"selection-color", "selection-background-color" and "alternate-background-color".

**Note:** Some styles do not use the palette for all drawing, for instance, if they make
use of native theme engines. This is the case for the Windows Vista and macOS styles.

**See also**
[QWidget::setPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#palette-prop)(),
[palette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#palette)(), and
[QStyle::polish](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#polish)().

PythonQt.Qt.QApplication.setStyle.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QApplication::setStyle([QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) \**style*)

Sets the application's GUI style to *style*. Ownership of the style object is
transferred to [QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html), so
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html) will delete the
style object on application exit or when a new style is set and the old style is still
the parent of the application object.

Example usage:

```
QApplication::setStyle(QStyleFactory::create("Fusion"));
```

When switching application styles, the color palette is set back to the initial colors
or the system defaults. This is necessary since certain styles have to adapt the color
palette to be fully style-guide compliant.

Setting the style before a palette has been set, i.e., before creating
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html), will cause the
application to use
[QStyle::standardPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#standardPalette)()
for the palette.

**Warning:** Qt style sheets are currently not supported for custom
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) subclasses. We plan to address
this in some future release.

**See also** [style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#style)(),
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html),
[setPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setPalette)(), and
[desktopSettingsAware](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#desktopSettingsAware)().

### `[static]` [QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) \*QApplication::setStyle(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*style*)

This is an overloaded function.

Requests a [QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) object for *style*
from the [QStyleFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstylefactory.html).

The string must be one of the
[QStyleFactory::keys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstylefactory.html#keys)(),
typically one of "windows", "windowsvista", "fusion", or "macintosh". Style names are
case insensitive.

Returns `nullptr` if an unknown *style* is passed, otherwise the

### startDragDistance : int

If you support drag and drop in your application, and want to start a drag and drop
operation after the user has moved the cursor a certain distance with a button held
down, you should use this property's value as the minimum distance required.

For example, if the mouse position of the click is stored in `startPos` and the current
position (e.g. in the mouse move event) is `currentPos`, you can find out if a drag
should be started with code like this:

```
if ((startPos - currentPos).manhattanLength() >=
        QApplication::startDragDistance())
    startTheDrag();
```

Qt uses this value internally, e.g. in
[QFileDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html).

The default value (if the platform doesn't provide a different default) is 10 pixels.

**Access functions:**

| void | **setStartDragDistance**(int *l*) |

**See also**

[QPoint::manhattanLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#manhattanLength)(),
and [Drag and Drop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#drag-and-drop).

PythonQt.Qt.QAuthenticator.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QAuthenticator class is usually used in the
[authenticationRequired()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkaccessmanager.html#authenticationRequired)
and
[proxyAuthenticationRequired()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkaccessmanager.html#proxyAuthenticationRequired)
signals of
[QNetworkAccessManager](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkaccessmanager.html)
and [QAbstractSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html). The
class provides a way to pass back the required authentication information to the socket
when accessing services that require authentication.

QAuthenticator supports the following authentication methods:

- Basic
- NTLM version 2
- Digest-MD5
- SPNEGO/Negotiate

### Options

In addition to the username and password required for authentication, a QAuthenticator
object can also contain additional options. The
[options](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qauthenticator.html#options)() function can
be used to query incoming options sent by the server; the
[setOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qauthenticator.html#setOption)() function
can be used to set outgoing options, to be processed by the authenticator calculation.
The options accepted and provided depend on the authentication type (see method()).

The following tables list known incoming options as well as accepted outgoing options.
The list of incoming options is not exhaustive, since servers may include additional
information at any time. The list of outgoing options is exhaustive, however, and no
unknown options will be treated or sent back to the server.

#### Basic

| Option | Direction | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `realm` | Incoming | [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) | Contains the realm of the authentication, the same as [realm](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qauthenticator.html#realm)() |

The Basic authentication mechanism supports no outgoing options.

#### NTLM version 2

The NTLM authentication mechanism currently supports no incoming or outgoing options. On
Windows, if no *user* has been set, domain\\user credentials will be searched for on the
local system to enable Single-Sign-On functionality.

#### Digest-MD5

| Option | Direction | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `realm` | Incoming | [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) | Contains the realm of the authentication, the same as [realm](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qauthenticator.html#realm)() |

The Digest-MD5 authentication mechanism supports no outgoing options.

#### SPNEGO/Negotiate

This authentication mechanism currently supports no incoming or outgoing options.

## Detailed Description

QBackingStore enables the use of
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) to paint on a
[QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html) with type RasterSurface. The
other way of rendering to a [QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html)
is through the use of OpenGL with
[QOpenGLContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglcontext.html).

A QBackingStore contains a buffered representation of the window contents, and thus
supports partial updates by using
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) to only update a sub region
of the window contents.

QBackingStore might be used by an application that wants to use
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) without OpenGL acceleration
and without the extra overhead of using the
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) or
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) UI stacks. For an
example of how to use QBackingStore see the [Raster Window
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-rasterwindow-example.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QBasicTimer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This is a fast, lightweight, and low-level class used by Qt internally. We recommend
using the higher-level [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) class
rather than this class if you want to use timers in your applications. Note that this
timer is a repeating timer that will send subsequent timer events unless the
[stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#stop)() function is called.

To use this class, create a QBasicTimer, and call its
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#start)() function with a
timeout interval and with a pointer to a
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass. When the timer
times out it will send a timer event to the
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass. The timer can be
stopped at any time using
[stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#stop)().
[isActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#isActive)() returns
`true` for a timer that is running; i.e. it has been started, has not reached the
timeout time, and has not been stopped. The timer's ID can be retrieved using
[timerId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#timerId)().

Objects of this class cannot be copied, but can be moved, so you can maintain a list of
basic timers by holding them in container that supports move-only types, e.g.
std::vector.

The [Wiggly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-wiggly-example.html)
example uses QBasicTimer to repaint a widget at regular intervals.

PythonQt.Qt.QBitArray.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QBitArray is an array that gives access to individual bits and provides operators
([AND](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-and),
[OR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7c),
[XOR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-5e), and
[NOT](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7e)) that work on
entire arrays of bits. It uses [implicit
sharing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) (copy-on-write) to
reduce memory usage and to avoid the needless copying of data.

The following code constructs a QBitArray containing 200 bits initialized to false (0):

```
QBitArray ba(200);
```

To initialize the bits to true, either pass `true` as second argument to the
constructor, or call [fill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#fill)()
later on.

QBitArray uses 0-based indexes, just like C\+\+ arrays. To access the bit at a
particular index position, you can use operator\[\](). On non-const bit arrays,
operator\[\]() returns a reference to a bit that can be used on the left side of an
assignment. For example:

```
QBitArray ba;
ba.resize(3);
ba[0] = true;
ba[1] = false;
ba[2] = true;
```

For technical reasons, it is more efficient to use
[testBit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#testBit)() and
[setBit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#setBit)() to access bits in
the array than operator\[\](). For example:

```
QBitArray ba(3);
ba.setBit(0, true);
ba.setBit(1, false);
ba.setBit(2, true);
```

QBitArray supports `&`
([AND](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-and)), `|`
([OR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7c)), `^`
([XOR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-5e)), `~`
([NOT](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7e)), as well as `&=`,
`|=`, and `^=`. These operators work in the same way as the built-in C\+\+ bitwise
operators of the same name. For example:

```
QBitArray x(5);
x.setBit(3, true);
// x: [ 0, 0, 0, 1, 0 ]

QBitArray y(5);
y.setBit(4, true);
// y: [ 0, 0, 0, 0, 1 ]

x |= y;
// x: [ 0, 0, 0, 1, 1 ]
```

For historical reasons, QBitArray distinguishes between a null bit array and an empty
bit array. A *null* bit array is a bit array that is initialized using QBitArray's
default constructor. An *empty* bit array is any bit array with size 0\. A null bit
array is always empty, but an empty bit array isn't necessarily null:

```
QBitArray().isNull();           // returns true
QBitArray().isEmpty();          // returns true

QBitArray(0).isNull();          // returns false
QBitArray(0).isEmpty();         // returns true

QBitArray(3).isNull();          // returns false
QBitArray(3).isEmpty();         // returns false
```

All functions except
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#isNull)() treat null bit
arrays the same as empty bit arrays; for example, QBitArray() compares equal to
QBitArray(0). We recommend that you always use
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#isEmpty)() and avoid
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#isNull)().

PythonQt.Qt.QBitArray.fill.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QBitArray::fill(bool *value*, int *size* \= -1)

Sets every bit in the bit array to *value*, returning true if successful; otherwise
returns `false`. If *size* is different from -1 (the default), the bit array is resized
to *size* beforehand.

Example:

```
QBitArray ba(8);
ba.fill(true);
// ba: [ 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 ]

ba.fill(false, 2);
// ba: [ 0, 0 ]
```

**See also** [resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#resize)().

### void QBitArray::fill(bool *value*, int *begin*, int *end*)

This is an overloaded function.

Sets bits at index positions *begin* up to (but not including) *end* to *value*.

*begin* must be a valid index position in the bit array (0 \<\= *begin* \<
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#size)()).

*end* must be either a valid index position or equal to
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#size)(), in which case the fill
operation runs until the end of the array (0 \<\= *end* \<\=
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#size)()).

Example:

```
QBitArray ba(4);
ba.fill(true, 1, 2);            // ba: [ 0, 1, 0, 0 ]
ba.fill(true, 1, 3);            // ba: [ 0, 1, 1, 0 ]
ba.fill(true, 1, 4);            // ba: [ 0, 1, 1, 1 ]
```
signatures: fill(self, val: bool, first: int, last: int) -> None
fill(self, val: bool, size: int=...) -> bool

PythonQt.Qt.QBitmap.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QBitmap class is a monochrome off-screen paint device used mainly for creating
custom [QCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcursor.html) and
[QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html) objects, constructing
[QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) objects, and for setting
masks for pixmaps and widgets.

QBitmap is a [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) subclass
ensuring a depth of 1, except for null objects which have a depth of 0\. If a pixmap
with a depth greater than 1 is assigned to a bitmap, the bitmap will be dithered
automatically.

Use the [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) objects
[Qt::color0](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum) and
[Qt::color1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum) when drawing
on a QBitmap object (or a [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html)
object with depth 1).

Painting with [Qt::color0](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum)
sets the bitmap bits to 0, and painting with
[Qt::color1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum) sets the bits
to 1\. For a bitmap, 0-bits indicate background (or transparent pixels) and 1-bits
indicate foreground (or opaque pixels). Use the
[clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html#clear)() function to set all the
bits to [Qt::color0](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum). Note
that using the [Qt::black](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum)
and [Qt::white](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum) colors make
no sense because the QColor::pixel() value is not necessarily 0 for black and 1 for
white.

The QBitmap class provides the
[transformed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html#transformed)() function
returning a transformed copy of the bitmap; use the
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) argument to translate,
scale, shear, and rotate the bitmap. In addition, QBitmap provides the static
[fromData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html#fromData)() function which
returns a bitmap constructed from the given `uchar` data, and the static
[fromImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html#fromImage)() function
returning a converted copy of a [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html)
object.

Just like the [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) class, QBitmap
is optimized by the use of implicit data sharing. For more information, see the
[Implicit Data Sharing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html)
documentation.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QBoxLayout takes the space it gets (from its parent layout or from the
[parentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#parentWidget)()), divides
it up into a row of boxes, and makes each managed widget fill one box.

![Horizontal box layout with five child
widgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qhboxlayout-with-5-children.png)

If the QBoxLayout's orientation is
[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) the boxes
are placed in a row, with suitable sizes. Each widget (or other box) will get at least
its minimum size and at most its maximum size. Any excess space is shared according to
the stretch factors (more about that below).

![Vertical box layout with five child
widgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qvboxlayout-with-5-children.png)

If the QBoxLayout's orientation is
[Qt::Vertical](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum), the boxes
are placed in a column, again with suitable sizes.

The easiest way to create a QBoxLayout is to use one of the convenience classes, e.g.
[QHBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhboxlayout.html) (for
[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) boxes) or
[QVBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvboxlayout.html) (for
[Qt::Vertical](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) boxes). You
can also use the QBoxLayout constructor directly, specifying its direction as
[LeftToRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#Direction-enum),
[RightToLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#Direction-enum),
[TopToBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#Direction-enum), or
[BottomToTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#Direction-enum).

If the QBoxLayout is not the top-level layout (i.e. it is not managing all of the
widget's area and children), you must add it to its parent layout before you can do
anything with it. The normal way to add a layout is by calling
parentLayout-\>[addLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addLayout)().

Once you have done this, you can add boxes to the QBoxLayout using one of four
functions:

- [addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addWidget)() to add a widget to the QBoxLayout and set the widget's stretch factor. (The stretch factor is along the row of boxes.)
- [addSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addSpacing)() to create an empty box; this is one of the functions you use to create nice and spacious dialogs. See below for ways to set margins.
- [addStretch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addStretch)() to create an empty, stretchable box.
- [addLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addLayout)() to add a box containing another [QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html) to the row and set that layout's stretch factor.

Use [insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#insertWidget)(),
[insertSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#insertSpacing)(),
[insertStretch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#insertStretch)() or
[insertLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#insertLayout)() to
insert a box at a specified position in the layout.

QBoxLayout also includes two margin widths:

- [setContentsMargins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#setContentsMargins)() sets the width of the outer border on each side of the widget. This is the width of the reserved space along each of the QBoxLayout's four sides.
- [setSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#setSpacing)() sets the width between neighboring boxes. (You can use [addSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addSpacing)() to get more space at a particular spot.)

The margin default is provided by the style. The default margin most Qt styles specify
is 9 for child widgets and 11 for windows. The spacing defaults to the same as the
margin width for a top-level layout, or to the same as the parent layout.

To remove a widget from a layout, call
[removeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#removeWidget)(). Calling
[QWidget::hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)() on a widget also
effectively removes the widget from the layout until
[QWidget::show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() is called.

You will almost always want to use
[QVBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvboxlayout.html) and
[QHBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhboxlayout.html) rather than
QBoxLayout because of their convenient constructors.

### void QBoxLayout::addStrut(int *size*)

[LeftToRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#Direction-enum)) to a

PythonQt.Qt.QBoxLayout.addWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QBoxLayout::addWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**widget*, int *stretch* \= 0, [Qt::Alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) *alignment* \= Qt::Alignment())

Adds *widget* to the end of this box layout, with a stretch factor of *stretch* and
alignment *alignment*.

The stretch factor applies only in the
[direction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#direction) of the
[QBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html), and is relative to the
other boxes and widgets in this
[QBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html). Widgets and boxes with
higher stretch factors grow more.

If the stretch factor is 0 and nothing else in the
[QBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html) has a stretch factor
greater than zero, the space is distributed according to the
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html):sizePolicy() of each widget
that's involved.

The alignment is specified by *alignment*. The default alignment is 0, which means that
the widget fills the entire cell.

**See also**
[insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#insertWidget)(),
[addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addItem)(),
[addLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addLayout)(),
[addStretch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addStretch)(),
[addSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addSpacing)(), and
[addStrut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#addStrut)().
signatures: addWidget(self, arg__1: PySide2.QtWidgets.QWidget, stretch: int=..., alignment: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.Alignment=...) -> None

the spacing property is valid, that value is returned. Otherwise, a value for the
spacing property is computed and returned. Since layout spacing in a widget is style

parent layout for the spacing().

[setSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html#setSpacing)().

PythonQt.Qt.QBrush.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A brush has a style, a color, a gradient and a texture.

The brush [style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#style)() defines the
fill pattern using the
[Qt::BrushStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum) enum. The
default brush style is
[Qt::NoBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum) (depending on
how you construct a brush). This style tells the painter to not fill shapes. The
standard style for filling is
[Qt::SolidPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum). The
style can be set when the brush is created using the appropriate constructor, and in
addition the [setStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#setStyle)()
function provides means for altering the style once the brush is constructed.

![Brush Styles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/brush-styles.png)

The brush [color](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#color)() defines the
color of the fill pattern. The color can either be one of Qt's predefined colors,
[Qt::GlobalColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum), or any
other custom [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html). The currently set
color can be retrieved and altered using the
[color](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#color)() and
[setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#setColor)() functions,
respectively.

The [gradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#gradient)() defines the
gradient fill used when the current style is either
[Qt::LinearGradientPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum),
[Qt::RadialGradientPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum)
or
[Qt::ConicalGradientPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum).
Gradient brushes are created by giving a
[QGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html) as a constructor argument
when creating the QBrush. Qt provides three different gradients:
[QLinearGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineargradient.html),
[QConicalGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qconicalgradient.html), and
[QRadialGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html) \- all of
which inherit [QGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html).

```
    QRadialGradient gradient(50, 50, 50, 50, 50);
    gradient.setColorAt(0, QColor::fromRgbF(0, 1, 0, 1));
    gradient.setColorAt(1, QColor::fromRgbF(0, 0, 0, 0));

    QBrush brush(gradient);
```

The [texture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#texture)() defines the
pixmap used when the current style is
[Qt::TexturePattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum). You
can create a brush with a texture by providing the pixmap when the brush is created or
by using [setTexture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#setTexture)().

Note that applying
[setTexture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#setTexture)() makes
[style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#style)() \=\=
[Qt::TexturePattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum),
regardless of previous style settings. Also, calling
[setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#setColor)() will not make a
difference if the style is a gradient. The same is the case if the style is
[Qt::TexturePattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum) style
unless the current texture is a
[QBitmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html).

The [isOpaque](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#isOpaque)() function
returns `true` if the brush is fully opaque otherwise false. A brush is considered
opaque if:

- The alpha component of the [color](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#color)() is 255\.
- Its [texture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#texture)() does not have an alpha channel and is not a [QBitmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html).
- The colors in the [gradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#gradient)() all have an alpha component that is 255\.

| Outlines | To specify the style and color of lines and outlines, use the [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html)'s [pen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpen.html) combined with [Qt::PenStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#PenStyle-enum) and [Qt::GlobalColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum): ``` QPainter painter(this);  painter.setBrush(Qt::cyan); painter.setPen(Qt::darkCyan); painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100,100);  painter.setBrush(Qt::NoBrush); painter.setPen(Qt::darkGreen); painter.drawRect(40, 40, 100, 100); ```  Note that, by default, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) renders the outline (using the currently set pen) when drawing shapes. Use [`painter.setPen(Qt::NoPen)`](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#PenStyle-enum) to disable this behavior. |
| --- | --- |

For more information about painting in general, see the [Paint
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/paintsystem.html).

### bool QBrush::isOpaque() const

Returns `true` if the brush is fully opaque otherwise false. A brush is considered
opaque if:

- The alpha component of the [color](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#color)() is 255\.
- Its [texture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#texture)() does not have an alpha channel and is not a [QBitmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html).
- The colors in the [gradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html#gradient)() all have an alpha component that is 255\.
- It is an extended radial gradient.

## Detailed Description

QBuffer allows you to access a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) using the
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) interface. The
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) is treated just as a
standard random-accessed file. Example:

```
    QBuffer buffer;
    char ch;

    buffer.open(QBuffer::ReadWrite);
    buffer.write("Qt rocks!");
    buffer.seek(0);
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == 'Q'
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == 't'
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == ' '
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == 'r'
```

By default, an internal [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)
buffer is created for you when you create a QBuffer. You can access this buffer directly
by calling [buffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#buffer)(). You can
also use QBuffer with an existing
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) by calling
[setBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#setBuffer)(), or by passing
your array to QBuffer's constructor.

Call [open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#open)() to open the buffer.
Then call [write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)() to write to the
buffer, and [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(),
[readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readAll)(), or
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)() to read from it.
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#size)() returns the current size
of the buffer, and you can seek to arbitrary positions in the buffer by calling
[seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#seek)(). When you are done with
accessing the buffer, call
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#close)().

The following code snippet shows how to write data to a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) using
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) and QBuffer:

```
    QByteArray byteArray;
    QBuffer buffer(&byteArray);
    buffer.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly);

    QDataStream out(&buffer);
    out << QApplication::palette();
```

Effectively, we convert the application's
[QPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html) into a byte array. Here's
how to read the data from the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html):

```
    QPalette palette;
    QBuffer buffer(&byteArray);
    buffer.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly);

    QDataStream in(&buffer);
    in >> palette;
```

[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) and
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) also provide
convenience constructors that take a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) and that create a
QBuffer behind the scenes.

QBuffer emits [readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)()
when new data has arrived in the buffer. By connecting to this signal, you can use
QBuffer to store temporary data before processing it. QBuffer also emits
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() every
time new data has been written to the buffer.

PythonQt.Qt.QBuffer.setBuffer.doc:

### void QBuffer::setBuffer([QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \**byteArray*)

Makes [QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) use the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) pointed to by
*byteArray* as its internal buffer. The caller is responsible for ensuring that
*byteArray* remains valid until the
[QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) is destroyed, or until
setBuffer() is called to change the buffer.
[QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) doesn't take ownership of the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html).

Does nothing if [isOpen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isOpen)() is
true.

If you open the buffer in write-only mode or read-write mode and write something into
the [QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html), *byteArray* will be
modified.

Example:

```
    QByteArray byteArray("abc");
    QBuffer buffer;
    buffer.setBuffer(&byteArray);
    buffer.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly);
    buffer.seek(3);
    buffer.write("def", 3);
    buffer.close();
    // byteArray == "abcdef"
```

If *byteArray* is `nullptr`, the buffer creates its own internal
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) to work on. This byte
array is initially empty.

**See also** [buffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#buffer)(),
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#setData)(), and
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#open)().

## Detailed Description

QButtonGroup provides an abstract container into which button widgets can be placed. It
does not provide a visual representation of this container (see
[QGroupBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgroupbox.html) for a container widget),
but instead manages the states of each of the buttons in the group.

An [exclusive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#exclusive-prop)
button group switches off all checkable (toggle) buttons except the one that has been
clicked. By default, a button group is exclusive. The buttons in a button group are
usually checkable [QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html)s,
[QCheckBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html)es (normally for
non-exclusive button groups), or
[QRadioButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradiobutton.html)s. If you create an
exclusive button group, you should ensure that one of the buttons in the group is
initially checked; otherwise, the group will initially be in a state where no buttons
are checked.

A button can be added to the group with
[addButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#addButton)() and
removed with
[removeButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#removeButton)(). If
the group is exclusive, the currently checked button is available with
[checkedButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#checkedButton)().
If a button is clicked, the
[buttonClicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#buttonClicked)()
signal is emitted; for a checkable button in an exclusive group this means that the
button has been checked. The list of buttons in the group is returned by
[buttons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#buttons)().

In addition, QButtonGroup can map between integers and buttons. You can assign an
integer id to a button with
[setId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#setId)(), and retrieve it
with [id](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#id)(). The id of the
currently checked button is available with
[checkedId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#checkedId)(), and there
is an overloaded signal
[buttonClicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#buttonClicked)()
which emits the id of the button. The id `-1` is reserved by QButtonGroup to mean "no
such button". The purpose of the mapping mechanism is to simplify the representation of
enum values in a user interface.

### exclusive : bool

This property holds whether the button group is exclusive

If this property is `true`, then only one button in the group can be checked at any
given time. The user can click on any button to check it, and that button will replace
the existing one as the checked button in the group.

In an exclusive group, the user cannot uncheck the currently checked button by clicking
on it; instead, another button in the group must be clicked to set the new checked
button for that group.

By default, this property is `true`.

**Access functions:**

| bool | **exclusive**() const |
