PythonQt.Qt.QByteArray.doc: Qt 5 reference: ## Detailed Description QByteArray can be used to store both raw bytes (including '\\0's) and traditional 8-bit '\\0'-terminated strings. Using QByteArray is much more convenient than using `const char *`. Behind the scenes, it always ensures that the data is followed by a '\\0' terminator, and uses [implicit sharing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) (copy-on-write) to reduce memory usage and avoid needless copying of data. In addition to QByteArray, Qt also provides the [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) class to store string data. For most purposes, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) is the class you want to use. It stores 16-bit Unicode characters, making it easy to store non-ASCII/non-Latin-1 characters in your application. Furthermore, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) is used throughout in the Qt API. The two main cases where QByteArray is appropriate are when you need to store raw binary data, and when memory conservation is critical (e.g., with Qt for Embedded Linux). One way to initialize a QByteArray is simply to pass a `const char *` to its constructor. For example, the following code creates a byte array of size 5 containing the data "Hello": ``` QByteArray ba("Hello"); ``` Although the [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() is 5, the byte array also maintains an extra '\\0' character at the end so that if a function is used that asks for a pointer to the underlying data (e.g. a call to [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)()), the data pointed to is guaranteed to be '\\0'-terminated. QByteArray makes a deep copy of the `const char *` data, so you can modify it later without experiencing side effects. (If for performance reasons you don't want to take a deep copy of the character data, use [QByteArray::fromRawData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromRawData)() instead.) Another approach is to set the size of the array using [resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)() and to initialize the data byte per byte. QByteArray uses 0-based indexes, just like C\+\+ arrays. To access the byte at a particular index position, you can use operator\[\](). On non-const byte arrays, operator\[\]() returns a reference to a byte that can be used on the left side of an assignment. For example: ``` QByteArray ba; ba.resize(5); ba[0] = 0x3c; ba[1] = 0xb8; ba[2] = 0x64; ba[3] = 0x18; ba[4] = 0xca; ``` For read-only access, an alternative syntax is to use [at](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#at)(): ``` for (int i = 0; i < ba.size(); ++i) { if (ba.at(i) >= 'a' && ba.at(i) <= 'f') cout << "Found character in range [a-f]" << Qt::endl; } ``` [at](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#at)() can be faster than operator\[\](), because it never causes a [deep copy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html#deep-copy) to occur. To extract many bytes at a time, use [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#left)(), [right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#right)(), or [mid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#mid)(). A QByteArray can embed '\\0' bytes. The [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() function always returns the size of the whole array, including embedded '\\0' bytes, but excluding the terminating '\\0' added by QByteArray. For example: ``` QByteArray ba1("ca\0r\0t"); ba1.size(); // Returns 2. ba1.constData(); // Returns "ca" with terminating \0. QByteArray ba2("ca\0r\0t", 3); ba2.size(); // Returns 3. ba2.constData(); // Returns "ca\0" with terminating \0. QByteArray ba3("ca\0r\0t", 4); ba3.size(); // Returns 4. ba3.constData(); // Returns "ca\0r" with terminating \0. const char cart[] = {'c', 'a', '\0', 'r', '\0', 't'}; QByteArray ba4(QByteArray::fromRawData(cart, 6)); ba4.size(); // Returns 6. ba4.constData(); // Returns "ca\0r\0t" without terminating \0. ``` If you want to obtain the length of the data up to and excluding the first '\\0' character, call [qstrlen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#qstrlen)() on the byte array. After a call to [resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)(), newly allocated bytes have undefined values. To set all the bytes to a particular value, call [fill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fill)(). To obtain a pointer to the actual character data, call [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)() or [constData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#constData)(). These functions return a pointer to the beginning of the data. The pointer is guaranteed to remain valid until a non-const function is called on the QByteArray. It is also guaranteed that the data ends with a '\\0' byte unless the QByteArray was created from a [raw data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromRawData). This '\\0' byte is automatically provided by QByteArray and is not counted in [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)(). QByteArray provides the following basic functions for modifying the byte data: [append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#append)(), [prepend](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#prepend)(), [insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#insert)(), [replace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#replace)(), and [remove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#remove)(). For example: ``` QByteArray x("and"); x.prepend("rock "); // x == "rock and" x.append(" roll"); // x == "rock and roll" x.replace(5, 3, "&"); // x == "rock & roll" ``` The [replace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#replace)() and [remove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#remove)() functions' first two arguments are the position from which to start erasing and the number of bytes that should be erased. When you [append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#append)() data to a non-empty array, the array will be reallocated and the new data copied to it. You can avoid this behavior by calling [reserve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#reserve)(), which preallocates a certain amount of memory. You can also call [capacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#capacity)() to find out how much memory QByteArray actually allocated. Data appended to an empty array is not copied. A frequent requirement is to remove whitespace characters from a byte array ('\\n', '\\t', ' ', etc.). If you want to remove whitespace from both ends of a QByteArray, use [trimmed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#trimmed)(). If you want to remove whitespace from both ends and replace multiple consecutive whitespaces with a single space character within the byte array, use [simplified](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#simplified)(). If you want to find all occurrences of a particular character or substring in a QByteArray, use [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)() or [lastIndexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#lastIndexOf)(). The former searches forward starting from a given index position, the latter searches backward. Both return the index position of the character or substring if they find it; otherwise, they return -1. For example, here's a typical loop that finds all occurrences of a particular substring: ``` QByteArray ba("We must be bold, very bold"); int j = 0; while ((j = ba.indexOf("", j)) != -1) { cout << "Found tag at index position " << j << Qt::endl; ++j; } ``` If you simply want to check whether a QByteArray contains a particular character or substring, use [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(). If you want to find out how many times a particular character or substring occurs in the byte array, use [count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#count-3)(). If you want to replace all occurrences of a particular value with another, use one of the two-parameter [replace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#replace)() overloads. [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)s can be compared using overloaded operators such as operator\<(), operator\<\=(), operator\=\=(), operator\>\=(), and so on. The comparison is based exclusively on the numeric values of the characters and is very fast, but is not what a human would expect. [QString::localeAwareCompare](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#localeAwareCompare)() is a better choice for sorting user-interface strings. For historical reasons, QByteArray distinguishes between a null byte array and an empty byte array. A *null* byte array is a byte array that is initialized using QByteArray's default constructor or by passing (const char \*)0 to the constructor. An *empty* byte array is any byte array with size 0\. A null byte array is always empty, but an empty byte array isn't necessarily null: ``` QByteArray().isNull(); // returns true QByteArray().isEmpty(); // returns true QByteArray("").isNull(); // returns false QByteArray("").isEmpty(); // returns true QByteArray("abc").isNull(); // returns false QByteArray("abc").isEmpty(); // returns false ``` All functions except [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isNull)() treat null byte arrays the same as empty byte arrays. For example, [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)() returns a valid pointer (*not* nullptr) to a '\\0' character for a byte array and QByteArray() compares equal to QByteArray(""). We recommend that you always use [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)() and avoid [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isNull)(). ### Maximum size and out-of-memory conditions The current version of QByteArray is limited to just under 2 GB (2^31 bytes) in size. The exact value is architecture-dependent, since it depends on the overhead required for managing the data block, but is no more than 32 bytes. Raw data blocks are also limited by the use of `int` type in the current version to 2 GB minus 1 byte. In case memory allocation fails, QByteArray will throw a `std::bad_alloc` exception. Out of memory conditions in the Qt containers are the only case where Qt will throw exceptions. Note that the operating system may impose further limits on applications holding a lot of allocated memory, especially large, contiguous blocks. Such considerations, the configuration of such behavior or any mitigation are outside the scope of the QByteArray API. ### Notes on Locale #### Number-String Conversions Functions that perform conversions between numeric data types and strings are performed in the C locale, irrespective of the user's locale settings. Use [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) to perform locale-aware conversions between numbers and strings. #### 8-bit Character Comparisons In QByteArray, the notion of uppercase and lowercase and of which character is greater than or less than another character is done in the Latin-1 locale. This affects functions that support a case insensitive option or that compare or lowercase or uppercase their arguments. Case insensitive operations and comparisons will be accurate if both strings contain only Latin-1 characters. Functions that this affects include [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(), [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)(), [lastIndexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#lastIndexOf)(), operator\<(), operator\<\=(), operator\>(), operator\>\=(), [isLower](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isLower)(), [isUpper](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isUpper)(), [toLower](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toLower)() and [toUpper](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toUpper)(). This issue does not apply to [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)s since they represent characters using Unicode.

PythonQt.Qt.QByteArray.append.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*)

Appends the byte array *ba* onto the end of this byte array.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("free");
QByteArray y("dom");
x.append(y);
// x == "freedom"
```

This is the same as
insert([size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)(), *ba*).

Note: [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) is an [implicitly
shared](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) class. Consequently,
if you append to an empty byte array, then the byte array will just share the data held
in *ba*. In this case, no copying of data is done, taking [constant
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#constant-time). If a shared
instance is modified, it will be copied (copy-on-write), taking [linear
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

If the byte array being appended to is not empty, a deep copy of the data is performed,
taking [linear time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

This operation typically does not suffer from allocation overhead, because
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) preallocates extra
space at the end of the data so that it may grow without reallocating for each append
operation.

**See also**
[operator\+\=](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#operator-2b-eq)(),
[prepend](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#prepend)(), and
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#insert)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(char *ch*)

This is an overloaded function.

Appends the character *ch* to this byte array.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(int *count*, char *ch*)

This is an overloaded function.

Appends *count* copies of character *ch* to this byte array and returns a reference to
this byte array.

If *count* is negative or zero nothing is appended to the byte array.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.7.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(const char \**str*)

This is an overloaded function.

Appends the string *str* to this byte array.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(const char \**str*, int *len*)

This function overloads append().

Appends the first *len* characters of the string *str* to this byte array and returns a
reference to this byte array.

If *len* is negative, the length of the string will be determined automatically using
[qstrlen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#qstrlen)(). If *len* is
zero or *str* is null, nothing is appended to the byte array. Ensure that *len* is *not*
longer than *str*.

### void QByteArray::chop(int *n*)

Removes *n* bytes from the end of the byte array.

If *n* is greater than
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)(), the result is an
empty byte array.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("STARTTLS\r\n");
ba.chop(2);                 // ba == "STARTTLS"
```

**See also** [truncate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#truncate)(),
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)(), and
[left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#left)().

Returns a decoded copy of the Base64 array *base64*, using the options defined by *options*. If *options* contains `IgnoreBase64DecodingErrors` (the default), the input is not checked for validity; invalid characters in the input are skipped, enabling the decoding process to continue with subsequent characters. If *options* contains `AbortOnBase64DecodingErrors`, then decoding will stop at the first invalid character. For example: ``` QByteArray::fromBase64("PHA+SGVsbG8/PC9wPg==", QByteArray::Base64Encoding); // returns "

Hello?

" QByteArray::fromBase64("PHA-SGVsbG8_PC9wPg==", QByteArray::Base64UrlEncoding); // returns "

Hello?

" ``` The algorithm used to decode Base64-encoded data is defined in [RFC 4648](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4648.txt). Returns the decoded data, or, if the `AbortOnBase64DecodingErrors` option was passed and the input data was invalid, an empty byte array. **Note:** The [fromBase64Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromBase64Encoding)() function is recommended in new code. Returns a decoded copy of the Base64 array *base64*. Input is not checked for validity; invalid characters in the input are skipped, enabling the decoding process to continue with subsequent characters. For example: ``` QByteArray text = QByteArray::fromBase64("UXQgaXMgZ3JlYXQh"); text.data(); // returns "Qt is great!" ``` The algorithm used to decode Base64-encoded data is defined in [RFC 4648](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4648.txt). **Note:** The [fromBase64Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromBase64Encoding)() function is recommended in new code. **See also** [toBase64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toBase64)() and [fromBase64Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromBase64Encoding)().

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::fromPercentEncoding(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*input*, char *percent* \= '%')

Returns a decoded copy of the URI/URL-style percent-encoded *input*. The *percent*
parameter allows you to replace the '%' character for another (for instance, '\_' or
'\=').

For example:

```
QByteArray text = QByteArray::fromPercentEncoding("Qt%20is%20great%33");
text.data();            // returns "Qt is great!"
```

**Note:** Given invalid input (such as a string containing the sequence "%G5", which is
not a valid hexadecimal number) the output will be invalid as well. As an example: the
sequence "%G5" could be decoded to 'W'.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[toPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toPercentEncoding)()
and
[QUrl::fromPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromPercentEncoding)().

### int QByteArray::indexOf(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*, int *from* \= 0\) const

Returns the index position of the first occurrence of the byte array *ba* in this byte
array, searching forward from index position *from*. Returns -1 if *ba* could not be
found.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("sticky question");
QByteArray y("sti");
x.indexOf(y);               // returns 0
x.indexOf(y, 1);            // returns 10
x.indexOf(y, 10);           // returns 10
x.indexOf(y, 11);           // returns -1
```

**See also**
[lastIndexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#lastIndexOf)(),
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(), and
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#count-3)().

### int QByteArray::indexOf(char *ch*, int *from* \= 0\) const

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the index position of the first occurrence of the character *ch* in the byte
array, searching forward from index position *from*. Returns -1 if *ch* could not be
found.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("ABCBA");
ba.indexOf("B");            // returns 1
ba.indexOf("B", 1);         // returns 1
ba.indexOf("B", 2);         // returns 3
ba.indexOf("X");            // returns -1
```

**See also**
[lastIndexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#lastIndexOf)() and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)().

found.

### bool QByteArray::isEmpty() const

Returns `true` if the byte array has size 0; otherwise returns `false`.

Example:

```
QByteArray().isEmpty();         // returns true
QByteArray("").isEmpty();       // returns true
QByteArray("abc").isEmpty();    // returns false
```

**See also** [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)().

PythonQt.Qt.QByteArray.isNull.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QByteArray::isNull() const

Returns `true` if this byte array is null; otherwise returns `false`.

Example:

```
QByteArray().isNull();          // returns true
QByteArray("").isNull();        // returns false
QByteArray("abc").isNull();     // returns false
```

Qt makes a distinction between null byte arrays and empty byte arrays for historical
reasons. For most applications, what matters is whether or not a byte array contains any
data, and this can be determined using
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)().

**See also** [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)().

### int QByteArray::lastIndexOf(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*, int *from* \= -1) const

Returns the index position of the last occurrence of the byte array *ba* in this byte
array, searching backward from index position *from*. If *from* is -1 (the default), the
search starts at the last byte. Returns -1 if *ba* could not be found.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("crazy azimuths");
QByteArray y("az");
x.lastIndexOf(y);           // returns 6
x.lastIndexOf(y, 6);        // returns 6
x.lastIndexOf(y, 5);        // returns 2
x.lastIndexOf(y, 1);        // returns -1
```

**See also** [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)(),
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(), and
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#count-3)().

### int QByteArray::lastIndexOf(char *ch*, int *from* \= -1) const

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the index position of the last occurrence of character *ch* in the byte array,
searching backward from index position *from*. If *from* is -1 (the default), the search
starts at the last ([size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() \-
1\) byte. Returns -1 if *ch* could not be found.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("ABCBA");
ba.lastIndexOf("B");        // returns 3
ba.lastIndexOf("B", 3);     // returns 3
ba.lastIndexOf("B", 2);     // returns 1
ba.lastIndexOf("X");        // returns -1
```

**See also** [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)() and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)().

searching backward from index position *from*. If *from* is -1 (the default), the search
starts at the last ([size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() \-
1\) byte. Returns -1 if *str* could not be found.

Returns a byte array of size *width* that contains this byte array padded by the *fill*

If *truncate* is false and the
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() of the byte array is

Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::number(int *n*, int *base* \= 10\)

Returns a byte array containing the string equivalent of the number *n* to base *base*
(10 by default). The *base* can be any value between 2 and 36\.

Example:

```
int n = 63;
QByteArray::number(n);              // returns "63"
QByteArray::number(n, 16);          // returns "3f"
QByteArray::number(n, 16).toUpper();  // returns "3F"
```

**Note:** The format of the number is not localized; the default C locale is used
irrespective of the user's locale.

**See also** [setNum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#setNum)() and
[toInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toInt)().

This is an overloaded function.

**See also** [toUInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toUInt)().

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::number(double *n*, char *f* \= 'g', int *prec* \= 6\)

This is an overloaded function.

Returns a byte array that contains the printed value of *n*, formatted in format *f*
with precision *prec*.

Argument *n* is formatted according to the *f* format specified, which is `g` by
default, and can be any of the following:

| Format | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `e` | format as \[-\]9.9e\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `E` | format as \[-\]9.9E\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `f` | format as \[-\]9.9 |
| `g` | use `e` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |
| `G` | use `E` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |

With 'e', 'E', and 'f', *prec* is the number of digits after the decimal point. With 'g'
and 'G', *prec* is the maximum number of significant digits (trailing zeroes are
omitted).

```
QByteArray ba = QByteArray::number(12.3456, 'E', 3);
// ba == 1.235E+01
```

**Note:** The format of the number is not localized; the default C locale is used
irrespective of the user's locale.

**See also** [toDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toDouble)().

PythonQt.Qt.QByteArray.prepend.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::prepend(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*)

Prepends the byte array *ba* to this byte array and returns a reference to this byte
array.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("ship");
QByteArray y("air");
x.prepend(y);
// x == "airship"
```

This is the same as insert(0, *ba*).

Note: [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) is an [implicitly
shared](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) class. Consequently,
if you prepend to an empty byte array, then the byte array will just share the data held
in *ba*. In this case, no copying of data is done, taking [constant
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#constant-time). If a shared
instance is modified, it will be copied (copy-on-write), taking [linear
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

If the byte array being prepended to is not empty, a deep copy of the data is performed,
taking [linear time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

**See also** [append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#append)() and
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#insert)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::remove(int *pos*, int *len*)

Removes *len* bytes from the array, starting at index position *pos*, and returns a
reference to the array.

If *pos* is out of range, nothing happens. If *pos* is valid, but *pos* \+ *len* is
larger than the size of the array, the array is truncated at position *pos*.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("Montreal");
ba.remove(1, 4);

### void QByteArray::reserve(int *size*)

Attempts to allocate memory for at least *size* bytes. If you know in advance how large
the byte array will be, you can call this function, and if you call
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)() often you are
likely to get better performance. If *size* is an underestimate, the worst that will
happen is that the [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) will
be a bit slower.

The sole purpose of this function is to provide a means of fine tuning
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)'s memory usage. In
general, you will rarely ever need to call this function. If you want to change the size
of the byte array, call
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)().

**See also** [squeeze](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#squeeze)() and
[capacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#capacity)().

### void QByteArray::resize(int *size*)

Sets the size of the byte array to *size* bytes.

If *size* is less than the current size, bytes are removed from the end.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::setNum(double *n*, char *f* \= 'g', int *prec* \= 6\)

This is an overloaded function.

Sets the byte array to the printed value of *n*, formatted in format *f* with precision
*prec*, and returns a reference to the byte array.

The format *f* can be any of the following:

| Format | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `e` | format as \[-\]9.9e\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `E` | format as \[-\]9.9E\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `f` | format as \[-\]9.9 |
| `g` | use `e` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |
| `G` | use `E` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |

With 'e', 'E', and 'f', *prec* is the number of digits after the decimal point. With 'g'
and 'G', *prec* is the maximum number of significant digits (trailing zeroes are
omitted).

**Note:** The format of the number is not localized; the default C locale is used
irrespective of the user's locale.

**See also** [toDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toDouble)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::simplified() const

Returns a byte array that has whitespace removed from the start and the end, and which
has each sequence of internal whitespace replaced with a single space.

Whitespace means any character for which the standard C\+\+ `isspace()` function returns
`true` in the C locale. This includes the ASCII isspace() function returns `true` in the
C locale. This includes the ASCII characters '\\t', '\\n', '\\v', '\\f', '\\r', and ' '.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("  lots\t of\nwhitespace\r\n ");
ba = ba.simplified();
// ba == "lots of whitespace";
```

**See also** [trimmed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#trimmed)().

PythonQt.Qt.QByteArray.size.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QByteArray::size() const

Returns the number of bytes in this byte array.

The last byte in the byte array is at position size() \- 1\. In addition,
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) ensures that the byte
at position size() is always '\\0', so that you can use the return value of
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)() and
[constData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#constData)() as arguments
to functions that expect '\\0'-terminated strings. If the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) object was created from
a [raw data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromRawData) that didn't
include the trailing null-termination character then
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) doesn't add it
automatically unless the [deep
copy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html#deep-copy) is created.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("Hello");
int n = ba.size();          // n == 5
ba.data()[0];               // returns 'H'
ba.data()[4];               // returns 'o'
ba.data()[5];               // returns '\0'
```

**See also** [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)() and
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)().

### double QByteArray::toDouble(bool \**ok* \= nullptr) const

Returns the byte array converted to a `double` value.

Returns an infinity if the conversion overflows or 0.0 if the conversion fails for other
reasons (e.g. underflow).

If *ok* is not `nullptr`, failure is reported by setting \**ok* to `false`, and success
by setting \**ok* to `true`.

```
QByteArray string("1234.56");
bool ok;
double a = string.toDouble(&ok);   // a == 1234.56, ok == true

string = "1234.56 Volt";
a = str.toDouble(&ok);             // a == 0, ok == false
```

**Warning:** The [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)
content may only contain valid numerical characters which includes the plus/minus sign,
the character e used in scientific notation, and the decimal point. Including the unit
or additional characters leads to a conversion error.

**Note:** The conversion of the number is performed in the default C locale,
irrespective of the user's locale.

This function ignores leading and trailing whitespace.

**See also** [number](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#number)().

QByteArray macAddress = QByteArray::fromHex("123456abcdef");
macAddress.toHex(':'); // returns "12:34:56:ab:cd:ef"
macAddress.toHex(0);   // returns "123456abcdef"

PythonQt.Qt.QByteArray.toInt.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QByteArray::toInt(bool \**ok* \= nullptr, int *base* \= 10\) const

Returns the byte array converted to an `int` using base *base*, which is 10 by default
and must be between 2 and 36, or 0\.

If *base* is 0, the base is determined automatically using the following rules: If the
byte array begins with "0x", it is assumed to be hexadecimal; if it begins with "0", it
is assumed to be octal; otherwise it is assumed to be decimal.

Returns 0 if the conversion fails.

If *ok* is not `nullptr`, failure is reported by setting \**ok* to `false`, and success
by setting \**ok* to `true`.

```
QByteArray str("FF");
bool ok;
int hex = str.toInt(&ok, 16);     // hex == 255, ok == true
int dec = str.toInt(&ok, 10);     // dec == 0, ok == false
```

**Note:** The conversion of the number is performed in the default C locale,
irrespective of the user's locale.

**See also** [number](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#number)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::toPercentEncoding(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*exclude* \= QByteArray(), const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*include* \= QByteArray(), char *percent* \= '%') const

Returns a URI/URL-style percent-encoded copy of this byte array. The *percent* parameter
allows you to override the default '%' character for another.

By default, this function will encode all characters that are not one of the following:

ALPHA ("a" to "z" and "A" to "Z") / DIGIT (0 to 9\) / "-" / "." / "\_" / "\~"

To prevent characters from being encoded pass them to *exclude*. To force characters to
be encoded pass them to *include*. The *percent* character is always encoded.

Example:

```
QByteArray text = "{a fishy string?}";
QByteArray ba = text.toPercentEncoding("{}", "s");
qDebug(ba.constData());
// prints "{a fi%73hy %73tring%3F}"
```

The hex encoding uses the numbers 0-9 and the uppercase letters A-F.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class is useful when you have a sequence of bytes that you want to repeatedly match
against some byte arrays (perhaps in a loop), or when you want to search for the same
sequence of bytes multiple times in the same byte array. Using a matcher object and
[indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#indexIn)() is faster
than matching a plain [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)
with [QByteArray::indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)()
if repeated matching takes place. This class offers no benefit if you are doing one-off
byte array matches.

Create the QByteArrayMatcher with the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) you want to search for.
Then call [indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#indexIn)()
on the [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) that you want to
search.

PythonQt.Qt.QByteArrayMatcher.indexIn.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QByteArrayMatcher::indexIn(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*ba*, int *from* \= 0\) const

Searches the byte array *ba*, from byte position *from* (default 0, i.e. from the first
byte), for the byte array
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() that was
set in the constructor or in the most recent call to
[setPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#setPattern)().
Returns the position where the
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() matched
in *ba*, or -1 if no match was found.

### int QByteArrayMatcher::indexIn(const char \**str*, int *len*, int *from* \= 0\) const

Searches the char string *str*, which has length *len*, from byte position *from*
(default 0, i.e. from the first byte), for the byte array
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() that was
set in the constructor or in the most recent call to
[setPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#setPattern)().
Returns the position where the
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() matched
in *str*, or -1 if no match was found.
signatures: indexIn(self, ba: PySide2.QtCore.QByteArray, from_: int=...) -> int

PythonQt.Qt.QCalendarWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/fusion-calendarwidget.png)

The widget is initialized with the current month and year, but QCalendarWidget provides
several public slots to change the year and month that is shown.

By default, today's date is selected, and the user can select a date using both mouse
and keyboard. The currently selected date can be retrieved using the
[selectedDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#selectedDate-prop)()
function. It is possible to constrain the user selection to a given date range by
setting the
[minimumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#minimumDate-prop)
and
[maximumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#maximumDate-prop)
properties. Alternatively, both properties can be set in one go using the
[setDateRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#setDateRange)()
convenience slot. Set the
[selectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#selectionMode-prop)
property to
[NoSelection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#SelectionMode-enum)
to prohibit the user from selecting at all. Note that a date also can be selected
programmatically using the
[setSelectedDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#selectedDate-prop)()
slot.

The currently displayed month and year can be retrieved using the
[monthShown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#monthShown)() and
[yearShown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#yearShown)()
functions, respectively.

A newly created calendar widget uses abbreviated day names, and both Saturdays and
Sundays are marked in red. The calendar grid is not visible. The week numbers are
displayed, and the first column day is the first day of the week for the calendar's
locale.

The notation of the days can be altered to a single letter abbreviations ("M" for
"Monday") by setting the
[horizontalHeaderFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#horizontalHeaderFormat-prop)
property to
[QCalendarWidget::SingleLetterDayNames](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#HorizontalHeaderFormat-enum).
Setting the same property to
[QCalendarWidget::LongDayNames](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#HorizontalHeaderFormat-enum)
makes the header display the complete day names. The week numbers can be removed by
setting the
[verticalHeaderFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#verticalHeaderFormat-prop)
property to
[QCalendarWidget::NoVerticalHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#VerticalHeaderFormat-enum).
The calendar grid can be turned on by setting the
[gridVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#gridVisible-prop)
property to true using the
[setGridVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#gridVisible-prop)()
function:

|  |
| --- |
| ``` QCalendarWidget *calendar; calendar->setGridVisible(true); ``` |

Finally, the day in the first column can be altered using the
[setFirstDayOfWeek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#firstDayOfWeek-prop)()
function.

The QCalendarWidget class also provides three signals,
[selectionChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#selectionChanged)(),
[activated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#activated)() and
[currentPageChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html#currentPageChanged)()
making it possible to respond to user interaction.

The rendering of the headers, weekdays or single days can be largely customized by
setting [QTextCharFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcharformat.html)'s for
some special weekday, a special date or for the rendering of the headers.

Only a subset of the properties in
[QTextCharFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcharformat.html) are used by
the calendar widget. Currently, the foreground, background and font properties are used
to determine the rendering of individual cells in the widget.

PythonQt.Qt.QCheckBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-checkbox.png)

A QCheckBox is an option button that can be switched on (checked) or off (unchecked).
Checkboxes are typically used to represent features in an application that can be
enabled or disabled without affecting others. Different types of behavior can be
implemented. For example, a
[QButtonGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html) can be used to
group check buttons logically, allowing exclusive checkboxes. However,
[QButtonGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html) does not provide
any visual representation.

The image below further illustrates the differences between exclusive and non-exclusive
checkboxes.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |

Whenever a checkbox is checked or cleared, it emits the signal
[stateChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html#stateChanged)().
Connect to this signal if you want to trigger an action each time the checkbox changes
state. You can use
[isChecked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)() to
query whether or not a checkbox is checked.

In addition to the usual checked and unchecked states, QCheckBox optionally provides a
third state to indicate "no change". This is useful whenever you need to give the user
the option of neither checking nor unchecking a checkbox. If you need this third state,
enable it with
[setTristate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html#tristate-prop)(), and
use [checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html#checkState)() to
query the current toggle state.

Just like [QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html), a checkbox
displays text, and optionally a small icon. The icon is set with
[setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)(). The text
can be set in the constructor or with
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(). A
shortcut key can be specified by preceding the preferred character with an ampersand.
For example:

```
QCheckBox *checkbox = new QCheckBox("C&ase sensitive", this);
```

In this example, the shortcut is *Alt\+A*. See the
[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html#mnemonic) documentation
for details. To display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&'.

Important inherited functions:
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(), pixmap(),
setPixmap(), accel(), setAccel(), isToggleButton(),
[setDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#down-prop)(),
[isDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#down-prop)(), isOn(),
[checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html#checkState)(),
[autoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop)(),
isExclusiveToggle(),
[group](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#group)(),
[setAutoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop)(),
[toggle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#toggle)(),
[pressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#pressed)(),
[released](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#released)(),
[clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#clicked)(),
[toggled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#toggled)(),
[checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html#checkState)(), and
[stateChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html#stateChanged)().

PythonQt.Qt.QChildEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Child events are sent immediately to objects when children are added or removed.

In both cases you can only rely on the child being a
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) (or, if
[QObject::isWidgetType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#isWidgetType)()
returns `true`, a [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html)). This is
because in the
[QEvent::ChildAdded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) case the
child is not yet fully constructed; in the
[QEvent::ChildRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) case it
might have already been destructed.

The handler for these events is

*mode* is
[QClipboard::Clipboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qclipboard.html#Mode-enum),

[QClipboard::Selection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qclipboard.html#Mode-enum),

[QClipboard::FindBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qclipboard.html#Mode-enum),

simpler wrappers for retrieving text, image, and pixmap data.

clipboard changes; either by calling one of the setter functions or externally by the

PythonQt.Qt.QCloseEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Close events are sent to widgets that the user wants to close, usually by choosing
"Close" from the window menu, or by clicking the **X** title bar button. They are also
sent when you call
[QWidget::close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#close)() to close a
widget programmatically.

Close events contain a flag that indicates whether the receiver wants the widget to be
closed or not. When a widget accepts the close event, it is hidden (and destroyed if it
was created with the
[Qt::WA\_DeleteOnClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
flag). If it refuses to accept the close event nothing happens. (Under X11 it is
possible that the window manager will forcibly close the window; but at the time of
writing we are not aware of any window manager that does this.)

The event handler
[QWidget::closeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#closeEvent)()
receives close events. The default implementation of this event handler accepts the
close event. If you do not want your widget to be hidden, or want some special handling,
you should reimplement the event handler and
[ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() the event.

The [closeEvent() in the Application
example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-mainwindows-application-example.html#close-event-handler)
shows a close event handler that asks whether to save a document before closing.

If you want the widget to be deleted when it is closed, create it with the
[Qt::WA\_DeleteOnClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
flag. This is very useful for independent top-level windows in a multi-window
application.

[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)s emits the
[destroyed()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#destroyed) signal when
they are deleted.

If the last top-level window is closed, the
[QGuiApplication::lastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#lastWindowClosed)()
signal is emitted.

The [isAccepted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accepted-prop)()
function returns `true` if the event's receiver has agreed to close the widget; call
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)() to agree to close the
widget and call [ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() if the
receiver of this event does not want the widget to be closed.

## Detailed Description

QCollator is initialized with a
[QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) and an optional collation
strategy. It tries to initialize the collator with the specified values. The collator
can then be used to compare and sort strings in a locale dependent fashion.

A QCollator object can be used together with template based sorting algorithms such as
std::sort to sort a list of QStrings.

In addition to the locale and collation strategy, several optional flags can be set that
influence the result of the collation.

## Detailed Description

A color is normally specified in terms of RGB (red, green, and blue) components, but it
is also possible to specify it in terms of HSV (hue, saturation, and value) and CMYK
(cyan, magenta, yellow and black) components. In addition a color can be specified using
a color name. The color name can be any of the SVG 1.0 color names.

| RGB | HSV | CMYK |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |

The QColor constructor creates the color based on RGB values. To create a QColor based
on either HSV or CMYK values, use the
[toHsv](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#toHsv)() and
[toCmyk](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#toCmyk)() functions
respectively. These functions return a copy of the color using the desired format. In
addition the static [fromRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#fromRgb)(),
[fromHsv](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#fromHsv)() and
[fromCmyk](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#fromCmyk)() functions create
colors from the specified values. Alternatively, a color can be converted to any of the
three formats using the
[convertTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#convertTo)() function
(returning a copy of the color in the desired format), or any of the
[setRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setRgb)(),
[setHsv](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setHsv)() and
[setCmyk](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setCmyk)() functions altering
*this* color's format. The [spec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#spec)()
function tells how the color was specified.

A color can be set by passing an RGB string (such as "#112233"), or an ARGB string (such
as "#ff112233") or a color name (such as "blue"), to the
[setNamedColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setNamedColor)()
function. The color names are taken from the SVG 1.0 color names. The
[name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#name)() function returns the name
of the color in the format "#RRGGBB". Colors can also be set using
[setRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setRgb)(),
[setHsv](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setHsv)() and
[setCmyk](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setCmyk)(). To get a lighter or
darker color use the [lighter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#lighter)()
and [darker](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#darker)() functions
respectively.

The [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#isValid)() function
indicates whether a QColor is legal at all. For example, a RGB color with RGB values out
of range is illegal. For performance reasons, QColor mostly disregards illegal colors,
and for that reason, the result of using an invalid color is undefined.

The color components can be retrieved individually, e.g with
[red](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#red)(),
[hue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#hue)() and
[cyan](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#cyan)(). The values of the color
components can also be retrieved in one go using the
[getRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#getRgb)(),
[getHsv](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#getHsv)() and getCmyk()
functions. Using the RGB color model, the color components can in addition be accessed
with [rgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#rgb)().

There are several related non-members:
[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) is a typdef for an
unsigned int representing the RGB value triplet (r, g, b). Note that it also can hold a
value for the alpha-channel (for more information, see the [Alpha-Blended
Drawing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#alpha-blended-drawing) section).
The [qRed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRed)(),
[qBlue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qBlue)() and
[qGreen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qGreen)() functions return the
respective component of the given
[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) value, while the
[qRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRgb)() and
[qRgba](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRgba)() functions create and
return the [QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) triplet
based on the given component values. Finally, the
[qAlpha](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qAlpha)() function returns the
alpha component of the provided
[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef), and the
[qGray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qGray)() function calculates and
return a gray value based on the given value.

QColor is platform and device independent. The
[QColormap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolormap.html) class maps the color to
the hardware.

For more information about painting in general, see the [Paint
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/paintsystem.html) documentation.

### Integer vs. Floating Point Precision

QColor supports floating point precision and provides floating point versions of all the
color components functions, e.g.
[getRgbF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#getRgbF)(),
[hueF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#hueF)() and
[fromCmykF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#fromCmykF)(). Note that since
the components are stored using 16-bit integers, there might be minor deviations between
the values set using, for example,
[setRgbF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setRgbF)() and the values
returned by the [getRgbF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#getRgbF)()
function due to rounding.

While the integer based functions take values in the range 0-255 (except
[hue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#hue)() which must have values
within the range 0-359), the floating point functions accept values in the range 0.0 \-
1.0.

### Alpha-Blended Drawing

QColor also support alpha-blended outlining and filling. The alpha channel of a color
specifies the transparency effect, 0 represents a fully transparent color, while 255
represents a fully opaque color. For example:

```
// Specify semi-transparent red
painter.setBrush(QColor(255, 0, 0, 127));
painter.drawRect(0, 0, width()/2, height());

// Specify semi-transparent blue
painter.setBrush(QColor(0, 0, 255, 127));
painter.drawRect(0, 0, width(), height()/2);
```

The code above produces the following output:

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/alphafill.png)

The alpha channel of a color can be retrieved and set using the
[alpha](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#alpha)() and
[setAlpha](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setAlpha)() functions if its
value is an integer, and
[alphaF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#alphaF)() and
[setAlphaF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setAlphaF)() if its value is
qreal (double). By default, the alpha-channel is set to 255 (opaque). To retrieve and
set *all* the RGB color components (including the alpha-channel) in one go, use the
[rgba](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#rgba)() and
[setRgba](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setRgba)() functions.

### Predefined Colors

There are 20 predefined QColor objects in the `QColorConstants` namespace, including
black, white, primary and secondary colors, darker versions of these colors, and three
shades of gray. Furthermore, the `QColorConstants::Svg` namespace defines QColor objects
for the standard [SVG color keyword
names](https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG11/types.html#ColorKeywords).

![Qt Colors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qt-colors.png)

The `QColorConstants::Color0`, `QColorConstants::Color1` and
`QColorConstants::Transparent` colors are used for special purposes.

`QColorConstants::Color0` (zero pixel value) and `QColorConstants::Color1` (non-zero
pixel value) are special colors for drawing in QBitmaps. Painting with
`QColorConstants::Color0` sets the bitmap bits to 0 (transparent; i.e., background), and
painting with c{QColorConstants::Color1} sets the bits to 1 (opaque; i.e., foreground).

`QColorConstants::Transparent` is used to indicate a transparent pixel. When painting
with this value, a pixel value will be used that is appropriate for the underlying pixel
format in use.

For historical reasons, the 20 predefined colors are also available in the
[Qt::GlobalColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum)
enumeration.

Finally, QColor recognizes a variety of color names (as strings); the static
[colorNames](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#colorNames)() function
returns a [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) color names
that QColor knows about.

### The Extended RGB Color Model

The extended RGB color model, also known as the scRGB color space, is the same the RGB
color model except it allows values under 0.0, and over 1.0. This makes it possible to
represent colors that would otherwise be outside the range of the RGB colorspace but
still use the same values for colors inside the RGB colorspace.

### The HSV Color Model

The RGB model is hardware-oriented. Its representation is close to what most monitors
show. In contrast, HSV represents color in a way more suited to the human perception of
color. For example, the relationships "stronger than", "darker than", and "the opposite
of" are easily expressed in HSV but are much harder to express in RGB.

HSV, like RGB, has three components:

- H, for hue, is in the range 0 to 359 if the color is chromatic (not gray), or meaningless if it is gray. It represents degrees on the color wheel familiar to most people. Red is 0 (degrees), green is 120, and blue is 240\.

  ![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qcolor-hue.png)
- S, for saturation, is in the range 0 to 255, and the bigger it is, the stronger the color is. Grayish colors have saturation near 0; very strong colors have saturation near 255\.

  ![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qcolor-saturation.png)
- V, for value, is in the range 0 to 255 and represents lightness or brightness of the color. 0 is black; 255 is as far from black as possible.

  ![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qcolor-value.png)

Here are some examples: pure red is H\=0, S\=255, V\=255; a dark red, moving slightly
towards the magenta, could be H\=350 (equivalent to -10), S\=255, V\=180; a grayish
light red could have H about 0 (say 350-359 or 0-10), S about 50-100, and S\=255.

Qt returns a hue value of -1 for achromatic colors. If you pass a hue value that is too
large, Qt forces it into range. Hue 360 or 720 is treated as 0; hue 540 is treated as
180\.

In addition to the standard HSV model, Qt provides an alpha-channel to feature
[alpha-blended
drawing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#alpha-blended-drawing).

### The HSL Color Model

HSL is similar to HSV, however instead of the Value parameter, HSL specifies a Lightness
parameter which maps somewhat differently to the brightness of the color.

Similarly, the HSL saturation value is not in general the same as the HSV saturation
value for the same color.
[hslSaturation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#hslSaturation)() provides
the color's HSL saturation value, while
[saturation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#saturation)() and
[hsvSaturation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#hsvSaturation)() provides
the HSV saturation value.

The hue value is defined to be the same in HSL and HSV.

### The CMYK Color Model

While the RGB and HSV color models are used for display on computer monitors, the CMYK
model is used in the four-color printing process of printing presses and some hard-copy
devices.

CMYK has four components, all in the range 0-255: cyan (C), magenta (M), yellow (Y) and
black (K). Cyan, magenta and yellow are called subtractive colors; the CMYK color model
creates color by starting with a white surface and then subtracting color by applying
the appropriate components. While combining cyan, magenta and yellow gives the color
black, subtracting one or more will yield any other color. When combined in various
percentages, these three colors can create the entire spectrum of colors.

Mixing 100 percent of cyan, magenta and yellow *does* produce black, but the result is
unsatisfactory since it wastes ink, increases drying time, and gives a muddy colour when
printing. For that reason, black is added in professional printing to provide a solid
black tone; hence the term 'four color process'.

In addition to the standard CMYK model, Qt provides an alpha-channel to feature
[alpha-blended
drawing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#alpha-blended-drawing).

### [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QColor) QColor::darker(int *factor* \= 200\) const

Returns a darker (or lighter) color, but does not change this object.

If the *factor* is greater than 100, this functions returns a darker color. Setting
*factor* to 300 returns a color that has one-third the brightness. If the *factor* is
less than 100, the return color is lighter, but we recommend using the
[lighter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#lighter)() function for this
purpose. If the *factor* is 0 or negative, the return value is unspecified.

The function converts the current color to HSV, divides the value (V) component by
*factor* and converts the color back to it's original color spec.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also** [lighter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#lighter)() and
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#isValid)().

### void QColor::getHsl(int \**h*, int \**s*, int \**l*, int \**a* \= nullptr) const

Sets the contents pointed to by *h*, *s*, *l*, and *a*, to the hue, saturation,
lightness, and alpha-channel (transparency) components of the color's HSL value.

These components can be retrieved individually using the
[hslHue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#hslHue)(),
[hslSaturation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#hslSaturation)(),
[lightness](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#lightness)() and
[alpha](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#alpha)() functions.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also** [getHslF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#getHslF)(),
[setHsl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#setHsl)(), and [The HSL Color
Model](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#the-hsl-color-model).

Qt 5 reference:

### [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QColor) QColor::lighter(int *factor* \= 150\) const

Returns a lighter (or darker) color, but does not change this object.

If the *factor* is greater than 100, this functions returns a lighter color. Setting
*factor* to 150 returns a color that is 50% brighter. If the *factor* is less than 100,
the return color is darker, but we recommend using the
[darker](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#darker)() function for this
purpose. If the *factor* is 0 or negative, the return value is unspecified.

The function converts the current color to HSV, multiplies the value (V) component by
*factor* and converts the color back to it's original color spec.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also** [darker](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#darker)() and
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#isValid)().

### void QColor::setNamedColor(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*)

Sets the RGB value of this [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) to
*name*, which may be in one of these formats:

- #RGB (each of R, G, and B is a single hex digit)
- #RRGGBB
- #AARRGGBB (Since 5.2)
- #RRRGGGBBB
- #RRRRGGGGBBBB
- A name from the list of colors defined in the list of [SVG color keyword names](https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG11/types.html#ColorKeywords) provided by the World Wide Web Consortium; for example, "steelblue" or "gainsboro". These color names work on all platforms. Note that these color names are *not* the same as defined by the [Qt::GlobalColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum) enums, e.g. "green" and [Qt::green](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum) does not refer to the same color.
- `transparent` \- representing the absence of a color.

The color is invalid if *name* cannot be parsed.

**See also** [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QColor)(),
[name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#name)(), and
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#isValid)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The color dialog's function is to allow users to choose colors. For example, you might
use this in a drawing program to allow the user to set the brush color.

The static functions provide modal color dialogs.

The static [getColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolordialog.html#getColor)()
function shows the dialog, and allows the user to specify a color. This function can
also be used to let users choose a color with a level of transparency: pass the
[ShowAlphaChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolordialog.html#ColorDialogOption-enum)
option as an additional argument.

The user can store
[customCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolordialog.html#customCount)()
different custom colors. The custom colors are shared by all color dialogs, and
remembered during the execution of the program. Use
[setCustomColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolordialog.html#setCustomColor)()
to set the custom colors, and use
[customColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolordialog.html#customColor)() to get
them.

When pressing the "Pick Screen Color" button, the cursor changes to a haircross and the
colors on the screen are scanned. The user can pick up one by clicking the mouse or the
Enter button. Pressing Escape restores the last color selected before entering this
mode.

The [Standard
Dialogs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-dialogs-standarddialogs-example.html)
example shows how to use QColorDialog as well as other built-in Qt dialogs.

![A color dialog in the Fusion widget
style.](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/fusion-colordialog.png)

[QColor::isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#isValid)()) color if

## Detailed Description

QColumnView displays a model in a number of QListViews, one for each hierarchy in the
tree. This is sometimes referred to as a cascading list.

The QColumnView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

QColumnView implements the interfaces defined by the
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) class to
allow it to display data provided by models derived from the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) class.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qcolumnview.png)

PythonQt.Qt.QComboBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-combobox.png)

A QComboBox provides a means of presenting a list of options to the user in a way that
takes up the minimum amount of screen space.

A combobox is a selection widget that displays the current item, and can pop up a list
of selectable items. A combobox may be editable, allowing the user to modify each item
in the list.

Comboboxes can contain pixmaps as well as strings; the
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#insertItem)() and
[setItemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setItemText)() functions
are suitably overloaded. For editable comboboxes, the function
[clearEditText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#clearEditText)() is
provided, to clear the displayed string without changing the combobox's contents.

There are three signals emitted if the current item of a combobox changes,
[currentIndexChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndexChanged)(),
[currentTextChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentTextChanged)()
and [activated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#activated)().
[currentIndexChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndexChanged)()
and
[currentTextChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentTextChanged)()
are always emitted regardless if the change was done programmatically or by user
interaction, while
[activated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#activated)() is only
emitted when the change is caused by user interaction. The
[highlighted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#highlighted)() signal is
emitted when the user highlights an item in the combobox popup list. All three signals
exist in two versions, one with a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) argument and one with an
`int` argument. If the user selects or highlights a pixmap, only the `int` signals are
emitted. Whenever the text of an editable combobox is changed the
[editTextChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#editTextChanged)()
signal is emitted.

When the user enters a new string in an editable combobox, the widget may or may not
insert it, and it can insert it in several locations. The default policy is
[InsertAtBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#InsertPolicy-enum)
but you can change this using
[setInsertPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#insertPolicy-prop)().

It is possible to constrain the input to an editable combobox using
[QValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html); see
[setValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setValidator)(). By
default, any input is accepted.

A combobox can be populated using the insert functions,
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#insertItem)() and
[insertItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#insertItems)() for
example. Items can be changed with
[setItemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setItemText)(). An item
can be removed with
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#removeItem)() and all
items can be removed with
[clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#clear)(). The text of the
current item is returned by
[currentText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentText-prop)(), and
the text of a numbered item is returned with text(). The current item can be set with
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndex-prop)().
The number of items in the combobox is returned by
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#count-prop)(); the maximum
number of items can be set with
[setMaxCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#maxCount-prop)(). You
can allow editing using
[setEditable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#editable-prop)(). For
editable comboboxes you can set auto-completion using
[setCompleter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setCompleter)() and
whether or not the user can add duplicates is set with
[setDuplicatesEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#duplicatesEnabled-prop)().

QComboBox uses the [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html) for its popup
list and to store its items. By default a
[QStandardItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html) stores
the items and a [QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) subclass
displays the popuplist. You can access the model and view directly (with
[model](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#model)() and
[view](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#view)()), but QComboBox also
provides functions to set and get item data (e.g.,
[setItemData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setItemData)() and
[itemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#itemText)()). You can also
set a new model and view (with
[setModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setModel)() and
[setView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setView)()). For the text
and icon in the combobox label, the data in the model that has the
[Qt::DisplayRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) and
[Qt::DecorationRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) is
used. Note that you cannot alter the
[SelectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#SelectionMode-enum)
of the [view](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#view)(), e.g., by using
[setSelectionMode()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionMode-prop).

PythonQt.Qt.QComboBox.activated.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QComboBox::activated(int *index*)

This signal is sent when the user chooses an item in the combobox. The item's *index* is
passed. Note that this signal is sent even when the choice is not changed. If you need
to know when the choice actually changes, use signal
[currentIndexChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndexChanged)()
or
[currentTextChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentTextChanged)().

**Note:** Signal *activated* is overloaded in this class. To connect to this signal by
using the function pointer syntax, Qt provides a convenient helper for obtaining the
function pointer as shown in this example:

```
connect(comboBox, QOverload<int>::of(&QComboBox::activated),
    [=](int index){ /* ... */ });
```

### `[signal]` void QComboBox::currentIndexChanged(int *index*)

This signal is sent whenever the
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndex-prop) in
the combobox changes either through user interaction or programmatically. The item's
*index* is passed or -1 if the combobox becomes empty or the

[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndex-prop).

signal by using the function pointer syntax, Qt provides a convenient helper for
obtaining the function pointer as shown in this example:

```

    [=](int index){ /* ... */ });
```

PythonQt.Qt.QComboBox.currentText.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### currentText : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the current text

If the combo box is editable, the current text is the value displayed by the line edit.
Otherwise, it is the value of the current item or an empty string if the combo box is
empty or no current item is set.

The setter setCurrentText() simply calls
[setEditText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#setEditText)() if the
combo box is editable. Otherwise, if there is a matching text in the list,
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndex-prop) is
set to the corresponding index.

### placeholderText : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

Sets a *placeholderText* text shown when no valid index is set

The *placeholderText* will be shown when an invalid index is set. The text is not
accessible in the dropdown list. When this function is called before items are added the
placeholder text will be shown, otherwise you have to call
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndex-prop)(-1)
programmatically if you want to show the placeholder text. Set an empty placeholder text
to reset the setting.

When the [QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html) is editable, use
[QLineEdit::setPlaceholderText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#placeholderText-prop)()

### void QComboBox::setCompleter([QCompleter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcompleter.html) \**completer*)

`nullptr`, auto completion is disabled.

By default, for an editable combo box, a
[QCompleter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcompleter.html) that performs case

[editable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#editable-prop) property
becomes `false`. Setting a completer on a
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html) that is not editable will

PythonQt.Qt.QCommandLineOption.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class is used to describe an option on the command line. It allows different ways
of defining the same option with multiple aliases possible. It is also used to describe
how the option is used \- it may be a flag (e.g. `-v`) or take a value (e.g. `-o file`).

Examples:

```
QCommandLineOption verboseOption("verbose", "Verbose mode. Prints out more information.");
QCommandLineOption outputOption(QStringList() << "o" << "output", "Write generated data into <file>.", "file");
```

### void QCommandLineOption::setValueName(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*valueName*)

Sets the name of the expected value, for the documentation, to *valueName*.

Options without a value assigned have a boolean-like behavior: either the user specifies
--option or they don't.

Options with a value assigned need to set a name for the expected value, for the
documentation of the option in the help output. An option with names `o` and `output`,
and a value name of `file` will appear as `-o, --output <file>`.

Call
[QCommandLineParser::value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#value)()
if you expect the option to be present only once, and
[QCommandLineParser::values](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#values)()
