### `[static]` QDate QDate::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*)

This is an overloaded function.

### `[static]` QDate QDate::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*, [QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) *cal*)

Returns the [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) represented by the
*string*, using the *format* given, or an invalid date if the string cannot be parsed.

Uses *cal* as calendar if supplied, else the Gregorian calendar. Ranges of values in the
format descriptions below are for the latter; they may be different for other calendars.

These expressions may be used for the format:

| Expression | Output |
| --- | --- |
| d | The day as a number without a leading zero (1 to 31\) |
| dd | The day as a number with a leading zero (01 to 31\) |
| ddd | The abbreviated localized day name (e.g. 'Mon' to 'Sun'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| dddd | The long localized day name (e.g. 'Monday' to 'Sunday'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| M | The month as a number without a leading zero (1 to 12\) |
| MM | The month as a number with a leading zero (01 to 12\) |
| MMM | The abbreviated localized month name (e.g. 'Jan' to 'Dec'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| MMMM | The long localized month name (e.g. 'January' to 'December'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| yy | The year as a two digit number (00 to 99\) |
| yyyy | The year as a four digit number, possibly plus a leading minus sign for negative years. |

**Note:** Unlike the other version of this function, day and month names must be given
in the user's local language. It is only possible to use the English names if the user's
language is English.

All other input characters will be treated as text. Any non-empty sequence of characters
enclosed in single quotes will also be treated (stripped of the quotes) as text and not
be interpreted as expressions. For example:

```
QDate date = QDate::fromString("1MM12car2003", "d'MM'MMcaryyyy");
// date is 1 December 2003
```

If the format is not satisfied, an invalid
[QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) is returned. The expressions that
don't expect leading zeroes (d, M) will be greedy. This means that they will use two
digits even if this will put them outside the accepted range of values and leaves too
few digits for other sections. For example, the following format string could have meant
January 30 but the M will grab two digits, resulting in an invalid date:

```
QDate date = QDate::fromString("130", "Md"); // invalid
```

For any field that is not represented in the format the following defaults are used:

| Field | Default value |
| --- | --- |
| Year | 1900 |
| Month | 1 |
| Day | 1 |

The following examples demonstrate the default values:

```
QDate::fromString("1.30", "M.d");           // January 30 1900
QDate::fromString("20000110", "yyyyMMdd");  // January 10, 2000
QDate::fromString("20000110", "yyyyMd");    // January 10, 2000
```

**Note:** If localized month and day names are used, please switch to using
[QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)().toDate() as
[QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) methods shall change to only
recognize English (C locale) names at Qt 6\.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toString-1)(),
[QDateTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)(),
[QTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#fromString)(), and
[QLocale::toDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDate)().
signatures: fromString(s: str, format: str, cal: PySide2.QtCore.QCalendar) -> PySide2.QtCore.QDate

### `[static]` bool QDate::isValid(int *year*, int *month*, int *day*)

This is an overloaded function.

Returns `true` if the specified date (*year*, *month*, and *day*) is valid in the
Gregorian calendar; otherwise returns `false`.

Example:

```
QDate::isValid(2002, 5, 17);  // true
QDate::isValid(2002, 2, 30);  // false (Feb 30 does not exist)
QDate::isValid(2004, 2, 29);  // true (2004 is a leap year)
QDate::isValid(2000, 2, 29);  // true (2000 is a leap year)
QDate::isValid(2006, 2, 29);  // false (2006 is not a leap year)
QDate::isValid(2100, 2, 29);  // false (2100 is not a leap year)
QDate::isValid(1202, 6, 6);   // true (even though 1202 is pre-Gregorian)
```

**See also** [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isNull)(),
[setDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#setDate)(), and

### int QDate::month([QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) *cal*) const

Returns the month-number for the date.

Numbers the months of the year starting with 1 for the first. Uses *cal* as calendar if
supplied, else the Gregorian calendar, for which the month numbering is as follows:

- 1 \= "January"
- 2 \= "February"
- 3 \= "March"
- 4 \= "April"
- 5 \= "May"
- 6 \= "June"
- 7 \= "July"
- 8 \= "August"
- 9 \= "September"
- 10 \= "October"
- 11 \= "November"
- 12 \= "December"

Returns 0 if the date is invalid. Note that some calendars may have more than 12 months
in some years.

**See also** [year](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#year-1)(),
[day](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#day-1)(), and
[QCalendar::partsFromDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#partsFromDate)().

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the date as a string. The *format* parameter determines the format of the
string.

If the *format* is
[Qt::TextDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
is formatted in the default way. The day and month names will be localized names using
the system locale, i.e.
[QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). An example
of this formatting is "Sat May 20 1995".

If the *format* is
[Qt::ISODate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
format corresponds to the ISO 8601 extended specification for representations of dates
and times, taking the form yyyy-MM-dd, where yyyy is the year, MM is the month of the
year (between 01 and 12), and dd is the day of the month between 01 and 31\.

The *format* options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with
[QLocale::system().toString(date,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale::system().toString(date,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

The *format* options
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with [QLocale().toString(date,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale().toString(date,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

If the *format* is
[Qt::RFC2822Date](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the
string is formatted in an [RFC 2822](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2822.txt)
compatible way. An example of this formatting is "20 May 1995".

If the date is invalid, an empty string will be returned.

**Warning:** The
[Qt::ISODate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum) format is only
valid for years in the range 0 to 9999\.

and [QLocale::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString)().

Qt 5 reference:

### int QDate::weekNumber(int \**yearNumber* \= nullptr) const

Returns the ISO 8601 week number (1 to 53).

Returns 0 if the date is invalid. Otherwise, returns the week number for the date. If
*yearNumber* is not `nullptr` (its default), stores the year as \**yearNumber*.

In accordance with ISO 8601, each week falls in the year to which most of its days
belong, in the Gregorian calendar. As ISO 8601's week starts on Monday, this is the year
in which the week's Thursday falls. Most years have 52 weeks, but some have 53\.

**Note:** \**yearNumber* is not always the same as
[year](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#year-1)(). For example, 1 January
2000 has week number 52 in the year 1999, and 31 December 2002 has week number 1 in the
year 2003\.

**See also** [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isValid)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDate.year.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QDate::year([QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) *cal*) const

Returns the year of this date.

Uses *cal* as calendar, if supplied, else the Gregorian calendar.

Returns 0 if the date is invalid. For some calendars, dates before their first year may
all be invalid.

If using a calendar which has a year 0, check using
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isValid)() if the return is 0\.
Such calendars use negative year numbers in the obvious way, with year 1 preceded by
year 0, in turn preceded by year -1 and so on.

Some calendars, despite having no year 0, have a conventional numbering of the years
before their first year, counting backwards from 1\. For example, in the proleptic
Gregorian calendar, successive years before 1 CE (the first year) are identified as 1
BCE, 2 BCE, 3 BCE and so on. For such calendars, negative year numbers are used to
indicate these years before year 1, with -1 indicating the year before 1\.

**See also** [month](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#month-1)(),
[day](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#day-1)(),
[QCalendar::hasYearZero](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#hasYearZero)(),
[QCalendar::isProleptic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#isProleptic)(),
and
[QCalendar::partsFromDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#partsFromDate)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QDateTime object encodes a calendar date and a clock time (a "datetime"). It combines
features of the [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) and
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) classes. It can read the current
datetime from the system clock. It provides functions for comparing datetimes and for
manipulating a datetime by adding a number of seconds, days, months, or years.

QDateTime can describe datetimes with respect to [local
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), to
[UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), to a specified [offset
from UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) or to a specified
[time zone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), in conjunction
with the [QTimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html) class. For
example, a time zone of "Europe/Berlin" will apply the daylight-saving rules as used in
Germany since 1970\. In contrast, an offset from UTC of \+3600 seconds is one hour ahead
of UTC (usually written in ISO standard notation as "UTC\+01:00"), with no
daylight-saving offset or changes. When using either local time or a specified time
zone, time-zone transitions such as the starts and ends of daylight-saving time (DST;
but see below) are taken into account. The choice of system used to represent a datetime
is described as its "timespec".

A QDateTime object is typically created either by giving a date and time explicitly in
the constructor, or by using a static function such as
[currentDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#currentDateTime)()
or
[fromMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromMSecsSinceEpoch)().
The date and time can be changed with
[setDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setDate)() and
[setTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setTime)(). A datetime can
also be set using the
[setMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setMSecsSinceEpoch)()
function that takes the time, in milliseconds, since 00:00:00 on January 1, 1970\. The
[fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)() function
returns a QDateTime, given a string and a date format used to interpret the date within
the string.

[QDateTime::currentDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#currentDateTime)()
returns a QDateTime that expresses the current time with respect to local time.
[QDateTime::currentDateTimeUtc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#currentDateTimeUtc)()
returns a QDateTime that expresses the current time with respect to UTC.

The [date](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#date)() and
[time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#time)() functions provide
access to the date and time parts of the datetime. The same information is provided in
textual format by the
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toString)() function.

QDateTime provides a full set of operators to compare two QDateTime objects, where
smaller means earlier and larger means later.

You can increment (or decrement) a datetime by a given number of milliseconds using
[addMSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addMSecs)(), seconds using
[addSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addSecs)(), or days using
[addDays](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addDays)(). Similarly, you
can use [addMonths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addMonths)() and
[addYears](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addYears)(). The
[daysTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#daysTo)() function returns
the number of days between two datetimes,
[secsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#secsTo)() returns the number
of seconds between two datetimes, and
[msecsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#msecsTo)() returns the
number of milliseconds between two datetimes. These operations are aware of
daylight-saving time (DST) and other time-zone transitions, where applicable.

Use [toTimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toTimeSpec)() to
express a datetime in local time or UTC,
[toOffsetFromUtc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toOffsetFromUtc)()
to express in terms of an offset from UTC, or
[toTimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toTimeZone)() to express
it with respect to a general time zone. You can use
[timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() to find out
what time-spec a QDateTime object stores its time relative to. When that is
[Qt::TimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), you can use
[timeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeZone)() to find out
which zone it is using.

**Note:** QDateTime does not account for leap seconds.

### Remarks

#### No Year 0

There is no year 0\. Dates in that year are considered invalid. The year -1 is the year
"1 before Christ" or "1 before current era." The day before 1 January 1 CE is 31
December 1 BCE.

#### Range of Valid Dates

The range of values that QDateTime can represent is dependent on the internal storage
implementation. QDateTime is currently stored in a qint64 as a serial msecs value
encoding the date and time. This restricts the date range to about \+/- 292 million
years, compared to the [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) range of
\+/- 2 billion years. Care must be taken when creating a QDateTime with extreme values
that you do not overflow the storage. The exact range of supported values varies
depending on the
[Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) and time zone.

#### Use of Timezones

QDateTime uses the system's time zone information to determine the current local time
zone and its offset from UTC. If the system is not configured correctly or not
up-to-date, QDateTime will give wrong results.

QDateTime likewise uses system-provided information to determine the offsets of other
timezones from UTC. If this information is incomplete or out of date, QDateTime will
give wrong results. See the
[QTimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html) documentation for more
details.

On modern Unix systems, this means QDateTime usually has accurate information about
historical transitions (including DST, see below) whenever possible. On Windows, where
the system doesn't support historical timezone data, historical accuracy is not
maintained with respect to timezone transitions, notably including DST.

#### Daylight-Saving Time (DST)

QDateTime takes into account transitions between Standard Time and Daylight-Saving Time.
For example, if the transition is at 2am and the clock goes forward to 3am, then there
is a "missing" hour from 02:00:00 to 02:59:59.999 which QDateTime considers to be
invalid. Any date arithmetic performed will take this missing hour into account and
return a valid result. For example, adding one minute to 01:59:59 will get 03:00:00.

The range of valid dates taking DST into account is 1970-01-01 to the present, and rules
are in place for handling DST correctly until 2037-12-31, but these could change. For
dates after 2037, QDateTime makes a *best guess* using the rules for year 2037, but we
can't guarantee accuracy; indeed, for *any* future date, the time-zone may change its
rules before that date comes around. For dates before 1970, QDateTime doesn't take DST
changes into account, even if the system's time zone database provides that information,
although it does take into account changes to the time-zone's standard offset, where
this information is available.

#### Offsets From UTC

There is no explicit size restriction on an offset from UTC, but there is an implicit
limit imposed when using the
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toString)() and
[fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)() methods
which use a \[\+\|-\]hh:mm format, effectively limiting the range to \+/- 99 hours and
59 minutes and whole minutes only. Note that currently no time zone lies outside the
range of \+/- 14 hours.

### [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::addDays([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *ndays*) const

Returns a [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) object
containing a datetime *ndays* days later than the datetime of this object (or earlier if
*ndays* is negative).

[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) and the
resulting date and time fall in the Standard Time to Daylight-Saving Time transition
hour then the result will be adjusted accordingly, i.e. if the transition is at 2am and
the clock goes forward to 3am and the result falls between 2am and 3am then the result
will be adjusted to fall after 3am.

**See also** [daysTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#daysTo)(),

### `[static]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QDateTime::currentMSecsSinceEpoch()

Returns the number of milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00 Universal Coordinated Time.
This number is like the POSIX time\_t variable, but expressed in milliseconds instead.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.7.

[currentDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#currentDateTime)(),
[currentDateTimeUtc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#currentDateTimeUtc)(),

[toTimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toTimeSpec)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDateTime.fromMSecsSinceEpoc.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::fromMSecsSinceEpoch([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *msecs*)

Returns a datetime whose date and time are the number of milliseconds, *msecs*, that
have passed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000, Coordinated Universal Time
([Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)), and converted to
[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum). On systems
that do not support time zones, the time will be set as if local time were
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

Note that there are possible values for *msecs* that lie outside the valid range of
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html), both negative and
positive. The behavior of this function is undefined for those values.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.7.

**See also**
[toMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toMSecsSinceEpoch)()
and
[setMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setMSecsSinceEpoch)().

### `[static]` [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::fromMSecsSinceEpoch([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *msecs*, [Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) *spec*, int *offsetSeconds* \= 0\)

Returns a datetime whose date and time are the number of milliseconds *msecs* that have
passed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000, Coordinated Universal Time
([Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)) and converted to
the given *spec*.

Note that there are possible values for *msecs* that lie outside the valid range of
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html), both negative and
positive. The behavior of this function is undefined for those values.

If the *spec* is not
[Qt::OffsetFromUTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) then the
*offsetSeconds* will be ignored. If the *spec* is
[Qt::OffsetFromUTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) and the
*offsetSeconds* is 0 then the spec will be set to
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), i.e. an offset of 0
seconds.

If *spec* is [Qt::TimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)
then the spec will be set to
[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), i.e. the
current system time zone.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

**See also**
[toMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toMSecsSinceEpoch)()
and
[setMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setMSecsSinceEpoch)().

### `[static]` [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::fromMSecsSinceEpoch([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *msecs*, const [QTimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html) \&*timeZone*)

Returns a datetime whose date and time are the number of milliseconds *msecs* that have
passed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000, Coordinated Universal Time
([Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)) and with the given
*timeZone*.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

**See also**
[fromSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromSecsSinceEpoch)().

### `[static]` [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, [Qt::DateFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum) *format* \= Qt::TextDate)

Returns the [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) represented
by the *string*, using the *format* given, or an invalid datetime if this is not
possible.

Note for [Qt::TextDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum): It
is recommended that you use the English short month names (e.g. "Jan"). Although
localized month names can also be used in Qt 5, they depend on the user's locale
settings.

**Note:** Support for localized dates, including the format options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Use
[QLocale::toDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDateTime)()
instead.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toString)()
and [QLocale::toDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDateTime)().

### `[static]` [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*)

This is an overloaded function.

### `[static]` [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*, [QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) *cal*)

Returns the [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) represented
by the *string*, using the *format* given, or an invalid datetime if the string cannot
be parsed.

Uses the calendar *cal* if supplied, else Gregorian.

In addition to the expressions, recognized in the format string to represent parts of
the date and time, by
[QDate::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#fromString)() and
[QTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#fromString)(), this
method supports:

| Expression | Output |
| --- | --- |
| t | the timezone (for example "CEST") |

All other input characters will be treated as text. Any non-empty sequence of characters
enclosed in single quotes will also be treated (stripped of the quotes) as text and not
be interpreted as expressions.

```
QTime time1 = QTime::fromString("131", "HHh");
// time1 is 13:00:00
QTime time1 = QTime::fromString("1apA", "1amAM");
// time1 is 01:00:00

QDateTime dateTime2 = QDateTime::fromString("M1d1y9800:01:02",
                                            "'M'M'd'd'y'yyhh:mm:ss");
// dateTime is 1 January 1998 00:01:02
```

If the format is not satisfied, an invalid
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) is returned. If the
format is satisfied but *string* represents an invalid date-time (e.g. in a gap skipped
by a time-zone transition), an invalid
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) is returned, whose
[toMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toMSecsSinceEpoch)()
represents a near-by date-time that is valid. Passing that to
[fromMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromMSecsSinceEpoch)()
will produce a valid date-time that isn't faithfully represented by the string parsed.

The expressions that don't have leading zeroes (d, M, h, m, s, z) will be greedy. This
means that they will use two digits even if this will put them outside the range and/or
leave too few digits for other sections.

```
QDateTime dateTime = QDateTime::fromString("130", "Mm"); // invalid
```

This could have meant 1 January 00:30.00 but the M will grab two digits.

Incorrectly specified fields of the *string* will cause an invalid
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) to be returned. For
example, consider the following code, where the two digit year 12 is read as 1912 (see
the table below for all field defaults); the resulting datetime is invalid because 23
April 1912 was a Tuesday, not a Monday:

```
QString string = "Monday, 23 April 12 22:51:41";
QString format = "dddd, d MMMM yy hh:mm:ss";
QDateTime invalid = QDateTime::fromString(string, format);
```

The correct code is:

```
QString string = "Tuesday, 23 April 12 22:51:41";
QString format = "dddd, d MMMM yy hh:mm:ss";
QDateTime valid = QDateTime::fromString(string, format);
```

For any field that is not represented in the format, the following defaults are used:

| Field | Default value |
| --- | --- |
| Year | 1900 |
| Month | 1 (January) |
| Day | 1 |
| Hour | 0 |
| Minute | 0 |
| Second | 0 |

For example:

```
QDateTime dateTime = QDateTime::fromString("1.30.1", "M.d.s");
// dateTime is January 30 in 1900 at 00:00:01.
dateTime = QDateTime::fromString("12", "yy");
// dateTime is January 1 in 1912 at 00:00:00.
```

**Note:** If localized month and day names are used, please switch to using
[QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)().toDateTime()
as [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) methods shall change
to only recognize English (C locale) names at Qt 6\.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toString)(),
[QDate::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#fromString)(),
[QTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#fromString)(), and
[QLocale::toDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDateTime)().

### bool QDateTime::isValid() const

Returns `true` if both the date and the time are valid and they are valid in the current
[Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), otherwise
returns `false`.

If the [timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() is
[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) or
[Qt::TimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) then the date
and time are checked to see if they fall in the Standard Time to Daylight-Saving Time
transition hour, i.e. if the transition is at 2am and the clock goes forward to 3am then
the time from 02:00:00 to 02:59:59.999 is considered to be invalid.

**See also**
[QDateTime::YearRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#YearRange-enum),
[QDate::isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isValid)(), and
[QTime::isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#isValid)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QDateTime::msecsTo(const [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) \&*other*) const

Returns the number of milliseconds from this datetime to the *other* datetime. If the
*other* datetime is earlier than this datetime, the value returned is negative.

Before performing the comparison, the two datetimes are converted to
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) to ensure that the
result is correct if daylight-saving (DST) applies to one of the two datetimes and but
not the other.

Returns 0 if either datetime is invalid.

**See also** [addMSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addMSecs)(),
[daysTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#daysTo)(), and
[QTime::msecsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#msecsTo)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDateTime.offsetFromUtc.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QDateTime::offsetFromUtc() const

Returns this date-time's Offset From UTC in seconds.

The result depends on
[timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)():

- `Qt::UTC` The offset is 0\.
- `Qt::OffsetFromUTC` The offset is the value originally set.
- `Qt::LocalTime` The local time's offset from UTC is returned.
- `Qt::TimeZone` The offset used by the time-zone is returned.

For the last two, the offset at this date and time will be returned, taking account of
Daylight-Saving Offset unless the date precedes the start of 1970\. The offset is the
difference between the local time or time in the given time-zone and UTC time; it is
positive in time-zones ahead of UTC (East of The Prime Meridian), negative for those
behind UTC (West of The Prime Meridian).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

**See also**
[setOffsetFromUtc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setOffsetFromUtc)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDateTime.secsTo.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QDateTime::secsTo(const [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) \&*other*) const

Returns the number of seconds from this datetime to the *other* datetime. If the *other*
datetime is earlier than this datetime, the value returned is negative.

Before performing the comparison, the two datetimes are converted to
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) to ensure that the
result is correct if daylight-saving (DST) applies to one of the two datetimes but not
the other.

Returns 0 if either datetime is invalid.

Example:

```
QDateTime now = QDateTime::currentDateTime();
QDateTime xmas(QDate(now.date().year(), 12, 25).startOfDay());
qDebug("There are %d seconds to Christmas", now.secsTo(xmas));
```

**See also** [addSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addSecs)(),
[daysTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#daysTo)(), and
[QTime::secsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#secsTo)().

### void QDateTime::setMSecsSinceEpoch([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *msecs*)

Sets the date and time given the number of milliseconds *msecs* that have passed since
1970-01-01T00:00:00.000, Coordinated Universal Time
([Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)). On systems that
do not support time zones this function will behave as if local time were
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

Note that passing the minimum of `qint64` (`std::numeric_limits<qint64>::min()`) to
*msecs* will result in undefined behavior.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.7.

**See also**
[toMSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toMSecsSinceEpoch)()
and
[setSecsSinceEpoch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setSecsSinceEpoch)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDateTime.setOffsetFromUtc.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QDateTime::setOffsetFromUtc(int *offsetSeconds*)

Sets the [timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() to
[Qt::OffsetFromUTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) and the
offset to *offsetSeconds*. The datetime will refer to a different point in time.

The maximum and minimum offset is 14 positive or negative hours. If *offsetSeconds* is
larger or smaller than that, then the result is undefined.

If *offsetSeconds* is 0 then the
[timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() will be set to
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

**See also** [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#isValid)() and
[offsetFromUtc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#offsetFromUtc)().

### void QDateTime::setTime(const [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) \&*time*)

Sets the time part of this datetime to *time*. If *time* is not valid, this function
sets it to midnight. Therefore, it's possible to clear any set time in a
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) by setting it to a
default [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html):

```
QDateTime dt = QDateTime::currentDateTime();
dt.setTime(QTime());
```

**See also** [time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#time)(),
[setDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setDate)(), and
[setTimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setTimeSpec)().

Qt 5 reference:

### void QDateTime::setTimeSpec([Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) *spec*)

Sets the time specification used in this datetime to *spec*. The datetime will refer to
a different point in time.

If *spec* is
[Qt::OffsetFromUTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) then the
[timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() will be set to
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), i.e. an effective
offset of 0\.

If *spec* is [Qt::TimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)
then the spec will be set to
[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), i.e. the
current system time zone.

Example:

```
QDateTime local(QDateTime::currentDateTime());
qDebug() << "Local time is:" << local;

QDateTime UTC(local);
UTC.setTimeSpec(Qt::UTC);
qDebug() << "UTC time is:" << UTC;

qDebug() << "There are" << local.secsTo(UTC) << "seconds difference between the datetimes.";
```

**See also** [timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)(),
[setDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setDate)(),
[setTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setTime)(),
[setTimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#setTimeZone)(), and
[Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

PythonQt.Qt.QDateTime.time.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QDateTime::toString([Qt::DateFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum) *format* \= Qt::TextDate) const

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the datetime as a string in the *format* given.

If the *format* is
[Qt::TextDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
is formatted in the default way. The day and month names will be localized names using
the system locale, i.e.
[QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). An example
of this formatting is "Wed May 20 03:40:13 1998".

If the *format* is
[Qt::ISODate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
format corresponds to the ISO 8601 extended specification for representations of dates
and times, taking the form yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss\[Z\|\[\+\|-\]HH:mm\], depending on the
[timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() of the
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html). If the
[timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() is
[Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), Z will be appended
to the string; if the
[timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)() is
[Qt::OffsetFromUTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), the
offset in hours and minutes from UTC will be appended to the string. To include
milliseconds in the ISO 8601 date, use the *format*
[Qt::ISODateWithMs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), which
corresponds to yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.zzz\[Z\|\[\+\|-\]HH:mm\].

The *format* options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with
[QLocale::system().toString(datetime,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale::system().toString(datetime,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

The *format* options
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with
[QLocale().toString(datetime,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale().toString(datetime,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

If the *format* is
[Qt::RFC2822Date](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the
string is formatted following [RFC 2822](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2822.txt).

If the datetime is invalid, an empty string will be returned.

**Warning:** The
[Qt::ISODate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum) format is only
valid for years in the range 0 to 9999\.

**See also**
[fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)(),
[QDate::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toString-1)(),
[QTime::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#toString)(), and
[QLocale::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString)().

### [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#QDateTime) QDateTime::toTimeSpec([Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) *spec*) const

Returns a copy of this datetime converted to the given time *spec*.

If *spec* is
[Qt::OffsetFromUTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) then it is
set to [Qt::UTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum). To set to a
spec of [Qt::OffsetFromUTC](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)
use
[toOffsetFromUtc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toOffsetFromUtc)().

If *spec* is [Qt::TimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum)
then it is set to
[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum), i.e. the
local Time Zone.

Example:

```
QDateTime local(QDateTime::currentDateTime());
QDateTime UTC(local.toTimeSpec(Qt::UTC));
qDebug() << "Local time is:" << local;
qDebug() << "UTC time is:" << UTC;
qDebug() << "No difference between times:" << local.secsTo(UTC);
```

**See also** [timeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#timeSpec)(),
[toTimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toTimeZone)(), and
[toOffsetFromUtc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toOffsetFromUtc)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDateTimeEdit.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-datetimeedit.png)

QDateTimeEdit allows the user to edit dates by using the keyboard or the arrow keys to
increase and decrease date and time values. The arrow keys can be used to move from
section to section within the QDateTimeEdit box. Dates and times appear in accordance
with the format set; see
[setDisplayFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#displayFormat-prop)().

```
QDateTimeEdit *dateEdit = new QDateTimeEdit(QDate::currentDate());
dateEdit->setMinimumDate(QDate::currentDate().addDays(-365));
dateEdit->setMaximumDate(QDate::currentDate().addDays(365));
dateEdit->setDisplayFormat("yyyy.MM.dd");
```

Here we've created a new QDateTimeEdit object initialized with today's date, and
restricted the valid date range to today plus or minus 365 days. We've set the order to
month, day, year.

The range of valid values for a QDateTimeEdit is controlled by the properties
[minimumDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDateTime-prop),
[maximumDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDateTime-prop),
and their respective date and time components. By default, any date-time from the start
of 100 CE to the end of 9999 CE is valid.

### Using a Pop-up Calendar Widget

QDateTimeEdit can be configured to allow a
[QCalendarWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendarwidget.html) to be used to
select dates. This is enabled by setting the
[calendarPopup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#calendarPopup-prop)
property. Additionally, you can supply a custom calendar widget for use as the calendar
pop-up by calling the
[setCalendarWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#setCalendarWidget)()
function. The existing calendar widget can be retrieved with
[calendarWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#calendarWidget)().

### Keyboard Tracking

When [keyboard
tracking](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#keyboardTracking-prop)
is enabled (the default), every keystroke of editing a field triggers signals for value
changes.

When the allowed
[range](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#setDateTimeRange) is
narrower than some time interval whose end it straddles, keyboard tracking prevents the
user editing the date or time to access the later part of the interval. For example, for
a range from 29.04.2020 to 02.05.2020 and an initial date of 30.04.2020, the user can
change neither the month (May 30th is outside the range) nor the day (April 2nd is
outside the range).

When keyboard tracking is disabled, changes are only signalled when focus leaves the
text field after edits have modified the content. This allows the user to edit via an
invalid date-time to reach a valid one.

### maximumDate : [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html)

Changing this property updates the date of the
[maximumDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDateTime-prop)
property while preserving the
[maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop)

[minimumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDate-prop) is
adjusted, if necessary, to ensure that the range remains valid. When this happens, the
[minimumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumTime-prop)
property is also adjusted if it is greater than the
[maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop)
property. Otherwise, changes to this property preserve the
[minimumDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDateTime-prop)
property.

This property can only be set to a valid
[QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) object describing a date on which
the current
[maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop)
property makes a valid [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html)
object. The latest date that setMaximumDate() accepts is the end of 9999 CE. This is the
default for this property. This default can be restored with

### void QDateTimeEdit::setDateRange(const [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) \&*min*, const [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) \&*max*)

Set the range of allowed dates for the date time edit.

This convenience function sets the
[minimumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDate-prop)
and
[maximumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDate-prop)
properties.

```
setDateRange(min, max);
```

is analogous to:

```
setMinimumDate(min);
setMaximumDate(max);
```

If either *min* or *max* is invalid, this function does nothing. This function preserves
the
[minimumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumTime-prop)
property. If *max* is less than *min*, the new
[maximumDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDateTime-prop)
property shall be the new
[minimumDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDateTime-prop)
property. If *max* is equal to *min* and the
[maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop)
property was less then the
[minimumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumTime-prop)
property, the
[maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop)
property is set to the
[minimumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumTime-prop)
property. Otherwise, this preserves the
[maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop)
property.

If the range is narrower then a time interval whose end it spans, for example a week
that spans the end of a month, users can only edit the date to one in the later part of
the range if keyboard-tracking is disabled.

**See also**
[minimumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDate-prop),
[maximumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDate-prop),

### void QDateTimeEdit::setTimeRange(const [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) \&*min*, const [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) \&*max*)

Set the range of allowed times for the date time edit.

This convenience function sets the
[minimumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumTime-prop)
and
[maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop)
properties.

Note that these only constrain the date time edit's value on, respectively, the
[minimumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDate-prop)
and
[maximumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDate-prop).
When these date properties do not coincide, times after *max* are allowed on dates
before
[maximumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDate-prop)
and times before *min* are allowed on dates after
[minimumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDate-prop).

```
setTimeRange(min, max);
```

is analogous to:

```
setMinimumTime(min);
setMaximumTime(max);
```

If either *min* or *max* is invalid, this function does nothing. This function preserves
the
[minimumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumDate-prop)
and
[maximumDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumDate-prop)
properties. If those properties coincide and *max* is less than *min*, *min* is used as
*max*.

If the range is narrower then a time interval whose end it spans, for example the
interval from ten to an hour to ten past the same hour, users can only edit the time to
one in the later part of the range if keyboard-tracking is disabled.

**See also**
[minimumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumTime-prop),

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Many desktop environments provide services that can be used by applications to perform
common tasks, such as opening a web page, in a way that is both consistent and takes
into account the user's application preferences.

This class contains functions that provide simple interfaces to these services that
indicate whether they succeeded or failed.

The [openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)()
function is used to open files located at arbitrary URLs in external applications. For
URLs that correspond to resources on the local filing system (where the URL scheme is
"file"), a suitable application will be used to open the file; otherwise, a web browser
will be used to fetch and display the file.

The user's desktop settings control whether certain executable file types are opened for
browsing, or if they are executed instead. Some desktop environments are configured to
prevent users from executing files obtained from non-local URLs, or to ask the user's
permission before doing so.

### URL Handlers

The behavior of the
[openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)() function
can be customized for individual URL schemes to allow applications to override the
default handling behavior for certain types of URLs.

The dispatch mechanism allows only one custom handler to be used for each URL scheme;
this is set using the
[setUrlHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#setUrlHandler)()
function. Each handler is implemented as a slot which accepts only a single
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) argument.

The existing handlers for each scheme can be removed with the
[unsetUrlHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#unsetUrlHandler)()
function. This returns the handling behavior for the given scheme to the default
behavior.

This system makes it easy to implement a help system, for example. Help could be
provided in labels and text browsers using **help://myapplication/mytopic** URLs, and by
registering a handler it becomes possible to display the help text inside the
application:

```
class MyHelpHandler : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
public:
    ...
public slots:
    void showHelp(const QUrl &url);
};

QDesktopServices::setUrlHandler("help", helpInstance, "showHelp");
```

If inside the handler you decide that you can't open the requested URL, you can just
call
[QDesktopServices::openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)()
again with the same argument, and it will try to open the URL using the appropriate
mechanism for the user's desktop environment.

Combined with platform specific settings, the schemes registered by the
[openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)() function
can also be exposed to other applications, opening up for application deep linking or a
very basic URL-based IPC mechanism.

**Note:** Since Qt 5, storageLocation() and displayName() are replaced by functionality
provided by the [QStandardPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandardpaths.html)
class.

PythonQt.Qt.QDesktopServices.openUrl.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` bool QDesktopServices::openUrl(const [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) \&*url*)

Opens the given *url* in the appropriate Web browser for the user's desktop environment,
and returns `true` if successful; otherwise returns `false`.

If the URL is a reference to a local file (i.e., the URL scheme is "file") then it will
be opened with a suitable application instead of a Web browser.

The following example opens a file on the Windows file system residing on a path that
contains spaces:

```
QDesktopServices::openUrl(QUrl("file:///C:/Program Files", QUrl::TolerantMode));
```

If a `mailto` URL is specified, the user's e-mail client will be used to open a composer
window containing the options specified in the URL, similar to the way `mailto` links
are handled by a Web browser.

For example, the following URL contains a recipient (`user@foo.com`), a subject
(`Test`), and a message body (`Just a test`):

```
mailto:user@foo.com?subject=Test&body=Just a test
```

**Warning:** Although many e-mail clients can send attachments and are Unicode-aware,
the user may have configured their client without these features. Also, certain e-mail
clients (e.g., Lotus Notes) have problems with long URLs.

**Warning:** A return value of `true` indicates that the application has successfully
requested the operating system to open the URL in an external application. The external
application may still fail to launch or fail to open the requested URL. This result will
not be reported back to the application.

**Warning:** URLs passed to this function on iOS will not load unless their schemes are
listed in the `LSApplicationQueriesSchemes` key of the application's Info.plist file.
For more information, see the Apple Developer Documentation for
[canOpenURL(\_:)](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiapplication/1622952-canopenurl).
For example, the following lines enable URLs with the HTTPS scheme:

```
<key>LSApplicationQueriesSchemes</key>
<array>
    <string>https</string>
</array>
```

**See also**
[setUrlHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#setUrlHandler)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDesktopServices.setUrlHandl.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QDesktopServices::setUrlHandler(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*scheme*, [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) \**receiver*, const char \**method*)

Sets the handler for the given *scheme* to be the handler *method* provided by the
*receiver* object.

This function provides a way to customize the behavior of
[openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)(). If
[openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)() is called
with a URL with the specified *scheme* then the given *method* on the *receiver* object
is called instead of
[QDesktopServices](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html) launching
an external application.

The provided method must be implemented as a slot that only accepts a single
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) argument.

```
class MyHelpHandler : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
public:
    ...
public slots:
    void showHelp(const QUrl &url);
};

QDesktopServices::setUrlHandler("help", helpInstance, "showHelp");
```

To use this function for receiving data from other apps on iOS you also need to add the
custom scheme to the `CFBundleURLSchemes` list in your Info.plist file:

```
<key>CFBundleURLTypes</key>
<array>
    <dict>
        <key>CFBundleURLSchemes</key>
        <array>
            <string>myapp</string>
        </array>
    </dict>
</array>
```

For more information, see the Apple Developer Documentation for [Communicating with
Other Apps Using Custom
URLs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/core_app/allowing_apps_and_websites_to_link_to_your_content/communicating_with_other_apps_using_custom_urls?language=objc).

**Warning:** It is not possible to claim support for some well known URL schemes,
including http and https. This is only allowed for Universal Links.

To claim support for http and https the above entry in the Info.plist file is not
allowed. This is only possible when you add your domain to the Entitlements file:

```
<key>com.apple.developer.associated-domains</key>
<array>
    <string>applinks:your.domain.com</string>
</array>
```

iOS will search for /.well-known/apple-app-site-association on your domain, when the
application is installed. If you want to listen to
https://your.domain.com/help?topic\=ABCDEF you need to provide the following content
there:

```
{
    "applinks": {
        "apps": [],
        "details": [{
            "appIDs" : [ "ABCDE12345.com.example.app" ],
            "components": [{
                "/": "/help",
                "?": { "topic": "?*"}
            }]
        }]
    }
}
```

For more information, see the Apple Developer Documentation for
<https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safariservices/supporting_associated_domains_in_your_app>\[Supporting
Associated Domains}.

If setUrlHandler() is used to set a new handler for a scheme which already has a
handler, the existing handler is simply replaced with the new one. Since
[QDesktopServices](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html) does not
take ownership of handlers, no objects are deleted when a handler is replaced.

Note that the handler will always be called from within the same thread that calls
[QDesktopServices::openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)().

You must call
[unsetUrlHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#unsetUrlHandler)()
before destroying the handler object, so the destruction of the handler object does not
overlap with concurrent invocations of
[openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)() using it.

**See also**
[openUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#openUrl)() and
[unsetUrlHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopservices.html#unsetUrlHandler)().
signatures: setUrlHandler(scheme: str, receiver: PySide2.QtCore.QObject, method: str) -> None

## Detailed Description

Systems with more than one graphics card and monitor can manage the physical screen
space available either as multiple desktops, or as a large virtual desktop.

This class provides information about the user's desktop, such as its total size, number
of screens, the geometry of each screen, and whether they are configured as separate
desktops or a single virtual desktop.

Widgets provided by Qt use this class to place tooltips, menus and dialog boxes on the
correct screen for their parent or application widgets. Applications can use this class
to obtain information that can be used to save window positions, or to place child
widgets and dialogs on one particular screen.

### Obtaining a Desktop Widget

The
[QApplication::desktop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication-obsolete.html#desktop)()
function is used to get an instance of QDesktopWidget.

The widget's
[screenGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget-obsolete.html#screenGeometry)()
function provides information about the geometry of the available screens with. The
number of screens available is returned by
[screenCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget-obsolete.html#screenCount-prop),
and the
[screenCountChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget-obsolete.html#screenCountChanged)()
signal is emitted when screens are added or removed. The screen number that a particular
point or widget is located in is returned by
[screenNumber](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget.html#screenNumber)().

### Screen Geometry

To obtain the dimensions of a particular screen, call the
[screenGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget-obsolete.html#screenGeometry)()
function. On some desktop environments, not all of the screen is available for
applications to use; for example, an application dock or menu bar may take up some
space. Use the
[availableGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget-obsolete.html#availableGeometry)()
function to obtain the available area for applications.

QDesktopWidget also inherits the
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) properties,
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#width-prop)() and
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#height-prop)(), which specify
the size of the desktop. However, for desktops with multiple screens, the size of the
desktop is the union of all the screen sizes, so
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#width-prop)() and
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#height-prop)() should *not* be
used for computing the size of a widget to be placed on one of the screens.

On systems that are configured to use the available screens as a single, large virtual
desktop, the
[virtualDesktop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget-obsolete.html#virtualDesktop-prop)
property will be set to true. In this case, the widget's size is usually the size of the
bounding rectangle of all the screens.

### Use of the Primary Screen

For an application, the screen where the main widget resides is the primary screen. This
is stored in the
[primaryScreen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdesktopwidget-obsolete.html#primaryScreen-prop)
property. All windows opened in the context of the application should be constrained to
the boundaries of the primary screen; for example, it would be inconvenient if a dialog
box popped up on a different screen, or split over two screens.

![Managing Multiple
Screens](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qdesktopwidget.png)

In the illustration above, Application One's primary screen is screen 0, and App Two's
primary screen is screen 1\.

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-dial.png)

QDial is used when the user needs to control a value within a program-definable range,
and the range either wraps around (for example, with angles measured from 0 to 359
degrees) or the dialog layout needs a square widget.

Since QDial inherits from
[QAbstractSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html), the dial
behaves in a similar way to a [slider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html).
When [wrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdial.html#wrapping-prop)() is false
(the default setting) there is no real difference between a slider and a dial. They both
share the same signals, slots and member functions. Which one you use depends on the
expectations of your users and on the type of application.

The dial initially emits
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#valueChanged)()
signals continuously while the slider is being moved; you can make it emit the signal
less often by disabling the
[tracking](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#tracking-prop)
property. The
[sliderMoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderMoved)()
signal is emitted continuously even when tracking is disabled.

The dial also emits
[sliderPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderPressed)()
and
[sliderReleased](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderReleased)()
signals when the mouse button is pressed and released. Note that the dial's value can
change without these signals being emitted since the keyboard and wheel can also be used
to change the value.

Unlike the slider, QDial attempts to draw a "nice" number of notches rather than one per
line step. If possible, the number of notches drawn is one per line step, but if there
aren't enough pixels to draw every one, QDial will skip notches to try and draw a
uniform set (e.g. by drawing every second or third notch).

Like the slider, the dial makes the
[QAbstractSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html) function
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop)()
available as a slot.

The dial's keyboard interface is fairly simple: The **left**/**up** and
**right**/**down** arrow keys adjust the dial's
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop) by the
defined
[singleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#singleStep-prop),
**Page Up** and **Page Down** by the defined
[pageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#pageStep-prop), and
the **Home** and **End** keys set the value to the defined
[minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#minimum-prop) and
[maximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#maximum-prop) values.

If you are using the mouse wheel to adjust the dial, the increment value is determined
by the lesser value of
[wheelScrollLines](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#wheelScrollLines-prop)
multiplied by
[singleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#singleStep-prop),
and [pageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#pageStep-prop).

PythonQt.Qt.QDialog.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A dialog window is a top-level window mostly used for short-term tasks and brief
communications with the user. QDialogs may be modal or modeless. QDialogs can provide a
[return value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#return), and they can
have [default buttons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#default).
QDialogs can also have a [QSizeGrip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizegrip.html)
in their lower-right corner, using
[setSizeGripEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#sizeGripEnabled-prop)().

Note that QDialog (and any other widget that has type `Qt::Dialog`) uses the parent
widget slightly differently from other classes in Qt. A dialog is always a top-level
widget, but if it has a parent, its default location is centered on top of the parent's
top-level widget (if it is not top-level itself). It will also share the parent's
taskbar entry.

Use the overload of the
[QWidget::setParent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setParent)()
function to change the ownership of a QDialog widget. This function allows you to
explicitly set the window flags of the reparented widget; using the overloaded function
will clear the window flags specifying the window-system properties for the widget (in
particular it will reset the
[Qt::Dialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum) flag).

**Note:** The parent relationship of the dialog does *not* imply that the dialog will
always be stacked on top of the parent window. To ensure that the dialog is always on
top, make the dialog modal. This also applies for child windows of the dialog itself. To
ensure that child windows of the dialog stay on top of the dialog, make the child
windows modal as well.

### Modal Dialogs

A **modal** dialog is a dialog that blocks input to other visible windows in the same
application. Dialogs that are used to request a file name from the user or that are used
to set application preferences are usually modal. Dialogs can be [application
modal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowModality-enum) (the default) or
[window modal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowModality-enum).

When an application modal dialog is opened, the user must finish interacting with the
dialog and close it before they can access any other window in the application. Window
modal dialogs only block access to the window associated with the dialog, allowing the
user to continue to use other windows in an application.

The most common way to display a modal dialog is to call its
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)() function. When the user
closes the dialog, [exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)() will
provide a useful [return value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#return).
To close the dialog and return the appropriate value, you must connect a default button,
e.g. an **OK** button to the
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#accept)() slot and a **Cancel**
button to the [reject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#reject)() slot.
Alternatively, you can call the
[done](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#done)() slot with `Accepted` or
`Rejected`.

An alternative is to call
[setModal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#modal-prop)(true) or
[setWindowModality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowModality-prop)(),
then [show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(). Unlike
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)(),
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() returns control to the
caller immediately. Calling
[setModal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#modal-prop)(true) is
especially useful for progress dialogs, where the user must have the ability to interact
with the dialog, e.g. to cancel a long running operation. If you use
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() and
[setModal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#modal-prop)(true) together to
perform a long operation, you must call
[QCoreApplication::processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)()
periodically during processing to enable the user to interact with the dialog. (See
[QProgressDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html).)

### Modeless Dialogs

A **modeless** dialog is a dialog that operates independently of other windows in the
same application. Find and replace dialogs in word-processors are often modeless to
allow the user to interact with both the application's main window and with the dialog.

Modeless dialogs are displayed using
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(), which returns control to
the caller immediately.

If you invoke the [show()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)
function after hiding a dialog, the dialog will be displayed in its original position.
This is because the window manager decides the position for windows that have not been
explicitly placed by the programmer. To preserve the position of a dialog that has been
moved by the user, save its position in your
[closeEvent()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#closeEvent) handler and
then move the dialog to that position, before showing it again.

### Default Button

A dialog's *default* button is the button that's pressed when the user presses Enter
(Return). This button is used to signify that the user accepts the dialog's settings and
wants to close the dialog. Use
[QPushButton::setDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#default-prop)(),
[QPushButton::isDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#default-prop)()
and
[QPushButton::autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)()
to set and control the dialog's default button.

### Escape Key

If the user presses the Esc key in a dialog,
[QDialog::reject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#reject)() will be
called. This will cause the window to close: The [close
event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcloseevent.html) cannot be
[ignored](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore).

### Extensibility

Extensibility is the ability to show the dialog in two ways: a partial dialog that shows
the most commonly used options, and a full dialog that shows all the options. Typically
an extensible dialog will initially appear as a partial dialog, but with a **More**
toggle button. If the user presses the **More** button down, the dialog is expanded. The
[Extension
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-dialogs-extension-example.html)
shows how to achieve extensible dialogs using Qt.

### Return Value (Modal Dialogs)

Modal dialogs are often used in situations where a return value is required, e.g. to
indicate whether the user pressed **OK** or **Cancel**. A dialog can be closed by
calling the [accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#accept)() or the
[reject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#reject)() slots, and
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)() will return `Accepted` or
`Rejected` as appropriate. The
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)() call returns the result
of the dialog. The result is also available from
[result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#result)() if the dialog has not
been destroyed.

In order to modify your dialog's close behavior, you can reimplement the functions
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#accept)(),
[reject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#reject)() or
[done](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#done)(). The
[closeEvent()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#closeEvent) function
should only be reimplemented to preserve the dialog's position or to override the
standard close or reject behavior.

### Code Examples

A modal dialog:

```
void EditorWindow::countWords()
{
    WordCountDialog dialog(this);
    dialog.setWordCount(document().wordCount());
    dialog.exec();
}
```

A modeless dialog:

```
void EditorWindow::find()
{
    if (!findDialog) {
        findDialog = new FindDialog(this);
        connect(findDialog, &FindDialog::findNext,
                this, &EditorWindow::findNext);
    }

    findDialog->show();
    findDialog->raise();
    findDialog->activateWindow();
}
```

### `[virtual slot]` void QDialog::done(int *r*)

Closes the dialog and sets its result code to *r*. The
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#finished)() signal will emit
*r*; if *r* is
[QDialog::Accepted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#DialogCode-enum) or
[QDialog::Rejected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#DialogCode-enum),
the [accepted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#accepted)() or the
[rejected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#rejected)() signals will also
be emitted, respectively.

If this dialog is shown with
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)(), done() also causes the
local event loop to finish, and
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)() to return *r*.

As with [QWidget::close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#close)(),
done() deletes the dialog if the
[Qt::WA\_DeleteOnClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
flag is set. If the dialog is the application's main widget, the application terminates.
If the dialog is the last window closed, the
[QApplication::lastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#lastWindowClosed)()
signal is emitted.

**See also** [accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#accept)(),
[reject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#reject)(),
[QApplication::activeWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activeWindow)(),
and
[QCoreApplication::quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)().

### `[virtual slot]` int QDialog::exec()

Shows the dialog as a [modal
dialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#modal-dialogs), blocking until
the user closes it. The function returns a
[DialogCode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#DialogCode-enum) result.

If the dialog is [application
modal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowModality-enum), users cannot
interact with any other window in the same application until they close the dialog. If
the dialog is [window
modal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowModality-enum), only interaction
with the parent window is blocked while the dialog is open. By default, the dialog is
application modal.

**Note:** Avoid using this function; instead, use `open()`. Unlike exec(),
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#open)() is asynchronous, and does
not spin an additional event loop. This prevents a series of dangerous bugs from
happening (e.g. deleting the dialog's parent while the dialog is open via exec()). When
using [open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#open)() you can connect to
the [finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#finished)() signal of
[QDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html) to be notified when the
dialog is closed.

**See also** [open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#open)(),
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(),
[result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#result)(), and
[setWindowModality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowModality-prop)().
