PythonQt.Qt.QDialogButtonBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Dialogs and message boxes typically present buttons in a layout that conforms to the
interface guidelines for that platform. Invariably, different platforms have different
layouts for their dialogs. QDialogButtonBox allows a developer to add buttons to it and
will automatically use the appropriate layout for the user's desktop environment.

Most buttons for a dialog follow certain roles. Such roles include:

- Accepting or rejecting the dialog.
- Asking for help.
- Performing actions on the dialog itself (such as resetting fields or applying changes).

There can also be alternate ways of dismissing the dialog which may cause destructive
results.

Most dialogs have buttons that can almost be considered standard (e.g. **OK** and
**Cancel** buttons). It is sometimes convenient to create these buttons in a standard
way.

There are a couple ways of using QDialogButtonBox. One ways is to create the buttons (or
button texts) yourself and add them to the button box, specifying their role.

```
    findButton = new QPushButton(tr("&Find"));
    findButton->setDefault(true);

    moreButton = new QPushButton(tr("&More"));
    moreButton->setCheckable(true);
    moreButton->setAutoDefault(false);
```

Alternatively, QDialogButtonBox provides several standard buttons (e.g. OK, Cancel,
Save) that you can use. They exist as flags so you can OR them together in the
constructor.

```
    buttonBox = new QDialogButtonBox(QDialogButtonBox::Ok
                                     | QDialogButtonBox::Cancel);

    connect(buttonBox, &QDialogButtonBox::accepted, this, &QDialog::accept);
    connect(buttonBox, &QDialogButtonBox::rejected, this, &QDialog::reject);
```

You can mix and match normal buttons and standard buttons.

Currently the buttons are laid out in the following way if the button box is horizontal:

| GnomeLayout Horizontal | Button box laid out in horizontal [GnomeLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) |
| --- | --- |
| KdeLayout Horizontal | Button box laid out in horizontal [KdeLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) |
| MacLayout Horizontal | Button box laid out in horizontal [MacLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) |
| WinLayout Horizontal | Button box laid out in horizontal [WinLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) |

The buttons are laid out the following way if the button box is vertical:

| [GnomeLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) | [KdeLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) | [MacLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) | [WinLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GnomeLayout Vertical | KdeLayout Vertical | MacLayout Vertical | WinLayout Vertical |

Additionally, button boxes that contain only buttons with
[ActionRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonRole-enum)
or [HelpRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonRole-enum)
can be considered modeless and have an alternate look on macOS:

| modeless horizontal [MacLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) | Screenshot of modeless horizontal MacLayout |
| --- | --- |
| modeless vertical [MacLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonLayout-enum) | Screenshot of modeless vertical MacLayout |

When a button is clicked in the button box, the
[clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#clicked)() signal is
emitted for the actual button is that is pressed. For convenience, if the button has an
[AcceptRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonRole-enum),
[RejectRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonRole-enum),
or [HelpRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#ButtonRole-enum),
the [accepted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#accepted)(),
[rejected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#rejected)(), or
[helpRequested](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialogbuttonbox.html#helpRequested)()
signals are emitted respectively.

If you want a specific button to be default you need to call
[QPushButton::setDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#default-prop)()
on it yourself. However, if there is no default button set and to preserve which button
is the default button across platforms when using the
[QPushButton::autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
property, the first push button with the accept role is made the default button when the
QDialogButtonBox is shown,

PythonQt.Qt.QDir.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QDir is used to manipulate path names, access information regarding paths and files,
and manipulate the underlying file system. It can also be used to access Qt's [resource
system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/resources.html).

Qt uses "/" as a universal directory separator in the same way that "/" is used as a
path separator in URLs. If you always use "/" as a directory separator, Qt will
translate your paths to conform to the underlying operating system.

A QDir can point to a file using either a relative or an absolute path. Absolute paths
begin with the directory separator (optionally preceded by a drive specification under
Windows). Relative file names begin with a directory name or a file name and specify a
path relative to the current directory.

Examples of absolute paths:

```
QDir("/home/user/Documents")
QDir("C:/Users")
```

On Windows, the second example above will be translated to `C:\Users` when used to
access files.

Examples of relative paths:

```
QDir("images/landscape.png")
```

You can use the [isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isRelative)()
or [isAbsolute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isAbsolute)() functions to
check if a QDir is using a relative or an absolute file path. Call
[makeAbsolute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#makeAbsolute)() to convert a
relative QDir to an absolute one.

**Note:** Paths starting with a colon (*:*) are always considered absolute, as they
denote a [QResource](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qresource.html).

### Navigation and Directory Operations

A directory's path can be obtained with the
[path](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#path)() function, and a new path set
with the [setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#setPath)() function. The
absolute path to a directory is found by calling
[absolutePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#absolutePath)().

The name of a directory is found using the
[dirName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#dirName)() function. This
typically returns the last element in the absolute path that specifies the location of
the directory. However, it can also return "." if the QDir represents the current
directory.

```
QDir("Documents/Letters/Applications").dirName() // "Applications"
QDir().dirName()                                 // "."
```

The path for a directory can also be changed with the
[cd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cd)() and
[cdUp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cdUp)() functions, both of which
operate like familiar shell commands. When
[cd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cd)() is called with the name of an
existing directory, the QDir object changes directory so that it represents that
directory instead. The [cdUp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cdUp)()
function changes the directory of the QDir object so that it refers to its parent
directory; i.e. cd("..") is equivalent to
[cdUp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cdUp)().

Directories can be created with
[mkdir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#mkdir)(), renamed with
[rename](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#rename)(), and removed with
[rmdir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#rmdir)().

You can test for the presence of a directory with a given name by using
[exists](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#exists-1)(), and the properties of
a directory can be tested with
[isReadable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isReadable)(),
[isAbsolute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isAbsolute)(),
[isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isRelative)(), and
[isRoot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isRoot)().

The [refresh](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#refresh)() function re-reads
the directory's data from disk.

### Files and Directory Contents

Directories contain a number of entries, representing files, directories, and symbolic
links. The number of entries in a directory is returned by
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#count)(). A string list of the
names of all the entries in a directory can be obtained with
[entryList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#entryList)(). If you need
information about each entry, use
[entryInfoList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#entryInfoList)() to obtain
a list of [QFileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html) objects.

Paths to files and directories within a directory can be constructed using
[filePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#filePath)() and
[absoluteFilePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#absoluteFilePath)(). The
[filePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#filePath)() function returns a
path to the specified file or directory relative to the path of the QDir object;
[absoluteFilePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#absoluteFilePath)()
returns an absolute path to the specified file or directory. Neither of these functions
checks for the existence of files or directory; they only construct paths.

```
QDir directory("Documents/Letters");
QString path = directory.filePath("contents.txt");
QString absolutePath = directory.absoluteFilePath("contents.txt");
```

Files can be removed by using the
[remove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#remove)() function. Directories
cannot be removed in the same way as files; use
[rmdir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#rmdir)() to remove them instead.

It is possible to reduce the number of entries returned by
[entryList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#entryList)() and
[entryInfoList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#entryInfoList)() by
applying filters to a QDir object. You can apply a name filter to specify a pattern with
wildcards that file names need to match, an attribute filter that selects properties of
entries and can distinguish between files and directories, and a sort order.

Name filters are lists of strings that are passed to
[setNameFilters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#setNameFilters)().
Attribute filters consist of a bitwise OR combination of Filters, and these are
specified when calling
[setFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#setFilter)(). The sort order is
specified using [setSorting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#setSorting)()
with a bitwise OR combination of
[SortFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#SortFlag-enum).

You can test to see if a filename matches a filter using the
[match](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#match)() function.

Filter and sort order flags may also be specified when calling
[entryList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#entryList)() and
[entryInfoList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#entryInfoList)() in order
to override previously defined behavior.

### The Current Directory and Other Special Paths

Access to some common directories is provided with a number of static functions that
return QDir objects. There are also corresponding functions for these that return
strings:

| QDir | [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) | Return Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [current](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#current)() | [currentPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#currentPath)() | The application's working directory |
| [home](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#home)() | [homePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#homePath)() | The user's home directory |
| [root](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#root)() | [rootPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#rootPath)() | The root directory |
| [temp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#temp)() | [tempPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#tempPath)() | The system's temporary directory |

The [setCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#setCurrent)() static
function can also be used to set the application's working directory.

If you want to find the directory containing the application's executable, see
[QCoreApplication::applicationDirPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#applicationDirPath)().

The [drives](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#drives)() static function
provides a list of root directories for each device that contains a filing system. On
Unix systems this returns a list containing a single root directory "/"; on Windows the
list will usually contain `C:/`, and possibly other drive letters such as `D:/`,
depending on the configuration of the user's system.

### Path Manipulation and Strings

Paths containing "." elements that reference the current directory at that point in the
path, ".." elements that reference the parent directory, and symbolic links can be
reduced to a canonical form using the
[canonicalPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#canonicalPath)() function.

Paths can also be simplified by using
[cleanPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cleanPath)() to remove
redundant "/" and ".." elements.

It is sometimes necessary to be able to show a path in the native representation for the
user's platform. The static
[toNativeSeparators](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#toNativeSeparators)()
function returns a copy of the specified path in which each directory separator is
replaced by the appropriate separator for the underlying operating system.

### Examples

Check if a directory exists:

```
QDir dir("example");
if (!dir.exists())
    qWarning("Cannot find the example directory");
```

(We could also use the static convenience function QFile::exists().)

Traversing directories and reading a file:

```
QDir dir = QDir::root();                 // "/"
if (!dir.cd("tmp")) {                    // "/tmp"
    qWarning("Cannot find the \"/tmp\" directory");
} else {
    QFile file(dir.filePath("ex1.txt")); // "/temporary/ex1.txt"
    if (!file.open(QIODevice::ReadWrite))
        qWarning("Cannot create the file %s", file.name());
}
```

A program that lists all the files in the current directory (excluding symbolic links),
sorted by size, smallest first:

```
#include <QDir>
#include <iostream>

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    QCoreApplication app(argc, argv);
    QDir dir;
    dir.setFilter(QDir::Files | QDir::Hidden | QDir::NoSymLinks);
    dir.setSorting(QDir::Size | QDir::Reversed);

    QFileInfoList list = dir.entryInfoList();
    std::cout << "     Bytes Filename" << std::endl;
    for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); ++i) {
        QFileInfo fileInfo = list.at(i);
        std::cout << qPrintable(QString("%1 %2").arg(fileInfo.size(), 10)
                                                .arg(fileInfo.fileName()));
        std::cout << std::endl;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### Platform Specific Issues

On Android, some limitations apply when dealing with [content
URIs](https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/providers/content-provider-basics#ContentURIs):

- Access permissions might be needed by prompting the user through the [QFileDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html) which implements Android's native file picker.
- Aim to follow the [Scoped storage](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage#scoped-storage) guidelines, such as using app specific directories instead of other public external directories. For more information, also see [storage best practices](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/use-cases).
- Due to the design of Qt APIs (e.g. [QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html)), it's not possible to fully integrate the latter APIs with Android's [MediaStore](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/provider/MediaStore) APIs.

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QDir::canonicalPath() const

Returns the canonical path, i.e. a path without symbolic links or redundant "." or ".."
elements.

On systems that do not have symbolic links this function will always return the same
string that [absolutePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#absolutePath)()
returns. If the canonical path does not exist (normally due to dangling symbolic links)
canonicalPath() returns an empty string.

Example:

```
QString bin = "/local/bin";         // where /local/bin is a symlink to /usr/bin
QDir binDir(bin);
QString canonicalBin = binDir.canonicalPath();
// canonicalBin now equals "/usr/bin"

QString ls = "/local/bin/ls";       // where ls is the executable "ls"
QDir lsDir(ls);
QString canonicalLs = lsDir.canonicalPath();
// canonicalLS now equals "/usr/bin/ls".
```

**See also** [path](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#path)(),
[absolutePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#absolutePath)(),
[exists](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#exists-1)(),
[cleanPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cleanPath)(),
[dirName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#dirName)(), and
[absoluteFilePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#absoluteFilePath)().

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QDir::cleanPath(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*path*)

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QDir::homePath()

Returns the absolute path of the user's home directory.

Under Windows this function will return the directory of the current user's profile.
Typically, this is:

```
C:/Users/Username
```

Use the
[toNativeSeparators](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#toNativeSeparators)()
function to convert the separators to the ones that are appropriate for the underlying
operating system.

If the directory of the current user's profile does not exist or cannot be retrieved,
the following alternatives will be checked (in the given order) until an existing and
available path is found:

1. The path specified by the `USERPROFILE` environment variable.
2. The path formed by concatenating the `HOMEDRIVE` and `HOMEPATH` environment variables.
3. The path specified by the `HOME` environment variable.
4. The path returned by the [rootPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#rootPath)() function (which uses the `SystemDrive` environment variable)
5. The `C:/` directory.

Under non-Windows operating systems the `HOME` environment variable is used if it
exists, otherwise the path returned by the
[rootPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#rootPath)().

**See also** [home](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#home)(),

PythonQt.Qt.QDir.removeRecursively.doc:

### bool QDir::removeRecursively()

Removes the directory, including all its contents.

Returns `true` if successful, otherwise false.

If a file or directory cannot be removed, removeRecursively() keeps going and attempts
to delete as many files and sub-directories as possible, then returns `false`.

If the directory was already removed, the method returns `true` (expected result already
reached).

Note: this function is meant for removing a small application-internal directory (such
as a temporary directory), but not user-visible directories. For user-visible
operations, it is rather recommended to report errors more precisely to the user, to
offer solutions in case of errors, to show progress during the deletion since it could
take several minutes, etc.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

### bool QDir::rename(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*oldName*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*newName*)

Renames a file or directory from *oldName* to *newName*, and returns true if successful;
otherwise returns `false`.

On most file systems, rename() fails only if *oldName* does not exist, or if a file with
the new name already exists. However, there are also other reasons why rename() can
fail. For example, on at least one file system rename() fails if *newName* points to an
open file.

If *oldName* is a file (not a directory) that can't be renamed right away, Qt will try
to copy *oldName* to *newName* and remove *oldName*.

**See also** QFile::rename().

### void QDir::setNameFilters(const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*nameFilters*)

[entryInfoList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#entryInfoList)() to the
list of filters specified by *nameFilters*.

Each name filter is a wildcard (globbing) filter that understands `*` and `?` wildcards.
See [QRegularExpression Wildcard
Matching](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregularexpression.html#wildcard-matching).

For example, the following code sets three name filters on a
[QDir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html) to ensure that only files with
extensions typically used for C\+\+ source files are listed:

```
    QStringList filters;
    filters << "*.cpp" << "*.cxx" << "*.cc";
    dir.setNameFilters(filters);
```

**See also** [nameFilters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#nameFilters)()
and [setFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#setFilter)().

### void QDir::setPath(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*path*)

of multiple separators. No check is made to see whether a directory with this path
actually exists; but you can check for yourself using
[exists](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#exists-1)().

The path can be either absolute or relative. Absolute paths begin with the directory
separator "/" (optionally preceded by a drive specification under Windows). Relative
file names begin with a directory name or a file name and specify a path relative to the
current directory. An example of an absolute path is the string "/temporary/quartz", a
relative path might look like "src/fatlib".

**See also** [path](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#path)(),
[absolutePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#absolutePath)(),

[cleanPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#cleanPath)(),
[dirName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#dirName)(),

[isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isRelative)(), and
[makeAbsolute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#makeAbsolute)().

### `[static]` void QDir::setSearchPaths(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*prefix*, const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*searchPaths*)

Sets or replaces Qt's search paths for file names with the prefix *prefix* to
*searchPaths*.

To specify a prefix for a file name, prepend the prefix followed by a single colon
(e.g., "images:undo.png", "xmldocs:books.xml"). *prefix* can only contain letters or
numbers (e.g., it cannot contain a colon, nor a slash).

Qt uses this search path to locate files with a known prefix. The search path entries
are tested in order, starting with the first entry.

```
QDir::setSearchPaths("icons", QStringList(QDir::homePath() + "/images"));
QDir::setSearchPaths("docs", QStringList(":/embeddedDocuments"));
...
QPixmap pixmap("icons:undo.png"); // will look for undo.png in QDir::homePath() + "/images"
QFile file("docs:design.odf"); // will look in the :/embeddedDocuments resource path
```

File name prefix must be at least 2 characters long to avoid conflicts with Windows
drive letters.

Search paths may contain paths to [The Qt Resource
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/resources.html).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also** [searchPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#searchPaths)().

PythonQt.Qt.QDirModel.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The usage of QDirModel is not recommended anymore. The
[QFileSystemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemmodel.html) class is a
more performant alternative.

This class provides access to the local filesystem, providing functions for renaming and
removing files and directories, and for creating new directories. In the simplest case,
it can be used with a suitable display widget as part of a browser or filer.

QDirModel keeps a cache with file information. The cache needs to be updated with
[refresh](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdirmodel.html#refresh)().

QDirModel can be accessed using the standard interface provided by
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html), but it
also provides some convenience functions that are specific to a directory model. The
[fileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdirmodel.html#fileInfo)() and
[isDir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdirmodel.html#isDir)() functions provide
information about the underlying files and directories related to items in the model.

Directories can be created and removed using
[mkdir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdirmodel.html#mkdir)(),
[rmdir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdirmodel.html#rmdir)(), and the model will
be automatically updated to take the changes into account.

**Note:** QDirModel requires an instance of
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QDockWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QDockWidget provides the concept of dock widgets, also know as tool palettes or utility
windows. Dock windows are secondary windows placed in the *dock widget area* around the
[central widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#centralWidget) in a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html).

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/mainwindow-docks.png)

Dock windows can be moved inside their current area, moved into new areas and floated
(e.g., undocked) by the end-user. The QDockWidget API allows the programmer to restrict
the dock widgets ability to move, float and close, as well as the areas in which they
can be placed.

### Appearance

A QDockWidget consists of a title bar and the content area. The title bar displays the
dock widgets [window
title](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowTitle-prop), a *float*
button and a *close* button. Depending on the state of the QDockWidget, the *float* and
*close* buttons may be either disabled or not shown at all.

The visual appearance of the title bar and buttons is dependent on the
[style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) in use.

A QDockWidget acts as a wrapper for its child widget, set with
[setWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html#setWidget)(). Custom
size hints, minimum and maximum sizes and size policies should be implemented in the
child widget. QDockWidget will respect them, adjusting its own constraints to include
the frame and title. Size constraints should not be set on the QDockWidget itself,
because they change depending on whether it is docked; a docked QDockWidget has no frame
and a smaller title bar.

**Note:** On macOS, if the QDockWidget has a native window handle (for example, if
[winId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#winId)() is called on it or the
child widget), then due to a limitation it will not be possible to drag the dock widget
when undocking. Starting the drag will undock the dock widget, but a second drag will be
needed to move the dock widget itself.

### floating : bool

This property holds whether the dock widget is floating

A floating dock widget is presented to the user as an independent window "on top" of its

being docked in the [QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html).

Qt 5 reference:

### void QDockWidget::setTitleBarWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*)

Sets an arbitrary *widget* as the dock widget's title bar. If *widget* is `nullptr`, any
custom title bar widget previously set on the dock widget is removed, but not deleted,
and the default title bar will be used instead.

If a title bar widget is set,
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) will not use native
window decorations when it is floated.

Here are some tips for implementing custom title bars:

- Mouse events that are not explicitly handled by the title bar widget must be ignored by calling [QMouseEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)(). These events then propagate to the [QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) parent, which handles them in the usual manner, moving when the title bar is dragged, docking and undocking when it is double-clicked, etc.
- When [DockWidgetVerticalTitleBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html#DockWidgetFeature-enum) is set on [QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html), the title bar widget is repositioned accordingly. In [resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#resizeEvent)(), the title bar should check what orientation it should assume:

  ```
  QDockWidget *dockWidget = qobject_cast<QDockWidget*>(parentWidget());
  if (dockWidget->features() & QDockWidget::DockWidgetVerticalTitleBar) {
      // I need to be vertical
  } else {
      // I need to be horizontal
  }
  ```
- The title bar widget must have a valid [QWidget::sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop)() and [QWidget::minimumSizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSizeHint-prop)(). These functions should take into account the current orientation of the title bar.
- It is not possible to remove a title bar from a dock widget. However, a similar effect can be achieved by setting a default constructed [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) as the title bar widget.

Using [qobject\_cast](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#qobject_cast)() as
shown above, the title bar widget has full access to its parent
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html). Hence it can perform
such operations as docking and hiding in response to user actions.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also**
[titleBarWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html#titleBarWidget)()
and
[DockWidgetVerticalTitleBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html#DockWidgetFeature-enum).

PythonQt.Qt.QDoubleSpinBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QDoubleSpinBox allows the user to choose a value by clicking the up and down buttons or
by pressing Up or Down on the keyboard to increase or decrease the value currently
displayed. The user can also type the value in manually. The spin box supports double
values but can be extended to use different strings with
[validate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#validate)(),
[textFromValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#textFromValue)()
and
[valueFromText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#valueFromText)().

Every time the value changes QDoubleSpinBox emits
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#valueChanged)()
and [textChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#textChanged)()
signals, the former providing a double and the latter a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). The
[textChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#textChanged)()
signal provides the value with both
[prefix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#prefix-prop)() and
[suffix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#suffix-prop)(). The
current value can be fetched with
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#value-prop)() and set
with [setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#value-prop)().

Note: QDoubleSpinBox will round numbers so they can be displayed with the current
precision. In a QDoubleSpinBox with decimals set to 2, calling
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#value-prop)(2.555)
will cause [value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#value-prop)()
to return 2.56.

Clicking the up and down buttons or using the keyboard accelerator's Up and Down arrows
will increase or decrease the current value in steps of size
[singleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#singleStep-prop)().
If you want to change this behavior you can reimplement the virtual function
[stepBy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#stepBy)(). The minimum
and maximum value and the step size can be set using one of the constructors, and can be
changed later with
[setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#minimum-prop)(),
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#maximum-prop)() and
[setSingleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#singleStep-prop)().
The spinbox has a default precision of 2 decimal places but this can be changed using
[setDecimals](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#decimals-prop)().

Most spin boxes are directional, but QDoubleSpinBox can also operate as a circular spin
box, i.e. if the range is 0.0-99.9 and the current value is 99.9, clicking "up" will
give 0 if
[wrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#wrapping-prop)() is
set to true. Use
[setWrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#wrapping-prop)()
if you want circular behavior.

The displayed value can be prepended and appended with arbitrary strings indicating, for
example, currency or the unit of measurement. See
[setPrefix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#prefix-prop)() and
[setSuffix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#suffix-prop)(). The
text in the spin box is retrieved with
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#text-prop)() (which
includes any
[prefix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#prefix-prop)() and
[suffix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#suffix-prop)()), or with
[cleanText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#cleanText-prop)()
(which has no
[prefix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#prefix-prop)(), no
[suffix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#suffix-prop)() and no
leading or trailing whitespace).

It is often desirable to give the user a special (often default) choice in addition to
the range of numeric values. See
[setSpecialValueText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#specialValueText-prop)()
for how to do this with QDoubleSpinBox.

**Note:** The displayed value of the QDoubleSpinBox is limited to 18 characters in
addition to eventual prefix and suffix content. This limitation is used to keep the
double spin box usable even with extremely large values.

### prefix : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the spin box's prefix

The prefix is prepended to the start of the displayed value. Typical use is to display a
unit of measurement or a currency symbol. For example:

```
spinbox->setPrefix("$");
```

To turn off the prefix display, set this property to an empty string. The default is no
prefix. The prefix is not displayed when
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#value-prop)() \=\=
[minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#minimum-prop)() and
[specialValueText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#specialValueText-prop)()
is set.

If no prefix is set, prefix() returns an empty string.

setRange(minimum, maximum);

setMinimum(minimum);

Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QDoubleSpinBox::textFromValue(double *value*) const

This virtual function is used by the spin box whenever it needs to display the given
*value*. The default implementation returns a string containing *value* printed using
[QWidget::locale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#locale-prop)().toString(*value*,
[QLatin1Char](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlatin1char.html)('f'),
[decimals](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#decimals-prop)()) and
will remove the thousand separator unless
[setGroupSeparatorShown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#showGroupSeparator-prop)()
is set. Reimplementations may return anything.

Note: [QDoubleSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html) does not
call this function for
[specialValueText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#specialValueText-prop)()
and that neither
[prefix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#prefix-prop)() nor
[suffix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html#suffix-prop)() should be
included in the return value.

If you reimplement this, you may also need to reimplement

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QDoubleValidator provides an upper bound, a lower bound, and a limit on the number of
digits after the decimal point. It does not provide a
[fixup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#fixup)() function.

You can set the acceptable range in one call with
[setRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#setRange)(), or with
[setBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#bottom-prop)() and
[setTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#top-prop)(). Set the
number of decimal places with
[setDecimals](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#decimals-prop)().
The [validate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#validate)()
function returns the validation state.

QDoubleValidator uses its
[locale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#locale)() to interpret the
number. For example, in the German locale, "1,234" will be accepted as the fractional
number 1.234. In Arabic locales, QDoubleValidator will accept Arabic digits.

**Note:** The
[QLocale::NumberOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#NumberOption-enum)
set on the [locale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#locale)() also
affect the way the number is interpreted. For example, since
[QLocale::RejectGroupSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#NumberOption-enum)
is not set by default, the validator will accept group separators. It is thus
recommended to use
[QLocale::toDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDouble)() to
obtain the numeric value.

### `[override virtual]` [QValidator::State](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) QDoubleValidator::validate([QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*input*, int \&*pos*) const

Reimplements:
[QValidator::validate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#validate)(QString
\&input, int \&pos) const.

Returns [Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if
the string *input* contains a double that is within the valid range and is in the
correct format.

Returns [Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if
*input* contains a double that is outside the range or is in the wrong format; e.g. is
empty.

Returns [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if the
*input* is not a double or with too many digits after the decimal point.

Note: If the valid range consists of just positive doubles (e.g. 0.0 to 100.0) and
*input* is a negative double then
[Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) is returned. If
[notation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#notation-prop)() is
set to
[StandardNotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#Notation-enum),
and the input contains more digits before the decimal point than a double in the valid
range may have, [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum)
is returned. If
[notation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#notation-prop)() is
[ScientificNotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html#Notation-enum),
and the input is not in the valid range,
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) is
returned. The value may yet become valid by changing the exponent.

By default, the *pos* parameter is not used by this validator.
signatures: validate(self, arg__1: str, arg__2: int) -> PySide2.QtGui.QValidator.State

PythonQt.Qt.QDrag.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Drag and drop is an intuitive way for users to copy or move data around in an
application, and is used in many desktop environments as a mechanism for copying data
between applications. Drag and drop support in Qt is centered around the QDrag class
that handles most of the details of a drag and drop operation.

The data to be transferred by the drag and drop operation is contained in a
[QMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html) object. This is specified
with the [setMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#setMimeData)()
function in the following way:

```
        QDrag *drag = new QDrag(this);
        QMimeData *mimeData = new QMimeData;

        mimeData->setText(commentEdit->toPlainText());
        drag->setMimeData(mimeData);
```

Note that [setMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#setMimeData)()
assigns ownership of the [QMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html)
object to the QDrag object. The QDrag must be constructed on the heap with a parent
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) to ensure that Qt can clean
up after the drag and drop operation has been completed.

A pixmap can be used to represent the data while the drag is in progress, and will move
with the cursor to the drop target. This pixmap typically shows an icon that represents
the MIME type of the data being transferred, but any pixmap can be set with
[setPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#setPixmap)(). The cursor's hot
spot can be given a position relative to the top-left corner of the pixmap with the
[setHotSpot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#setHotSpot)() function. The
following code positions the pixmap so that the cursor's hot spot points to the center
of its bottom edge:

```
    drag->setHotSpot(QPoint(drag->pixmap().width()/2,
                            drag->pixmap().height()));
```

**Note:** On X11, the pixmap may not be able to keep up with the mouse movements if the
hot spot causes the pixmap to be displayed directly under the cursor.

The source and target widgets can be found with
[source](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#source)() and
[target](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#target)(). These functions are
often used to determine whether drag and drop operations started and finished at the
same widget, so that special behavior can be implemented.

QDrag only deals with the drag and drop operation itself. It is up to the developer to
decide when a drag operation begins, and how a QDrag object should be constructed and
used. For a given widget, it is often necessary to reimplement
[mousePressEvent()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mousePressEvent) to
determine whether the user has pressed a mouse button, and reimplement
[mouseMoveEvent()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseMoveEvent) to
check whether a QDrag is required.

PythonQt.Qt.QDrag.exec.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [Qt::DropAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DropAction-enum) QDrag::exec([Qt::DropActions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DropAction-enum) *supportedActions* \= Qt::MoveAction)

Starts the drag and drop operation and returns a value indicating the requested drop
action when it is completed. The drop actions that the user can choose from are
specified in *supportedActions*. The default proposed action will be selected among the
allowed actions in the following order: Move, Copy and Link.

**Note:** On Linux and macOS, the drag and drop operation can take some time, but this
function does not block the event loop. Other events are still delivered to the
application while the operation is performed. On Windows, the Qt event loop is blocked
during the operation.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also** [cancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#cancel)().

### [Qt::DropAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DropAction-enum) QDrag::exec([Qt::DropActions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DropAction-enum) *supportedActions*, [Qt::DropAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DropAction-enum) *defaultDropAction*)

Starts the drag and drop operation and returns a value indicating the requested drop
action when it is completed. The drop actions that the user can choose from are
specified in *supportedActions*.

The *defaultDropAction* determines which action will be proposed when the user performs
a drag without using modifier keys.

**Note:** On Linux and macOS, the drag and drop operation can take some time, but this
function does not block the event loop. Other events are still delivered to the
application while the operation is performed. On Windows, the Qt event loop is blocked
during the operation. However,
[QDrag::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html#exec)() on Windows causes
processEvents() to be called frequently to keep the GUI responsive. If any loops or
operations are called while a drag operation is active, it will block the drag
operation.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

PythonQt.Qt.QDragEnterEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A widget must accept this event in order to receive the [drag move
events](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragmoveevent.html) that are sent while the
drag and drop action is in progress. The drag enter event is always immediately followed
by a drag move event.

QDragEnterEvent inherits most of its functionality from
[QDragMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragmoveevent.html), which in turn
inherits most of its functionality from
[QDropEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QDragLeaveEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This event is always preceded by a
[QDragEnterEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragenterevent.html) and a series
of [QDragMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragmoveevent.html)s. It is not
sent if a [QDropEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html) is sent
instead.

PythonQt.Qt.QDragMoveEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A widget will receive drag move events repeatedly while the drag is within its
boundaries, if it accepts [drop
events](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#acceptDrops-prop) and [enter
events](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#dragEnterEvent). The widget
should examine the event to see what kind of
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#mimeData) it provides, and
call the [accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragmoveevent.html#accept-1)()
function to accept the drop if appropriate.

The rectangle supplied by the
[answerRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragmoveevent.html#answerRect)()
function can be used to restrict drops to certain parts of the widget. For example, we
can check whether the rectangle intersects with the geometry of a certain child widget
and only call
[acceptProposedAction()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#acceptProposedAction)
if that is the case.

Note that this class inherits most of its functionality from
[QDropEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html).

### void QDragMoveEvent::accept(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rectangle*)

The same as accept(), but also notifies that future moves will also be acceptable if
they remain within the *rectangle* given on the widget. This can improve performance,
but may also be ignored by the underlying system.

If the rectangle is empty, drag move events will be sent continuously. This is useful if
the source is scrolling in a timer event.

PythonQt.Qt.QDropEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

When a widget [accepts drop
events](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#acceptDrops-prop), it will
receive this event if it has accepted the most recent
[QDragEnterEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragenterevent.html) or
[QDragMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdragmoveevent.html) sent to it.

The drop event contains a proposed action, available from
[proposedAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#proposedAction)(),
for the widget to either accept or ignore. If the action can be handled by the widget,
you should call the
[acceptProposedAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#acceptProposedAction)()
function. Since the proposed action can be a combination of
[Qt::DropAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DropAction-enum) values, it
may be useful to either select one of these values as a default action or ask the user
to select their preferred action.

If the proposed drop action is not suitable, perhaps because your custom widget does not
support that action, you can replace it with any of the [possible drop
actions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#possibleActions) by calling
[setDropAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#setDropAction)() with
your preferred action. If you set a value that is not present in the bitwise OR
combination of values returned by
[possibleActions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#possibleActions)(),
the default copy action will be used. Once a replacement drop action has been set, call
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)() instead of
[acceptProposedAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#acceptProposedAction)()
to complete the drop operation.

The [mimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdropevent.html#mimeData)() function
provides the data dropped on the widget in a
[QMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html) object. This contains
information about the MIME type of the data in addition to the data itself.

PythonQt.Qt.QEasingCurve.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Easing curves describe a function that controls how the speed of the interpolation
between 0 and 1 should be. Easing curves allow transitions from one value to another to
appear more natural than a simple constant speed would allow. The QEasingCurve class is
usually used in conjunction with the
[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) and
[QPropertyAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpropertyanimation.html) classes
but can be used on its own. It is usually used to accelerate the interpolation from zero
velocity (ease in) or decelerate to zero velocity (ease out). Ease in and ease out can
also be combined in the same easing curve.

To calculate the speed of the interpolation, the easing curve provides the function
[valueForProgress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#valueForProgress)(),
where the *progress* argument specifies the progress of the interpolation: 0 is the
start value of the interpolation, 1 is the end value of the interpolation. The returned
value is the effective progress of the interpolation. If the returned value is the same
as the input value for all input values the easing curve is a linear curve. This is the
default behaviour.

For example,

```
    QEasingCurve easing(QEasingCurve::InOutQuad);

    for (qreal t = 0.0; t < 1.0; t += 0.1)
        qWarning() << "Effective progress" << t << "is"
                   << easing.valueForProgress(t);
```

will print the effective progress of the interpolation between 0 and 1\.

When using a
[QPropertyAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpropertyanimation.html), the
associated easing curve will be used to control the progress of the interpolation
between startValue and endValue:

```
    QPropertyAnimation animation;
    animation.setStartValue(0);
    animation.setEndValue(1000);
    animation.setDuration(1000);
    animation.setEasingCurve(QEasingCurve::InOutQuad);
```

The ability to set an amplitude, overshoot, or period depends on the QEasingCurve type.
Amplitude access is available to curves that behave as springs such as elastic and
bounce curves. Changing the amplitude changes the height of the curve. Period access is
only available to elastic curves and setting a higher period slows the rate of bounce.
Only curves that have "boomerang" behaviors such as the
[InBack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum),
[OutBack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum),
[InOutBack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum), and
[OutInBack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum) have
overshoot settings. These curves will interpolate beyond the end points and return to
the end point, acting similar to a boomerang.

The [Easing Curves
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-animation-easing-example.html)
contains samples of QEasingCurve types and lets you change the curve settings.

### void QEasingCurve::addTCBSegment(const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \&*nextPoint*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *t*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *c*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *b*)

Adds a segment of a TCB bezier spline to define a custom easing curve. It is only
applicable if [type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#type)() is
[QEasingCurve::TCBSpline](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum).
The spline has to start explicitly at (0.0, 0.0) and has to end at (1.0, 1.0) to be a
valid easing curve. The tension *t* changes the length of the tangent vector. The
continuity *c* changes the sharpness in change between the tangents. The bias *b*
changes the direction of the tangent vector. *nextPoint* is the sample position. All
three parameters are valid between -1 and 1 and define the tangent of the control point.

and endpoint always have a bias of -1 and 1, since the outer tangent is not defined.

PythonQt.Qt.QElapsedTimer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QElapsedTimer class is usually used to quickly calculate how much time has elapsed
between two events. Its API is similar to that of
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html), so code that was using that can
be ported quickly to the new class.

However, unlike [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html), QElapsedTimer
tries to use monotonic clocks if possible. This means it's not possible to convert
QElapsedTimer objects to a human-readable time.

The typical use-case for the class is to determine how much time was spent in a slow
operation. The simplest example of such a case is for debugging purposes, as in the
following example:

```
    QElapsedTimer timer;
    timer.start();

    slowOperation1();

    qDebug() << "The slow operation took" << timer.elapsed() << "milliseconds";
```

In this example, the timer is started by a call to start() and the elapsed time is
calculated by the elapsed() function.

The time elapsed can also be used to recalculate the time available for another
operation, after the first one is complete. This is useful when the execution must
complete within a certain time period, but several steps are needed. The `waitFor`-type
functions in [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) and its
subclasses are good examples of such need. In that case, the code could be as follows:

```
void executeSlowOperations(int timeout)
{
    QElapsedTimer timer;
    timer.start();
    slowOperation1();

    int remainingTime = timeout - timer.elapsed();
    if (remainingTime > 0)
        slowOperation2(remainingTime);
}
```

Another use-case is to execute a certain operation for a specific timeslice. For this,
QElapsedTimer provides the hasExpired() convenience function, which can be used to
determine if a certain number of milliseconds has already elapsed:

```
void executeOperationsForTime(int ms)
{
    QElapsedTimer timer;
    timer.start();

    while (!timer.hasExpired(ms))
        slowOperation1();
}
```

It is often more convenient to use
[QDeadlineTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdeadlinetimer.html) in this case,
which counts towards a timeout in the future instead of tracking elapsed time.

### Reference Clocks

QElapsedTimer will use the platform's monotonic reference clock in all platforms that
support it (see QElapsedTimer::isMonotonic()). This has the added benefit that
QElapsedTimer is immune to time adjustments, such as the user correcting the time. Also
unlike [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html), QElapsedTimer is immune
to changes in the timezone settings, such as daylight-saving periods.

On the other hand, this means QElapsedTimer values can only be compared with other
values that use the same reference. This is especially true if the time since the
reference is extracted from the QElapsedTimer object
(QElapsedTimer::msecsSinceReference()) and serialised. These values should never be
exchanged across the network or saved to disk, since there's no telling whether the
computer node receiving the data is the same as the one originating it or if it has
rebooted since.

It is, however, possible to exchange the value with other processes running on the same
machine, provided that they also use the same reference clock. QElapsedTimer will always
use the same clock, so it's safe to compare with the value coming from another process
in the same machine. If comparing to values produced by other APIs, you should check
that the clock used is the same as QElapsedTimer (see QElapsedTimer::clockType()).

An error message widget consists of a text label and a checkbox. The checkbox lets the
user control whether the same error message will be displayed again in the future,
typically displaying the text, "Show this message again" translated into the appropriate
local language.

For production applications, the class can be used to display messages which the user
only needs to see once. To use QErrorMessage like this, you create the dialog in the
usual way, and show it by calling the
[showMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qerrormessage.html#showMessage)() slot
or connecting signals to it.

The static
[qtHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qerrormessage.html#qtHandler)() function
installs a message handler using
[qInstallMessageHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qInstallMessageHandler)()
and creates a QErrorMessage that displays
[qDebug](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qDebug)(),
[qWarning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qWarning)() and
[qFatal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qFatal)() messages. This is
most useful in environments where no console is available to display warnings and error
messages.

In both cases QErrorMessage will queue pending messages and display them in order, with
each new message being shown as soon as the user has accepted the previous message. Once
the user has specified that a message is not to be shown again it is automatically
skipped, and the dialog will show the next appropriate message in the queue.

The [Standard
Dialogs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-dialogs-standarddialogs-example.html)
example shows how to use QErrorMessage as well as other built-in Qt dialogs.

PythonQt.Qt.QEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt's main event loop
([QCoreApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)())
fetches native window system events from the event queue, translates them into QEvents,
and sends the translated events to
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)s.

In general, events come from the underlying window system
([spontaneous](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#spontaneous)() returns
`true`), but it is also possible to manually send events using
[QCoreApplication::sendEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendEvent)()
and
[QCoreApplication::postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#postEvent)()
([spontaneous](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#spontaneous)() returns
`false`).

[QObjects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) receive events by having
their [QObject::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#event)() function
called. The function can be reimplemented in subclasses to customize event handling and
add additional event types;
[QWidget::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)() is a notable
example. By default, events are dispatched to event handlers like
[QObject::timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent)() and
[QWidget::mouseMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseMoveEvent)().
[QObject::installEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#installEventFilter)()
allows an object to intercept events destined for another object.

The basic QEvent contains only an event type parameter and an "accept" flag. The accept
flag set with [accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)(), and
cleared with [ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)(). It is
set by default, but don't rely on this as subclasses may choose to clear it in their
constructor.

Subclasses of QEvent contain additional parameters that describe the particular event.

PythonQt.Qt.QEventLoop.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

At any time, you can create a QEventLoop object and call
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exec)() on it to start a local
event loop. From within the event loop, calling
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exit)() will force
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exec)() to return.

PythonQt.Qt.QEventLoop.exec.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QEventLoop::exec([QEventLoop::ProcessEventsFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum) *flags* \= AllEvents)

Enters the main event loop and waits until
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exit)() is called. Returns the
value that was passed to
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exit)().

If *flags* are specified, only events of the types allowed by the *flags* will be
processed.

It is necessary to call this function to start event handling. The main event loop
receives events from the window system and dispatches these to the application widgets.

Generally speaking, no user interaction can take place before calling exec(). As a
special case, modal widgets like
[QMessageBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html) can be used before
calling exec(), because modal widgets use their own local event loop.

To make your application perform idle processing (i.e. executing a special function
whenever there are no pending events), use a
[QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) with 0 timeout. More
sophisticated idle processing schemes can be achieved using
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#processEvents)().

**See also**
[QCoreApplication::quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)(),
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exit)(), and
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#processEvents)().

PythonQt.Qt.QEventLoop.exit.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QEventLoop::exit(int *returnCode* \= 0\)

Tells the event loop to exit with a return code.

After this function has been called, the event loop returns from the call to
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exec)(). The
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exec)() function returns
*returnCode*.

By convention, a *returnCode* of 0 means success, and any non-zero value indicates an
error.

Note that unlike the C library function of the same name, this function *does* return to
the caller \-- it is event processing that stops.

**See also**
[QCoreApplication::quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)(),
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#quit)(), and
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#exec)().

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QEventLoop::processEvents([QEventLoop::ProcessEventsFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum) *flags* \= ...)

Processes some pending events that match *flags*. Returns `true` if pending events were
handled; otherwise returns `false`.

This function is especially useful if you have a long running operation and want to show
its progress without allowing user input; i.e. by using the
[ExcludeUserInputEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum)
flag.

This function is simply a wrapper for
[QAbstractEventDispatcher::processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracteventdispatcher.html#processEvents)().
See the documentation for that function for details.

### void QEventLoop::processEvents([QEventLoop::ProcessEventsFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum) *flags*, int *maxTime*)

Process pending events that match *flags* for a maximum of *maxTime* milliseconds, or
until there are no more events to process, whichever is shorter. This function is
especially useful if you have a long running operation and want to show its progress
without allowing user input, i.e. by using the
[ExcludeUserInputEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum)
flag.

**Notes:**

- This function does not process events continuously; it returns after all available events are processed.
- Specifying the [WaitForMoreEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum) flag makes no sense and will be ignored.

## Detailed Description

Expose events are sent to windows when an area of the window is invalidated, for example
when window exposure in the windowing system changes.

A Window with a client area that is completely covered by another window, or is
otherwise not visible may be considered obscured by Qt and may in such cases not receive
expose events.

The event handler
[QWindow::exposeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#exposeEvent)()
receives expose events.

PythonQt.Qt.QFile.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QFile is an I/O device for reading and writing text and binary files and
[resources](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/resources.html). A QFile may be used by
itself or, more conveniently, with a
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) or
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html).

The file name is usually passed in the constructor, but it can be set at any time using
setFileName(). QFile expects the file separator to be '/' regardless of operating
system. The use of other separators (e.g., '\\') is not supported.

You can check for a file's existence using exists(), and remove a file using remove().
(More advanced file system related operations are provided by
[QFileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html) and
[QDir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html).)

The file is opened with
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)(), closed with
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#close)(), and flushed with
[flush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#flush)(). Data is usually
read and written using
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) or
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html), but you can also
call the [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html)-inherited
functions [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(),
[readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readAll)(),
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)(). QFile also inherits
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(),
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)(), and
[ungetChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#ungetChar)(), which work
one character at a time.

The size of the file is returned by
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#size)(). You can get the
current file position using
[pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#pos)(), or move to a new file
position using [seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#seek)(). If
you've reached the end of the file,
[atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#atEnd)() returns `true`.

### Reading Files Directly

The following example reads a text file line by line:

```
    QFile file("in.txt");
    if (!file.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly | QIODevice::Text))
        return;

    while (!file.atEnd()) {
        QByteArray line = file.readLine();
        process_line(line);
    }
```

The
[QIODevice::Text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum)
flag passed to [open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)() tells Qt
to convert Windows-style line terminators ("\\r\\n") into C\+\+-style terminators
("\\n"). By default, QFile assumes binary, i.e. it doesn't perform any conversion on the
bytes stored in the file.

### Using Streams to Read Files

The next example uses [QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html)
to read a text file line by line:

```
    QFile file("in.txt");
    if (!file.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly | QIODevice::Text))
        return;

    QTextStream in(&file);
    while (!in.atEnd()) {
        QString line = in.readLine();
        process_line(line);
    }
```

[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) takes care of
converting the 8-bit data stored on disk into a 16-bit Unicode
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). By default, it assumes that
the user system's local 8-bit encoding is used (e.g., UTF-8 on most unix based operating
systems; see
[QTextCodec::codecForLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#codecForLocale)()
for details). This can be changed using
[QTextStream::setCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setCodec)().

To write text, we can use operator\<\<(), which is overloaded to take a
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) on the left and
various data types (including
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)) on the right:

```
    QFile file("out.txt");
    if (!file.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly | QIODevice::Text))
        return;

    QTextStream out(&file);
    out << "The magic number is: " << 49 << "\n";
```

[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) is similar, in that
you can use operator\<\<() to write data and operator\>\>() to read it back. See the
class documentation for details.

When you use QFile, [QFileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html), and
[QDir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html) to access the file system with Qt,
you can use Unicode file names. On Unix, these file names are converted to an 8-bit
encoding. If you want to use standard C\+\+ APIs (`<cstdio>` or `<iostream>`) or
platform-specific APIs to access files instead of QFile, you can use the
[encodeName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html#encodeName)() and
[decodeName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html#decodeName)() functions to
convert between Unicode file names and 8-bit file names.

On Unix, there are some special system files (e.g. in `/proc`) for which
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#size)() will always return 0,
yet you may still be able to read more data from such a file; the data is generated in
direct response to you calling
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(). In this case, however,
you cannot use [atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#atEnd)() to
determine if there is more data to read (since
[atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#atEnd)() will return true
for a file that claims to have size 0). Instead, you should either call
[readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readAll)(), or call
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() or
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() repeatedly
until no more data can be read. The next example uses
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) to read
`/proc/modules` line by line:

```
    QFile file("/proc/modules");
    if (!file.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly | QIODevice::Text))
        return;

    QTextStream in(&file);
    QString line = in.readLine();
    while (!line.isNull()) {
        process_line(line);
        line = in.readLine();
    }
```

### Signals

Unlike other [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html)
implementations, such as
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html), QFile does not emit
the [aboutToClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#aboutToClose)(),
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)(), or
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signals. This
implementation detail means that QFile is not suitable for reading and writing certain
types of files, such as device files on Unix platforms.

### Platform Specific Issues

File permissions are handled differently on Unix-like systems and Windows. In a non
[writable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isWritable) directory on
Unix-like systems, files cannot be created. This is not always the case on Windows,
where, for instance, the 'My Documents' directory usually is not writable, but it is
still possible to create files in it.

Qt's understanding of file permissions is limited, which affects especially the
[QFile::setPermissions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#setPermissions)()
function. On Windows, Qt will set only the legacy read-only flag, and that only when
none of the Write\* flags are passed. Qt does not manipulate access control lists
(ACLs), which makes this function mostly useless for NTFS volumes. It may still be of
use for USB sticks that use VFAT file systems. POSIX ACLs are not manipulated, either.

On Android, some limitations apply when dealing with [content
URIs](https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/providers/content-provider-basics#ContentURIs):

- Access permissions might be needed by prompting the user through the [QFileDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html) which implements Android's native file picker.
- Aim to follow the [Scoped storage](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage#scoped-storage) guidelines, such as using app specific directories instead of other public external directories. For more information, also see [storage best practices](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/use-cases).
- Due to the design of Qt APIs (e.g. QFile), it's not possible to fully integrate the latter APIs with Android's [MediaStore](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/provider/MediaStore) APIs.

## Detailed Description

QFileDevice is the base class for I/O devices that can read and write text and binary
files and [resources](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/resources.html).
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) offers the main functionality,
QFileDevice serves as a base class for sharing functionality with other file devices
such as [QTemporaryFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html), by
providing all the operations that can be done on files that have been opened by
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) or
[QTemporaryFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html).

### `[override virtual]` bool QFileDevice::atEnd() const

Reimplements:
[QIODevice::atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#atEnd)() const.

Returns `true` if the end of the file has been reached; otherwise returns false.

For regular empty files on Unix (e.g. those in `/proc`), this function returns `true`,
since the file system reports that the size of such a file is 0\. Therefore, you should
not depend on atEnd() when reading data from such a file, but rather call
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() until no more data can
be read.

for a map to succeed but the file does not need to stay open after the memory has been

PythonQt.Qt.QFileDevice.seek.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[override virtual]` bool QFileDevice::seek([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *pos*)

Reimplements:
[QIODevice::seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)(qint64 pos).

For random-access devices, this function sets the current position to *pos*, returning
true on success, or false if an error occurred. For sequential devices, the default
behavior is to do nothing and return false.

Seeking beyond the end of a file: If the position is beyond the end of a file, then
seek() will not immediately extend the file. If a write is performed at this position,
then the file will be extended. The content of the file between the previous end of file
and the newly written data is UNDEFINED and varies between platforms and file systems.
