PythonQt.Qt.QGLWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QGLWidget provides functionality for displaying OpenGL graphics integrated into a Qt
application. It is very simple to use. You inherit from it and use the subclass like any
other [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), except that you have
the choice between using [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html)
and standard OpenGL rendering commands.

**Note:** This class is part of the legacy [Qt
OpenGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtopengl-index.html) module and, like the
other `QGL` classes, should be avoided in the new applications. Instead, starting from
Qt 5.4, prefer using
[QOpenGLWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwidget.html) and the `QOpenGL`
classes.

QGLWidget provides three convenient virtual functions that you can reimplement in your
subclass to perform the typical OpenGL tasks:

- [paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)() \- Renders the OpenGL scene. Gets called whenever the widget needs to be updated.
- [resizeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeGL)() \- Sets up the OpenGL viewport, projection, etc. Gets called whenever the widget has been resized (and also when it is shown for the first time because all newly created widgets get a resize event automatically).
- [initializeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#initializeGL)() \- Sets up the OpenGL rendering context, defines display lists, etc. Gets called once before the first time [resizeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeGL)() or [paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)() is called.

Here is a rough outline of how a QGLWidget subclass might look:

```
class MyGLDrawer : public QGLWidget
{
    Q_OBJECT        // must include this if you use Qt signals/slots

public:
    MyGLDrawer(QWidget *parent)
        : QGLWidget(parent) {}

protected:

    void initializeGL() override
    {
        // Set up the rendering context, define display lists etc.:
        ...
        glClearColor(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
        glEnable(GL_DEPTH_TEST);
        ...
    }

    void resizeGL(int w, int h) override
    {
        // setup viewport, projection etc.:
        glViewport(0, 0, (GLint)w, (GLint)h);
        ...
        glFrustum(...);
        ...
    }

    void paintGL() override
    {
        // draw the scene:
        ...
        glRotatef(...);
        glMaterialfv(...);
        glBegin(GL_QUADS);
        glVertex3f(...);
        glVertex3f(...);
        ...
        glEnd();
        ...
    }

};
```

If you need to trigger a repaint from places other than
[paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)() (a typical
example is when using [timers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) to
animate scenes), you should call the widget's
[updateGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#updateGL)() function.

Your widget's OpenGL rendering context is made current when
[paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)(),
[resizeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeGL)(), or
[initializeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#initializeGL)() is
called. If you need to call the standard OpenGL API functions from other places (e.g. in
your widget's constructor or in your own paint functions), you must call
[makeCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#makeCurrent)() first.

QGLWidget provides functions for requesting a new display
[format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglformat.html) and you can also create
widgets with customized rendering
[contexts](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglcontext.html).

You can also share OpenGL display lists between QGLWidget objects (see the documentation
of the QGLWidget constructors for details).

Note that under Windows, the
[QGLContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglcontext.html) belonging to a
QGLWidget has to be recreated when the QGLWidget is reparented. This is necessary due to
limitations on the Windows platform. This will most likely cause problems for users that
have subclassed and installed their own
[QGLContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglcontext.html) on a QGLWidget. It is
possible to work around this issue by putting the QGLWidget inside a dummy widget and
then reparenting the dummy widget, instead of the QGLWidget. This will side-step the
issue altogether, and is what we recommend for users that need this kind of
functionality.

On macOS, when Qt is built with Cocoa support, a QGLWidget can't have any sibling
widgets placed ontop of itself. This is due to limitations in the Cocoa API and is not
supported by Apple.

### Overlays

The QGLWidget creates a GL overlay context in addition to the normal context if overlays
are supported by the underlying system.

If you want to use overlays, you specify it in the
[format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglformat.html). (Note: Overlay must be
requested in the format passed to the QGLWidget constructor.) Your GL widget should also
implement some or all of these virtual methods:

- [paintOverlayGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintOverlayGL)()
- [resizeOverlayGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeOverlayGL)()
- [initializeOverlayGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#initializeOverlayGL)()

These methods work in the same way as the normal
[paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)() etc. functions,
except that they will be called when the overlay context is made current. You can
explicitly make the overlay context current by using
[makeOverlayCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#makeOverlayCurrent)(),
and you can access the overlay context directly (e.g. to ask for its transparent color)
by calling
[overlayContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#overlayContext)().

On X servers in which the default visual is in an overlay plane, non-GL Qt windows can
also be used for overlays.

### Painting Techniques

As described above, subclass QGLWidget to render pure 3D content in the following way:

- Reimplement the [QGLWidget::initializeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#initializeGL)() and [QGLWidget::resizeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeGL)() to set up the OpenGL state and provide a perspective transformation.
- Reimplement [QGLWidget::paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)() to paint the 3D scene, calling only OpenGL functions to draw on the widget.

It is also possible to draw 2D graphics onto a QGLWidget subclass, it is necessary to
reimplement
[QGLWidget::paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintEvent)()
and do the following:

- Construct a [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) object.
- Initialize it for use on the widget with the [QPainter::begin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#begin)() function.
- Draw primitives using [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html)'s member functions.
- Call [QPainter::end](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#end)() to finish painting.

### Threading

As of Qt version 4.8, support for doing threaded GL rendering has been improved. There
are three scenarios that we currently support:

- 1\. Buffer swapping in a thread.

  Swapping buffers in a double buffered context may be a synchronous, locking call that
  may be a costly operation in some GL implementations. Especially so on embedded devices.
  It's not optimal to have the CPU idling while the GPU is doing a buffer swap. In those
  cases it is possible to do the rendering in the main thread and do the actual buffer
  swap in a separate thread. This can be done with the following steps:

  1\. Call [doneCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#doneCurrent)()
  in the main thread when the rendering is finished.

  2\. Call
  [QGLContext::moveToThread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglcontext.html#moveToThread)(swapThread)
  to transfer ownership of the context to the swapping thread.

  3\. Notify the swapping thread that it can grab the context.

  4\. Make the rendering context current in the swapping thread with
  [makeCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#makeCurrent)() and then
  call [swapBuffers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#swapBuffers)().

  5\. Call [doneCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#doneCurrent)()
  in the swapping thread.

  6\. Call
  [QGLContext::moveToThread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglcontext.html#moveToThread)([qApp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#qApp)-\>[thread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#thread)())
  and notify the main thread that swapping is done.

  Doing this will free up the main thread so that it can continue with, for example,
  handling UI events or network requests. Even if there is a context swap involved, it may
  be preferable compared to having the main thread wait while the GPU finishes the swap
  operation. Note that this is highly implementation dependent.
- 2\. Texture uploading in a thread.

  Doing texture uploads in a thread may be very useful for applications handling large
  amounts of images that needs to be displayed, like for instance a photo gallery
  application. This is supported in Qt through the existing
  [bindTexture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#bindTexture)() API. A
  simple way of doing this is to create two sharing QGLWidgets. One is made current in the
  main GUI thread, while the other is made current in the texture upload thread. The
  widget in the uploading thread is never shown, it is only used for sharing textures with
  the main thread. For each texture that is bound via
  [bindTexture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#bindTexture)(), notify
  the main thread so that it can start using the texture.
- 3\. Using [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) to draw into a QGLWidget in a thread.

  In Qt 4.8, it is possible to draw into a QGLWidget using a
  [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) in a separate thread. Note
  that this is also possible for QGLPixelBuffers and QGLFramebufferObjects. Since this is
  only supported in the GL 2 paint engine, OpenGL 2.0 or OpenGL ES 2.0 is required.

  QGLWidgets can only be created in the main GUI thread. This means a call to
  [doneCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#doneCurrent)() is
  necessary to release the GL context from the main thread, before the widget can be drawn
  into by another thread. You then need to call
  [QGLContext::moveToThread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglcontext.html#moveToThread)()
  to transfer ownership of the context to the thread in which you want to make it current.
  Also, the main GUI thread will dispatch resize and paint events to a QGLWidget when the
  widget is resized, or parts of it becomes exposed or needs redrawing. It is therefore
  necessary to handle those events because the default implementations inside QGLWidget
  will try to make the QGLWidget's context current, which again will interfere with any
  threads rendering into the widget. Reimplement
  [QGLWidget::paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintEvent)()
  and
  [QGLWidget::resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeEvent)()
  to notify the rendering thread that a resize or update is necessary, and be careful not
  to call the base class implementation. If you are rendering an animation, it might not
  be necessary to handle the paint event at all since the rendering thread is doing
  regular updates. Then it would be enough to reimplement
  [QGLWidget::paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintEvent)()
  to do nothing.

As a general rule when doing threaded rendering: be aware that binding and releasing
contexts in different threads have to be synchronized by the user. A GL rendering
context can only be current in one thread at any time. If you try to open a
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) on a QGLWidget and the
widget's rendering context is current in another thread, it will fail.

In addition to this, rendering using raw GL calls in a separate thread is supported.

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) QGLWidget::grabFrameBuffer(bool *withAlpha* \= false)

Returns an image of the frame buffer. If *withAlpha* is true the alpha channel is
included.

Depending on your hardware, you can explicitly select which color buffer to grab with a
glReadBuffer() call before calling this function.

On QNX the back buffer is not preserved when
[swapBuffers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#swapBuffers)() is
called. The back buffer where this function reads from, might thus not contain the same
content as the front buffer. In order to retrieve what is currently visible on the
screen, [swapBuffers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#swapBuffers)()
has to be executed prior to this function call.

[resizeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeGL)(), and then once
whenever the widget has been assigned a new QGLContext. Reimplement it in a subclass.

display lists, etc.

[makeCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#makeCurrent)() because

that it operates on the widget's overlay context instead of the widget's main context.
This means that initializeOverlayGL() is called once before the first call to
[paintOverlayGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintOverlayGL)() or
[resizeOverlayGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeOverlayGL)().

display lists, etc. for the overlay context.

[makeOverlayCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#makeOverlayCurrent)()
because this has already been done when this function is called.

PythonQt.Qt.QGLWidget.renderPixmap.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) QGLWidget::renderPixmap(int *w* \= 0, int *h* \= 0, bool *useContext* \= false)

Renders the current scene on a pixmap and returns the pixmap.

You can use this method on both visible and invisible
[QGLWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html) objects.

Internally the function renders into a framebuffer object and performs pixel readback.
This has a performance penalty, meaning that this function is not suitable to be called
at a high frequency.

After creating and binding the framebuffer object, the function will call
[initializeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#initializeGL)(),
[resizeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeGL)(), and
[paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)(). On the next
normal update
[initializeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#initializeGL)() and
[resizeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#resizeGL)() will be
triggered again since the size of the destination pixmap and the
[QGLWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html)'s size may differ.

The size of the pixmap will be *w* pixels wide and *h* pixels high unless one of these
parameters is 0 (the default), in which case the pixmap will have the same size as the
widget.

Care must be taken when using framebuffer objects in
[paintGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#paintGL)() in combination
with this function. To switch back to the default framebuffer, use
[QGLFramebufferObject::bindDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglframebufferobject.html#bindDefault)().
Binding FBO 0 is wrong since renderPixmap() uses a custom framebuffer instead of the one
provided by the windowing system.

*useContext* is ignored. Historically this parameter enabled the usage of the existing
GL context. This is not supported anymore since additional contexts are never created.

Overlays are not rendered onto the pixmap.

If the GL rendering context and the desktop have different bit depths, the result will
most likely look surprising.

Note that the creation of display lists, modifications of the view frustum etc. should
be done from within
[initializeGL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglwidget.html#initializeGL)(). If
this is not done, the temporary QGLContext will not be initialized properly, and the
rendered pixmap may be incomplete/corrupted.
signatures: renderPixmap(self, w: int=..., h: int=..., useContext: bool=...) -> PySide2.QtGui.QPixmap

*x* and *y* are specified in window coordinates, with the origin in the upper left-hand

**Note:** This function clears the stencil buffer.

**Note:** This function is not supported on OpenGL/ES systems.

**Note:** This function temporarily disables depth-testing when the text is drawn.

**Note:** This function can only be used inside a
[QPainter::beginNativePainting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#beginNativePainting)()/[QPainter::endNativePainting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#endNativePainting)()

PythonQt.Qt.QGesture.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Gesture objects are not constructed directly by developers. They are created by the
[QGestureRecognizer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html) object
that is registered with the application; see
[QGestureRecognizer::registerRecognizer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#registerRecognizer)().

For an overview of gesture handling in Qt and information on using gestures in your
applications, see the [Gestures in Widgets and Graphics
View](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/gestures-overview.html) document.

### Gesture Properties

The class has a list of properties that can be queried by the user to get some
gesture-specific arguments. For example, the pinch gesture has a scale factor that is
exposed as a property.

Developers of custom gesture recognizers can add additional properties in order to
provide additional information about a gesture. This can be done by adding new dynamic
properties to a QGesture object, or by subclassing the QGesture class (or one of its
subclasses).

### Lifecycle of a Gesture Object

A QGesture instance is implicitly created when needed and is owned by Qt. Developers
should never destroy them or store them for later use as Qt may destroy particular
instances of them and create new ones to replace them.

The registered gesture recognizer monitors the input events for the target object via
its [recognize()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)
function, updating the properties of the gesture object as required.

The gesture object may be delivered to the target object in a
[QGestureEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html) if the
corresponding gesture is active or has just been canceled. Each event that is delivered
contains a list of gesture objects, since support for more than one gesture may be
enabled for the target object. Due to the way events are handled in Qt, gesture events
may be filtered by other objects.

PythonQt.Qt.QGestureEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QGestureEvent class contains a list of gestures, which can be obtained using the
[gestures](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#gestures)() function.

The gestures are either active or canceled. A list of those that are currently being
executed can be obtained using the
[activeGestures](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#activeGestures)()
function. A list of those which were previously active and have been canceled can be
accessed using the
[canceledGestures](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#canceledGestures)()
function. A gesture might be canceled if the current window loses focus, for example, or
because of a timeout, or for other reasons.

If the event handler does not accept the event by calling the generic
[QEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)() function, all
individual [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object that were
not accepted and in the
[Qt::GestureStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GestureState-enum) state
will be propagated up the parent widget chain until a widget accepts them individually,
by calling
[QGestureEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#accept)()
for each of them, or an event filter consumes the event.

### Further Reading

For an overview of gesture handling in Qt and information on using gestures in your
applications, see the [Gestures in Widgets and Graphics
View](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/gestures-overview.html) document.

### void QGestureEvent::setAccepted([QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) \**gesture*, bool *value*)

Sets the accept flag of the given *gesture* object to the specified *value*.

Setting the accept flag indicates that the event receiver wants the *gesture*. Unwanted
gestures may be propagated to the parent widget.

By default, gestures in events of type
[QEvent::Gesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) are
accepted, and gestures in
[QEvent::GestureOverride](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Gesture recognizers are responsible for creating and managing
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) objects and monitoring
input events sent to [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html) subclasses.
QGestureRecognizer is the base class for implementing custom gestures.

Developers that only need to provide gesture recognition for standard gestures do not
need to use this class directly. Instances will be created behind the scenes by the
framework.

For an overview of gesture handling in Qt and information on using gestures in your
applications, see the [Gestures in Widgets and Graphics
View](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/gestures-overview.html) document.

### Recognizing Gestures

The process of recognizing gestures involves filtering input events sent to specific
objects, and modifying the associated
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) objects to include relevant
information about the user's input.

Gestures are created when the framework calls
[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#create)() to handle
user input for a particular instance of a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) or
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html) subclass. A
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object is created for each
widget or item that is configured to use gestures.

Once a [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) has been created for
a target object, the gesture recognizer will receive events for it in its
[recognize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)()
handler function.

When a gesture is canceled, the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#reset)() function is
called, giving the recognizer the chance to update the appropriate properties in the
corresponding [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object.

### Supporting New Gestures

To add support for new gestures, you need to derive from QGestureRecognizer to create a
custom recognizer class, construct an instance of this class, and register it with the
application by calling
[QGestureRecognizer::registerRecognizer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#registerRecognizer)().
You can also subclass [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) to
create a custom gesture class, or rely on dynamic properties to express specific details
of the gesture you want to handle.

Your custom QGestureRecognizer subclass needs to reimplement the
[recognize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)()
function to handle and filter the incoming input events for
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html) subclasses.
Although the logic for gesture recognition is implemented in this function, you can
store persistent information about the state of the recognition process in the
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object supplied. The
[recognize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)()
function must return a value of
[QGestureRecognizer::Result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#ResultFlag-enum)
that indicates the state of recognition for a given gesture and target object. This
determines whether or not a gesture event will be delivered to a target object.

If you choose to represent a gesture by a custom
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) subclass, you will need to
reimplement the
[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#create)() function
to construct instances of your gesture class. Similarly, you may need to reimplement the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#reset)() function if
your custom gesture objects need to be specially handled when a gesture is canceled.

PythonQt.Qt.QGlyphRun.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

When Qt displays a string of text encoded in Unicode, it will first convert the Unicode
points into a list of glyph indexes and a list of positions based on one or more fonts.
The Unicode representation of the text and the
[QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) object will in this case serve as
a convenient abstraction that hides the details of what actually takes place when
displaying the text on-screen. For instance, by the time the text actually reaches the
screen, it may be represented by a set of fonts in addition to the one specified by the
user, e.g. in case the originally selected font did not support all the writing systems
contained in the text.

Under certain circumstances, it can be useful as an application developer to have more
low-level control over which glyphs in a specific font are drawn to the screen. This
could for instance be the case in applications that use an external font engine and text
shaper together with Qt. QGlyphRun provides an interface to the raw data needed to get
text on the screen. It contains a list of glyph indexes, a position for each glyph and a
font.

It is the user's responsibility to ensure that the selected font actually contains the
provided glyph indexes.

[QTextLayout::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#glyphRuns)()
or
[QTextFragment::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextfragment.html#glyphRuns)()
can be used to convert unicode encoded text into a list of QGlyphRun objects, and
[QPainter::drawGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawGlyphRun)()
can be used to draw the glyphs.

**Note:** Please note that [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html)
is considered local to the thread in which it is constructed. This in turn means that a
new [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) will have to be created
and set on the QGlyphRun if it is moved to a different thread. If the QGlyphRun contains
a reference to a [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) from a
different thread than the current, it will not be possible to draw the glyphs using a
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html), as the
[QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) is considered invalid and
inaccessible in this case.

Qt 5 reference:

### void QGlyphRun::setBoundingRect(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*boundingRect*)

Sets the bounding rect of the glyphs in this
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html) to be *boundingRect*.
This rectangle will be returned by
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#boundingRect)() unless
it is empty, in which case the bounding rectangle of the glyphs in the glyph run will be
returned instead.

**Note:** Unless you are implementing text shaping, you should not have to use this
function. It is used specifically when the
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html) should represent an area
which is smaller than the area of the glyphs it contains. This could happen e.g. if the
glyph run is retrieved by calling
[QTextLayout::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#glyphRuns)()
and the specified range only includes part of a ligature (where two or more characters
are combined to a single glyph.) When this is the case, the bounding rect should only
include the appropriate part of the ligature glyph, based on a calculation of the
average width of the characters in the ligature.

In order to support such a case (an example is selections which should be drawn with a
different color than the main text color), it is necessary to clip the painting
mechanism to the rectangle returned from
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#boundingRect)() to
avoid drawing the entire ligature glyph.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#boundingRect)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt currently supports three types of gradient fills:

- *Linear* gradients interpolate colors between start and end points.
- *Simple* radial gradients interpolate colors between a focal point and end points on a circle surrounding it.
- *Extended* radial gradients interpolate colors between a center and a focal circle.
- *Conical* gradients interpolate colors around a center point.

A gradient's type can be retrieved using the
[type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#type)() function. Each of the
types is represented by a subclass of QGradient:

| [QLinearGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineargradient.html) | [QRadialGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html) | [QConicalGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qconicalgradient.html) |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |

The colors in a gradient are defined using stop points of the
[QGradientStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#QGradientStop-typedef)
type; i.e., a position and a color. Use the
[setColorAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setColorAt)() function to
define a single stop point. Alternatively, use the
[setStops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setStops)() function to
define several stop points in one go. Note that the latter function *replaces* the
current set of stop points.

It is the gradient's complete set of stop points (accessible through the
[stops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#stops)() function) that
describes how the gradient area should be filled. If no stop points have been specified,
a gradient of black at 0 to white at 1 is used.

A diagonal linear gradient from black at (100, 100\) to white at (200, 200\) could be
specified like this:

```
    QLinearGradient linearGrad(QPointF(100, 100), QPointF(200, 200));
    linearGrad.setColorAt(0, Qt::black);
    linearGrad.setColorAt(1, Qt::white);
```

A gradient can have an arbitrary number of stop points. The following would create a
radial gradient starting with red in the center, blue and then green on the edges:

```
    QRadialGradient radialGrad(QPointF(100, 100), 100);
    radialGrad.setColorAt(0, Qt::red);
    radialGrad.setColorAt(0.5, Qt::blue);
    radialGrad.setColorAt(1, Qt::green);
```

It is possible to repeat or reflect the gradient outside its area by specifiying the
[spread method](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) using the
[setSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setSpread)() function. The
default is to pad the outside area with the color at the closest stop point. The
currently set [spread
method](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) can be retrieved
using the [spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#spread)() function.
The [QGradient::Spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum)
enum defines three different methods:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [PadSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) | [RepeatSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) | [ReflectSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) |

Note that the [setSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setSpread)()
function only has effect for linear and radial gradients. The reason is that the conical
gradient is closed by definition, i.e. the *conical* gradient fills the entire circle
from 0 \- 360 degrees, while the boundary of a radial or a linear gradient can be
specified through its radius or final stop points, respectively.

The gradient coordinates can be specified in logical coordinates, relative to device
coordinates, or relative to object bounding box coordinates. The [coordinate
mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#CoordinateMode-enum) can be set
using the
[setCoordinateMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setCoordinateMode)()
function. The default is
[LogicalMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#CoordinateMode-enum),
where the gradient coordinates are specified in the same way as the object coordinates.
To retrieve the currently set [coordinate
mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#CoordinateMode-enum) use
[coordinateMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#coordinateMode)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The graphics anchor provides an API that enables you to query and manipulate the
properties an anchor has. When an anchor is added to the layout with
[QGraphicsAnchorLayout::addAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchor)(),
a QGraphicsAnchor instance is returned where the properties are initialized to their
default values. The properties can then be further changed, and they will be picked up
the next time the layout is activated.

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsAnchor.sizePolicy.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### sizePolicy : [QSizePolicy::Policy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum)

This property holds the size policy for the
[QGraphicsAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html).

By setting the size policy on an anchor you can configure how the anchor can resize
itself from its preferred spacing. For instance, if the anchor has the size policy
[QSizePolicy::Minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum),
the spacing is the minimum size of the anchor. However, its size can grow up to the
anchors maximum size. If the default size policy is
[QSizePolicy::Fixed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum),
the anchor can neither grow or shrink, which means that the only size the anchor can
have is the spacing.
[QSizePolicy::Fixed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum) is
the default size policy.
[QGraphicsAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html) always has a
minimum spacing of 0 and a very large maximum spacing.

**Access functions:**

| QSizePolicy::Policy | **sizePolicy**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setSizePolicy**(QSizePolicy::Policy *policy*) |

**See also**
[QGraphicsAnchor::spacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html#spacing-prop).

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsAnchorLayout.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The anchor layout allows developers to specify how widgets should be placed relative to
each other, and to the layout itself. The specification is made by adding anchors to the
layout by calling
[addAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchor)(),
[addAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchors)()
or
[addCornerAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addCornerAnchors)().

Existing anchors in the layout can be accessed with the
[anchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#anchor)()
function. Items that are anchored are automatically added to the layout, and if items
are removed, all their anchors will be automatically removed.

![Using an anchor layout to align simple colored
widgets.](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/simpleanchorlayout-example.png)

Anchors are always set up between edges of an item, where the "center" is also
considered to be an edge. Consider the following example:

```
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorLeft, a, Qt::AnchorRight);
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorTop, a, Qt::AnchorBottom);
```

Here, the right edge of item `a` is anchored to the left edge of item `b` and the bottom
edge of item `a` is anchored to the top edge of item `b`, with the result that item `b`
will be placed diagonally to the right and below item `b`.

The
[addCornerAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addCornerAnchors)()
function provides a simpler way of anchoring the corners of two widgets than the two
individual calls to
[addAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchor)()
shown in the code above. Here, we see how a widget can be anchored to the top-left
corner of the enclosing layout:

```
layout->addCornerAnchors(a, Qt::TopLeftCorner, layout, Qt::TopLeftCorner);
```

In cases where anchors are used to match the widths or heights of widgets, it is
convenient to use the
[addAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchors)()
function. As with the other functions for specifying anchors, it can also be used to
anchor a widget to a layout.

### Size Hints and Size Policies in an Anchor Layout

QGraphicsAnchorLayout respects each item's size hints and size policies. Note that there
are some properties of
[QSizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html) that are [not
respected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#known-issues).

### Spacing within an Anchor Layout

The layout may distribute some space between the items. If the spacing has not been
explicitly specified, the actual amount of space will usually be 0\.

However, if the first edge is the *opposite* of the second edge (e.g., the right edge of
the first widget is anchored to the left edge of the second widget), the size of the
anchor will be queried from the style through a pixel metric:
[PM\_LayoutHorizontalSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PixelMetric-enum)
for horizontal anchors and
[PM\_LayoutVerticalSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PixelMetric-enum)
for vertical anchors.

If the spacing is negative, the items will overlap to some extent.

### Known Issues

There are some features that QGraphicsAnchorLayout currently does not support. This
might change in the future, so avoid using these features if you want to avoid any
future regressions in behaviour:

- Stretch factors are not respected.
- [QSizePolicy::ExpandFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#PolicyFlag-enum) is not respected.
- Height for width is not respected.

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsAnchorLayout.addAnc.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QGraphicsAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html) \*QGraphicsAnchorLayout::addAnchor([QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**firstItem*, [Qt::AnchorPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AnchorPoint-enum) *firstEdge*, [QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**secondItem*, [Qt::AnchorPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AnchorPoint-enum) *secondEdge*)

Creates an anchor between the edge *firstEdge* of item *firstItem* and the edge
*secondEdge* of item *secondItem*. The spacing of the anchor is picked up from the
style. Anchors between a layout edge and an item edge will have a size of 0\. If there
is already an anchor between the edges, the new anchor will replace the old one.

*firstItem* and *secondItem* are automatically added to the layout if they are not part
of the layout. This means that
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#count)() can
increase by up to 2\.

The spacing an anchor will get depends on the type of anchor. For instance, anchors from
the Right edge of one item to the Left edge of another (or vice versa) will use the
default horizontal spacing. The same behaviour applies to Bottom to Top anchors, (but
they will use the default vertical spacing). For all other anchor combinations, the
spacing will be 0\. All anchoring functions will follow this rule.

The spacing can also be set manually by using
[QGraphicsAnchor::setSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html#spacing-prop)()
method.

Calling this function where *firstItem* or *secondItem* are ancestors of the layout have
undefined behaviour.

**See also**
[addAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchors)()
and
[addCornerAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addCornerAnchors)().

### void QGraphicsAnchorLayout::addAnchors([QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**firstItem*, [QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**secondItem*, [Qt::Orientations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) *orientations* \= ...)

Anchors two or four edges of *firstItem* with the corresponding edges of *secondItem*,
so that *firstItem* has the same size as *secondItem* in the dimensions specified by
*orientations*.

For example, the following example anchors the left and right edges of two items to
match their widths:

```
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorLeft, c, Qt::AnchorLeft);
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorRight, c, Qt::AnchorRight);
```

This can also be achieved using the following line of code:

```
layout->addAnchors(b, c, Qt::Horizontal);
```

### void QGraphicsAnchorLayout::addCornerAnchors([QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**firstItem*, [Qt::Corner](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Corner-enum) *firstCorner*, [QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**secondItem*, [Qt::Corner](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Corner-enum) *secondCorner*)

Creates two anchors between *firstItem* and *secondItem* specified by the corners,
*firstCorner* and *secondCorner*, where one is for the horizontal edge and another one
for the vertical edge.

This is a convenience function, since anchoring corners can be expressed as anchoring
two edges. For instance:

```
layout->addAnchor(a, Qt::AnchorTop, layout, Qt::AnchorTop);
layout->addAnchor(a, Qt::AnchorLeft, layout, Qt::AnchorLeft);
```

This can also be achieved with the following line of code:

```
layout->addCornerAnchors(a, Qt::TopLeftCorner, layout, Qt::TopLeftCorner);
```

If there is already an anchor between the edge pairs, it will be replaced by the anchors
that this function specifies.

*firstItem* and *secondItem* are automatically added to the layout if they are not part
of the layout. This means that
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#count)() can
increase by up to 2\.

**See also**
[addAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchor)()
and
[addAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchors)().

## Detailed Description

A blur effect blurs the source. This effect is useful for reducing details, such as when
the source loses focus and you want to draw attention to other elements. The level of
detail can be modified using the
[setBlurRadius](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#blurRadius-prop)()
function. Use
[setBlurHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#blurHints-prop)()
to choose the blur hints.

By default, the blur radius is 5 pixels. The blur radius is specified in device
coordinates.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicseffect-blur.png)

## Detailed Description

A drop shadow effect renders the source with a drop shadow. The color of the drop shadow
can be modified using the
[setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html#color-prop)()
function. The drop shadow offset can be modified using the
[setOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html#offset-prop)()
function and the blur radius of the drop shadow can be changed with the
[setBlurRadius](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html#blurRadius-prop)()
function.

By default, the drop shadow is a semi-transparent dark gray
([QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html)(63, 63, 63, 180)) shadow,
blurred with a radius of 1 at an offset of 8 pixels towards the lower right. The drop
shadow offset is specified in device coordinates.

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsEffect.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Effects alter the appearance of elements by hooking into the rendering pipeline and
operating between the source (e.g., a
[QGraphicsPixmapItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html)) and
the destination device (e.g.,
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html)'s viewport).
Effects can be disabled by calling
[setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#enabled-prop)(false).
If effects are disabled, the source is rendered directly.

To add a visual effect to a
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html), for example, you
can use one of the standard effects, or alternately, create your own effect by creating
a subclass of QGraphicsEffect. The effect can then be installed on the item using
[QGraphicsItem::setGraphicsEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setGraphicsEffect)().

Qt provides the following standard effects:

- [QGraphicsBlurEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html) \- blurs the item by a given radius
- [QGraphicsDropShadowEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html) \- renders a dropshadow behind the item
- [QGraphicsColorizeEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicscolorizeeffect.html) \- renders the item in shades of any given color
- [QGraphicsOpacityEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsopacityeffect.html) \- renders the item with an opacity

|  | |
| --- | --- |
|  |  |
|  |  |

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicseffect-widget.png)

For more information on how to use each effect, refer to the specific effect's
documentation.

To create your own custom effect, create a subclass of QGraphicsEffect (or any other
existing effects) and reimplement the virtual function
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)(). This function is
called whenever the effect needs to redraw. The
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)() function takes
the painter with which to draw as an argument. For more information, refer to the
documentation for
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)(). In the
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)() function you can
call
[sourcePixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#sourcePixmap)()
to get a pixmap of the graphics effect source which you can then process.

If your effect changes, use
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#update)() to request
for a redraw. If your custom effect changes the bounding rectangle of the source, e.g.,
a radial glow effect may need to apply an extra margin, you can reimplement the virtual
[boundingRectFor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#boundingRectFor)()
function, and call
[updateBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#updateBoundingRect)()
to notify the framework whenever this rectangle changes. The virtual
[sourceChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#sourceChanged)()
function is called to notify the effects that the source has changed in some way \-
e.g., if the source is a
[QGraphicsRectItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html) and its
rectangle parameters have changed.

### enabled : bool

This property holds whether the effect is enabled or not.

If an effect is disabled, the source will be rendered with as normal, with no
interference from the effect. If the effect is enabled, the source will be rendered with
the effect applied.

This property is enabled by default.

Using this property, you can disable certain effects on slow platforms, in order to
ensure that the user interface is responsive.

## Detailed Description

QGraphicsEllipseItem respresents an ellipse with a fill and an outline, and you can also
use it for ellipse segments (see
[startAngle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#startAngle)(),
[spanAngle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#spanAngle)()).

|  |  |
| --- | --- |

To set the item's ellipse, pass a
[QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) to QGraphicsEllipseItem's
constructor, or call
[setRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#setRect)(). The
[rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#rect)() function
returns the current ellipse geometry.

QGraphicsEllipseItem uses the rect and the pen width to provide a reasonable
implementation of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#boundingRect)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#shape)(), and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#contains)(). The
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#paint)() function
draws the ellipse using the item's associated pen and brush, which you can set by
calling
[setPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setPen)()
and
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setBrush)().

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsGridLayout.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The most common way to use QGraphicsGridLayout is to construct an object on the heap
with no parent, add widgets and layouts by calling
[addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#addItem)(), and
finally assign the layout to a widget by calling
[QGraphicsWidget::setLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#setLayout)().
QGraphicsGridLayout automatically computes the dimensions of the grid as you add items.

```
QGraphicsScene scene;
QGraphicsWidget *textEdit = scene.addWidget(new QTextEdit);
QGraphicsWidget *pushButton = scene.addWidget(new QPushButton);

QGraphicsGridLayout *layout = new QGraphicsGridLayout;
layout->addItem(textEdit, 0, 0);
layout->addItem(pushButton, 0, 1);

QGraphicsWidget *form = new QGraphicsWidget;
form->setLayout(layout);
scene.addItem(form);
```

The layout takes ownership of the items. In some cases when the layout item also
inherits from [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html)
(such as
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget))
there will be a ambiguity in ownership because the layout item belongs to two ownership
hierarchies. See the documentation of
[QGraphicsLayoutItem::setOwnedByLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setOwnedByLayout)()
how to handle this. You can access each item in the layout by calling
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#count)() and
[itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#itemAt)(). Calling
[removeAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#removeAt)() will
remove an item from the layout, without destroying it.

### Size Hints and Size Policies in QGraphicsGridLayout

QGraphicsGridLayout respects each item's size hints and size policies, and when a cell
in the grid has more space than the items can fill, each item is arranged according to
the layout's alignment for that item. You can set an alignment for each item by calling
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#setAlignment)(),
and check the alignment for any item by calling
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#alignment)().
You can also set the alignment for an entire row or column by calling
[setRowAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#setRowAlignment)()
and
[setColumnAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#setColumnAlignment)()
respectively. By default, items are aligned to the top left.

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsItem.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It provides a light-weight foundation for writing your own custom items. This includes
defining the item's geometry, collision detection, its painting implementation and item
interaction through its event handlers. QGraphicsItem is part of the [Graphics View
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html)

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-items.png)

For convenience, Qt provides a set of standard graphics items for the most common
shapes. These are:

- [QGraphicsEllipseItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html) provides an ellipse item
- [QGraphicsLineItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslineitem.html) provides a line item
- [QGraphicsPathItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspathitem.html) provides an arbitrary path item
- [QGraphicsPixmapItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html) provides a pixmap item
- [QGraphicsPolygonItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html) provides a polygon item
- [QGraphicsRectItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html) provides a rectangular item
- [QGraphicsSimpleTextItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicssimpletextitem.html) provides a simple text label item
- [QGraphicsTextItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicstextitem.html) provides an advanced text browser item

All of an item's geometric information is based on its local coordinate system. The
item's position, [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#pos)(), is
the only function that does not operate in local coordinates, as it returns a position
in parent coordinates. [The Graphics View Coordinate
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#the-graphics-view-coordinate-system)
describes the coordinate system in detail.

You can set whether an item should be visible (i.e., drawn, and accepting events), by
calling
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setVisible)(). Hiding
an item will also hide its children. Similarly, you can enable or disable an item by
calling
[setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setEnabled)(). If you
disable an item, all its children will also be disabled. By default, items are both
visible and enabled. To toggle whether an item is selected or not, first enable
selection by setting the
[ItemIsSelectable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flag, and then call
[setSelected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setSelected)().
Normally, selection is toggled by the scene, as a result of user interaction.

To write your own graphics item, you first create a subclass of QGraphicsItem, and then
start by implementing its two pure virtual public functions:
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)(),
which returns an estimate of the area painted by the item, and
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)(), which implements
the actual painting. For example:

```
class SimpleItem : public QGraphicsItem
{
public:
    QRectF boundingRect() const override
    {
        qreal penWidth = 1;
        return QRectF(-10 - penWidth / 2, -10 - penWidth / 2,
                      20 + penWidth, 20 + penWidth);
    }

    void paint(QPainter *painter, const QStyleOptionGraphicsItem *option,
               QWidget *widget) override
    {
        painter->drawRoundedRect(-10, -10, 20, 20, 5, 5);
    }
};
```

The [boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)()
function has many different purposes.
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) bases its item
index on
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)(),
and [QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) uses it both
for culling invisible items, and for determining the area that needs to be recomposed
when drawing overlapping items. In addition, QGraphicsItem's collision detection
mechanisms use
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() to
provide an efficient cut-off. The fine grained collision algorithm in
[collidesWithItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#collidesWithItem)()
is based on calling
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)(), which returns an
accurate outline of the item's shape as a
[QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html).

[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) expects all
items
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() and
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)() to remain
unchanged unless it is notified. If you want to change an item's geometry in any way,
you must first call
[prepareGeometryChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#prepareGeometryChange)()
to allow [QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) to
update its bookkeeping.

Collision detection can be done in two ways:

1. Reimplement [shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)() to return an accurate shape for your item, and rely on the default implementation of [collidesWithItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#collidesWithItem)() to do shape-shape intersection. This can be rather expensive if the shapes are complex.
2. Reimplement [collidesWithItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#collidesWithItem)() to provide your own custom item and shape collision algorithm.

The [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)()
function can be called to determine whether the item *contains* a point or not. This
function can also be reimplemented by the item. The default behavior of
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)() is based on
calling [shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)().

Items can contain other items, and also be contained by other items. All items can have
a parent item and a list of children. Unless the item has no parent, its position is in
*parent* coordinates (i.e., the parent's local coordinates). Parent items propagate both
their position and their transformation to all children.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-parentchild.png)

### Transformations

QGraphicsItem supports projective transformations in addition to its base position,
[pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#pos)(). There are several
ways to change an item's transformation. For simple transformations, you can call either
of the convenience functions
[setRotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setRotation)() or
[setScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setScale)(), or you can
pass any transformation matrix to
[setTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransform)().
For advanced transformation control you also have the option of setting several combined
transformations by calling
[setTransformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransformations)().

Item transformations accumulate from parent to child, so if both a parent and child item
are rotated 90 degrees, the child's total transformation will be 180 degrees. Similarly,
if the item's parent is scaled to 2x its original size, its children will also be twice
as large. An item's transformation does not affect its own local geometry; all geometry
functions (e.g.,
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)(),
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)(), and all the
mapping functions) still operate in local coordinates. For convenience, QGraphicsItem
provides the functions
[sceneTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneTransform)(),
which returns the item's total transformation matrix (including its position and all
parents' positions and transformations), and
[scenePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scenePos)(), which
returns its position in scene coordinates. To reset an item's matrix, call
[resetTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#resetTransform)().

Certain transformation operations produce a different outcome depending on the order in
which they are applied. For example, if you scale an transform, and then rotate it, you
may get a different result than if the transform was rotated first. However, the order
you set the transformation properties on QGraphicsItem does not affect the resulting
transformation; QGraphicsItem always applies the properties in a fixed, defined order:

- The item's base transform is applied ([transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)())
- The item's transformations list is applied in order ([transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations)())
- The item is rotated relative to its transform origin point ([rotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#rotation)(), [transformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformOriginPoint)())
- The item is scaled relative to its transform origin point ([scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scale-1)(), [transformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformOriginPoint)())

### Painting

The [paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() function is
called by [QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) to
paint the item's contents. The item has no background or default fill of its own;
whatever is behind the item will shine through all areas that are not explicitly painted
in this function. You can call
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)() to schedule a
repaint, optionally passing the rectangle that needs a repaint. Depending on whether or
not the item is visible in a view, the item may or may not be repainted; there is no
equivalent to
[QWidget::repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() in
QGraphicsItem.

Items are painted by the view, starting with the parent items and then drawing children,
in ascending stacking order. You can set an item's stacking order by calling
[setZValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setZValue)(), and test
it by calling [zValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#zValue)(),
where items with low z-values are painted before items with high z-values. Stacking
order applies to sibling items; parents are always drawn before their children.

### Sorting

All items are drawn in a defined, stable order, and this same order decides which items
will receive mouse input first when you click on the scene. Normally you don't have to
worry about sorting, as the items follow a "natural order", following the logical
structure of the scene.

An item's children are stacked on top of the parent, and sibling items are stacked by
insertion order (i.e., in the same order that they were either added to the scene, or
added to the same parent). If you add item A, and then B, then B will be on top of A. If
you then add C, the items' stacking order will be A, then B, then C.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-zorder.png)

This example shows the stacking order of all limbs of the robot from the [Drag and Drop
Robot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-graphicsview-dragdroprobot-example.html)
example. The torso is the root item (all other items are children or descendants of the
torso), so it is drawn first. Next, the head is drawn, as it is the first item in the
torso's list of children. Then the upper left arm is drawn. As the lower arm is a child
of the upper arm, the lower arm is then drawn, followed by the upper arm's next sibling,
which is the upper right arm, and so on.

For advanced users, there are ways to alter how your items are sorted:

- You can call [setZValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setZValue)() on an item to explicitly stack it on top of, or under, other sibling items. The default Z value for an item is 0\. Items with the same Z value are stacked by insertion order.
- You can call [stackBefore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#stackBefore)() to reorder the list of children. This will directly modify the insertion order.
- You can set the [ItemStacksBehindParent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum) flag to stack a child item behind its parent.

The stacking order of two sibling items also counts for each item's children and
descendant items. So if one item is on top of another, then all its children will also
be on top of all the other item's children as well.

### Events

QGraphicsItem receives events from
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) through the
virtual function
[sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)(). This
function distributes the most common events to a set of convenience event handlers:

- [contextMenuEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contextMenuEvent)() handles context menu events
- [focusInEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusInEvent)() and [focusOutEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusOutEvent)() handle focus in and out events
- [hoverEnterEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverEnterEvent)(), [hoverMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverMoveEvent)(), and [hoverLeaveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverLeaveEvent)() handles hover enter, move and leave events
- [inputMethodEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#inputMethodEvent)() handles input events, for accessibility support
- [keyPressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#keyPressEvent)() and [keyReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#keyReleaseEvent)() handle key press and release events
- [mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)(), [mouseMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseMoveEvent)(), [mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(), and [mouseDoubleClickEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseDoubleClickEvent)() handles mouse press, move, release, click and double-click events

You can filter events for any other item by installing event filters. This functionality
is separate from Qt's regular event filters (see
[QObject::installEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#installEventFilter)()),
which only work on subclasses of
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html). After installing your item
as an event filter for another item by calling
[installSceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#installSceneEventFilter)(),
the filtered events will be received by the virtual function
[sceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEventFilter)().
You can remove item event filters by calling
[removeSceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#removeSceneEventFilter)().

### Custom Data

Sometimes it's useful to register custom data with an item, be it a custom item, or a
standard item. You can call
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setData)() on any item
to store data in it using a key-value pair (the key being an integer, and the value is a
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)). To get custom data from
an item, call [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#data)(). This
functionality is completely untouched by Qt itself; it is provided for the user's
convenience.

### `[virtual]` void QGraphicsItem::advance(int *phase*)

This virtual function is called twice for all items by the
[QGraphicsScene::advance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#advance)()
slot. In the first phase, all items are called with *phase* \=\= 0, indicating that
items on the scene are about to advance, and then all items are called with *phase* \=\=

animation.

[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) and
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) and use the

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsItem.boundingRect.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual]` [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QGraphicsItem::boundingRect() const

This pure virtual function defines the outer bounds of the item as a rectangle; all
painting must be restricted to inside an item's bounding rect.
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) uses this to
determine whether the item requires redrawing.

Although the item's shape can be arbitrary, the bounding rect is always rectangular, and
it is unaffected by the items' transformation.

If you want to change the item's bounding rectangle, you must first call
[prepareGeometryChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#prepareGeometryChange)().
This notifies the scene of the imminent change, so that it can update its item geometry
index; otherwise, the scene will be unaware of the item's new geometry, and the results
are undefined (typically, rendering artifacts are left within the view).

Reimplement this function to let
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) determine what
parts of the widget, if any, need to be redrawn.

Note: For shapes that paint an outline / stroke, it is important to include half the pen
width in the bounding rect. It is not necessary to compensate for antialiasing, though.

Example:

```
QRectF CircleItem::boundingRect() const
{
    qreal penWidth = 1;
    return QRectF(-radius - penWidth / 2, -radius - penWidth / 2,
                  diameter + penWidth, diameter + penWidth);
}
```

**See also**
[boundingRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRegion)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)(),
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)(), [The
Graphics View Coordinate
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#the-graphics-view-coordinate-system),
and
[prepareGeometryChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#prepareGeometryChange)().

PythonQt.Qt.QGraphicsItem.boundingRegion.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) QGraphicsItem::boundingRegion(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*itemToDeviceTransform*) const

Returns the bounding region for this item. The coordinate space of the returned region
depends on *itemToDeviceTransform*. If you pass an identity
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) as a parameter, this
function will return a local coordinate region.

The bounding region describes a coarse outline of the item's visual contents. Although
it's expensive to calculate, it's also more precise than
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)(),
and it can help to avoid unnecessary repainting when an item is updated. This is
particularly efficient for thin items (e.g., lines or simple polygons). You can tune the
granularity for the bounding region by calling
[setBoundingRegionGranularity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setBoundingRegionGranularity)().
The default granularity is 0; in which the item's bounding region is the same as its
bounding rect.

*itemToDeviceTransform* is the transformation from item coordinates to device
coordinates. If you want this function to return a
[QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) in scene coordinates, you can
pass
[sceneTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneTransform)()
as an argument.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[boundingRegionGranularity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRegionGranularity)().

Qt 5 reference:

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QGraphicsItem::boundingRegionGranularity() const

Returns the item's bounding region granularity; a value between and including 0 and 1\.
The default value is 0 (i.e., the lowest granularity, where the bounding region
corresponds to the item's bounding rectangle).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[setBoundingRegionGranularity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setBoundingRegionGranularity)().

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QGraphicsItem::childrenBoundingRect() const

Returns the bounding rect of this item's descendants (i.e., its children, their
children, etc.) in local coordinates. The rectangle will contain all descendants after
they have been mapped to local coordinates. If the item has no children, this function
returns an empty [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html).

This does not include this item's own bounding rect; it only returns its descendants'
accumulated bounding rect. If you need to include this item's bounding rect, you can add
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() to
childrenBoundingRect() using QRectF::operator\|().

This function is linear in complexity; it determines the size of the returned bounding
rect by iterating through all descendants.

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() and
[sceneBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneBoundingRect)().
