### `[signal]` void QGuiApplication::commitDataRequest([QSessionManager](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html) \&*manager*)

This signal deals with [session
management](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/ipc.html#session-management). It is
emitted when the
[QSessionManager](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html) wants the
application to commit all its data.

Usually this means saving all open files, after getting permission from the user.
Furthermore you may want to provide a means by which the user can cancel the shutdown.

You should not exit the application within this signal. Instead, the session manager may
or may not do this afterwards, depending on the context.

**Warning:** Within this signal, no user interaction is possible, *unless* you ask the
*manager* for explicit permission. See
[QSessionManager::allowsInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsInteraction)()
and
[QSessionManager::allowsErrorInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsErrorInteraction)()
for details and example usage.

**Note:** You should use
[Qt::DirectConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ConnectionType-enum)
when connecting to this signal.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[setFallbackSessionManagementEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#setFallbackSessionManagementEnabled)(),
[isSessionRestored](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#isSessionRestored)(),
[sessionId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#sessionId)(),
[saveStateRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#saveStateRequest)(),
and [Session
Management](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/ipc.html#session-management).

### `[static]` int QGuiApplication::exec()

Enters the main event loop and waits until
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() is called, and
then returns the value that was set to
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() (which is 0 if
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() is called via
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)()).

It is necessary to call this function to start event handling. The main event loop
receives events from the window system and dispatches these to the application widgets.

Generally, no user interaction can take place before calling exec().

To make your application perform idle processing, e.g., executing a special function
whenever there are no pending events, use a
[QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) with 0 timeout. More advanced
idle processing schemes can be achieved using
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)().

We recommend that you connect clean-up code to the
[aboutToQuit()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#aboutToQuit)
signal, instead of putting it in your application's `main()` function. This is because,
on some platforms, the
[QApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#exec)() call
may not return.

**See also**
[quitOnLastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#quitOnLastWindowClosed-prop),
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)(),
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)(),
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)(),
and
[QCoreApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)().

PythonQt.Qt.QGuiApplication.isFallbackSe.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` bool QGuiApplication::isFallbackSessionManagementEnabled()

Returns whether
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) will use
fallback session management.

The default is `true`.

If this is `true` and the session manager allows user interaction,
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) will try to
close toplevel windows after
[commitDataRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#commitDataRequest)()
has been emitted. If a window cannot be closed, session shutdown will be canceled and
the application will keep running.

Fallback session management only benefits applications that have an "are you sure you
want to close this window?" feature or other logic that prevents closing a toplevel
window depending on certain conditions, and that do nothing to explicitly implement
session management. In applications that *do* implement session management using the
proper session management API, fallback session management interferes and may break
session management logic.

**Warning:** If all windows *are* closed due to fallback session management and
[quitOnLastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#quitOnLastWindowClosed-prop)()
is `true`, the application will quit before it is explicitly instructed to quit through
the platform's session management protocol. That violation of protocol may prevent the
platform session manager from saving application state.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.6.

**See also**
[setFallbackSessionManagementEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#setFallbackSessionManagementEnabled)(),
[QSessionManager::allowsInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsInteraction)(),
[saveStateRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#saveStateRequest)(),
[commitDataRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#commitDataRequest)(),
and [Session
Management](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/ipc.html#session-management).

### `[static]` [Qt::KeyboardModifiers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#KeyboardModifier-enum) QGuiApplication::keyboardModifiers()

Returns the current state of the modifier keys on the keyboard. The current state is
updated sychronously as the event queue is emptied of events that will spontaneously
change the keyboard state
([QEvent::KeyPress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and

Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html) \*QGuiApplication::modalWindow()

Returns the most recently shown modal window. If no modal windows are visible, this
function returns zero.

A modal window is a window which has its
[modality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#modality-prop) property set
to [Qt::WindowModal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowModality-enum) or
[Qt::ApplicationModal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowModality-enum).
A modal window must be closed before the user can continue with other parts of the
program.

Modal window are organized in a stack. This function returns the modal window at the top
of the stack.

**See also**
[Qt::WindowModality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowModality-enum) and
[QWindow::setModality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#modality-prop)().

Qt 5 reference:

### platformName : const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the name of the underlying platform plugin.

The QPA platform plugins are located in `qtbase\src\plugins\platforms`. At the time of
writing, the following platform plugin names are supported:

- `android`
- `cocoa` is a platform plugin for macOS.
- `directfb`
- `eglfs` is a platform plugin for running Qt5 applications on top of EGL and OpenGL ES 2.0 without an actual windowing system (like X11 or Wayland). For more information, see [EGLFS](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/vxworks.html#eglfs).
- `ios` (also used for tvOS)
- `kms` is an experimental platform plugin using kernel modesetting and [DRM](http://dri.freedesktop.org/wiki/DRM) (Direct Rendering Manager).
- `linuxfb` writes directly to the framebuffer. For more information, see [LinuxFB](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/embedded-linux.html#linuxfb).
- `minimal` is provided as an examples for developers who want to write their own platform plugins. However, you can use the plugin to run GUI applications in environments without a GUI, such as servers.
- `minimalegl` is an example plugin.
- `offscreen`
- `openwfd`
- `qnx`
- `windows`
- `wayland` is a platform plugin for modern Linux desktops and some embedded systems.
- `xcb` is the X11 plugin used on regular desktop Linux platforms.

For more information about the platform plugins for embedded Linux devices, see [Qt for
Embedded Linux](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/embedded-linux.html).

**Access functions:**

| --- | --- |

### `[static]` [Qt::KeyboardModifiers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#KeyboardModifier-enum) QGuiApplication::queryKeyboardModifiers()

Queries and returns the state of the modifier keys on the keyboard. Unlike
[keyboardModifiers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#keyboardModifiers),
this method returns the actual keys held on the input device at the time of calling the
method.

It does not rely on the keypress events having been received by this process, which
makes it possible to check the modifiers while moving a window, for instance. Note that
in most cases, you should use
[keyboardModifiers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#keyboardModifiers)(),
which is faster and more accurate since it contains the state of the modifiers as they
were when the currently processed event was received.

**See also**
[keyboardModifiers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#keyboardModifiers)().

PythonQt.Qt.QGuiApplication.saveStateReq.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QGuiApplication::saveStateRequest([QSessionManager](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html) \&*manager*)

This signal deals with [session
management](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/ipc.html#session-management). It is
invoked when the [session
manager](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html) wants the application
to preserve its state for a future session.

For example, a text editor would create a temporary file that includes the current
contents of its edit buffers, the location of the cursor and other aspects of the
current editing session.

You should never exit the application within this signal. Instead, the session manager
may or may not do this afterwards, depending on the context. Furthermore, most session
managers will very likely request a saved state immediately after the application has
been started. This permits the session manager to learn about the application's restart
policy.

**Warning:** Within this signal, no user interaction is possible, *unless* you ask the
*manager* for explicit permission. See
[QSessionManager::allowsInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsInteraction)()
and
[QSessionManager::allowsErrorInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsErrorInteraction)()
for details.

**Note:** You should use
[Qt::DirectConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ConnectionType-enum)
when connecting to this signal.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[isSessionRestored](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#isSessionRestored)(),
[sessionId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#sessionId)(),
[commitDataRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#commitDataRequest)(),
and [Session
Management](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/ipc.html#session-management).

### `[static]` void QGuiApplication::setDesktopSettingsAware(bool *on*)

Sets whether Qt should use the system's standard colors, fonts, etc., to *on*. By
default, this is `true`.

This function must be called before creating the

    QApplication app(argc, argv);

    return app.exec();
}
```

PythonQt.Qt.QGuiApplication.setOverrideC.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QGuiApplication::setOverrideCursor(const [QCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcursor.html) \&*cursor*)

Sets the application override cursor to *cursor*.

Application override cursors are intended for showing the user that the application is
in a special state, for example during an operation that might take some time.

This cursor will be displayed in all the application's widgets until
[restoreOverrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#restoreOverrideCursor)()
or another setOverrideCursor() is called.

Application cursors are stored on an internal stack. setOverrideCursor() pushes the
cursor onto the stack, and
[restoreOverrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#restoreOverrideCursor)()
pops the active cursor off the stack.
[changeOverrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#changeOverrideCursor)()
changes the curently active application override cursor.

Every setOverrideCursor() must eventually be followed by a corresponding
[restoreOverrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#restoreOverrideCursor)(),
otherwise the stack will never be emptied.

Example:

```
QGuiApplication::setOverrideCursor(QCursor(Qt::WaitCursor));
calculateHugeMandelbrot();              // lunch time...
QGuiApplication::restoreOverrideCursor();
```

**See also**
[overrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#overrideCursor)(),
[restoreOverrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#restoreOverrideCursor)(),
[changeOverrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#changeOverrideCursor)(),
and [QWidget::setCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#cursor-prop)().

### `[static]` void QGuiApplication::sync()

Function that can be used to sync Qt state with the Window Systems state.

This function will first empty Qts events by calling
[QCoreApplication::processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)(),
then the platform plugin will sync up with the windowsystem, and finally Qts events will
be delived by another call to
[QCoreApplication::processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)();

This function is timeconsuming and its use is discouraged.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

PythonQt.Qt.QHeaderView.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QHeaderView displays the headers used in item views such as the
[QTableView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html) and
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) classes. It takes the
place of Qt3's `QHeader` class previously used for the same purpose, but uses the Qt's
model/view architecture for consistency with the item view classes.

The QHeaderView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

The header gets the data for each section from the model using the
[QAbstractItemModel::headerData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#headerData)()
function. You can set the data by using
[QAbstractItemModel::setHeaderData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setHeaderData)().

Each header has an
[orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#orientation)() and a
number of sections, given by the
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#count)() function. A section
refers to a part of the header \- either a row or a column, depending on the
orientation.

Sections can be moved and resized using
[moveSection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#moveSection)() and
[resizeSection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#resizeSection)();
they can also be hidden and shown with
[hideSection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#hideSection)() and
[showSection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#showSection)().

Each section of a header is described by a section ID, specified by its section(), and
can be located at a particular
[visualIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#visualIndex)() in the
header. A section can have a sort indicator set with
[setSortIndicator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSortIndicator)();
this indicates whether the items in the associated item view will be sorted in the order
given by the section.

For a horizontal header the section is equivalent to a column in the model, and for a
vertical header the section is equivalent to a row in the model.

### Moving Header Sections

A header can be fixed in place, or made movable with
[setSectionsMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionsMovable)().
It can be made clickable with
[setSectionsClickable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionsClickable)(),
and has resizing behavior in accordance with
[setSectionResizeMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionResizeMode)().

**Note:** Double-clicking on a header to resize a section only applies for visible rows.

A header will emit
[sectionMoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#sectionMoved)() if
the user moves a section,
[sectionResized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#sectionResized)()
if the user resizes a section, and
[sectionClicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#sectionClicked)()
as well as
[sectionHandleDoubleClicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#sectionHandleDoubleClicked)()
in response to mouse clicks. A header will also emit
[sectionCountChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#sectionCountChanged)().

You can identify a section using the
[logicalIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#logicalIndex)() and
[logicalIndexAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#logicalIndexAt)()
functions, or by its index position, using the
[visualIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#visualIndex)() and
[visualIndexAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#visualIndexAt)()
functions. The visual index will change if a section is moved, but the logical index
will not change.

### Appearance

[QTableWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtablewidget.html) and
[QTableView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html) create default headers.
If you want the headers to be visible, you can use
[setVisible()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop).

Not all [ItemDataRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum)s
will have an effect on a QHeaderView. If you need to draw other roles, you can subclass
QHeaderView and reimplement
[paintEvent()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#paintEvent).
QHeaderView respects the following item data roles, unless they are in conflict with the
style (which can happen for styles that follow the desktop theme):

[TextAlignmentRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum),
[DisplayRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum),
[FontRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum),
[DecorationRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum),
[ForegroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum), and
[BackgroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum).

**Note:** Each header renders the data for each section itself, and does not rely on a
delegate. As a result, calling a header's
[setItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setItemDelegate)()
function will have no effect.

### firstSectionMovable : bool

This property holds whether the first column can be moved by the user

This property controls whether the first column can be moved by the user. In a
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html), the first column holds
the tree structure and is therefore non-movable by default, even after
[setSectionsMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionsMovable)(true).

It can be made movable again, for instance in the case of flat lists without a tree
structure, by calling this method. In such a scenario, it is recommended to call
[QTreeView::setRootIsDecorated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#rootIsDecorated-prop)(false)
as well.

Setting it to true has no effect unless
[setSectionsMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionsMovable)(true)
is called as well.

This property was introduced in Qt 5.11.

**Access functions:**

| bool | **isFirstSectionMovable**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setFirstSectionMovable**(bool *movable*) |

**See also**
[setSectionsMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionsMovable)().

PythonQt.Qt.QHeaderView.setResizeContent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QHeaderView::setResizeContentsPrecision(int *precision*)

Sets how precise [QHeaderView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html)
should calculate the size when
[ResizeToContents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#ResizeMode-enum)
is used. A low value will provide a less accurate but fast auto resize while a higher
value will provide a more accurate resize that however can be slow.

The number *precision* specifies how many sections that should be consider when
calculating the preferred size.

The default value is 1000 meaning that a horizontal column with auto-resize will look at
maximum 1000 rows on calculating when doing an auto resize.

Special value 0 means that it will look at only the visible area. Special value -1 will
imply looking at all elements.

This value is used in
[QTableView::sizeHintForColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#sizeHintForColumn)(),
[QTableView::sizeHintForRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#sizeHintForRow)()
and
[QTreeView::sizeHintForColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#sizeHintForColumn)().
Reimplementing these functions can make this function not having an effect.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

**See also**
[resizeContentsPrecision](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#resizeContentsPrecision)(),
[setSectionResizeMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionResizeMode)(),
[resizeSections](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#resizeSections-1)(),
[QTableView::sizeHintForColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#sizeHintForColumn)(),
[QTableView::sizeHintForRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#sizeHintForRow)(),
and
[QTreeView::sizeHintForColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#sizeHintForColumn)().

PythonQt.Qt.QHideEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This event is sent just before
[QWidget::hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)() returns, and
also when a top-level window has been hidden (iconified) by the user.

If [spontaneous](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#spontaneous)() is true,
the event originated outside the application. In this case, the user hid the window
using the window manager controls, either by iconifying the window or by switching to
another virtual desktop where the window is not visible. The window will become hidden
but not withdrawn. If the window was iconified,
[QWidget::isMinimized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimized-prop)()
returns `true`.

PythonQt.Qt.QHostAddress.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class holds an IPv4 or IPv6 address in a platform- and protocol-independent manner.

QHostAddress is normally used with the
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html),
[QTcpServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpserver.html), and
[QUdpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html) to connect to a host or
to set up a server.

A host address is set with
[setAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#setAddress)(), and
retrieved with
[toIPv4Address](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#toIPv4Address)(),
[toIPv6Address](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#toIPv6Address)(),
or [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#toString)(). You can
check the type with
[protocol](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#protocol)().

**Note:** Please note that QHostAddress does not do DNS lookups.
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) is needed for that.

The class also supports common predefined addresses:
[Null](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#SpecialAddress-enum),
[LocalHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#SpecialAddress-enum),
[LocalHostIPv6](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#SpecialAddress-enum),
[Broadcast](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#SpecialAddress-enum),
and [Any](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#SpecialAddress-enum).

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QHostAddress::isInSubnet(const [QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#QHostAddress) \&*subnet*, int *netmask*) const

Returns `true` if this IP is in the subnet described by the network prefix *subnet* and
netmask *netmask*.

An IP is considered to belong to a subnet if it is contained between the lowest and the
highest address in that subnet. In the case of IP version 4, the lowest address is the
network address, while the highest address is the broadcast address.

The *subnet* argument does not have to be the actual network address (the lowest address
in the subnet). It can be any valid IP belonging to that subnet. In particular, if it is
equal to the IP address held by this object, this function will always return true
(provided the netmask is a valid value).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also**
[parseSubnet](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#parseSubnet)().

### bool QHostAddress::isInSubnet(const [QPair](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpair.html)\<[QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#QHostAddress), int\> \&*subnet*) const

This is an overloaded function.

Returns `true` if this IP is in the subnet described by *subnet*. The
[QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html) member of *subnet*
contains the network prefix and the int (second) member contains the netmask (prefix
length).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.
signatures: isInSubnet(self, subnet: PySide2.QtNetwork.QHostAddress, netmask: int) -> bool

PythonQt.Qt.QHostAddress.parseSubnet.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QPair](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpair.html)\<[QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#QHostAddress), int\> QHostAddress::parseSubnet(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*subnet*)

Parses the IP and subnet information contained in *subnet* and returns the network
prefix for that network and its prefix length.

The IP address and the netmask must be separated by a slash (/).

This function supports arguments in the form:

- 123.123.123.123/n where n is any value between 0 and 32
- 123.123.123.123/255.255.255.255
- \<ipv6-address\>/n where n is any value between 0 and 128

For IP version 4, this function accepts as well missing trailing components (i.e., less
than 4 octets, like "192.168.1"), followed or not by a dot. If the netmask is also
missing in that case, it is set to the number of octets actually passed (in the example
above, it would be 24, for 3 octets).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also**
[isInSubnet](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#isInSubnet)().

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QHostAddress::scopeId() const

Returns the scope ID of an IPv6 address. For IPv4 addresses, or if the address does not
contain a scope ID, an empty [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)
is returned.

The IPv6 scope ID specifies the scope of *reachability* for non-global IPv6 addresses,
limiting the area in which the address can be used. All IPv6 addresses are associated
with such a reachability scope. The scope ID is used to disambiguate addresses that are
not guaranteed to be globally unique.

IPv6 specifies the following four levels of reachability:

- Node-local: Addresses that are only used for communicating with services on the same interface (e.g., the loopback interface "::1").
- Link-local: Addresses that are local to the network interface (*link*). There is always one link-local address for each IPv6 interface on your host. Link-local addresses ("fe80...") are generated from the MAC address of the local network adaptor, and are not guaranteed to be unique.
- Global: For globally routable addresses, such as public servers on the Internet.

When using a link-local or site-local address for IPv6 connections, you must specify the
scope ID. The scope ID for a link-local address is usually the same as the interface
name (e.g., "eth0", "en1") or number (e.g., "1", "2").

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also**
[setScopeId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#setScopeId)(),
[QNetworkInterface](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkinterface.html), and
[QNetworkInterface::interfaceFromName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkinterface.html#interfaceFromName).

### void QHostAddress::setScopeId(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*id*)

Sets the IPv6 scope ID of the address to *id*. If the address protocol is not IPv6, this
function does nothing. The scope ID may be set as an interface name (such as "eth0" or
"en1") or as an integer representing the interface index. If *id* is an interface name,
[QtNetwork](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtnetwork-module.html) will convert to an
interface index using
[QNetworkInterface::interfaceIndexFromName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkinterface.html#interfaceIndexFromName)()
before calling the operating system networking functions.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also** [scopeId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#scopeId)(),
[QNetworkInterface](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkinterface.html), and
[QNetworkInterface::interfaceFromName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkinterface.html#interfaceFromName).

Returns the IPv4 address as a number.

For example, if the address is 127.0.0.1, the returned value is 2130706433 (i.e.

[IPv6Protocol](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#NetworkLayerProtocol-enum),

Returns the IPv4 address as a number.

For example, if the address is 127.0.0.1, the returned value is 2130706433 (i.e.
0x7f000001).

This value is valid if the

### Q\_IPV6ADDR QHostAddress::toIPv6Address() const

Returns the IPv6 address as a Q\_IPV6ADDR structure. The structure consists of 16
unsigned characters.

```
Q_IPV6ADDR addr = hostAddr.toIPv6Address();
// addr contains 16 unsigned characters

for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {
    // process addr[i]
}
```

This value is valid if the
[protocol](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#protocol)() is
[IPv6Protocol](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#NetworkLayerProtocol-enum).
If the protocol is
[IPv4Protocol](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#NetworkLayerProtocol-enum),
then the address is returned an an IPv4 mapped IPv6 address. (RFC4291)

**See also**
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#toString)().

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QHostAddress::toString() const

Returns the address as a string.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QHostInfo finds the IP address(es) associated with a host name, or the host name
associated with an IP address. The class provides two static convenience functions: one
that works asynchronously and emits a signal once the host is found, and one that blocks
and returns a QHostInfo object.

To look up a host's IP addresses asynchronously, call
[lookupHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#lookupHost)(), which
takes the host name or IP address, a receiver object, and a slot signature as arguments
and returns an ID. You can abort the lookup by calling
[abortHostLookup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#abortHostLookup)()
with the lookup ID.

Example:

```
// To find the IP address of qt-project.org
QHostInfo::lookupHost("qt-project.org",
                      this, SLOT(printResults(QHostInfo)));

// To find the host name for 4.2.2.1
QHostInfo::lookupHost("4.2.2.1",
                      this, SLOT(printResults(QHostInfo)));
```

The slot is invoked when the results are ready. The results are stored in a QHostInfo
object. Call [addresses](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#addresses)()
to get the list of IP addresses for the host, and
[hostName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#hostName)() to get the host
name that was looked up.

If the lookup failed, [error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#error)()
returns the type of error that occurred.
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#errorString)() gives a
human-readable description of the lookup error.

If you want a blocking lookup, use the
[QHostInfo::fromName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#fromName)()
function:

```
QHostInfo info = QHostInfo::fromName("qt-project.org");
```

QHostInfo supports Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) through the IDNA and Punycode
standards.

To retrieve the name of the local host, use the static
[QHostInfo::localHostName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#localHostName)()
function.

QHostInfo uses the mechanisms provided by the operating system to perform the lookup. As
per {https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6724}{RFC 6724} there is no guarantee that all IP
addresses registered for a domain or host will be returned.

**Note:** Since Qt 4.6.1 QHostInfo is using multiple threads for DNS lookup instead of
one dedicated DNS thread. This improves performance, but also changes the order of
signal emissions when using
[lookupHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#lookupHost)() compared to
previous versions of Qt.

**Note:** Since Qt 4.6.3 QHostInfo is using a small internal 60 second DNS cache for
performance improvements.

PythonQt.Qt.QHostInfo.fromName.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#QHostInfo) QHostInfo::fromName(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*)

Looks up the IP address(es) for the given host *name*. The function blocks during the
lookup which means that execution of the program is suspended until the results of the
lookup are ready. Returns the result of the lookup in a
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) object.

If you pass a literal IP address to *name* instead of a host name,
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) will search for the
domain name for the IP (i.e.,
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) will perform a *reverse*
lookup). On success, the returned
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) will contain both the
resolved domain name and IP addresses for the host name.

**See also**
[lookupHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#lookupHost)().

PythonQt.Qt.QHostInfo.lookupHost.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` int QHostInfo::lookupHost(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*, [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) \**receiver*, const char \**member*)

Looks up the IP address(es) associated with host name *name*, and returns an ID for the
lookup. When the result of the lookup is ready, the slot or signal *member* in
*receiver* is called with a
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) argument. The
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) object can then be
inspected to get the results of the lookup.

The lookup is performed by a single function call, for example:

```
QHostInfo::lookupHost("www.kde.org",
                      this, SLOT(lookedUp(QHostInfo)));
```

The implementation of the slot prints basic information about the addresses returned by
the lookup, or reports an error if it failed:

```
void MyWidget::lookedUp(const QHostInfo &host)
{
    if (host.error() != QHostInfo::NoError) {
        qDebug() << "Lookup failed:" << host.errorString();
        return;
    }

    const auto addresses = host.addresses();
    for (const QHostAddress &address : addresses)
        qDebug() << "Found address:" << address.toString();
}
```

If you pass a literal IP address to *name* instead of a host name,
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) will search for the
domain name for the IP (i.e.,
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) will perform a *reverse*
lookup). On success, the resulting
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) will contain both the
resolved domain name and IP addresses for the host name. Example:

```
QHostInfo::lookupHost("4.2.2.1",
                      this, SLOT(lookedUp(QHostInfo)));
```

**Note:** There is no guarantee on the order the signals will be emitted if you start
multiple requests with lookupHost().

**See also**
[abortHostLookup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#abortHostLookup)(),
[addresses](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#addresses)(),
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#error)(), and
[fromName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#fromName)().

### `[static]` template \<typename Functor\> int QHostInfo::lookupHost(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*, Functor *functor*)

This is an overloaded function.

Looks up the IP address(es) associated with host name *name*, and returns an ID for the
lookup. When the result of the lookup is ready, the *functor* is called with a
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) argument. The
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) object can then be
inspected to get the results of the lookup.

The *functor* will be run in the thread that makes the call to lookupHost; that thread
must have a running Qt event loop.

**Note:** There is no guarantee on the order the signals will be emitted if you start
multiple requests with lookupHost().

This function was introduced in Qt 5.9.

**See also**
[abortHostLookup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#abortHostLookup)(),
[addresses](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#addresses)(),
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#error)(), and
[fromName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#fromName)().

### `[static]` template \<typename Functor\> int QHostInfo::lookupHost(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*, const [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) \**context*, Functor *functor*)

This is an overloaded function.

Looks up the IP address(es) associated with host name *name*, and returns an ID for the
lookup. When the result of the lookup is ready, the *functor* is called with a
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) argument. The
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) object can then be
inspected to get the results of the lookup.

If *context* is destroyed before the lookup completes, the *functor* will not be called.
The *functor* will be run in the thread of *context*. The context's thread must have a
running Qt event loop.

Here is an alternative signature for the function:

```
lookupHost(const QString &name, const QObject *receiver, PointerToMemberFunction function)
```

In this case, when the result of the lookup is ready, the slot or signal `function` in
`receiver` is called with a
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) argument. The
[QHostInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html) object can then be
inspected to get the results of the lookup.

**Note:** There is no guarantee on the order the signals will be emitted if you start
multiple requests with lookupHost().

This function was introduced in Qt 5.9.

**See also**
[abortHostLookup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#abortHostLookup)(),
[addresses](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostinfo.html#addresses)(),

## Detailed Description

Mouse events occur when a mouse cursor is moved into, out of, or within a widget, and if
the widget has the
[Qt::WA\_Hover](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute.

The function [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhoverevent.html#pos)() gives the
current cursor position, while
[oldPos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhoverevent.html#oldPos)() gives the old
mouse position.

There are a few similarities between the events
[QEvent::HoverEnter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[QEvent::HoverLeave](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum), and the
events [QEvent::Enter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[QEvent::Leave](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum). However, they
are slightly different because we do an update() in the event handler of
[HoverEnter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[HoverLeave](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).

[QEvent::HoverMove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) is also
slightly different from
[QEvent::MouseMove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum). Let us
consider a top-level window A containing a child B which in turn contains a child C (all
with mouse tracking enabled):

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/hoverevents.png)

Now, if you move the cursor from the top to the bottom in the middle of A, you will get
the following
[QEvent::MouseMove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events:

1. A::MouseMove
2. B::MouseMove
3. C::MouseMove

You will get the same events for
[QEvent::HoverMove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum), except
that the event always propagates to the top-level regardless whether the event is
accepted or not. It will only stop propagating with the
[Qt::WA\_NoMousePropagation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute.

In this case the events will occur in the following way:

1. A::HoverMove
2. A::HoverMove, B::HoverMove
3. A::HoverMove, B::HoverMove, C::HoverMove

PythonQt.Qt.QHttpPart.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QHttpPart class holds a body part to be used inside a HTTP multipart MIME message
(which is represented by the
[QHttpMultiPart](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhttpmultipart.html) class). A
QHttpPart consists of a header block and a data block, which are separated by each other
by two consecutive new lines. An example for one part would be:

```
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="text"

here goes the body
```

For setting headers, use
[setHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhttppart.html#setHeader)() and
[setRawHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhttppart.html#setRawHeader)(), which
behave exactly like
[QNetworkRequest::setHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkrequest.html#setHeader)()
and
[QNetworkRequest::setRawHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkrequest.html#setRawHeader)().

For reading small pieces of data, use
[setBody](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhttppart.html#setBody)(); for larger data
blocks like e.g. images, use
[setBodyDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhttppart.html#setBodyDevice)(). The
latter method saves memory by not copying the data internally, but reading directly from
the device. This means that the device must be opened and readable at the moment when
the multipart message containing the body part is sent on the network via
[QNetworkAccessManager::post](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkaccessmanager.html#post)().

To construct a QHttpPart with a small body, consider the following snippet (this
produces the data shown in the example above):

```
QHttpPart textPart;
textPart.setHeader(QNetworkRequest::ContentTypeHeader, QVariant("text/plain"));
textPart.setHeader(QNetworkRequest::ContentDispositionHeader, QVariant("form-data; name=\"text\""));
textPart.setBody("here goes the body");
```

To construct a QHttpPart reading from a device (e.g. a file), the following can be
applied:

```
QHttpPart imagePart;
imagePart.setHeader(QNetworkRequest::ContentTypeHeader, QVariant("image/jpeg"));
imagePart.setHeader(QNetworkRequest::ContentDispositionHeader, QVariant("form-data; name=\"image\""));
imagePart.setRawHeader("Content-ID", "my@content.id"); // add any headers you like via setRawHeader()
QFile *file = new QFile("image.jpg");
file->open(QIODevice::ReadOnly);
imagePart.setBodyDevice(file);
```

Be aware that QHttpPart does not take ownership of the device when set, so it is the
developer's responsibility to destroy it when it is not needed anymore. A good idea
might be to set the multipart message as parent object for the device, as documented at
the documentation for
[QHttpMultiPart](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhttpmultipart.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QIODevice provides both a common implementation and an abstract interface for devices
that support reading and writing of blocks of data, such as
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html),
[QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) and
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html). QIODevice is abstract
and cannot be instantiated, but it is common to use the interface it defines to provide
device-independent I/O features. For example, Qt's XML classes operate on a QIODevice
pointer, allowing them to be used with various devices (such as files and buffers).

Before accessing the device,
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)() must be called to set
the correct
[OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) (such as
[ReadOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) or
[ReadWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum)). You
can then write to the device with
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)(), and read by
calling either [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), or
[readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readAll)(). Call
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#close)() when you are done
with the device.

QIODevice distinguishes between two types of devices: random-access devices and
sequential devices.

- Random-access devices support seeking to arbitrary positions using [seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)(). The current position in the file is available by calling [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#pos)(). [QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) and [QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) are examples of random-access devices.
- Sequential devices don't support seeking to arbitrary positions. The data must be read in one pass. The functions [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#pos)() and [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#size)() don't work for sequential devices. [QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html) and [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) are examples of sequential devices.

You can use
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)() to
determine the type of device.

QIODevice emits
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() when new data
is available for reading; for example, if new data has arrived on the network or if
additional data is appended to a file that you are reading from. You can call
[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)() to
determine the number of bytes that are currently available for reading. It's common to
use [bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)()
together with the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal when
programming with asynchronous devices such as
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html), where fragments of
data can arrive at arbitrary points in time. QIODevice emits the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal
every time a payload of data has been written to the device. Use
[bytesToWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesToWrite)() to
determine the current amount of data waiting to be written.

Certain subclasses of QIODevice, such as
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html) and
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html), are asynchronous. This
means that I/O functions such as
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() always return
immediately, while communication with the device itself may happen when control goes
back to the event loop. QIODevice provides functions that allow you to force these
operations to be performed immediately, while blocking the calling thread and without
entering the event loop. This allows QIODevice subclasses to be used without an event
loop, or in a separate thread:

- [waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)() \- This function suspends operation in the calling thread until new data is available for reading.
- [waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)() \- This function suspends operation in the calling thread until one payload of data has been written to the device.
- waitFor....() \- Subclasses of QIODevice implement blocking functions for device-specific operations. For example, [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) has a function called [waitForStarted()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted) which suspends operation in the calling thread until the process has started.

Calling these functions from the main, GUI thread, may cause your user interface to
freeze. Example:

```
QProcess gzip;
gzip.start("gzip", QStringList() << "-c");
if (!gzip.waitForStarted())
    return false;

gzip.write("uncompressed data");

QByteArray compressed;
while (gzip.waitForReadyRead())
    compressed += gzip.readAll();
```

By subclassing QIODevice, you can provide the same interface to your own I/O devices.
Subclasses of QIODevice are only required to implement the protected
[readData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readData)() and
[writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)() functions.
QIODevice uses these functions to implement all its convenience functions, such as
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)(). QIODevice also
handles access control for you, so you can safely assume that the device is opened in
write mode if [writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)()
is called.

Some subclasses, such as [QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) and
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html), are implemented using
a memory buffer for intermediate storing of data. This reduces the number of required
device accessing calls, which are often very slow. Buffering makes functions like
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)() and
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)() fast, as they can
operate on the memory buffer instead of directly on the device itself. Certain I/O
operations, however, don't work well with a buffer. For example, if several users open
the same device and read it character by character, they may end up reading the same
data when they meant to read a separate chunk each. For this reason, QIODevice allows
you to bypass any buffering by passing the Unbuffered flag to
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)(). When subclassing
QIODevice, remember to bypass any buffer you may use when the device is open in
Unbuffered mode.

Usually, the incoming data stream from an asynchronous device is fragmented, and chunks
of data can arrive at arbitrary points in time. To handle incomplete reads of data
structures, use the transaction mechanism implemented by QIODevice. See
[startTransaction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#startTransaction)()
and related functions for more details.

Some sequential devices support communicating via multiple channels. These channels
represent separate streams of data that have the property of independently sequenced
delivery. Once the device is opened, you can determine the number of channels by calling
the
[readChannelCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readChannelCount)()
and
[writeChannelCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeChannelCount)()
functions. To switch between channels, call
[setCurrentReadChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#setCurrentReadChannel)()
and
[setCurrentWriteChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#setCurrentWriteChannel)(),
respectively. QIODevice also provides additional signals to handle asynchronous
communication on a per-channel basis.

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::atEnd() const

Returns `true` if the current read and write position is at the end of the device (i.e.
there is no more data available for reading on the device); otherwise returns `false`.

For some devices, atEnd() can return true even though there is more data to read. This
special case only applies to devices that generate data in direct response to you
calling [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() (e.g., `/dev`
or `/proc` files on Unix and macOS, or console input / `stdin` on all platforms).

**See also**
[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)(),
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(), and
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)().

used with sequential devices to determine the number of bytes to allocate in a buffer
before reading.

Subclasses that reimplement this function must call the base implementation in order to
include the size of the buffer of
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). Example:

```
qint64 CustomDevice::bytesAvailable() const
{
    return buffer.size() + QIODevice::bytesAvailable();
}
```

[bytesToWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesToWrite)(),
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)(), and
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)().

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::bytesWritten([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *bytes*)

This signal is emitted every time a payload of data has been written to the device's
current write channel. The *bytes* argument is set to the number of bytes that were
written in this payload.

bytesWritten() is not emitted recursively; if you reenter the event loop or call
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)()
inside a slot connected to the bytesWritten() signal, the signal will not be reemitted
(although
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)()
may still return true).

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::canReadLine() const

Returns `true` if a complete line of data can be read from the device; otherwise returns
`false`.

Note that unbuffered devices, which have no way of determining what can be read, always
return false.

This function is often called in conjunction with the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal.

Subclasses that reimplement this function must call the base implementation in order to
include the contents of the
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html)'s buffer. Example:

```
bool CustomDevice::canReadLine() const
{
    return buffer.contains('\n') || QIODevice::canReadLine();
}
```

**See also** [readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)()
and [readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)().

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::channelBytesWritten(int *channel*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *bytes*)

This signal is emitted every time a payload of data has been written to the device. The
*bytes* argument is set to the number of bytes that were written in this payload, while

Returns `true` if data can be read from the device; otherwise returns false. Use
[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)() to
determine how many bytes can be read.

This is a convenience function which checks if the
[OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) of the
device contains the
[ReadOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) flag.

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.isSequential.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::isSequential() const

Returns `true` if this device is sequential; otherwise returns false.

Sequential devices, as opposed to a random-access devices, have no concept of a start,
an end, a size, or a current position, and they do not support seeking. You can only
read from the device when it reports that data is available. The most common example of
a sequential device is a network socket. On Unix, special files such as /dev/zero and
fifo pipes are sequential.

Regular files, on the other hand, do support random access. They have both a size and a
current position, and they also support seeking backwards and forwards in the data
stream. Regular files are non-sequential.

**See also**
[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)().

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.peek.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::peek(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads at most *maxSize* bytes from the device into *data*, without side effects (i.e.,
if you call [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() after
peek(), you will get the same data). Returns the number of bytes read. If an error
occurs, such as when attempting to peek a device opened in
[WriteOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) mode,
this function returns -1.

0 is returned when no more data is available for reading.

Example:

```
bool isExeFile(QFile *file)
{
    char buf[2];
    if (file->peek(buf, sizeof(buf)) == sizeof(buf))
        return (buf[0] == 'M' && buf[1] == 'Z');
    return false;
}
```

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QIODevice::peek([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

This is an overloaded function.

Peeks at most *maxSize* bytes from the device, returning the data peeked as a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html).

Example:

```
bool isExeFile(QFile *file)
{
    return file->peek(2) == "MZ";
}
```

This function has no way of reporting errors; returning an empty
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) can mean either that no
data was currently available for peeking, or that an error occurred.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

### `[virtual]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::pos() const

For random-access devices, this function returns the position that data is written to or
read from. For sequential devices or closed devices, where there is no concept of a
"current position", 0 is returned.

The current read/write position of the device is maintained internally by
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), so reimplementing this
function is not necessary. When subclassing
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), use
[QIODevice::seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)() to notify
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) about changes in the
device position.

**See also**
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)() and
[seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::read(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads at most *maxSize* bytes from the device into *data*, and returns the number of
bytes read. If an error occurs, such as when attempting to read from a device opened in
[WriteOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) mode,
this function returns -1.

0 is returned when no more data is available for reading. However, reading past the end
of the stream is considered an error, so this function returns -1 in those cases (that
is, reading on a closed socket or after a process has died).

**See also** [readData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readData)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QIODevice::read([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

This is an overloaded function.

Reads at most *maxSize* bytes from the device, and returns the data read as a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html).

This function has no way of reporting errors; returning an empty
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) can mean either that no
data was currently available for reading, or that an error occurred.

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::readChannelFinished()

This signal is emitted when the input (reading) stream is closed in this device. It is
emitted as soon as the closing is detected, which means that there might still be data
available for reading with
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also** [atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#atEnd)() and

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.readData.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual protected]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::readData(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads up to *maxSize* bytes from the device into *data*, and returns the number of bytes
read or -1 if an error occurred.

If there are no bytes to be read and there can never be more bytes available (examples
include socket closed, pipe closed, sub-process finished), this function returns -1.

This function is called by
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). Reimplement this
function when creating a subclass of
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

When reimplementing this function it is important that this function reads all the
required data before returning. This is required in order for
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) to be able to operate
on the class. [QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) assumes
all the requested information was read and therefore does not retry reading if there was
a problem.

This function might be called with a maxSize of 0, which can be used to perform
post-reading operations.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and
[writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)().
signatures: readData(self, data: str, maxlen: int) -> int

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.readLine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::readLine(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

This function reads a line of ASCII characters from the device, up to a maximum of
*maxSize* \- 1 bytes, stores the characters in *data*, and returns the number of bytes
read. If a line could not be read but no error occurred, this function returns 0\. If an
error occurs, this function returns the length of what could be read, or -1 if nothing
was read.

A terminating '\\0' byte is always appended to *data*, so *maxSize* must be larger than
1\.

Data is read until either of the following conditions are met:

- The first '\\n' character is read.
- *maxSize* \- 1 bytes are read.
- The end of the device data is detected.

For example, the following code reads a line of characters from a file:

```
QFile file("box.txt");
if (file.open(QFile::ReadOnly)) {
    char buf[1024];
    qint64 lineLength = file.readLine(buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (lineLength != -1) {
        // the line is available in buf
    }
}
```

The newline character ('\\n') is included in the buffer. If a newline is not encountered
before maxSize \- 1 bytes are read, a newline will not be inserted into the buffer. On
windows newline characters are replaced with '\\n'.

This function calls
[readLineData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLineData)(), which
is implemented using repeated calls to
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(). You can provide
a more efficient implementation by reimplementing
[readLineData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLineData)() in your
own subclass.

**See also** [getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(),
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(), and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QIODevice::readLine([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize* \= 0\)

This is an overloaded function.

Reads a line from the device, but no more than *maxSize* characters, and returns the
result as a byte array.

This function has no way of reporting errors; returning an empty
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) can mean either that no
data was currently available for reading, or that an error occurred.

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.readLineData.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::readLineData(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads up to *maxSize* characters into *data* and returns the number of characters read.

This function is called by
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and provides
its base implementation, using
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(). Buffered devices
can improve the performance of
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() by
reimplementing this function.

[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() appends a '\\0'
byte to *data*; readLineData() does not need to do this.

If you reimplement this function, be careful to return the correct value: it should
return the number of bytes read in this line, including the terminating newline, or 0 if
there is no line to be read at this point. If an error occurs, it should return -1 if
and only if no bytes were read. Reading past EOF is considered an error.
signatures: readLineData(self, data: str, maxlen: int) -> int

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.readyRead.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::readyRead()

This signal is emitted once every time new data is available for reading from the
device's current read channel. It will only be emitted again once new data is available,
such as when a new payload of network data has arrived on your network socket, or when a
new block of data has been appended to your device.

readyRead() is not emitted recursively; if you reenter the event loop or call
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)()
inside a slot connected to the readyRead() signal, the signal will not be reemitted
(although
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)()
may still return true).

Note for developers implementing classes derived from
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html): you should always emit
readyRead() when new data has arrived (do not emit it only because there's data still to
be read in your buffers). Do not emit readyRead() in other conditions.

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::reset()

Note that when using a
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) on a

true on success, or false if an error occurred. For sequential devices, the default

[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html)'s built-in buffer.

### void QIODevice::ungetChar(char *c*)

Puts the character *c* back into the device, and decrements the current position unless
the position is 0\. This function is usually called to "undo" a
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)() operation, such
as when writing a backtracking parser.

If *c* was not previously read from the device, the behavior is undefined.

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.waitForBytesWritte.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::waitForBytesWritten(int *msecs*)

For buffered devices, this function waits until a payload of buffered written data has
been written to the device and the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal
has been emitted, or until *msecs* milliseconds have passed. If msecs is -1, this
function will not time out. For unbuffered devices, it returns immediately.

Returns `true` if a payload of data was written to the device; otherwise returns `false`
(i.e. if the operation timed out, or if an error occurred).

This function can operate without an event loop. It is useful when writing non-GUI
applications and when performing I/O operations in a non-GUI thread.

If called from within a slot connected to the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal,
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() will
not be reemitted.

Reimplement this function to provide a blocking API for a custom device. The default
implementation does nothing, and returns `false`.

**Warning:** Calling this function from the main (GUI) thread might cause your user
interface to freeze.

**See also**
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)().

PythonQt.Qt.QIODevice.waitForReadyRead.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::waitForReadyRead(int *msecs*)

Blocks until new data is available for reading and the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal has
been emitted, or until *msecs* milliseconds have passed. If msecs is -1, this function
will not time out.

Returns `true` if new data is available for reading; otherwise returns false (if the
operation timed out or if an error occurred).

This function can operate without an event loop. It is useful when writing non-GUI
applications and when performing I/O operations in a non-GUI thread.

If called from within a slot connected to the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal,
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() will not be
reemitted.

Reimplement this function to provide a blocking API for a custom device. The default
implementation does nothing, and returns `false`.

**Warning:** Calling this function from the main (GUI) thread might cause your user
interface to freeze.

**See also**
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)().

### `[pure virtual protected]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::writeData(const char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Writes up to *maxSize* bytes from *data* to the device. Returns the number of bytes
written, or -1 if an error occurred.

This function is called by
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). Reimplement this
function when creating a subclass of
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

available before returning. This is required in order for

on the class. [QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) assumes
all the information was written and therefore does not retry writing if there was a
problem.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)().
