PythonQt.Qt.QIcon.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QIcon can generate smaller, larger, active, and disabled pixmaps from the set of
pixmaps it is given. Such pixmaps are used by Qt widgets to show an icon representing a
particular action.

The simplest use of QIcon is to create one from a
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) file or resource, and then
use it, allowing Qt to work out all the required icon styles and sizes. For example:

```
QToolButton *button = new QToolButton;
button->setIcon(QIcon("open.xpm"));
```

To undo a QIcon, simply set a null icon in its place:

```
button->setIcon(QIcon());
```

Use the
[QImageReader::supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)()
and
[QImageWriter::supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportedImageFormats)()
functions to retrieve a complete list of the supported file formats.

When you retrieve a pixmap using
pixmap([QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html), Mode, State), and no
pixmap for this given size, mode and state has been added with
[addFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#addFile)() or
[addPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#addPixmap)(), then QIcon will
generate one on the fly. This pixmap generation happens in a
[QIconEngine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html). The default engine
scales pixmaps down if required, but never up, and it uses the current style to
calculate a disabled appearance. By using custom icon engines, you can customize every
aspect of generated icons. With
[QIconEnginePlugin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengineplugin.html) it is
possible to register different icon engines for different file suffixes, making it
possible for third parties to provide additional icon engines to those included with Qt.

**Note:** Since Qt 4.2, an icon engine that supports SVG is included.

### Making Classes that Use QIcon

If you write your own widgets that have an option to set a small pixmap, consider
allowing a QIcon to be set for that pixmap. The Qt class
[QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html) is an example of such
a widget.

Provide a method to set a QIcon, and when you draw the icon, choose whichever pixmap is
appropriate for the current state of your widget. For example:

```
void MyWidget::drawIcon(QPainter *painter, QPoint pos)
{
    QPixmap pixmap = icon.pixmap(QSize(22, 22),
                                   isEnabled() ? QIcon::Normal
                                               : QIcon::Disabled,
                                   isChecked() ? QIcon::On
                                               : QIcon::Off);
    painter->drawPixmap(pos, pixmap);
}
```

You might also make use of the `Active` mode, perhaps making your widget `Active` when
the mouse is over the widget (see
[QWidget::enterEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enterEvent)()),
while the mouse is pressed pending the release that will activate the function, or when
it is the currently selected item. If the widget can be toggled, the "On" mode might be
used to draw a different icon.

![QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/icon.png)

**Note:** QIcon needs a
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) instance
before the icon is created.

### High DPI Icons

There are two ways that QIcon supports [high
DPI](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/highdpi.html) icons: via
[addFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#addFile)() and
[fromTheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#fromTheme)().

[addFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#addFile)() is useful if you have
your own custom directory structure and do not need to use the [freedesktop.org Icon
Theme
Specification](https://standards.freedesktop.org/icon-theme-spec/icon-theme-spec-latest.html).
Icons created via this approach use Qt's ["@nx" high DPI
syntax](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#high-resolution-versions-of-images).

Using [fromTheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#fromTheme)() is
necessary if you plan on following the Icon Theme Specification. To make QIcon use the
high DPI version of an image, add an additional entry to the appropriate `index.theme`
file:

```
[Icon Theme]
Name=Test
Comment=Test Theme

Directories=32x32/actions,32x32@2/actions

[32x32/actions]
Size=32
Context=Actions
Type=Fixed

# High DPI version of the entry above.
[32x32@2/actions]
Size=32
Scale=2
Type=Fixed
```

Your icon theme directory would then look something like this:

```
├── 32x32
│   └── actions
│       └── appointment-new.png
├── 32x32@2
│   └── actions
│       └── appointment-new.png
└── index.theme
```

### void QIcon::addFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*, const [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html) \&*size* \= QSize(), [QIcon::Mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#Mode-enum) *mode* \= Normal, [QIcon::State](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#State-enum) *state* \= Off)

Adds an image from the file with the given *fileName* to the icon, as a specialization
for *size*, *mode* and *state*. The file will be loaded on demand. Note: custom icon
engines are free to ignore additionally added pixmaps.

If *fileName* contains a relative path (e.g. the filename only) the relevant file must
be found relative to the runtime working directory.

The file name can refer to an actual file on disk or to one of the application's
embedded resources. See the [Resource
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/resources.html) overview for details on how
to embed images and other resource files in the application's executable.

Use the
[QImageReader::supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)()
and
[QImageWriter::supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportedImageFormats)()
functions to retrieve a complete list of the supported file formats.

If a high resolution version of the image exists (identified by the suffix `@2x` on the
base name), it is automatically loaded and added with the *device pixel ratio* set to a
value of 2\. This can be disabled by setting the environment variable
`QT_HIGHDPI_DISABLE_2X_IMAGE_LOADING` (see
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html)).

**Note:** When you add a non-empty filename to a
[QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html), the icon becomes non-null, even
if the file doesn't exist or points to a corrupt file.

**See also** [addPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#addPixmap)() and
[QPixmap::devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#devicePixelRatio)().

PythonQt.Qt.QIcon.fromTheme.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#QIcon) QIcon::fromTheme(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*)

Returns the [QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html) corresponding to
*name* in the current icon theme.

The latest version of the freedesktop icon specification and naming specification can be
obtained here:

- <http://standards.freedesktop.org/icon-theme-spec/icon-theme-spec-latest.html>
- <http://standards.freedesktop.org/icon-naming-spec/icon-naming-spec-latest.html>

To fetch an icon from the current icon theme:

```
    QIcon undoicon = QIcon::fromTheme("edit-undo");
```

**Note:** By default, only X11 will support themed icons. In order to use themed icons
on Mac and Windows, you will have to bundle a compliant theme in one of your
[themeSearchPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#themeSearchPaths)() and
set the appropriate
[themeName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#themeName)().

**Note:** Qt will make use of GTK's icon-theme.cache if present to speed up the lookup.
These caches can be generated using gtk-update-icon-cache:
<https://developer.gnome.org/gtk3/stable/gtk-update-icon-cache.html>.

**Note:** If an icon can't be found in the current theme, then it will be searched in
[fallbackSearchPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html#fallbackSearchPaths)()
as an unthemed icon.

## Detailed Description

Icon drag events are sent to widgets when the main icon of a window has been dragged
away. On macOS, this happens when the proxy icon of a window is dragged off the title
bar.

It is normal to begin using drag and drop in response to this event.

PythonQt.Qt.QIconEngine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

An icon engine provides the rendering functions for a
[QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html). Each icon has a corresponding
icon engine that is responsible for drawing the icon with a requested size, mode and
state.

The icon is rendered by the
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html#paint)() function, and the
icon can additionally be obtained as a pixmap with the
[pixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html#pixmap)() function (the
default implementation simply uses
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html#paint)() to achieve this).
The [addPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html#addPixmap)()
function can be used to add new pixmaps to the icon engine, and is used by
[QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html) to add specialized custom
pixmaps.

The [paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html#paint)(),
[pixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html#pixmap)(), and
[addPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiconengine.html#addPixmap)() functions
are all virtual, and can therefore be reimplemented in subclasses of QIconEngine.

PythonQt.Qt.QImage.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt provides four classes for handling image data: QImage,
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html),
[QBitmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html) and
[QPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html). QImage is designed and
optimized for I/O, and for direct pixel access and manipulation, while
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) is designed and optimized for
showing images on screen. [QBitmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html) is
only a convenience class that inherits
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html), ensuring a depth of 1\.
Finally, the [QPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html) class is a
paint device that records and replays
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) commands.

Because QImage is a [QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html)
subclass, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) can be used to
draw directly onto images. When using
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) on a QImage, the painting
can be performed in another thread than the current GUI thread.

The QImage class supports several image formats described by the
[Format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum) enum. These include
monochrome, 8-bit, 32-bit and alpha-blended images which are available in all versions
of Qt 4.x.

QImage provides a collection of functions that can be used to obtain a variety of
information about the image. There are also several functions that enables
transformation of the image.

QImage objects can be passed around by value since the QImage class uses [implicit data
sharing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html). QImage objects can
also be streamed and compared.

**Note:** If you would like to load QImage objects in a static build of Qt, refer to the
[Plugin HowTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/plugins-howto.html).

**Warning:** Painting on a QImage with the format
[QImage::Format\_Indexed8](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum)
is not supported.

### Reading and Writing Image Files

QImage provides several ways of loading an image file: The file can be loaded when
constructing the QImage object, or by using the
[load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#load)() or
[loadFromData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#loadFromData)() functions
later on. QImage also provides the static
[fromData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#fromData)() function,
constructing a QImage from the given data. When loading an image, the file name can
either refer to an actual file on disk or to one of the application's embedded
resources. See [The Qt Resource
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/resources.html) overview for details on how
to embed images and other resource files in the application's executable.

Simply call the [save](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#save)() function
to save a QImage object.

The complete list of supported file formats are available through the
[QImageReader::supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)()
and
[QImageWriter::supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportedImageFormats)()
functions. New file formats can be added as plugins. By default, Qt supports the
following formats:

| Format | Description | Qt's support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMP | Windows Bitmap | Read/write |
| GIF | Graphic Interchange Format (optional) | Read |
| JPG | Joint Photographic Experts Group | Read/write |
| JPEG | Joint Photographic Experts Group | Read/write |
| PNG | Portable Network Graphics | Read/write |
| PBM | Portable Bitmap | Read |
| PGM | Portable Graymap | Read |
| PPM | Portable Pixmap | Read/write |
| XBM | X11 Bitmap | Read/write |
| XPM | X11 Pixmap | Read/write |

### Image Information

QImage provides a collection of functions that can be used to obtain a variety of
information about the image:

|  | Available Functions |
| --- | --- |
| Geometry | The [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#size)(), [width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#width)(), [height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#height)(), [dotsPerMeterX](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#dotsPerMeterX)(), and [dotsPerMeterY](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#dotsPerMeterY)() functions provide information about the image size and aspect ratio. The [rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#rect)() function returns the image's enclosing rectangle. The [valid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#valid)() function tells if a given pair of coordinates is within this rectangle. The [offset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#offset)() function returns the number of pixels by which the image is intended to be offset by when positioned relative to other images, which also can be manipulated using the [setOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setOffset)() function. |
| Colors | The color of a pixel can be retrieved by passing its coordinates to the [pixel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixel)() function. The [pixel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixel)() function returns the color as a [QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) value indepedent of the image's format. In case of monochrome and 8-bit images, the [colorCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#colorCount)() and [colorTable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#colorTable)() functions provide information about the color components used to store the image data: The [colorTable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#colorTable)() function returns the image's entire color table. To obtain a single entry, use the [pixelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixelIndex)() function to retrieve the pixel index for a given pair of coordinates, then use the [color](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#color)() function to retrieve the color. Note that if you create an 8-bit image manually, you have to set a valid color table on the image as well.  The [hasAlphaChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#hasAlphaChannel)() function tells if the image's format respects the alpha channel, or not. The [allGray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#allGray)() and [isGrayscale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#isGrayscale)() functions tell whether an image's colors are all shades of gray.  See also the [Pixel Manipulation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixel-manipulation) and [Image Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-transformations) sections. |
| Text | The [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#text)() function returns the image text associated with the given text key. An image's text keys can be retrieved using the [textKeys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#textKeys)() function. Use the [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setText)() function to alter an image's text. |
| Low-level information | The [depth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#depth)() function returns the depth of the image. The supported depths are 1 (monochrome), 8, 16, 24 and 32 bits. The [bitPlaneCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#bitPlaneCount)() function tells how many of those bits that are used. For more information see the [Image Formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-formats) section. The [format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#format)(), [bytesPerLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#bytesPerLine)(), and [sizeInBytes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#sizeInBytes)() functions provide low-level information about the data stored in the image.  The [cacheKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#cacheKey)() function returns a number that uniquely identifies the contents of this QImage object. |

### Pixel Manipulation

The functions used to manipulate an image's pixels depend on the image format. The
reason is that monochrome and 8-bit images are index-based and use a color lookup table,
while 32-bit images store ARGB values directly. For more information on image formats,
see the [Image Formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-formats)
section.

In case of a 32-bit image, the
[setPixel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setPixel)() function can be
used to alter the color of the pixel at the given coordinates to any other color
specified as an ARGB quadruplet. To make a suitable
[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) value, use the
[qRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRgb)() (adding a default alpha
component to the given RGB values, i.e. creating an opaque color) or
[qRgba](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRgba)() function. For example:

| 32-bit | |
| --- | --- |
|  | ``` QImage image(3, 3, QImage::Format_RGB32); QRgb value;  value = qRgb(189, 149, 39); // 0xffbd9527 image.setPixel(1, 1, value);  value = qRgb(122, 163, 39); // 0xff7aa327 image.setPixel(0, 1, value); image.setPixel(1, 0, value);  value = qRgb(237, 187, 51); // 0xffedba31 image.setPixel(2, 1, value); ``` |

In case of a 8-bit and monchrome images, the pixel value is only an index from the
image's color table. So the
[setPixel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setPixel)() function can only
be used to alter the color of the pixel at the given coordinates to a predefined color
from the image's color table, i.e. it can only change the pixel's index value. To alter
or add a color to an image's color table, use the
[setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setColor)() function.

An entry in the color table is an ARGB quadruplet encoded as an
[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) value. Use the
[qRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRgb)() and
[qRgba](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRgba)() functions to make a
suitable [QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) value for
use with the [setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setColor)()
function. For example:

| 8-bit | |
| --- | --- |
|  | ``` QImage image(3, 3, QImage::Format_Indexed8); QRgb value;  value = qRgb(122, 163, 39); // 0xff7aa327 image.setColor(0, value);  value = qRgb(237, 187, 51); // 0xffedba31 image.setColor(1, value);  value = qRgb(189, 149, 39); // 0xffbd9527 image.setColor(2, value);  image.setPixel(0, 1, 0); image.setPixel(1, 0, 0); image.setPixel(1, 1, 2); image.setPixel(2, 1, 1); ``` |

For images with more than 8-bit per color-channel. The methods
[setPixelColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setPixelColor)() and
[pixelColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixelColor)() can be used to
set and get with [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) values.

QImage also provide the
[scanLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#scanLine)() function which
returns a pointer to the pixel data at the scanline with the given index, and the
[bits](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#bits)() function which returns a
pointer to the first pixel data (this is equivalent to `scanLine(0)`).

### Image Formats

Each pixel stored in a QImage is represented by an integer. The size of the integer
varies depending on the format. QImage supports several image formats described by the
[Format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum) enum.

Monochrome images are stored using 1-bit indexes into a color table with at most two
colors. There are two different types of monochrome images: big endian (MSB first) or
little endian (LSB first) bit order.

8-bit images are stored using 8-bit indexes into a color table, i.e. they have a single
byte per pixel. The color table is a
[QVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvector.html)\<[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef)\>,
and the [QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) typedef is
equivalent to an unsigned int containing an ARGB quadruplet on the format 0xAARRGGBB.

32-bit images have no color table; instead, each pixel contains an
[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) value. There are
three different types of 32-bit images storing RGB (i.e. 0xffRRGGBB), ARGB and
premultiplied ARGB values respectively. In the premultiplied format the red, green, and
blue channels are multiplied by the alpha component divided by 255\.

An image's format can be retrieved using the
[format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#format)() function. Use the
[convertToFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#convertToFormat)()
functions to convert an image into another format. The
[allGray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#allGray)() and
[isGrayscale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#isGrayscale)() functions
tell whether a color image can safely be converted to a grayscale image.

### Image Transformations

QImage supports a number of functions for creating a new image that is a transformed
version of the original: The
[createAlphaMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#createAlphaMask)()
function builds and returns a 1-bpp mask from the alpha buffer in this image, and the
[createHeuristicMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#createHeuristicMask)()
function creates and returns a 1-bpp heuristic mask for this image. The latter function
works by selecting a color from one of the corners, then chipping away pixels of that
color starting at all the edges.

The [mirrored](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#mirrored)() function
returns a mirror of the image in the desired direction, the
[scaled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#scaled)() returns a copy of the
image scaled to a rectangle of the desired measures, and the
[rgbSwapped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#rgbSwapped)() function
constructs a BGR image from a RGB image.

The [scaledToWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#scaledToWidth)() and
[scaledToHeight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#scaledToHeight)()
functions return scaled copies of the image.

The transformed() function returns a copy of the image that is transformed with the
given transformation matrix and transformation mode: Internally, the transformation
matrix is adjusted to compensate for unwanted translation, i.e. transformed() returns
the smallest image containing all transformed points of the original image. The static
trueMatrix() function returns the actual matrix used for transforming the image.

There are also functions for changing attributes of an image in-place:

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [setDotsPerMeterX](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setDotsPerMeterX)() | Defines the aspect ratio by setting the number of pixels that fit horizontally in a physical meter. |
| [setDotsPerMeterY](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setDotsPerMeterY)() | Defines the aspect ratio by setting the number of pixels that fit vertically in a physical meter. |
| [fill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#fill)() | Fills the entire image with the given pixel value. |
| [invertPixels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#invertPixels)() | Inverts all pixel values in the image using the given [InvertMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#InvertMode-enum) value. |
| [setColorTable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setColorTable)() | Sets the color table used to translate color indexes. Only monochrome and 8-bit formats. |
| [setColorCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#setColorCount)() | Resizes the color table. Only monochrome and 8-bit formats. |

Returns a sub-area of the image as a new image.

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#QImage) QImage::createAlphaMask([Qt::ImageConversionFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ImageConversionFlag-enum) *flags* \= Qt::AutoColor) const

Builds and returns a 1-bpp mask from the alpha buffer in this image. Returns a null
image if the image's format is
[QImage::Format\_RGB32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum).

The *flags* argument is a bitwise-OR of the
[Qt::ImageConversionFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ImageConversionFlag-enum),
and controls the conversion process. Passing 0 for flags sets all the default options.

The returned image has little-endian bit order (i.e. the image's format is
[QImage::Format\_MonoLSB](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum)),
which you can convert to big-endian
([QImage::Format\_Mono](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum))
using the
[convertToFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#convertToFormat)()
function.

**See also**
[createHeuristicMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#createHeuristicMask)()
and [Image
Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-transformations).

PythonQt.Qt.QImage.createHeuristicMask.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#QImage) QImage::createHeuristicMask(bool *clipTight* \= true) const

Creates and returns a 1-bpp heuristic mask for this image.

The function works by selecting a color from one of the corners, then chipping away
pixels of that color starting at all the edges. The four corners vote for which color is
to be masked away. In case of a draw (this generally means that this function is not
applicable to the image), the result is arbitrary.

The returned image has little-endian bit order (i.e. the image's format is
[QImage::Format\_MonoLSB](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum)),
which you can convert to big-endian
([QImage::Format\_Mono](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum))
using the
[convertToFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#convertToFormat)()
function.

If *clipTight* is true (the default) the mask is just large enough to cover the pixels;
otherwise, the mask is larger than the data pixels.

Note that this function disregards the alpha buffer.

**See also**
[createAlphaMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#createAlphaMask)() and
[Image
Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-transformations).

PythonQt.Qt.QImage.fill.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QImage::fill([uint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#uint-typedef) *pixelValue*)

Fills the entire image with the given *pixelValue*.

If the depth of this image is 1, only the lowest bit is used. If you say fill(0),
fill(2), etc., the image is filled with 0s. If you say fill(1), fill(3), etc., the image
is filled with 1s. If the depth is 8, the lowest 8 bits are used and if the depth is 16
the lowest 16 bits are used.

Note: [QImage::pixel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixel)() returns
the color of the pixel at the given coordinates while QColor::pixel() returns the pixel
value of the underlying window system (essentially an index value), so normally you will
want to use [QImage::pixel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixel)() to
use a color from an existing image or
[QColor::rgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#rgb)() to use a specific
color.

**See also** [depth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#depth)() and [Image
Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-transformations).

### void QImage::fill(const [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) \&*color*)

This is an overloaded function.

Fills the entire image with the given *color*.

If the depth of the image is 1, the image will be filled with 1 if *color* equals
[Qt::color1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum); it will
otherwise be filled with 0\.

If the depth of the image is 8, the image will be filled with the index corresponding
the *color* in the color table if present; it will otherwise be filled with 0\.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

### void QImage::fill([Qt::GlobalColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum) *color*)

This is an overloaded function.

Fills the image with the given *color*, described as a standard global color.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

### void QImage::invertPixels([QImage::InvertMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#InvertMode-enum) *mode* \= InvertRgb)

Inverts all pixel values in the image.

The given invert *mode* only have a meaning when the image's depth is 32\. The default
*mode* is [InvertRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#InvertMode-enum),
which leaves the alpha channel unchanged. If the *mode* is
[InvertRgba](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#InvertMode-enum), the alpha
bits are also inverted.

Inverting an 8-bit image means to replace all pixels using color index *i* with a pixel
using color index 255 minus *i*. The same is the case for a 1-bit image. Note that the
color table is *not* changed.

If the image has a premultiplied alpha channel, the image is first converted to an
unpremultiplied image format to be inverted and then converted back.

**See also** [Image
Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-transformations).

### bool QImage::load(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*, const char \**format* \= nullptr)

Loads an image from the file with the given *fileName*. Returns `true` if the image was
successfully loaded; otherwise invalidates the image and returns `false`.

The loader attempts to read the image using the specified *format*, e.g., PNG or JPG. If
*format* is not specified (which is the default), it is auto-detected based on the
file's suffix and header. For details, see
[QImageReader::setAutoDetectImageFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setAutoDetectImageFormat)().

The file name can either refer to an actual file on disk or to one of the application's
embedded resources. See the [Resource
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/resources.html) overview for details on how
to embed images and other resource files in the application's executable.

**See also** [Reading and Writing Image
Files](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#reading-and-writing-image-files).

### bool QImage::save(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*, const char \**format* \= nullptr, int *quality* \= -1) const

Saves the image to the file with the given *fileName*, using the given image file
*format* and *quality* factor. If *format* is `nullptr`,
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) will attempt to guess the
format by looking at *fileName*'s suffix.

The *quality* factor must be in the range 0 to 100 or -1. Specify 0 to obtain small
compressed files, 100 for large uncompressed files, and -1 (the default) to use the
default settings.

Returns `true` if the image was successfully saved; otherwise returns `false`.

**See also** [Reading and Writing Image
Files](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#reading-and-writing-image-files).

This function writes a [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) to the
given *device*.

This can, for example, be used to save an image directly into a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html):

```
        QImage image;
        QByteArray ba;
        QBuffer buffer(&ba);
        buffer.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly);

```

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#QImage) QImage::scaled(const [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html) \&*size*, [Qt::AspectRatioMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AspectRatioMode-enum) *aspectRatioMode* \= Qt::IgnoreAspectRatio, [Qt::TransformationMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TransformationMode-enum) *transformMode* \= Qt::FastTransformation) const

Returns a copy of the image scaled to a rectangle defined by the given *size* according
to the given *aspectRatioMode* and *transformMode*.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qimage-scaling.png)

- If *aspectRatioMode* is [Qt::IgnoreAspectRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AspectRatioMode-enum), the image is scaled to *size*.
- If *aspectRatioMode* is [Qt::KeepAspectRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AspectRatioMode-enum), the image is scaled to a rectangle as large as possible inside *size*, preserving the aspect ratio.
- If *aspectRatioMode* is [Qt::KeepAspectRatioByExpanding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AspectRatioMode-enum), the image is scaled to a rectangle as small as possible outside *size*, preserving the aspect ratio.

If the given *size* is empty, this function returns a null image.

**See also** [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#isNull)() and

### [uchar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#uchar-typedef) \*QImage::scanLine(int *i*)

Returns a pointer to the pixel data at the scanline with index *i*. The first scanline
is at index 0\.

The scanline data is as minimum 32-bit aligned. For 64-bit formats it follows the native
alignment of 64-bit integers (64-bit for most platforms, but notably 32-bit on i386).

**Warning:** If you are accessing 32-bpp image data, cast the returned pointer to
`QRgb*` ([QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) has a
32-bit size) and use it to read/write the pixel value. You cannot use the `uchar*`
pointer directly, because the pixel format depends on the byte order on the underlying
platform. Use [qRed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qRed)(),
[qGreen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qGreen)(),
[qBlue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qBlue)(), and
[qAlpha](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#qAlpha)() to access the pixels.

**See also**
[bytesPerLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#bytesPerLine)(),
[bits](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#bits)(), [Pixel
Manipulation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#pixel-manipulation), and
[constScanLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#constScanLine)().

### void QImage::setAlphaChannel(const [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#QImage) \&*alphaChannel*)

Sets the alpha channel of this image to the given *alphaChannel*.

If *alphaChannel* is an 8 bit alpha image, the alpha values are used directly.
Otherwise, *alphaChannel* is converted to 8 bit grayscale and the intensity of the pixel
values is used.

If the image already has an alpha channel, the existing alpha channel is multiplied with
the new one. If the image doesn't have an alpha channel it will be converted to a format
that does.

The operation is similar to painting *alphaChannel* as an alpha image over this image
using `QPainter::CompositionMode_DestinationIn`.

**See also**
[hasAlphaChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#hasAlphaChannel)(),
[alphaChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage-obsolete.html#alphaChannel)(),

Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-transformations),

### void QImage::setDevicePixelRatio([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *scaleFactor*)

Sets the device pixel ratio for the image. This is the ratio between image pixels and
device-independent pixels.

The default *scaleFactor* is 1.0. Setting it to something else has two effects:

QPainters that are opened on the image will be scaled. For example, painting on a
200x200 image if with a ratio of 2.0 will result in effective (device-independent)
painting bounds of 100x100.

Code paths in Qt that calculate layout geometry based on the image size will take the
ratio into account: [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html) layoutSize \=
image.[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#size)() /
image.[devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#devicePixelRatio)()
The net effect of this is that the image is displayed as high-DPI image rather than a
large image (see [Drawing High Resolution Versions of Pixmaps and
Images](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawing-high-resolution-versions-of-pixmaps-and-images)).

**See also**
[devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#devicePixelRatio)().

### void QImage::setText(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*key*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*)

Sets the image text to the given *text* and associate it with the given *key*.

If you just want to store a single text block (i.e., a "comment" or just a description),
you can either pass an empty key, or use a generic key like "Description".

The image text is embedded into the image data when you call
[save](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#save)() or
[QImageWriter::write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#write)().

Not all image formats support embedded text. You can find out if a specific image or
format supports embedding text by using
[QImageWriter::supportsOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportsOption)().
We give an example:

```
    QImageWriter writer;
    writer.setFormat("png");
    if (writer.supportsOption(QImageIOHandler::Description))
        qDebug() << "Png supports embedded text";
```

You can use
[QImageWriter::supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportedImageFormats)()
to find out which image formats are available to you.

**See also** [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#text)() and
[textKeys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#textKeys)().

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#QImage) QImage::transformed(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*matrix*, [Qt::TransformationMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TransformationMode-enum) *mode* \= Qt::FastTransformation) const

Returns a copy of the image that is transformed using the given transformation *matrix*
and transformation *mode*.

The returned image will normally have the same {Image Formats}{format} as the original
image. However, a complex transformation may result in an image where not all pixels are
covered by the transformed pixels of the original image. In such cases, those background
pixels will be assigned a transparent color value, and the transformed image will be
given a format with an alpha channel, even if the orginal image did not have that.

The transformation *matrix* is internally adjusted to compensate for unwanted
translation; i.e. the image produced is the smallest image that contains all the
transformed points of the original image. Use the trueMatrix() function to retrieve the
actual matrix used for transforming an image.

Unlike the other overload, this function can be used to perform perspective
transformations on images.

**See also**
[trueMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage-obsolete.html#trueMatrix)() and
[Image
Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#image-transformations).
signatures: transformed(self, matrix: PySide2.QtGui.QMatrix, mode: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.TransformationMode=...) -> PySide2.QtGui.QImage

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt uses QImageIOHandler for reading and writing images through
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) and
[QImageWriter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html). You can also
derive from this class to write your own image format handler using Qt's plugin
mechanism.

Call [setDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#setDevice)() to
assign a device to the handler, and
[setFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#setFormat)() to
assign a format to it. One QImageIOHandler may support more than one image format.
[canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#canRead)() returns
`true` if an image can be read from the device, and
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#read)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#write)() return true if
reading or writing an image was completed successfully.

QImageIOHandler also has support for animations formats, through the functions
[loopCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#loopCount)(),
[imageCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#imageCount)(),
[nextImageDelay](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#nextImageDelay)()
and
[currentImageNumber](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#currentImageNumber)().

In order to determine what options an image handler supports, Qt will call
[supportsOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#supportsOption)()
and [setOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#setOption)().
Make sure to reimplement these functions if you can provide support for any of the
options in the
[ImageOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#ImageOption-enum)
enum.

To write your own image handler, you must at least reimplement
[canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#canRead)() and
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#read)(). Then create a
[QImageIOPlugin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html) that can create
the handler. Finally, install your plugin, and
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) and
[QImageWriter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html) will then
automatically load the plugin, and start using it.

### `[pure virtual]` bool QImageIOHandler::canRead() const

Returns `true` if an image can be read from the device (i.e., the image format is
supported, the device can be read from and the initial header information suggests that
the image can be read); otherwise returns `false`.

When reimplementing canRead(), make sure that the I/O device
([device](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#device)()) is left in
its original state (e.g., by using peek() rather than
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#read)()).

PythonQt.Qt.QImageIOPlugin.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QImageIOPlugin is a factory for creating
[QImageIOHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html) objects,
which are used internally by
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) and
[QImageWriter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html) to add support for
different image formats to Qt.

Writing an image I/O plugin is achieved by subclassing this base class, reimplementing
the pure virtual functions
[capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)()
and [create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#create)(), and
exporting the class with the
[Q\_PLUGIN\_METADATA](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtplugin.html#Q_PLUGIN_METADATA)()
macro. See [How to Create Qt
Plugins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/plugins-howto.html) for details.

An image format plugin can support three capabilities: reading
([CanRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum)),
writing
([CanWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum)) and
*incremental* reading
([CanReadIncremental](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum)).
Reimplement
[capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)() in
you subclass to expose the capabilities of your image format.

[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#create)() should create
an instance of your
[QImageIOHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html) subclass,
with the provided device and format properly set, and return this handler.

The json metadata file for the plugin needs to contain information about the image
formats the plugins supports, together with the corresponding MIME types (one for each
format). For a jpeg plugin, this could, for example, look as follows:

```
{
  "Keys": [ "jpg", "jpeg" ],
  "MimeTypes": [ "image/jpeg", "image/jpeg" ]
}
```

Different plugins can support different capabilities. For example, you may have one
plugin that supports reading the GIF format, and another that supports writing. Qt will
select the correct plugin for the job, depending on the return value of
[capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)().
If several plugins support the same capability, Qt will select one arbitrarily.

PythonQt.Qt.QImageIOPlugin.capabilities.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual]` [QImageIOPlugin::Capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum) QImageIOPlugin::capabilities([QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) \**device*, const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*format*) const

Returns the capabilities of the plugin, based on the data in *device* and the format
*format*. If *device* is `0`, it should simply report whether the format can be read or
written. Otherwise, it should attempt to determine whether the given format (or any
format supported by the plugin if *format* is empty) can be read from or written to
*device*. It should do this without changing the state of *device* (typically by using
[QIODevice::peek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#peek)()).

For example, if the
[QImageIOPlugin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html) supports the
BMP format, *format* is either empty or `"bmp"`, and the data in the device starts with
the characters `"BM"`, this function should return
[CanRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum). If
*format* is `"bmp"`, *device* is `0` and the handler supports both reading and writing,
this function should return
[CanRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum) \|
[CanWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum).

Format names are always given in lower case.

PythonQt.Qt.QImageReader.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The most common way to read images is through
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) and
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html)'s constructors, or by calling
[QImage::load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#load)() and
[QPixmap::load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#load)(). QImageReader is
a specialized class which gives you more control when reading images. For example, you
can read an image into a specific size by calling
[setScaledSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setScaledSize)(),
and you can select a clip rect, effectively loading only parts of an image, by calling
[setClipRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setClipRect)().
Depending on the underlying support in the image format, this can save memory and speed
up loading of images.

To read an image, you start by constructing a QImageReader object. Pass either a file
name or a device pointer, and the image format to QImageReader's constructor. You can
then set several options, such as the clip rect (by calling
[setClipRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setClipRect)()) and
scaled size (by calling
[setScaledSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setScaledSize)()).
[canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#canRead)() returns the
image if the QImageReader can read the image (i.e., the image format is supported and
the device is open for reading). Call
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)() to read the image.

If any error occurs when reading the image,
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)() will return a null
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html). You can then call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#error)() to find the type
of error that occurred, or
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#errorString)() to get
a human readable description of what went wrong.

**Note:** QImageReader assumes exclusive control over the file or device that is
assigned. Any attempts to modify the assigned file or device during the lifetime of the
QImageReader object will yield undefined results.

### Formats

Call
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)()
for a list of formats that QImageReader can read. QImageReader supports all built-in
image formats, in addition to any image format plugins that support reading. Call
[supportedMimeTypes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedMimeTypes)()
to obtain a list of supported MIME types, which for example can be passed to
[QFileDialog::setMimeTypeFilters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html#setMimeTypeFilters)().

QImageReader autodetects the image format by default, by looking at the provided
(optional) format string, the file name suffix, and the data stream contents. You can
enable or disable this feature, by calling
[setAutoDetectImageFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setAutoDetectImageFormat)().

### High Resolution Versions of Images

It is possible to provide high resolution versions of images should a scaling between
*device pixels* and *device independent pixels* be in effect.

The high resolution version is marked by the suffix `@2x` on the base name. The image
read will have its *device pixel ratio* set to a value of 2\.

This can be disabled by setting the environment variable
`QT_HIGHDPI_DISABLE_2X_IMAGE_LOADING`.

### bool QImageReader::canRead() const

Returns `true` if an image can be read for the device (i.e., the image format is
supported, and the device seems to contain valid data); otherwise returns `false`.

canRead() is a lightweight function that only does a quick test to see if the image data
is valid. [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)() may still
return false after canRead() returns `true`, if the image data is corrupt.

**Note:** A [QMimeDatabase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html)
lookup is normally a better approach than this function for identifying potentially
non-image files or data.

For images that support animation, canRead() returns `false` when all frames have been
read.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)(),
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)(),
and [QMimeDatabase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html).

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) QImageReader::read()

Reads an image from the device. On success, the image that was read is returned;
otherwise, a null [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) is returned.
You can then call [error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#error)()
to find the type of error that occurred, or
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#errorString)() to get
a human readable description of the error.

For image formats that support animation, calling read() repeatedly will return the next
frame. When all frames have been read, a null image will be returned.

**See also** [canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#canRead)(),
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)(),
[supportsAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportsAnimation)(),
and [QMovie](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmovie.html).

### bool QImageReader::read([QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) \**image*)

This is an overloaded function.

Reads an image from the device into *image*, which must point to a
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html). Returns `true` on success;
otherwise, returns `false`.

If *image* has same format and size as the image data that is about to be read, this
function may not need to allocate a new image before reading. Because of this, it can be
faster than the other read() overload, which always constructs a new image; especially
when reading several images with the same format and size.

```
QImage icon(64, 64, QImage::Format_RGB32);
QImageReader reader("icon_64x64.bmp");
if (reader.read(&icon)) {
    // Display icon
}
```

For image formats that support animation, calling read() repeatedly will return the next
frame. When all frames have been read, a null image will be returned.

**See also** [canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#canRead)(),
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)(),
[supportsAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportsAnimation)(),
and [QMovie](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmovie.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QImageReader.setAutoDetectIm.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QImageReader::setAutoDetectImageFormat(bool *enabled*)

If *enabled* is true, image format autodetection is enabled; otherwise, it is disabled.
By default, autodetection is enabled.

[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) uses an extensive
approach to detecting the image format; firstly, if you pass a file name to
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html), it will attempt to
detect the file extension if the given file name does not point to an existing file, by
appending supported default extensions to the given file name, one at a time. It then
uses the following approach to detect the image format:

- Image plugins are queried first, based on either the optional format string, or the file name suffix (if the source device is a file). No content detection is done at this stage. [QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) will choose the first plugin that supports reading for this format.
- If no plugin supports the image format, Qt's built-in handlers are checked based on either the optional format string, or the file name suffix.
- If no capable plugins or built-in handlers are found, each plugin is tested by inspecting the content of the data stream.
- If no plugins could detect the image format based on data contents, each built-in image handler is tested by inspecting the contents.
- Finally, if all above approaches fail, [QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) will report failure when trying to read the image.

By disabling image format autodetection,
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) will only query the
plugins and built-in handlers based on the format string (i.e., no file name extensions
are tested).

**See also**
[autoDetectImageFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#autoDetectImageFormat)(),
[QImageIOHandler::canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#canRead)(),
and
[QImageIOPlugin::capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)().

### void QImageReader::setDecideFormatFromContent(bool *ignored*)

If *ignored* is set to true, then the image reader will ignore specified formats or file
extensions and decide which plugin to use only based on the contents in the datastream.

Setting this flag means that all image plugins gets loaded. Each plugin will read the
first bytes in the image data and decide if the plugin is compatible or not.

### void QImageReader::setQuality(int *quality*)

Sets the quality setting of the image format to *quality*.

Some image formats, in particular lossy ones, entail a tradeoff between a) visual
quality of the resulting image, and b) decoding execution time. This function sets the
level of that tradeoff for image formats that support it.

In case of scaled image reading, the quality setting may also influence the tradeoff
level between visual quality and execution speed of the scaling algorithm.

The value range of *quality* depends on the image format. For example, the "jpeg" format
supports a quality range from 0 (low visual quality) to 100 (high visual quality).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also** [quality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#quality)()
and
[setScaledSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setScaledSize)().

### bool QImageReader::supportsOption([QImageIOHandler::ImageOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#ImageOption-enum) *option*) const

Returns `true` if the reader supports *option*; otherwise returns false.

Different image formats support different options. Call this function to determine
whether a certain option is supported by the current format. For example, the PNG format
allows you to embed text into the image's metadata (see
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#text)()), and the BMP format

```

if (reader.supportsOption(QImageIOHandler::Size))
    qDebug() << "Size:" << reader.size();
```

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[QImageWriter::supportsOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportsOption)().

PythonQt.Qt.QImageWriter.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QImageWriter supports setting format specific options, such as compression level and
quality, prior to storing the image. If you do not need such options, you can use
[QImage::save](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#save)() or
[QPixmap::save](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#save)() instead.

To store an image, you start by constructing a QImageWriter object. Pass either a file
name or a device pointer, and the image format to QImageWriter's constructor. You can
then set several options, such as quality (by calling
[setQuality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#setQuality)()).
[canWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#canWrite)() returns
`true` if QImageWriter can write the image (i.e., the image format is supported and the
device is open for writing). Call
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#write)() to write the image
to the device.

If any error occurs when writing the image,
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#write)() will return false.
You can then call [error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#error)()
to find the type of error that occurred, or
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#errorString)() to get
a human readable description of what went wrong.

Call
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportedImageFormats)()
for a list of formats that QImageWriter can write. QImageWriter supports all built-in
image formats, in addition to any image format plugins that support writing.

**Note:** QImageWriter assumes exclusive control over the file or device that is
assigned. Any attempts to modify the assigned file or device during the lifetime of the
QImageWriter object will yield undefined results. If immediate access to a resource is
desired, the use of a scope is the recommended method.

For example:

```
    QString imagePath(QStringLiteral("path/image.jpeg"));
    QImage image(64, 64, QImage::Format_RGB32);
    image.fill(Qt::red);
    {
        QImageWriter writer(imagePath);
        writer.write(image);
    }

    QFile::rename(imagePath,
                  QStringLiteral("path/other_image.jpeg"));
```

### void QImageWriter::setQuality(int *quality*)

Sets the quality setting of the image format to *quality*.

Some image formats, in particular lossy ones, entail a tradeoff between a) visual
quality of the resulting image, and b) encoding execution time and compression level.
This function sets the level of that tradeoff for image formats that support it. For
other formats, this value is ignored.

The value range of *quality* depends on the image format. For example, the "jpeg" format
supports a quality range from 0 (low visual quality, high compression) to 100 (high
visual quality, low compression).

**See also** [quality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#quality)().

### void QImageWriter::setSubType(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*type*)

This is an image format specific function that sets the subtype of the image to *type*.
Subtype can be used by a handler to determine which format it should use while saving
the image.

For example, saving an image in DDS format with A8R8G8R8 subtype:

```
QImageWriter writer("some/image.dds");
if (writer.supportsOption(QImageIOHandler::SubType))
    writer.setSubType("A8R8G8B8");
writer.write(image);
```

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

Sets the image text associated with the key *key* to *text*. This is useful for storing
copyright information or other information about the image. Example:

```
QImage image("some/image.jpeg");
QImageWriter writer("images/outimage.png", "png");
writer.setText("Author", "John Smith");
writer.write(image);
```

If you want to store a single block of data (e.g., a comment), you can pass an empty
key, or use a generic key like "Description".

The key and text will be embedded into the image data after calling
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#write)().

Support for this option is implemented through
[QImageIOHandler::Description](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#ImageOption-enum).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

Formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimageformats-index.html) module provides

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The input value can be a string, a number or an item from a list. A label must be set to
tell the user what they should enter.

Five static convenience functions are provided:
[getText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getText)(),
[getMultiLineText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getMultiLineText)(),
[getInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getInt)(),
[getDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getDouble)(), and
[getItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getItem)(). All the
functions can be used in a similar way, for example:

```
    bool ok;
    QString text = QInputDialog::getText(this, tr("QInputDialog::getText()"),
                                         tr("User name:"), QLineEdit::Normal,
                                         QDir::home().dirName(), &ok);
    if (ok && !text.isEmpty())
        textLabel->setText(text);
```

The `ok` variable is set to true if the user clicks **OK**; otherwise, it is set to
false.

![Input Dialogs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/inputdialogs.png)

The [Standard
Dialogs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-dialogs-standarddialogs-example.html)
example shows how to use QInputDialog as well as other built-in Qt dialogs.

### `[static]` double QInputDialog::getDouble([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**parent*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*title*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*label*, double *value* \= 0, double *min* \= -2147483647, double *max* \= 2147483647, int *decimals* \= 1, bool \**ok* \= nullptr, [Qt::WindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum) *flags* \= Qt::WindowFlags(), double *step* \= 1\)

Static convenience function to get a floating point number from the user.

*title* is the text which is displayed in the title bar of the dialog. *label* is the
text which is shown to the user (it should say what should be entered). *value* is the
default floating point number that the line edit will be set to. *min* and *max* are the
minimum and maximum values the user may choose. *decimals* is the maximum number of
decimal places the number may have. *step* is the amount by which the values change as
the user presses the arrow buttons to increment or decrement the value.

If *ok* is nonnull, \**ok* will be set to true if the user pressed **OK** and to false
if the user pressed **Cancel**. The dialog's parent is *parent*. The dialog will be
modal and uses the widget *flags*.

This function returns the floating point number which has been entered by the user.

Use this static function like this:

```
    bool ok;
    double d = QInputDialog::getDouble(this, tr("QInputDialog::getDouble()"),
                                       tr("Amount:"), 37.56, -10000, 10000, 2, &ok,
                                       Qt::WindowFlags(), 1);
    if (ok)
        doubleLabel->setText(QString("$%1").arg(d));
```

**See also** [getText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getText)(),
[getInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getInt)(),
[getItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getItem)(), and
[getMultiLineText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getMultiLineText)().

Static convenience function to let the user select an item from a string list.

*title* is the text which is displayed in the title bar of the dialog. *label* is the
text which is shown to the user (it should say what should be entered). *items* is the
string list which is inserted into the combo box. *current* is the number of the item
which should be the current item. *inputMethodHints* is the input method hints that will
be used if the combo box is editable and an input method is active.

select one of the existing items.

the user pressed **Cancel**. The dialog's parent is *parent*. The dialog will be modal
and uses the widget *flags*.

current text of the combo box.

Use this static function like this:

```

    items << tr("Spring") << tr("Summer") << tr("Fall") << tr("Winter");

    bool ok;
    QString item = QInputDialog::getItem(this, tr("QInputDialog::getItem()"),
                                         tr("Season:"), items, 0, false, &ok);

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QInputDialog::getText([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**parent*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*title*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*label*, [QLineEdit::EchoMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum) *mode* \= QLineEdit::Normal, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text* \= QString(), bool \**ok* \= nullptr, [Qt::WindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum) *flags* \= Qt::WindowFlags(), [Qt::InputMethodHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#InputMethodHint-enum) *inputMethodHints* \= Qt::ImhNone)

Static convenience function to get a string from the user.

*title* is the text which is displayed in the title bar of the dialog. *label* is the
text which is shown to the user (it should say what should be entered). *text* is the
default text which is placed in the line edit. *mode* is the echo mode the line edit
will use. *inputMethodHints* is the input method hints that will be used in the edit
widget if an input method is active.

If *ok* is nonnull *\*ok* will be set to true if the user pressed **OK** and to false if
the user pressed **Cancel**. The dialog's parent is *parent*. The dialog will be modal
and uses the specified widget *flags*.

If the dialog is accepted, this function returns the text in the dialog's line edit. If
the dialog is rejected, a null
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) is returned.

Use this static function like this:

```
    bool ok;
    QString text = QInputDialog::getText(this, tr("QInputDialog::getText()"),
                                         tr("User name:"), QLineEdit::Normal,
                                         QDir::home().dirName(), &ok);
    if (ok && !text.isEmpty())
        textLabel->setText(text);
```

**See also** [getInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getInt)(),
[getDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getDouble)(),
[getItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getItem)(), and
[getMultiLineText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getMultiLineText)().
signatures: getText(parent: PySide2.QtWidgets.QWidget, title: str, label: str, echo: PySide2.QtWidgets.QLineEdit.EchoMode, text: str=..., flags: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.WindowFlags=..., inputMethodHints: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.InputMethodHints=...) -> typing.Tuple[str, bool]

### void QInputDialog::open([QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**receiver*, const char \**member*)

This function connects one of its signals to the slot specified by *receiver* and
*member*. The specific signal depends on the arguments that are specified in *member*.
These are:

- [textValueSelected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#textValueSelected)() if *member* has a [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) for its first argument.
- [intValueSelected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#intValueSelected)() if *member* has an int for its first argument.
- [doubleValueSelected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#doubleValueSelected)() if *member* has a double for its first argument.
- [accepted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#accepted)() if *member* has NO arguments.

The signal will be disconnected from the slot when the dialog is closed.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.
signatures: open(self, receiver: PySide2.QtCore.QObject, member: str) -> None

## Detailed Description

QInputMethod is used by the text editors for integrating to the platform text input
methods and more commonly by application views for querying various text input
method-related information like virtual keyboard visibility and keyboard dimensions.

Qt Quick also provides access to QInputMethod in QML through [Qt global
object](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qml-qtqml-qt.html) as `Qt.inputMethod`
property.

### `[slot]` void QInputMethod::commit()

Commits the word user is currently composing to the editor. The function is mostly
needed by the input methods with text prediction features and by the methods where the
script used for typing characters is different from the script that actually gets
appended to the editor. Any kind of action that interrupts the text composing needs to
flush the composing state by calling the commit() function, for example when the cursor
is moved elsewhere.

PythonQt.Qt.QInputMethod.update.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QInputMethod::update([Qt::InputMethodQueries](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#InputMethodQuery-enum) *queries*)

Called by the input item to inform the platform input methods when there has been state
changes in editor's input method query attributes. When calling the function *queries*
parameter has to be used to tell what has changes, which input method can use to make
queries for attributes it's interested with
[QInputMethodQueryEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodqueryevent.html).

In particular calling update whenever the cursor position changes is important as that
often causes other query attributes like surrounding text and text selection to change
as well. The attributes that often change together with cursor position have been
grouped in
[Qt::ImQueryInput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#InputMethodQuery-enum)
value for convenience.
