### bool QLibrary::unload()

Unloads the library and returns `true` if the library could be unloaded; otherwise
returns `false`.

This happens automatically on application termination, so you shouldn't normally need to
call this function.

If other instances of [QLibrary](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html) are
using the same library, the call will fail, and unloading will only happen when every
instance has called unload().

Note that on Mac OS X 10.3 (Panther), dynamic libraries cannot be unloaded.

**See also** [resolve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#resolve)() and
[load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#load)().

## Detailed Description

Many pieces of information are established when Qt is configured and built. This class
provides an abstraction for accessing that information. By using the static functions of
this class, an application can obtain information about the instance of the Qt library
which the application is using at run-time.

You can also use a `qt.conf` file to override the hard-coded paths that are compiled
into the Qt library. For more information, see the [Using
qt.conf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt-conf.html) documentation.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QLine describes a finite length line (or a line segment) on a two-dimensional surface.
The start and end points of the line are specified using integer point accuracy for
coordinates. Use the [QLineF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html)
constructor to retrieve a floating point copy.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |

The positions of the line's start and end points can be retrieved using the
[p1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#p1)(),
[x1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#x1)(),
[y1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#y1)(),
[p2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#p2)(),
[x2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#x2)(), and
[y2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#y2)() functions. The
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#dy)() functions return the horizontal
and vertical components of the line. Use
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#isNull)() to determine whether
the QLine represents a valid line or a null line.

Finally, the line can be translated a given offset using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#translate)() function.

PythonQt.Qt.QLineEdit.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-lineedit.png)

A line edit allows the user to enter and edit a single line of plain text with a useful
collection of editing functions, including undo and redo, cut and paste, and drag and
drop (see
[setDragEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#dragEnabled-prop)()).

By changing the
[echoMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#echoMode-prop)() of a line
edit, it can also be used as a "write-only" field, for inputs such as passwords.

The length of the text can be constrained to
[maxLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#maxLength-prop)(). The
text can be arbitrarily constrained using a
[validator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#validator)() or an
[inputMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#inputMask-prop)(), or
both. When switching between a validator and an input mask on the same line edit, it is
best to clear the validator or input mask to prevent undefined behavior.

A related class is [QTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) which
allows multi-line, rich text editing.

You can change the text with
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() or
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#insert)(). The text is
retrieved with [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)();
the displayed text (which may be different, see
[EchoMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum)) is
retrieved with
[displayText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#displayText-prop)().
Text can be selected with
[setSelection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#setSelection)() or
[selectAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#selectAll)(), and the
selection can be [cut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#cut)(),
[copy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#copy)()ied and
[paste](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#paste)()d. The text can be
aligned with
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#alignment-prop)().

When the text changes the
[textChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#textChanged)() signal is
emitted; when the text changes other than by calling
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() the
[textEdited](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#textEdited)() signal is
emitted; when the cursor is moved the
[cursorPositionChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#cursorPositionChanged)()
signal is emitted; and when the Return or Enter key is pressed the
[returnPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#returnPressed)()
signal is emitted.

When editing is finished, either because the line edit lost focus or Return/Enter is
pressed the
[editingFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#editingFinished)()
signal is emitted.

Note that if there is a validator set on the line edit, the
[returnPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#returnPressed)()/[editingFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#editingFinished)()
signals will only be emitted if the validator returns
[QValidator::Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).

By default, QLineEdits have a frame as specified by platform style guides; you can turn
it off by calling
[setFrame](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#frame-prop)(false).

The default key bindings are described below. The line edit also provides a context menu
(usually invoked by a right mouse click) that presents some of these editing options.

| Keypress | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Left Arrow | Moves the cursor one character to the left. |
| Shift\+Left Arrow | Moves and selects text one character to the left. |
| Right Arrow | Moves the cursor one character to the right. |
| Shift\+Right Arrow | Moves and selects text one character to the right. |
| Home | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the line. |
| End | Moves the cursor to the end of the line. |
| Backspace | Deletes the character to the left of the cursor. |
| Ctrl\+Backspace | Deletes the word to the left of the cursor. |
| Delete | Deletes the character to the right of the cursor. |
| Ctrl\+Delete | Deletes the word to the right of the cursor. |
| Ctrl\+A | Select all. |
| Ctrl\+C | Copies the selected text to the clipboard. |
| Ctrl\+Insert | Copies the selected text to the clipboard. |
| Ctrl\+K | Deletes to the end of the line. |
| Ctrl\+V | Pastes the clipboard text into line edit. |
| Shift\+Insert | Pastes the clipboard text into line edit. |
| Ctrl\+X | Deletes the selected text and copies it to the clipboard. |
| Shift\+Delete | Deletes the selected text and copies it to the clipboard. |
| Ctrl\+Z | Undoes the last operation. |
| Ctrl\+Y | Redoes the last undone operation. |

Any other key sequence that represents a valid character, will cause the character to be
inserted into the line edit.

### clearButtonEnabled : bool

This property holds whether the line edit displays a clear button when it is not empty.

Qt 5 reference:

### `[override virtual protected]` void QLineEdit::contextMenuEvent([QContextMenuEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcontextmenuevent.html) \**event*)

Reimplements:
[QWidget::contextMenuEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#contextMenuEvent)(QContextMenuEvent
\*event).

Shows the standard context menu created with
[createStandardContextMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#createStandardContextMenu)().

If you do not want the line edit to have a context menu, you can set its
[contextMenuPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#contextMenuPolicy-prop)
to
[Qt::NoContextMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ContextMenuPolicy-enum).
If you want to customize the context menu, reimplement this function. If you want to
extend the standard context menu, reimplement this function, call
[createStandardContextMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#createStandardContextMenu)()
and extend the menu returned.

```
void LineEdit::contextMenuEvent(QContextMenuEvent *event)
{
    QMenu *menu = createStandardContextMenu();
    menu->addAction(tr("My Menu Item"));
    //...
    menu->exec(event->globalPos());
    delete menu;
}
```

The *event* parameter is used to obtain the position where the mouse cursor was when the
event was generated.

**See also**
[setContextMenuPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#contextMenuPolicy-prop)().

### echoMode : [EchoMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum)

This property holds the line edit's echo mode.

The echo mode determines how the text entered in the line edit is displayed (or echoed)
to the user.

The most common setting is
[Normal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum), in which the
text entered by the user is displayed verbatim, but
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html) also supports modes that
allow the entered text to be suppressed or obscured: these include
[NoEcho](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum),
[Password](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum) and
[PasswordEchoOnEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum).

The widget's display and the ability to copy or drag the text is affected by this
setting.

By default, this property is set to
[Normal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum).

**Access functions:**

PythonQt.Qt.QLineEdit.inputMask.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### inputMask : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the validation input mask.

If no mask is set, inputMask() returns an empty string.

Sets the [QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html)'s validation
mask. Validators can be used instead of, or in conjunction with masks; see
[setValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#setValidator)().

Unset the mask and return to normal
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html) operation by passing an
empty string ("").

The input mask is an input template string. It can contain the following elements:

| Mask Characters | Defines the [Category](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#Category-enum) of input characters that are considered valid in this position |
| --- | --- |
| Meta Characters | Various special meanings |
| Separators | All other characters are regarded as immutable separators |

The following table shows the mask and meta characters that can be used in an input
mask.

| Mask Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `A` | character of the Letter category required, such as A-Z, a-z. |
| `a` | character of the Letter category permitted but not required. |
| `N` | character of the Letter or Number category required, such as A-Z, a-z, 0-9. |
| `n` | character of the Letter or Number category permitted but not required. |
| `X` | Any non-blank character required. |
| `x` | Any non-blank character permitted but not required. |
| `9` | character of the Number category required, e.g 0-9. |
| `0` | character of the Number category permitted but not required. |
| `D` | character of the Number category and larger than zero required, such as 1-9 |
| `d` | character of the Number category and larger than zero permitted but not required, such as 1-9. |
| `#` | character of the Number category, or plus/minus sign permitted but not required. |
| `H` | Hexadecimal character required. A-F, a-f, 0-9. |
| `h` | Hexadecimal character permitted but not required. |
| `B` | Binary character required. 0-1. |
| `b` | Binary character permitted but not required. |
| Meta Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `>` | All following alphabetic characters are uppercased. |
| `<` | All following alphabetic characters are lowercased. |
| `!` | Switch off case conversion. |
| `;c` | Terminates the input mask and sets the *blank* character to *c*. |
| `[ ] { }` | Reserved. |
| `\` | Use `\` to escape the special characters listed above to use them as separators. |

When created or cleared, the line edit will be filled with a copy of the input mask
string where the meta characters have been removed, and the mask characters have been
replaced with the *blank* character (by default, a `space`).

When an input mask is set, the
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() method returns a
modified copy of the line edit content where all the *blank* characters have been
removed. The unmodified content can be read using
[displayText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#displayText-prop)().

The
[hasAcceptableInput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#acceptableInput-prop)()
method returns false if the current content of the line edit does not fulfil the
requirements of the input mask.

Examples:

| Mask | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `000.000.000.000;_` | IP address; blanks are `_`. |
| `HH:HH:HH:HH:HH:HH;_` | MAC address |
| `0000-00-00` | ISO Date; blanks are `space` |
| `>AAAAA-AAAAA-AAAAA-AAAAA-AAAAA;#` | License number; blanks are `#` and all (alphabetic) characters are converted to uppercase. |

To get range control (e.g., for an IP address) use masks together with
[validators](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#setValidator).

**Access functions:**

| QString | **inputMask**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setInputMask**(const QString \&*inputMask*) |

**See also**
[maxLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#maxLength-prop),
[QChar::isLetter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#isLetter)(),
[QChar::isNumber](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#isNumber)(), and
[QChar::digitValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#digitValue)().

### `[signal]` void QLineEdit::inputRejected()

This signal is emitted when the user presses a key that is not considered to be
acceptable input. For example, if a key press results in a validator's validate() call
to return Invalid. Another case is when trying to enter in more characters beyond the
maximum length of the line edit.

Note: This signal will still be emitted in a case where part of the text is accepted but
not all of it is. For example, if there is a maximum length set and the clipboard text
is longer than the maximum length when it is pasted.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.12.

### modified : bool

This property holds whether the line edit's contents has been modified by the user.

The modified flag is never read by
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html); it has a default value
of false and is changed to true whenever the user changes the line edit's contents.

This is useful for things that need to provide a default value but do not start out
knowing what the default should be (perhaps it depends on other fields on the form).
Start the line edit without the best default, and when the default is known, if
modified() returns `false` (the user hasn't entered any text), insert the default value.

Calling [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() resets
the modified flag to false.

### void QLineEdit::setValidator(const [QValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html) \**v*)

Sets the validator for values of line edit to *v*.

The line edit's
[returnPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#returnPressed)() and
[editingFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#editingFinished)()
signals will only be emitted if *v* validates the line edit's content as
[Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum). The user
may change the content to any
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) value
during editing, but will be prevented from editing the text to a value that *v*
validates as [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).

This allows you to constrain the text that shall finally be entered when editing is
done, while leaving users with enough freedom to edit the text from one valid state to
another.

If *v* \=\= 0, setValidator() removes the current input validator. The initial setting
is to have no input validator (i.e. any input is accepted up to
[maxLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#maxLength-prop)()).

**See also** [validator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#validator)(),
[hasAcceptableInput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#acceptableInput-prop)(),
[QIntValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qintvalidator.html),
[QDoubleValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html), and
[QRegExpValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregexpvalidator.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QLineF.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QLineF describes a finite length line (or line segment) on a two-dimensional surface.
QLineF defines the start and end points of the line using floating point accuracy for
coordinates. Use the [toLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#toLine)()
function to retrieve an integer based copy of this line.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |

The positions of the line's start and end points can be retrieved using the
[p1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#p1)(),
[x1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#x1)(),
[y1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#y1)(),
[p2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#p2)(),
[x2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#x2)(), and
[y2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#y2)() functions. The
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#dy)() functions return the
horizontal and vertical components of the line, respectively.

The line's length can be retrieved using the
[length](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#length)() function, and altered
using the [setLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#setLength)()
function. Similarly, [angle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#angle)() and
[setAngle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#setAngle)() are respectively
used for retrieving and altering the angle of the line. Use the
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#isNull)() function to determine
whether the QLineF represents a valid line or a null line.

The [intersects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#intersects)() function
determines the
[IntersectionType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#IntersectionType-alias)
for this line and a given line, while the
[angleTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#angleTo)() function returns the
angle between the lines. In addition, the
[unitVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#unitVector)() function
returns a line that has the same starting point as this line, but with a length of only
1, while the
[normalVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#normalVector)() function
returns a line that is perpendicular to this line with the same starting point and
length.

Finally, the line can be translated a given offset using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#translate)() function, and
can be traversed using the
[pointAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#pointAt)() function.

### Constraints

[QLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html) is limited to the minimum and
maximum values for the `int` type. Operations on a
[QLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html) that could potentially result in
values outside this range will result in undefined behavior.

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QLineF::angle() const

Returns the angle of the line in degrees.

The return value will be in the range of values from 0.0 up to but not including 360.0.
The angles are measured counter-clockwise from a point on the x-axis to the right of the
origin (x \> 0).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also** [setAngle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#setAngle)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLineF.angleTo.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QLineF::angleTo(const [QLineF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#QLineF) \&*line*) const

Returns the angle (in degrees) from this line to the given *line*, taking the direction
of the lines into account. If the lines do not intersect within their range, it is the
intersection point of the extended lines that serves as origin (see
QLineF::UnboundedIntersection).

The returned value represents the number of degrees you need to add to this line to make
it have the same angle as the given *line*, going counter-clockwise.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[intersect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef-obsolete.html#intersect)().

Returns `true` if the line does not have distinct start and end points; otherwise
returns `false`. The start and end points are considered distinct if
[qFuzzyCompare](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qFuzzyCompare)() can
distinguish them in at least one coordinate.

[length](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#length)() is not zero.

**See also**
[qFuzzyCompare](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qFuzzyCompare)() and

## Detailed Description

Linear gradients interpolate colors between start and end points. Outside these points
the gradient is either padded, reflected or repeated depending on the currently set
[spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) method:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [PadSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) (default) | [ReflectSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) | [RepeatSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) |

The colors in a gradient is defined using stop points of the
[QGradientStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#QGradientStop-typedef)
type, i.e. a position and a color. Use the
[QGradient::setColorAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setColorAt)()
or the
[QGradient::setStops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setStops)()
function to define the stop points. It is the gradient's complete set of stop points
that describes how the gradient area should be filled. If no stop points have been
specified, a gradient of black at 0 to white at 1 is used.

In addition to the functions inherited from
[QGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html), the QLinearGradient
class provides the
[finalStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineargradient.html#finalStop)()
function which returns the final stop point of the gradient, and the
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineargradient.html#start)() function
returning the start point of the gradient.

PythonQt.Qt.QListView.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-listview.png)

A QListView presents items stored in a model, either as a simple non-hierarchical list,
or as a collection of icons. This class is used to provide lists and icon views that
were previously provided by the `QListBox` and `QIconView` classes, but using the more
flexible approach provided by Qt's model/view architecture.

The QListView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

This view does not display horizontal or vertical headers; to display a list of items
with a horizontal header, use
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) instead.

QListView implements the interfaces defined by the
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) class to
allow it to display data provided by models derived from the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) class.

Items in a list view can be displayed using one of two view modes: In
[ListMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#ViewMode-enum), the items
are displayed in the form of a simple list; in
[IconMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#ViewMode-enum), the list
view takes the form of an *icon view* in which the items are displayed with icons like
files in a file manager. By default, the list view is in
[ListMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#ViewMode-enum). To change
the view mode, use the
[setViewMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#viewMode-prop)()
function, and to determine the current view mode, use
[viewMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#viewMode-prop)().

Items in these views are laid out in the direction specified by the
[flow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#flow-prop)() of the list view.
The items may be fixed in place, or allowed to move, depending on the view's
[movement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#movement-prop)() state.

If the items in the model cannot be completely laid out in the direction of flow, they
can be wrapped at the boundary of the view widget; this depends on
[isWrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#isWrapping-prop)(). This
property is useful when the items are being represented by an icon view.

The [resizeMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#resizeMode-prop)()
and [layoutMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#layoutMode-prop)()
govern how and when the items are laid out. Items are spaced according to their
[spacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#spacing-prop)(), and can
exist within a notional grid of size specified by
[gridSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#gridSize-prop)(). The items
can be rendered as large or small icons depending on their
[iconSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#iconSize-prop)().

### Improving Performance

It is possible to give the view hints about the data it is handling in order to improve
its performance when displaying large numbers of items. One approach that can be taken
for views that are intended to display items with equal sizes is to set the
[uniformItemSizes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#uniformItemSizes-prop)
property to true.

### flow : [Flow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum)

This property holds which direction the items layout should flow.

If this property is
[LeftToRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum), the items
will be laid out left to right. If the
[isWrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#isWrapping-prop) property
is `true`, the layout will wrap when it reaches the right side of the visible area. If
this property is
[TopToBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum), the items
will be laid out from the top of the visible area, wrapping when it reaches the bottom.

Setting this property when the view is visible will cause the items to be laid out
again.

By default, this property is set to
[TopToBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum).

**Access functions:**

| QListView::Flow | **flow**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setFlow**(QListView::Flow *flow*) |

**See also**
[viewMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#viewMode-prop).

### gridSize : [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html)

This property holds the size of the layout grid

This property is the size of the grid in which the items are laid out. The default is an
empty size which means that there is no grid and the layout is not done in a grid.
Setting this property to a non-empty size switches on the grid layout. (When a grid
layout is in force the
[spacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#spacing-prop) property is
ignored.)

Setting this property when the view is visible will cause the items to be laid out

This property holds whether the items can be moved freely, are snapped to a grid, or

This property determines how the user can move the items in the view.
[Static](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Movement-enum) means that the

by the [gridSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#gridSize-prop)
property.

Setting this property when the view is visible will cause the items to be laid out

PythonQt.Qt.QListWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-listview.png)

QListWidget is a convenience class that provides a list view similar to the one supplied
by [QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html), but with a classic
item-based interface for adding and removing items. QListWidget uses an internal model
to manage each
[QListWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html) in the list.

For a more flexible list view widget, use the
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) class with a standard
model.

List widgets are constructed in the same way as other widgets:

```
    QListWidget *listWidget = new QListWidget(this);
```

The
[selectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionMode-prop)()
of a list widget determines how many of the items in the list can be selected at the
same time, and whether complex selections of items can be created. This can be set with
the
[setSelectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionMode-prop)()
function.

There are two ways to add items to the list: they can be constructed with the list
widget as their parent widget, or they can be constructed with no parent widget and
added to the list later. If a list widget already exists when the items are constructed,
the first method is easier to use:

```
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Oak"), listWidget);
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Fir"), listWidget);
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Pine"), listWidget);
```

If you need to insert a new item into the list at a particular position, then it should
be constructed without a parent widget. The
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#insertItem)() function
should then be used to place it within the list. The list widget will take ownership of
the item.

```
    QListWidgetItem *newItem = new QListWidgetItem;
    newItem->setText(itemText);
    listWidget->insertItem(row, newItem);
```

For multiple items,
[insertItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#insertItems)() can be
used instead. The number of items in the list is found with the
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#count-prop)() function. To
remove items from the list, use
[takeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#takeItem)().

The current item in the list can be found with
[currentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#currentItem)(), and
changed with
[setCurrentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#setCurrentItem)().
The user can also change the current item by navigating with the keyboard or clicking on
a different item. When the current item changes, the
[currentItemChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#currentItemChanged)()
signal is emitted with the new current item and the item that was previously current.

PythonQt.Qt.QListWidgetItem.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QListWidgetItem represents a single item in a
[QListWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html). Each item can hold
several pieces of information, and will display them appropriately.

The item view convenience classes use a classic item-based interface rather than a pure
model/view approach. For a more flexible list view widget, consider using the
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) class with a standard
model.

List items can be inserted automatically into a list, when they are constructed, by
specifying the list widget:

```
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Hazel"), listWidget);
```

Alternatively, list items can also be created without a parent widget, and later
inserted into a list using
[QListWidget::insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#insertItem)().

List items are typically used to display
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#text)() and an
[icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#icon)(). These are set
with the [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setText)()
and [setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setIcon)()
functions. The appearance of the text can be customized with
[setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setFont)(),
[setForeground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setForeground)(),
and
[setBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setBackground)().
Text in list items can be aligned using the
[setTextAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setTextAlignment)()
function. Tooltips, status tips and "What's This?" help can be added to list items with
[setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setToolTip)(),
[setStatusTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setStatusTip)(),
and
[setWhatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setWhatsThis)().

By default, items are enabled, selectable, checkable, and can be the source of drag and
drop operations.

Each item's flags can be changed by calling
[setFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setFlags)() with the
appropriate value (see
[Qt::ItemFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum)). Checkable
items can be checked, unchecked and partially checked with the
[setCheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setCheckState)()
function. The corresponding
[checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#checkState)()
function indicates the item's current check state.

The [isHidden](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#isHidden)()
function can be used to determine whether the item is hidden. To hide an item, use
[setHidden](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setHidden)().

### Subclassing

When subclassing QListWidgetItem to provide custom items, it is possible to define new
types for them enabling them to be distinguished from standard items. For subclasses
that require this feature, ensure that you call the base class constructor with a new
type value equal to or greater than
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#ItemType-enum),
within *your* constructor.

PythonQt.Qt.QLocalServer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class makes it possible to accept incoming local socket connections.

Call [listen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#listen)() to have the
server start listening for incoming connections on a specified key. The
[newConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#newConnection)()
signal is then emitted each time a client connects to the server.

Call
[nextPendingConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#nextPendingConnection)()
to accept the pending connection as a connected
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html). The function
returns a pointer to a
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) that can be used
for communicating with the client.

If an error occurs,
[serverError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#serverError)()
returns the type of error, and
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#errorString)() can be
called to get a human readable description of what happened.

When listening for connections, the name which the server is listening on is available
through [serverName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#serverName)().

Calling [close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#close)() makes
QLocalServer stop listening for incoming connections.

Although QLocalServer is designed for use with an event loop, it's possible to use it
without one. In that case, you must use
[waitForNewConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#waitForNewConnection)(),
which blocks until either a connection is available or a timeout expires.

### `[virtual protected]` void QLocalServer::incomingConnection([quintptr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quintptr-typedef) *socketDescriptor*)

This virtual function is called by
[QLocalServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html) when a new
connection is available. *socketDescriptor* is the native socket descriptor for the
accepted connection.

The base implementation creates a
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html), sets the socket
descriptor and then stores the
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) in an internal list
of pending connections. Finally
[newConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#newConnection)() is
emitted.

Reimplement this function to alter the server's behavior when a connection is available.

**See also**
[newConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#newConnection)(),
[nextPendingConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#nextPendingConnection)(),
and
[QLocalSocket::setSocketDescriptor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#setSocketDescriptor)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLocalServer.listen.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QLocalServer::listen(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*)

Tells the server to listen for incoming connections on *name*. If the server is
currently listening then it will return false. Return true on success otherwise false.

*name* can be a single name and
[QLocalServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html) will determine the
correct platform specific path.
[serverName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#serverName)() will
return the name that is passed into listen.

Usually you would just pass in a name like "foo", but on Unix this could also be a path
such as "/temporary/foo" and on Windows this could be a pipe path such as
"\\\\.\\pipe\\foo"

**Note:** On Unix if the server crashes without closing listen will fail with
AddressInUseError. To create a new server the file should be removed. On Windows two
local servers can listen to the same pipe at the same time, but any connections will go
to one of the server.

**See also**
[serverName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#serverName)(),
[isListening](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#isListening)(), and
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#close)().

### bool QLocalServer::listen([qintptr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qintptr-typedef) *socketDescriptor*)

Instructs the server to listen for incoming connections on *socketDescriptor*. The
property returns `false` if the server is currently listening. It returns `true` on
success; otherwise, it returns `false`. The socket must be ready to accept new
connections with no extra platform-specific functions called. The socket is set into
non-blocking mode.

[serverName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#serverName)(),
[fullServerName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#fullServerName)()
may return a string with a name if this option is supported by the platform; otherwise,
they return an empty [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also**
[isListening](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#isListening)() and
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#close)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLocalServer.nextPendingConn.doc:

### `[virtual]` [QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) \*QLocalServer::nextPendingConnection()

Returns the next pending connection as a connected
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) object.

The socket is created as a child of the server, which means that it is automatically
deleted when the [QLocalServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html)
object is destroyed. It is still a good idea to delete the object explicitly when you
are done with it, to avoid wasting memory.

`nullptr` is returned if this function is called when there are no pending connections.

**See also**

### void QLocalServer::setMaxPendingConnections(int *numConnections*)

Sets the maximum number of pending accepted connections to *numConnections*.
[QLocalServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html) will accept no more
than *numConnections* incoming connections before
[nextPendingConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#nextPendingConnection)()
is called.

Note: Even though [QLocalServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html)
will stop accepting new connections after it has reached its maximum number of pending
connections, the operating system may still keep them in queue which will result in

Qt 5 reference:

### socketOptions : [SocketOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#SocketOption-enum)

The setSocketOptions method controls how the socket operates. For example the socket may
restrict access to what user ids can connect to the socket.

These options must be set before
[listen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#listen)() is called.

In some cases, such as with Unix domain sockets on Linux, the access to the socket will
be determined by file system permissions, and are created based on the umask. Setting
the access flags will override this and will restrict or permit access as specified.

Other Unix-based operating systems, such as macOS, do not honor file permissions for
Unix domain sockets and by default have WorldAccess and these permission flags will have
no effect.

On Windows,
[UserAccessOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#SocketOption-enum)
is sufficient to allow a non elevated process to connect to a local server created by an
elevated process run by the same user.
[GroupAccessOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#SocketOption-enum)
refers to the primary group of the process (see TokenPrimaryGroup in the Windows
documentation).
[OtherAccessOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#SocketOption-enum)
refers to the well known "Everyone" group.

By default none of the flags are set, access permissions are the platform default.

This property was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also** [listen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#listen)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLocalServer.waitForNewConne.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QLocalServer::waitForNewConnection(int *msec* \= 0, bool \**timedOut* \= nullptr)

Waits for at most *msec* milliseconds or until an incoming connection is available.
Returns `true` if a connection is available; otherwise returns `false`. If the operation
timed out and *timedOut* is not `nullptr`, \*timedOut will be set to true.

This is a blocking function call. Its use is ill-advised in a single-threaded GUI
application, since the whole application will stop responding until the function
returns. waitForNewConnection() is mostly useful when there is no event loop available.

The non-blocking alternative is to connect to the
[newConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#newConnection)()
signal.

If msec is -1, this function will not time out.

**See also**
[hasPendingConnections](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#hasPendingConnections)()
and
[nextPendingConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalserver.html#nextPendingConnection)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLocalSocket.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

On Windows this is a named pipe and on Unix this is a local domain socket.

If an error occurs,
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#error)() returns the type
of error, and
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#errorString)() can be
called to get a human readable description of what happened.

Although QLocalSocket is designed for use with an event loop, it's possible to use it
without one. In that case, you must use
[waitForConnected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#waitForConnected)(),
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#waitForReadyRead)(),
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#waitForBytesWritten)(),
and
[waitForDisconnected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#waitForDisconnected)()
which blocks until the operation is complete or the timeout expires.

### void QLocalSocket::connectToServer([QIODevice::OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) *openMode* \= ReadWrite)

Attempts to make a connection to
[serverName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#serverName)().
[setServerName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#setServerName)()
must be called before you open the connection. Alternatively you can use
connectToServer(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&name,
[OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum)
[openMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#openMode));

The socket is opened in the given *openMode* and first enters
[ConnectingState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#LocalSocketState-enum).
If a connection is established,
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) enters
[ConnectedState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#LocalSocketState-enum)
and emits [connected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#connected)().

After calling this function, the socket can emit
[errorOccurred](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#errorOccurred)() to
signal that an error occurred.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.1.

### bool QLocalSocket::flush()

This function writes as much as possible from the internal write buffer to the socket,
without blocking. If any data was written, this function returns `true`; otherwise false
is returned.

Call this function if you need
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) to start sending
buffered data immediately. The number of bytes successfully written depends on the
operating system. In most cases, you do not need to call this function, because
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) will start sending
data automatically once control goes back to the event loop. In the absence of an event
loop, call
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#waitForBytesWritten)()
instead.

**See also** [write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() and
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#waitForBytesWritten)().

### void QLocalSocket::setReadBufferSize([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *size*)

Sets the size of [QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html)'s
internal read buffer to be *size* bytes.

If the buffer size is limited to a certain size,
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) won't buffer more
than this size of data. Exceptionally, a buffer size of 0 means that the read buffer is
unlimited and all incoming data is buffered. This is the default.

This option is useful if you only read the data at certain points in time (e.g., in a
real-time streaming application) or if you want to protect your socket against receiving
too much data, which may eventually cause your application to run out of memory.

**See also**
[readBufferSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#readBufferSize)()
and [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

### [qintptr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qintptr-typedef) QLocalSocket::socketDescriptor() const

Returns the native socket descriptor of the
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) object if this is
available; otherwise returns -1.

The socket descriptor is not available when
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) is in
[UnconnectedState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#LocalSocketState-enum).

- On Windows, the returned value is a [Winsock 2 Socket Handle](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/ms740522(v=vs.85).aspx).

- On all other UNIX-like operating systems, the type is a file descriptor representing a socket.

**See also**
[setSocketDescriptor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#setSocketDescriptor)().

### bool QLocalSocket::waitForConnected(int *msecs* \= 30000\)

Waits until the socket is connected, up to *msecs* milliseconds. If the connection has
been established, this function returns `true`; otherwise it returns `false`. In the
case where it returns `false`, you can call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#error)() to determine the
cause of the error.

The following example waits up to one second for a connection to be established:

```
socket->connectToServer("market");
if (socket->waitForConnected(1000))
    qDebug("Connected!");
```

If *msecs* is -1, this function will not time out.

**See also**
[connectToServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#connectToServer)()
and [connected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#connected)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLocalSocket.waitForDisconne.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QLocalSocket::waitForDisconnected(int *msecs* \= 30000\)

Waits until the socket has disconnected, up to *msecs* milliseconds. If the connection
was successfully disconnected, this function returns `true`; otherwise it returns
`false` (if the operation timed out, if an error occurred, or if this
[QLocalSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html) is already
disconnected). In the case where it returns `false`, you can call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#error)() to determine the
cause of the error.

The following example waits up to one second for a connection to be closed:

```
socket->disconnectFromServer();
if (socket->state() == QLocalSocket::UnconnectedState
    || socket->waitForDisconnected(1000)) {
    qDebug("Disconnected!");
}
```

If *msecs* is -1, this function will not time out.

**See also**
[disconnectFromServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#disconnectFromServer)()
and [close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocalsocket.html#close)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QLocale is initialized with a language/country pair in its constructor and offers
number-to-string and string-to-number conversion functions similar to those in
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

Example:

```
QLocale egyptian(QLocale::Arabic, QLocale::Egypt);
QString s1 = egyptian.toString(1.571429E+07, 'e');
QString s2 = egyptian.toString(10);

double d = egyptian.toDouble(s1);
int i = egyptian.toInt(s2);
```

QLocale supports the concept of a default locale, which is determined from the system's
locale settings at application startup. The default locale can be changed by calling the
static member
[setDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#setDefault)(). Setting the
default locale has the following effects:

- If a QLocale object is constructed with the default constructor, it will use the default locale's settings.
- [QString::toInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#toInt)(), [QString::toDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#toDouble)(), etc., interpret the string according to the default locale. If this fails, it falls back on the "C" locale.
- [QString::arg](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#arg)() uses the default locale to format a number when its position specifier in the format string contains an 'L', e.g. "%L1".

The following example illustrates how to use QLocale directly:

```
QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(QLocale::Hebrew, QLocale::Israel));
QLocale hebrew; // Constructs a default QLocale
QString s1 = hebrew.toString(15714.3, 'e');

bool ok;
double d;

QLocale::setDefault(QLocale::C);
d = QString("1234,56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == false, d == 0
d = QString("1234.56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == true,  d == 1234.56

QLocale::setDefault(QLocale::German);
d = QString("1234,56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == false, d == 0
d = QString("1234.56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == true,  d == 1234.56

QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(QLocale::English, QLocale::UnitedStates));
QString str = QString("%1 %L2 %L3")
      .arg(12345).arg(12345).arg(12345, 0, 16);
// str == "12345 12,345 3039"
```

When a language/country pair is specified in the constructor, one of three things can
happen:

- If the language/country pair is found in the database, it is used.
- If the language is found but the country is not, or if the country is `AnyCountry`, the language is used with the most appropriate available country (for example, Germany for German),
- If neither the language nor the country are found, QLocale defaults to the default locale (see [setDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#setDefault)()).

Use [language](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#language)() and
[country](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#country)() to determine the
actual language and country values used.

An alternative method for constructing a QLocale object is by specifying the locale
name.

```
QLocale korean("ko");
QLocale swiss("de_CH");
```

This constructor converts the locale name to a language/country pair; it does not use
the system locale database.

**Note:** For the current keyboard input locale take a look at
[QInputMethod::locale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethod.html#locale-prop)().

QLocale's data is based on Common Locale Data Repository v39.

PythonQt.Qt.QLocale.c.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#QLocale) QLocale::c()

Returns a [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) object initialized
to the "C" locale.

This locale is based on en\_US but with various quirks of its own, such as simplified
number formatting and its own date formatting. It implements the POSIX standards that
describe the behavior of standard library functions of the "C" programming language.

Among other things, this means its collation order is based on the ASCII values of
letters, so that (for case-sensitive sorting) all upper-case letters sort before any
lower-case one (rather than each letter's upper- and lower-case forms sorting adjacent
to one another, before the next letter's two forms).

**See also** [system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)().

### `[static]` void QLocale::setDefault(const [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#QLocale) \&*locale*)

Sets the global default locale to *locale*. These values are used when a
[QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) object is constructed with no

application startup, before any non-GUI threads are created.

Parses the date/time string given in *string* and returns the time. See
[QDateTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)()
for information on the expressions that can be used with this function.

**Note:** The month and day names used must be given in the user's local language.

If the string could not be parsed, returns an invalid
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html). If the string can be
parsed and represents an invalid date-time (e.g. in a gap skipped by a time-zone
transition), an invalid [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html)
is returned, whose toMSecsSinceEpoch() represents a near-by date-time that is valid.
Passing that to fromMSecsSinceEpoch() will produce a valid date-time that isn't
faithfully represented by the string parsed.

### double QLocale::toDouble(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*s*, bool \**ok* \= nullptr) const

Returns the double represented by the localized string *s*.

Returns an infinity if the conversion overflows or 0.0 if the conversion fails for any
other reason (e.g. underflow).

If *ok* is not `nullptr`, failure is reported by setting \**ok* to `false`, and success
by setting \**ok* to `true`.

This function does not fall back to the 'C' locale if the string cannot be interpreted
in this locale.

```
bool ok;
double d;

QLocale c(QLocale::C);
d = c.toDouble("1234.56", &ok);  // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = c.toDouble("1,234.56", &ok); // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = c.toDouble("1234,56", &ok);  // ok == false, d == 0

QLocale german(QLocale::German);
d = german.toDouble("1234,56", &ok);  // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = german.toDouble("1.234,56", &ok); // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = german.toDouble("1234.56", &ok);  // ok == false, d == 0

d = german.toDouble("1.234", &ok);    // ok == true,  d == 1234.0
```

Notice that the last conversion returns 1234.0, because '.' is the thousands group
separator in the German locale.

This function ignores leading and trailing whitespace.

**See also** [toFloat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toFloat)(),
[toInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toInt)(), and
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLockFile.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A lock file can be used to prevent multiple processes from accessing concurrently the
same resource. For instance, a configuration file on disk, or a socket, a port, a region
of shared memory...

Serialization is only guaranteed if all processes that access the shared resource use
QLockFile, with the same file path.

QLockFile supports two use cases: to protect a resource for a short-term operation (e.g.
verifying if a configuration file has changed before saving new settings), and for
long-lived protection of a resource (e.g. a document opened by a user in an editor) for
an indefinite amount of time.

When protecting for a short-term operation, it is acceptable to call
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)() and wait until any
running operation finishes. When protecting a resource over a long time, however, the
application should always call
[setStaleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#setStaleLockTime)(0)
and then [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() with a
short timeout, in order to warn the user that the resource is locked.

If the process holding the lock crashes, the lock file stays on disk and can prevent any
other process from accessing the shared resource, ever. For this reason, QLockFile tries
to detect such a "stale" lock file, based on the process ID written into the file. To
cover the situation that the process ID got reused meanwhile, the current process name
is compared to the name of the process that corresponds to the process ID from the lock
file. If the process names differ, the lock file is considered stale. Additionally, the
last modification time of the lock file (30s by default, for the use case of a
short-lived operation) is taken into account. If the lock file is found to be stale, it
will be deleted.

For the use case of protecting a resource over a long time, you should therefore call
[setStaleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#setStaleLockTime)(0),
and when [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() returns
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum),
inform the user that the document is locked, possibly using
[getLockInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#getLockInfo)() for more
details.

**Note:** On Windows, this class has problems detecting a stale lock if the machine's
hostname contains characters outside the US-ASCII character set.

PythonQt.Qt.QLockFile.getLockInfo.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QLockFile::getLockInfo([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) \**pid*, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \**hostname*, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \**appname*) const

Retrieves information about the current owner of the lock file.

If [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() returns
`false`, and [error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#error)() returns
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum),
this function can be called to find out more information about the existing lock file:

- the PID of the application (returned in *pid*)
- the *hostname* it's running on (useful in case of networked filesystems),
- the name of the application which created it (returned in *appname*),

Note that [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)()
automatically deleted the file if there is no running application with this PID, so
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum) can
only happen if there is an application with this PID (it could be unrelated though).

This can be used to inform users about the existing lock file and give them the choice
to delete it. After removing the file using
[removeStaleLockFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#removeStaleLockFile)(),
the application can call
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() again.

This function returns `true` if the information could be successfully retrieved, false
if the lock file doesn't exist or doesn't contain the expected data. This can happen if
the lock file was deleted between the time where
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() failed and the
call to this function. Simply call
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() again if this
happens.

### bool QLockFile::lock()

Creates the lock file.

If another process (or another thread) has created the lock file already, this function
will block until that process (or thread) releases it.

Calling this function multiple times on the same lock from the same thread without
unlocking first is not allowed. This function will *dead-lock* when the file is locked
recursively.

Returns `true` if the lock was acquired, false if it could not be acquired due to an
unrecoverable error, such as no permissions in the parent directory.

**See also** [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#unlock)() and
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLockFile.removeStaleLockFil.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QLockFile::removeStaleLockFile()

Attempts to forcefully remove an existing lock file.

Calling this is not recommended when protecting a short-lived operation:
[QLockFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html) already takes care of
removing lock files after they are older than
[staleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#staleLockTime)().

This method should only be called when protecting a resource for a long time, i.e. with
[staleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#staleLockTime)(0), and
after [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() returned
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum), and
the user agreed on removing the lock file.

Returns `true` on success, false if the lock file couldn't be removed. This happens on
Windows, when the application owning the lock is still running.

PythonQt.Qt.QLockFile.setStaleLockTime.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QLockFile::setStaleLockTime(int *staleLockTime*)

Sets *staleLockTime* to be the time in milliseconds after which a lock file is
considered stale. The default value is 30000, i.e. 30 seconds. If your application
typically keeps the file locked for more than 30 seconds (for instance while saving
megabytes of data for 2 minutes), you should set a bigger value using
setStaleLockTime().

The value of *staleLockTime* is used by
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)() and
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() in order to
determine when an existing lock file is considered stale, i.e. left over by a crashed
process. This is useful for the case where the PID got reused meanwhile, so one way to
detect a stale lock file is by the fact that it has been around for a long time.

**See also**
[staleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#staleLockTime)().

PythonQt.Qt.QLockFile.tryLock.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QLockFile::tryLock(int *timeout* \= 0\)

Attempts to create the lock file. This function returns `true` if the lock was obtained;
otherwise it returns `false`. If another process (or another thread) has created the
lock file already, this function will wait for at most *timeout* milliseconds for the
lock file to become available.

Note: Passing a negative number as the *timeout* is equivalent to calling
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)(), i.e. this function
will wait forever until the lock file can be locked if *timeout* is negative.

If the lock was obtained, it must be released with
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#unlock)() before another
process (or thread) can successfully lock it.

Calling this function multiple times on the same lock from the same thread without
unlocking first is not allowed, this function will *always* return false when attempting
to lock the file recursively.

**See also** [lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)() and
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#unlock)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

### Qt Main Window Framework

A main window provides a framework for building an application's user interface. Qt has
QMainWindow and its [related
classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/widget-classes.html#main-window-and-related-classes)
for main window management. QMainWindow has its own layout to which you can add
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html)s,
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html)s, a
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html), and a
[QStatusBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html). The layout has a
center area that can be occupied by any kind of widget. You can see an image of the
layout below.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/mainwindowlayout.png)

**Note:** Creating a main window without a central widget is not supported. You must
have a central widget even if it is just a placeholder.

### Creating Main Window Components

A central widget will typically be a standard Qt widget such as a
[QTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) or a
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html). Custom widgets
can also be used for advanced applications. You set the central widget with
`setCentralWidget()`.

Main windows have either a single (SDI) or multiple (MDI) document interface. You create
MDI applications in Qt by using a
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html) as the central widget.

We will now examine each of the other widgets that can be added to a main window. We
give examples on how to create and add them.

#### Creating Menus

Qt implements menus in [QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) and
QMainWindow keeps them in a
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html).
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html)s are added to the menus,
which display them as menu items.

You can add new menus to the main window's menu bar by calling `menuBar()`, which
returns the [QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html) for the window,
and then add a menu with
[QMenuBar::addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html#addMenu)().

QMainWindow comes with a default menu bar, but you can also set one yourself with
`setMenuBar()`. If you wish to implement a custom menu bar (i.e., not use the
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html) widget), you can set it
with `setMenuWidget()`.

An example of how to create menus follows:

```
    void MainWindow::createMenus()
    {
        fileMenu = menuBar()->addMenu(tr("&File"));
        fileMenu->addAction(newAct);
        fileMenu->addAction(openAct);
        fileMenu->addAction(saveAct);
```

The `createPopupMenu()` function creates popup menus when the main window receives
context menu events. The default implementation generates a menu with the checkable
actions from the dock widgets and toolbars. You can reimplement `createPopupMenu()` for
a custom menu.

#### Creating Toolbars

Toolbars are implemented in the
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) class. You add a toolbar to
a main window with `addToolBar()`.

You control the initial position of toolbars by assigning them to a specific
[Qt::ToolBarArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ToolBarArea-enum). You can
split an area by inserting a toolbar break \- think of this as a line break in text
editing \- with `addToolBarBreak()` or `insertToolBarBreak()`. You can also restrict
placement by the user with
[QToolBar::setAllowedAreas](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#allowedAreas-prop)()
and
[QToolBar::setMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#movable-prop)().

The size of toolbar icons can be retrieved with `iconSize()`. The sizes are platform
dependent; you can set a fixed size with `setIconSize()`. You can alter the appearance
of all tool buttons in the toolbars with `setToolButtonStyle()`.

An example of toolbar creation follows:

```
    void MainWindow::createToolBars()
    {
        fileToolBar = addToolBar(tr("File"));
        fileToolBar->addAction(newAct);
```

#### Creating Dock Widgets

Dock widgets are implemented in the
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) class. A dock widget
is a window that can be docked into the main window. You add dock widgets to a main
window with `addDockWidget()`.

There are four dock widget areas as given by the
[Qt::DockWidgetArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DockWidgetArea-enum)
enum: left, right, top, and bottom. You can specify which dock widget area that should
occupy the corners where the areas overlap with `setCorner()`. By default each area can
only contain one row (vertical or horizontal) of dock widgets, but if you enable nesting
with `setDockNestingEnabled()`, dock widgets can be added in either direction.

Two dock widgets may also be stacked on top of each other. A
[QTabBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html) is then used to select which
of the widgets should be displayed.

We give an example of how to create and add dock widgets to a main window:

```
    QDockWidget *dockWidget = new QDockWidget(tr("Dock Widget"), this);
    dockWidget->setAllowedAreas(Qt::LeftDockWidgetArea |
                                Qt::RightDockWidgetArea);
    dockWidget->setWidget(dockWidgetContents);
    addDockWidget(Qt::LeftDockWidgetArea, dockWidget);
```

#### The Status Bar

You can set a status bar with `setStatusBar()`, but one is created the first time
`statusBar()` (which returns the main window's status bar) is called. See
[QStatusBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html) for information on how
to use it.

### Storing State

QMainWindow can store the state of its layout with `saveState()`; it can later be
retrieved with `restoreState()`. It is the position and size (relative to the size of
the main window) of the toolbars and dock widgets that are stored.

### animated : bool

This property holds whether manipulating dock widgets and tool bars is animated

When a dock widget or tool bar is dragged over the main window, the main window adjusts
its contents to indicate where the dock widget or tool bar will be docked if it is
dropped. Setting this property causes
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) to move its contents
in a smooth animation. Clearing this property causes the contents to snap into their new
positions.

By default, this property is set. It may be cleared if the main window contains widgets
which are slow at resizing or repainting themselves.

Setting this property is identical to setting the
[AnimatedDocks](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#DockOption-enum)
option using
[setDockOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#dockOptions-prop)().

This property was introduced in Qt 4.2.

### dockNestingEnabled : bool

This property holds whether docks can be nested

If this property is `false`, dock areas can only contain a single row (horizontal or
vertical) of dock widgets. If this property is `true`, the area occupied by a dock
widget can be split in either direction to contain more dock widgets.

Dock nesting is only necessary in applications that contain a lot of dock widgets. It
gives the user greater freedom in organizing their main window. However, dock nesting
leads to more complex (and less intuitive) behavior when a dock widget is dragged over
the main window, since there are more ways in which a dropped dock widget may be placed
in the dock area.

Setting this property is identical to setting the
[AllowNestedDocks](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#DockOption-enum)
option using
[setDockOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#dockOptions-prop)().

This property was introduced in Qt 4.2.

### void QMainWindow::resizeDocks(const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) \*\> \&*docks*, const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<int\> \&*sizes*, [Qt::Orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) *orientation*)

Resizes the dock widgets in the list *docks* to the corresponding size in pixels from
the list *sizes*. If *orientation* is
[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum), adjusts
the width, otherwise adjusts the height of the dock widgets. The sizes will be adjusted
such that the maximum and the minimum sizes are respected and the
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) itself will not be
resized. Any additional/missing space is distributed amongst the widgets according to
the relative weight of the sizes.

Example:

```
    resizeDocks({blueWidget, yellowWidget}, {20 , 40}, Qt::Horizontal);
```

If the blue and the yellow widget are nested on the same level they will be resized such
that the yellowWidget is twice as big as the blueWidget

If some widgets are grouped in tabs, only one widget per group should be specified.
Widgets not in the list might be changed to respect the constraints.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.6.
signatures: resizeDocks(self, docks: typing.Sequence[PySide2.QtWidgets.QDockWidget], sizes: shibokensupport.typing27.Sequence, orientation: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.Orientation) -> None
