### bool QMainWindow::restoreState(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*state*, int *version* \= 0\)

Restores the *state* of this mainwindow's toolbars and dockwidgets. Also restores the
corner settings too. The *version* number is compared with that stored in *state*. If
they do not match, the mainwindow's state is left unchanged, and this function returns
`false`; otherwise, the state is restored, and this function returns `true`.

To restore geometry saved using
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html), you can use code like
this:

```
void MainWindow::readSettings()
{
    QSettings settings("MyCompany", "MyApp");
    restoreGeometry(settings.value("myWidget/geometry").toByteArray());
    restoreState(settings.value("myWidget/windowState").toByteArray());
}
```

**See also**
[saveState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#saveState)(),
[QWidget::saveGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#saveGeometry)(),
[QWidget::restoreGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#restoreGeometry)(),
and
[restoreDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreDockWidget)().
signatures: restoreState(self, state: PySide2.QtCore.QByteArray, version: int=...) -> bool

PythonQt.Qt.QMainWindow.saveState.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QMainWindow::saveState(int *version* \= 0\) const

Saves the current state of this mainwindow's toolbars and dockwidgets. This includes the
corner settings which can be set with
[setCorner](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#setCorner)(). The
*version* number is stored as part of the data.

The [objectName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#objectName-prop)
property is used to identify each
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) and
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html). You should make sure
that this property is unique for each
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) and
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) you add to the
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html)

To restore the saved state, pass the return value and *version* number to
[restoreState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreState)().

To save the geometry when the window closes, you can implement a close event like this:

```
void MyMainWindow::closeEvent(QCloseEvent *event)
{
    QSettings settings("MyCompany", "MyApp");
    settings.setValue("geometry", saveGeometry());
    settings.setValue("windowState", saveState());
    QMainWindow::closeEvent(event);
}
```

**See also**
[restoreState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreState)(),
[QWidget::saveGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#saveGeometry)(),
and
[QWidget::restoreGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#restoreGeometry)().

PythonQt.Qt.QMainWindow.splitDockWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QMainWindow::splitDockWidget([QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) \**first*, [QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) \**second*, [Qt::Orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) *orientation*)

Splits the space covered by the *first* dock widget into two parts, moves the *first*
dock widget into the first part, and moves the *second* dock widget into the second
part.

The *orientation* specifies how the space is divided: A
[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) split
places the second dock widget to the right of the first; a
[Qt::Vertical](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) split places
the second dock widget below the first.

*Note*: if *first* is currently in a tabbed docked area, *second* will be added as a new
tab, not as a neighbor of *first*. This is because a single tab can contain only one
dock widget.

*Note*: The
[Qt::LayoutDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#LayoutDirection-enum)
influences the order of the dock widgets in the two parts of the divided area. When
right-to-left layout direction is enabled, the placing of the dock widgets will be
reversed.

**See also**
[tabifyDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#tabifyDockWidget)(),
[addDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#addDockWidget)(),
and
[removeDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#removeDockWidget)().
signatures: splitDockWidget(self, after: PySide2.QtWidgets.QDockWidget, dockwidget: PySide2.QtWidgets.QDockWidget, orientation: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.Orientation) -> None

`true` only if all margins are set to zero.

QMargin objects can be streamed as well as compared.

PythonQt.Qt.QMatrix.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A matrix specifies how to translate, scale, shear or rotate the coordinate system, and
is typically used when rendering graphics. QMatrix, in contrast to
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html), does not allow
perspective transformations.
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) is the recommended
transformation class in Qt.

A QMatrix object can be built using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#setMatrix)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#scale)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#rotate)(),
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#translate)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#shear)() functions.
Alternatively, it can be built by applying [basic matrix
operations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#basic-matrix-operations).
The matrix can also be defined when constructed, and it can be reset to the identity
matrix (the default) using the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#reset)() function.

The QMatrix class supports mapping of graphic primitives: A given point, line, polygon,
region, or painter path can be mapped to the coordinate system defined by *this* matrix
using the [map](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#map)() function. In case
of a rectangle, its coordinates can be transformed using the
[mapRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#mapRect)() function. A
rectangle can also be transformed into a *polygon* (mapped to the coordinate system
defined by *this* matrix), using the
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#mapToPolygon)() function.

QMatrix provides the
[isIdentity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#isIdentity)() function
which returns `true` if the matrix is the identity matrix, and the
[isInvertible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#isInvertible)() function
which returns `true` if the matrix is non-singular (i.e. AB \= BA \= I). The
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#inverted)() function returns
an inverted copy of *this* matrix if it is invertible (otherwise it returns the identity
matrix). In addition, QMatrix provides the
[determinant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#determinant)() function
returning the matrix's determinant.

Finally, the QMatrix class supports matrix multiplication, and objects of the class can
be streamed as well as compared.

### Rendering Graphics

When rendering graphics, the matrix defines the transformations but the actual
transformation is performed by the drawing routines in
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html).

By default, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) operates on the
associated device's own coordinate system. The standard coordinate system of a
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) has its origin
located at the top-left position. The *x* values increase to the right; *y* values
increase downward. For a complete description, see the [coordinate
system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html) documentation.

[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) has functions to translate,
scale, shear and rotate the coordinate system without using a QMatrix. For example:

|  | ``` void SimpleTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.rotate(45);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QMatrix"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

Although these functions are very convenient, it can be more efficient to build a
QMatrix and call
[QPainter::setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter-obsolete.html#setMatrix)()
if you want to perform more than a single transform operation. For example:

|  | ``` void CombinedTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      QMatrix matrix;     matrix.translate(50, 50);     matrix.rotate(45);     matrix.scale(0.5, 1.0);     painter.setMatrix(matrix);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QMatrix"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

### Basic Matrix Operations

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qmatrix-representation.png)

A QMatrix object contains a 3 x 3 matrix. The `dx` and `dy` elements specify horizontal
and vertical translation. The `m11` and `m22` elements specify horizontal and vertical
scaling. And finally, the `m21` and `m12` elements specify horizontal and vertical
*shearing*.

QMatrix transforms a point in the plane to another point using the following formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
```

The point *(x, y)* is the original point, and *(x', y')* is the transformed point. *(x',
y')* can be transformed back to *(x, y)* by performing the same operation on the
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#inverted)() matrix.

The various matrix elements can be set when constructing the matrix, or by using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#setMatrix)() function later
on. They can also be manipulated using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#translate)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#rotate)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#scale)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#shear)() convenience functions,
The currently set values can be retrieved using the
[m11](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m11)(),
[m12](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m12)(),
[m21](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m21)(),
[m22](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m22)(),
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#dy)() functions.

Translation is the simplest transformation. Setting `dx` and `dy` will move the
coordinate system `dx` units along the X axis and `dy` units along the Y axis. Scaling
can be done by setting `m11` and `m22`. For example, setting `m11` to 2 and `m22` to 1.5
will double the height and increase the width by 50%. The identity matrix has `m11` and
`m22` set to 1 (all others are set to 0\) mapping a point to itself. Shearing is
controlled by `m12` and `m21`. Setting these elements to values different from zero will
twist the coordinate system. Rotation is achieved by carefully setting both the shearing
factors and the scaling factors.

Here's the combined transformations example using basic matrix operations:

|  | ``` void BasicOperations::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     double pi = 3.14;      double a    = pi/180 * 45.0;     double sina = sin(a);     double cosa = cos(a);      QMatrix translationMatrix(1, 0, 0, 1, 50.0, 50.0);     QMatrix rotationMatrix(cosa, sina, -sina, cosa, 0, 0);     QMatrix scalingMatrix(0.5, 0, 0, 1.0, 0, 0);      QMatrix matrix;     matrix =  scalingMatrix * rotationMatrix * translationMatrix;      QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.setMatrix(matrix);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QMatrix"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

PythonQt.Qt.QMatrix4x4.doc:

## Detailed Description

The QMatrix4x4 class in general is treated as a row-major matrix, in that the
constructors and
[operator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#operator-28-29)()
functions take data in row-major format, as is familiar in C-style usage.

Internally the data is stored as column-major format, so as to be optimal for passing to
OpenGL functions, which expect column-major data.

When using these functions be aware that they return data in **column-major** format:

- [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#data)()

Qt 5 reference:

### void QMatrix4x4::optimize()

Optimize the usage of this matrix from its current elements.

Some operations such as
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#translate)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#scale)(), and
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#rotate)() can be performed
more efficiently if the matrix being modified is already known to be the identity, a
previous [translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#translate)(), a
previous [scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#scale)(), etc.

Normally the [QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html) class
keeps track of this special type internally as operations are performed. However, if the
matrix is modified directly with operator()() or
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#data)(), then
[QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html) will lose track of the
special type and will revert to the safest but least efficient operations thereafter.

By calling optimize() after directly modifying the matrix, the programmer can force
[QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html) to recover the special
type if the elements appear to conform to one of the known optimized types.

**See also** operator()(),
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#data)(), and
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#translate)().

The returned [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) is formed
by simply dropping the third row and third column of the

the z co-ordinate. The value of 1024 corresponds to the projection factor used by
[QTransform::rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#rotate)() for
the x and y axes.

If *distanceToPlane* is zero, then the returned
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) is formed by simply
dropping the third row and third column of the
[QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html). This is suitable for

PythonQt.Qt.QMdiArea.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QMdiArea functions, essentially, like a window manager for MDI windows. For instance, it
draws the windows it manages on itself and arranges them in a cascading or tile pattern.
QMdiArea is commonly used as the center widget in a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) to create MDI
applications, but can also be placed in any layout. The following code adds an area to a
main window:

```
    QMainWindow *mainWindow = new QMainWindow;
    mainWindow->setCentralWidget(mdiArea);
```

Unlike the window managers for top-level windows, all window flags
([Qt::WindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum)) are
supported by QMdiArea as long as the flags are supported by the current widget style. If
a specific flag is not supported by the style (e.g., the
[WindowShadeButtonHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum)),
you can still shade the window with showShaded().

Subwindows in QMdiArea are instances of
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html). They are added
to an MDI area with
[addSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#addSubWindow)(). It is
common to pass a [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), which is
set as the internal widget, to this function, but it is also possible to pass a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) directly.The
class inherits [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), and you can
use the same API as with a normal top-level window when programming.
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) also has behavior
that is specific to MDI windows. See the
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) class description
for more details.

A subwindow becomes active when it gets the keyboard focus, or when
[setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setFocus-1)() is called. The
user activates a window by moving focus in the usual ways. The MDI area emits the
[subWindowActivated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#subWindowActivated)()
signal when the active window changes, and the
[activeSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activeSubWindow)()
function returns the active subwindow.

The convenience function
[subWindowList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#subWindowList)()
returns a list of all subwindows. This information could be used in a popup menu
containing a list of windows, for example.

The subwindows are sorted by the current
[WindowOrder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#WindowOrder-enum). This
is used for the
[subWindowList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#subWindowList)() and
for
[activateNextSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activateNextSubWindow)()
and
[activatePreviousSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activatePreviousSubWindow)().
Also, it is used when cascading or tiling the windows with
[cascadeSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#cascadeSubWindows)()
and [tileSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#tileSubWindows)().

QMdiArea provides two built-in layout strategies for subwindows:
[cascadeSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#cascadeSubWindows)()
and [tileSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#tileSubWindows)().
Both are slots and are easily connected to menu entries.

PythonQt.Qt.QMdiArea.activeSubWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) \*QMdiArea::activeSubWindow() const

Returns a pointer to the current active subwindow. If no window is currently active,
`nullptr` is returned.

Subwindows are treated as top-level windows with respect to window state, i.e., if a
widget outside the MDI area is the active window, no subwindow will be active. Note that
if a widget in the window in which the MDI area lives gains focus, the window will be
activated.

**See also**
[setActiveSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#setActiveSubWindow)()
and [Qt::WindowState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum).

PythonQt.Qt.QMdiArea.addSubWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) \*QMdiArea::addSubWindow([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*, [Qt::WindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum) *windowFlags* \= Qt::WindowFlags())

Adds *widget* as a new subwindow to the MDI area. If *windowFlags* are non-zero, they
will override the flags set on the widget.

The *widget* can be either a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) or another
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) (in which case the MDI area
will create a subwindow and set the *widget* as the internal widget).

**Note:** Once the subwindow has been added, its parent will be the *viewport widget* of
the [QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html).

```
    QMdiArea mdiArea;
    QMdiSubWindow *subWindow1 = new QMdiSubWindow;
    subWindow1->setWidget(internalWidget1);
    subWindow1->setAttribute(Qt::WA_DeleteOnClose);
    mdiArea.addSubWindow(subWindow1);

    QMdiSubWindow *subWindow2 =
        mdiArea.addSubWindow(internalWidget2);
```

When you create your own subwindow, you must set the
[Qt::WA\_DeleteOnClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
widget attribute if you want the window to be deleted when closed in the MDI area. If
not, the window will be hidden and the MDI area will not activate the next subwindow.

Returns the [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) that
is added to the MDI area.

**See also**
[removeSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#removeSubWindow)().
signatures: addSubWindow(self, widget: PySide2.QtWidgets.QWidget, flags: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.WindowFlags=...) -> PySide2.QtWidgets.QMdiSubWindow

### void QMdiArea::removeSubWindow([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*)

Removes *widget* from the MDI area. The *widget* must be either a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) or a widget that
is the internal widget of a subwindow. Note *widget* is never actually deleted by
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html). If a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) is passed in, its
parent is set to `nullptr` and it is removed; but if an internal widget is passed in,
the child widget is set to `nullptr` and the
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) is *not* removed.

[addSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#addSubWindow)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QMdiSubWindow represents a top-level window in a
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html), and consists of a title
bar with window decorations, an internal widget, and (depending on the current style) a
window frame and a size grip. QMdiSubWindow has its own layout, which consists of the
title bar and a center area for the internal widget.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qmdisubwindowlayout.png)

The most common way to construct a QMdiSubWindow is to call
[QMdiArea::addSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#addSubWindow)()
with the internal widget as the argument. You can also create a subwindow yourself, and
set an internal widget by calling
[setWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#setWidget)().

You use the same API when programming with subwindows as with regular top-level windows
(e.g., you can call functions such as
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(),
[hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)(),
[showMaximized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#showMaximized)(), and
[setWindowTitle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowTitle-prop)()).

### Subwindow Handling

QMdiSubWindow also supports behavior specific to subwindows in an MDI area.

By default, each QMdiSubWindow is visible inside the MDI area viewport when moved
around, but it is also possible to specify transparent window movement and resizing
behavior, where only the outline of a subwindow is updated during these operations. The
[setOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#setOption)() function
is used to enable this behavior.

The [isShaded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#isShaded)()
function detects whether the subwindow is currently shaded (i.e., the window is
collapsed so that only the title bar is visible). To enter shaded mode, call
[showShaded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#showShaded)().
QMdiSubWindow emits the
[windowStateChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#windowStateChanged)()
signal whenever the window state has changed (e.g., when the window becomes minimized,
or is restored). It also emits
[aboutToActivate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#aboutToActivate)()
before it is activated.

In keyboard-interactive mode, the windows are moved and resized with the keyboard. You
can enter this mode through the system menu of the window. The
[keyboardSingleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#keyboardSingleStep-prop)
and
[keyboardPageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#keyboardPageStep-prop)
properties control the distance the widget is moved or resized for each keypress event.
When shift is pressed down page step is used; otherwise single step is used.

You can also change the active window with the keyboard. By pressing the control and tab
keys at the same time, the next (using the current
[WindowOrder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#WindowOrder-enum))
subwindow will be activated. By pressing control, shift, and tab, you will activate the
previous window. This is equivalent to calling
[activateNextSubWindow()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activateNextSubWindow)
and
[activatePreviousSubWindow()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activatePreviousSubWindow).
Note that these shortcuts overrides global shortcuts, but not the
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html)s shortcuts.

### void QMdiSubWindow::setSystemMenu([QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) \**systemMenu*)

Sets *systemMenu* as the current system menu for this subwindow.

By default, each [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html)
has a standard system menu.

QActions for the system menu created by
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) will
automatically be updated depending on the current window state; e.g., the minimize
action will be disabled after the window is minimized.

QActions added by the user are not updated by
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html).

[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) takes ownership
of *systemMenu*; you do not have to delete it. Any existing menus will be deleted.

**See also**
[systemMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#systemMenu)() and
[showSystemMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#showSystemMenu)().

PythonQt.Qt.QMenu.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/fusion-menu.png)

A menu widget is a selection menu. It can be either a pull-down menu in a menu bar or a
standalone context menu. Pull-down menus are shown by the menu bar when the user clicks
on the respective item or presses the specified shortcut key. Use
[QMenuBar::addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html#addMenu)() to
insert a menu into a menu bar. Context menus are usually invoked by some special
keyboard key or by right-clicking. They can be executed either asynchronously with
[popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#popup)() or synchronously with
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#exec)(). Menus can also be invoked
in response to button presses; these are just like context menus except for how they are
invoked.

### Actions

A menu consists of a list of action items. Actions are added with the
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addAction)(),
[addActions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#addActions)() and
[insertAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#insertAction)()
functions. An action is represented vertically and rendered by
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html). In addition, actions can have
a text label, an optional icon drawn on the very left side, and shortcut key sequence
such as "Ctrl\+X".

The existing actions held by a menu can be found with
[actions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#actions)().

There are four kinds of action items: separators, actions that show a submenu, widgets,
and actions that perform an action. Separators are inserted with
[addSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addSeparator)(), submenus
with [addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addMenu)(), and all other
items are considered action items.

When inserting action items you usually specify a receiver and a slot. The receiver will
be notified whenever the item is
[triggered()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#triggered). In addition,
QMenu provides two signals,
[triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#triggered)() and
[hovered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#hovered)(), which signal the
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) that was triggered from the
menu.

You clear a menu with [clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#clear)() and
remove individual action items with
[removeAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#removeAction)().

A QMenu can also provide a tear-off menu. A tear-off menu is a top-level window that
contains a copy of the menu. This makes it possible for the user to "tear off"
frequently used menus and position them in a convenient place on the screen. If you want
this functionality for a particular menu, insert a tear-off handle with
[setTearOffEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#tearOffEnabled-prop)().
When using tear-off menus, bear in mind that the concept isn't typically used on
Microsoft Windows so some users may not be familiar with it. Consider using a
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) instead.

Widgets can be inserted into menus with the
[QWidgetAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html) class. Instances
of this class are used to hold widgets, and are inserted into menus with the
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addAction)() overload that
takes a [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html). If the
[QWidgetAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html) fires the
[triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#triggered)() signal, the menu
will close.

**Warning:** To make QMenu visible on the screen,
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#exec)() or
[popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#popup)() should be used instead of
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)().

### QMenu on macOS with Qt Build Against Cocoa

QMenu can be inserted only once in a menu/menubar. Subsequent insertions will have no
effect or will result in a disabled menu item.

See the
[Menus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-mainwindows-menus-example.html)
example for an example of how to use
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html) and QMenu in your
application.

**Important inherited functions:**
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addAction)(),
[removeAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#removeAction)(),
[clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#clear)(),
[addSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addSeparator)(), and
[addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addMenu)().

PythonQt.Qt.QMenu.exec.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \*QMenu::exec()

Executes this menu synchronously.

This is equivalent to `exec(pos())`.

This returns the triggered [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) in
either the popup menu or one of its submenus, or `nullptr` if no item was triggered
(normally because the user pressed Esc).

In most situations you'll want to specify the position yourself, for example, the
current mouse position:

```
exec(QCursor::pos());
```

or aligned to a widget:

```
exec(somewidget.mapToGlobal(QPoint(0,0)));
```

or in reaction to a [QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html)
\*e:

```
exec(e->globalPos());
```

### [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \*QMenu::exec(const [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) \&*p*, [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \**action* \= nullptr)

This is an overloaded function.

Executes this menu synchronously.

Pops up the menu so that the action *action* will be at the specified *global* position
*p*. To translate a widget's local coordinates into global coordinates, use
[QWidget::mapToGlobal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mapToGlobal)().

This returns the triggered [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) in
either the popup menu or one of its submenus, or `nullptr` if no item was triggered
(normally because the user pressed Esc).

Note that all signals are emitted as usual. If you connect a
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) to a slot and call the menu's
exec(), you get the result both via the signal-slot connection and in the return value
of exec().

Common usage is to position the menu at the current mouse position:

```
exec(QCursor::pos());
```

or aligned to a widget:

```
exec(somewidget.mapToGlobal(QPoint(0, 0)));
```

or in reaction to a [QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html)
\*e:

```
exec(e->globalPos());
```

When positioning a menu with exec() or
[popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#popup)(), bear in mind that you
cannot rely on the menu's current
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#size-prop)(). For performance
reasons, the menu adapts its size only when necessary. So in many cases, the size before
and after the show is different. Instead, use
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#sizeHint)() which calculates
the proper size depending on the menu's current contents.

**See also** [popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#popup)() and
[QWidget::mapToGlobal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mapToGlobal)().

### `[static]` [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \*QMenu::exec([QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \*\> *actions*, const [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) \&*pos*, [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \**at* \= nullptr, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**parent* \= nullptr)

This is an overloaded function.

Executes a menu synchronously.

The menu's actions are specified by the list of *actions*. The menu will pop up so that
the specified action, *at*, appears at global position *pos*. If *at* is not specified
then the menu appears at position *pos*. *parent* is the menu's parent widget;
specifying the parent will provide context when *pos* alone is not enough to decide
where the menu should go (e.g., with multiple desktops or when the parent is embedded in
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html)).

The function returns the triggered
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) in either the popup menu or
one of its submenus, or `nullptr` if no item was triggered (normally because the user
pressed Esc).

This is equivalent to:

```
QMenu menu;
QAction *at = actions[0]; // Assumes actions is not empty
for (QAction *a : qAsConst(actions))
    menu.addAction(a);
menu.exec(pos, at);
```

**See also** [popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#popup)() and
[QWidget::mapToGlobal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mapToGlobal)().

### `[signal]` void QMenu::hovered([QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \**action*)

This signal is emitted when a menu action is highlighted; *action* is the action that

### `[signal]` void QMenu::triggered([QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \**action*)

Normally, you connect each menu action's
[triggered()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#triggered) signal to its

PythonQt.Qt.QMenuBar.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A menu bar consists of a list of pull-down menu items. You add menu items with
[addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html#addMenu)(). For example,
assuming that `menubar` is a pointer to a QMenuBar and `fileMenu` is a pointer to a
[QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html), the following statement inserts
the menu into the menu bar:

```
menubar->addMenu(fileMenu);
```

The ampersand in the menu item's text sets Alt\+F as a shortcut for this menu. (You can
use "\&\&" to get a real ampersand in the menu bar.)

There is no need to lay out a menu bar. It automatically sets its own geometry to the
top of the parent widget and changes it appropriately whenever the parent is resized.

### Usage

In most main window style applications you would use the
[menuBar()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#menuBar) function
provided in [QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html), adding
[QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html)s to the menu bar and adding
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html)s to the pop-up menus.

Example (from the
[Menus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-mainwindows-menus-example.html)
example):

```
    fileMenu = menuBar()->addMenu(tr("&File"));
    fileMenu->addAction(newAct);
```

Menu items may be removed with
[removeAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#removeAction)().

Widgets can be added to menus by using instances of the
[QWidgetAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html) class to hold
them. These actions can then be inserted into menus in the usual way; see the
[QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) documentation for more details.

### Platform Dependent Look and Feel

Different platforms have different requirements for the appearance of menu bars and
their behavior when the user interacts with them. For example, Windows systems are often
configured so that the underlined character mnemonics that indicate keyboard shortcuts
for items in the menu bar are only shown when the **Alt** key is pressed.

### QMenuBar as a Global Menu Bar

On macOS and on certain Linux desktop environments such as Ubuntu Unity, QMenuBar is a
wrapper for using the system-wide menu bar. If you have multiple menu bars in one dialog
the outermost menu bar (normally inside a widget with widget flag
[Qt::Window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum)) will be used
for the system-wide menu bar.

Qt for macOS also provides a menu bar merging feature to make QMenuBar conform more
closely to accepted macOS menu bar layout. The merging functionality is based on string
matching the title of a [QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) entry.
These strings are translated (using
[QObject::tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)()) in the "QMenuBar"
context. If an entry is moved its slots will still fire as if it was in the original
place. The table below outlines the strings looked for and where the entry is placed if
matched:

| String matches | Placement | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| about.\* | Application Menu \| About \<application name\> | The application name is fetched from the `Info.plist` file (see note below). If this entry is not found no About item will appear in the Application Menu. |
| config, options, setup, settings or preferences | Application Menu \| Preferences | If this entry is not found the Settings item will be disabled |
| quit or exit | Application Menu \| Quit \<application name\> | If this entry is not found a default Quit item will be created to call [QCoreApplication::quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)() |

You can override this behavior by using the
[QAction::menuRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#menuRole-prop)()
property.

If you want all windows in a Mac application to share one menu bar, you must create a
menu bar that does not have a parent. Create a parent-less menu bar this way:

```
QMenuBar *menuBar = new QMenuBar(nullptr);
```

**Note:** Do *not* call
[QMainWindow::menuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#menuBar)() to
create the shared menu bar, because that menu bar will have the
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) as its parent. That
menu bar would only be displayed for the parent
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html).

**Note:** The text used for the application name in the macOS menu bar is obtained from
the value set in the `Info.plist` file in the application's bundle. See [Qt for macOS \-
Deployment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/macos-deployment.html) for more
information.

**Note:** On Linux, if the com.canonical.AppMenu.Registrar service is available on the
D-Bus session bus, then Qt will communicate with it to install the application's menus
into the global menu bar, as described.

### Examples

The [Menus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-mainwindows-menus-example.html)
example shows how to use QMenuBar and
[QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html). The other [main window
application examples](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/examples-mainwindow.html) also
provide menus using these classes.

### template \<typename Obj, typename PointerToMemberFunctionOrFunctor\> [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \*QMenuBar::addAction(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, const Obj \**receiver*, PointerToMemberFunctionOrFunctor *method*)

This convenience function creates a new action with the given *text*. The action's
[triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html#triggered)() signal is

### nativeMenuBar : bool

This property holds whether or not a menubar will be used as a native menubar on
platforms that support it

This property specifies whether or not the menubar should be used as a native menubar on
platforms that support it. The currently supported platforms are macOS, and Linux
desktops which use the com.canonical.dbusmenu D-Bus interface (such as Ubuntu Unity). If
this property is `true`, the menubar is used in the native menubar and is not in the
window of its parent; if `false` the menubar remains in the window. On other platforms,
setting this attribute has no effect, and reading this attribute will always return
`false`.

The default is to follow whether the
[Qt::AA\_DontUseNativeMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ApplicationAttribute-enum)
attribute is set for the application. Explicitly setting this property overrides the
presence (or absence) of the attribute.

This property was introduced in Qt 4.6.

PythonQt.Qt.QMessageAuthenticationCode.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QMessageAuthenticationCode supports all cryptographic hashes which are supported by
[QCryptographicHash](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcryptographichash.html).

To generate message authentication code, pass hash algorithm
[QCryptographicHash::Algorithm](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcryptographichash.html#Algorithm-enum)
to constructor, then set key and message by
[setKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#setKey)()
and
[addData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#addData)()
functions. Result can be acquired by
[result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#result)()
function.

```
    QByteArray key = "key";
    QByteArray message = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    ...
    QMessageAuthenticationCode code(QCryptographicHash::Sha1);
    code.setKey(key);
    code.addData(message);
    code.result().toHex();      // returns "de7c9b85b8b78aa6bc8a7a36f70a90701c9db4d9"
```

Alternatively, this effect can be achieved by providing message, key and method to
[hash](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#hash)()
method.

```
    QMessageAuthenticationCode::hash(message, key, QCryptographicHash::Sha1).toHex();
```

PythonQt.Qt.QMessageBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A message box displays a primary
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#text-prop) to alert the user
to a situation, an [informative
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#informativeText-prop) to
further explain the alert or to ask the user a question, and an optional [detailed
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#detailedText-prop) to provide
even more data if the user requests it. A message box can also display an
[icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#icon-prop) and [standard
buttons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#standardButtons-prop) for
accepting a user response.

Two APIs for using QMessageBox are provided, the property-based API, and the static
functions. Calling one of the static functions is the simpler approach, but it is less
flexible than using the property-based API, and the result is less informative. Using
the property-based API is recommended.

### The Property-based API

To use the property-based API, construct an instance of QMessageBox, set the desired
properties, and call [exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#exec)()
to show the message. The simplest configuration is to set only the [message
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#text-prop) property.

```
QMessageBox msgBox;
msgBox.setText("The document has been modified.");
msgBox.exec();
```

The user must click the **OK** button to dismiss the message box. The rest of the GUI is
blocked until the message box is dismissed.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/msgbox1.png)

A better approach than just alerting the user to an event is to also ask the user what
to do about it. Store the question in the [informative
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#informativeText-prop)
property, and set the [standard
buttons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#standardButtons-prop)
property to the set of buttons you want as the set of user responses. The buttons are
specified by combining values from
[StandardButtons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#StandardButton-enum)
using the bitwise OR operator. The display order for the buttons is platform-dependent.
For example, on Windows, **Save** is displayed to the left of **Cancel**, whereas on Mac
OS, the order is reversed.

Mark one of your standard buttons to be your [default
button](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#defaultButton).

```
QMessageBox msgBox;
msgBox.setText("The document has been modified.");
msgBox.setInformativeText("Do you want to save your changes?");
msgBox.setStandardButtons(QMessageBox::Save | QMessageBox::Discard | QMessageBox::Cancel);
msgBox.setDefaultButton(QMessageBox::Save);
int ret = msgBox.exec();
```

This is the approach recommended in the [macOS
Guidelines](http://developer.apple.com/library/mac/documentation/UserExperience/Conceptual/AppleHIGuidelines/Windows/Windows.html#//apple_ref/doc/uid/20000961-BABCAJID).
Similar guidelines apply for the other platforms, but note the different ways the
[informative
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#informativeText-prop) is
handled for different platforms.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/msgbox2.png)

The [exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#exec)() slot returns the
[StandardButtons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#StandardButton-enum)
value of the button that was clicked.

```
switch (ret) {
  case QMessageBox::Save:
      // Save was clicked
      break;
  case QMessageBox::Discard:
      // Don't Save was clicked
      break;
  case QMessageBox::Cancel:
      // Cancel was clicked
      break;
  default:
      // should never be reached
      break;
}
```

To give the user more information to help him answer the question, set the [detailed
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#detailedText-prop) property.
If the [detailed
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#detailedText-prop) property is
set, the **Show Details...** button will be shown.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/msgbox3.png)

Clicking the **Show Details...** button displays the detailed text.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/msgbox4.png)

#### Rich Text and the Text Format Property

The [detailed
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#detailedText-prop) property is
always interpreted as plain text. The [main
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#text-prop) and [informative
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#informativeText-prop)
properties can be either plain text or rich text. These strings are interpreted
according to the setting of the [text
format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#textFormat-prop) property.
The default setting is
[auto-text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFormat-enum).

Note that for some plain text strings containing XML meta-characters, the auto-text
[rich text detection
test](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt-sub-qtgui.html#mightBeRichText) may fail
causing your plain text string to be interpreted incorrectly as rich text. In these rare
cases, use
[Qt::convertFromPlainText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt-sub-qtgui.html#convertFromPlainText)()
to convert your plain text string to a visually equivalent rich text string, or set the
[text format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#textFormat-prop)
property explicitly with
[setTextFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#textFormat-prop)().

#### Severity Levels and the Icon and Pixmap Properties

QMessageBox supports four predefined message severity levels, or message types, which
really only differ in the predefined icon they each show. Specify one of the four
predefined message types by setting the
[icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#icon-prop) property to one of
the [predefined icons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum).
The following rules are guidelines:

|  | [Question](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum) | For asking a question during normal operations. |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | [Information](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum) | For reporting information about normal operations. |
|  | [Warning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum) | For reporting non-critical errors. |
|  | [Critical](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum) | For reporting critical errors. |

[Predefined icons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum) are
not defined by QMessageBox, but provided by the style. The default value is [No
Icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum). The message boxes
are otherwise the same for all cases. When using a standard icon, use the one
recommended in the table, or use the one recommended by the style guidelines for your
platform. If none of the standard icons is right for your message box, you can use a
custom icon by setting the [icon
pixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#iconPixmap-prop) property
instead of setting the
[icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#icon-prop) property.

In summary, to set an icon, use *either*
[setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#icon-prop)() for one of
the standard icons, *or*
[setIconPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#iconPixmap-prop)()
for a custom icon.

### The Static Functions API

Building message boxes with the static functions API, although convenient, is less
flexible than using the property-based API, because the static function signatures lack
parameters for setting the [informative
text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#informativeText-prop) and
[detailed text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#detailedText-prop)
properties. One work-around for this has been to use the `title` parameter as the
message box main text and the `text` parameter as the message box informative text.
Because this has the obvious drawback of making a less readable message box, platform
guidelines do not recommend it. The *Microsoft Windows User Interface Guidelines*
recommend using the [application
name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#applicationName-prop) as
the [window's
title](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#setWindowTitle), which means
that if you have an informative text in addition to your main text, you must concatenate
it to the `text` parameter.

Note that the static function signatures have changed with respect to their button
parameters, which are now used to set the [standard
buttons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#standardButtons-prop) and
the [default button](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#defaultButton).

Static functions are available for creating
[information](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#information)(),
[question](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#question)(),
[warning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#warning)(), and
[critical](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#critical)() message
boxes.

```
int ret = QMessageBox::warning(this, tr("My Application"),
                               tr("The document has been modified.\n"
                                  "Do you want to save your changes?"),
                               QMessageBox::Save | QMessageBox::Discard
                               | QMessageBox::Cancel,
                               QMessageBox::Save);
```

The [Standard
Dialogs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-dialogs-standarddialogs-example.html)
example shows how to use QMessageBox and the other built-in Qt dialogs.

### Advanced Usage

If the [standard
buttons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#StandardButton-enum) are
not flexible enough for your message box, you can use the
[addButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#addButton)() overload
that takes a text and a
[ButtonRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#ButtonRole-enum) to add
custom buttons. The
[ButtonRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#ButtonRole-enum) is
used by QMessageBox to determine the ordering of the buttons on screen (which varies
according to the platform). You can test the value of
[clickedButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#clickedButton)()
after calling [exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#exec)(). For
example,

```
QMessageBox msgBox;
QPushButton *connectButton = msgBox.addButton(tr("Connect"), QMessageBox::ActionRole);
QPushButton *abortButton = msgBox.addButton(QMessageBox::Abort);

msgBox.exec();

if (msgBox.clickedButton() == connectButton) {
    // connect
} else if (msgBox.clickedButton() == abortButton) {
    // abort
}
```

### Default and Escape Keys

The default button (i.e., the button activated when **Enter** is pressed) can be
specified using
[setDefaultButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#setDefaultButton)().
If a default button is not specified, QMessageBox tries to find one based on the [button
roles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#ButtonRole-enum) of the
buttons used in the message box.

The escape button (the button activated when **Esc** is pressed) can be specified using
[setEscapeButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#setEscapeButton)().
If an escape button is not specified, QMessageBox tries to find one using these rules:

1. If there is only one button, it is the button activated when **Esc** is pressed.
2. If there is a [Cancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#StandardButton-enum) button, it is the button activated when **Esc** is pressed.
3. If there is exactly one button having either [the Reject role](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#ButtonRole-enum) or the [the No role](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#ButtonRole-enum), it is the button activated when **Esc** is pressed.

When an escape button can't be determined using these rules, pressing **Esc** has no
effect.

### `[static]` void QMessageBox::about([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**parent*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*title*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*)

Displays a simple about box with title *title* and text *text*. The about box's parent
is *parent*.

about() looks for a suitable icon in four locations:

1. It prefers [parent-\>icon()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowIcon-prop) if that exists.
2. If not, it tries the top-level widget containing *parent*.
3. If that fails, it tries the [active window.](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activeWindow)
4. As a last resort it uses the Information icon.

The about box has a single button labelled "OK". On macOS, the about box is popped up as
a modeless window; on other platforms, it is currently application modal.

**See also**
[QWidget::windowIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowIcon-prop)()
and
[QApplication::activeWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activeWindow)().

standard buttons, this function returns a
[StandardButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#StandardButton-enum)
value indicating the standard button that was clicked. When using
[QMessageBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html) with custom buttons,
this function returns an opaque value; use
[clickedButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#clickedButton)() to
determine which button was clicked.

**Note:** The [result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#result)()
function returns also
[StandardButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#StandardButton-enum)
value instead of
[QDialog::DialogCode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#DialogCode-enum).

Users cannot interact with any other window in the same application until they close the
dialog, either by clicking a button or by using a mechanism provided by the window
system.

**See also** [show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() and
[result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#result)().

This property holds the message box's icon

The icon of the message box can be specified with one of the values:

- [QMessageBox::NoIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum)
- [QMessageBox::Question](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum)

[QMessageBox::NoIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#Icon-enum).

style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#style). You can also set a custom
pixmap for the icon by setting the [icon
pixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessagebox.html#iconPixmap-prop) property.

**Warning:** Do not delete *parent* during the execution of the dialog. If you want to

## Detailed Description

Class information items are simple *name*\--*value* pairs that are specified using
[Q\_CLASSINFO](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_CLASSINFO)() in the
source code. The information can be retrieved using
[name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaclassinfo.html#name)() and
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaclassinfo.html#value)(). For example:

```
class MyClass
{
    Q_OBJECT
    Q_CLASSINFO("author", "Sabrina Schweinsteiger")
    Q_CLASSINFO("url", "http://doc.moosesoft.co.uk/1.0/")

public:
    ...
};
```

This mechanism is free for you to use in your Qt applications. Qt doesn't use it for any
of its classes.

enumerator's name. The enumerator's keys (names of each enumerated item) are returned by
[key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#key)(); use
[keyCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#keyCount)() to find the
number of keys. [isFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#isFlag)()
returns whether the enumerator is meant to be used as a flag, meaning that its values
can be combined using the OR operator.

The conversion functions
[keyToValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#keyToValue)(),
[valueToKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#valueToKey)(),
[keysToValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#keysToValue)(), and
[valueToKeys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#valueToKeys)() allow
conversion between the integer representation of an enumeration or set value and its
literal representation. The
[scope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#scope)() function returns the
class scope this enumerator was declared in.

PythonQt.Qt.QMetaMethod.tag.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### const char \*QMetaMethod::tag() const

Returns the tag associated with this method.

Tags are special macros recognized by `moc` that make it possible to add extra
information about a method.

Tag information can be added in the following way in the function declaration:

```
    // In the class MainWindow declaration
    #ifndef Q_MOC_RUN
    // define the tag text as empty, so the compiler doesn't see it
    #  define MY_CUSTOM_TAG
    #endif
    ...
    private slots:
        MY_CUSTOM_TAG void testFunc();
```

and the information can be accessed by using:

```
    MainWindow win;
    win.show();

    int functionIndex = win.metaObject()->indexOfSlot("testFunc()");
    QMetaMethod mm = win.metaObject()->method(functionIndex);
    qDebug() << mm.tag(); // prints MY_CUSTOM_TAG
```

For the moment, `moc` will extract and record all tags, but it will not handle any of
them specially. You can use the tags to annotate your methods differently, and treat
them according to the specific needs of your application.

**Note:** Since Qt 5.0, `moc` expands preprocessor macros, so it is necessary to
surround the definition with `#ifndef` `Q_MOC_RUN`, as shown in the example above. This
was not required in Qt 4\. The code as shown above works with Qt 4 too.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The Qt [Meta-Object System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/metaobjects.html) in Qt
is responsible for the signals and slots inter-object communication mechanism, runtime
type information, and the Qt property system. A single QMetaObject instance is created
for each [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass that is
used in an application, and this instance stores all the meta-information for the
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass. This object is
available as
[QObject::metaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#metaObject)().

This class is not normally required for application programming, but it is useful if you
write meta-applications, such as scripting engines or GUI builders.

The functions you are most likely to find useful are these:

- [className](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#className)() returns the name of a class.
- [superClass](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#superClass)() returns the superclass's meta-object.
- [method](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#method)() and [methodCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#methodCount)() provide information about a class's meta-methods (signals, slots and other [invokable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_INVOKABLE) member functions).
- [enumerator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#enumerator)() and [enumeratorCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#enumeratorCount)() and provide information about a class's enumerators.
- [propertyCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#propertyCount)() and [property](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#property)() provide information about a class's properties.
- [constructor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#constructor)() and [constructorCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#constructorCount)() provide information about a class's meta-constructors.

The index functions
[indexOfConstructor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfConstructor)(),
[indexOfMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfMethod)(),
[indexOfEnumerator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfEnumerator)(),
and
[indexOfProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfProperty)()
map names of constructors, member functions, enumerators, or properties to indexes in
the meta-object. For example, Qt uses
[indexOfMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfMethod)()
internally when you connect a signal to a slot.

Classes can also have a list of *name*\--*value* pairs of additional class information,
stored in [QMetaClassInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaclassinfo.html)
objects. The number of pairs is returned by
[classInfoCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#classInfoCount)(),
single pairs are returned by
[classInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#classInfo)(), and you
can search for pairs with
[indexOfClassInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfClassInfo)().

**Note:** Operations that use the meta object system are generally thread- safe, as
QMetaObjects are typically static read-only instances generated at compile time.
However, if meta objects are dynamically modified by the application (for instance, when
using [QQmlPropertyMap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qqmlpropertymap.html)), then
the application has to explicitly synchronize access to the respective meta object.

### int QMetaObject::methodCount() const

Returns the number of methods in this class, including the number of methods provided by
each base class. These include signals and slots as well as normal member functions.

Use code like the following to obtain a
[QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) containing the
methods specific to a given class:

```
const QMetaObject* metaObject = obj->metaObject();
QStringList methods;
for(int i = metaObject->methodOffset(); i < metaObject->methodCount(); ++i)
    methods << QString::fromLatin1(metaObject->method(i).methodSignature());
```

**See also** [method](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#method)(),
[methodOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#methodOffset)(), and
[indexOfMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfMethod)().

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QMetaObject::normalizedSignature(const char \**method*)

Normalizes the signature of the given *method*.

Qt uses normalized signatures to decide whether two given signals and slots are
compatible. Normalization reduces whitespace to a minimum, moves 'const' to the front
where appropriate, removes 'const' from value types and replaces const references with
values.

**See also**
[checkConnectArgs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#checkConnectArgs)()
and
[normalizedType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#normalizedType)().

PythonQt.Qt.QMetaProperty.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Property meta-data is obtained from an object's meta-object. See
[QMetaObject::property](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#property)()
and
[QMetaObject::propertyCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#propertyCount)()
for details.

### Property Meta-Data

A property has a [name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#name)()
and a [type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#type)(), as well as
various attributes that specify its behavior:
[isReadable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isReadable)(),
[isWritable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isWritable)(),
[isDesignable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isDesignable)(),
[isScriptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isScriptable)(),
[revision](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#revision)(), and
[isStored](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isStored)().

If the property is an enumeration,
[isEnumType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isEnumType)() returns
`true`; if the property is an enumeration that is also a flag (i.e. its values can be
combined using the OR operator),
[isEnumType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isEnumType)() and
[isFlagType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isFlagType)() both
return true. The enumerator for these types is available from
[enumerator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#enumerator)().

The property's values are set and retrieved with
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#read)(),
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#write)(), and
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#reset)(); they can also be
changed through [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)'s set and get
functions. See
[QObject::setProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#setProperty)()
and [QObject::property](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#property)() for
details.

### Copying and Assignment

QMetaProperty objects can be copied by value. However, each copy will refer to the same
underlying property meta-data.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The class is used as a helper to marshall types in
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) and in queued
signals and slots connections. It associates a type name to a type so that it can be
created and destructed dynamically at run-time. Declare new types with
[Q\_DECLARE\_METATYPE](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Q_DECLARE_METATYPE)()
to make them available to
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) and other
template-based functions. Call
[qRegisterMetaType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#qRegisterMetaType-1)()
to make types available to non-template based functions, such as the queued signal and
slot connections.

Any class or struct that has a public default constructor, a public copy constructor,
and a public destructor can be registered.

The following code allocates and destructs an instance of `MyClass`:

```
int id = QMetaType::type("MyClass");
if (id != QMetaType::UnknownType) {
    void *myClassPtr = QMetaType::create(id);
    ...
    QMetaType::destroy(id, myClassPtr);
    myClassPtr = 0;
}
```

If we want the stream operators `operator<<()` and `operator>>()` to work on
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) objects that
store custom types, the custom type must provide `operator<<()` and `operator>>()`
operators.

Compares the objects at *lhs* and *rhs*. Both objects need to be of type *typeId*.

PythonQt.Qt.QMetaType.construct.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void \*QMetaType::construct(int *type*, void \**where*, const void \**copy*)

Constructs a value of the given *type* in the existing memory addressed by *where*, that
is a copy of *copy*, and returns *where*. If *copy* is zero, the value is default
constructed.

This is a low-level function for explicitly managing the memory used to store the type.
Consider calling [create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#create)() if
you don't need this level of control (that is, use "new" rather than "placement new").

You must ensure that *where* points to a location that can store a value of type *type*,
and that *where* is suitably aligned. The type's size can be queried by calling
[sizeOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#sizeOf-1)().

The rule of thumb for alignment is that a type is aligned to its natural boundary, which
is the smallest power of 2 that is bigger than the type, unless that alignment is larger
than the maximum useful alignment for the platform. For practical purposes, alignment
larger than 2 \* sizeof(void\*) is only necessary for special hardware instructions
(e.g., aligned SSE loads and stores on x86).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also** [destruct](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#destruct)()
and [sizeOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#sizeOf-1)().

### void \*QMetaType::construct(void \**where*, const void \**copy* \= 0\) const

Constructs a value of the type that this
[QMetaType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html) instance was constructed
for in the existing memory addressed by *where*, that is a copy of *copy*, and returns
*where*. If *copy* is zero, the value is default constructed.

This is a low-level function for explicitly managing the memory used to store the type.
Consider calling [create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#create)() if
you don't need this level of control (that is, use "new" rather than "placement new").

You must ensure that *where* points to a location where the new value can be stored and
that *where* is suitably aligned. The type's size can be queried by calling
[sizeOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#sizeOf-1)().

The rule of thumb for alignment is that a type is aligned to its natural boundary, which
is the smallest power of 2 that is bigger than the type, unless that alignment is larger
than the maximum useful alignment for the platform. For practical purposes, alignment
larger than 2 \* sizeof(void\*) is only necessary for special hardware instructions
(e.g., aligned SSE loads and stores on x86).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

### const [QMetaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html) \*QMetaType::metaObject() const

Returns a [QMetaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html) relative to
this type.

If the type is a pointer type to a subclass of
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html),
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains
[QMetaType::PointerToQObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#TypeFlag-enum)
and this function returns the corresponding
[QMetaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html). This can be used in
combination with
[QMetaObject::newInstance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#newInstance)()
to create QObjects of this type.

If the type is a [Q\_GADGET](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_GADGET),
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains
[QMetaType::IsGadget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#TypeFlag-enum).
If the type is a pointer to a
[Q\_GADGET](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_GADGET),
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains
[QMetaType::PointerToGadget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#TypeFlag-enum).
In both cases, this function returns its
[QMetaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html). This can be used to
retrieve [QMetaMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetamethod.html) and
[QMetaProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html) and use them on a
pointer of this type for example, as given by QVariant::data().

If the type is an enumeration,
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains
[QMetaType::IsEnumeration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#TypeFlag-enum).
In this case, this function returns the
[QMetaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html) of the enclosing

[Q\_ENUM](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_ENUM) or `nullptr`
otherwise.
