### `[pure virtual]` void QPaintEngine::updateState(const [QPaintEngineState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html) \&*state*)

Reimplement this function to update the state of a paint engine.

When implemented, this function is responsible for checking the paint engine's current
*state* and update the properties that are changed. Use the
[QPaintEngineState::state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#state)()
function to find out which properties that must be updated, then use the corresponding
[get function](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#getfunction) to
retrieve the current values for the given properties.

**See also**
[QPaintEngineState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QPaintEngineState.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QPaintEngineState records which properties that have changed since the last time the
paint engine was updated, as well as their current value.

Which properties that have changed can at any time be retrieved using the
[state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#state)() function.
This function returns an instance of the
[QPaintEngine::DirtyFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum)
type which stores an OR combination of
[QPaintEngine::DirtyFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum)
values. The
[QPaintEngine::DirtyFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum)
enum defines whether a property has changed since the last update or not.

If a property is marked with a dirty flag, its current value can be retrieved using the
corresponding get function:

| Property Flag | Current Property Value |
| --- | --- |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [backgroundBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#backgroundBrush)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyBackgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [backgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#backgroundMode)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [brush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#brush)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyBrushOrigin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [brushOrigin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#brushOrigin)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyClipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) *or* [QPaintEngine::DirtyClipPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [clipOperation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#clipOperation)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyClipPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [clipPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#clipPath)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyClipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [clipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#clipRegion)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyCompositionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [compositionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#compositionMode)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#font)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#transform)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyClipEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [isClipEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#isClipEnabled)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [pen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#pen)() |
| [QPaintEngine::DirtyHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#DirtyFlag-enum) | [renderHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#renderHints)() |

The QPaintEngineState class also provide the
[painter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintenginestate.html#painter)() function
which returns a pointer to the painter that is currently updating the paint engine.

An instance of this class, representing the current state of the active paint engine, is
passed as argument to the
[QPaintEngine::updateState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html#updateState)()
function. The only situation in which you will have to use this class directly is when
implementing your own paint engine.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Paint events are sent to widgets that need to update themselves, for instance when part
of a widget is exposed because a covering widget was moved.

The event contains a
[region](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html#region)() that needs to be
updated, and a [rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html#rect)() that
is the bounding rectangle of that region. Both are provided because many widgets cannot
make much use of [region](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html#region)(),
and [rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html#rect)() can be much
faster than
[region](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html#region)().boundingRect().

### Automatic Clipping

Painting is clipped to
[region](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html#region)() during the
processing of a paint event. This clipping is performed by Qt's paint system and is
independent of any clipping that may be applied to a
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) used to draw on the paint
device.

As a result, the value returned by
[QPainter::clipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#clipRegion)() on
a newly-constructed [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) will
not reflect the clip region that is used by the paint system.

PythonQt.Qt.QPainter.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QPainter provides highly optimized functions to do most of the drawing GUI programs
require. It can draw everything from simple lines to complex shapes like pies and
chords. It can also draw aligned text and pixmaps. Normally, it draws in a "natural"
coordinate system, but it can also do view and world transformation. QPainter can
operate on any object that inherits the
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) class.

The common use of QPainter is inside a widget's paint event: Construct and customize
(e.g. set the pen or the brush) the painter. Then draw. Remember to destroy the QPainter
object after drawing. For example:

```
void SimpleExampleWidget::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *)
{
    QPainter painter(this);
    painter.setPen(Qt::blue);
    painter.setFont(QFont("Arial", 30));
    painter.drawText(rect(), Qt::AlignCenter, "Qt");
}
```

The core functionality of QPainter is drawing, but the class also provide several
functions that allows you to customize QPainter's settings and its rendering quality,
and others that enable clipping. In addition you can control how different shapes are
merged together by specifying the painter's composition mode.

The [isActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#isActive)() function
indicates whether the painter is active. A painter is activated by the
[begin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#begin)() function and the
constructor that takes a
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) argument. The
[end](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#end)() function, and the
destructor, deactivates it.

Together with the [QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html)
and [QPaintEngine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html) classes,
QPainter form the basis for Qt's paint system. QPainter is the class used to perform
drawing operations. [QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html)
represents a device that can be painted on using a QPainter.
[QPaintEngine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintengine.html) provides the
interface that the painter uses to draw onto different types of devices. If the painter
is active, [device](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#device)() returns
the paint device on which the painter paints, and
[paintEngine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#paintEngine)() returns
the paint engine that the painter is currently operating on. For more information, see
the [Paint System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/paintsystem.html).

Sometimes it is desirable to make someone else paint on an unusual
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html). QPainter supports
a static function to do this, setRedirected().

**Warning:** When the paintdevice is a widget, QPainter can only be used inside a
paintEvent() function or in a function called by paintEvent().

### Settings

There are several settings that you can customize to make QPainter draw according to
your preferences:

- [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#font)() is the font used for drawing text. If the painter [isActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#isActive)(), you can retrieve information about the currently set font, and its metrics, using the [fontInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#fontInfo)() and [fontMetrics](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#fontMetrics)() functions respectively.
- [brush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#brush)() defines the color or pattern that is used for filling shapes.
- [pen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#pen)() defines the color or stipple that is used for drawing lines or boundaries.
- [backgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#backgroundMode)() defines whether there is a [background](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#background)() or not, i.e it is either [Qt::OpaqueMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum) or [Qt::TransparentMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum).
- [background](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#background)() only applies when [backgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#backgroundMode)() is [Qt::OpaqueMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum) and [pen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#pen)() is a stipple. In that case, it describes the color of the background pixels in the stipple.
- [brushOrigin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#brushOrigin)() defines the origin of the tiled brushes, normally the origin of widget's background.
- [viewport](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#viewport)(), [window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#window)(), [worldTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#worldTransform)() make up the painter's coordinate transformation system. For more information, see the [Coordinate Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#coordinate-transformations) section and the [Coordinate System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html) documentation.
- [hasClipping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#hasClipping)() tells whether the painter clips at all. (The paint device clips, too.) If the painter clips, it clips to [clipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#clipRegion)().
- [layoutDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#layoutDirection)() defines the layout direction used by the painter when drawing text.
- [worldMatrixEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#worldMatrixEnabled)() tells whether world transformation is enabled.
- [viewTransformEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#viewTransformEnabled)() tells whether view transformation is enabled.

Note that some of these settings mirror settings in some paint devices, e.g.
[QWidget::font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop)(). The
[QPainter::begin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#begin)() function (or
equivalently the QPainter constructor) copies these attributes from the paint device.

You can at any time save the QPainter's state by calling the
[save](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#save)() function which saves all
the available settings on an internal stack. The
[restore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#restore)() function pops them
back.

### Drawing Pixmaps and Images

There are functions to draw pixmaps/images, namely
[drawPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPixmap)(),
[drawImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawImage)() and
[drawTiledPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawTiledPixmap)().
Both [drawPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPixmap)() and
[drawImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawImage)() produce the
same result, except that
[drawPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPixmap)() is faster
on-screen while
[drawImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawImage)() may be faster
on a [QPrinter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html) or other devices.

There is a [drawPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPicture)()
function that draws the contents of an entire
[QPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html). The
[drawPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPicture)() function
is the only function that disregards all the painter's settings as
[QPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html) has its own settings.

#### Drawing High Resolution Versions of Pixmaps and Images

High resolution versions of pixmaps have a *device pixel ratio* value larger than 1 (see
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html),
[QPixmap::devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#devicePixelRatio)()).
Should it match the value of the underlying
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html), it is drawn
directly onto the device with no additional transformation applied.

This is for example the case when drawing a
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) of 64x64 pixels size with a
device pixel ratio of 2 onto a high DPI screen which also has a device pixel ratio of
2\. Note that the pixmap is then effectively 32x32 pixels in *user space*. Code paths in
Qt that calculate layout geometry based on the pixmap size will use this size. The net
effect of this is that the pixmap is displayed as high DPI pixmap rather than a large
pixmap.

### Rendering Quality

To get the optimal rendering result using QPainter, you should use the platform
independent [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) as paint device;
i.e. using [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) will ensure that the
result has an identical pixel representation on any platform.

The QPainter class also provides a means of controlling the rendering quality through
its [RenderHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum) enum
and the support for floating point precision: All the functions for drawing primitives
has a floating point version. These are often used in combination with the
[QPainter::Antialiasing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum)
render hint.

|  | **Concentric Circles Example** The [Concentric Circles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-concentriccircles-example.html) example shows the improved rendering quality that can be obtained using floating point precision and anti-aliasing when drawing custom widgets.  The application's main window displays several widgets which are drawn using the various combinations of precision and anti-aliasing. |
| --- | --- |

The [RenderHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum) enum
specifies flags to QPainter that may or may not be respected by any given engine.
[QPainter::Antialiasing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum)
indicates that the engine should antialias edges of primitives if possible,
[QPainter::TextAntialiasing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum)
indicates that the engine should antialias text if possible, and the
[QPainter::SmoothPixmapTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum)
indicates that the engine should use a smooth pixmap transformation algorithm.

The [renderHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#renderHints)()
function returns a flag that specifies the rendering hints that are set for this
painter. Use the
[setRenderHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setRenderHint)()
function to set or clear the currently set
[RenderHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum).

### Coordinate Transformations

Normally, the QPainter operates on the device's own coordinate system (usually pixels),
but QPainter has good support for coordinate transformations.

| nop | [rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#rotate)() | [scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#scale)() | [translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#translate)() |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |  |

The most commonly used transformations are scaling, rotation, translation and shearing.
Use the [scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#scale)() function to
scale the coordinate system by a given offset, the
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#rotate)() function to rotate
it clockwise and
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#translate)() to translate
it (i.e. adding a given offset to the points). You can also twist the coordinate system
around the origin using the
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#shear)() function. See the
[Affine
Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-affine-example.html)
example for a visualization of a sheared coordinate system.

See also the
[Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-transformations-example.html)
example which shows how transformations influence the way that QPainter renders graphics
primitives. In particular it shows how the order of transformations affects the result.

| **Affine Transformations Example** The [Affine Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-affine-example.html) example shows Qt's ability to perform affine transformations on painting operations. The demo also allows the user to experiment with the transformation operations and see the results immediately. |  |
| --- | --- |

All the tranformation operations operate on the transformation
[worldTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#worldTransform)(). A
matrix transforms a point in the plane to another point. For more information about the
transformation matrix, see the [Coordinate
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html) and
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) documentation.

The
[setWorldTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setWorldTransform)()
function can replace or add to the currently set
[worldTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#worldTransform)(). The
[resetTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#resetTransform)()
function resets any transformations that were made using
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#translate)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#scale)(),
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#shear)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#rotate)(),
[setWorldTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setWorldTransform)(),
[setViewport](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setViewport)() and
[setWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setWindow)() functions. The
[deviceTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#deviceTransform)()
returns the matrix that transforms from logical coordinates to device coordinates of the
platform dependent paint device. The latter function is only needed when using platform
painting commands on the platform dependent handle, and the platform does not do
transformations nativly.

When drawing with QPainter, we specify points using logical coordinates which then are
converted into the physical coordinates of the paint device. The mapping of the logical
coordinates to the physical coordinates are handled by QPainter's
[combinedTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#combinedTransform)(),
a combination of [viewport](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#viewport)()
and [window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#window)() and
[worldTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#worldTransform)(). The
[viewport](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#viewport)() represents the
physical coordinates specifying an arbitrary rectangle, the
[window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#window)() describes the same
rectangle in logical coordinates, and the
[worldTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#worldTransform)() is
identical with the transformation matrix.

See also [Coordinate System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html)

### Clipping

QPainter can clip any drawing operation to a rectangle, a region, or a vector path. The
current clip is available using the functions
[clipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#clipRegion)() and
[clipPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#clipPath)(). Whether paths
or regions are preferred (faster) depends on the underlying
[paintEngine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#paintEngine)(). For
example, the [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) paint engine
prefers paths while the X11 paint engine prefers regions. Setting a clip is done in the
painters logical coordinates.

After QPainter's clipping, the paint device may also clip. For example, most widgets
clip away the pixels used by child widgets, and most printers clip away an area near the
edges of the paper. This additional clipping is not reflected by the return value of
[clipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#clipRegion)() or
[hasClipping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#hasClipping)().

### Composition Modes

QPainter provides the
[CompositionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#CompositionMode-enum)
enum which defines the Porter-Duff rules for digital image compositing; it describes a
model for combining the pixels in one image, the source, with the pixels in another
image, the destination.

The two most common forms of composition are
[Source](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#CompositionMode-enum) and
[SourceOver](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#CompositionMode-enum).
[Source](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#CompositionMode-enum) is used
to draw opaque objects onto a paint device. In this mode, each pixel in the source
replaces the corresponding pixel in the destination. In
[SourceOver](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#CompositionMode-enum)
composition mode, the source object is transparent and is drawn on top of the
destination.

Note that composition transformation operates pixelwise. For that reason, there is a
difference between using the graphic primitive itself and its bounding rectangle: The
bounding rect contains pixels with alpha \=\= 0 (i.e the pixels surrounding the
primitive). These pixels will overwrite the other image's pixels, effectively clearing
those, while the primitive only overwrites its own area.

|  | **Composition Modes Example** The [Composition Modes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-composition-example.html) example, available in Qt's examples directory, allows you to experiment with the various composition modes and see the results immediately. |
| --- | --- |

### Limitations

If you are using coordinates with Qt's raster-based paint engine, it is important to
note that, while coordinates greater than \+/- 215 can be used, any painting performed
with coordinates outside this range is not guaranteed to be shown; the drawing may be
clipped. This is due to the use of `short int` in the implementation.

The outlines generated by Qt's stroker are only an approximation when dealing with
curved shapes. It is in most cases impossible to represent the outline of a bezier curve
segment using another bezier curve segment, and so Qt approximates the curve outlines by
using several smaller curves. For performance reasons there is a limit to how many
curves Qt uses for these outlines, and thus when using large pen widths or scales the
outline error increases. To generate outlines with smaller errors it is possible to use
the [QPainterPathStroker](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html)
class, which has the setCurveThreshold member function which let's the user specify the
error tolerance. Another workaround is to convert the paths to polygons first and then
draw the polygons instead.

### Performance

QPainter is a rich framework that allows developers to do a great variety of graphical
operations, such as gradients, composition modes and vector graphics. And QPainter can
do this across a variety of different hardware and software stacks. Naturally the
underlying combination of hardware and software has some implications for performance,
and ensuring that every single operation is fast in combination with all the various
combinations of composition modes, brushes, clipping, transformation, etc, is close to
an impossible task because of the number of permutations. As a compromise we have
selected a subset of the QPainter API and backends, where performance is guaranteed to
be as good as we can sensibly get it for the given combination of hardware and software.

The backends we focus on as high-performance engines are:

- Raster \- This backend implements all rendering in pure software and is always used to render into QImages. For optimal performance only use the format types [QImage::Format\_ARGB32\_Premultiplied](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum), [QImage::Format\_RGB32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum) or [QImage::Format\_RGB16](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum). Any other format, including [QImage::Format\_ARGB32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum), has significantly worse performance. This engine is used by default for [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html).
- OpenGL 2.0 (ES) \- This backend is the primary backend for hardware accelerated graphics. It can be run on desktop machines and embedded devices supporting the OpenGL 2.0 or OpenGL/ES 2.0 specification. This includes most graphics chips produced in the last couple of years. The engine can be enabled by using QPainter onto a [QOpenGLWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwidget.html).

These operations are:

- Simple transformations, meaning translation and scaling, pluss 0, 90, 180, 270 degree rotations.
- `drawPixmap()` in combination with simple transformations and opacity with non-smooth transformation mode (`QPainter::SmoothPixmapTransform` not enabled as a render hint).
- Rectangle fills with solid color, two-color linear gradients and simple transforms.
- Rectangular clipping with simple transformations and intersect clip.
- Composition Modes `QPainter::CompositionMode_Source` and [QPainter::CompositionMode\_SourceOver](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#CompositionMode-enum).
- Rounded rectangle filling using solid color and two-color linear gradients fills.
- 3x3 patched pixmaps, via qDrawBorderPixmap.

This list gives an indication of which features to safely use in an application where
performance is critical. For certain setups, other operations may be fast too, but
before making extensive use of them, it is recommended to benchmark and verify them on
the system where the software will run in the end. There are also cases where expensive
operations are ok to use, for instance when the result is cached in a
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QPainter.begin.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QPainter::begin([QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) \**device*)

Begins painting the paint *device* and returns `true` if successful; otherwise returns
`false`.

Notice that all painter settings
([setPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setPen)(),
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setBrush)() etc.) are reset
to default values when begin() is called.

The errors that can occur are serious problems, such as these:

```
painter->begin(0); // impossible - paint device cannot be 0

QPixmap image(0, 0);
painter->begin(&image); // impossible - image.isNull() == true;

painter->begin(myWidget);
painter2->begin(myWidget); // impossible - only one painter at a time
```

Note that most of the time, you can use one of the constructors instead of begin(), and
that [end](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#end)() is automatically done
at destruction.

**Warning:** A paint device can only be painted by one painter at a time.

**Warning:** Painting on a [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) with
the format
[QImage::Format\_Indexed8](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum)
is not supported.

**See also** [end](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#end)() and
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#QPainter)().

PythonQt.Qt.QPainter.beginNativePainting.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QPainter::beginNativePainting()

Flushes the painting pipeline and prepares for the user issuing commands directly to the
underlying graphics context. Must be followed by a call to
[endNativePainting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#endNativePainting)().

Note that only the states the underlying paint engine changes will be reset to their
respective default states. The states we reset may change from release to release. The
following states are currently reset in the OpenGL 2 engine:

- blending is disabled
- the depth, stencil and scissor tests are disabled
- the active texture unit is reset to 0
- the depth mask, depth function and the clear depth are reset to their default values
- the stencil mask, stencil operation and stencil function are reset to their default values
- the current color is reset to solid white

If, for example, the OpenGL polygon mode is changed by the user inside a
beginNativePaint()/[endNativePainting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#endNativePainting)()
block, it will not be reset to the default state by
[endNativePainting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#endNativePainting)().
Here is an example that shows intermixing of painter commands and raw OpenGL commands:

```
QPainter painter(this);
painter.fillRect(0, 0, 128, 128, Qt::green);
painter.beginNativePainting();

glEnable(GL_SCISSOR_TEST);
glScissor(0, 0, 64, 64);

glClearColor(1, 0, 0, 1);
glClear(GL_COLOR_BUFFER_BIT);

glDisable(GL_SCISSOR_TEST);

painter.endNativePainting();
```

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[endNativePainting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#endNativePainting)().

### void QPainter::drawArc(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*, int *startAngle*, int *spanAngle*)

Draws the arc defined by the given *rectangle*, *startAngle* and *spanAngle*.

The *startAngle* and *spanAngle* must be specified in 1/16th of a degree, i.e. a full

| --- | --- |

### void QPainter::drawConvexPolygon(const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \**points*, int *pointCount*)

Draws the convex polygon defined by the first *pointCount* points in the array *points*
using the current pen.

|  | ``` static const QPointF points[4] = {     QPointF(10.0, 80.0),     QPointF(20.0, 10.0),     QPointF(80.0, 30.0),     QPointF(90.0, 70.0) };  QPainter painter(this); painter.drawConvexPolygon(points, 4); ``` |
| --- | --- |

The first point is implicitly connected to the last point, and the polygon is filled
with the current [brush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#brush)(). If
the supplied polygon is not convex, i.e. it contains at least one angle larger than 180
degrees, the results are undefined.

On some platforms (e.g. X11), the drawConvexPolygon() function can be faster than the
[drawPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPolygon)() function.

**See also**
[drawPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPolygon)(),
[drawPolyline](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPolyline)(), and
[Coordinate System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html).

### void QPainter::drawGlyphRun(const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \&*position*, const [QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html) \&*glyphs*)

Draws the glyphs represented by *glyphs* at *position*. The *position* gives the edge of
the baseline for the string of glyphs. The glyphs will be retrieved from the font
selected on *glyphs* and at offsets given by the positions in *glyphs*.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

**See also**
[QGlyphRun::setRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#setRawFont)(),
[QGlyphRun::setPositions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#setPositions)(),
and
[QGlyphRun::setGlyphIndexes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#setGlyphIndexes)().

### void QPainter::drawImage(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*target*, const [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) \&*image*, const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*source*, [Qt::ImageConversionFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ImageConversionFlag-enum) *flags* \= Qt::AutoColor)

Draws the rectangular portion *source* of the given *image* into the *target* rectangle
in the paint device.

**Note:** The image is scaled to fit the rectangle, if both the image and rectangle size
disagree.

**Note:** See [Drawing High Resolution Versions of Pixmaps and
Images](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawing-high-resolution-versions-of-pixmaps-and-images)
on how this is affected by
[QImage::devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#devicePixelRatio)().

If the image needs to be modified to fit in a lower-resolution result (e.g. converting
from 32-bit to 8-bit), use the *flags* to specify how you would prefer this to happen.

| ``` QRectF target(10.0, 20.0, 80.0, 60.0); QRectF source(0.0, 0.0, 70.0, 40.0); QImage image(":/images/myImage.png");  QPainter painter(this); painter.drawImage(target, image, source); ``` |
| --- |

**See also** [drawPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPixmap)()
and
[QImage::devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#devicePixelRatio)().

### void QPainter::drawPicture(const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \&*point*, const [QPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html) \&*picture*)

Replays the given *picture* at the given *point*.

The [QPicture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html) class is a paint device
that records and replays [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html)
commands. A picture serializes the painter commands to an IO device in a
platform-independent format. Everything that can be painted on a widget or pixmap can
also be stored in a picture.

This function does exactly the same as
[QPicture::play](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html#play)() when called
with *point* \= [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html)(0, 0).

| ``` QPicture picture; QPointF point(10.0, 20.0) picture.load("drawing.pic");  QPainter painter(this); painter.drawPicture(0, 0, picture); ``` |
| --- |

**See also** [QPicture::play](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpicture.html#play)().

### void QPainter::drawPie(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*, int *startAngle*, int *spanAngle*)

Draws a pie defined by the given *rectangle*, *startAngle* and *spanAngle*.

The pie is filled with the current
[brush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#brush)().

The startAngle and spanAngle must be specified in 1/16th of a degree, i.e. a full circle
equals 5760 (16 \* 360). Positive values for the angles mean counter-clockwise while
negative values mean the clockwise direction. Zero degrees is at the 3 o'clock position.

|  | ``` QRectF rectangle(10.0, 20.0, 80.0, 60.0); int startAngle = 30 * 16; int spanAngle = 120 * 16;  QPainter painter(this); painter.drawPie(rectangle, startAngle, spanAngle); ``` |
| --- | --- |

**See also**
[drawEllipse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawEllipse)(),
[drawChord](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawChord)(), and
[Coordinate System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html).

### void QPainter::drawPixmap(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*target*, const [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) \&*pixmap*, const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*source*)

Draws the rectangular portion *source* of the given *pixmap* into the given *target* in
the paint device.

**Note:** The pixmap is scaled to fit the rectangle, if both the pixmap and rectangle
size disagree.

**Note:** See [Drawing High Resolution Versions of Pixmaps and
Images](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawing-high-resolution-versions-of-pixmaps-and-images)
on how this is affected by
[QPixmap::devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#devicePixelRatio)().

| ``` QRectF target(10.0, 20.0, 80.0, 60.0); QRectF source(0.0, 0.0, 70.0, 40.0); QPixmap pixmap(":myPixmap.png");  QPainter(this); painter.drawPixmap(target, pixmap, source); ``` |
| --- |

If *pixmap* is a [QBitmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html) it is drawn
with the bits that are "set" using the pens color. If
[backgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#backgroundMode) is
[Qt::OpaqueMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum), the "unset"
bits are drawn using the color of the background brush; if
[backgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#backgroundMode) is
[Qt::TransparentMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum), the
"unset" bits are transparent. Drawing bitmaps with gradient or texture colors is not
supported.

**See also** [drawImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawImage)()
and
[QPixmap::devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#devicePixelRatio)().

This is an overloaded function.

Draws the rectangular portion with the origin (*sx*, *sy*), width *sw* and height *sh*,
of the given *pixmap* , at the point (*x*, *y*), with a width of *w* and a height of
*h*. If sw or sh are equal to zero the width/height of the pixmap is used and adjusted
by the offset sx/sy;

### void QPainter::drawPixmap(int *x*, int *y*, const [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) \&*pixmap*, int *sx*, int *sy*, int *sw*, int *sh*)

This is an overloaded function.

Draws a pixmap at (*x*, *y*) by copying a part of the given *pixmap* into the paint

(*x*, *y*) specifies the top-left point in the paint device that is to be drawn onto.

(*sw*, *sh*) specifies the size of the pixmap that is to be drawn. The default, (0, 0\)

positions with different scale, rotation and opacity. *fragments* is an array of

This function is potentially faster than multiple calls to

backend can optimize state changes.

### void QPainter::drawPolygon(const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \**points*, int *pointCount*, [Qt::FillRule](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum) *fillRule* \= Qt::OddEvenFill)

Draws the polygon defined by the first *pointCount* points in the array *points* using
the current pen and brush.

|  | ``` static const QPointF points[4] = {     QPointF(10.0, 80.0),     QPointF(20.0, 10.0),     QPointF(80.0, 30.0),     QPointF(90.0, 70.0) };  QPainter painter(this); painter.drawPolygon(points, 4); ``` |

The first point is implicitly connected to the last point, and the polygon is filled
with the current [brush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#brush)().

If *fillRule* is
[Qt::WindingFill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum), the polygon
is filled using the winding fill algorithm. If *fillRule* is
[Qt::OddEvenFill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum), the polygon
is filled using the odd-even fill algorithm. See
[Qt::FillRule](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum) for a more
detailed description of these fill rules.

### void QPainter::drawStaticText(const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \&*topLeftPosition*, const [QStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html) \&*staticText*)

Draws the given *staticText* at the given *topLeftPosition*.

The text will be drawn using the font and the transformation set on the painter. If the
font and/or transformation set on the painter are different from the ones used to
initialize the layout of the
[QStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html), then the layout will
have to be recalculated. Use
[QStaticText::prepare](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html#prepare)() to
initialize *staticText* with the font and transformation with which it will later be
drawn.

If *topLeftPosition* is not the same as when *staticText* was initialized, or when it
was last drawn, then there will be a slight overhead when translating the text to its
new position.

**Note:** If the painter's transformation is not affine, then *staticText* will be drawn
using regular calls to
[drawText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawText)(), losing any
potential for performance improvement.

**Note:** The y-position is used as the top of the font.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.7.

**See also** [QStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html).

### void QPainter::drawText(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*, int *flags*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \**boundingRect* \= nullptr)

This is an overloaded function.

Draws the given *text* within the provided *rectangle*. The *rectangle* along with
alignment *flags* defines the anchors for the *text*.

|  | ``` QPainter painter(this); painter.drawText(rect, Qt::AlignCenter, tr("Qt\nProject")); ``` |
| --- | --- |

The *boundingRect* (if not null) is set to what the bounding rectangle should be in
order to enclose the whole text. For example, in the following image, the dotted line
represents *boundingRect* as calculated by the function, and the dashed line represents
*rectangle*:

|  | ``` QPainter painter(this); QFont font = painter.font(); font.setPixelSize(48); painter.setFont(font);  const QRect rectangle = QRect(0, 0, 100, 50); QRect boundingRect; painter.drawText(rectangle, 0, tr("Hello"), &boundingRect);  QPen pen = painter.pen(); pen.setStyle(Qt::DotLine); painter.setPen(pen); painter.drawRect(boundingRect.adjusted(0, 0, -pen.width(), -pen.width()));  pen.setStyle(Qt::DashLine); painter.setPen(pen); painter.drawRect(rectangle.adjusted(0, 0, -pen.width(), -pen.width())); ``` |
| --- | --- |

The *flags* argument is a bitwise OR of the following flags:

- [Qt::AlignLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::AlignRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::AlignHCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::AlignJustify](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::AlignTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::AlignBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::AlignVCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::AlignCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum)
- [Qt::TextDontClip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum)
- [Qt::TextSingleLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum)
- [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum)
- [Qt::TextShowMnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum)
- [Qt::TextWordWrap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum)
- [Qt::TextIncludeTrailingSpaces](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum)

By default, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) draws text
anti-aliased.

**Note:** The y-coordinate of *rectangle* is used as the top of the font.

|  | ``` QPainter painter(this); QFont font = painter.font(); font.setPixelSize(48); painter.setFont(font);  const QRect rectangle = QRect(0, 0, 100, 50); QRect boundingRect; painter.drawText(rectangle, 0, tr("Hello"), &boundingRect);  QPen pen = painter.pen(); pen.setStyle(Qt::DotLine); painter.setPen(pen); painter.drawRect(boundingRect.adjusted(0, 0, -pen.width(), -pen.width()));  pen.setStyle(Qt::DashLine); painter.setPen(pen); painter.drawRect(rectangle.adjusted(0, 0, -pen.width(), -pen.width())); ``` |
| --- | --- |

By default, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) draws text
anti-aliased.

**Note:** The y-coordinate of *rectangle* is used as the top of the font.

### void QPainter::drawText(int *x*, int *y*, int *width*, int *height*, int *flags*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \**boundingRect* \= nullptr)

This is an overloaded function.

Draws the given *text* within the rectangle with origin (*x*, *y*), *width* and
*height*.

The *boundingRect* (if not null) is set to the what the bounding rectangle should be in
order to enclose the whole text. For example, in the following image, the dotted line
represents *boundingRect* as calculated by the function, and the dashed line represents
the rectangle defined by *x*, *y*, *width* and *height*:

|  | ``` QPainter painter(this); QFont font = painter.font(); font.setPixelSize(48); painter.setFont(font);  const QRect rectangle = QRect(0, 0, 100, 50); QRect boundingRect; painter.drawText(rectangle, 0, tr("Hello"), &boundingRect);  QPen pen = painter.pen(); pen.setStyle(Qt::DotLine); painter.setPen(pen); painter.drawRect(boundingRect.adjusted(0, 0, -pen.width(), -pen.width()));  pen.setStyle(Qt::DashLine); painter.setPen(pen); painter.drawRect(rectangle.adjusted(0, 0, -pen.width(), -pen.width())); ``` |

### void QPainter::drawTiledPixmap(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*, const [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) \&*pixmap*, const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \&*position* \= QPointF())

Draws a tiled *pixmap*, inside the given *rectangle* with its origin at the given
*position*.

Calling drawTiledPixmap() is similar to calling
[drawPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPixmap)() several
times to fill (tile) an area with a pixmap, but is potentially much more efficient
depending on the underlying window system.

drawTiledPixmap() will produce the same visual tiling pattern on high-dpi displays (with
devicePixelRatio \> 1), compared to normal- dpi displays. Set the devicePixelRatio on
the *pixmap* to control the tile size. For example, setting it to 2 halves the tile
width and height (on both 1x and 2x displays), and produces high-resolution output on 2x
displays.

The *position* offset is always in the painter coordinate system, indepentent of display
devicePixelRatio.

**See also**
[drawPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPixmap)().

### void QPainter::drawTiledPixmap(int *x*, int *y*, int *width*, int *height*, const [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) \&*pixmap*, int *sx* \= 0, int *sy* \= 0\)

*pixmap* that is to be drawn; this defaults to (0, 0).

### void QPainter::setBackground(const [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html) \&*brush*)

Sets the background brush of the painter to the given *brush*.

The background brush is the brush that is filled in when drawing opaque text, stippled
lines and bitmaps. The background brush has no effect in transparent background mode
(which is the default).

**See also**
[background](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#background)(),
[setBackgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setBackgroundMode)(),

### void QPainter::setBackgroundMode([Qt::BGMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum) *mode*)

Sets the background mode of the painter to the given *mode*

[Qt::TransparentMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum) (the
default) draws stippled lines and text without setting the background pixels.
[Qt::OpaqueMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BGMode-enum) fills these
space with the current background color.

Note that in order to draw a bitmap or pixmap transparently, you must use
[QPixmap::setMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#setMask)().

**See also**
[backgroundMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#backgroundMode)(),
[setBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setBackground)(), and
[Settings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#settings).

### void QPainter::setFont(const [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) \&*font*)

Sets the painter's font to the given *font*.

This font is used by subsequent
[drawText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawText)() functions. The
text color is the same as the pen color.

If you set a font that isn't available, Qt finds a close match.
[font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#font)() will return what you set
using setFont() and
[fontInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#fontInfo)() returns the font
actually being used (which may be the same).

**See also** [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#font)(),
[drawText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawText)(), and

PythonQt.Qt.QPainterPath.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A painter path is an object composed of a number of graphical building blocks, such as
rectangles, ellipses, lines, and curves. Building blocks can be joined in closed
subpaths, for example as a rectangle or an ellipse. A closed path has coinciding start
and end points. Or they can exist independently as unclosed subpaths, such as lines and
curves.

A QPainterPath object can be used for filling, outlining, and clipping. To generate
fillable outlines for a given painter path, use the
[QPainterPathStroker](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html)
class. The main advantage of painter paths over normal drawing operations is that
complex shapes only need to be created once; then they can be drawn many times using
only calls to the
[QPainter::drawPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPath)()
function.

QPainterPath provides a collection of functions that can be used to obtain information
about the path and its elements. In addition it is possible to reverse the order of the
elements using the
[toReversed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toReversed)()
function. There are also several functions to convert this painter path object into a
polygon representation.

### Composing a QPainterPath

A QPainterPath object can be constructed as an empty path, with a given start point, or
as a copy of another QPainterPath object. Once created, lines and curves can be added to
the path using the
[lineTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#lineTo)(),
[arcTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#arcTo)(),
[cubicTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#cubicTo)() and
[quadTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#quadTo)() functions. The
lines and curves stretch from the
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
to the position passed as argument.

The
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
of the QPainterPath object is always the end position of the last subpath that was added
(or the initial start point). Use the
[moveTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#moveTo)() function to move
the
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
without adding a component. The
[moveTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#moveTo)() function
implicitly starts a new subpath, and closes the previous one. Another way of starting a
new subpath is to call the
[closeSubpath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#closeSubpath)()
function which closes the current path by adding a line from the
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
back to the path's start position. Note that the new path will have (0, 0\) as its
initial
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)().

QPainterPath class also provides several convenience functions to add closed subpaths to
a painter path:
[addEllipse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#addEllipse)(),
[addPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#addPath)(),
[addRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#addRect)(),
[addRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#addRegion)() and
[addText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#addText)(). The
[addPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#addPolygon)() function
adds an *unclosed* subpath. In fact, these functions are all collections of
[moveTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#moveTo)(),
[lineTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#lineTo)() and
[cubicTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#cubicTo)() operations.

In addition, a path can be added to the current path using the
[connectPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#connectPath)()
function. But note that this function will connect the last element of the current path
to the first element of given one by adding a line.

Below is a code snippet that shows how a QPainterPath object can be used:

|  | ``` QPainterPath path; path.addRect(20, 20, 60, 60);  path.moveTo(0, 0); path.cubicTo(99, 0,  50, 50,  99, 99); path.cubicTo(0, 99,  50, 50,  0, 0);  QPainter painter(this); painter.fillRect(0, 0, 100, 100, Qt::white); painter.setPen(QPen(QColor(79, 106, 25), 1, Qt::SolidLine,                     Qt::FlatCap, Qt::MiterJoin)); painter.setBrush(QColor(122, 163, 39));  painter.drawPath(path); ``` |
| --- | --- |

The painter path is initially empty when constructed. We first add a rectangle, which is
a closed subpath. Then we add two bezier curves which together form a closed subpath
even though they are not closed individually. Finally we draw the entire path. The path
is filled using the default fill rule,
[Qt::OddEvenFill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum). Qt provides
two methods for filling paths:

| [Qt::OddEvenFill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum) | [Qt::WindingFill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum) |
| --- | --- |
|  |  |

See the [Qt::FillRule](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum)
documentation for the definition of the rules. A painter path's currently set fill rule
can be retrieved using the
[fillRule](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#fillRule)() function,
and altered using the
[setFillRule](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#setFillRule)()
function.

### QPainterPath Information

The QPainterPath class provides a collection of functions that returns information about
the path and its elements.

The
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
function returns the end point of the last subpath that was added (or the initial start
point). The
[elementAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#elementAt)() function
can be used to retrieve the various subpath elements, the *number* of elements can be
retrieved using the
[elementCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#elementCount)()
function, and the
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#isEmpty)() function tells
whether this QPainterPath object contains any elements at all.

The
[controlPointRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#controlPointRect)()
function returns the rectangle containing all the points and control points in this
path. This function is significantly faster to compute than the exact
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#boundingRect)()
which returns the bounding rectangle of this painter path with floating point precision.

Finally, QPainterPath provides the
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#contains)() function
which can be used to determine whether a given point or rectangle is inside the path,
and the [intersects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#intersects)()
function which determines if any of the points inside a given rectangle also are inside
this path.

### QPainterPath Conversion

For compatibility reasons, it might be required to simplify the representation of a
painter path: QPainterPath provides the
[toFillPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygon)(),
[toFillPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygons)()
and
[toSubpathPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toSubpathPolygons)()
functions which convert the painter path into a polygon. The
[toFillPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygon)()
returns the painter path as one single polygon, while the two latter functions return a
list of polygons.

The
[toFillPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygons)()
and
[toSubpathPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toSubpathPolygons)()
functions are provided because it is usually faster to draw several small polygons than
to draw one large polygon, even though the total number of points drawn is the same. The
difference between the two is the *number* of polygons they return: The
[toSubpathPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toSubpathPolygons)()
creates one polygon for each subpath regardless of intersecting subpaths (i.e.
overlapping bounding rectangles), while the
[toFillPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygons)()
functions creates only one polygon for overlapping subpaths.

The
[toFillPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygon)()
and
[toFillPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygons)()
functions first convert all the subpaths to polygons, then uses a rewinding technique to
make sure that overlapping subpaths can be filled using the correct fill rule. Note that
rewinding inserts additional lines in the polygon so the outline of the fill polygon
does not match the outline of the path.

### Examples

Qt provides the [Painter Paths
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-painterpaths-example.html)
and the [Vector Deformation
example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-deform-example.html)
which are located in Qt's example directory.

The [Painter Paths
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-painterpaths-example.html)
shows how painter paths can be used to build complex shapes for rendering and lets the
user experiment with the filling and stroking. The [Vector Deformation
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-deform-example.html)
shows how to use QPainterPath to draw text.

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QPainterPath::angleAtPercent([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *t*) const

Returns the angle of the path tangent at the percentage *t*. The argument *t* has to be
between 0 and 1\.

Positive values for the angles mean counter-clockwise while negative values mean the
clockwise direction. Zero degrees is at the 3 o'clock position.

Note that similarly to the other percent methods, the percentage measurement is not
linear with regards to the length if curves are present in the path. When curves are
present the percentage argument is mapped to the t parameter of the Bezier equations.

### void QPainterPath::arcTo(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *startAngle*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *sweepLength*)

Creates an arc that occupies the given *rectangle*, beginning at the specified
*startAngle* and extending *sweepLength* degrees counter-clockwise.

Angles are specified in degrees. Clockwise arcs can be specified using negative angles.

Note that this function connects the starting point of the arc to the current position
if they are not already connected. After the arc has been added, the current position is
the last point in arc. To draw a line back to the first point, use the
[closeSubpath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#closeSubpath)()
function.

|  | ``` QLinearGradient myGradient; QPen myPen;  QPointF center, startPoint;  QPainterPath myPath; myPath.moveTo(center); myPath.arcTo(boundingRect, startAngle,              sweepLength);  QPainter painter(this); painter.setBrush(myGradient); painter.setPen(myPen); painter.drawPath(myPath); ``` |
| --- | --- |

[arcMoveTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#arcMoveTo)(),
[addEllipse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#addEllipse)(),
[QPainter::drawArc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawArc)(),
[QPainter::drawPie](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPie)(), and

QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#composing-a-qpainterpath).

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QPainterPath::intersects(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*) const

Returns `true` if any point in the given *rectangle* intersects the path; otherwise
returns `false`.

There is an intersection if any of the lines making up the rectangle crosses a part of
the path or if any part of the rectangle overlaps with any area enclosed by the path.
This function respects the current
[fillRule](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#fillRule) to determine
what is considered inside the path.

**See also**
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#contains)().

### bool QPainterPath::intersects(const [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#QPainterPath) \&*p*) const

Returns `true` if the current path intersects at any point the given path *p*. Also
returns `true` if the current path contains or is contained by any part of *p*.

Set operations on paths will treat the paths as areas. Non-closed paths will be treated
as implicitly closed.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also**
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#contains)().

### [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#QPainterPath) QPainterPath::simplified() const

PythonQt.Qt.QPainterPath.toFillPolygon.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QPolygonF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpolygonf.html) QPainterPath::toFillPolygon(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*matrix* \= QTransform()) const

Converts the path into a polygon using the
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) *matrix*, and returns
the polygon.

The polygon is created by first converting all subpaths to polygons, then using a
rewinding technique to make sure that overlapping subpaths can be filled using the
correct fill rule.

Note that rewinding inserts addition lines in the polygon so the outline of the fill
polygon does not match the outline of the path.

**See also**
[toSubpathPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toSubpathPolygons)(),
[toFillPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygons)(),
and [QPainterPath
Conversion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#qpainterpath-conversion).

PythonQt.Qt.QPainterPath.toFillPolygons.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### QList\<[QPolygonF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpolygonf.html)\> QPainterPath::toFillPolygons(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*matrix* \= QTransform()) const

Converts the path into a list of polygons using the
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) *matrix*, and returns
the list.

The function differs from the
[toFillPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygon)()
function in that it creates several polygons. It is provided because it is usually
faster to draw several small polygons than to draw one large polygon, even though the
total number of points drawn is the same.

The toFillPolygons() function differs from the
[toSubpathPolygons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toSubpathPolygons)()
function in that it create only polygon for subpaths that have overlapping bounding
rectangles.

Like the
[toFillPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#toFillPolygon)()
function, this function uses a rewinding technique to make sure that overlapping
subpaths can be filled using the correct fill rule. Note that rewinding inserts addition
lines in the polygons so the outline of the fill polygon does not match the outline of
the path.

## Detailed Description

By calling the
[createStroke](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#createStroke)()
function, passing a given
[QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) as argument, a new
painter path representing the outline of the given path is created. The newly created
painter path can then be filled to draw the original painter path's outline.

You can control the various design aspects (width, cap styles, join styles and dash
pattern) of the outlining using the following functions:

- [setWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#setWidth)()
- [setCapStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#setCapStyle)()
- [setJoinStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#setJoinStyle)()
- [setDashPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#setDashPattern)()

The
[setDashPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#setDashPattern)()
function accepts both a
[Qt::PenStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#PenStyle-enum) object and a
vector representation of the pattern as argument.

In addition you can specify a curve's threshold, controlling the granularity with which
a curve is drawn, using the
[setCurveThreshold](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#setCurveThreshold)()
function. The default threshold is a well adjusted value (0.25), and normally you should
not need to modify it. However, you can make the curve's appearance smoother by
decreasing its value.

You can also control the miter limit for the generated outline using the
[setMiterLimit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#setMiterLimit)()
function. The miter limit describes how far from each join the miter join can extend.
The limit is specified in the units of width so the pixelwise miter limit will be
`miterlimit * width`. This value is only used if the join style is
[Qt::MiterJoin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#PenJoinStyle-enum).

The painter path generated by the
[createStroke](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html#createStroke)()
function should only be used for outlining the given painter path. Otherwise it may
cause unexpected behavior. Generated outlines also require the
[Qt::WindingFill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FillRule-enum) rule which
is set by default.

## Detailed Description

Once a [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) object is
constructed, subpaths like lines and curves can be added to the path (creating
[QPainterPath::LineToElement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#ElementType-enum)
and
[QPainterPath::CurveToElement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#ElementType-enum)
components).

The lines and curves stretch from the
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
to the position passed as argument. The
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
of the [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) object is
always the end position of the last subpath that was added (or the initial start point).
The [moveTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#moveTo)() function can
be used to move the
[currentPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#currentPosition)()
without adding a line or curve, creating a
[QPainterPath::MoveToElement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html#ElementType-enum)
component.

## Detailed Description

The *sourceLeft*, *sourceTop*, *width* and *height* variables are used as a source
rectangle within the pixmap passed into the
[QPainter::drawPixmapFragments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawPixmapFragments)()
function. The variables *x*, *y*, *width* and *height* are used to calculate the target
rectangle that is drawn. *x* and *y* denotes the center of the target rectangle. The
*width* and *height* in the target rectangle is scaled by the *scaleX* and *scaleY*
values. The resulting target rectangle is then rotated *rotation* degrees around the
*x*, *y* center point.

PythonQt.Qt.QPalette.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A palette consists of three color groups: *Active*, *Disabled*, and *Inactive*. All
widgets in Qt contain a palette and use their palette to draw themselves. This makes the
user interface easily configurable and easier to keep consistent.

If you create a new widget we strongly recommend that you use the colors in the palette
rather than hard-coding specific colors.

The color groups:

- The Active group is used for the window that has keyboard focus.
- The Inactive group is used for other windows.
- The Disabled group is used for widgets (not windows) that are disabled for some reason.

Both active and inactive windows can contain disabled widgets. (Disabled widgets are
often called *inaccessible* or *grayed out*.)

In most styles, Active and Inactive look the same.

Colors and brushes can be set for particular roles in any of a palette's color groups
with [setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#setColor)() and
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#setBrush)(). A color group
contains a group of colors used by widgets for drawing themselves. We recommend that
widgets use color group roles from the palette such as "foreground" and "base" rather
than literal colors like "red" or "turquoise". The color roles are enumerated and
defined in the
[ColorRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorRole-enum)
documentation.

We strongly recommend that you use the default palette of the current style (returned by
[QGuiApplication::palette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#palette)())
and modify that as necessary. This is done by Qt's widgets when they are drawn.

To modify a color group you call the functions
[setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#setColor)() and
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#setBrush)(), depending on
whether you want a pure color or a pixmap pattern.

There are also corresponding
[color](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#color)() and
[brush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#brush)() getters, and a
commonly used convenience function to get the
[ColorRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorRole-enum) for the
current [ColorGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorGroup-enum):
[window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#window)(),
[windowText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#windowText)(),
[base](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#base)(), etc.

You can copy a palette using the copy constructor and test to see if two palettes are
*identical* using
[isCopyOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#isCopyOf)().

QPalette is optimized by the use of [implicit
sharing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html), so it is very
efficient to pass QPalette objects as arguments.

**Warning:** Some styles do not use the palette for all drawing, for instance, if they
make use of native theme engines. This is the case for both the Windows Vista and the
macOS styles.

### lastOffset : [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html)

This property holds the last offset recorded for this gesture

The last offset contains the change in position of the user's input as reported in the
[offset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpangesture.html#offset-prop) property when
a previous gesture event was delivered for this gesture.

If no previous event was delivered with information about this gesture (i.e., this
gesture object contains information about the first movement in the gesture) then this
property contains a zero size.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QParallelAnimationGroup--a [container for
animations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html)--starts all its
animations when it is
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#start) itself,
i.e., runs all animations in parallel. The animation group finishes when the longest
lasting animation has finished.

You can treat QParallelAnimationGroup as any other
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html), e.g.,
pause, resume, or add it to other animation groups.

```
    QParallelAnimationGroup *group = new QParallelAnimationGroup;
    group->addAnimation(anim1);
    group->addAnimation(anim2);

    group->start();
```

## Detailed Description

If you wish to introduce a delay between animations in a
[QSequentialAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsequentialanimationgroup.html),
you can insert a QPauseAnimation. This class does not animate anything, but does not
[finish](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#finished) before a
specified number of milliseconds have elapsed from when it was started. You specify the
duration of the pause in the constructor. It can also be set directly with
[setDuration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpauseanimation.html#duration-prop)().

It is not necessary to construct a QPauseAnimation yourself.
[QSequentialAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsequentialanimationgroup.html)
provides the convenience functions
[addPause()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsequentialanimationgroup.html#addPause)
and
[insertPause()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsequentialanimationgroup.html#insertPause).
These functions simply take the number of milliseconds the pause should last.
