### bool QPrinter::setPageOrientation([QPageLayout::Orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Orientation-enum) *orientation*)

Sets the page *orientation* to
[QPageLayout::Portrait](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Orientation-enum)
or
[QPageLayout::Landscape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Orientation-enum).

The printer driver reads this setting and prints the page using the specified
orientation.

On Windows and Mac, this option can be changed while printing and will take effect from
the next call to [newPage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#newPage)().

To obtain the current
[QPageLayout::Orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Orientation-enum)
use
[pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)().orientation().

Returns true if the page orientation was successfully set to *orientation*.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.3.

**See also** [pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)()
and [setPageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPageLayout)().

[pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)().pageSize().

PythonQt.Qt.QProcess.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

### Running a Process

To start a process, pass the name and command line arguments of the program you want to
run as arguments to [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)().
Arguments are supplied as individual strings in a
[QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html).

Alternatively, you can set the program to run with
[setProgram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProgram)() and
[setArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setArguments)(), and
then call [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() or
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#open)().

For example, the following code snippet runs the analog clock example in the Fusion
style on X11 platforms by passing strings containing "-style" and "fusion" as two items
in the list of arguments:

```
    QObject *parent;
    ...
    QString program = "./path/to/Qt/examples/widgets/analogclock";
    QStringList arguments;
    arguments << "-style" << "fusion";

    QProcess *myProcess = new QProcess(parent);
    myProcess->start(program, arguments);
```

QProcess then enters the
[Starting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessState-enum) state,
and when the program has started, QProcess enters the
[Running](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessState-enum) state and
emits [started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)().

QProcess allows you to treat a process as a sequential I/O device. You can write to and
read from the process just as you would access a network connection using
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html). You can then write to
the process's standard input by calling
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)(), and read the
standard output by calling
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(). Because it
inherits [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), QProcess can
also be used as an input source for QXmlReader, or for generating data to be uploaded
using
[QNetworkAccessManager](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkaccessmanager.html).

When the process exits, QProcess reenters the
[NotRunning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessState-enum) state
(the initial state), and emits
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#finished)().

The [finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#finished)() signal
provides the exit code and exit status of the process as arguments, and you can also
call [exitCode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#exitCode)() to obtain
the exit code of the last process that finished, and
[exitStatus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#exitStatus)() to obtain
its exit status. If an error occurs at any point in time, QProcess will emit the
[errorOccurred](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#errorOccurred)()
signal. You can also call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#error)() to find the type of
error that occurred last, and
[state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#state)() to find the current
process state.

**Note:** QProcess is not supported on
[VxWorks](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/vxworks.html), iOS, tvOS, watchOS, or the
Universal Windows Platform.

### Communicating via Channels

Processes have two predefined output channels: The standard output channel (`stdout`)
supplies regular console output, and the standard error channel (`stderr`) usually
supplies the errors that are printed by the process. These channels represent two
separate streams of data. You can toggle between them by calling
[setReadChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setReadChannel)().
QProcess emits
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() when data is
available on the current read channel. It also emits
[readyReadStandardOutput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readyReadStandardOutput)()
when new standard output data is available, and when new standard error data is
available,
[readyReadStandardError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readyReadStandardError)()
is emitted. Instead of calling
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), or
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(), you can
explicitly read all data from either of the two channels by calling
[readAllStandardOutput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readAllStandardOutput)()
or
[readAllStandardError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readAllStandardError)().

The terminology for the channels can be misleading. Be aware that the process's output
channels correspond to QProcess's *read* channels, whereas the process's input channels
correspond to QProcess's *write* channels. This is because what we read using QProcess
is the process's output, and what we write becomes the process's input.

QProcess can merge the two output channels, so that standard output and standard error
data from the running process both use the standard output channel. Call
[setProcessChannelMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProcessChannelMode)()
with
[MergedChannels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum)
before starting the process to activate this feature. You also have the option of
forwarding the output of the running process to the calling, main process, by passing
[ForwardedChannels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum)
as the argument. It is also possible to forward only one of the output channels \-
typically one would use
[ForwardedErrorChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum),
but
[ForwardedOutputChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum)
also exists. Note that using channel forwarding is typically a bad idea in GUI
applications \- you should present errors graphically instead.

Certain processes need special environment settings in order to operate. You can set
environment variables for your process by calling
[setProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProcessEnvironment)().
To set a working directory, call
[setWorkingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setWorkingDirectory)().
By default, processes are run in the current working directory of the calling process.

The positioning and the screen Z-order of windows belonging to GUI applications started
with QProcess are controlled by the underlying windowing system. For Qt 5 applications,
the positioning can be specified using the `-qwindowgeometry` command line option; X11
applications generally accept a `-geometry` command line option.

### Synchronous Process API

QProcess provides a set of functions which allow it to be used without an event loop, by
suspending the calling thread until certain signals are emitted:

- [waitForStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted)() blocks until the process has started.
- [waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForReadyRead)() blocks until new data is available for reading on the current read channel.
- [waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForBytesWritten)() blocks until one payload of data has been written to the process.
- [waitForFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForFinished)() blocks until the process has finished.

Calling these functions from the main thread (the thread that calls
[QApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#exec)()) may
cause your user interface to freeze.

The following example runs `gzip` to compress the string "Qt rocks!", without an event
loop:

```
    QProcess gzip;
    gzip.start("gzip", QStringList() << "-c");
    if (!gzip.waitForStarted())
        return false;

    gzip.write("Qt rocks!");
    gzip.closeWriteChannel();

    if (!gzip.waitForFinished())
        return false;

    QByteArray result = gzip.readAll();
```

### Notes for Windows Users

Some Windows commands (for example, `dir`) are not provided by separate applications,
but by the command interpreter itself. If you attempt to use QProcess to execute these
commands directly, it won't work. One possible solution is to execute the command
interpreter itself (`cmd.exe` on some Windows systems), and ask the interpreter to
execute the desired command.

PythonQt.Qt.QProcess.closeWriteChannel.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QProcess::closeWriteChannel()

Schedules the write channel of
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) to be closed. The channel
will close once all data has been written to the process. After calling this function,
any attempts to write to the process will fail.

Closing the write channel is necessary for programs that read input data until the
channel has been closed. For example, the program "more" is used to display text data in
a console on both Unix and Windows. But it will not display the text data until
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html)'s write channel has been
closed. Example:

```
QProcess more;
more.start("more");
more.write("Text to display");
more.closeWriteChannel();
// QProcess will emit readyRead() once "more" starts printing
```

The write channel is implicitly opened when

### void QProcess::setStandardInputFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*)

Redirects the process' standard input to the file indicated by *fileName*. When an input
redirection is in place, the
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) object will be in read-only
mode (calling [write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() will
result in error).

To make the process read EOF right away, pass
[nullDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#nullDevice)() here. This
is cleaner than using
[closeWriteChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#closeWriteChannel)()
before writing any data, because it can be set up prior to starting the process.

If the file *fileName* does not exist at the moment
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() is called or is not
readable, starting the process will fail.

Calling setStandardInputFile() after the process has started has no effect.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[setStandardOutputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardOutputFile)(),
[setStandardErrorFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardErrorFile)(),
and
[setStandardOutputProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardOutputProcess)().

### void QProcess::setStandardOutputFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*, [QIODevice::OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) *mode* \= Truncate)

Redirects the process' standard output to the file *fileName*. When the redirection is
in place, the standard output read channel is closed: reading from it using
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() will always fail, as
will
[readAllStandardOutput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readAllStandardOutput)().

To discard all standard output from the process, pass
[nullDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#nullDevice)() here. This
is more efficient than simply never reading the standard output, as no
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) buffers are filled.

If the file *fileName* doesn't exist at the moment
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() is called, it will be
created. If it cannot be created, the starting will fail.

If the file exists and *mode* is
[QIODevice::Truncate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum),
the file will be truncated. Otherwise (if *mode* is
[QIODevice::Append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum)),
the file will be appended to.

Calling setStandardOutputFile() after the process has started has no effect.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[setStandardInputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardInputFile)(),
[setStandardErrorFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardErrorFile)(),
and
[setStandardOutputProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardOutputProcess)().

### void QProcess::setStandardOutputProcess([QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#QProcess) \**destination*)

Pipes the standard output stream of this process to the *destination* process' standard
input.

The following shell command:

```
command1 | command2
```

Can be accomplished with [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html)
with the following code:

### void QProcess::start(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*program*, const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*arguments*, [QIODevice::OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) *mode* \= ReadWrite)

Starts the given *program* in a new process, passing the command line arguments in
*arguments*.

The [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) object will immediately
enter the Starting state. If the process starts successfully,
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) will emit
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)(); otherwise,
[errorOccurred](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#errorOccurred)() will
be emitted.

**Note:** Processes are started asynchronously, which means the
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)() and
[errorOccurred](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#errorOccurred)()
signals may be delayed. Call
[waitForStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted)() to
make sure the process has started (or has failed to start) and those signals have been
emitted.

**Note:** No further splitting of the arguments is performed.

**Windows:** The arguments are quoted and joined into a command line that is compatible
with the `CommandLineToArgvW()` Windows function. For programs that have different
command line quoting requirements, you need to use
[setNativeArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setNativeArguments)().
One notable program that does not follow the `CommandLineToArgvW()` rules is cmd.exe
and, by consequence, all batch scripts.

The [OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) is
set to *mode*.

If the [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) object is already
running a process, a warning may be printed at the console, and the existing process
will continue running unaffected.

**See also** [processId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#processId)(),
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)(),
[waitForStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted)(), and
[setNativeArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setNativeArguments)().

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QProcess::startDetached([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) \**pid* \= nullptr)

Starts the program set by
[setProgram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProgram)() with
arguments set by
[setArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setArguments)() in a new
process, and detaches from it. Returns `true` on success; otherwise returns `false`. If
the calling process exits, the detached process will continue to run unaffected.

**Unix:** The started process will run in its own session and act like a daemon.

The process will be started in the directory set by
[setWorkingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setWorkingDirectory)().
If
[workingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#workingDirectory)()
is empty, the working directory is inherited from the calling process.

If the function is successful then \**pid* is set to the process identifier of the
started process. Note that the child process may exit and the PID may become invalid
without notice. Furthermore, after the child process exits, the same PID may be recycled
and used by a completely different process. User code should be careful when using this
variable, especially if one intends to forcibly terminate the process by operating
system means.

Only the following property setters are supported by startDetached():

- [setArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setArguments)()
- [setCreateProcessArgumentsModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setCreateProcessArgumentsModifier)()
- [setNativeArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setNativeArguments)()
- [setProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProcessEnvironment)()
- [setProgram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProgram)()
- [setStandardErrorFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardErrorFile)()
- [setStandardInputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardInputFile)()
- [setStandardOutputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardOutputFile)()
- [setWorkingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setWorkingDirectory)()

All other properties of the [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html)
object are ignored.

**Note:** The called process inherits the console window of the calling process. To
suppress console output, redirect standard/error output to
[QProcess::nullDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#nullDevice)().

This function was introduced in Qt 5.10.

**See also** [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)(),
[startDetached](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#startDetached-1)(const
QString \&program, const QStringList \&arguments, const QString \&workingDirectory,
qint64 \*pid), and
[startDetached](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess-obsolete.html#startDetached-2)(const
QString \&command).

### `[static]` bool QProcess::startDetached(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*program*, const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*arguments*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*workingDirectory* \= QString(), [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) \**pid* \= nullptr)

This function overloads startDetached().

Starts the program *program* with the arguments *arguments* in a new process, and
detaches from it. Returns `true` on success; otherwise returns `false`. If the calling
process exits, the detached process will continue to run unaffected.

Argument handling is identical to the respective
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() overload.

The process will be started in the directory *workingDirectory*. If *workingDirectory*
is empty, the working directory is inherited from the calling process.

If the function is successful then \**pid* is set to the process identifier of the
started process.

**See also** [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)().

### `[static]` [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) QProcess::systemEnvironment()

Returns the environment of the calling process as a list of key\=value pairs. Example:

```
QStringList environment = QProcess::systemEnvironment();
// environment = {"PATH=/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin",
//                "USER=greg", "HOME=/home/greg"}

This function does not cache the system environment. Therefore, it's possible to obtain
an updated version of the environment if low-level C library functions like `setenv` or
`putenv` have been called.

variables, which is a non-trivial operation.

[QProcessEnvironment::systemEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html#systemEnvironment)()

### `[slot]` void QProcess::terminate()

Attempts to terminate the process.

The process may not exit as a result of calling this function (it is given the chance to
prompt the user for any unsaved files, etc).

On Windows, terminate() posts a WM\_CLOSE message to all top-level windows of the
process and then to the main thread of the process itself. On Unix and macOS the
`SIGTERM` signal is sent.

Console applications on Windows that do not run an event loop, or whose event loop does
not handle the WM\_CLOSE message, can only be terminated by calling
[kill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#kill)().

**See also** [kill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#kill)().

### bool QProcess::waitForFinished(int *msecs* \= 30000\)

Blocks until the process has finished and the
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#finished)() signal has been
emitted, or until *msecs* milliseconds have passed.

Returns `true` if the process finished; otherwise returns `false` (if the operation
timed out, if an error occurred, or if this
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) is already finished).

This function can operate without an event loop. It is useful when writing non-GUI
applications and when performing I/O operations in a non-GUI thread.

**Warning:** Calling this function from the main (GUI) thread might cause your user
interface to freeze.

If msecs is -1, this function will not time out.

**See also** [finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#finished)(),
[waitForStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted)(),

PythonQt.Qt.QProcessEnvironment.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A process's environment is composed of a set of key\=value pairs known as environment
variables. The QProcessEnvironment class wraps that concept and allows easy manipulation
of those variables. It's meant to be used along with
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html), to set the environment for
child processes. It cannot be used to change the current process's environment.

The environment of the calling process can be obtained using
[QProcessEnvironment::systemEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html#systemEnvironment)().

On Unix systems, the variable names are case-sensitive. Note that the Unix environment
allows both variable names and contents to contain arbitrary binary data (except for the
NUL character). QProcessEnvironment will preserve such variables, but does not support
manipulating variables whose names or values cannot be encoded by the current locale
settings (see
[QTextCodec::codecForLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#codecForLocale)).

On Windows, the variable names are case-insensitive, but case-preserving.
QProcessEnvironment behaves accordingly.

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-progressbar.png)

A progress bar is used to give the user an indication of the progress of an operation
and to reassure them that the application is still running.

The progress bar uses the concept of *steps*. You set it up by specifying the minimum
and maximum possible step values, and it will display the percentage of steps that have
been completed when you later give it the current step value. The percentage is
calculated by dividing the progress
([value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#value-prop)() \-
[minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#minimum-prop)()) divided
by [maximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#maximum-prop)() \-
[minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#minimum-prop)().

You can specify the minimum and maximum number of steps with
[setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#minimum-prop)() and
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#maximum-prop). The
current number of steps is set with
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#value-prop)(). The
progress bar can be rewound to the beginning with
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#reset)().

If minimum and maximum both are set to 0, the bar shows a busy indicator instead of a
percentage of steps. This is useful, for example, when using QNetworkAccessManager to
download items when they are unable to determine the size of the item being downloaded.

PythonQt.Qt.QProgressDialog.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A progress dialog is used to give the user an indication of how long an operation is
going to take, and to demonstrate that the application has not frozen. It can also give
the user an opportunity to abort the operation.

A common problem with progress dialogs is that it is difficult to know when to use them;
operations take different amounts of time on different hardware. QProgressDialog offers
a solution to this problem: it estimates the time the operation will take (based on time
for steps), and only shows itself if that estimate is beyond
[minimumDuration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#minimumDuration-prop)()
(4 seconds by default).

Use [setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#minimum-prop)()
and [setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#maximum-prop)()
or the constructor to set the number of "steps" in the operation and call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() as the
operation progresses. The number of steps can be chosen arbitrarily. It can be the
number of files copied, the number of bytes received, the number of iterations through
the main loop of your algorithm, or some other suitable unit. Progress starts at the
value set by
[setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#minimum-prop)(),
and the progress dialog shows that the operation has finished when you call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() with
the value set by
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#maximum-prop)() as
its argument.

The dialog automatically resets and hides itself at the end of the operation. Use
[setAutoReset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#autoReset-prop)()
and
[setAutoClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#autoClose-prop)()
to change this behavior. Note that if you set a new maximum (using
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#maximum-prop)() or
[setRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setRange)()) that
equals your current
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)(), the
dialog will not close regardless.

There are two ways of using QProgressDialog: modal and modeless.

Compared to a modeless QProgressDialog, a modal QProgressDialog is simpler to use for
the programmer. Do the operation in a loop, call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() at
intervals, and check for cancellation with
[wasCanceled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#wasCanceled-prop)().
For example:

```
    QProgressDialog progress("Copying files...", "Abort Copy", 0, numFiles, this);
    progress.setWindowModality(Qt::WindowModal);

    for (int i = 0; i < numFiles; i++) {
        progress.setValue(i);

        if (progress.wasCanceled())
            break;
        //... copy one file
    }
    progress.setValue(numFiles);
```

A modeless progress dialog is suitable for operations that take place in the background,
where the user is able to interact with the application. Such operations are typically
based on [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) (or
[QObject::timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent)()) or
[QSocketNotifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html); or performed
in a separate thread. A
[QProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html) in the status bar
of your main window is often an alternative to a modeless progress dialog.

You need to have an event loop to be running, connect the
[canceled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#canceled)() signal to
a slot that stops the operation, and call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() at
intervals. For example:

```
// Operation constructor
Operation::Operation(QObject *parent)
    : QObject(parent), steps(0)
{
    pd = new QProgressDialog("Operation in progress.", "Cancel", 0, 100);
    connect(pd, &QProgressDialog::canceled, this, &Operation::cancel);
    t = new QTimer(this);
    connect(t, &QTimer::timeout, this, &Operation::perform);
    t->start(0);
}

void Operation::perform()
{
    pd->setValue(steps);
    //... perform one percent of the operation
    steps++;
    if (steps > pd->maximum())
        t->stop();
}

void Operation::cancel()
{
    t->stop();
    //... cleanup
}
```

In both modes the progress dialog may be customized by replacing the child widgets with
custom widgets by using
[setLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setLabel)(),
[setBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setBar)(), and
[setCancelButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setCancelButton)().
The functions
[setLabelText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#labelText-prop)()
and
[setCancelButtonText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setCancelButtonText)()
set the texts shown.

![A progress dialog shown in the Fusion widget
style.](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/fusion-progressdialog.png)

PythonQt.Qt.QPropertyAnimation.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QPropertyAnimation interpolates over [Qt
properties](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/properties.html). As property values are
stored in [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)s, the class
inherits [QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html),
and supports animation of the same [meta
types](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) as its super class.

A class declaring properties must be a
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html). To make it possible to
animate a property, it must provide a setter (so that QPropertyAnimation can set the
property's value). Note that this makes it possible to animate many of Qt's widgets.
Let's look at an example:

```
    QPropertyAnimation *animation = new QPropertyAnimation(myWidget, "geometry");
    animation->setDuration(10000);
    animation->setStartValue(QRect(0, 0, 100, 30));
    animation->setEndValue(QRect(250, 250, 100, 30));

    animation->start();
```

The property name and the [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)
instance of which property should be animated are passed to the constructor. You can
then specify the start and end value of the property. The procedure is equal for
properties in classes you have implemented yourself--just check with
[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) that your
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) type is supported.

The [QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) class
description explains how to set up the animation in detail. Note, however, that if a
start value is not set, the property will start at the value it had when the
QPropertyAnimation instance was created.

QPropertyAnimation works like a charm on its own. For complex animations that, for
instance, contain several objects,
[QAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html) is provided.
An animation group is an animation that can contain other animations, and that can
manage when its animations are played. Look at
[QParallelAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qparallelanimationgroup.html)
for an example.

PythonQt.Qt.QPushButton.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-pushbutton.png)

The push button, or command button, is perhaps the most commonly used widget in any
graphical user interface. Push (click) a button to command the computer to perform some
action, or to answer a question. Typical buttons are OK, Apply, Cancel, Close, Yes, No
and Help.

A command button is rectangular and typically displays a text label describing its
action. A shortcut key can be specified by preceding the preferred character with an
ampersand in the text. For example:

```
QPushButton *button = new QPushButton("&Download", this);
```

In this example the shortcut is *Alt\+D*. See the
[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html#mnemonic) documentation
for details (to display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&').

Push buttons display a textual label, and optionally a small icon. These can be set
using the constructors and changed later using
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)() and
[setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)(). If the
button is disabled, the appearance of the text and icon will be manipulated with respect
to the GUI style to make the button look "disabled".

A push button emits the signal
[clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#clicked)() when it is
activated by the mouse, the Spacebar or by a keyboard shortcut. Connect to this signal
to perform the button's action. Push buttons also provide less commonly used signals,
for example [pressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#pressed)()
and [released](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#released)().

Command buttons in dialogs are by default auto-default buttons, i.e., they become the
default push button automatically when they receive the keyboard input focus. A default
button is a push button that is activated when the user presses the Enter or Return key
in a dialog. You can change this with
[setAutoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)().
Note that auto-default buttons reserve a little extra space which is necessary to draw a
default-button indicator. If you do not want this space around your buttons, call
[setAutoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)(false).

Being so central, the button widget has grown to accommodate a great many variations in
the past decade. The Microsoft style guide now shows about ten different states of
Windows push buttons and the text implies that there are dozens more when all the
combinations of features are taken into consideration.

The most important modes or states are:

- Available or not (grayed out, disabled).
- Standard push button, toggling push button or menu button.
- On or off (only for toggling push buttons).
- Default or normal. The default button in a dialog can generally be "clicked" using the Enter or Return key.
- Auto-repeat or not.
- Pressed down or not.

As a general rule, use a push button when the application or dialog window performs an
action when the user clicks on it (such as Apply, Cancel, Close and Help) *and* when the
widget is supposed to have a wide, rectangular shape with a text label. Small, typically
square buttons that change the state of the window rather than performing an action
(such as the buttons in the top-right corner of the
[QFileDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html)) are not command
buttons, but tool buttons. Qt provides a special class
([QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html)) for these buttons.

If you need toggle behavior (see
[setCheckable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkable-prop)())
or a button that auto-repeats the activation signal when being pushed down like the
arrows in a scroll bar (see
[setAutoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop)()),
a command button is probably not what you want. When in doubt, use a tool button.

**Note:** On macOS when a push button's width becomes smaller than 50 or its height
becomes smaller than 30, the button's corners are changed from round to square. Use the
[setMinimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)()
function to prevent this behavior.

A variation of a command button is a menu button. These provide not just one command,
but several, since when they are clicked they pop up a menu of options. Use the method
[setMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#setMenu)() to associate a
popup menu with a push button.

Other classes of buttons are option buttons (see
[QRadioButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradiobutton.html)) and check boxes
(see [QCheckBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html)).

In Qt, the [QAbstractButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html)
base class provides most of the modes and other API, and QPushButton provides GUI logic.
See [QAbstractButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html) for more
information about the API.

### autoDefault : bool

This property holds whether the push button is an auto default button

If this property is set to true then the push button is an auto default button.

In some GUI styles a default button is drawn with an extra frame around it, up to 3
pixels or more. Qt automatically keeps this space free around auto-default buttons,
i.e., auto-default buttons may have a slightly larger size hint.

This property's default is true for buttons that have a
[QDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html) parent; otherwise it defaults
to false.

See the [default](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#default) property for
details of how [default](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#default) and
auto-default interact.

PythonQt.Qt.QPushButton.default.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### default : bool

This property holds whether the push button is the default button

Default and autodefault buttons decide what happens when the user presses enter in a
dialog.

A button with this property set to true (i.e., the dialog's *default* button,) will
automatically be pressed when the user presses enter, with one exception: if an
*autoDefault* button currently has focus, the
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
button is pressed. When the dialog has
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
buttons but no default button, pressing enter will press either the
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
button that currently has focus, or if no button has focus, the next
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
button in the focus chain.

In a dialog, only one push button at a time can be the default button. This button is
then displayed with an additional frame (depending on the GUI style).

The default button behavior is provided only in dialogs. Buttons can always be clicked
from the keyboard by pressing Spacebar when the button has focus.

If the default property is set to false on the current default button while the dialog
is visible, a new default will automatically be assigned the next time a push button in
the dialog receives focus.

This property's default is false.

**Access functions:**

| bool | **isDefault**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setDefault**(*bool*) |

### flat : bool

This property holds whether the button border is raised

This property's default is false. If this property is set, most styles will not paint
the button background unless the button is being pressed.
[setAutoFillBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#autoFillBackground-prop)()
can be used to ensure that the background is filled using the
[QPalette::Button](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorRole-enum)
brush.

## Detailed Description

Quaternions are used to represent rotations in 3D space, and consist of a 3D rotation
axis specified by the x, y, and z coordinates, and a scalar representing the rotation
angle.

### `[static]` [QQuaternion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#QQuaternion) QQuaternion::nlerp(const [QQuaternion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#QQuaternion) \&*q1*, const [QQuaternion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#QQuaternion) \&*q2*, float *t*)

Interpolates along the shortest linear path between the rotational positions *q1* and
*q2*. The value *t* should be between 0 and 1, indicating the distance to travel between
*q1* and *q2*. The result will be
[normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#normalized)().

equal to 1, then *q2* will be returned.

[slerp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#slerp)() and will give
approximate results to spherical interpolation that are good enough for some
applications.

**See also** [slerp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#slerp)().

PythonQt.Qt.QRadialGradient.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt supports both simple and extended radial gradients.

Simple radial gradients interpolate colors between a focal point and end points on a
circle surrounding it. Extended radial gradients interpolate colors between a focal
circle and a center circle. Points outside the cone defined by the two circles will be
transparent. For simple radial gradients the focal point is adjusted to lie inside the
center circle, whereas the focal point can have any position in an extended radial
gradient.

Outside the end points the gradient is either padded, reflected or repeated depending on
the currently set
[spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) method:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [PadSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) (default) | [ReflectSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) | [RepeatSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) |

The colors in a gradient is defined using stop points of the
[QGradientStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#QGradientStop-typedef)
type, i.e. a position and a color. Use the
[QGradient::setColorAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setColorAt)()
or the
[QGradient::setStops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setStops)()
function to define the stop points. It is the gradient's complete set of stop points
that describes how the gradient area should be filled. If no stop points have been
specified, a gradient of black at 0 to white at 1 is used.

In addition to the functions inherited from
[QGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html), the QRadialGradient
class provides the
[center](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html#center)(),
[focalPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html#focalPoint)() and
[radius](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html#radius)() functions
returning the gradient's center, focal point and radius respectively.

PythonQt.Qt.QRadioButton.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-radiobutton.png)

A QRadioButton is an option button that can be switched on (checked) or off (unchecked).
Radio buttons typically present the user with a "one of many" choice. In a group of
radio buttons, only one radio button at a time can be checked; if the user selects
another button, the previously selected button is switched off.

Radio buttons are
[autoExclusive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoExclusive-prop)
by default. If auto-exclusive is enabled, radio buttons that belong to the same parent
widget behave as if they were part of the same exclusive button group. If you need
multiple exclusive button groups for radio buttons that belong to the same parent
widget, put them into a
[QButtonGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html).

Whenever a button is switched on or off, it emits the
[toggled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#toggled)() signal.
Connect to this signal if you want to trigger an action each time the button changes
state. Use
[isChecked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)() to
see if a particular button is selected.

Just like [QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html), a radio
button displays text, and optionally a small icon. The icon is set with
[setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)(). The text
can be set in the constructor or with
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(). A
shortcut key can be specified by preceding the preferred character with an ampersand in
the text. For example:

```
QRadioButton *button = new QRadioButton("Search from the &cursor", this);
```

In this example the shortcut is *Alt\+c*. See the
[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html#mnemonic) documentation
for details. To display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&'.

Important inherited members:
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QRasterWindow is a [QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html) with a
raster-based, non-OpenGL surface. On top of the functionality offered by
[QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html), QRasterWindow adds a virtual
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevicewindow.html#paintEvent)()
function and the possibility to open a
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) on itself. The underlying
paint engine will be the raster one, meaning that all drawing will happen on the CPU.
For performing accelerated, OpenGL-based drawing, use
[QOpenGLWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwindow.html) instead.

Internally the class is thin wrapper for
[QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html) and
[QBackingStore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbackingstore.html) and is very
similar to the [Raster Window
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-rasterwindow-example.html) that uses
these classes directly.

PythonQt.Qt.QRawFont.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

**Note:** QRawFont is a low level class. For most purposes
[QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) is a more appropriate class.

Most commonly, when presenting text in a user interface, the exact fonts used to render
the characters is to some extent unknown. This can be the case for several reasons: For
instance, the actual, physical fonts present on the target system could be unexpected to
the developers, or the text could contain user selected styles, sizes or writing systems
that are not supported by font chosen in the code.

Therefore, Qt's [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) class really
represents a query for fonts. When text is interpreted, Qt will do its best to match the
text to the query, but depending on the support, different fonts can be used behind the
scenes.

For most use cases, this is both expected and necessary, as it minimizes the possibility
of text in the user interface being undisplayable. In some cases, however, more direct
control over the process might be useful. It is for these use cases the QRawFont class
exists.

A QRawFont object represents a single, physical instance of a given font in a given
pixel size. I.e. in the typical case it represents a set of TrueType or OpenType font
tables and uses a user specified pixel size to convert metrics into logical pixel units.
It can be used in combination with the
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html) class to draw specific
glyph indexes at specific positions, and also have accessors to some relevant data in
the physical font.

QRawFont only provides support for the main font technologies: GDI and DirectWrite on
Windows platforms,
[FreeType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-attribution-freetype.html#freetype)
on Linux platforms and CoreText on macOS. For other font back-ends, the APIs will be
disabled.

QRawFont can be constructed in a number of ways:

- It can be constructed by calling QTextLayout::glyphs() or QTextFragment::glyphs(). The returned QGlyphs objects will contain QRawFont objects which represent the actual fonts used to render each portion of the text.
- It can be constructed by passing a [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) object to [QRawFont::fromFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#fromFont)(). The function will return a QRawFont object representing the font that will be selected as response to the [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) query and the selected writing system.
- It can be constructed by passing a file name or [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) directly to the QRawFont constructor, or by calling [loadFromFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromFile)() or [loadFromData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromData)(). In this case, the font will not be registered in [QFontDatabase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontdatabase.html), and it will not be available as part of regular font selection.

QRawFont is considered local to the thread in which it is constructed (either using a
constructor, or by calling
[loadFromData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromData)() or
[loadFromFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromFile)()). The
QRawFont cannot be moved to a different thread, but will have to be recreated in the
thread in question.

**Note:** For the requirement of caching glyph indexes and font selections for static
text to avoid reshaping and relayouting in the inner loop of an application, a better
choice is the [QStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html) class,
since it optimizes the memory cost of the cache and also provides the possibility of
paint engine specific caches for an additional speed-up.

PythonQt.Qt.QRawFont.alphaMapForGlyph.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) QRawFont::alphaMapForGlyph([quint32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint32-typedef) *glyphIndex*, [QRawFont::AntialiasingType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#AntialiasingType-enum) *antialiasingType* \= SubPixelAntialiasing, const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*transform* \= QTransform()) const

This function returns a rasterized image of the glyph at the given *glyphIndex* in the
underlying font, using the *transform* specified. If the
[QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) is not valid, this function
will return an invalid [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html).

If the font is a color font, then the resulting image will contain the rendered glyph at
the current pixel size. In this case, the *antialiasingType* will be ignored.

Otherwise, if *antialiasingType* is set to
[QRawFont::SubPixelAntialiasing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#AntialiasingType-enum),
then the resulting image will be in
[QImage::Format\_RGB32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum) and
the RGB values of each pixel will represent the subpixel opacities of the pixel in the
rasterization of the glyph. Otherwise, the image will be in the format of
[QImage::Format\_Indexed8](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum)
and each pixel will contain the opacity of the pixel in the rasterization.

**See also**
[pathForGlyph](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#pathForGlyph)() and
[QPainter::drawGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawGlyphRun)().
signatures: alphaMapForGlyph(self, glyphIndex: int, antialiasingType: PySide2.QtGui.QRawFont.AntialiasingType=..., transform: PySide2.QtGui.QTransform=...) -> PySide2.QtGui.QImage

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QRawFont::ascent() const

Returns the ascent of this [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html)
in pixel units.

The ascent of a font is the distance from the baseline to the highest position
characters extend to. In practice, some font designers break this rule, e.g. when they
put more than one accent on top of a character, or to accommodate an unusual character
in an exotic language, so it is possible (though rare) that this value will be too
small.

**See also**
[QFontMetricsF::ascent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#ascent)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A read-write lock is a synchronization tool for protecting resources that can be
accessed for reading and writing. This type of lock is useful if you want to allow
multiple threads to have simultaneous read-only access, but as soon as one thread wants
to write to the resource, all other threads must be blocked until the writing is
complete.

In many cases, QReadWriteLock is a direct competitor to
[QMutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html). QReadWriteLock is a good
choice if there are many concurrent reads and writing occurs infrequently.

Example:

```
QReadWriteLock lock;

void ReaderThread::run()
{
    ...
    lock.lockForRead();
    read_file();
    lock.unlock();
    ...
}

void WriterThread::run()
{
    ...
    lock.lockForWrite();
    write_file();
    lock.unlock();
    ...
}
```

To ensure that writers aren't blocked forever by readers, readers attempting to obtain a
lock will not succeed if there is a blocked writer waiting for access, even if the lock
is currently only accessed by other readers. Also, if the lock is accessed by a writer
and another writer comes in, that writer will have priority over any readers that might
also be waiting.

Like [QMutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html), a QReadWriteLock can be
recursively locked by the same thread when constructed with
[QReadWriteLock::Recursive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#RecursionMode-enum)
as
[QReadWriteLock::RecursionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#RecursionMode-enum).
In such cases, [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#unlock)()
must be called the same number of times
[lockForWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#lockForWrite)() or
[lockForRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#lockForRead)() was
called. Note that the lock type cannot be changed when trying to lock recursively, i.e.
it is not possible to lock for reading in a thread that already has locked for writing
(and vice versa).

### bool QReadWriteLock::tryLockForRead()

Attempts to lock for reading. If the lock was obtained, this function returns `true`,
otherwise it returns `false` instead of waiting for the lock to become available, i.e.
it does not block.

The lock attempt will fail if another thread has locked for writing.

If the lock was obtained, the lock must be unlocked with
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#unlock)() before another
thread can successfully lock it for writing.

It is not possible to lock for read if the thread already has locked for write.

**See also** [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#unlock)()
and [lockForRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#lockForRead)().

### bool QReadWriteLock::tryLockForRead(int *timeout*)

This is an overloaded function.

Attempts to lock for reading. This function returns `true` if the lock was obtained;
otherwise it returns `false`. If another thread has locked for writing, this function
will wait for at most *timeout* milliseconds for the lock to become available.

Note: Passing a negative number as the *timeout* is equivalent to calling
[lockForRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#lockForRead)(),
i.e. this function will wait forever until lock can be locked for reading when *timeout*
is negative.

If the lock was obtained, the lock must be unlocked with
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#unlock)() before another
thread can successfully lock it for writing.

It is not possible to lock for read if the thread already has locked for write.

**See also** [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#unlock)()
and [lockForRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#lockForRead)().

PythonQt.Qt.QRect.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A rectangle is normally expressed as a top-left corner and a size. The size (width and
height) of a QRect is always equivalent to the mathematical rectangle that forms the
basis for its rendering.

A QRect can be constructed with a set of left, top, width and height integers, or from a
[QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) and a
[QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html). The following code creates two
identical rectangles.

```
QRect r1(100, 200, 11, 16);
QRect r2(QPoint(100, 200), QSize(11, 16));
```

There is a third constructor that creates a QRect using the top-left and bottom-right
coordinates, but we recommend that you avoid using it. The rationale is that for
historical reasons the values returned by the
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)() and
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() functions deviate from
the true bottom-right corner of the rectangle.

The QRect class provides a collection of functions that return the various rectangle
coordinates, and enable manipulation of these. QRect also provides functions to move the
rectangle relative to the various coordinates. In addition there is a
[moveTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#moveTo)() function that moves the
rectangle, leaving its top left corner at the given coordinates. Alternatively, the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#translate)() function moves
the rectangle the given offset relative to the current position, and the
[translated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#translated)() function
returns a translated copy of this rectangle.

The [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#size)() function returns the
rectangle's dimensions as a [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html). The
dimensions can also be retrieved separately using the
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#width)() and
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#height)() functions. To
manipulate the dimensions use the
[setSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setSize)(),
[setWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setWidth)() or
[setHeight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setHeight)() functions.
Alternatively, the size can be changed by applying either of the functions setting the
rectangle coordinates, for example,
[setBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setBottom)() or
[setRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setRight)().

The [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#contains)() function tells
whether a given point is inside the rectangle or not, and the
[intersects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#intersects)() function
returns `true` if this rectangle intersects with a given rectangle. The QRect class also
provides the [intersected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#intersected)()
function which returns the intersection rectangle, and the
[united](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#united)() function which returns
the rectangle that encloses the given rectangle and this:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [intersected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#intersected)() | [united](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#united)() |

The [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isEmpty)() function returns
`true` if [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)() \>
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() or
[top](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#top)() \>
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)(). Note that an empty
rectangle is not valid: The
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isValid)() function returns
`true` if [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)() \<\=
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() *and*
[top](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#top)() \<\=
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)(). A null rectangle
([isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isNull)() \=\= true) on the
other hand, has both width and height set to 0\.

Note that due to the way QRect and
[QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) are defined, an empty QRect is
defined in essentially the same way as
[QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html).

Finally, QRect objects can be streamed as well as compared.

### Rendering

When using an
[anti-aliased](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum)
painter, the boundary line of a QRect will be rendered symmetrically on both sides of
the mathematical rectangle's boundary line. But when using an aliased painter (the
default) other rules apply.

Then, when rendering with a one pixel wide pen the QRect's boundary line will be
rendered to the right and below the mathematical rectangle's boundary line.

When rendering with a two pixels wide pen the boundary line will be split in the middle
by the mathematical rectangle. This will be the case whenever the pen is set to an even
number of pixels, while rendering with a pen with an odd number of pixels, the spare
pixel will be rendered to the right and below the mathematical rectangle as in the one
pixel case.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Logical representation | One pixel wide pen |
|  |  |
| Two pixel wide pen | Three pixel wide pen |

### Coordinates

The QRect class provides a collection of functions that return the various rectangle
coordinates, and enable manipulation of these. QRect also provides functions to move the
rectangle relative to the various coordinates.

For example the [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)(),
[setLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setLeft)() and
[moveLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#moveLeft)() functions as an
example: [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)() returns the
x-coordinate of the rectangle's left edge,
[setLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setLeft)() sets the left edge of
the rectangle to the given x coordinate (it may change the width, but will never change
the rectangle's right edge) and
[moveLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#moveLeft)() moves the entire
rectangle horizontally, leaving the rectangle's left edge at the given x coordinate and
its size unchanged.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qrect-coordinates.png)

Note that for historical reasons the values returned by the
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)() and
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() functions deviate from
the true bottom-right corner of the rectangle: The
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() function returns
*[left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)() \+
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#width)() \- 1* and the
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)() function returns
*[top](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#top)() \+
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#height)() \- 1*. The same is the
case for the point returned by the
[bottomRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottomRight)() convenience
function. In addition, the x and y coordinate of the
[topRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#topRight)() and
[bottomLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottomLeft)() functions,
respectively, contain the same deviation from the true right and bottom edges.

We recommend that you use [x](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#x)() \+
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#width)() and
[y](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#y)() \+
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#height)() to find the true
bottom-right corner, and avoid
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() and
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)(). Another solution is to
use [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html): The
[QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) class defines a rectangle in
the plane using floating point accuracy for coordinates, and the
[QRectF::right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#right)() and
[QRectF::bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#bottom)() functions *do*
return the right and bottom coordinates.

It is also possible to add offsets to this rectangle's coordinates using the
[adjust](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#adjust)() function, as well as
retrieve a new rectangle based on adjustments of the original one using the
[adjusted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#adjusted)() function. If either
of the width and height is negative, use the
[normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#normalized)() function to
retrieve a rectangle where the corners are swapped.

In addition, QRect provides the
[getCoords](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#getCoords)() function which
extracts the position of the rectangle's top-left and bottom-right corner, and the
[getRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#getRect)() function which
extracts the rectangle's top-left corner, width and height. Use the
[setCoords](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setCoords)() and
[setRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#setRect)() function to
manipulate the rectangle's coordinates and dimensions in one go.

### Constraints

QRect is limited to the minimum and maximum values for the `int` type. Operations on a
QRect that could potentially result in values outside this range will result in
undefined behavior.

### bool QRect::isEmpty() const

Returns `true` if the rectangle is empty, otherwise returns `false`.

An empty rectangle has a [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)() \>
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() or
[top](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#top)() \>
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)(). An empty rectangle is
not valid (i.e., isEmpty() \=\=
![isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isValid)()).

Use the [normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#normalized)()
function to retrieve a rectangle where the corners are swapped.

**See also** [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isNull)(),
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isValid)(), and
[normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#normalized)().

### bool QRect::isNull() const

Returns `true` if the rectangle is a null rectangle, otherwise returns `false`.

A null rectangle has both the width and the height set to 0 (i.e.,
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() \=\=
[left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)() \- 1 and
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)() \=\=
[top](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#top)() \- 1). A null rectangle is
also empty, and hence is not valid.

**See also** [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isEmpty)() and
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isValid)().

PythonQt.Qt.QRect.isValid.doc:

### bool QRect::isValid() const

Returns `true` if the rectangle is valid, otherwise returns `false`.

A valid rectangle has a [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#left)()
\<\= [right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#right)() and
[top](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#top)() \<\=
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#bottom)(). Note that non-trivial
operations like intersections are not defined for invalid rectangles. A valid rectangle
is not empty (i.e., isValid() \=\=
![isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isEmpty)()).

**See also** [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isNull)(),
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#isEmpty)(), and
[normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html#normalized)().

PythonQt.Qt.QRectF.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A rectangle is normally expressed as a top-left corner and a size. The size (width and
height) of a QRectF is always equivalent to the mathematical rectangle that forms the
basis for its rendering.

A QRectF can be constructed with a set of left, top, width and height coordinates, or
from a [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) and a
[QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizef.html). The following code creates two
identical rectangles.

```
QRectF r1(100.0, 200.1, 11.2, 16.3);
QRectF r2(QPointF(100.0, 200.1), QSizeF(11.2, 16.3));
```

There is also a third constructor creating a QRectF from a
[QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html), and a corresponding
[toRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#toRect)() function that returns
a [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) object based on the values of
this rectangle (note that the coordinates in the returned rectangle are rounded to the
nearest integer).

The QRectF class provides a collection of functions that return the various rectangle
coordinates, and enable manipulation of these. QRectF also provides functions to move
the rectangle relative to the various coordinates. In addition there is a
[moveTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#moveTo)() function that moves
the rectangle, leaving its top left corner at the given coordinates. Alternatively, the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#translate)() function moves
the rectangle the given offset relative to the current position, and the
[translated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#translated)() function
returns a translated copy of this rectangle.

The [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#size)() function returns the
rectangle's dimensions as a [QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizef.html).
The dimensions can also be retrieved separately using the
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#width)() and
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#height)() functions. To
manipulate the dimensions use the
[setSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setSize)(),
[setWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setWidth)() or
[setHeight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setHeight)() functions.
Alternatively, the size can be changed by applying either of the functions setting the
rectangle coordinates, for example,
[setBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setBottom)() or
[setRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setRight)().

The [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#contains)() function tells
whether a given point is inside the rectangle or not, and the
[intersects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#intersects)() function
returns `true` if this rectangle intersects with a given rectangle (otherwise false).
The QRectF class also provides the
[intersected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#intersected)() function
which returns the intersection rectangle, and the
[united](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#united)() function which returns
the rectangle that encloses the given rectangle and this:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [intersected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#intersected)() | [united](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#united)() |

The [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#isEmpty)() function returns
`true` if the rectangle's width or height is less than, or equal to, 0\. Note that an
empty rectangle is not valid: The
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#isValid)() function returns
`true` if both width and height is larger than 0\. A null rectangle
([isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#isNull)() \=\= true) on the
other hand, has both width and height set to 0\.

Note that due to the way [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) and
QRectF are defined, an empty QRectF is defined in essentially the same way as
[QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html).

Finally, QRectF objects can be streamed as well as compared.

### Rendering

When using an
[anti-aliased](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum)
painter, the boundary line of a QRectF will be rendered symmetrically on both sides of
the mathematical rectangle's boundary line. But when using an aliased painter (the
default) other rules apply.

Then, when rendering with a one pixel wide pen the QRectF's boundary line will be
rendered to the right and below the mathematical rectangle's boundary line.

When rendering with a two pixels wide pen the boundary line will be split in the middle
by the mathematical rectangle. This will be the case whenever the pen is set to an even
number of pixels, while rendering with a pen with an odd number of pixels, the spare
pixel will be rendered to the right and below the mathematical rectangle as in the one
pixel case.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Logical representation | One pixel wide pen |
|  |  |
| Two pixel wide pen | Three pixel wide pen |

### Coordinates

The QRectF class provides a collection of functions that return the various rectangle
coordinates, and enable manipulation of these. QRectF also provides functions to move
the rectangle relative to the various coordinates.

For example: the [bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#bottom)(),
[setBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setBottom)() and
[moveBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#moveBottom)() functions:
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#bottom)() returns the
y-coordinate of the rectangle's bottom edge,
[setBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setBottom)() sets the bottom
edge of the rectangle to the given y coordinate (it may change the height, but will
never change the rectangle's top edge) and
[moveBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#moveBottom)() moves the
entire rectangle vertically, leaving the rectangle's bottom edge at the given y
coordinate and its size unchanged.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qrectf-coordinates.png)

It is also possible to add offsets to this rectangle's coordinates using the
[adjust](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#adjust)() function, as well as
retrieve a new rectangle based on adjustments of the original one using the
[adjusted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#adjusted)() function. If
either of the width and height is negative, use the
[normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#normalized)() function to
retrieve a rectangle where the corners are swapped.

In addition, QRectF provides the
[getCoords](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#getCoords)() function which
extracts the position of the rectangle's top-left and bottom-right corner, and the
[getRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#getRect)() function which
extracts the rectangle's top-left corner, width and height. Use the
[setCoords](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setCoords)() and
[setRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#setRect)() function to
manipulate the rectangle's coordinates and dimensions in one go.

### bool QRectF::isValid() const

A valid rectangle has a [width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#width)()
\> 0 and [height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#height)() \> 0\. Note
that non-trivial operations like intersections are not defined for invalid rectangles. A
valid rectangle is not empty (i.e., isValid() \=\=
![isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#isEmpty)()).

**See also** [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#isNull)(),
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#isEmpty)(), and
[normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#normalized)().
