## Detailed Description

QSslSocket establishes a secure, encrypted TCP connection you can use for transmitting
encrypted data. It can operate in both client and server mode, and it supports modern
SSL protocols, including SSL 3 and TLS 1.2. By default, QSslSocket uses only SSL
protocols which are considered to be secure
([QSsl::SecureProtocols](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qssl.html#SslProtocol-enum)),
but you can change the SSL protocol by calling
[setProtocol](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#setProtocol)() as long
as you do it before the handshake has started.

SSL encryption operates on top of the existing TCP stream after the socket enters the
[ConnectedState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum).
There are two simple ways to establish a secure connection using QSslSocket: With an
immediate SSL handshake, or with a delayed SSL handshake occurring after the connection
has been established in unencrypted mode.

The most common way to use QSslSocket is to construct an object and start a secure
connection by calling
[connectToHostEncrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#connectToHostEncrypted)().
This method starts an immediate SSL handshake once the connection has been established.

```
QSslSocket *socket = new QSslSocket(this);
connect(socket, SIGNAL(encrypted()), this, SLOT(ready()));

socket->connectToHostEncrypted("imap.example.com", 993);
```

As with a plain [QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html),
QSslSocket enters the
[HostLookupState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum),
[ConnectingState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum),
and finally the
[ConnectedState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum),
if the connection is successful. The handshake then starts automatically, and if it
succeeds, the
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() signal is
emitted to indicate the socket has entered the encrypted state and is ready for use.

Note that data can be written to the socket immediately after the return from
[connectToHostEncrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#connectToHostEncrypted)()
(i.e., before the
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() signal is
emitted). The data is queued in QSslSocket until after the
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() signal is
emitted.

An example of using the delayed SSL handshake to secure an existing connection is the
case where an SSL server secures an incoming connection. Suppose you create an SSL
server class as a subclass of
[QTcpServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpserver.html). You would override
[QTcpServer::incomingConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpserver.html#incomingConnection)()
with something like the example below, which first constructs an instance of QSslSocket
and then calls
[setSocketDescriptor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#setSocketDescriptor)()
to set the new socket's descriptor to the existing one passed in. It then initiates the
SSL handshake by calling
[startServerEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startServerEncryption)().

```
void SslServer::incomingConnection(qintptr socketDescriptor)
{
    QSslSocket *serverSocket = new QSslSocket;
    if (serverSocket->setSocketDescriptor(socketDescriptor)) {
        addPendingConnection(serverSocket);
        connect(serverSocket, &QSslSocket::encrypted, this, &SslServer::ready);
        serverSocket->startServerEncryption();
    } else {
        delete serverSocket;
    }
}
```

If an error occurs, QSslSocket emits the sslErrors() signal. In this case, if no action
is taken to ignore the error(s), the connection is dropped. To continue, despite the
occurrence of an error, you can call
[ignoreSslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#ignoreSslErrors)(),
either from within this slot after the error occurs, or any time after construction of
the QSslSocket and before the connection is attempted. This will allow QSslSocket to
ignore the errors it encounters when establishing the identity of the peer. Ignoring
errors during an SSL handshake should be used with caution, since a fundamental
characteristic of secure connections is that they should be established with a
successful handshake.

Once encrypted, you use QSslSocket as a regular
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html). When
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() is emitted,
you can call [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[canReadLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#canReadLine)() and
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), or
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)() to read decrypted
data from QSslSocket's internal buffer, and you can call
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)() to write data
back to the peer. QSslSocket will automatically encrypt the written data for you, and
emit
[encryptedBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encryptedBytesWritten)()
once the data has been written to the peer.

As a convenience, QSslSocket supports
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html)'s blocking functions
[waitForConnected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForConnected)(),
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForReadyRead)(),
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForBytesWritten)(),
and
[waitForDisconnected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForDisconnected)().
It also provides
[waitForEncrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForEncrypted)(),
which will block the calling thread until an encrypted connection has been established.

```
QSslSocket socket;
socket.connectToHostEncrypted("http.example.com", 443);
if (!socket.waitForEncrypted()) {
    qDebug() << socket.errorString();
    return false;
}

socket.write("GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n");
while (socket.waitForReadyRead())
    qDebug() << socket.readAll().data();
```

QSslSocket provides an extensive, easy-to-use API for handling cryptographic ciphers,
private keys, and local, peer, and Certification Authority (CA) certificates. It also
provides an API for handling errors that occur during the handshake phase.

The following features can also be customized:

- The socket's cryptographic cipher suite can be customized before the handshake phase with [QSslConfiguration::setCiphers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslconfiguration.html#setCiphers)() and QSslConfiguration::setDefaultCiphers().
- The socket's local certificate and private key can be customized before the handshake phase with [setLocalCertificate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#setLocalCertificate)() and [setPrivateKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#setPrivateKey)().
- The CA certificate database can be extended and customized with [QSslConfiguration::addCaCertificate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslconfiguration.html#addCaCertificate)(), [QSslConfiguration::addCaCertificates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslconfiguration.html#addCaCertificates)().

To extend the list of *default* CA certificates used by the SSL sockets during the SSL
handshake you must update the default configuration, as in the snippet below:

```
QList<QSslCertificate> certificates = getCertificates();
QSslConfiguration configuration = QSslConfiguration::defaultConfiguration();
configuration.addCaCertificates(certificates);
QSslConfiguration::setDefaultConfiguration(configuration);
```

**Note:** If available, root certificates on Unix (excluding macOS) will be loaded on
demand from the standard certificate directories. If you do not want to load root
certificates on demand, you need to call either
[QSslConfiguration::defaultConfiguration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslconfiguration.html#defaultConfiguration)().setCaCertificates()
before the first SSL handshake is made in your application (for example, via passing
QSslSocket::systemCaCertificates() to it), or call
[QSslConfiguration::defaultConfiguration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslconfiguration.html#defaultConfiguration)()::setCaCertificates()
on your QSslSocket instance prior to the SSL handshake.

For more information about ciphers and certificates, refer to
[QSslCipher](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslcipher.html) and
[QSslCertificate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslcertificate.html).

This product includes software developed by the OpenSSL Project for use in the OpenSSL
Toolkit (<http://www.openssl.org/>).

**Note:** Be aware of the difference between the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal
and the
[encryptedBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encryptedBytesWritten)()
signal. For a [QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html),
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() will
get emitted as soon as data has been written to the TCP socket. For a QSslSocket,
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() will
get emitted when the data is being encrypted and
[encryptedBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encryptedBytesWritten)()
will get emitted as soon as data has been written to the TCP socket.

### void QSslSocket::connectToHostEncrypted(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*hostName*, [quint16](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint16-typedef) *port*, [QIODevice::OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) *mode* \= ReadWrite, [QAbstractSocket::NetworkLayerProtocol](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#NetworkLayerProtocol-enum) *protocol* \= AnyIPProtocol)

Starts an encrypted connection to the device *hostName* on *port*, using *mode* as the
[OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum). This is
equivalent to calling
[connectToHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#connectToHost)()
to establish the connection, followed by a call to
[startClientEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startClientEncryption)().
The *protocol* parameter can be used to specify which network protocol to use (eg. IPv4
or IPv6).

[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) first enters the
[HostLookupState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum).
Then, after entering either the event loop or one of the waitFor...() functions, it
enters the
[ConnectingState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum),
emits [connected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#connected)(),
and then initiates the SSL client handshake. At each state change,
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) emits signal
[stateChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#stateChanged)().

After initiating the SSL client handshake, if the identity of the peer can't be
established, signal sslErrors() is emitted. If you want to ignore the errors and
continue connecting, you must call
[ignoreSslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#ignoreSslErrors)(),
either from inside a slot function connected to the sslErrors() signal, or prior to
entering encrypted mode. If
[ignoreSslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#ignoreSslErrors)()
is not called, the connection is dropped, signal
[disconnected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#disconnected)()
is emitted, and [QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) returns
to the
[UnconnectedState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum).

If the SSL handshake is successful,
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) emits
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)().

```
QSslSocket socket;
connect(&socket, SIGNAL(encrypted()), receiver, SLOT(socketEncrypted()));

socket.connectToHostEncrypted("imap", 993);
socket->write("1 CAPABILITY\r\n");
```

**Note:** The example above shows that text can be written to the socket immediately
after requesting the encrypted connection, before the
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() signal has
been emitted. In such cases, the text is queued in the object and written to the socket
*after* the connection is established and the
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() signal has
been emitted.

The default for *mode* is
[ReadWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum).

If you want to create a [QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html)
on the server side of a connection, you should instead call
[startServerEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startServerEncryption)()
upon receiving the incoming connection through
[QTcpServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpserver.html).

**See also**
[connectToHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#connectToHost)(),
[startClientEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startClientEncryption)(),
[waitForConnected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForConnected)(),
and
[waitForEncrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForEncrypted)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QSslSocket::encryptedBytesAvailable() const

Returns the number of encrypted bytes that are awaiting decryption. Normally, this
function will return 0 because

### bool QSslSocket::flush()

This function writes as much as possible from the internal write buffer to the
underlying network socket, without blocking. If any data was written, this function
returns `true`; otherwise false is returned.

Call this function if you need
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) to start sending
buffered data immediately. The number of bytes successfully written depends on the
operating system. In most cases, you do not need to call this function, because
[QAbstractSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html) will start
sending data automatically once control goes back to the event loop. In the absence of
an event loop, call
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForBytesWritten)()
instead.

**See also** [write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() and
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#waitForBytesWritten)().

PythonQt.Qt.QSslSocket.ignoreSslErrors.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QSslSocket::ignoreSslErrors()

This slot tells [QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) to
ignore errors during [QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html)'s
handshake phase and continue connecting. If you want to continue with the connection
even if errors occur during the handshake phase, then you must call this slot, either
from a slot connected to sslErrors(), or before the handshake phase. If you don't call
this slot, either in response to errors or before the handshake, the connection will be
dropped after the sslErrors() signal has been emitted.

If there are no errors during the SSL handshake phase (i.e., the identity of the peer is
established with no problems),
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) will not emit the
sslErrors() signal, and it is unnecessary to call this function.

**Warning:** Be sure to always let the user inspect the errors reported by the
sslErrors() signal, and only call this method upon confirmation from the user that
proceeding is ok. If there are unexpected errors, the connection should be aborted.
Calling this method without inspecting the actual errors will most likely pose a
security risk for your application. Use it with great care!

**See also**
[sslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket-obsolete.html#sslErrors)().

### void QSslSocket::ignoreSslErrors(const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QSslError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslerror.html)\> \&*errors*)

This is an overloaded function.

This method tells [QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) to
ignore only the errors given in *errors*.

**Note:** Because most SSL errors are associated with a certificate, for most of them
you must set the expected certificate this SSL error is related to. If, for instance,
you want to connect to a server that uses a self-signed certificate, consider the
following snippet:

```
QList<QSslCertificate> cert = QSslCertificate::fromPath(QLatin1String("server-certificate.pem"));
QSslError error(QSslError::SelfSignedCertificate, cert.at(0));
QList<QSslError> expectedSslErrors;
expectedSslErrors.append(error);

QSslSocket socket;
socket.ignoreSslErrors(expectedSslErrors);
socket.connectToHostEncrypted("server.tld", 443);
```

Multiple calls to this function will replace the list of errors that were passed in
previous calls. You can clear the list of errors you want to ignore by calling this
function with an empty list.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[sslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket-obsolete.html#sslErrors)() and
[sslHandshakeErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#sslHandshakeErrors)().

### bool QSslSocket::isEncrypted() const

Returns `true` if the socket is encrypted; otherwise, false is returned.

An encrypted socket encrypts all data that is written by calling
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)() before the data
is written to the network, and decrypts all incoming data as the data is received from
the network, before you call
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() or
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)().

[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) emits
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() when it
enters encrypted mode.

You can call
[sessionCipher](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#sessionCipher)() to
find which cryptographic cipher is used to encrypt and decrypt your data.

Qt 5 reference:

### [QSslCertificate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslcertificate.html) QSslSocket::peerCertificate() const

Returns the peer's digital certificate (i.e., the immediate certificate of the host you
are connected to), or a null certificate, if the peer has not assigned a certificate.

The peer certificate is checked automatically during the handshake phase, so this
function is normally used to fetch the certificate for display or for connection
diagnostic purposes. It contains information about the peer, including its host name,
the certificate issuer, and the peer's public key.

Because the peer certificate is set during the handshake phase, it is safe to access the
peer certificate from a slot connected to the sslErrors() signal or the
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() signal.

If a null certificate is returned, it can mean the SSL handshake failed, or it can mean
the host you are connected to doesn't have a certificate, or it can mean there is no
connection.

If you want to check the peer's complete chain of certificates, use
[peerCertificateChain](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#peerCertificateChain)()
to get them all at once.

**See also**
[peerCertificateChain](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#peerCertificateChain)().

Returns the peer's chain of digital certificates, or an empty list of certificates.

Peer certificates are checked automatically during the handshake phase. This function is
normally used to fetch certificates for display, or for performing connection
diagnostics. Certificates contain information about the peer and the certificate
issuers, including host name, issuer names, and issuer public keys.

The peer certificates are set in
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) during the handshake
phase, so it is safe to call this function from a slot connected to the sslErrors()

If an empty list is returned, it can mean the SSL handshake failed, or it can mean the
host you are connected to doesn't have a certificate, or it can mean there is no
connection.

If you want to get only the peer's immediate certificate, use
[peerCertificate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#peerCertificate)().

### `[signal]` void QSslSocket::peerVerifyError(const [QSslError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslerror.html) \&*error*)

[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) can emit this signal
several times during the SSL handshake, before encryption has been established, to
indicate that an error has occurred while establishing the identity of the peer. The
*error* is usually an indication that
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) is unable to securely

to this signal, you can manually choose to tear down the connection from inside the
connected slot before the handshake has completed. If no action is taken,
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) will proceed to
emitting QSslSocket::sslErrors().

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

[sslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket-obsolete.html#sslErrors)().

### `[signal]` void QSslSocket::preSharedKeyAuthenticationRequired([QSslPreSharedKeyAuthenticator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslpresharedkeyauthenticator.html) \**authenticator*)

[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) emits this signal when
it negotiates a PSK ciphersuite, and therefore a PSK authentication is then required.

information in a slot connected to this signal, by filling in the passed *authenticator*

cause the handshake to fail, and therefore the connection to be aborted.

the application.

### void QSslSocket::setLocalCertificate(const [QSslCertificate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslcertificate.html) \&*certificate*)

Sets the socket's local certificate to *certificate*. The local certificate is necessary
if you need to confirm your identity to the peer. It is used together with the private
key; if you set the local certificate, you must also set the private key.

The local certificate and private key are always necessary for server sockets, but are
also rarely used by client sockets if the server requires the client to authenticate.

**Note:** Secure Transport SSL backend on macOS may update the default keychain (the
default is probably your login keychain) by importing your local certificates and keys.
This can also result in system dialogs showing up and asking for permission when your
application is using these private keys. If such behavior is undesired, set the
QT\_SSL\_USE\_TEMPORARY\_KEYCHAIN environment variable to a non-zero value; this will
prompt [QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) to use its own
temporary keychain.

Sets the maximum number of certificates in the peer's certificate chain to be checked

PythonQt.Qt.QSslSocket.sslErrors.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QSslSocket::sslErrors(const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QSslError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslerror.html)\> \&*errors*)

[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) emits this signal after
the SSL handshake to indicate that one or more errors have occurred while establishing
the identity of the peer. The errors are usually an indication that
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) is unable to securely
identify the peer. Unless any action is taken, the connection will be dropped after this
signal has been emitted.

If you want to continue connecting despite the errors that have occurred, you must call
[QSslSocket::ignoreSslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#ignoreSslErrors)()
from inside a slot connected to this signal. If you need to access the error list at a
later point, you can call
[sslHandshakeErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#sslHandshakeErrors)().

*errors* contains one or more errors that prevent
[QSslSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html) from verifying the
identity of the peer.

**Note:** You cannot use
[Qt::QueuedConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ConnectionType-enum)
when connecting to this signal, or calling
[QSslSocket::ignoreSslErrors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#ignoreSslErrors)()
will have no effect.

**Note:** Signal *sslErrors* is overloaded in this class. To connect to this signal by
using the function pointer syntax, Qt provides a convenient helper for obtaining the
function pointer as shown in this example:

```
connect(sslSocket, QOverload<const QList<QSslError> &>::of(&QSslSocket::sslErrors),
    [=](const QList<QSslError> &errors){ /* ... */ });
```

**See also**
[peerVerifyError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#peerVerifyError)().

### `[slot]` void QSslSocket::startClientEncryption()

Starts a delayed SSL handshake for a client connection. This function can be called when
the socket is in the
[ConnectedState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum)
but still in the
[UnencryptedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#SslMode-enum). If
it is not yet connected, or if it is already encrypted, this function has no effect.

Clients that implement STARTTLS functionality often make use of delayed SSL handshakes.
Most other clients can avoid calling this function directly by using
[connectToHostEncrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#connectToHostEncrypted)()
instead, which automatically performs the handshake.

**See also**
[connectToHostEncrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#connectToHostEncrypted)()
and
[startServerEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startServerEncryption)().

PythonQt.Qt.QSslSocket.startServerEncryp.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QSslSocket::startServerEncryption()

Starts a delayed SSL handshake for a server connection. This function can be called when
the socket is in the
[ConnectedState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum)
but still in
[UnencryptedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#SslMode-enum). If
it is not connected or it is already encrypted, the function has no effect.

For server sockets, calling this function is the only way to initiate the SSL handshake.
Most servers will call this function immediately upon receiving a connection, or as a
result of having received a protocol-specific command to enter SSL mode (e.g, the server
may respond to receiving the string "STARTTLS\\r\\n" by calling this function).

The most common way to implement an SSL server is to create a subclass of
[QTcpServer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpserver.html) and reimplement
[QTcpServer::incomingConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpserver.html#incomingConnection)().
The returned socket descriptor is then passed to
[QSslSocket::setSocketDescriptor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#setSocketDescriptor)().

**See also**
[connectToHostEncrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#connectToHostEncrypted)()
and
[startClientEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startClientEncryption)().

### bool QSslSocket::waitForEncrypted(int *msecs* \= 30000\)

Waits until the socket has completed the SSL handshake and has emitted
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)(), or *msecs*
milliseconds, whichever comes first. If
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)() has been
emitted, this function returns true; otherwise (e.g., the socket is disconnected, or the
SSL handshake fails), false is returned.

The following example waits up to one second for the socket to be encrypted:

```
socket->connectToHostEncrypted("imap", 993);
if (socket->waitForEncrypted(1000))
    qDebug("Encrypted!");
```

If msecs is -1, this function will not time out.

**See also**
[startClientEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startClientEncryption)(),
[startServerEncryption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#startServerEncryption)(),
[encrypted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsslsocket.html#encrypted)(), and

PythonQt.Qt.QStackedLayout.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QStackedLayout can be used to create a user interface similar to the one provided by
[QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html). There is also a
convenience [QStackedWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html)
class built on top of QStackedLayout.

A QStackedLayout can be populated with a number of child widgets ("pages"). For example:

```
    QWidget *firstPageWidget = new QWidget;
    QWidget *secondPageWidget = new QWidget;
    QWidget *thirdPageWidget = new QWidget;

    QStackedLayout *stackedLayout = new QStackedLayout;
    stackedLayout->addWidget(firstPageWidget);
    stackedLayout->addWidget(secondPageWidget);
    stackedLayout->addWidget(thirdPageWidget);

    QVBoxLayout *mainLayout = new QVBoxLayout;
    mainLayout->addLayout(stackedLayout);
    setLayout(mainLayout);
```

QStackedLayout provides no intrinsic means for the user to switch page. This is
typically done through a [QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html)
or a [QListWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html) that stores the
titles of the QStackedLayout's pages. For example:

```
    QComboBox *pageComboBox = new QComboBox;
    pageComboBox->addItem(tr("Page 1"));
    pageComboBox->addItem(tr("Page 2"));
    pageComboBox->addItem(tr("Page 3"));
    connect(pageComboBox, QOverload<int>::of(&QComboBox::activated),
            stackedLayout, &QStackedLayout::setCurrentIndex);
```

When populating a layout, the widgets are added to an internal list. The
[indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#indexOf)() function returns
the index of a widget in that list. The widgets can either be added to the end of the
list using the
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#addWidget)()
function, or inserted at a given index using the
[insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#insertWidget)()
function. The
[removeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#removeWidget)() function
removes the widget at the given index from the layout. The number of widgets contained
in the layout, can be obtained using the
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#count-prop)() function.

The [widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#widget)() function
returns the widget at a given index position. The index of the widget that is shown on
screen is given by
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#currentIndex-prop)()
and can be changed using
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#currentIndex-prop)().
In a similar manner, the currently shown widget can be retrieved using the
[currentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#currentWidget)()
function, and altered using the
[setCurrentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#setCurrentWidget)()
function.

Whenever the current widget in the layout changes or a widget is removed from the
layout, the
[currentChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#currentChanged)()
and
[widgetRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html#widgetRemoved)()
signals are emitted respectively.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QStackedWidget can be used to create a user interface similar to the one provided by
[QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html). It is a convenience
layout widget built on top of the
[QStackedLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html) class.

Like [QStackedLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html),
QStackedWidget can be constructed and populated with a number of child widgets
("pages"):

```
    QWidget *firstPageWidget = new QWidget;
    QWidget *secondPageWidget = new QWidget;
    QWidget *thirdPageWidget = new QWidget;

    QStackedWidget *stackedWidget = new QStackedWidget;
    stackedWidget->addWidget(firstPageWidget);
    stackedWidget->addWidget(secondPageWidget);
    stackedWidget->addWidget(thirdPageWidget);

    QVBoxLayout *layout = new QVBoxLayout;
    layout->addWidget(stackedWidget);
    setLayout(layout);
```

QStackedWidget provides no intrinsic means for the user to switch page. This is
typically done through a [QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html)
or a [QListWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html) that stores the
titles of the QStackedWidget's pages. For example:

```
    QComboBox *pageComboBox = new QComboBox;
    pageComboBox->addItem(tr("Page 1"));
    pageComboBox->addItem(tr("Page 2"));
    pageComboBox->addItem(tr("Page 3"));
    connect(pageComboBox, QOverload<int>::of(&QComboBox::activated),
            stackedWidget, &QStackedWidget::setCurrentIndex);
```

When populating a stacked widget, the widgets are added to an internal list. The
[indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#indexOf)() function
returns the index of a widget in that list. The widgets can either be added to the end
of the list using the
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#addWidget)()
function, or inserted at a given index using the
[insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#insertWidget)()
function. The
[removeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#removeWidget)()
function removes a widget from the stacked widget. The number of widgets contained in
the stacked widget can be obtained using the
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#count-prop)() function.

The [widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#widget)() function
returns the widget at a given index position. The index of the widget that is shown on
screen is given by
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#currentIndex-prop)()
and can be changed using
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#currentIndex-prop)().
In a similar manner, the currently shown widget can be retrieved using the
[currentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#currentWidget)()
function, and altered using the
[setCurrentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#setCurrentWidget)()
function.

Whenever the current widget in the stacked widget changes or a widget is removed from
the stacked widget, the
[currentChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#currentChanged)()
and
[widgetRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html#widgetRemoved)()
signals are emitted respectively.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Items usually contain text, icons, or checkboxes.

Each item can have its own background brush which is set with the
[setBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setBackground)()
function. The current background brush can be found with
[background](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#background)(). The
text label for each item can be rendered with its own font and brush. These are
specified with the
[setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setFont)() and
[setForeground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setForeground)()
functions, and read with
[font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#font)() and
[foreground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#foreground)().

By default, items are enabled, editable, selectable, checkable, and can be used both as
the source of a drag and drop operation and as a drop target. Each item's flags can be
changed by calling
[setFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setFlags)(). Checkable
items can be checked and unchecked with the
[setCheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setCheckState)()
function. The corresponding
[checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#checkState)()
function indicates whether the item is currently checked.

You can store application-specific data in an item by calling
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setData)().

Each item can have a two-dimensional table of child items. This makes it possible to
build hierarchies of items. The typical hierarchy is the tree, in which case the child
table is a table with a single column (a list).

The dimensions of the child table can be set with
[setRowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setRowCount)() and
[setColumnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setColumnCount)().
Items can be positioned in the child table with
[setChild](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setChild)(). Get a
pointer to a child item with
[child](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#child)(). New rows and
columns of children can also be inserted with
[insertRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#insertRow)() and
[insertColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#insertColumn)(), or
appended with
[appendRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#appendRow)() and
[appendColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#appendColumn)().
When using the append and insert functions, the dimensions of the child table will grow
as needed.

An existing row of children can be removed with
[removeRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#removeRow)() or
[takeRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#takeRow)();
correspondingly, a column can be removed with
[removeColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#removeColumn)() or
[takeColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#takeColumn)().

An item's children can be sorted by calling
[sortChildren](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#sortChildren)().

### Subclassing

When subclassing QStandardItem to provide custom items, it is possible to define new
types for them so that they can be distinguished from the base class. The
[type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#type)() function should be
reimplemented to return a new type value equal to or greater than
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#ItemType-enum).

Reimplement [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#data)() and
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#setData)() if you want
to perform custom handling of data queries and/or control how an item's data is
represented.

Reimplement [clone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#clone)() if
you want
[QStandardItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html) to be
able to create instances of your custom item class on demand (see
[QStandardItemModel::setItemPrototype](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#setItemPrototype)()).

Reimplement [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#read)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#write)() if you want to
control how items are represented in their serialized form.

Reimplement
[operator\<](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#operator-lt)() if you
want to control the semantics of item comparison.

PythonQt.Qt.QStandardItemModel.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QStandardItemModel can be used as a repository for standard Qt data types. It is one of
the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's
[model/view](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html) framework.

QStandardItemModel provides a classic item-based approach to working with the model. The
items in a QStandardItemModel are provided by
[QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html).

QStandardItemModel implements the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html)
interface, which means that the model can be used to provide data in any view that
supports that interface (such as
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html),
[QTableView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html) and
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html), and your own custom
views). For performance and flexibility, you may want to subclass
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) to
provide support for different kinds of data repositories. For example, the QDirModel
provides a model interface to the underlying file system.

When you want a list or tree, you typically create an empty QStandardItemModel and use
[appendRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#appendRow)() to
add items to the model, and
[item](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#item)() to access an
item. If your model represents a table, you typically pass the dimensions of the table
to the QStandardItemModel constructor and use
[setItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#setItem)() to
position items into the table. You can also use
[setRowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#setRowCount)()
and
[setColumnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#setColumnCount)()
to alter the dimensions of the model. To insert items, use
[insertRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#insertRow)() or
[insertColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#insertColumn)(),
and to remove items, use
[removeRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRow)() or
[removeColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeColumn)().

You can set the header labels of your model with
[setHorizontalHeaderLabels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#setHorizontalHeaderLabels)()
and
[setVerticalHeaderLabels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#setVerticalHeaderLabels)().

You can search for items in the model with
[findItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#findItems)(), and
sort the model by calling
[sort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#sort)().

Call [clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#clear)() to
remove all items from the model.

An example usage of QStandardItemModel to create a table:

```
QStandardItemModel model(4, 4);
for (int row = 0; row < model.rowCount(); ++row) {
    for (int column = 0; column < model.columnCount(); ++column) {
        QStandardItem *item = new QStandardItem(QString("row %0, column %1").arg(row).arg(column));
        model.setItem(row, column, item);
    }
}
```

An example usage of QStandardItemModel to create a tree:

```
QStandardItemModel model;
QStandardItem *parentItem = model.invisibleRootItem();
for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
    QStandardItem *item = new QStandardItem(QString("item %0").arg(i));
    parentItem->appendRow(item);
    parentItem = item;
}
```

After setting the model on a view, you typically want to react to user actions, such as
an item being clicked. Since a
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) provides
[QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html)-based signals and
functions, you need a way to obtain the
[QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html) that corresponds
to a given [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html), and vice
versa.
[itemFromIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#itemFromIndex)()
and
[indexFromItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#indexFromItem)()
provide this mapping. Typical usage of
[itemFromIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#itemFromIndex)()
includes obtaining the item at the current index in a view, and obtaining the item that
corresponds to an index carried by a
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) signal,
such as
[QAbstractItemView::clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#clicked)().
First you connect the view's signal to a slot in your class:

```
QTreeView *treeView = new QTreeView(this);
treeView->setModel(myStandardItemModel);
connect(treeView, &QTreeView::clicked,
        this, &MyWidget::clicked);
```

When you receive the signal, you call
[itemFromIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#itemFromIndex)()
on the given model index to get a pointer to the item:

```
void MyWidget::clicked(const QModelIndex &index)
{
    QStandardItem *item = myStandardItemModel->itemFromIndex(index);
    // Do stuff with the item ...
}
```

Conversely, you must obtain the
[QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) of an item when you
want to invoke a model/view function that takes an index as argument. You can obtain the
index either by using the model's
[indexFromItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#indexFromItem)()
function, or, equivalently, by calling
[QStandardItem::index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#index)():

```
treeView->scrollTo(item->index());
```

You are, of course, not required to use the item-based approach; you could instead rely
entirely on the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html)
interface when working with the model, or use a combination of the two as appropriate.

### [QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html) \*QStandardItemModel::itemFromIndex(const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*index*) const

Returns a pointer to the
[QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html) associated with
the given *index*.

Calling this function is typically the initial step when processing
[QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html)-based signals from a
view, such as
[QAbstractItemView::activated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#activated)().
In your slot, you call itemFromIndex(), with the
[QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) carried by the signal
as argument, to obtain a pointer to the corresponding
[QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html).

Note that this function will lazily create an item for the index (using
[itemPrototype](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#itemPrototype)()),
and set it in the parent item's child table, if no item already exists at that index.

If *index* is an invalid index, this function returns `nullptr`.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[indexFromItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#indexFromItem)().

### void QStandardItemModel::setItemPrototype(const [QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html) \**item*)

Sets the item prototype for the model to the specified *item*. The model takes ownership
of the prototype.

The item prototype acts as a
[QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html) factory, by
relying on the
[QStandardItem::clone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#clone)()
function. To provide your own prototype, subclass
[QStandardItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html), reimplement
[QStandardItem::clone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#clone)()
and set the prototype to be an instance of your custom class. Whenever
[QStandardItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html) needs
to create an item on demand (for instance, when a view or item delegate calls
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#setData)())), the
new items will be instances of your custom class.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[itemPrototype](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemmodel.html#itemPrototype)()
and
[QStandardItem::clone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditem.html#clone)().

## Detailed Description

This class contains functions to query standard locations on the local filesystem, for
common tasks such as user-specific directories or system-wide configuration directories.

PythonQt.Qt.QStandardPaths.findExecutabl.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QStandardPaths::findExecutable(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*executableName*, const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*paths* \= QStringList())

Finds the executable named *executableName* in the specified *paths*, or the system
paths if paths is empty.

On most operating systems the system path is determined by the `PATH` environment
variable. The directories where to search for the executable can be set in the paths
argument. To search in both your own paths and the system paths, call findExecutable
twice, once with paths set and once with paths empty. Symlinks are not resolved in order
to preserve behavior for the case of executables whose behavior depends on the name they
are invoked with .

**Note:** On Windows, the usual executable extensions (from the PATHEXT environment
variable) are automatically appended. For example, the findExecutable("foo") call finds
`foo.exe` or `foo.bat` if present.

Returns the absolute file path to the executable, or an empty string if not found.

If the given \\n executableName is an absolute path pointing to an executable its clean
path is returned.

PythonQt.Qt.QStandardPaths.setTestModeEn.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QStandardPaths::setTestModeEnabled(bool *testMode*)

If *testMode* is `true`, this enables a special "test mode" in
[QStandardPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandardpaths.html), which changes
writable locations to point to test directories. This prevents auto tests from reading
or writing to the current user's configuration.

It affects the locations into which test programs might write files:
`GenericDataLocation`, `DataLocation`, `ConfigLocation`, `GenericConfigLocation`,
`AppConfigLocation`, `GenericCacheLocation`, and `CacheLocation`. Other locations are
not affected.

On Unix, `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set to `~/.qttest/share`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set to
`~/.qttest/config`, and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is set to `~/.qttest/cache`.

On macOS, data goes to `~/.qttest/Application Support`, cache goes to `~/.qttest/Cache`,
and config goes to `~/.qttest/Preferences`.

On Windows, everything goes to a "qttest" directory under `%APPDATA%`.

PythonQt.Qt.QState.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QState objects can have child states, and can have transitions to other states. QState
is part of [The State Machine
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html).

The [addTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#addTransition)()
function adds a transition. The
[removeTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#removeTransition)()
function removes a transition. The
[transitions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#transitions)() function
returns the state's outgoing transitions.

The [assignProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#assignProperty)()
function is used for defining property assignments that should be performed when a state
is entered.

Top-level states must be passed a
[QStateMachine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html) object as their
parent state, or added to a state machine using
[QStateMachine::addState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#addState)().

### States with Child States

The [childMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#childMode) property
determines how child states are treated. For non-parallel state groups, the
[setInitialState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#setInitialState)()
function must be called to set the initial state. The child states are mutually
exclusive states, and the state machine needs to know which child state to enter when
the parent state is the target of a transition.

The state emits the
[QState::finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#finished)() signal
when a final child state
([QFinalState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfinalstate.html)) is entered.

The [setErrorState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#setErrorState)() sets
the state's error state. The error state is the state that the state machine will
transition to if an error is detected when attempting to enter the state (e.g. because
no initial state has been set).

### void QState::addTransition([QAbstractTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html) \**transition*)

Adds the given *transition*. The transition has this state as the source. This state
takes ownership of the transition.

### [QSignalTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsignaltransition.html) \*QState::addTransition(const [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**sender*, const char \**signal*, [QAbstractState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html#QAbstractState) \**target*)

Adds a transition associated with the given *signal* of the given *sender* object, and
returns the new

PythonQt.Qt.QStateMachine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QStateMachine is based on the concepts and notation of
[Statecharts](http://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~dharel/SCANNED.PAPERS/Statecharts.pdf).
QStateMachine is part of [The State Machine
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html).

A state machine manages a set of states (classes that inherit from
[QAbstractState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html)) and
transitions (descendants of
[QAbstractTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html))
between those states; these states and transitions define a state graph. Once a state
graph has been built, the state machine can execute it. QStateMachine's execution
algorithm is based on the [State Chart XML (SCXML)](http://www.w3.org/TR/scxml/)
algorithm. The framework's
[overview](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html) gives several state
graphs and the code to build them.

Use the [addState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#addState)()
function to add a top-level state to the state machine. States are removed with the
[removeState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#removeState)()
function. Removing states while the machine is running is discouraged.

Before the machine can be started, the [initial
state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#initialState) must be set. The
initial state is the state that the machine enters when started. You can then
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#start)() the state
machine. The [started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#started)()
signal is emitted when the initial state is entered.

The machine is event driven and keeps its own event loop. Events are posted to the
machine through
[postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#postEvent)(). Note
that this means that it executes asynchronously, and that it will not progress without a
running event loop. You will normally not have to post events to the machine directly as
Qt's transitions, e.g.,
[QEventTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventtransition.html) and its
subclasses, handle this. But for custom transitions triggered by events,
[postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#postEvent)() is
useful.

The state machine processes events and takes transitions until a top-level final state
is entered; the state machine then emits the
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#finished)() signal. You can
also [stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#stop)() the state
machine explicitly. The
[stopped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#stopped)() signal is
emitted in this case.

The following snippet shows a state machine that will finish when a button is clicked:

```
QPushButton button;

QStateMachine machine;
QState *s1 = new QState();
s1->assignProperty(&button, "text", "Click me");

QFinalState *s2 = new QFinalState();
s1->addTransition(&button, &QPushButton::clicked, s2);

machine.addState(s1);
machine.addState(s2);
machine.setInitialState(s1);
machine.start();
```

This code example uses [QState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html), which
inherits [QAbstractState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html). The
[QState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html) class provides a state that you
can use to set properties and invoke methods on
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)s when the state is entered or
exited. It also contains convenience functions for adding transitions, e.g.,
[QSignalTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsignaltransition.html)s as in
this example. See the [QState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html) class
description for further details.

If an error is encountered, the machine will look for an [error
state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#errorState), and if one is
available, it will enter this state. The types of errors possible are described by the
[Error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#Error-enum) enum. After
the error state is entered, the type of the error can be retrieved with
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#error)(). The execution of
the state graph will not stop when the error state is entered. If no error state applies
to the erroneous state, the machine will stop executing and an error message will be
printed to the console.

**Note:** Important: setting the
[ChildMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#ChildMode-enum) of a state
machine to parallel
([ParallelStates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#ChildMode-enum))
results in an invalid state machine. It can only be set to (or kept as)
[ExclusiveStates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#ChildMode-enum).

milliseconds. Returns an identifier associated with the delayed event, or -1 if the

the event and deletes it once it has been processed.

PythonQt.Qt.QStaticText.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QStaticText provides a way to cache layout data for a block of text so that it can be
drawn more efficiently than by using
[QPainter::drawText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawText)() in
which the layout information is recalculated with every call.

The class primarily provides an optimization for cases where the text, its font and the
transformations on the painter are static over several paint events. If the text or its
layout is changed for every iteration,
[QPainter::drawText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawText)() is the
more efficient alternative, since the static text's layout would have to be recalculated
to take the new state into consideration.

Translating the painter will not cause the layout of the text to be recalculated, but
will cause a very small performance impact on drawStaticText(). Altering any other parts
of the painter's transformation or the painter's font will cause the layout of the
static text to be recalculated. This should be avoided as often as possible to maximize
the performance benefit of using QStaticText.

In addition, only affine transformations are supported by drawStaticText(). Calling
drawStaticText() on a projected painter will perform slightly worse than using the
regular drawText() call, so this should be avoided.

```
class MyWidget: public QWidget
{
public:
    MyWidget(QWidget *parent = 0) : QWidget(parent), m_staticText("This is static text")

protected:
    void paintEvent(QPaintEvent *)
    {
        QPainter painter(this);
        painter.drawStaticText(0, 0, m_staticText);
    }

private:
    QStaticText m_staticText;
};
```

The QStaticText class can be used to mimic the behavior of
[QPainter::drawText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawText)() to a
specific point with no boundaries, and also when
[QPainter::drawText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawText)() is
called with a bounding rectangle.

If a bounding rectangle is not required, create a QStaticText object without setting a
preferred text width. The text will then occupy a single line.

If you set a text width on the QStaticText object, this will bound the text. The text
will be formatted so that no line exceeds the given width. The text width set for
QStaticText will not automatically be used for clipping. To achieve clipping in addition
to line breaks, use
[QPainter::setClipRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setClipRect)().
The position of the text is decided by the argument passed to
[QPainter::drawStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawStaticText)()
and can change from call to call with a minimal impact on performance.

For extra convenience, it is possible to apply formatting to the text using the HTML
subset supported by
[QTextDocument](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextdocument.html). QStaticText will
attempt to guess the format of the input text using
[Qt::mightBeRichText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt-sub-qtgui.html#mightBeRichText)(),
and interpret it as rich text if this function returns `true`. To force QStaticText to
display its contents as either plain text or rich text, use the function
[QStaticText::setTextFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html#setTextFormat)()
and pass in, respectively,
[Qt::PlainText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFormat-enum) and
[Qt::RichText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFormat-enum).

QStaticText can only represent text, so only HTML tags which alter the layout or
appearance of the text will be respected. Adding an image to the input HTML, for
instance, will cause the image to be included as part of the layout, affecting the
positions of the text glyphs, but it will not be displayed. The result will be an empty
area the size of the image in the output. Similarly, using tables will cause the text to
be laid out in table format, but the borders will not be drawn.

If it's the first time the static text is drawn, or if the static text, or the painter's
font has been altered since the last time it was drawn, the text's layout has to be
recalculated. On some paint engines, changing the matrix of the painter will also cause
the layout to be recalculated. In particular, this will happen for any engine except for
the OpenGL2 paint engine. Recalculating the layout will impose an overhead on the
[QPainter::drawStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawStaticText)()
call where it occurs. To avoid this overhead in the paint event, you can call
[prepare](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html#prepare)() ahead of time
to ensure that the layout is calculated.

### void QStaticText::prepare(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*matrix* \= QTransform(), const [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) \&*font* \= QFont())

When drawStaticText() is called, the layout of the

on any other paint engine than the OpenGL2 engine, if the painter's matrix has been

To avoid the overhead of creating the layout the first time you draw the
[QStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html) after making changes,
you can use the prepare() function and pass in the *matrix* and *font* you expect to use

## Detailed Description

Each status indicator falls into one of three categories:

- *Temporary* \- briefly occupies most of the status bar. Used to explain tool tip texts or menu entries, for example.
- *Normal* \- occupies part of the status bar and may be hidden by temporary messages. Used to display the page and line number in a word processor, for example.
- *Permanent* \- is never hidden. Used for important mode indications, for example, some applications put a Caps Lock indicator in the status bar.

QStatusBar lets you display all three types of indicators.

Typically, a request for the status bar functionality occurs in relation to a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) object.
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) provides a main
application window, with a menu bar, tool bars, dock widgets *and* a status bar around a
large central widget. The status bar can be retrieved using the
[QMainWindow::statusBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#statusBar)()
function, and replaced using the
[QMainWindow::setStatusBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#setStatusBar)()
function.

Use the [showMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#showMessage)()
slot to display a *temporary* message:

```
void MainWindow::createStatusBar()
{
    statusBar()->showMessage(tr("Ready"));
}
```

To remove a temporary message, use the
[clearMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#clearMessage)() slot,
or set a time limit when calling
[showMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#showMessage)(). For
example:

```
void MainWindow::print()
{
#if defined(QT_PRINTSUPPORT_LIB) && QT_CONFIG(printdialog)
    QTextDocument *document = textEdit->document();
    QPrinter printer;

    QPrintDialog dlg(&printer, this);
    if (dlg.exec() != QDialog::Accepted) {
        return;
    }

    document->print(&printer);
    statusBar()->showMessage(tr("Ready"), 2000);
#endif
}
```

Use the
[currentMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#currentMessage)()
function to retrieve the temporary message currently shown. The QStatusBar class also
provide the
[messageChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#messageChanged)()
signal which is emitted whenever the temporary status message changes.

*Normal* and *Permanent* messages are displayed by creating a small widget
([QLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html),
[QProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html) or even
[QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html)) and then adding it
to the status bar using the
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#addWidget)() or the
[addPermanentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#addPermanentWidget)()
function. Use the
[removeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#removeWidget)()
function to remove such messages from the status bar.

```
statusBar()->addWidget(new MyReadWriteIndication);
```

By default QStatusBar provides a
[QSizeGrip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizegrip.html) in the lower-right
corner. You can disable it using the
[setSizeGripEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#sizeGripEnabled-prop)()
function. Use the
[isSizeGripEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#sizeGripEnabled-prop)()
function to determine the current status of the size grip.

![A status bar shown in the Fusion widget
style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/fusion-statusbar-sizegrip.png)

### void QStatusBar::addPermanentWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*, int *stretch* \= 0\)

Adds the given *widget* permanently to this status bar, reparenting the widget if it
isn't already a child of this
[QStatusBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html) object. The *stretch*
parameter is used to compute a suitable size for the given *widget* as the status bar
grows and shrinks. The default stretch factor is 0, i.e giving the widget a minimum of
space.

Permanently means that the widget may not be obscured by temporary messages. It is is
located at the far right of the status bar.

[removeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#removeWidget)(), and

### `[slot]` void QStatusBar::showMessage(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*message*, int *timeout* \= 0\)

Hides the normal status indications and displays the given *message* for the specified
number of milli-seconds (*timeout*). If *timeout* is 0 (default), the *message* remains
displayed until the
[clearMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#clearMessage)() slot
is called or until the showMessage() slot is called again to change the message.

Note that showMessage() is called to show temporary explanations of tool tip texts, so
passing a *timeout* of 0 is not sufficient to display a [permanent
message](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#permanent-message).

**See also**
[messageChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#messageChanged)(),
[currentMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html#currentMessage)(),

PythonQt.Qt.QStatusTipEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Status tips can be set on a widget using the
[QWidget::setStatusTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#statusTip-prop)()
function. They are shown in the status bar when the mouse cursor enters the widget. For
example:

| ``` MainWindow::MainWindow(QWidget *parent)     : QMainWindow(parent) {     QWidget *myWidget = new QWidget;     myWidget->setStatusTip(tr("This is my widget."));      setCentralWidget(myWidget);     ... } ``` | Widget with status tip. |
| --- | --- |

Status tips can also be set on actions using the
[QAction::setStatusTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#statusTip-prop)()
function:

| ``` MainWindow::MainWindow(QWidget *parent)     : QMainWindow(parent) {     QMenu *fileMenu = menuBar()->addMenu(tr("File"));      QAction *newAct = new QAction(tr("&New"), this);     newAct->setStatusTip(tr("Create a new file."));     fileMenu->addAction(newAct);     ... } ``` | Action with status tip. |
| --- | --- |

Finally, status tips are supported for the item view classes through the
[Qt::StatusTipRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) enum
value.

### void QStorageInfo::refresh()

Resets [QStorageInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstorageinfo.html)'s internal
cache.

[QStorageInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstorageinfo.html) caches information

[QStorageInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstorageinfo.html) retrieves
information during object construction and/or when calling the
[setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstorageinfo.html#setPath)() method. You
have to manually reset the cache by calling this function to update storage information.

Returns the mount point of the filesystem this
[QStorageInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstorageinfo.html) object represents.

On Windows, it returns the volume letter in case the volume is not mounted to a

## Detailed Description

QStringListModel is an editable model that can be used for simple cases where you need
to display a number of strings in a view widget, such as a
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) or a
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html).

The model provides all the standard functions of an editable model, representing the
data in the string list as a model with one column and a number of rows equal to the
number of items in the list.

Model indexes corresponding to items are obtained with the
[index()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractlistmodel.html#index) function,
and item flags are obtained with
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#flags)(). Item data is
read with the [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#data)()
function and written with
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#setData)(). The
number of rows (and number of items in the string list) can be found with the
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#rowCount)()
function.

The model can be constructed with an existing string list, or strings can be set later
with the
[setStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#setStringList)()
convenience function. Strings can also be inserted in the usual way with the
[insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#insertRows)()
function, and removed with
[removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#removeRows)(). The
contents of the string list can be retrieved with the
[stringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlistmodel.html#stringList)()
convenience function.

An example usage of QStringListModel:

```
    QStringListModel *model = new QStringListModel();
    QStringList list;
    list << "a" << "b" << "c";
    model->setStringList(list);
```

## Detailed Description

This class is useful when you have a sequence of
[QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html)s that you want to repeatedly
match against some strings (perhaps in a loop), or when you want to search for the same
sequence of characters multiple times in the same string. Using a matcher object and
[indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringmatcher.html#indexIn)() is faster
than matching a plain [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) with
[QString::indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#indexOf)() if
repeated matching takes place. This class offers no benefit if you are doing one-off
string matches.

Create the QStringMatcher with the
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) you want to search for. Then
call [indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringmatcher.html#indexIn)() on the
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) that you want to search.
