PythonQt.Qt.QStyle.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt contains a set of QStyle subclasses that emulate the styles of the different
platforms supported by Qt (QWindowsStyle, QMacStyle etc.). By default, these styles are
built into the Qt GUI module. Styles can also be made available as plugins.

Qt's built-in widgets use QStyle to perform nearly all of their drawing, ensuring that
they look exactly like the equivalent native widgets. The diagram below shows a
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html) in nine different styles.

![Nine combo boxes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qstyle-comboboxes.png)

Topics:

### Setting a Style

The style of the entire application can be set using the
[QApplication::setStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setStyle)()
function. It can also be specified by the user of the application, using the `-style`
command-line option:

```
./myapplication -style windows
```

If no style is specified, Qt will choose the most appropriate style for the user's
platform or desktop environment.

A style can also be set on an individual widget using the
[QWidget::setStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setStyle)()
function.

### Developing Style-Aware Custom Widgets

If you are developing custom widgets and want them to look good on all platforms, you
can use QStyle functions to perform parts of the widget drawing, such as
[drawItemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawItemText)(),
[drawItemPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawItemPixmap)(),
[drawPrimitive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawPrimitive)(),
[drawControl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawControl)(), and
[drawComplexControl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawComplexControl)().

Most QStyle draw functions take four arguments:

- an enum value specifying which graphical element to draw
- a [QStyleOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoption.html) specifying how and where to render that element
- a [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) that should be used to draw the element
- a [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) on which the drawing is performed (optional)

For example, if you want to draw a focus rectangle on your widget, you can write:

```
void MyWidget::paintEvent(QPaintEvent * /* event */)
{
    QPainter painter(this);

    QStyleOptionFocusRect option;
    option.initFrom(this);
    option.backgroundColor = palette().color(QPalette::Background);

    style()->drawPrimitive(QStyle::PE_FrameFocusRect, &option, &painter, this);
}
```

QStyle gets all the information it needs to render the graphical element from
[QStyleOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoption.html). The widget is
passed as the last argument in case the style needs it to perform special effects (such
as animated default buttons on macOS), but it isn't mandatory. In fact, you can use
QStyle to draw on any paint device, not just widgets, by setting the
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) properly.

[QStyleOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoption.html) has various
subclasses for the various types of graphical elements that can be drawn. For example,
[PE\_FrameFocusRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PrimitiveElement-enum)
expects a
[QStyleOptionFocusRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoptionfocusrect.html)
argument.

To ensure that drawing operations are as fast as possible,
[QStyleOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoption.html) and its subclasses
have public data members. See the
[QStyleOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoption.html) class documentation
for details on how to use it.

For convenience, Qt provides the
[QStylePainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstylepainter.html) class, which
combines a QStyle, a [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html), and a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html). This makes it possible to
write

```
    QStylePainter painter(this);
    ...
    painter.drawPrimitive(QStyle::PE_FrameFocusRect, option);
```

instead of

```
    QPainter painter(this);
    ...
    style()->drawPrimitive(QStyle::PE_FrameFocusRect, &option, &painter, this);
```

### Creating a Custom Style

You can create a custom look and feel for your application by creating a custom style.
There are two approaches to creating a custom style. In the static approach, you either
choose an existing QStyle class, subclass it, and reimplement virtual functions to
provide the custom behavior, or you create an entire QStyle class from scratch. In the
dynamic approach, you modify the behavior of your system style at runtime. The static
approach is described below. The dynamic approach is described in
[QProxyStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qproxystyle.html).

The first step in the static approach is to pick one of the styles provided by Qt from
which you will build your custom style. Your choice of QStyle class will depend on which
style resembles your desired style the most. The most general class that you can use as
a base is [QCommonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommonstyle.html) (not
QStyle). This is because Qt requires its styles to be
[QCommonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommonstyle.html)s.

Depending on which parts of the base style you want to change, you must reimplement the
functions that are used to draw those parts of the interface. To illustrate this, we
will modify the look of the spin box arrows drawn by QWindowsStyle. The arrows are
*primitive elements* that are drawn by the
[drawPrimitive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawPrimitive)()
function, so we need to reimplement that function. We need the following class
declaration:

```
class CustomStyle : public QProxyStyle
{
    Q_OBJECT

public:
    CustomStyle();
    ~CustomStyle() {}

    void drawPrimitive(PrimitiveElement element, const QStyleOption *option,
                       QPainter *painter, const QWidget *widget) const override;
};
```

To draw its up and down arrows,
[QSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html) uses the
[PE\_IndicatorSpinUp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PrimitiveElement-enum)
and
[PE\_IndicatorSpinDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PrimitiveElement-enum)
primitive elements. Here's how to reimplement the
[drawPrimitive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawPrimitive)() function
to draw them differently:

```
void CustomStyle::drawPrimitive(PrimitiveElement element, const QStyleOption *option,
                                QPainter *painter, const QWidget *widget) const
{
    if (element == PE_IndicatorSpinUp || element == PE_IndicatorSpinDown) {
        QPolygon points(3);
        int x = option->rect.x();
        int y = option->rect.y();
        int w = option->rect.width() / 2;
        int h = option->rect.height() / 2;
        x += (option->rect.width() - w) / 2;
        y += (option->rect.height() - h) / 2;

        if (element == PE_IndicatorSpinUp) {
            points[0] = QPoint(x, y + h);
            points[1] = QPoint(x + w, y + h);
            points[2] = QPoint(x + w / 2, y);
        } else { // PE_SpinBoxDown
            points[0] = QPoint(x, y);
            points[1] = QPoint(x + w, y);
            points[2] = QPoint(x + w / 2, y + h);
        }

        if (option->state & State_Enabled) {
            painter->setPen(option->palette.mid().color());
            painter->setBrush(option->palette.buttonText());
        } else {
            painter->setPen(option->palette.buttonText().color());
            painter->setBrush(option->palette.mid());
        }
        painter->drawPolygon(points);
    } else {
    QProxyStyle::drawPrimitive(element, option, painter, widget);
    }
}
```

Notice that we don't use the `widget` argument, except to pass it on to the
QWindowStyle::drawPrimitive() function. As mentioned earlier, the information about what
is to be drawn and how it should be drawn is specified by a
[QStyleOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoption.html) object, so there is
no need to ask the widget.

If you need to use the `widget` argument to obtain additional information, be careful to
ensure that it isn't 0 and that it is of the correct type before using it. For example:

```
    const QSpinBox *spinBox = qobject_cast<const QSpinBox *>(widget);
    if (spinBox) {
    ...
    }
```

When implementing a custom style, you cannot assume that the widget is a
[QSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html) just because the enum value
is called
[PE\_IndicatorSpinUp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PrimitiveElement-enum)
or
[PE\_IndicatorSpinDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PrimitiveElement-enum).

The documentation for the
[Styles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-styles-example.html)
example covers this topic in more detail.

**Warning:** Qt style sheets are currently not supported for custom QStyle subclasses.
We plan to address this in some future release.

### Using a Custom Style

There are several ways of using a custom style in a Qt application. The simplest way is
to pass the custom style to the
[QApplication::setStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setStyle)()
static function before creating the
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html) object:

```
#include <QtWidgets>

#include "customstyle.h"

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    QApplication::setStyle(new CustomStyle);
    QApplication app(argc, argv);
    QSpinBox spinBox;
    spinBox.show();
    return app.exec();
}
```

You can call
[QApplication::setStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setStyle)()
at any time, but by calling it before the constructor, you ensure that the user's
preference, set using the `-style` command-line option, is respected.

You may want to make your custom style available for use in other applications, which
may not be yours and hence not available for you to recompile. The Qt Plugin system
makes it possible to create styles as plugins. Styles created as plugins are loaded as
shared objects at runtime by Qt itself. Please refer to the [Qt
Plugin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/plugins-howto.html) documentation for more
information on how to go about creating a style plugin.

Compile your plugin and put it into Qt's `plugins/styles` directory. We now have a
pluggable style that Qt can load automatically. To use your new style with existing
applications, simply start the application with the following argument:

```
./myapplication -style custom
```

The application will use the look and feel from the custom style you implemented.

### Right-to-Left Desktops

Languages written from right to left (such as Arabic and Hebrew) usually also mirror the
whole layout of widgets, and require the light to come from the screen's top-right
corner instead of top-left.

If you create a custom style, you should take special care when drawing asymmetric
elements to make sure that they also look correct in a mirrored layout. An easy way to
test your styles is to run applications with the `-reverse` command-line option or to
call
[QApplication::setLayoutDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#layoutDirection-prop)()
in your `main()` function.

Here are some things to keep in mind when making a style work well in a right-to-left
environment:

- [subControlRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#subControlRect)() and [subElementRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#subElementRect)() return rectangles in screen coordinates
- [QStyleOption::direction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoption.html#direction-var) indicates in which direction the item should be drawn in
- If a style is not right-to-left aware it will display items as if it were left-to-right
- [visualRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#visualRect)(), [visualPos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#visualPos)(), and [visualAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#visualAlignment)() are helpful functions that will translate from logical to screen representations.
- [alignedRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#alignedRect)() will return a logical rect aligned for the current direction

### Styles in Item Views

The painting of items in views is performed by a delegate. Qt's default delegate,
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html), is
also used for calculating bounding rectangles of items, and their sub-elements for the
various kind of item [data
roles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum)
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html)
supports. See the
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html) class
description to find out which datatypes and roles are supported. You can read more about
item data roles in [Model/View
Programming](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

When [QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html)
paints its items, it draws
[CE\_ItemViewItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#ControlElement-enum),
and calculates their size with
[CT\_ItemViewItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#ContentsType-enum).
Note also that it uses
[SE\_ItemViewItemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#SubElement-enum)
to set the size of editors. When implementing a style to customize drawing of item
views, you need to check the implementation of
[QCommonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommonstyle.html) (and any other
subclasses from which your style inherits). This way, you find out which and how other
style elements are painted, and you can then reimplement the painting of elements that
should be drawn differently.

We include a small example where we customize the drawing of item backgrounds.

```
    switch (element) {
        case (PE_PanelItemViewItem): {
            painter->save();

            QPoint topLeft = option->rect.topLeft();
            QPoint bottomRight = option->rect.topRight();
            QLinearGradient backgroundGradient(topLeft, bottomRight);
            backgroundGradient.setColorAt(0.0, QColor(Qt::yellow).lighter(190));
            backgroundGradient.setColorAt(1.0, Qt::white);
            painter->fillRect(option->rect, QBrush(backgroundGradient));

            painter->restore();
        break;
        }
        default:
            QProxyStyle::drawPrimitive(element, option, painter, widget);
    }
```

The primitive element
[PE\_PanelItemViewItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PrimitiveElement-enum)
is responsible for painting the background of items, and is called from
[QCommonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommonstyle.html)'s implementation of
[CE\_ItemViewItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#ControlElement-enum).

To add support for drawing of new datatypes and item data roles, it is necessary to
create a custom delegate. But if you only need to support the datatypes implemented by
the default delegate, a custom style does not need an accompanying delegate. The
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html) class
description gives more information on custom delegates.

The drawing of item view headers is also done by the style, giving control over size of
header items and row and column sizes.

Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` void QStyle::polish([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**widget*)

Initializes the appearance of the given *widget*.

This function is called for every widget at some point after it has been fully created
but just *before* it is shown for the very first time.

Note that the default implementation does nothing. Reasonable actions in this function
might be to call the QWidget::setBackgroundMode() function for the widget. Do not use
the function to set, for example, the geometry. Reimplementing this function provides a
back-door through which the appearance of a widget can be changed, but with Qt's style
engine it is rarely necessary to implement this function; reimplement
[drawItemPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawItemPixmap)(),
[drawItemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawItemText)(),
[drawPrimitive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#drawPrimitive)(), etc.
instead.

The [QWidget::inherits](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#inherits)()
function may provide enough information to allow class-specific customizations. But
because new [QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) subclasses are
expected to work reasonably with all current and *future* widgets, limited use of
hard-coded customization is recommended.

**See also** [unpolish](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#unpolish)().

### `[static]` int QStyle::sliderPositionFromValue(int *min*, int *max*, int *logicalValue*, int *span*, bool *upsideDown* \= false)

Converts the given *logicalValue* to a pixel position. The *min* parameter maps to 0,
*max* maps to *span* and other values are distributed evenly in-between.

This function can handle the entire integer range without overflow, providing that
*span* is less than 4096\.

By default, this function assumes that the maximum value is on the right for horizontal
items and on the bottom for vertical items. Set the *upsideDown* parameter to true to
reverse this behavior.

**See also**
[sliderValueFromPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#sliderValueFromPosition)().

### `[virtual]` void QStyle::unpolish([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**widget*)

Uninitialize the given *widget*'s appearance.

This function is the counterpart to
[polish](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#polish)(). It is called for
every polished widget whenever the style is dynamically changed; the former style has to
unpolish its settings before the new style can polish them again.

Note that unpolish() will only be called if the widget is destroyed. This can cause
problems in some cases, e.g, if you remove a widget from the UI, cache it, and then
reinsert it after the style has changed; some of Qt's classes cache their widgets.

**See also** [polish](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#polish)().

PythonQt.Qt.QStyleFactory.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The [QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) class is an abstract base
class that encapsulates the look and feel of a GUI. QStyleFactory creates a
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) object using the
[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstylefactory.html#create)() function and a
key identifying the style. The styles are either built-in or dynamically loaded from a
style plugin (see [QStylePlugin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleplugin.html)).

The valid keys can be retrieved using the
[keys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstylefactory.html#keys)() function. Typically
they include "windows" and "fusion". Depending on the platform, "windowsvista" and
"macintosh" may be available. Note that keys are case insensitive.

Creates and returns a [QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) object
that matches the given *key*, or returns `nullptr` if no matching style is found.

Both built-in styles and styles from style plugins are queried for a matching style.

**Note:** The keys used are case insensitive.

## Detailed Description

QStyleHintReturn and its subclasses are used to pass information from a style back to
the querying widget. This is most useful when the return value from
[QStyle::styleHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#styleHint)() does not
provide enough detail; for example, when a mask is to be returned.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

An object of this class, obtained from
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html), provides
access to certain global user interface parameters of the current platform.

Access is read only; typically the platform itself provides the user a way to tune these
parameters.

Access to these parameters are useful when implementing custom user interface
components, in that they allow the components to exhibit the same behaviour and feel as
other components.

### startDragDistance : const int

This property holds the distance, in pixels, that the mouse must be moved with a button
held down before a drag and drop operation will begin.

If you support drag and drop in your application, and want to start a drag and drop
operation after the user has moved the cursor a certain distance with a button held
down, you should use this property's value as the minimum distance required.

For example, if the mouse position of the click is stored in `startPos` and the current
position (e.g. in the mouse move event) is `currentPos`, you can find out if a drag
should be started with code like this:

```
if ((startPos - currentPos).manhattanLength() >=
        QApplication::startDragDistance())
    startTheDrag();
```

**Access functions:**

| int | **startDragDistance**() const |
| --- | --- |

**Notifier signal:**

| void | **startDragDistanceChanged**(int *startDragDistance*) |
| --- | --- |

## Detailed Description

QStyleOptionButton contains all the information that
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) functions need to draw
graphical elements like
[QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html),
[QCheckBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html), and
[QRadioButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradiobutton.html).

For performance reasons, the access to the member variables is direct (i.e., using the
`.` or `->` operator). This low-level feel makes the structures straightforward to use
and emphasizes that these are simply parameters used by the style functions.

For an example demonstrating how style options can be used, see the
[Styles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-styles-example.html)
example.

implement extensions without breaking compatibility. If you use

example.

PythonQt.Qt.QStyleOptionGraphicsItem.lev.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QStyleOptionGraphicsItem::levelOfDetailFromTransform(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*worldTransform*)

Returns the level of detail from the *worldTransform*.

Its value represents the maximum value of the height and width of a unity rectangle,
mapped using the *worldTransform* of the painter used to draw the item. By default, if
no transformations are applied, its value is 1\. If zoomed out 1:2, the level of detail
will be 0.5, and if zoomed in 2:1, its value is 2\.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[QGraphicsScene::minimumRenderSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#minimumRenderSize-prop)().

PythonQt.Qt.QStylePlugin.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QStylePlugin is a simple plugin interface that makes it easy to create custom styles
that can be loaded dynamically into applications using the
[QStyleFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstylefactory.html) class.

Writing a style plugin is achieved by subclassing this base class, reimplementing the
pure virtual [create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleplugin.html#create)()
function, and exporting the class using the
[Q\_PLUGIN\_METADATA](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtplugin.html#Q_PLUGIN_METADATA)()
macro.

```
class MyStylePlugin : public QStylePlugin
{
    Q_OBJECT
    Q_PLUGIN_METADATA(IID "org.qt-project.Qt.QStyleFactoryInterface" FILE "mystyleplugin.json")
public:
    MyStylePlugin(QObject *parent = 0);

    QStyle *create(const QString &key) override;
};
```

The json metadata file `mystyleplugin.json` for the plugin needs to contain information
about the names of the styles the plugins supports as follows:

```
{ "Keys": [ "Rocket", "Starbuster" ] }
```

See [How to Create Qt Plugins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/plugins-howto.html)
for details.

PythonQt.Qt.QStyledItemDelegate.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

When displaying data from models in Qt item views, e.g., a
[QTableView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html), the individual items
are drawn by a delegate. Also, when an item is edited, it provides an editor widget,
which is placed on top of the item view while editing takes place. QStyledItemDelegate
is the default delegate for all Qt item views, and is installed upon them when they are
created.

The QStyledItemDelegate class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html). The delegate
allows the display and editing of items to be developed independently from the model and
view.

The data of items in models are assigned an
[ItemDataRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum); each item
can store a [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) for each role.
QStyledItemDelegate implements display and editing for the most common datatypes
expected by users, including booleans, integers, and strings.

The data will be drawn differently depending on which role they have in the model. The
following table describes the roles and the data types the delegate can handle for each
of them. It is often sufficient to ensure that the model returns appropriate data for
each of the roles to determine the appearance of items in views.

| Role | Accepted Types |
| --- | --- |
| [Qt::BackgroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html) ( |
| [Qt::BackgroundColorRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) (obsolete; use [Qt::BackgroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) instead) |
| [Qt::CheckStateRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [Qt::CheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#CheckState-enum) |
| [Qt::DecorationRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html), [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html), [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) and [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) |
| [Qt::DisplayRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) and types with a string representation |
| [Qt::EditRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | See [QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html) for details |
| [Qt::FontRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) |
| [Qt::SizeHintRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html) |
| [Qt::TextAlignmentRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [Qt::Alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) |
| [Qt::ForegroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html) ( |
| [Qt::TextColorRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) (obsolete; use [Qt::ForegroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) instead) |

Editors are created with a
[QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html); a
default static instance provided by
[QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html) is
installed on all item delegates. You can set a custom factory using
[setItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#setItemEditorFactory)()
or set a new default factory with
[QItemEditorFactory::setDefaultFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html#setDefaultFactory)().
It is the data stored in the item model with the
[EditRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) that is edited.
See the [QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html)
class for a more high-level introduction to item editor factories. The [Color Editor
Factory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-itemviews-coloreditorfactory-example.html)
example shows how to create custom editors with a factory.

### Subclassing QStyledItemDelegate

If the delegate does not support painting of the data types you need or you want to
customize the drawing of items, you need to subclass QStyledItemDelegate, and
reimplement [paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#paint)()
and possibly
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#sizeHint)(). The
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#paint)() function is
called individually for each item, and with
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#sizeHint)(), you
can specify the hint for each of them.

When reimplementing
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#paint)(), one would
typically handle the datatypes one would like to draw and use the superclass
implementation for other types.

The painting of check box indicators are performed by the current style. The style also
specifies the size and the bounding rectangles in which to draw the data for the
different data roles. The bounding rectangle of the item itself is also calculated by
the style. When drawing already supported datatypes, it is therefore a good idea to ask
the style for these bounding rectangles. The
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) class description describes
this in more detail.

If you wish to change any of the bounding rectangles calculated by the style or the
painting of check box indicators, you can subclass
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html). Note, however, that the size
of the items can also be affected by reimplementing
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#sizeHint)().

It is possible for a custom delegate to provide editors without the use of an editor
item factory. In this case, the following virtual functions must be reimplemented:

- [createEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#createEditor)() returns the widget used to change data from the model and can be reimplemented to customize editing behavior.
- [setEditorData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#setEditorData)() provides the widget with data to manipulate.
- [updateEditorGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#updateEditorGeometry)() ensures that the editor is displayed correctly with respect to the item view.
- [setModelData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html#setModelData)() returns updated data to the model.

The [Star
Delegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-itemviews-stardelegate-example.html)
example creates editors by reimplementing these methods.

### QStyledItemDelegate vs. QItemDelegate

Since Qt 4.4, there are two delegate classes:
[QItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html) and
QStyledItemDelegate. However, the default delegate is QStyledItemDelegate. These two
classes are independent alternatives to painting and providing editors for items in
views. The difference between them is that QStyledItemDelegate uses the current style to
paint its items. We therefore recommend using QStyledItemDelegate as the base class when
implementing custom delegates or when working with Qt style sheets. The code required
for either class should be equal unless the custom delegate needs to use the style for
drawing.

If you wish to customize the painting of item views, you should implement a custom
style. Please see the [QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) class
documentation for details.

\*watched, QEvent \*event).

Returns `true` if the given *editor* is a valid
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and the given *event* is
handled; otherwise returns `false`. The following key press events are handled by
default:

- **Tab**
- **Backtab**
- **Enter**
- **Return**
- **Esc**

If the *editor*'s type is [QTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html)
or [QPlainTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qplaintextedit.html) then
**Enter** and **Return** keys are *not* handled.

In the case of **Tab**, **Backtab**, **Enter** and **Return** key press events, the
*editor*'s data is committed to the model and the editor is closed. If the *event* is a
**Tab** key press the view will open an editor on the next item in the view. Likewise,
if the *event* is a **Backtab** key press the view will open an editor on the *previous*
item in the view.

If the event is a **Esc** key press event, the *editor* is closed *without* committing
its data.

**See also**
[commitData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#commitData)()
and
[closeEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#closeEditor)().

PythonQt.Qt.QSurfaceFormat.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The format includes the size of the color buffers, red, green, and blue; the size of the
alpha buffer; the size of the depth and stencil buffers; and number of samples per pixel
for multisampling. In addition, the format contains surface configuration parameters
such as OpenGL profile and version for rendering, whether or not to enable stereo
buffers, and swap behaviour.

**Note:** When troubleshooting context or window format issues, it can be helpful to
enable the logging category `qt.qpa.gl`. Depending on the platform, this may print
useful debug information when it comes to OpenGL initialization and the native visual or
framebuffer configurations which QSurfaceFormat gets mapped to.

### `[static]` void QSurfaceFormat::setDefaultFormat(const [QSurfaceFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsurfaceformat.html#QSurfaceFormat) \&*format*)

Sets the global default surface *format*.

This format is used by default in
[QOpenGLContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglcontext.html),
[QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html),
[QOpenGLWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwidget.html) and similar
classes.

It can always be overridden on a per-instance basis by using the class in question's own
setFormat() function. However, it is often more convenient to set the format for all
windows once at the start of the application. It also guarantees proper behavior in
cases where shared contexts are required, because settings the format via this function
guarantees that all contexts and surfaces, even the ones created internally by Qt, will
use the same format.

**Note:** When setting
[Qt::AA\_ShareOpenGLContexts](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ApplicationAttribute-enum),
it is strongly recommended to place the call to this function before the construction of
the [QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) or
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html). Otherwise *format*
will not be applied to the global share context and therefore issues may arise with
context sharing afterwards.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also**
[defaultFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsurfaceformat.html#defaultFormat)().

### void QSurfaceFormat::setSwapInterval(int *interval*)

Sets the preferred swap interval. The swap interval specifies the minimum number of
video frames that are displayed before a buffer swap occurs. This can be used to sync
the GL drawing into a window to the vertical refresh of the screen.

Setting an *interval* value of 0 will turn the vertical refresh syncing off, any value
higher than 0 will turn the vertical syncing on. Setting *interval* to a higher value,
for example 10, results in having 10 vertical retraces between every buffer swap.

The default interval is 1\.

Changing the swap interval may not be supported by the underlying platform. In this
case, the request will be silently ignored.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.3.

**See also**
[swapInterval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsurfaceformat.html#swapInterval)().

PythonQt.Qt.QSvgGenerator.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This paint device represents a Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) drawing. Like QPrinter, it
is designed as a write-only device that generates output in a specific format.

To write an SVG file, you first need to configure the output by setting the
[fileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvggenerator.html#fileName-prop) or
[outputDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvggenerator.html#outputDevice-prop)
properties. It is usually necessary to specify the size of the drawing by setting the
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvggenerator.html#size-prop) property, and in
some cases where the drawing will be included in another, the
[viewBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvggenerator.html#viewBox) property also
needs to be set.

```
    QSvgGenerator generator;
    generator.setFileName(path);
    generator.setSize(QSize(200, 200));
    generator.setViewBox(QRect(0, 0, 200, 200));
    generator.setTitle(tr("SVG Generator Example Drawing"));
    generator.setDescription(tr("An SVG drawing created by the SVG Generator "
                                "Example provided with Qt."));
```

Other meta-data can be specified by setting the *title*, *description* and *resolution*
properties.

As with other [QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html)
subclasses, a [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) object is
used to paint onto an instance of this class:

```
    QPainter painter;
    painter.begin(&generator);
    ...
    painter.end();
```

Painting is performed in the same way as for any other paint device. However, it is
necessary to use the
[QPainter::begin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#begin)() and
[end()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#end) to explicitly begin and
end painting on the device.

The [SVG Generator
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtsvg-svggenerator-example.html) shows how
the same painting commands can be used for painting a widget and writing an SVG file.

PythonQt.Qt.QSvgRenderer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Using QSvgRenderer, Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) can be rendered onto any
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) subclass, including
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html),
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html), and QGLWidget.

QSvgRenderer provides an API that supports basic features of SVG rendering, such as
loading and rendering of static drawings, and more interactive features like animation.
Since the rendering is performed using
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html), SVG drawings can be
rendered on any subclass of
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html).

SVG drawings are either loaded when an QSvgRenderer is constructed, or loaded later
using the [load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#load)() functions.
Data is either supplied directly as serialized XML, or indirectly using a file name. If
a valid file has been loaded, either when the renderer is constructed or at some later
time, [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#isValid)() returns
true; otherwise it returns false. QSvgRenderer provides the
[render](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#render)() slot to render
the current document, or the current frame of an animated document, using a given
painter.

The [defaultSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#defaultSize)()
function provides information about the amount of space that is required to render the
currently loaded SVG file. This is useful for paint devices, such as
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), that often need to supply a
size hint to their parent layout. The default size of a drawing may differ from its
visible area, found using the
[viewBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#viewBox) property.

Animated SVG drawings are supported, and can be controlled with a simple collection of
functions and properties:

- The [animated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#animated)() function indicates whether a drawing contains animation information.
- The [framesPerSecond](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#framesPerSecond-prop) property contains the rate at which the animation plays.

Finally, the QSvgRenderer class provides the
[repaintNeeded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html#repaintNeeded)()
signal which is emitted whenever the rendering of the document needs to be updated.

PythonQt.Qt.QSvgWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class enables developers to display SVG drawings alongside standard widgets, and is
used in much the same way as [QLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html) is
used for displaying text and bitmap images.

Since QSvgWidget is a subclass of
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), SVG drawings are rendered
using the properties of the display. More control can be exercised over the rendering
process with the [QSvgRenderer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgrenderer.html)
class, as this can be used to paint onto other paint devices, such as
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) and QGLWidget. The renderer
used by the widget can be obtained with the
[renderer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgwidget.html#renderer)() function.

Each QSvgWidget can be constructed with the file name of a SVG file, or they can be
constructed without a specific file to render and one can be supplied later. The
[load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgwidget.html#load)() functions provide two
different ways to load an SVG file: they accept either the file name of an SVG file or a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) containing the
serialized XML representation of an SVG file.

By default, the widget provides a size hint to reflect the size of the drawing that it
displays. If no data has been loaded, the widget provides the default
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) size hint. Subclass this
class and reimplement
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsvgwidget.html#sizeHint)() if you need to
customize this behavior.

### `[protected]` void QSyntaxHighlighter::setCurrentBlockUserData([QTextBlockUserData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextblockuserdata.html) \**data*)

Attaches the given *data* to the current text block. The ownership is passed to the
underlying text document, i.e. the provided
[QTextBlockUserData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextblockuserdata.html) object
will be deleted if the corresponding text block gets deleted.

[QTextBlockUserData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextblockuserdata.html) can be
used to store custom settings. In the case of syntax highlighting, it is in particular
interesting as cache storage for information that you may figure out while parsing the
paragraph's text.

For example while parsing the text, you can keep track of parenthesis characters that
you encounter ('{\[(' and the like), and store their relative position and the actual
[QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html) in a simple class derived from
[QTextBlockUserData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextblockuserdata.html):

```
struct ParenthesisInfo
{
    QChar char;
    int position;
};

struct BlockData : public QTextBlockUserData
{
    QVector<ParenthesisInfo> parentheses;
};
```

During cursor navigation in the associated editor, you can ask the current
[QTextBlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextblock.html) (retrieved using the
[QTextCursor::block](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcursor.html#block)()
function) if it has a user data object set and cast it to your `BlockData` object. Then
you can check if the current cursor position matches with a previously recorded
parenthesis position, and, depending on the type of parenthesis (opening or closing),
find the next opening or closing parenthesis on the same level.

In this way you can do a visual parenthesis matching and highlight from the current
cursor position to the matching parenthesis. That makes it easier to spot a missing
parenthesis in your code and to find where a corresponding opening/closing parenthesis
is when editing parenthesis intensive code.

**See also**
[currentBlockUserData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsyntaxhighlighter.html#currentBlockUserData)()
and
[QTextBlock::setUserData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextblock.html#setUserData)().

Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::buildAbi()

Returns the full architecture string that Qt was compiled for. This string is useful for
identifying different, incompatible builds. For example, it can be used as an identifier
to request an upgrade package from a server.

The values returned from this function are kept stable as follows: the mandatory
components of the result will not change in future versions of Qt, but optional suffixes
may be added.

The returned value is composed of three or more parts, separated by dashes ("-"). They
are:

| Component | Value |
| --- | --- |
| CPU Architecture | The same as [QSysInfo::buildCpuArchitecture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#buildCpuArchitecture)(), such as "arm", "i386", "mips" or "x86\_64" |
| Endianness | "little\_endian" or "big\_endian" |
| Word size | Whether it's a 32- or 64-bit application. Possible values are: "llp64" (Windows 64-bit), "lp64" (Unix 64-bit), "ilp32" (32-bit) |
| (Optional) ABI | Zero or more components identifying different ABIs possible in this architecture. Currently, Qt has optional ABI components for ARM and MIPS processors: one component is the main ABI (such as "eabi", "o32", "n32", "o64"); another is whether the calling convention is using hardware floating point registers ("hardfloat" is present). Additionally, if Qt was configured with `-qreal float`, the ABI option tag "qreal\_float" will be present. If Qt was configured with another type as qreal, that type is present after "qreal\_", with all characters other than letters and digits escaped by an underscore, followed by two hex digits. For example, `-qreal long double` becomes "qreal\_long\_20double". |

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also**
[QSysInfo::buildCpuArchitecture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#buildCpuArchitecture)().

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::kernelType()

Returns the type of the operating system kernel Qt was compiled for. It's also the
kernel the application is running on, unless the host operating system is running a form
of compatibility or virtualization layer.

Values returned by this function are stable and will not change over time, so
applications can rely on the returned value as an identifier, except that new OS kernel
types may be added over time.

On Windows, this function returns the type of Windows kernel, like "winnt". On Unix
systems, it returns the same as the output of `uname -s` (lowercased).

**Note:** This function may return surprising values: it returns "linux" for all
operating systems running Linux (including Android), "qnx" for all operating systems
running QNX, "freebsd" for Debian/kFreeBSD, and "darwin" for macOS and iOS. For
information on the type of product the application is running on, see
[productType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#productType)().

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also** [QFileSelector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileselector.html),

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::productType()

Returns the product name of the operating system this application is running in. If the
application is running on some sort of emulation or virtualization layer (such as WINE
on a Unix system), this function will inspect the emulation / virtualization layer.

Values returned by this function are stable and will not change over time, so
applications can rely on the returned value as an identifier, except that new OS types
may be added over time.

**Linux and Android note**: this function returns "android" for Linux systems running
Android userspace, notably when using the Bionic library. For all other Linux systems,
regardless of C library being used, it tries to determine the distribution name and
returns that. If determining the distribution name failed, it returns "unknown".

**macOS note**: this function returns "osx" for all macOS systems, regardless of Apple
naming convention. The returned string will be updated for Qt 6\. Note that this
function erroneously returned "macos" for macOS 10.12 in Qt versions 5.6.2, 5.7.1, and
5.8.0.

**Darwin, iOS, tvOS, and watchOS note**: this function returns "ios" for iOS systems,
"tvos" for tvOS systems, "watchos" for watchOS systems, and "darwin" in case the system
could not be determined.

**[FreeBSD](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcore-attribution-freebsd.html#freebsd)
note**: this function returns "debian" for Debian/kFreeBSD and "unknown" otherwise.

**Windows note**: this function "winrt" for WinRT builds, and "windows" for normal
desktop builds.

For other Unix-type systems, this function usually returns "unknown".

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also** [QFileSelector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileselector.html),

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A semaphore is a generalization of a mutex. While a mutex can be locked only once, a
semaphore can be acquired multiple times. Typically, a semaphore is used to protect a
certain number of identical resources.

Like its lighter counterpart
[QSemaphore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsemaphore.html), a QSystemSemaphore can
be accessed from multiple [threads](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html).
Unlike [QSemaphore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsemaphore.html), a
QSystemSemaphore can also be accessed from multiple
[processes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html). This means
QSystemSemaphore is a much heavier class, so if your application doesn't need to access
your semaphores across multiple processes, you will probably want to use
[QSemaphore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsemaphore.html).

Semaphores support two fundamental operations,
[acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)() and
[release](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#release)():

[acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)() tries to
acquire one resource. If there isn't a resource available, the call blocks until a
resource becomes available. Then the resource is acquired and the call returns.

[release](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#release)() releases
one resource so it can be acquired by another process. The function can also be called
with a parameter n \> 1, which releases n resources.

A system semaphore is created with a string key that other processes can use to use the
same semaphore.

Example: Create a system semaphore

```
QSystemSemaphore sem("market", 3, QSystemSemaphore::Create);
                             // resources available == 3
sem.acquire();               // resources available == 2
sem.acquire();               // resources available == 1
sem.acquire();               // resources available == 0
sem.release();               // resources available == 1
sem.release(2);              // resources available == 3
```

A typical application of system semaphores is for controlling access to a circular
buffer shared by a producer process and a consumer processes.

### Platform-Specific Behavior

When using this class, be aware of the following platform differences:

**Windows:** QSystemSemaphore does not own its underlying system semaphore. Windows owns
it. This means that when all instances of QSystemSemaphore for a particular key have
been destroyed, either by having their destructors called, or because one or more
processes crash, Windows removes the underlying system semaphore.

**Unix:**

- QSystemSemaphore owns the underlying system semaphore in Unix systems. This means that the last process having an instance of QSystemSemaphore for a particular key must remove the underlying system semaphore in its destructor. If the last process crashes without running the QSystemSemaphore destructor, Unix does not automatically remove the underlying system semaphore, and the semaphore survives the crash. A subsequent process that constructs a QSystemSemaphore with the same key will then be given the existing system semaphore. In that case, if the QSystemSemaphore constructor has specified its [access mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum) as [Open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum), its initial resource count will not be reset to the one provided but remain set to the value it received in the crashed process. To protect against this, the first process to create a semaphore for a particular key (usually a server), must pass its [access mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum) as [Create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum), which will force Unix to reset the resource count in the underlying system semaphore.
- When a process using QSystemSemaphore terminates for any reason, Unix automatically reverses the effect of all acquire operations that were not released. Thus if the process acquires a resource and then exits without releasing it, Unix will release that resource.

### bool QSystemSemaphore::acquire()

Acquires one of the resources guarded by this semaphore, if there is one available, and
returns `true`. If all the resources guarded by this semaphore have already been
acquired, the call blocks until one of them is released by another process or thread
having a semaphore with the same key.

If false is returned, a system error has occurred. Call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#error)() to get a value
of
[QSystemSemaphore::SystemSemaphoreError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#SystemSemaphoreError-enum)
that indicates which error occurred.

**See also**
[release](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#release)().

PythonQt.Qt.QSystemSemaphore.release.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QSystemSemaphore::release(int *n* \= 1\)

Releases *n* resources guarded by the semaphore. Returns `true` unless there is a system
error.

Example: Create a system semaphore having five resources; acquire them all and then
release them all.

```
QSystemSemaphore sem("market", 5, QSystemSemaphore::Create);
for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i)  // acquire all 5 resources
    sem.acquire();
sem.release(5);              // release the 5 resources
```

This function can also "create" resources. For example, immediately following the
sequence of statements above, suppose we add the statement:

```
sem.release(10);          // "create" 10 new resources
```

Ten new resources are now guarded by the semaphore, in addition to the five that already
existed. You would not normally use this function to create more resources.

**See also**
[acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)().

## Detailed Description

Modern operating systems usually provide a special area on the desktop, called the
*system tray* or *notification area*, where long-running applications can display icons
and short messages.

![The system tray on Windows
XP.](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/system-tray.png)

The QSystemTrayIcon class can be used on the following platforms:

- All supported versions of Windows.
- All window managers and independent tray implementations for X11 that implement the <http://standards.freedesktop.org/systemtray-spec/systemtray-spec-0.2.html freedesktop.org> XEmbed system tray specification.
- All X11 desktop environments that implement the D-Bus <http://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Specifications/StatusNotifierItem/StatusNotifierItem> specification, including recent versions of KDE and Unity.
- All supported versions of macOS.

To check whether a system tray is present on the user's desktop, call the
[QSystemTrayIcon::isSystemTrayAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemtrayicon.html#isSystemTrayAvailable)()
static function.

To add a system tray entry, create a QSystemTrayIcon object, call
[setContextMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemtrayicon.html#setContextMenu)()
to provide a context menu for the icon, and call
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemtrayicon.html#show)() to make it
visible in the system tray. Status notification messages ("balloon messages") can be
displayed at any time using
[showMessage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemtrayicon.html#showMessage)().

If the system tray is unavailable when a system tray icon is constructed, but becomes
available later, QSystemTrayIcon will automatically add an entry for the application in
the system tray if the icon is
[visible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemtrayicon.html#visible-prop).

The [activated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemtrayicon.html#activated)()
signal is emitted when the user activates the icon.

Only on X11, when a tooltip is requested, the QSystemTrayIcon receives a
[QHelpEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhelpevent.html) of type
[QEvent::ToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).
Additionally, the QSystemTrayIcon receives wheel events of type
[QEvent::Wheel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum). These are not
supported on any other platform. Note: Since GNOME Shell version 3.26, not all
[QSystemTrayIcon::ActivationReason](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemtrayicon.html#ActivationReason-enum)
are supported by the system without shell extensions installed.

## Detailed Description

QTabBar is straightforward to use; it draws the tabs using one of the predefined
[shapes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#Shape-enum), and emits a signal
when a tab is selected. It can be subclassed to tailor the look and feel. Qt also
provides a ready-made [QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html).

Each tab has a [tabText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabText)(), an
optional [tabIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabIcon)(), an
optional [tabToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabToolTip)(),
optional [tabWhatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabWhatsThis)()
and optional [tabData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabData)(). The
tabs's attributes can be changed with
[setTabText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#setTabText)(),
[setTabIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#setTabIcon)(),
[setTabToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#setTabToolTip)(),
[setTabWhatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#setTabWhatsThis) and
[setTabData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#setTabData)(). Each tabs
can be enabled or disabled individually with
[setTabEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#setTabEnabled)().

Each tab can display text in a distinct color. The current text color for a tab can be
found with the
[tabTextColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabTextColor)() function.
Set the text color for a particular tab with
[setTabTextColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#setTabTextColor)().

Tabs are added using [addTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#addTab)(),
or inserted at particular positions using
[insertTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#insertTab)(). The total
number of tabs is given by
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#count-prop)(). Tabs can be
removed from the tab bar with
[removeTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#removeTab)(). Combining
[removeTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#removeTab)() and
[insertTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#insertTab)() allows you to
move tabs to different positions.

The [shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#shape-prop) property defines
the tabs' appearance. The choice of shape is a matter of taste, although tab dialogs
(for preferences and similar) invariably use
[RoundedNorth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#Shape-enum). Tab controls
in windows other than dialogs almost always use either
[RoundedSouth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#Shape-enum) or
[TriangularSouth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#Shape-enum). Many
spreadsheets and other tab controls in which all the pages are essentially similar use
[TriangularSouth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#Shape-enum), whereas
[RoundedSouth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#Shape-enum) is used
mostly when the pages are different (e.g. a multi-page tool palette). The default in
QTabBar is [RoundedNorth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#Shape-enum).

The most important part of QTabBar's API is the
[currentChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#currentChanged)()
signal. This is emitted whenever the current tab changes (even at startup, when the
current tab changes from 'none'). There is also a slot,
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#currentIndex-prop)(),
which can be used to select a tab programmatically. The function
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#currentIndex-prop)()
returns the index of the current tab,
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#count-prop) holds the number of
tabs.

QTabBar creates automatic mnemonic keys in the manner of
[QAbstractButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html); e.g. if a
tab's label is "\&Graphics", Alt\+G becomes a shortcut key for switching to that tab.

The following virtual functions may need to be reimplemented in order to tailor the look
and feel or store extra data with each tab:

- [tabSizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabSizeHint)() calcuates the size of a tab.
- [tabInserted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabInserted)() notifies that a new tab was added.
- [tabRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabRemoved)() notifies that a tab was removed.
- [tabLayoutChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabLayoutChange)() notifies that the tabs have been re-laid out.
- [paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#paintEvent)() paints all tabs.

For subclasses, you might also need the
[tabRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabRect)() functions which
returns the visual geometry of a single tab.

### int QTabBar::insertTab(int *index*, const [QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html) \&*icon*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*)

This is an overloaded function.

Inserts a new tab with icon *icon* and text *text* at position *index*. If *index* is
out of range, the new tab is appended. Returns the new tab's index.

If the [QTabBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html) was empty before this
function is called, the inserted tab becomes the current tab.

Inserting a new tab at an index less than or equal to the current index will increment
the current index, but keep the current tab.

### void QTabBar::setTabButton(int *index*, [QTabBar::ButtonPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#ButtonPosition-enum) *position*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*)

Sets *widget* on the tab *index*. The widget is placed on the left or right hand side
depending upon the *position*.

Any previously set widget in *position* is hidden.

The tab bar will take ownership of the widget and so all widgets set here will be
deleted by the tab bar when it is destroyed unless you separately reparent the widget
after setting some other widget (or `nullptr`).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also** [tabButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabButton)()
and [tabsClosable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html#tabsClosable-prop)().

PythonQt.Qt.QTabWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-tabwidget.png)

A tab widget provides a tab bar (see
[QTabBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html)) and a "page area" that is
used to display pages related to each tab. By default, the tab bar is shown above the
page area, but different configurations are available (see
[TabPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#TabPosition-enum)).
Each tab is associated with a different widget (called a page). Only the current page is
shown in the page area; all the other pages are hidden. The user can show a different
page by clicking on its tab or by pressing its Alt\+*letter* shortcut if it has one.

The normal way to use QTabWidget is to do the following:

1. Create a QTabWidget.
2. Create a [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) for each of the pages in the tab dialog, but do not specify parent widgets for them.
3. Insert child widgets into the page widget, using layouts to position them as normal.
4. Call [addTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#addTab)() or [insertTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#insertTab)() to put the page widgets into the tab widget, giving each tab a suitable label with an optional keyboard shortcut.

The position of the tabs is defined by
[tabPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#tabPosition-prop),
their shape by
[tabShape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#tabShape-prop).

The signal
[currentChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#currentChanged)() is
emitted when the user selects a page.

The current page index is available as
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#currentIndex-prop)(),
the current page widget with
[currentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#currentWidget)(). You
can retrieve a pointer to a page widget with a given index using
[widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#widget)(), and can find the
index position of a widget with
[indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#indexOf)(). Use
[setCurrentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#setCurrentWidget)()
or
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#currentIndex-prop)()
to show a particular page.

You can change a tab's text and icon using
[setTabText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#setTabText)() or
[setTabIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#setTabIcon)(). A tab and
its associated page can be removed with
[removeTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#removeTab)().

Each tab is either enabled or disabled at any given time (see
[setTabEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#setTabEnabled)()). If
a tab is enabled, the tab text is drawn normally and the user can select that tab. If it
is disabled, the tab is drawn in a different way and the user cannot select that tab.
Note that even if a tab is disabled, the page can still be visible, for example if all
of the tabs happen to be disabled.

Tab widgets can be a very good way to split up a complex dialog. An alternative is to
use a [QStackedWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html) for which
you provide some means of navigating between pages, for example, a
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) or a
[QListWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html).

Most of the functionality in QTabWidget is provided by a
[QTabBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html) (at the top, providing the
tabs) and a [QStackedWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html)
(most of the area, organizing the individual pages).

### int QTabWidget::addTab([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**page*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*label*)

Adds a tab with the given *page* and *label* to the tab widget, and returns the index of
the tab in the tab bar. Ownership of *page* is passed on to the

If the tab's *label* contains an ampersand, the letter following the ampersand is used
as a shortcut for the tab, e.g. if the label is "Bro\&wse" then Alt\+W becomes a
shortcut which will move the focus to this tab.

**Note:** If you call addTab() after
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(), the layout system will
try to adjust to the changes in its widgets hierarchy and may cause flicker. To prevent
this, you can set the
[QWidget::updatesEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#updatesEnabled-prop)
property to false prior to changes; remember to set the property to true when the
changes are done, making the widget receive paint events again.

[insertTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#insertTab)().

### int QTabWidget::insertTab(int *index*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**page*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*label*)

Inserts a tab with the given *label* and *page* into the tab widget at the specified
*index*, and returns the index of the inserted tab in the tab bar. Ownership of *page*
is passed on to the [QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html).

The label is displayed in the tab and may vary in appearance depending on the
configuration of the tab widget.

If the tab's *label* contains an ampersand, the letter following the ampersand is used
as a shortcut for the tab, e.g. if the label is "Bro\&wse" then Alt\+W becomes a
shortcut which will move the focus to this tab.

If *index* is out of range, the tab is simply appended. Otherwise it is inserted at the
specified position.

If the [QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html) was empty before
this function is called, the new page becomes the current page. Inserting a new tab at
an index less than or equal to the current index will increment the current index, but
keep the current page.

**Note:** If you call insertTab() after
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(), the layout system will
try to adjust to the changes in its widgets hierarchy and may cause flicker. To prevent
this, you can set the
[QWidget::updatesEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#updatesEnabled-prop)
property to false prior to changes; remember to set the property to true when the
changes are done, making the widget receive paint events again.

**See also** [addTab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#addTab)().

geometry of the widget is determined based on the widget's
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#sizeHint)() and the
[style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#style)().

Passing `nullptr` shows no widget in the corner.

All widgets set here will be deleted by the tab widget when it is destroyed unless you
separately reparent the widget after setting some other corner widget (or `nullptr`).

[North](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#TabPosition-enum) and
[South](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#TabPosition-enum) tab
positions; other orientations are known to not work properly.

### void QTabWidget::setTabEnabled(int *index*, bool *enable*)

If *enable* is true, the page at position *index* is enabled; otherwise the page at
position *index* is disabled. The page's tab is redrawn appropriately.

[QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html) uses
[QWidget::setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop)()
internally, rather than keeping a separate flag.

Note that even a disabled tab/page may be visible. If the page is visible already,
[QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html) will not hide it; if
all the pages are disabled,
[QTabWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html) will show one of them.

**See also**
[isTabEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabwidget.html#isTabEnabled)() and

PythonQt.Qt.QTableView.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-tableview.png)

A QTableView implements a table view that displays items from a model. This class is
used to provide standard tables that were previously provided by the QTable class, but
using the more flexible approach provided by Qt's model/view architecture.

The QTableView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

QTableView implements the interfaces defined by the
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) class to
allow it to display data provided by models derived from the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) class.

### Navigation

You can navigate the cells in the table by clicking on a cell with the mouse, or by
using the arrow keys. Because QTableView enables
[tabKeyNavigation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#tabKeyNavigation-prop)
by default, you can also hit Tab and Backtab to move from cell to cell.

### Visual Appearance

The table has a vertical header that can be obtained using the
[verticalHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#verticalHeader)()
function, and a horizontal header that is available through the
[horizontalHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#horizontalHeader)()
function. The height of each row in the table can be found by using
[rowHeight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#rowHeight)(); similarly,
the width of columns can be found using
[columnWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#columnWidth)(). Since
both of these are plain widgets, you can hide either of them using their
[hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)() functions. Each header is
configured with its
[highlightSections](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#highlightSections-prop)
and
[sectionsClickable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#sectionsClickable)
properties set to `true`.

Rows and columns can be hidden and shown with
[hideRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#hideRow)(),
[hideColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#hideColumn)(),
[showRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#showRow)(), and
[showColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#showColumn)(). They can
be selected with
[selectRow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#selectRow)() and
[selectColumn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#selectColumn)(). The
table will show a grid depending on the
[showGrid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#showGrid-prop) property.

The items shown in a table view, like those in the other item views, are rendered and
edited using standard
[delegates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html). However, for
some tasks it is sometimes useful to be able to insert widgets in a table instead.
Widgets are set for particular indexes with the
[setIndexWidget()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setIndexWidget)
function, and later retrieved with
[indexWidget()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#indexWidget).

|  | By default, the cells in a table do not expand to fill the available space. You can make the cells fill the available space by stretching the last header section. Access the relevant header using [horizontalHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#horizontalHeader)() or [verticalHeader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#verticalHeader)() and set the header's [stretchLastSection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#stretchLastSection-prop) property.  To distribute the available space according to the space requirement of each column or row, call the view's [resizeColumnsToContents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#resizeColumnsToContents)() or [resizeRowsToContents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#resizeRowsToContents)() functions. |
| --- | --- |

### Coordinate Systems

For some specialized forms of tables it is useful to be able to convert between row and
column indexes and widget coordinates. The
[rowAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#rowAt)() function provides
the y-coordinate within the view of the specified row; the row index can be used to
obtain a corresponding y-coordinate with
[rowViewportPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#rowViewportPosition)().
The [columnAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#columnAt)() and
[columnViewportPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html#columnViewportPosition)()
functions provide the equivalent conversion operations between x-coordinates and column
indexes.
