PythonQt.Qt.QTime.fromString.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` QTime QTime::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, [Qt::DateFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum) *format* \= Qt::TextDate)

Returns the time represented in the *string* as a
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) using the *format* given, or an
invalid time if this is not possible.

Note that fromString() uses a "C" locale encoded string to convert milliseconds to a
float value. If the default locale is not "C", this may result in two conversion
attempts (if the conversion fails for the default locale). This should be considered an
implementation detail.

**Note:** Support for localized dates, including the format options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Use
[QLocale::toTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toTime)() instead.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#toString)() and
[QLocale::toTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toTime)().

### `[static]` QTime QTime::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*)

Returns the [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) represented by the
*string*, using the *format* given, or an invalid time if the string cannot be parsed.

These expressions may be used for the format:

| Expression | Output |
| --- | --- |
| h | The hour without a leading zero (0 to 23 or 1 to 12 if AM/PM display) |
| hh | The hour with a leading zero (00 to 23 or 01 to 12 if AM/PM display) |
| H | The hour without a leading zero (0 to 23, even with AM/PM display) |
| HH | The hour with a leading zero (00 to 23, even with AM/PM display) |
| m | The minute without a leading zero (0 to 59\) |
| mm | The minute with a leading zero (00 to 59\) |
| s | The whole second, without any leading zero (0 to 59\) |
| ss | The whole second, with a leading zero where applicable (00 to 59\) |
| z | The fractional part of the second, to go after a decimal point, without trailing zeroes (0 to 999). Thus "`s.z`" reports the seconds to full available (millisecond) precision without trailing zeroes. |
| zzz | The fractional part of the second, to millisecond precision, including trailing zeroes where applicable (000 to 999). |
| AP or A | Interpret as an AM/PM time. *A/AP* will match an upper-case version of either [QLocale::amText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#amText)() or [QLocale::pmText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#pmText)(). |
| ap or a | Interpret as an am/pm time. *a/ap* will match a lower-case version of either [QLocale::amText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#amText)() or [QLocale::pmText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#pmText)(). |

All other input characters will be treated as text. Any non-empty sequence of characters
enclosed in single quotes will also be treated (stripped of the quotes) as text and not
be interpreted as expressions.

```
QTime time = QTime::fromString("1mm12car00", "m'mm'hcarss");
// time is 12:01.00
```

If the format is not satisfied, an invalid
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) is returned. Expressions that do
not expect leading zeroes to be given (h, m, s and z) are greedy. This means that they
will use two digits even if this puts them outside the range of accepted values and
leaves too few digits for other sections. For example, the following string could have
meant 00:07:10, but the m will grab two digits, resulting in an invalid time:

```
QTime time = QTime::fromString("00:710", "hh:ms"); // invalid
```

Any field that is not represented in the format will be set to zero. For example:

```
QTime time = QTime::fromString("1.30", "m.s");
// time is 00:01:30.000
```

**Note:** If localized forms of am or pm (the AP, ap, A or a formats) are used, please
switch to using
[QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)().toTime() as
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) methods shall change to only
recognize English (C locale) at Qt 6\.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#toString)(),
[QDateTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)(),
[QDate::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#fromString)(), and
[QLocale::toTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toTime)().

### int QTime::restart()

Sets this time to the current time and returns the number of milliseconds that have
elapsed since the last time start() or restart() was called.

This function is guaranteed to be atomic and is thus very handy for repeated
measurements. Call start() to start the first measurement, and restart() for each later
measurement.

Note that the counter wraps to zero 24 hours after the last call to start() or
restart().

**Warning:** If the system's clock setting has been changed since the last time start()
or restart() was called, the result is undefined. This can happen when daylight-saving
time is turned on or off.

**See also** [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime-obsolete.html#start)(),
[elapsed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime-obsolete.html#elapsed)(), and
[currentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#currentTime)().

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the time as a string. The *format* parameter determines the format of the
string.

If *format* is
[Qt::TextDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
format is HH:mm:ss; e.g. 1 second before midnight would be "23:59:59".

If *format* is
[Qt::ISODate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
format corresponds to the ISO 8601 extended specification for representations of dates,
represented by HH:mm:ss. To include milliseconds in the ISO 8601 date, use the *format*
[Qt::ISODateWithMs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), which
corresponds to HH:mm:ss.zzz.

The *format* options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum):,
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with:
[QLocale::system().toString(time,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale::system().toString(time,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

The *format* options
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with: [QLocale().toString(time,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale().toString(time,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

If the *format* is
[Qt::RFC2822Date](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the
string is formatted in an [RFC 2822](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2822.txt)
compatible way. An example of this formatting is "23:59:20".

If the time is invalid, an empty string will be returned.

**See also** [fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#fromString)(),
[QDate::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toString-1)(),
[QDateTime::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toString)(), and
[QLocale::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString)().

PythonQt.Qt.QTimeLine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It's most commonly used to animate a GUI control by calling a slot periodically. You can
construct a timeline by passing its duration in milliseconds to QTimeLine's constructor.
The timeline's duration describes for how long the animation will run. Then you set a
suitable frame range by calling
[setFrameRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#setFrameRange)().
Finally connect the
[frameChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#frameChanged)() signal
to a suitable slot in the widget you wish to animate (for example,
[setValue()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#value-prop) in
[QProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html)). When you proceed
to calling [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#start)(), QTimeLine
will enter Running state, and start emitting
[frameChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#frameChanged)() at
regular intervals, causing your widget's connected property's value to grow from the
lower end to the upper and of your frame range, at a steady rate. You can specify the
update interval by calling
[setUpdateInterval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#updateInterval-prop)().
When done, QTimeLine enters
[NotRunning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#State-enum) state, and
emits [finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#finished)().

Example:

```
...
progressBar = new QProgressBar(this);
progressBar->setRange(0, 100);

// Construct a 1-second timeline with a frame range of 0 - 100
QTimeLine *timeLine = new QTimeLine(1000, this);
timeLine->setFrameRange(0, 100);
connect(timeLine, &QTimeLine::frameChanged, progressBar, &QProgressBar::setValue);

// Clicking the push button will start the progress bar animation
pushButton = new QPushButton(tr("Start animation"), this);
connect(pushButton, &QPushButton::clicked, timeLine, &QTimeLine::start);
...
```

By default the timeline runs once, from its beginning to its end, upon which you must
call [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#start)() again to restart
from the beginning. To make the timeline loop, you can call
[setLoopCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#loopCount-prop)(),
passing the number of times the timeline should run before finishing. The direction can
also be changed, causing the timeline to run backward, by calling
[setDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#direction-prop)(). You
can also pause and unpause the timeline while it's running by calling
[setPaused](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#setPaused)(). For
interactive control, the
[setCurrentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#currentTime-prop)()
function is provided, which sets the time position of the time line directly. Although
most useful in
[NotRunning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#State-enum) state (e.g.,
connected to a
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueChanged)() signal
in a [QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html)), this function can be
called at any time.

The frame interface is useful for standard widgets, but QTimeLine can be used to control
any type of animation. The heart of QTimeLine lies in the
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)()
function, which generates a *value* between 0 and 1 for a given time. This value is
typically used to describe the steps of an animation, where 0 is the first step of an
animation, and 1 is the last step. When running, QTimeLine generates values between 0
and 1 by calling
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)() and
emitting
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueChanged)(). By
default,
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)() applies
an interpolation algorithm to generate these value. You can choose from a set of
predefined timeline algorithms by calling
[setEasingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#easingCurve-prop)().

Note that, by default, QTimeLine uses
[QEasingCurve::InOutSine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum),
which provides a value that grows slowly, then grows steadily, and finally grows slowly.
For a custom timeline, you can reimplement
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)(), in
which case QTimeLine's
[easingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#easingCurve-prop)
property is ignored.

### `[slot]` void QTimeLine::start()

Starts the timeline. [QTimeLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html) will
enter Running state, and once it enters the event loop, it will update its current time,
frame and value at regular intervals. The default interval is 40 ms (i.e., 25 times per
second). You can change the update interval by calling
[setUpdateInterval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#updateInterval-prop)().

The timeline will start from position 0, or the end if going backward. If you want to
resume a stopped timeline without restarting, you can call
[resume](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#resume)() instead.

**See also** [resume](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#resume)(),
[updateInterval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#updateInterval-prop)(),
[frameChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#frameChanged)(), and
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueChanged)().

### `[virtual]` [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QTimeLine::valueForTime(int *msec*) const

Returns the timeline value for the time *msec*. The returned value, which varies
depending on the curve shape, is always between 0 and 1\. If *msec* is 0, the default

## Detailed Description

This class provides a stateless calculator for time zone conversions between UTC and the
local time in a specific time zone. By default it uses the host system time zone data to
perform these conversions.

This class is primarily designed for use in
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html); most applications will
not need to access this class directly and should instead use
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) with a
[Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) of
[Qt::TimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

**Note:** For consistency with
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html), QTimeZone does not
account for leap seconds.

### Remarks

#### IANA Time Zone IDs

QTimeZone uses the IANA time zone IDs as defined in the IANA Time Zone Database
(http://www.iana.org/time-zones). This is to ensure a standard ID across all supported
platforms. Most platforms support the IANA IDs and the IANA Database natively, but for
Windows a mapping is required to the native IDs. See below for more details.

The IANA IDs can and do change on a regular basis, and can vary depending on how
recently the host system data was updated. As such you cannot rely on any given ID
existing on any host system. You must use
[availableTimeZoneIds](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#availableTimeZoneIds)()
to determine what IANA IDs are available.

The IANA IDs and database are also know as the Olson IDs and database, named after their
creator.

#### UTC Offset Time Zones

A default UTC time zone backend is provided which is always guaranteed to be available.
This provides a set of generic Offset From UTC time zones in the range UTC-14:00 to
UTC\+14:00. These time zones can be created using either the standard ISO format names
"UTC\+00:00" as listed by
[availableTimeZoneIds](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#availableTimeZoneIds)(),
or using the number of offset seconds.

#### Windows Time Zones

Windows native time zone support is severely limited compared to the standard IANA TZ
Database. Windows time zones cover larger geographic areas and are thus less accurate in
their conversions. They also do not support as much historic conversion data and so may
only be accurate for the current year.

QTimeZone uses a conversion table derived form the Unicode CLDR data to map between IANA
IDs and Windows IDs. Depending on your version of Windows and Qt, this table may not be
able to provide a valid conversion, in which "UTC" will be returned.

QTimeZone provides a public API to use this conversion table. The Windows ID used is the
Windows Registry Key for the time zone which is also the MS Exchange EWS ID as well, but
is different to the Time Zone Name (TZID) and COD code used by MS Exchange in versions
before 2007\.

#### System Time Zone

QTimeZone does not support any concept of a system or default time zone. If you require
a [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) that uses the current
system time zone at any given moment then you should use a
[Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) of
[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

The method
[systemTimeZoneId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#systemTimeZoneId)()
returns the current system IANA time zone ID which on Unix-like systems will always be
correct. On Windows this ID is translated from the Windows system ID using an internal
translation table and the user's selected country. As a consequence there is a small
chance any Windows install may have IDs not known by Qt, in which case "UTC" will be
returned.

Creating a new QTimeZone instance using the system time zone ID will only produce a
fixed named copy of the time zone, it will not change if the system time zone changes.

#### Time Zone Offsets

The difference between UTC and the local time in a time zone is expressed as an offset
in seconds from UTC, i.e. the number of seconds to add to UTC to obtain the local time.
The total offset is comprised of two component parts, the standard time offset and the
daylight-saving time offset. The standard time offset is the number of seconds to add to
UTC to obtain standard time in the time zone. The daylight-saving time offset is the
number of seconds to add to the standard time offset to obtain daylight-saving time
(abbreviated DST and sometimes called "daylight time" or "summer time") in the time
zone.

Note that the standard and DST offsets for a time zone may change over time as countries
have changed DST laws or even their standard time offset.

#### License

This class includes data obtained from the CLDR data files under the terms of the
Unicode Data Files and Software License. See [Unicode Common Locale Data Repository
(CLDR)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcore-attribution-unicode-cldr.html#unicode-cldr)
for details.

### int QTimeZone::offsetFromUtc(const [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) \&*atDateTime*) const

Returns the total effective offset at the given *atDateTime*, i.e. the number of seconds
to add to UTC to obtain the local time. This includes any DST offset that may be in
effect, i.e. it is the sum of
[standardTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#standardTimeOffset)()
and
[daylightTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#daylightTimeOffset)()
for the given datetime.

For example, for the time zone "Europe/Berlin" the standard time offset is \+3600
seconds and the DST offset is \+3600 seconds. During standard time offsetFromUtc() will
return \+3600 (UTC\+01:00), and during DST it will return \+7200 (UTC\+02:00).

**See also**
[standardTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#standardTimeOffset)()
and
[daylightTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#daylightTimeOffset)().

PythonQt.Qt.QTimer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QTimer class provides a high-level programming interface for timers. To use it,
create a QTimer, connect its
[timeout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout)() signal to the
appropriate slots, and call
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#start-1)(). From then on, it will
emit the [timeout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout)() signal at
constant intervals.

Example for a one second (1000 millisecond) timer (from the [Analog
Clock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-analogclock-example.html)
example):

```
    QTimer *timer = new QTimer(this);
    connect(timer, &QTimer::timeout, this, QOverload<>::of(&AnalogClock::update));
    timer->start(1000);
```

From then on, the `update()` slot is called every second.

You can set a timer to time out only once by calling
[setSingleShot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#singleShot-prop)(true).
You can also use the static
[QTimer::singleShot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#singleShot)()
function to call a slot after a specified interval:

```
    QTimer::singleShot(200, this, &Foo::updateCaption);
```

In multithreaded applications, you can use QTimer in any thread that has an event loop.
To start an event loop from a non-GUI thread, use
[QThread::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html#exec)(). Qt uses the
timer's [thread affinity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#thread) to
determine which thread will emit the
[timeout()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout) signal. Because of
this, you must start and stop the timer in its thread; it is not possible to start a
timer from another thread.

As a special case, a QTimer with a timeout of 0 will time out as soon as possible,
though the ordering between zero timers and other sources of events is unspecified. Zero
timers can be used to do some work while still providing a snappy user interface:

```
    QTimer *timer = new QTimer(this);
    connect(timer, &QTimer::timeout, this, &Foo::processOneThing);
    timer->start();
```

From then on, `processOneThing()` will be called repeatedly. It should be written in
such a way that it always returns quickly (typically after processing one data item) so
that Qt can deliver events to the user interface and stop the timer as soon as it has
done all its work. This is the traditional way of implementing heavy work in GUI
applications, but as multithreading is nowadays becoming available on more and more
platforms, we expect that zero-millisecond QTimer objects will gradually be replaced by
[QThread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html)s.

### Accuracy and Timer Resolution

The accuracy of timers depends on the underlying operating system and hardware. Most
platforms support a resolution of 1 millisecond, though the accuracy of the timer will
not equal this resolution in many real-world situations.

The accuracy also depends on the [timer
type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum). For
[Qt::PreciseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum), QTimer
will try to keep the accuracy at 1 millisecond. Precise timers will also never time out
earlier than expected.

For [Qt::CoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum) and
[Qt::VeryCoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum) types,
QTimer may wake up earlier than expected, within the margins for those types: 5% of the
interval for
[Qt::CoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum) and 500 ms
for [Qt::VeryCoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum).

All timer types may time out later than expected if the system is busy or unable to
provide the requested accuracy. In such a case of timeout overrun, Qt will emit
[timeout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout)() only once, even if
multiple timeouts have expired, and then will resume the original interval.

### Alternatives to QTimer

An alternative to using QTimer is to call
[QObject::startTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#startTimer)() for
your object and reimplement the
[QObject::timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent)()
event handler in your class (which must inherit
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)). The disadvantage is that
[timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timerEvent)() does not
support such high-level features as single-shot timers or signals.

Another alternative is
[QBasicTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html). It is typically less
cumbersome than using
[QObject::startTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#startTimer)()
directly. See [Timers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/timers.html) for an overview
of all three approaches.

Some operating systems limit the number of timers that may be used; Qt tries to work
around these limitations.

### `[slot]` void QTimer::start()

This function overloads start().

Starts or restarts the timer with the timeout specified in
[interval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#interval-prop).

If the timer is already running, it will be
[stopped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#stop) and restarted.

If [singleShot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#singleShot) is true, the
timer will be activated only once.

### `[slot]` void QTimer::start(int *msec*)

This is an overloaded function.

Starts or restarts the timer with a timeout of duration *msec* milliseconds.

If the timer is already running, it will be
[stopped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#stop) and restarted.

If [singleShot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#singleShot) is true, the
timer will be activated only once.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.8.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Timer events are sent at regular intervals to objects that have started one or more
timers. Each timer has a unique identifier. A timer is started with
[QObject::startTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#startTimer)().

The [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) class provides a high-level
programming interface that uses signals instead of events. It also provides single-shot
timers.

The event handler
[QObject::timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent)()
receives timer events.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Toolbar buttons are added by adding *actions*, using
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addAction)() or
[insertAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#insertAction)(). Groups
of buttons can be separated using
[addSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addSeparator)() or
[insertSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#insertSeparator)().
If a toolbar button is not appropriate, a widget can be inserted instead using
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addWidget)() or
[insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#insertWidget)().
Examples of suitable widgets are
[QSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html),
[QDoubleSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html), and
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html). When a toolbar button is
pressed, it emits the
[actionTriggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#actionTriggered)()
signal.

A toolbar can be fixed in place in a particular area (e.g., at the top of the window),
or it can be movable between toolbar areas; see
[setMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#movable-prop)(),
[isMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#movable-prop)(),
[allowedAreas](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#allowedAreas-prop)() and
[isAreaAllowed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#isAreaAllowed)().

When a toolbar is resized in such a way that it is too small to show all the items it
contains, an extension button will appear as the last item in the toolbar. Pressing the
extension button will pop up a menu containing the items that do not currently fit in
the toolbar.

When a QToolBar is not a child of a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html), it loses the ability
to populate the extension pop up with widgets added to the toolbar using
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addWidget)(). Please use
widget actions created by inheriting
[QWidgetAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html) and implementing
[QWidgetAction::createWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html#createWidget)()
instead.

PythonQt.Qt.QToolBar.addWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \*QToolBar::addWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*)

Adds the given *widget* to the toolbar as the toolbar's last item.

The toolbar takes ownership of *widget*.

If you add a [QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html) with
this method, the toolbar's
[Qt::ToolButtonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ToolButtonStyle-enum)
will not be respected.

**Note:** You should use
[QAction::setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#visible-prop)() to
change the visibility of the widget. Using
[QWidget::setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)(),
[QWidget::show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() and
[QWidget::hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)() does not work.

**See also**
[insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#insertWidget)().

### toolButtonStyle : [Qt::ToolButtonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ToolButtonStyle-enum)

This property holds the style of toolbar buttons

This property defines the style of all tool buttons that are added as
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html)s. Note that if you add a
[QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html) with the
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addWidget)() method, it
will not get this button style.

To have the style of toolbuttons follow the system settings, set this property to
[Qt::ToolButtonFollowStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ToolButtonStyle-enum).
On Unix, the user settings from the desktop environment will be used. On other
platforms,
[Qt::ToolButtonFollowStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ToolButtonStyle-enum)
means icon only.

The default is
[Qt::ToolButtonIconOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ToolButtonStyle-enum).

PythonQt.Qt.QToolBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A toolbox is a widget that displays a column of tabs one above the other, with the
current item displayed below the current tab. Every tab has an index position within the
column of tabs. A tab's item is a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html).

Each item has an
[itemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#itemText)(), an optional
[itemIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#itemIcon)(), an optional
[itemToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#itemToolTip)(), and a
[widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#widget)(). The item's
attributes can be changed with
[setItemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemText)(),
[setItemIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemIcon)(), and
[setItemToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemToolTip)().
Each item can be enabled or disabled individually with
[setItemEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemEnabled)().

Items are added using
[addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#addItem)(), or inserted at
particular positions using
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#insertItem)(). The total
number of items is given by
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#count-prop)(). Items can be
deleted with delete, or removed from the toolbox with
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#removeItem)(). Combining
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#removeItem)() and
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#insertItem)() allows you
to move items to different positions.

The index of the current item widget is returned by
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#currentIndex-prop)(),
and set with
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#currentIndex-prop)().
The index of a particular item can be found using
[indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#indexOf)(), and the item at a
given index is returned by item().

The [currentChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#currentChanged)()
signal is emitted when the current item is changed.

PythonQt.Qt.QToolButton.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A tool button is a special button that provides quick-access to specific commands or
options. As opposed to a normal command button, a tool button usually doesn't show a
text label, but shows an icon instead.

Tool buttons are normally created when new
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) instances are created with
[QToolBar::addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addAction)() or
existing actions are added to a toolbar with
[QToolBar::addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addAction)(). It
is also possible to construct tool buttons in the same way as any other widget, and
arrange them alongside other widgets in layouts.

One classic use of a tool button is to select tools; for example, the "pen" tool in a
drawing program. This would be implemented by using a QToolButton as a toggle button
(see
[setCheckable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkable-prop)()).

QToolButton supports auto-raising. In auto-raise mode, the button draws a 3D frame only
when the mouse points at it. The feature is automatically turned on when a button is
used inside a [QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html). Change it
with
[setAutoRaise](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#autoRaise-prop)().

A tool button's icon is set as [QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html).
This makes it possible to specify different pixmaps for the disabled and active state.
The disabled pixmap is used when the button's functionality is not available. The active
pixmap is displayed when the button is auto-raised because the mouse pointer is hovering
over it.

The button's look and dimension is adjustable with
[setToolButtonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#toolButtonStyle-prop)()
and
[setIconSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#iconSize-prop)().
When used inside a [QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) in a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html), the button
automatically adjusts to
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html)'s settings (see
[QMainWindow::setToolButtonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#toolButtonStyle-prop)()
and
[QMainWindow::setIconSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#iconSize-prop)()).
Instead of an icon, a tool button can also display an arrow symbol, specified with
[arrowType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#arrowType-prop).

A tool button can offer additional choices in a popup menu. The popup menu can be set
using [setMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#setMenu)(). Use
[setPopupMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#popupMode-prop)() to
configure the different modes available for tool buttons with a menu set. The default
mode is DelayedPopupMode which is sometimes used with the "Back" button in a web
browser. After pressing and holding the button down for a while, a menu pops up showing
a list of possible pages to jump to. The timeout is style dependent, see
[QStyle::SH\_ToolButton\_PopupDelay](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#StyleHint-enum).

### `[slot]` void QToolButton::setDefaultAction([QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \**action*)

Sets the default action to *action*.

If a tool button has a default action, the action defines the following properties of
the button:

- [checkable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkable-prop)
- [checked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)
- [enabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop)
- [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop)
- [icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)
- [popupMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#popupMode-prop) (assuming the action has a menu)
- [statusTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#statusTip-prop)
- [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)
- [toolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#toolTip-prop)
- [whatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#whatsThis-prop)

Other properties, such as
[autoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop),

PythonQt.Qt.QToolTip.doc:
Qt 5 reference: ## Detailed Description The tip is a short piece of text reminding the user of the widget's function. It is drawn immediately below the given position in a distinctive black-on-yellow color combination. The tip can be any [rich text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) formatted string. Rich text displayed in a tool tip is implicitly word-wrapped unless specified differently with `

`. The simplest and most common way to set a widget's tool tip is by calling its [QWidget::setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#toolTip-prop)() function. It is also possible to show different tool tips for different regions of a widget, by using a [QHelpEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhelpevent.html) of type [QEvent::ToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum). Intercept the help event in your widget's [event()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event) function and call [QToolTip::showText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#showText)() with the text you want to display. The [Tooltips](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-tooltips-example.html) example illustrates this technique. If you are calling [QToolTip::hideText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#hideText)(), or [QToolTip::showText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#showText)() with an empty string, as a result of a [ToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)-event you should also call [ignore()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore) on the event, to signal that you don't want to start any tooltip specific modes. Note that, if you want to show tooltips in an item view, the model/view architecture provides functionality to set an item's tool tip; e.g., the [QTableWidgetItem::setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtablewidgetitem.html#setToolTip)() function. However, if you want to provide custom tool tips in an item view, you must intercept the help event in the [QAbstractItemView::viewportEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#viewportEvent)() function and handle it yourself. The default tool tip color and font can be customized with [setPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#setPalette)() and [setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#setFont)(). When a tooltip is currently on display, [isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#isVisible)() returns `true` and [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#text)() the currently visible text. **Note:** Tool tips use the inactive color group of [QPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html), because tool tips are not active windows.

### `[static]` void QToolTip::showText(const [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) \&*pos*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**w*, const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rect*)

Shows *text* as a tool tip, with the global position *pos* as the point of interest. The
tool tip will be shown with a platform specific offset from this point of interest.

If you specify a non-empty rect the tip will be hidden as soon as you move your cursor
out of this area.

The *rect* is in the coordinates of the widget you specify with *w*. If the *rect* is
not empty you must specify a widget. Otherwise this argument can be `nullptr` but it is
used to determine the appropriate screen on multi-head systems.

If *text* is empty the tool tip is hidden. If the text is the same as the currently
shown tooltip, the tip will *not* move. You can force moving by first hiding the tip
with an empty text, and then showing the new tip at the new position.

## Detailed Description

Each [QTouchEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html) contains a
QTouchDevice pointer to allow accessing device-specific properties like type and
capabilities. It is the responsibility of the platform or generic plug-ins to register
the available touch devices via QWindowSystemInterface before generating any touch
events. Applications do not need to instantiate this class, they should just access the
global instances pointed to by
[QTouchEvent::device](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#device)().

## Detailed Description

### Enabling Touch Events

Touch events occur when pressing, releasing, or moving one or more touch points on a
touch device (such as a touch-screen or track-pad). To receive touch events, widgets
have to have the
[Qt::WA\_AcceptTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute set and graphics items need to have the
[acceptTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setAcceptTouchEvents)
attribute set to true.

When using
[QAbstractScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html) based
widgets, you should enable the
[Qt::WA\_AcceptTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute on the scroll area's
[viewport](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#viewport).

Similarly to [QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html), Qt
automatically grabs each touch point on the first press inside a widget, and the widget
will receive all updates for the touch point until it is released. Note that it is
possible for a widget to receive events for numerous touch points, and that multiple
widgets may be receiving touch events at the same time.

### Event Handling

All touch events are of type
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum),
[QEvent::TouchUpdate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum),
[QEvent::TouchEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) or
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).
Reimplement [QWidget::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)() or
[QAbstractScrollArea::viewportEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#viewportEvent)()
for widgets and
[QGraphicsItem::sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)()
for items in a graphics view to receive touch events.

Unlike widgets, QWindows receive touch events always, there is no need to opt in. When
working directly with a [QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html), it
is enough to reimplement
[QWindow::touchEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#touchEvent)().

The [QEvent::TouchUpdate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[QEvent::TouchEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events are
sent to the widget or item that accepted the
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event. If
the [QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event
is not accepted and not filtered by an event filter, then no further touch events are
sent until the next
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).

Some systems may send an event of type
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum). Upon
receiving this event applications are requested to ignore the entire active touch
sequence. For example in a composited system the compositor may decide to treat certain
gestures as system-wide gestures. Whenever such a decision is made (the gesture is
recognized), the clients will be notified with a
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event so
they can update their state accordingly.

The [touchPoints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#touchPoints)()
function returns a list of all touch points contained in the event. Note that this list
may be empty, for example in case of a
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event.
Information about each touch point can be retrieved using the
[QTouchEvent::TouchPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent-touchpoint.html)
class. The
[Qt::TouchPointState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TouchPointState-enum)
enum describes the different states that a touch point may have.

**Note:** The list of
[touchPoints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#touchPoints)() will
never be partial: A touch event will always contain a touch point for each existing
physical touch contacts targetting the window or widget to which the event is sent. For
instance, assuming that all touches target the same window or widget, an event with a
condition of
[touchPoints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#touchPoints)().count()\=\=2
is guaranteed to imply that the number of fingers touching the touchscreen or touchpad
is exactly two.

### Event Delivery and Propagation

By default, [QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html)
translates the first touch point in a QTouchEvent into a
[QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html). This makes it
possible to enable touch events on existing widgets that do not normally handle
QTouchEvent. See below for information on some special considerations needed when doing
this.

[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) is the
first touch event sent to a widget. The
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event
contains a special accept flag that indicates whether the receiver wants the event. By
default, the event is accepted. You should call
[ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() if the touch event is
not handled by your widget. The
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event is
propagated up the parent widget chain until a widget accepts it with
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)(), or an event filter
consumes it. For QGraphicsItems, the
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event is
propagated to items under the mouse (similar to mouse event propagation for
QGraphicsItems).

### Touch Point Grouping

As mentioned above, it is possible that several widgets can be receiving QTouchEvents at
the same time. However, Qt makes sure to never send duplicate
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events to
the same widget, which could theoretically happen during propagation if, for example,
the user touched 2 separate widgets in a
[QGroupBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgroupbox.html) and both widgets ignored
the [QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
event.

To avoid this, Qt will group new touch points together using the following rules:

- When the first touch point is detected, the destination widget is determined firstly by the location on screen and secondly by the propagation rules.
- When additional touch points are detected, Qt first looks to see if there are any active touch points on any ancestor or descendent of the widget under the new touch point. If there are, the new touch point is grouped with the first, and the new touch point will be sent in a single QTouchEvent to the widget that handled the first touch point. (The widget under the new touch point will not receive an event).

This makes it possible for sibling widgets to handle touch events independently while
making sure that the sequence of QTouchEvents is always correct.

### Mouse Events and Touch Event Synthesizing

QTouchEvent delivery is independent from that of
[QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html). The application
flags
[Qt::AA\_SynthesizeTouchForUnhandledMouseEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ApplicationAttribute-enum)
and
[Qt::AA\_SynthesizeMouseForUnhandledTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ApplicationAttribute-enum)
can be used to enable or disable automatic synthesizing of touch events to mouse events
and mouse events to touch events.

### Caveats

- As mentioned above, enabling touch events means multiple widgets can be receiving touch events simultaneously. Combined with the default [QWidget::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)() handling for QTouchEvents, this gives you great flexibility in designing touch user interfaces. Be aware of the implications. For example, it is possible that the user is moving a [QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html) with one finger and pressing a [QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html) with another. The signals emitted by these widgets will be interleaved.
- Recursion into the event loop using one of the exec() methods (e.g., [QDialog::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)() or [QMenu::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#exec)()) in a QTouchEvent event handler is not supported. Since there are multiple event recipients, recursion may cause problems, including but not limited to lost events and unexpected infinite recursion.
- QTouchEvents are not affected by a [mouse grab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabMouse) or an [active pop-up widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activePopupWidget). The behavior of QTouchEvents is undefined when opening a pop-up or grabbing the mouse while there are more than one active touch points.

PythonQt.Qt.QTouchEvent__TouchPoint.rawS.doc:

### [QVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvector.html)\<[QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html)\> TouchPoint::rawScreenPositions() const

Returns the raw, unfiltered positions for the touch point. The positions are in native
screen coordinates. To get local coordinates you can use mapFromGlobal() of the
[QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html) returned by
[QTouchEvent::window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#window)().

**Note:** Returns an empty vector if the touch device's capabilities do not include
[QTouchDevice::RawPositions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchdevice.html#CapabilityFlag-enum).

**Note:** Native screen coordinates refer to the native orientation of the screen which,
in case of mobile devices, is typically portrait. This means that on systems capable of
screen orientation changes the positions in this list will not reflect the current
orientation (unlike
[pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent-touchpoint.html#pos)(),
[screenPos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent-touchpoint.html#screenPos)(),
etc.) and will always be reported in the native orientation.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also**
[QTouchDevice::capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchdevice.html#capabilities)(),
[device](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#device)(), and
[window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#window)().

PythonQt.Qt.QTransform.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A transformation specifies how to translate, scale, shear, rotate or project the
coordinate system, and is typically used when rendering graphics.

QTransform differs from QMatrix in that it is a true 3x3 matrix, allowing perspective
transformations. QTransform's toAffine() method allows casting QTransform to QMatrix. If
a perspective transformation has been specified on the matrix, then the conversion will
cause loss of data.

QTransform is the recommended transformation class in Qt.

A QTransform object can be built using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#setMatrix)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#scale)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#rotate)(),
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#translate)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#shear)() functions.
Alternatively, it can be built by applying [basic matrix
operations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#basic-matrix-operations).
The matrix can also be defined when constructed, and it can be reset to the identity
matrix (the default) using the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#reset)() function.

The QTransform class supports mapping of graphic primitives: A given point, line,
polygon, region, or painter path can be mapped to the coordinate system defined by
*this* matrix using the [map](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#map)()
function. In case of a rectangle, its coordinates can be transformed using the
[mapRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#mapRect)() function. A
rectangle can also be transformed into a *polygon* (mapped to the coordinate system
defined by *this* matrix), using the
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#mapToPolygon)()
function.

QTransform provides the
[isIdentity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#isIdentity)() function
which returns `true` if the matrix is the identity matrix, and the
[isInvertible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#isInvertible)()
function which returns `true` if the matrix is non-singular (i.e. AB \= BA \= I). The
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#inverted)() function
returns an inverted copy of *this* matrix if it is invertible (otherwise it returns the
identity matrix), and
[adjoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#adjoint)() returns the
matrix's classical adjoint. In addition, QTransform provides the
[determinant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#determinant)() function
which returns the matrix's determinant.

Finally, the QTransform class supports matrix multiplication, addition and subtraction,
and objects of the class can be streamed as well as compared.

### Rendering Graphics

When rendering graphics, the matrix defines the transformations but the actual
transformation is performed by the drawing routines in
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html).

By default, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) operates on the
associated device's own coordinate system. The standard coordinate system of a
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) has its origin
located at the top-left position. The *x* values increase to the right; *y* values
increase downward. For a complete description, see the [coordinate
system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html) documentation.

[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) has functions to translate,
scale, shear and rotate the coordinate system without using a QTransform. For example:

|  | ``` void SimpleTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.rotate(45);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QTransform"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

Although these functions are very convenient, it can be more efficient to build a
QTransform and call
[QPainter::setTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setTransform)()
if you want to perform more than a single transform operation. For example:

|  | ``` void CombinedTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      QTransform transform;     transform.translate(50, 50);     transform.rotate(45);     transform.scale(0.5, 1.0);     painter.setTransform(transform);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QTransform"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

### Basic Matrix Operations

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qtransform-representation.png)

A QTransform object contains a 3 x 3 matrix. The `m31` (`dx`) and `m32` (`dy`) elements
specify horizontal and vertical translation. The `m11` and `m22` elements specify
horizontal and vertical scaling. The `m21` and `m12` elements specify horizontal and
vertical *shearing*. And finally, the `m13` and `m23` elements specify horizontal and
vertical projection, with `m33` as an additional projection factor.

QTransform transforms a point in the plane to another point using the following
formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
if (!isAffine()) {
    w' = m13*x + m23*y + m33
    x' /= w'
    y' /= w'
}
```

The point *(x, y)* is the original point, and *(x', y')* is the transformed point. *(x',
y')* can be transformed back to *(x, y)* by performing the same operation on the
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#inverted)() matrix.

The various matrix elements can be set when constructing the matrix, or by using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#setMatrix)() function
later on. They can also be manipulated using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#translate)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#rotate)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#scale)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#shear)() convenience
functions. The currently set values can be retrieved using the
[m11](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m11)(),
[m12](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m12)(),
[m13](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m13)(),
[m21](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m21)(),
[m22](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m22)(),
[m23](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m23)(),
[m31](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m31)(),
[m32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m32)(),
[m33](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m33)(),
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#dy)() functions.

Translation is the simplest transformation. Setting `dx` and `dy` will move the
coordinate system `dx` units along the X axis and `dy` units along the Y axis. Scaling
can be done by setting `m11` and `m22`. For example, setting `m11` to 2 and `m22` to 1.5
will double the height and increase the width by 50%. The identity matrix has `m11`,
`m22`, and `m33` set to 1 (all others are set to 0\) mapping a point to itself. Shearing
is controlled by `m12` and `m21`. Setting these elements to values different from zero
will twist the coordinate system. Rotation is achieved by setting both the shearing
factors and the scaling factors. Perspective transformation is achieved by setting both
the projection factors and the scaling factors.

#### Combining Transforms

Here's the combined transformations example using basic matrix operations:

|  | ``` void BasicOperations::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     const double a = qDegreesToRadians(45.0);     double sina = sin(a);     double cosa = cos(a);      QTransform scale(0.5, 0, 0, 1.0, 0, 0);     QTransform rotate(cosa, sina, -sina, cosa, 0, 0);     QTransform translate(1, 0, 0, 1, 50.0, 50.0);      QTransform transform = scale * rotate * translate;      QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.setTransform(transform);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QTransform"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

The combined transform first scales each operand, then rotates it, and finally
translates it, just as in the order in which the product of its factors is written. This
means the point to which the transforms are applied is implicitly multiplied on the left
with the transform to its right.

#### Relation to Matrix Notation

The matrix notation in QTransform is the transpose of a commonly-taught convention which
represents transforms and points as matrices and vectors. That convention multiplies its
matrix on the left and column vector to the right. In other words, when several
transforms are applied to a point, the right-most matrix acts directly on the vector
first. Then the next matrix to the left acts on the result of the first operation \- and
so on. As a result, that convention multiplies the matrices that make up a composite
transform in the reverse of the order in QTransform, as you can see in [Combining
Transforms](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#combining-transforms).
Transposing the matrices, and combining them to the right of a row vector that
represents the point, lets the matrices of transforms appear, in their product, in the
order in which we think of the transforms being applied to the point.

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QTransform::mapRect(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*) const

Creates and returns a [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) object
that is a copy of the given *rectangle*, mapped into the coordinate system defined by
this matrix.

The rectangle's coordinates are transformed using the following formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
if (!isAffine()) {
    w' = m13*x + m23*y + m33
    x' /= w'
    y' /= w'
}
```

If rotation or shearing has been specified, this function returns the *bounding*
rectangle. To retrieve the exact region the given *rectangle* maps to, use the
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#mapToPolygon)()
function instead.

### [QTransform::TransformationType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#TransformationType-enum) QTransform::type() const

Returns the transformation type of this matrix.

The transformation type is the highest enumeration value capturing all of the matrix's
transformations. For example, if the matrix both scales and shears, the type would be
`TxShear`, because `TxShear` has a higher enumeration value than `TxScale`.

Knowing the transformation type of a matrix is useful for optimization: you can often
handle specific types more optimally than handling the generic case.

PythonQt.Qt.QTranslator.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

An object of this class contains a set of translations from a source language to a
target language. QTranslator provides functions to look up translations in a translation
file. Translation files are created using [Qt
Linguist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtlinguist-index.html).

The most common use of QTranslator is to: load a translation file, and install it using
[QCoreApplication::installTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#installTranslator)().

Here's an example `main()` function using the QTranslator:

```
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    QApplication app(argc, argv);

    QTranslator translator;
    // look up e.g. :/i18n/myapp_de.qm
    if (translator.load(QLocale(), QLatin1String("myapp"), QLatin1String("_"), QLatin1String(":/i18n")))
        QCoreApplication::installTranslator(&translator);

    QPushButton hello(QCoreApplication::translate("main", "Hello world!"));
    hello.resize(100, 30);

    hello.show();
    return app.exec();
}
```

Note that the translator must be created *before* the application's widgets.

Most applications will never need to do anything else with this class. The other
functions provided by this class are useful for applications that work on translator
files.

### Looking up Translations

It is possible to look up a translation using
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html#translate)() (as
[tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)() and
[QCoreApplication::translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#translate)()
do). The [translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html#translate)()
function takes up to three parameters:

- The *context* \- usually the class name for the [tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)() caller.
- The *source text* \- usually the argument to [tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)().
- The *disambiguation* \- an optional string that helps disambiguate different uses of the same text in the same context.

For example, the "Cancel" in a dialog might have "Anuluj" when the program runs in
Polish (in this case the source text would be "Cancel"). The context would (normally) be
the dialog's class name; there would normally be no comment, and the translated text
would be "Anuluj".

But it's not always so simple. The Spanish version of a printer dialog with settings for
two-sided printing and binding would probably require both "Activado" and "Activada" as
translations for "Enabled". In this case the source text would be "Enabled" in both
cases, and the context would be the dialog's class name, but the two items would have
disambiguations such as "two-sided printing" for one and "binding" for the other. The
disambiguation enables the translator to choose the appropriate gender for the Spanish
version, and enables Qt to distinguish between translations.

### Using Multiple Translations

Multiple translation files can be installed in an application. Translations are searched
for in the reverse order in which they were installed, so the most recently installed
translation file is searched for translations first and the earliest translation file is
searched last. The search stops as soon as a translation containing a matching string is
found.

This mechanism makes it possible for a specific translation to be "selected" or given
priority over the others; simply uninstall the translator from the application by
passing it to the
[QCoreApplication::removeTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#removeTranslator)()
function and reinstall it with
[QCoreApplication::installTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#installTranslator)().
It will then be the first translation to be searched for matching strings.

### bool QTranslator::load(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*filename*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*directory* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*search\_delimiters* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*suffix* \= QString())

Loads *filename* \+ *suffix* (".qm" if the *suffix* is not specified), which may be an
absolute file name or relative to *directory*. Returns `true` if the translation is
successfully loaded; otherwise returns `false`.

If *directory* is not specified, the current directory is used (i.e., as
[currentPath()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#currentPath)).

The previous contents of this translator object are discarded.

If the file name does not exist, other file names are tried in the following order:

1. File name without *suffix* appended.
2. File name with text after a character in *search\_delimiters* stripped ("\_." is the default for *search\_delimiters* if it is an empty string) and *suffix*.
3. File name stripped without *suffix* appended.
4. File name stripped further, etc.

For example, an application running in the fr\_CA locale (French-speaking Canada) might
call load("foo.fr\_ca", "/opt/foolib"). load() would then try to open the first existing
readable file from this list:

1. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_ca.qm`
2. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_ca`
3. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr.qm`
4. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr`
5. `/opt/foolib/foo.qm`
6. `/opt/foolib/foo`

Usually, it is better to use the QTranslator::load(const
[QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&) function instead, because
it uses
[QLocale::uiLanguages](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#uiLanguages)()
and not simply the locale name, which refers to the formatting of dates and numbers and
not necessarily the UI language.

### bool QTranslator::load(const [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) \&*locale*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*filename*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*prefix* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*directory* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*suffix* \= QString())

Loads *filename* \+ *prefix* \+ [ui language
name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#uiLanguages) \+ *suffix* (".qm" if
the *suffix* is not specified), which may be an absolute file name or relative to
*directory*. Returns `true` if the translation is successfully loaded; otherwise returns
`false`.

The previous contents of this translator object are discarded.

If the file name does not exist, other file names are tried in the following order:

1. File name without *suffix* appended.
2. File name with ui language part after a "\_" character stripped and *suffix*.
3. File name with ui language part stripped without *suffix* appended.
4. File name with ui language part stripped further, etc.

For example, an application running in the *locale* with the following [ui
languages](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#uiLanguages) \- "es",
"fr-CA", "de" might call load(QLocale(), "foo", ".", "/opt/foolib", ".qm"). load() would
replace '-' (dash) with '\_' (underscore) in the ui language and then try to open the
first existing readable file from this list:

1. `/opt/foolib/foo.es.qm`
2. `/opt/foolib/foo.es`
3. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_CA.qm`
4. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_CA`
5. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr.qm`
6. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr`
7. `/opt/foolib/foo.de.qm`
8. `/opt/foolib/foo.de`
9. `/opt/foolib/foo.qm`
10. `/opt/foolib/foo`.
11. `/opt/foolib/foo`

On operating systems where file system is case sensitive,
[QTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html) also tries to load a
lower-cased version of the locale name.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

is found, also tries (*context*, *sourceText*, ""). If that still fails, returns a null
string.

**Note:** Incomplete translations may result in unexpected behavior: If no translation
for (*context*, *sourceText*, "") is provided, the method might in this case actually
return a translation for a different *disambiguation*.

If *n* is not -1, it is used to choose an appropriate form for the translation (e.g. "%n
file found" vs. "%n files found").

If you need to programmatically insert translations into a
[QTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html), this function can be
reimplemented.

PythonQt.Qt.QTreeView.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-treeview.png)

A QTreeView implements a tree representation of items from a model. This class is used
to provide standard hierarchical lists that were previously provided by the `QListView`
class, but using the more flexible approach provided by Qt's model/view architecture.

The QTreeView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

QTreeView implements the interfaces defined by the
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) class to
allow it to display data provided by models derived from the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) class.

It is simple to construct a tree view displaying data from a model. In the following
example, the contents of a directory are supplied by a
[QFileSystemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemmodel.html) and
displayed as a tree:

```
    QFileSystemModel *model = new QFileSystemModel;
    model->setRootPath(QDir::currentPath());
    QTreeView *tree = new QTreeView(splitter);
    tree->setModel(model);
```

The model/view architecture ensures that the contents of the tree view are updated as
the model changes.

Items that have children can be in an expanded (children are visible) or collapsed
(children are hidden) state. When this state changes a
[collapsed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#collapsed)() or
[expanded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#expanded)() signal is
emitted with the model index of the relevant item.

The amount of indentation used to indicate levels of hierarchy is controlled by the
[indentation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#indentation-prop)
property.

Headers in tree views are constructed using the
[QHeaderView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html) class and can be
hidden using `header()->hide()`. Note that each header is configured with its
[stretchLastSection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#stretchLastSection-prop)
property set to true, ensuring that the view does not waste any of the space assigned to
it for its header. If this value is set to true, this property will override the resize
mode set on the last section in the header.

By default, all columns in a tree view are movable except the first. To disable movement
of these columns, use
[QHeaderView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html)'s
[setSectionsMovable()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionsMovable)
function. For more information about rearranging sections, see [Moving Header
Sections](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#moving-header-sections).

### Key Bindings

QTreeView supports a set of key bindings that enable the user to navigate in the view
and interact with the contents of items:

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Up | Moves the cursor to the item in the same column on the previous row. If the parent of the current item has no more rows to navigate to, the cursor moves to the relevant item in the last row of the sibling that precedes the parent. |
| Down | Moves the cursor to the item in the same column on the next row. If the parent of the current item has no more rows to navigate to, the cursor moves to the relevant item in the first row of the sibling that follows the parent. |
| Left | Hides the children of the current item (if present) by collapsing a branch. |
| Minus | Same as Left. |
| Right | Reveals the children of the current item (if present) by expanding a branch. |
| Plus | Same as Right. |
| Asterisk | Expands the current item and all its children (if present). |
| PageUp | Moves the cursor up one page. |
| PageDown | Moves the cursor down one page. |
| Home | Moves the cursor to an item in the same column of the first row of the first top-level item in the model. |
| End | Moves the cursor to an item in the same column of the last row of the last top-level item in the model. |
| F2 | In editable models, this opens the current item for editing. The Escape key can be used to cancel the editing process and revert any changes to the data displayed. |

### Improving Performance

It is possible to give the view hints about the data it is handling in order to improve
its performance when displaying large numbers of items. One approach that can be taken
for views that are intended to display items with equal heights is to set the
[uniformRowHeights](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#uniformRowHeights-prop)
property to true.

### indentation : int

indentation of the items in the tree view.

This property holds the indentation measured in pixels of the items for each level in
the tree view. For top-level items, the indentation specifies the horizontal distance
from the viewport edge to the items in the first column; for child items, it specifies
their indentation from their parent items.

By default, the value of this property is style dependent. Thus, when the style changes,
this property updates from it. Calling setIndentation() stops the updates, calling
resetIndentation() will restore default behavior.

### rootIsDecorated : bool

This property holds whether to show controls for expanding and collapsing top-level
items

Items with children are typically shown with controls to expand and collapse them,
allowing their children to be shown or hidden. If this property is false, these controls
are not shown for top-level items. This can be used to make a single level tree
structure appear like a simple list of items.

By default, this property is `true`.
