### sortingEnabled : bool

This property holds whether sorting is enabled

If this property is `true`, sorting is enabled for the tree; if the property is false,
sorting is not enabled. The default value is false.

**Note:** In order to avoid performance issues, it is recommended that sorting is
enabled *after* inserting the items into the tree. Alternatively, you could also insert
the items into a list before inserting the items into the tree.

This property was introduced in Qt 4.2.

### wordWrap : bool

This property holds the item text word-wrapping policy

If this property is `true` then the item text is wrapped where necessary at word-breaks;
otherwise it is not wrapped at all. This property is `false` by default.

Note that even if wrapping is enabled, the cell will not be expanded to fit all text.
Ellipsis will be inserted according to the current
[textElideMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#textElideMode-prop).

This property was introduced in Qt 4.3.

PythonQt.Qt.QTreeWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-treeview.png)

The QTreeWidget class is a convenience class that provides a standard tree widget with a
classic item-based interface similar to that used by the
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) class in Qt 3\. This
class is based on Qt's Model/View architecture and uses a default model to hold items,
each of which is a
[QTreeWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html).

Developers who do not need the flexibility of the Model/View framework can use this
class to create simple hierarchical lists very easily. A more flexible approach involves
combining a [QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) with a
standard item model. This allows the storage of data to be separated from its
representation.

In its simplest form, a tree widget can be constructed in the following way:

```
QTreeWidget *treeWidget = new QTreeWidget();
treeWidget->setColumnCount(1);
QList<QTreeWidgetItem *> items;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i)
    items.append(new QTreeWidgetItem(static_cast<QTreeWidget *>(nullptr), QStringList(QString("item: %1").arg(i))));
treeWidget->insertTopLevelItems(0, items);
```

Before items can be added to the tree widget, the number of columns must be set with
[setColumnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#columnCount-prop)().
This allows each item to have one or more labels or other decorations. The number of
columns in use can be found with the
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#columnCount-prop)()
function.

The tree can have a header that contains a section for each column in the widget. It is
easiest to set up the labels for each section by supplying a list of strings with
[setHeaderLabels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#setHeaderLabels)(),
but a custom header can be constructed with a
[QTreeWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html) and inserted
into the tree with the
[setHeaderItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#setHeaderItem)()
function.

The items in the tree can be sorted by column according to a predefined sort order. If
sorting is enabled, the user can sort the items by clicking on a column header. Sorting
can be enabled or disabled by calling
[setSortingEnabled()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#sortingEnabled-prop).
The
[isSortingEnabled()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#sortingEnabled-prop)
function indicates whether sorting is enabled.

[autoFillBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#autoFillBackground-prop)

widget, use [QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) and subclass
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html)
instead.

This function cannot be called before the item hierarchy has been set up, i.e., the
[QTreeWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html) that will
hold *widget* must have been added to the view before *widget* is set.

**Note:** The tree takes ownership of the widget.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

[itemWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#itemWidget)() and

PythonQt.Qt.QTreeWidgetItem.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Tree widget items are used to hold rows of information for tree widgets. Rows usually
contain several columns of data, each of which can contain a text label and an icon.

The QTreeWidgetItem class is a convenience class that replaces the QListViewItem class
in Qt 3\. It provides an item for use with the
[QTreeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html) class.

Items are usually constructed with a parent that is either a
[QTreeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html) (for top-level items)
or a QTreeWidgetItem (for items on lower levels of the tree). For example, the following
code constructs a top-level item to represent cities of the world, and adds a entry for
Oslo as a child item:

```
    QTreeWidgetItem *cities = new QTreeWidgetItem(treeWidget);
    cities->setText(0, tr("Cities"));
    QTreeWidgetItem *osloItem = new QTreeWidgetItem(cities);
    osloItem->setText(0, tr("Oslo"));
    osloItem->setText(1, tr("Yes"));
```

Items can be added in a particular order by specifying the item they follow when they
are constructed:

```
    QTreeWidgetItem *planets = new QTreeWidgetItem(treeWidget, cities);
    planets->setText(0, tr("Planets"));
```

Each column in an item can have its own background brush which is set with the
[setBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setBackground)()
function. The current background brush can be found with
[background](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#background)(). The
text label for each column can be rendered with its own font and brush. These are
specified with the
[setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setFont)() and
[setForeground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setForeground)()
functions, and read with
[font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#font)() and
[foreground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#foreground)().

The main difference between top-level items and those in lower levels of the tree is
that a top-level item has no
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#parent)(). This
information can be used to tell the difference between items, and is useful to know when
inserting and removing items from the tree. Children of an item can be removed with
[takeChild](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#takeChild)() and
inserted at a given index in the list of children with the
[insertChild](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#insertChild)()
function.

By default, items are enabled, selectable, checkable, and can be the source of a drag
and drop operation. Each item's flags can be changed by calling
[setFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setFlags)() with the
appropriate value (see
[Qt::ItemFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum)). Checkable
items can be checked and unchecked with the
[setCheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setCheckState)()
function. The corresponding
[checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#checkState)()
function indicates whether the item is currently checked.

### Subclassing

When subclassing QTreeWidgetItem to provide custom items, it is possible to define new
types for them so that they can be distinguished from standard items. The constructors
for subclasses that require this feature need to call the base class constructor with a
new type value equal to or greater than
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#ItemType-enum).

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a lightweight, unreliable, datagram-oriented,
connectionless protocol. It can be used when reliability isn't important. QUdpSocket is
a subclass of [QAbstractSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html)
that allows you to send and receive UDP datagrams.

The most common way to use this class is to bind to an address and port using
[bind](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#bind)(), then call
[writeDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#writeDatagram)() and
[readDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#readDatagram)() /
[receiveDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#receiveDatagram)()
to transfer data. If you want to use the standard
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) functions
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(),
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)(), etc., you must first
connect the socket directly to a peer by calling
[connectToHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#connectToHost)().

The socket emits the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal
every time a datagram is written to the network. If you just want to send datagrams, you
don't need to call
[bind](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#bind)().

The [readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal is
emitted whenever datagrams arrive. In that case,
[hasPendingDatagrams](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#hasPendingDatagrams)()
returns `true`. Call
[pendingDatagramSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#pendingDatagramSize)()
to obtain the size of the first pending datagram, and
[readDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#readDatagram)() or
[receiveDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#receiveDatagram)()
to read it.

**Note:** An incoming datagram should be read when you receive the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal,
otherwise this signal will not be emitted for the next datagram.

Example:

```
void Server::initSocket()
{
    udpSocket = new QUdpSocket(this);
    udpSocket->bind(QHostAddress::LocalHost, 7755);

    connect(udpSocket, &QUdpSocket::readyRead,
            this, &Server::readPendingDatagrams);
}

void Server::readPendingDatagrams()
{
    while (udpSocket->hasPendingDatagrams()) {
        QNetworkDatagram datagram = udpSocket->receiveDatagram();
        processTheDatagram(datagram);
    }
}
```

QUdpSocket also supports UDP multicast. Use
[joinMulticastGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#joinMulticastGroup)()
and
[leaveMulticastGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#leaveMulticastGroup)()
to control group membership, and
[QAbstractSocket::MulticastTtlOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketOption-enum)
and
[QAbstractSocket::MulticastLoopbackOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketOption-enum)
to set the TTL and loopback socket options. Use
[setMulticastInterface](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#setMulticastInterface)()
to control the outgoing interface for multicast datagrams, and
[multicastInterface](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#multicastInterface)()
to query it.

With QUdpSocket, you can also establish a virtual connection to a UDP server using
[connectToHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#connectToHost)()
and then use [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() to exchange datagrams
without specifying the receiver for each datagram.

The [Broadcast
Sender](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtnetwork-broadcastsender-example.html),
[Broadcast
Receiver](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtnetwork-broadcastreceiver-example.html),
[Multicast
Sender](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtnetwork-multicastsender-example.html), and
[Multicast
Receiver](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtnetwork-multicastreceiver-example.html)
examples illustrate how to use QUdpSocket in applications.

### bool QUdpSocket::joinMulticastGroup(const [QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html) \&*groupAddress*)

Joins the multicast group specified by *groupAddress* on the default interface chosen by
the operating system. The socket must be in
[BoundState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketState-enum),
otherwise an error occurs.

Note that if you are attempting to join an IPv4 group, your socket must not be bound
using IPv6 (or in dual mode, using
[QHostAddress::Any](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#SpecialAddress-enum)).
You must use
[QHostAddress::AnyIPv4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#SpecialAddress-enum)
instead.

This function returns `true` if successful; otherwise it returns `false` and sets the
socket error accordingly.

**Note:** Joining IPv6 multicast groups without an interface selection is not supported
in all operating systems. Consider using the overload where the interface is specified.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

**See also**
[leaveMulticastGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#leaveMulticastGroup)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QUdpSocket::readDatagram(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*, [QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html) \**address* \= nullptr, [quint16](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint16-typedef) \**port* \= nullptr)

Receives a datagram no larger than *maxSize* bytes and stores it in *data*. The sender's
host address and port is stored in \**address* and \**port* (unless the pointers are
`nullptr`).

Returns the size of the datagram on success; otherwise returns -1.

If *maxSize* is too small, the rest of the datagram will be lost. To avoid loss of data,
call
[pendingDatagramSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#pendingDatagramSize)()
to determine the size of the pending datagram before attempting to read it. If *maxSize*
is 0, the datagram will be discarded.

**See also**
[writeDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#writeDatagram)(),
[hasPendingDatagrams](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#hasPendingDatagrams)(),
and
[pendingDatagramSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#pendingDatagramSize)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QUdpSocket::writeDatagram(const char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *size*, const [QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html) \&*address*, [quint16](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint16-typedef) *port*)

Sends the datagram at *data* of size *size* to the host address *address* at port
*port*. Returns the number of bytes sent on success; otherwise returns -1.

Datagrams are always written as one block. The maximum size of a datagram is highly
platform-dependent, but can be as low as 8192 bytes. If the datagram is too large, this
function will return -1 and
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#error)() will return
[DatagramTooLargeError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#SocketError-enum).

Sending datagrams larger than 512 bytes is in general disadvised, as even if they are
sent successfully, they are likely to be fragmented by the IP layer before arriving at
their final destination.

**Warning:** Calling this function on a connected UDP socket may result in an error and
no packet being sent. If you are using a connected socket, use
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() to send datagrams.

**See also**
[readDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html#readDatagram)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QUdpSocket::writeDatagram(const [QNetworkDatagram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkdatagram.html) \&*datagram*)

This is an overloaded function.

Sends the datagram *datagram* to the host address and port numbers contained in
*datagram*, using the network interface and hop count limits also set there. If the
destination address and port numbers are unset, this function will send to the address
that was passed to
[connectToHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractsocket.html#connectToHost)().

If the destination address is IPv6 with a non-empty [scope
id](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html#scopeId) but differs from the
interface index in *datagram*, it is undefined which interface the operating system will
choose to send on.

The function returns the number of bytes sent if it succeeded or -1 if it encountered an
error.

**Warning:** Calling this function on a connected UDP socket may result in an error and
no packet being sent. If you are using a connected socket, use
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() to send datagrams.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.8.

**See also**
[QNetworkDatagram::setDestination](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkdatagram.html#setDestination)(),
[QNetworkDatagram::setHopLimit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkdatagram.html#setHopLimit)(),
and
[QNetworkDatagram::setInterfaceIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkdatagram.html#setInterfaceIndex)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QUdpSocket::writeDatagram(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*datagram*, const [QHostAddress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhostaddress.html) \&*host*, [quint16](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint16-typedef) *port*)

This is an overloaded function.

Sends the datagram *datagram* to the host address *host* and at port *port*.

PythonQt.Qt.QUiLoader.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

In addition, you can customize or create your own user interface by deriving your own
loader class.

If you have a custom component or an application that embeds *Qt Designer*, you can also
use the [QFormBuilder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qformbuilder.html) class
provided by the [QtDesigner](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtdesigner-module.html)
module to create user interfaces from UI files.

The QUiLoader class provides a collection of functions allowing you to create widgets
based on the information stored in UI files (created with *Qt Designer*) or available in
the specified plugin paths. The specified plugin paths can be retrieved using the
[pluginPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#pluginPaths)() function.
Similarly, the contents of a UI file can be retrieved using the
[load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#load)() function. For example:

```
MyWidget::MyWidget(QWidget *parent)
    : QWidget(parent)
{
    QUiLoader loader;
    QFile file(":/forms/myform.ui");
    file.open(QFile::ReadOnly);
    QWidget *myWidget = loader.load(&file, this);
    file.close();

    QVBoxLayout *layout = new QVBoxLayout;
    layout->addWidget(myWidget);
    setLayout(layout);
}
```

By including the user interface in the form's resources (`myform.qrc`), we ensure that
it will be present at run-time:

```
<!DOCTYPE RCC><RCC version="1.0">
<qresource prefix="/forms">
<file>myform.ui</file>
</qresource>
</RCC>
```

The
[availableWidgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#availableWidgets)()
function returns a [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html)
with the class names of the widgets available in the specified plugin paths. To create
these widgets, simply use the
[createWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#createWidget)()
function. For example:

```
QWidget *loadCustomWidget(QWidget *parent)
{
    QUiLoader loader;
    QWidget *myWidget;

    QStringList availableWidgets = loader.availableWidgets();

    if (availableWidgets.contains("AnalogClock"))
        myWidget = loader.createWidget("AnalogClock", parent);

    return myWidget;
}
```

To make a custom widget available to the loader, you can use the
[addPluginPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#addPluginPath)()
function; to remove all available widgets, you can call the
[clearPluginPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#clearPluginPaths)()
function.

The [createAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#createAction)(),
[createActionGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#createActionGroup)(),
[createLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#createLayout)(), and
[createWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quiloader.html#createWidget)()
functions are used internally by the QUiLoader class whenever it has to create an
action, action group, layout, or widget respectively. For that reason, you can subclass
the QUiLoader class and reimplement these functions to intervene the process of
constructing a user interface. For example, you might want to have a list of the actions
created when loading a form or creating a custom widget.

For a complete example using the QUiLoader class, see the [Calculator Builder
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtdesigner-calculatorbuilder-example.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QUndoCommand.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

For an overview of Qt's Undo Framework, see the [overview
document](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundo.html).

A QUndoCommand represents a single editing action on a document; for example, inserting
or deleting a block of text in a text editor. QUndoCommand can apply a change to the
document with [redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() and
undo the change with
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)(). The implementations
for these functions must be provided in a derived class.

```
class AppendText : public QUndoCommand
{
public:
    AppendText(QString *doc, const QString &text)
        : m_document(doc), m_text(text) { setText("append text"); }
    void undo() override
        { m_document->chop(m_text.length()); }
    void redo() override
        { m_document->append(m_text); }
private:
    QString *m_document;
    QString m_text;
};
```

A QUndoCommand has an associated
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#text)(). This is a short
string describing what the command does. It is used to update the text properties of the
stack's undo and redo actions; see
[QUndoStack::createUndoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createUndoAction)()
and
[QUndoStack::createRedoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createRedoAction)().

QUndoCommand objects are owned by the stack they were pushed on.
[QUndoStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html) deletes a command if it
has been undone and a new command is pushed. For example:

```
MyCommand *command1 = new MyCommand();
stack->push(command1);
MyCommand *command2 = new MyCommand();
stack->push(command2);

stack->undo();

MyCommand *command3 = new MyCommand();
stack->push(command3); // command2 gets deleted
```

In effect, when a command is pushed, it becomes the top-most command on the stack.

To support command compression, QUndoCommand has an
[id](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#id)() and the virtual function
[mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)(). These
functions are used by
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)().

To support command macros, a QUndoCommand object can have any number of child commands.
Undoing or redoing the parent command will cause the child commands to be undone or
redone. A command can be assigned to a parent explicitly in the constructor. In this
case, the command will be owned by the parent.

The parent in this case is usually an empty command, in that it doesn't provide its own
implementation of [undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)()
and [redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)(). Instead, it
uses the base implementations of these functions, which simply call
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)() or
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() on all its children.
The parent should, however, have a meaningful
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#text)().

```
QUndoCommand *insertRed = new QUndoCommand(); // an empty command
insertRed->setText("insert red text");

new InsertText(document, idx, text, insertRed); // becomes child of insertRed
new SetColor(document, idx, text.length(), Qt::red, insertRed);

stack.push(insertRed);
```

Another way to create macros is to use the convenience functions
[QUndoStack::beginMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#beginMacro)()
and
[QUndoStack::endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)().

### `[virtual]` int QUndoCommand::id() const

Returns the ID of this command.

A command ID is used in command compression. It must be an integer unique to this
command's class, or -1 if the command doesn't support compression.

If the command supports compression this function must be overridden in the derived
class to return the correct ID. The base implementation returns -1.

[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)() will only
try to merge two commands if they have the same ID, and the ID is not -1.

**See also**
[mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)() and
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)().

PythonQt.Qt.QUndoCommand.mergeWith.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QUndoCommand::mergeWith(const [QUndoCommand](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#QUndoCommand) \**command*)

Attempts to merge this command with *command*. Returns `true` on success; otherwise
returns `false`.

If this function returns `true`, calling this command's
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() must have the same
effect as redoing both this command and *command*. Similarly, calling this command's
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)() must have the same
effect as undoing *command* and this command.

[QUndoStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html) will only try to merge
two commands if they have the same id, and the id is not -1.

The default implementation returns `false`.

```
bool AppendText::mergeWith(const QUndoCommand *other)
{
    if (other->id() != id()) // make sure other is also an AppendText command
        return false;
    m_text += static_cast<const AppendText*>(other)->m_text;
    return true;
}
```

**See also** [id](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#id)() and
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)().

### `[virtual]` void QUndoCommand::undo()

Reverts a change to the document. After undo() is called, the state of the document
should be the same as before
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() was called. This
function must be implemented in the derived class. Calling
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)(),
[QUndoStack::undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#undo)() or
[QUndoStack::redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)() from this
function leads to undefined beahavior.

The default implementation calls undo() on all child commands in reverse order.

**See also** [redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)().

## Detailed Description

For an overview of the Qt's undo framework, see the
[overview](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundo.html).

An application often has multiple undo stacks, one for each opened document. At the same
time, an application usually has one undo action and one redo action, which triggers
undo or redo in the active document.

QUndoGroup is a group of
[QUndoStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html) objects, one of which
may be active. It has an
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#undo)() and
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#redo)() slot, which calls
[QUndoStack::undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#undo)() and
[QUndoStack::redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)() for the
active stack. It also has the functions
[createUndoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#createUndoAction)()
and
[createRedoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#createRedoAction)().
The actions returned by these functions behave in the same way as those returned by
[QUndoStack::createUndoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createUndoAction)()
and
[QUndoStack::createRedoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createRedoAction)()
of the active stack.

Stacks are added to a group with
[addStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#addStack)() and removed
with [removeStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#removeStack)(). A
stack is implicitly added to a group when it is created with the group as its parent
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html).

It is the programmer's responsibility to specify which stack is active by calling
[QUndoStack::setActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#active-prop)(),
usually when the associated document window receives focus. The active stack may also be
set with
[setActiveStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#setActiveStack)(),
and is returned by
[activeStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#activeStack)().

When a stack is added to a group using
[addStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#addStack)(), the group
does not take ownership of the stack. This means the stack has to be deleted separately
from the group. When a stack is deleted, it is automatically removed from a group. A
stack may belong to only one group. Adding it to another group will cause it to be
removed from the previous group.

A QUndoGroup is also useful in conjunction with
[QUndoView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundoview.html). If a
[QUndoView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundoview.html) is set to watch a group
using
[QUndoView::setGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundoview.html#setGroup)(), it
will update itself to display the active stack.

PythonQt.Qt.QUndoStack.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

For an overview of Qt's Undo Framework, see the [overview
document](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundo.html).

An undo stack maintains a stack of commands that have been applied to a document.

New commands are pushed on the stack using
[push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)(). Commands can be
undone and redone using
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#undo)() and
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)(), or by triggering the
actions returned by
[createUndoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createUndoAction)()
and
[createRedoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createRedoAction)().

QUndoStack keeps track of the *current* command. This is the command which will be
executed by the next call to
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)(). The index of this
command is returned by
[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#index)(). The state of the
edited object can be rolled forward or back using
[setIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#setIndex)(). If the
top-most command on the stack has already been redone,
[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#index)() is equal to
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#count)().

QUndoStack provides support for undo and redo actions, command compression, command
macros, and supports the concept of a *clean state*.

### Undo and Redo Actions

QUndoStack provides convenient undo and redo
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) objects, which can be
inserted into a menu or a toolbar. When commands are undone or redone, QUndoStack
updates the text properties of these actions to reflect what change they will trigger.
The actions are also disabled when no command is available for undo or redo. These
actions are returned by
[QUndoStack::createUndoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createUndoAction)()
and
[QUndoStack::createRedoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createRedoAction)().

### Command Compression and Macros

Command compression is useful when several commands can be compressed into a single
command that can be undone and redone in a single operation. For example, when a user
types a character in a text editor, a new command is created. This command inserts the
character into the document at the cursor position. However, it is more convenient for
the user to be able to undo or redo typing of whole words, sentences, or paragraphs.
Command compression allows these single-character commands to be merged into a single
command which inserts or deletes sections of text. For more information, see
[QUndoCommand::mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)()
and [push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)().

A command macro is a sequence of commands, all of which are undone and redone in one go.
Command macros are created by giving a command a list of child commands. Undoing or
redoing the parent command will cause the child commands to be undone or redone. Command
macros may be created explicitly by specifying a parent in the
[QUndoCommand](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html) constructor, or by
using the convenience functions
[beginMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#beginMacro)() and
[endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)().

Although command compression and macros appear to have the same effect to the user, they
often have different uses in an application. Commands that perform small changes to a
document may be usefully compressed if there is no need to individually record them, and
if only larger changes are relevant to the user. However, for commands that need to be
recorded individually, or those that cannot be compressed, it is useful to use macros to
provide a more convenient user experience while maintaining a record of each command.

### Clean State

QUndoStack supports the concept of a clean state. When the document is saved to disk,
the stack can be marked as clean using
[setClean](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#setClean)(). Whenever the
stack returns to this state through undoing and redoing commands, it emits the signal
[cleanChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#cleanChanged)(). This
signal is also emitted when the stack leaves the clean state. This signal is usually
used to enable and disable the save actions in the application, and to update the
document's title to reflect that it contains unsaved changes.

### Obsolete Commands

QUndoStack is able to delete commands from the stack if the command is no longer needed.
One example may be to delete a command when two commands are merged together in such a
way that the merged command has no function. This can be seen with move commands where
the user moves their mouse to one part of the screen and then moves it to the original
position. The merged command results in a mouse movement of 0\. This command can be
deleted since it serves no purpose. Another example is with networking commands that
fail due to connection issues. In this case, the command is to be removed from the stack
because the [redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)() and
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#undo)() functions have no
function since there was connection issues.

A command can be marked obsolete with the
[QUndoCommand::setObsolete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#setObsolete)()
function. The
[QUndoCommand::isObsolete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#isObsolete)()
flag is checked in
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)(),
[QUndoStack::undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#undo)(),
[QUndoStack::redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)(), and
[QUndoStack::setIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#setIndex)()
after calling
[QUndoCommand::undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)(),
[QUndoCommand::redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() and
[QUndoCommand](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html):mergeWith() where
applicable.

If a command is set obsolete and the clean index is greater than or equal to the current
command index, then the clean index will be reset when the command is deleted from the
stack.

### active : bool

This property holds the active status of this stack.

An application often has multiple undo stacks, one for each opened document. The active
stack is the one associated with the currently active document. If the stack belongs to
a [QUndoGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html), calls to
[QUndoGroup::undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#undo)() or
[QUndoGroup::redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html#redo)() will be
forwarded to this stack when it is active. If the
[QUndoGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html) is watched by a
[QUndoView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundoview.html), the view will display
the contents of this stack when it is active. If the stack does not belong to a
[QUndoGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html), making it active has
no effect.

It is the programmer's responsibility to specify which stack is active by calling
setActive(), usually when the associated document window receives focus.

PythonQt.Qt.QUndoStack.beginMacro.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QUndoStack::beginMacro(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*)

Begins composition of a macro command with the given *text* description.

An empty command described by the specified *text* is pushed on the stack. Any
subsequent commands pushed on the stack will be appended to the empty command's children
until [endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)() is
called.

Calls to beginMacro() and
[endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)() may be nested,
but every call to beginMacro() must have a matching call to
[endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)().

While a macro is being composed, the stack is disabled. This means that:

- [indexChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#indexChanged)() and [cleanChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#cleanChanged)() are not emitted,
- [canUndo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#canUndo)() and [canRedo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#canRedo)() return false,
- calling [undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#undo)() or [redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)() has no effect,
- the undo/redo actions are disabled.

The stack becomes enabled and appropriate signals are emitted when
[endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)() is called for
the outermost macro.

```
stack.beginMacro("insert red text");
stack.push(new InsertText(document, idx, text));
stack.push(new SetColor(document, idx, text.length(), Qt::red));
stack.endMacro(); // indexChanged() is emitted
```

This code is equivalent to:

```
QUndoCommand *insertRed = new QUndoCommand(); // an empty command
insertRed->setText("insert red text");

new InsertText(document, idx, text, insertRed); // becomes child of insertRed
new SetColor(document, idx, text.length(), Qt::red, insertRed);

stack.push(insertRed);
```

**See also** [endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)().

### int QUndoStack::cleanIndex() const

Returns the clean index. This is the index at which
[setClean](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#setClean)() was called.

A stack may not have a clean index. This happens if a document is saved, some commands
are undone, then a new command is pushed. Since
[push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)() deletes all the undone
commands before pushing the new command, the stack can't return to the clean state
again. In this case, this function returns -1. The -1 may also be returned after an
explicit call to
[resetClean](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#resetClean)().

**See also** [isClean](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#isClean)() and
[setClean](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#setClean)().

PythonQt.Qt.QUndoStack.push.doc:

### void QUndoStack::push([QUndoCommand](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html) \**cmd*)

Pushes *cmd* on the stack or merges it with the most recently executed command. In
either case, executes *cmd* by calling its
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#redo)() function.

If *cmd*'s id is not -1, and if the id is the same as that of the most recently executed
command, [QUndoStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html) will attempt
to merge the two commands by calling
[QUndoCommand::mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)()
on the most recently executed command. If
[QUndoCommand::mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)()
returns `true`, *cmd* is deleted.

After calling
[QUndoCommand::redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() and,
if applicable,
[QUndoCommand::mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)(),
[QUndoCommand::isObsolete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#isObsolete)()
will be called for *cmd* or the merged command. If
[QUndoCommand::isObsolete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#isObsolete)()
returns `true`, then *cmd* or the merged command will be deleted from the stack.

In all other cases *cmd* is simply pushed on the stack.

If commands were undone before *cmd* was pushed, the current command and all commands
above it are deleted. Hence *cmd* always ends up being the top-most on the stack.

Once a command is pushed, the stack takes ownership of it. There are no getters to
return the command, since modifying it after it has been executed will almost always
lead to corruption of the document's state.

**See also**
[QUndoCommand::id](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#id)() and
[QUndoCommand::mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)().

### `[slot]` void QUndoStack::redo()

Redoes the current command by calling
[QUndoCommand::redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)().
Increments the current command index.

If the stack is empty, or if the top command on the stack has already been redone, this
function does nothing.

If
[QUndoCommand::isObsolete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#isObsolete)()
returns true for the current command, then the command will be deleted from the stack.
Additionally, if the clean index is greater than or equal to the current command index,
then the clean index is reset.

**See also** [undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#undo)() and
[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#index)().

### `[slot]` void QUndoStack::resetClean()

[cleanChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#cleanChanged)() if the

### `[slot]` void QUndoStack::undo()

Undoes the command below the current command by calling
[QUndoCommand::undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)().
Decrements the current command index.

If the stack is empty, or if the bottom command on the stack has already been undone,

After the command is undone, if
[QUndoCommand::isObsolete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#isObsolete)()
returns `true`, then the command will be deleted from the stack. Additionally, if the
clean index is greater than or equal to the current command index, then the clean index
is reset.

[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#index)().

### undoLimit : int

This property holds the maximum number of commands on this stack.

When the number of commands on a stack exceedes the stack's undoLimit, commands are
deleted from the bottom of the stack. Macro commands (commands with child commands) are
treated as one command. The default value is 0, which means that there is no limit.

This property may only be set when the undo stack is empty, since setting it on a
non-empty stack might delete the command at the current index. Calling setUndoLimit() on
a non-empty stack prints a warning and does nothing.

This property was introduced in Qt 4.3.

## Detailed Description

QUndoView is a [QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) which
displays the list of commands pushed on an undo stack. The most recently executed
command is always selected. Selecting a different command results in a call to
[QUndoStack::setIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#setIndex)(),
rolling the state of the document backwards or forward to the new command.

The stack can be set explicitly with
[setStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundoview.html#setStack)(). Alternatively,
a [QUndoGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundogroup.html) object can be set
with [setGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundoview.html#setGroup)(). The view
will then update itself automatically whenever the active stack of the group changes.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qundoview.png)

PythonQt.Qt.QUrl.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It can parse and construct URLs in both encoded and unencoded form. QUrl also has
support for internationalized domain names (IDNs).

The most common way to use QUrl is to initialize it via the constructor by passing a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). Otherwise,
[setUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUrl)() can also be used.

URLs can be represented in two forms: encoded or unencoded. The unencoded representation
is suitable for showing to users, but the encoded representation is typically what you
would send to a web server. For example, the unencoded URL
"http://bühler.example.com/List of applicants.xml" would be sent to the server as
"http://xn--bhler-kva.example.com/List%20of%20applicants.xml".

A URL can also be constructed piece by piece by calling
[setScheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setScheme)(),
[setUserName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserName)(),
[setPassword](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPassword)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)(),
[setPort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPort)(),
[setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPath)(),
[setQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setQuery)() and
[setFragment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setFragment)(). Some
convenience functions are also available:
[setAuthority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setAuthority)() sets the
user name, password, host and port.
[setUserInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserInfo)() sets the user
name and password at once.

Call [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() to check if the
URL is valid. This can be done at any point during the constructing of a URL. If
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() returns `false`, you
should [clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#clear)() the URL before
proceeding, or start over by parsing a new URL with
[setUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUrl)().

Constructing a query is particularly convenient through the use of the
[QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) class and its methods
[QUrlQuery::setQueryItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQueryItems)(),
[QUrlQuery::addQueryItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#addQueryItem)()
and
[QUrlQuery::removeQueryItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#removeQueryItem)().
Use
[QUrlQuery::setQueryDelimiters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQueryDelimiters)()
to customize the delimiters used for generating the query string.

For the convenience of generating encoded URL strings or query strings, there are two
static functions called
[fromPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromPercentEncoding)()
and
[toPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toPercentEncoding)()
which deal with percent encoding and decoding of
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) objects.

[fromLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromLocalFile)() constructs
a QUrl by parsing a local file path.
[toLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toLocalFile)() converts a URL
to a local file path.

The human readable representation of the URL is fetched with
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toString)(). This representation
is appropriate for displaying a URL to a user in unencoded form. The encoded form
however, as returned by
[toEncoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toEncoded)(), is for internal
use, passing to web servers, mail clients and so on. Both forms are technically correct
and represent the same URL unambiguously \-- in fact, passing either form to QUrl's
constructor or to [setUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUrl)() will
yield the same QUrl object.

QUrl conforms to the URI specification from [RFC
3986](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.txt) (Uniform Resource Identifier: Generic
Syntax), and includes scheme extensions from [RFC
1738](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1738.txt) (Uniform Resource Locators). Case
folding rules in QUrl conform to [RFC 3491](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3491.txt)
(Nameprep: A Stringprep Profile for Internationalized Domain Names (IDN)). It is also
compatible with the [file URI
specification](http://freedesktop.org/wiki/Specifications/file-uri-spec/) from
freedesktop.org, provided that the locale encodes file names using UTF-8 (required by
IDN).

#### Relative URLs vs Relative Paths

Calling [isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isRelative)() will
return whether or not the URL is relative. A relative URL has no
[scheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#scheme). For example:

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("main.qml").isRelative();          // true: no scheme
    qDebug() << QUrl("qml/main.qml").isRelative();      // true: no scheme
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:main.qml").isRelative();     // false: has "file" scheme
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:qml/main.qml").isRelative(); // false: has "file" scheme
```

Notice that a URL can be absolute while containing a relative path, and vice versa:

```
    // Absolute URL, relative path
    QUrl url("file:file.txt");
    qDebug() << url.isRelative();                 // false: has "file" scheme
    qDebug() << QDir::isAbsolutePath(url.path()); // false: relative path

    // Relative URL, absolute path
    url = QUrl("/home/user/file.txt");
    qDebug() << url.isRelative();                 // true: has no scheme
    qDebug() << QDir::isAbsolutePath(url.path()); // true: absolute path
```

A relative URL can be resolved by passing it as an argument to
[resolved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#resolved)(), which returns an
absolute URL. [isParentOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isParentOf)() is
used for determining whether one URL is a parent of another.

#### Error checking

QUrl is capable of detecting many errors in URLs while parsing it or when components of
the URL are set with individual setter methods (like
[setScheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setScheme)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)() or
[setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPath)()). If the parsing or
setter function is successful, any previously recorded error conditions will be
discarded.

By default, QUrl setter methods operate in
[QUrl::TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum),
which means they accept some common mistakes and mis-representation of data. An
alternate method of parsing is
[QUrl::StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), which
applies further checks. See
[QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) for a
description of the difference of the parsing modes.

QUrl only checks for conformance with the URL specification. It does not try to verify
that high-level protocol URLs are in the format they are expected to be by handlers
elsewhere. For example, the following URIs are all considered valid by QUrl, even if
they do not make sense when used:

- "http:/filename.html"
- "mailto://example.com"

When the parser encounters an error, it signals the event by making
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() return false and
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toString)() /
[toEncoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toEncoded)() return an empty
string. If it is necessary to show the user the reason why the URL failed to parse, the
error condition can be obtained from QUrl by calling
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#errorString)(). Note that
this message is highly technical and may not make sense to end-users.

QUrl is capable of recording only one error condition. If more than one error is found,
it is undefined which error is reported.

#### Character Conversions

Follow these rules to avoid erroneous character conversion when dealing with URLs and
strings:

- When creating a [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) to contain a URL from a [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) or a char\*, always use [QString::fromUtf8](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#fromUtf8)().

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::fileName([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= FullyDecoded) const

Returns the name of the file, excluding the directory path.

Note that, if this [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) object is given
a path ending in a slash, the name of the file is considered empty.

If the path doesn't contain any slash, it is fully returned as the fileName.

Example:

```

// url.adjusted(RemoveFilename) == "http://qt-project.org/support/"
// url.fileName() == "file.html"

The *options* argument controls how to format the file name component. All values
produce an unambiguous result. With
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
all percent-encoded sequences are decoded; otherwise, the returned value may contain
some percent-encoded sequences for some control sequences not representable in decoded
form in [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

**See also** [path](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#path)().

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::fromAce(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*domain*)

Returns the Unicode form of the given domain name *domain*, which is encoded in the
ASCII Compatible Encoding (ACE). The result of this function is considered equivalent to
*domain*.

If the value in *domain* cannot be encoded, it will be converted to
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) and returned.

The ASCII Compatible Encoding (ACE) is defined by RFC 3490, RFC 3491 and RFC 3492\. It
is part of the Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) specification,
which allows for domain names (like `"example.com"`) to be written using international
characters.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

PythonQt.Qt.QUrl.fromLocalFile.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::fromLocalFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*localFile*)

Returns a [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) representation of
*localFile*, interpreted as a local file. This function accepts paths separated by
slashes as well as the native separator for this platform.

This function also accepts paths with a doubled leading slash (or backslash) to indicate
a remote file, as in "//servername/path/to/file.txt". Note that only certain platforms
can actually open this file using
[QFile::open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)().

An empty *localFile* leads to an empty URL (since Qt 5.4).

```
    qDebug() << QUrl::fromLocalFile("file.txt");            // QUrl("file:file.txt")
    qDebug() << QUrl::fromLocalFile("/home/user/file.txt"); // QUrl("file:///home/user/file.txt")
    qDebug() << QUrl::fromLocalFile("file:file.txt");       // doesn't make sense; expects path, not url with scheme
```

In the first line in snippet above, a file URL is constructed from a local, relative
path. A file URL with a relative path only makes sense if there is a base URL to resolve
it against. For example:

```
    QUrl url = QUrl::fromLocalFile("file.txt");
    QUrl baseUrl = QUrl("file:/home/user/");
    // wrong: prints QUrl("file:file.txt"), as url already has a scheme
    qDebug() << baseUrl.resolved(url);
```

To resolve such a URL, it's necessary to remove the scheme beforehand:

```
    // correct: prints QUrl("file:///home/user/file.txt")
    url.setScheme(QString());
    qDebug() << baseUrl.resolved(url);
```

For this reason, it is better to use a relative URL (that is, no scheme) for relative
file paths:

```
    QUrl url = QUrl("file.txt");
    QUrl baseUrl = QUrl("file:/home/user/");
    // prints QUrl("file:///home/user/file.txt")
    qDebug() << baseUrl.resolved(url);
```

**See also** [toLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toLocalFile)(),
[isLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isLocalFile)(), and
[QDir::toNativeSeparators](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#toNativeSeparators)().

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::fromPercentEncoding(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*input*)

PythonQt.Qt.QUrl.fromUserInput.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::fromUserInput(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*userInput*)

Returns a valid URL from a user supplied *userInput* string if one can be deducted. In
the case that is not possible, an invalid
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl)() is returned.

Most applications that can browse the web, allow the user to input a URL in the form of
a plain string. This string can be manually typed into a location bar, obtained from the
clipboard, or passed in via command line arguments.

When the string is not already a valid URL, a best guess is performed, making various
web related assumptions.

In the case the string corresponds to a valid file path on the system, a file:// URL is
constructed, using
[QUrl::fromLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromLocalFile)().

If that is not the case, an attempt is made to turn the string into a http:// or ftp://
URL. The latter in the case the string starts with 'ftp'. The result is then passed
through [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html)'s tolerant parser, and in
the case or success, a valid [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) is
returned, or else a [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl)().



#### Examples:

- qt-project.org becomes http://qt-project.org
- ftp.qt-project.org becomes ftp://ftp.qt-project.org
- hostname becomes http://hostname
- /home/user/test.html becomes file:///home/user/test.html

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

### `[static]` [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::fromUserInput(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*userInput*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*workingDirectory*, [QUrl::UserInputResolutionOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#UserInputResolutionOption-enum) *options* \= DefaultResolution)

Returns a valid URL from a user supplied *userInput* string if one can be deduced. In
the case that is not possible, an invalid
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl)() is returned.

This overload takes a *workingDirectory* path, in order to be able to handle relative
paths. This is especially useful when handling command line arguments. If
*workingDirectory* is empty, no handling of relative paths will be done, so this method
will behave like its one argument overload.

By default, an input string that looks like a relative path will only be treated as such
if the file actually exists in the given working directory.

If the application can handle files that don't exist yet, it should pass the flag
[AssumeLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#UserInputResolutionOption-enum)
in *options*.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.
signatures: fromUserInput(userInput: str, workingDirectory: str, options: PySide2.QtCore.QUrl.UserInputResolutionOptions=...) -> PySide2.QtCore.QUrl

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::host([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= FullyDecoded) const

Returns the host of the URL if it is defined; otherwise an empty string is returned.

The *options* argument controls how the hostname will be formatted. The
[QUrl::EncodeUnicode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)

All other flags are ignored. Host names cannot contain control or percent characters, so
the returned value can be considered fully decoded.

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::password([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= FullyDecoded) const

Note that
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
may cause data loss if those non-representable sequences are present. It is recommended
to use that value when the result will be used in a non-URL context, such as setting in

a login.

PythonQt.Qt.QUrl.path.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::path([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= FullyDecoded) const

Returns the path of the URL.

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:file.txt").path();                   // "file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("/home/user/file.txt").path();             // "/home/user/file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("http://www.example.com/test/123").path(); // "/test/123"
```

The *options* argument controls how to format the path component. All values produce an
unambiguous result. With
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
all percent-encoded sequences are decoded; otherwise, the returned value may contain
some percent-encoded sequences for some control sequences not representable in decoded
form in [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

Note that
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
may cause data loss if those non-representable sequences are present. It is recommended
to use that value when the result will be used in a non-URL context, such as sending to
an FTP server.

An example of data loss is when you have non-Unicode percent-encoded sequences and use
[FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
(the default):

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("/foo%FFbar").path();
```

In this example, there will be some level of data loss because the `%FF` cannot be
converted.

Data loss can also occur when the path contains sub-delimiters (such as `+`):

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("/foo+bar%2B").path(); // "/foo+bar+"
```

Other decoding examples:

```
    const QUrl url("/temporary/Mambo %235%3F.mp3");
    qDebug() << url.path(QUrl::FullyDecoded);  // "/temporary/Mambo #5?.mp3"
    qDebug() << url.path(QUrl::PrettyDecoded); // "/temporary/Mambo #5?.mp3"
    qDebug() << url.path(QUrl::FullyEncoded);  // "/temporary/Mambo%20%235%3F.mp3"
```

**See also** [setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPath)().

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::query([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= PrettyDecoded) const

Returns the query string of the URL if there's a query string, or an empty result if
not. To determine if the parsed URL contained a query string, use
[hasQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasQuery)().

The *options* argument controls how to format the query component. All values produce an
unambiguous result. With
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
all percent-encoded sequences are decoded; otherwise, the returned value may contain
some percent-encoded sequences for some control sequences not representable in decoded

PythonQt.Qt.QUrl.resolved.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::resolved(const [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) \&*relative*) const

Returns the result of the merge of this URL with *relative*. This URL is used as a base
to convert *relative* to an absolute URL.

If *relative* is not a relative URL, this function will return *relative* directly.
Otherwise, the paths of the two URLs are merged, and the new URL returned has the scheme
and authority of the base URL, but with the merged path, as in the following example:

```
QUrl baseUrl("http://qt.digia.com/Support/");
QUrl relativeUrl("../Product/Library/");
qDebug(baseUrl.resolved(relativeUrl).toString());
// prints "http://qt.digia.com/Product/Library/"
```

Calling resolved() with ".." returns a
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) whose directory is one level higher
than the original. Similarly, calling resolved() with "../.." removes two levels from
the path. If *relative* is "/", the path becomes "/".

### void QUrl::setAuthority(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*authority*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *mode* \= TolerantMode)

Sets the authority of the URL to *authority*.

The authority of a URL is the combination of user info, a host name and a port. All of
these elements are optional; an empty authority is therefore valid.

The user info and host are separated by a '@', and the host and port are separated by a
':'. If the user info is empty, the '@' must be omitted; although a stray ':' is
permitted if the port is empty.

The following example shows a valid authority string:

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-authority.png)

The *authority* data is interpreted according to *mode*: in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), any '%'
characters must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal characters and some characters
(including space) are not allowed in undecoded form. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) (the
default), all characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will
correct stray '%' not followed by two hex characters.

This function does not allow *mode* to be
[QUrl::DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum). To
set fully decoded data, call
[setUserName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserName)(),
[setPassword](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPassword)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)() and
[setPort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPort)() individually.

**See also** [authority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#authority)(),
[setUserInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserInfo)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)(), and
[setPort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPort)().

PythonQt.Qt.QUrl.setIdnWhitelist.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QUrl::setIdnWhitelist(const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*list*)

Sets the whitelist of Top-Level Domains (TLDs) that are allowed to have non-ASCII
characters in domains to the value of *list*.

Note that if you call this function, you need to do so *before* you start any threads
that might access
[idnWhitelist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#idnWhitelist)().

Qt comes with a default list that contains the Internet top-level domains that have
published support for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and rules to guarantee that
no deception can happen between similarly-looking characters (such as the Latin
lowercase letter `'a'` and the Cyrillic equivalent, which in most fonts are visually
identical).

This list is periodically maintained, as registrars publish new rules.

This function is provided for those who need to manipulate the list, in order to add or
remove a TLD. It is not recommended to change its value for purposes other than testing,
as it may expose users to security risks.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[idnWhitelist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#idnWhitelist)().

Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrl::setQuery(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*query*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *mode* \= TolerantMode)

Sets the query string of the URL to *query*.

This function is useful if you need to pass a query string that does not fit into the
key-value pattern, or that uses a different scheme for encoding special characters than
what is suggested by [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html).

Passing a value of QString() to *query* (a null
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)) unsets the query completely.
However, passing a value of
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)("") will set the query to an
empty value, as if the original URL had a lone "?".

The *query* data is interpreted according to *mode*: in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), any '%'
characters must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal characters and some characters
(including space) are not allowed in undecoded form. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), all
characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will correct stray '%'
not followed by two hex characters. In
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), '%' stand
for themselves and encoded characters are not possible.

Query strings often contain percent-encoded sequences, so use of
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) is
discouraged. One special sequence to be aware of is that of the plus character ('\+').
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) does not convert spaces to plus
characters, even though HTML forms posted by web browsers do. In order to represent an
actual plus character in a query, the sequence "%2B" is usually used. This function will
leave "%2B" sequences untouched in
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) or
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum).

**See also** [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#query)() and
[hasQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasQuery)().

### void QUrl::setQuery(const [QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) \&*query*)

This is an overloaded function.

Sets the query string of the URL to *query*.

This function reconstructs the query string from the
[QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) object and sets on this
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) object. This function does not have
parsing parameters because the
[QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) contains data that is
already parsed.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also** [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#query)() and
[hasQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasQuery)().

PythonQt.Qt.QUrl.setScheme.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrl::setScheme(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*scheme*)

Sets the scheme of the URL to *scheme*. As a scheme can only contain ASCII characters,
no conversion or decoding is done on the input. It must also start with an ASCII letter.

The scheme describes the type (or protocol) of the URL. It's represented by one or more
ASCII characters at the start the URL.

A scheme is strictly [RFC 3986](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc3986.txt)-compliant: `scheme
= ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "-" / "." )`

The following example shows a URL where the scheme is "ftp":

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-authority2.png)

To set the scheme, the following call is used:

```
    QUrl url;
    url.setScheme("ftp");
```

The scheme can also be empty, in which case the URL is interpreted as relative.

**See also** [scheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#scheme)() and
[isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isRelative)().

### void QUrl::setUrl(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*url*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *parsingMode* \= TolerantMode)

Parses *url* and sets this object to that value.
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) will automatically percent encode
all characters that are not allowed in a URL and decode the percent-encoded sequences
that represent an unreserved character (letters, digits, hyphens, undercores, dots and
tildes). All other characters are left in their original forms.

Parses the *url* using the parser mode *parsingMode*. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) (the
default), [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) will correct certain
mistakes, notably the presence of a percent character ('%') not followed by two
hexadecimal digits, and it will accept any character in any position. In
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), encoding
mistakes will not be tolerated and [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html)
will also check that certain forbidden characters are not present in unencoded form. If
an error is detected in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum),
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() will return false. The
parsing mode
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) is not
permitted in this context and will produce a run-time warning.

**See also** [url](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#url)() and
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toString)().

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QUrl::toAce(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*domain*)

Returns the ASCII Compatible Encoding of the given domain name *domain*. The result of
this function is considered equivalent to *domain*.

The ASCII-Compatible Encoding (ACE) is defined by RFC 3490, RFC 3491 and RFC 3492\. It
is part of the Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) specification,
which allows for domain names (like `"example.com"`) to be written using international
characters.

This function returns an empty
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) if *domain* is not a
valid hostname. Note, in particular, that IPv6 literals are not valid domain names.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::toLocalFile() const

Returns the path of this URL formatted as a local file path. The path returned will use
forward slashes, even if it was originally created from one with backslashes.

If this URL contains a non-empty hostname, it will be encoded in the returned value in
the form found on SMB networks (for example, "//servername/path/to/file.txt").

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:file.txt").toLocalFile();            // "file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:/home/user/file.txt").toLocalFile(); // "/home/user/file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("file.txt").toLocalFile();                 // ""; wasn't a local file as it had no scheme
```

Note: if the path component of this URL contains a non-UTF-8 binary sequence (such as
%80), the behaviour of this function is undefined.

**See also**
[fromLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromLocalFile)() and
[isLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isLocalFile)().
