### geometry : [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html)

This property holds the geometry of the widget relative to its parent and excluding the
window frame

When changing the geometry, the widget, if visible, receives a move event
([moveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#moveEvent)()) and/or a
resize event
([resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#resizeEvent)())
immediately. If the widget is not currently visible, it is guaranteed to receive
appropriate events before it is shown.

The size component is adjusted if it lies outside the range defined by
[minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)() and
[maximumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#maximumSize-prop)().

**Warning:** Calling setGeometry() inside
[resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#resizeEvent)() or
[moveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#moveEvent)() can lead to
infinite recursion.

See the [Window
Geometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/application-windows.html#window-geometry)
documentation for an overview of geometry issues with windows.

By default, this property contains a value that depends on the user's platform and
screen geometry.

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.grabKeyboard.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QWidget::grabKeyboard()

Grabs the keyboard input.

This widget receives all keyboard events until
[releaseKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseKeyboard)() is
called; other widgets get no keyboard events at all. Mouse events are not affected. Use
[grabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabMouse)() if you want to
grab that.

The focus widget is not affected, except that it doesn't receive any keyboard events.
[setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setFocus-1)() moves the focus
as usual, but the new focus widget receives keyboard events only after
[releaseKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseKeyboard)() is
called.

If a different widget is currently grabbing keyboard input, that widget's grab is
released first.

**See also**
[releaseKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseKeyboard)(),
[grabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabMouse)(),
[releaseMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseMouse)(), and
[focusWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusWidget)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.grabMouse.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QWidget::grabMouse()

Grabs the mouse input.

This widget receives all mouse events until
[releaseMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseMouse)() is
called; other widgets get no mouse events at all. Keyboard events are not affected. Use
[grabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabKeyboard)() if you
want to grab that.

**Warning:** Bugs in mouse-grabbing applications very often lock the terminal. Use this
function with extreme caution, and consider using the `-nograb` command line option
while debugging.

It is almost never necessary to grab the mouse when using Qt, as Qt grabs and releases
it sensibly. In particular, Qt grabs the mouse when a mouse button is pressed and keeps
it until the last button is released.

**Note:** Only visible widgets can grab mouse input. If
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)() returns
`false` for a widget, that widget cannot call grabMouse().

**Note:** On Windows, grabMouse() only works when the mouse is inside a window owned by
the process. On macOS, grabMouse() only works when the mouse is inside the frame of that
widget.

**See also**
[releaseMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseMouse)(),
[grabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabKeyboard)(), and
[releaseKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseKeyboard)().

### void QWidget::grabMouse(const [QCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcursor.html) \&*cursor*)

This function overloads grabMouse().

Grabs the mouse input and changes the cursor shape.

The cursor will assume shape *cursor* (for as long as the mouse focus is grabbed) and
this widget will be the only one to receive mouse events until
[releaseMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseMouse)() is
called().

**Warning:** Grabbing the mouse might lock the terminal.

**Note:** See the note in
[QWidget::grabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabMouse)().

**See also**
[releaseMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseMouse)(),
[grabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabKeyboard)(),
[releaseKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseKeyboard)(),
and [setCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#cursor-prop)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.grabShortcut.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QWidget::grabShortcut(const [QKeySequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html) \&*key*, [Qt::ShortcutContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ShortcutContext-enum) *context* \= Qt::WindowShortcut)

Adds a shortcut to Qt's shortcut system that watches for the given *key* sequence in the
given *context*. If the *context* is
[Qt::ApplicationShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ShortcutContext-enum),
the shortcut applies to the application as a whole. Otherwise, it is either local to
this widget,
[Qt::WidgetShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ShortcutContext-enum),
or to the window itself,
[Qt::WindowShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ShortcutContext-enum).

If the same *key* sequence has been grabbed by several widgets, when the *key* sequence
occurs a [QEvent::Shortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
event is sent to all the widgets to which it applies in a non-deterministic order, but
with the \`\`ambiguous'' flag set to true.

**Warning:** You should not normally need to use this function; instead create
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html)s with the shortcut key
sequences you require (if you also want equivalent menu options and toolbar buttons), or
create [QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html)s if you just need
key sequences. Both [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) and
[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html) handle all the event
filtering for you, and provide signals which are triggered when the user triggers the
key sequence, so are much easier to use than this low-level function.

**See also**
[releaseShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#releaseShortcut)() and
[setShortcutEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setShortcutEnabled)().
signatures: grabShortcut(self, key: PySide2.QtGui.QKeySequence, context: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.ShortcutContext=...) -> int

### `[slot]` void QWidget::hide()

Hides the widget. This function is equivalent to
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)(false).

**Note:** If you are working with
[QDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html) or its subclasses and you

**See also** [hideEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hideEvent)(),
[isHidden](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#isHidden)(),

Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::hideEvent([QHideEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhideevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive widget hide events. The
event is passed in the *event* parameter.

Hide events are sent to widgets immediately after they have been hidden.

Note: A widget receives spontaneous show and hide events when its mapping status is
changed by the window system, e.g. a spontaneous hide event when the user minimizes the
window, and a spontaneous show event when the window is restored again. After receiving
a spontaneous hide event, a widget is still considered visible in the sense of
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)().

**See also** [visible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop),
[event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)(), and
[QHideEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhideevent.html).

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::inputMethodEvent([QInputMethodEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive
Input Method composition events. This handler is called when the state of the input
method changes.

Note that when creating custom text editing widgets, the
[Qt::WA\_InputMethodEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
window attribute must be set explicitly (using the
[setAttribute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setAttribute)() function)
in order to receive input method events.

The default implementation calls event-\>ignore(), which rejects the Input Method event.
See the [QInputMethodEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html)
documentation for more details.

**See also** [event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)() and
[QInputMethodEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.inputMethodHints.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### inputMethodHints : [Qt::InputMethodHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#InputMethodHint-enum)

What input method specific hints the widget has.

This is only relevant for input widgets. It is used by the input method to retrieve
hints as to how the input method should operate. For example, if the
[Qt::ImhFormattedNumbersOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#InputMethodHint-enum)
flag is set, the input method may change its visual components to reflect that only
numbers can be entered.

**Warning:** Some widgets require certain flags in order to work as intended. To set a
flag, do `w->setInputMethodHints(w->inputMethodHints()|f)` instead of

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QWidget::isEnabledTo(const [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**ancestor*) const

Returns `true` if this widget would become enabled if *ancestor* is enabled; otherwise
returns `false`.

This is the case if neither the widget itself nor every parent up to but excluding
*ancestor* has been explicitly disabled.

isEnabledTo(0) returns false if this widget or any if its ancestors was explicitly
disabled.

The word ancestor here means a parent widget within the same window.

Therefore isEnabledTo(0) stops at this widget's window, unlike
[isEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop)() which also
takes parent windows into considerations.

**See also**
[setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop)() and
[enabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop).

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QWidget::isHidden() const

Returns `true` if the widget is hidden, otherwise returns `false`.

A hidden widget will only become visible when
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() is called on it. It will
not be automatically shown when the parent is shown.

To check visibility, use
![isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)() instead
(notice the exclamation mark).

isHidden() implies
![isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)(), but a
widget can be not visible and not hidden at the same time. This is the case for widgets
that are children of widgets that are not visible.

Widgets are hidden if:

- they were created as independent windows,
- they were created as children of visible widgets,
- [hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)() or [setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)(false) was called.

### bool QWidget::isVisibleTo(const [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**ancestor*) const

Returns `true` if this widget would become visible if *ancestor* is shown; otherwise
returns `false`.

The true case occurs if neither the widget itself nor any parent up to but excluding
*ancestor* has been explicitly hidden.

This function will still return true if the widget is obscured by other windows on the
screen, but could be physically visible if it or they were to be moved.

isVisibleTo(0) is identical to
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)().

**See also** [show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(),
[hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)(), and
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.isWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QWidget::isWindow() const

Returns `true` if the widget is an independent window, otherwise returns `false`.

A window is a widget that isn't visually the child of any other widget and that usually
has a frame and a [window
title](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowTitle-prop).

A window can have a [parent
widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#parentWidget). It will then be
grouped with its parent and deleted when the parent is deleted, minimized when the
parent is minimized etc. If supported by the window manager, it will also have a common
taskbar entry with its parent.

[QDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html) and
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) widgets are by
default windows, even if a parent widget is specified in the constructor. This behavior
is specified by the
[Qt::Window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum) flag.

**See also** [window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#window)(),
[isModal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#modal-prop)(), and
[parentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#parentWidget)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.keyPressEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::keyPressEvent([QKeyEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeyevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive key
press events for the widget.

A widget must call
[setFocusPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusPolicy-prop)() to
accept focus initially and have focus in order to receive a key press event.

If you reimplement this handler, it is very important that you call the base class
implementation if you do not act upon the key.

The default implementation closes popup widgets if the user presses the key sequence for
[QKeySequence::Cancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#StandardKey-enum)
(typically the Escape key). Otherwise the event is ignored, so that the widget's parent
can interpret it.

Note that [QKeyEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeyevent.html) starts with
isAccepted() \=\= true, so you do not need to call
[QKeyEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)() \- just do
not call the base class implementation if you act upon the key.

**See also**
[keyReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#keyReleaseEvent)(),
[setFocusPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusPolicy-prop)(),
[focusInEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusInEvent)(),
[focusOutEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusOutEvent)(),
[event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)(),
[QKeyEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeyevent.html), and [Tetrix
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-tetrix-example.html).

### maximumSize : [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html)

This property holds the widget's maximum size in pixels

The widget cannot be resized to a larger size than the maximum widget size.

By default, this property contains a size in which both width and height have values of
16777215\.

**Note:** The definition of the `QWIDGETSIZE_MAX` macro limits the maximum size of
widgets.

### minimumSize : [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html)

This property holds the widget's minimum size

The widget cannot be resized to a smaller size than the minimum widget size. The
widget's size is forced to the minimum size if the current size is smaller.

The minimum size set by this function will override the minimum size defined by
[QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html). In order to unset the
minimum size, use a value of `QSize(0, 0)`.

By default, this property contains a size with zero width and height.

| --- | --- |

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.minimumSizeHint.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### minimumSizeHint : const [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html)

This property holds the recommended minimum size for the widget

If the value of this property is an invalid size, no minimum size is recommended.

The default implementation of minimumSizeHint() returns an invalid size if there is no
layout for this widget, and returns the layout's minimum size otherwise. Most built-in
widgets reimplement minimumSizeHint().

[QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html) will never resize a widget to
a size smaller than the minimum size hint unless
[minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)() is set
or the size policy is set to QSizePolicy::Ignore. If
[minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)() is
set, the minimum size hint will be ignored.

**Access functions:**

| virtual QSize | **minimumSizeHint**() const |
| --- | --- |

**See also** [QSize::isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#isValid)(),
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#size-prop)(),
[setMinimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)(),
and [sizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizePolicy-prop)().

Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::mouseDoubleClickEvent([QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive
mouse double click events for the widget.

The default implementation calls
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mousePressEvent)().

**Note:** The widget will also receive mouse press and mouse release events in addition
to the double click event. And if another widget that overlaps this widget disappears in
response to press or release events, then this widget will only receive the double click
event. It is up to the developer to ensure that the application interprets these events
correctly.

**See also**
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mousePressEvent)(),
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(),
[mouseMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseMoveEvent)(),
[event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)(), and
[QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.mouseMoveEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::mouseMoveEvent([QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive
mouse move events for the widget.

If mouse tracking is switched off, mouse move events only occur if a mouse button is
pressed while the mouse is being moved. If mouse tracking is switched on, mouse move
events occur even if no mouse button is pressed.

[QMouseEvent::pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html#pos)() reports
the position of the mouse cursor, relative to this widget. For press and release events,
the position is usually the same as the position of the last mouse move event, but it
might be different if the user's hand shakes. This is a feature of the underlying window
system, not Qt.

If you want to show a tooltip immediately, while the mouse is moving (e.g., to get the
mouse coordinates with
[QMouseEvent::pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html#pos)() and show
them as a tooltip), you must first enable mouse tracking as described above. Then, to
ensure that the tooltip is updated immediately, you must call
[QToolTip::showText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#showText)()
instead of [setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#toolTip-prop)()
in your implementation of mouseMoveEvent().

**See also**
[setMouseTracking](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseTracking-prop)(),
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mousePressEvent)(),
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(),
[mouseDoubleClickEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseDoubleClickEvent)(),
[event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)(),
[QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html), and [Scribble
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-scribble-example.html).

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::mousePressEvent([QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive
mouse press events for the widget.

If you create new widgets in the mousePressEvent() the
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseReleaseEvent)()
may not end up where you expect, depending on the underlying window system (or X11
window manager), the widgets' location and maybe more.

The default implementation implements the closing of popup widgets when you click
outside the window. For other widget types it does nothing.

**See also**
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(),
[mouseDoubleClickEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseDoubleClickEvent)(),

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.nativeEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` bool QWidget::nativeEvent(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*eventType*, void \**message*, long \**result*)

This special event handler can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive native platform
events identified by *eventType* which are passed in the *message* parameter.

In your reimplementation of this function, if you want to stop the event being handled
by Qt, return true and set *result*. The *result* parameter has meaning only on Windows.
If you return false, this native event is passed back to Qt, which translates the event
into a Qt event and sends it to the widget.

**Note:** Events are only delivered to this event handler if the widget has a native
window handle.

**Note:** This function superseedes the event filter functions x11Event(), winEvent()
and macEvent() of Qt 4\.

| Platform | Event Type Identifier | Message Type | Result Type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Windows | "windows\_generic\_MSG" | MSG \* | LRESULT |
| macOS | "NSEvent" | NSEvent \* |  |
| XCB | "xcb\_generic\_event\_t" | xcb\_generic\_event\_t \* |  |

**See also**
[QAbstractNativeEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractnativeeventfilter.html).
signatures: nativeEvent(self, eventType: PySide2.QtCore.QByteArray, message: int) -> typing.Tuple[bool, int]

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.paintEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::paintEvent([QPaintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive paint events passed in
*event*.

A paint event is a request to repaint all or part of a widget. It can happen for one of
the following reasons:

- [repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() or [update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() was invoked,
- the widget was obscured and has now been uncovered, or
- many other reasons.

Many widgets can simply repaint their entire surface when asked to, but some slow
widgets need to optimize by painting only the requested region:
[QPaintEvent::region](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html#region)().
This speed optimization does not change the result, as painting is clipped to that
region during event processing.
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) and
[QTableView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html) do this, for example.

Qt also tries to speed up painting by merging multiple paint events into one. When
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() is called several
times or the window system sends several paint events, Qt merges these events into one
event with a larger region (see
[QRegion::united](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#united)()). The
[repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() function does not
permit this optimization, so we suggest using
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() whenever possible.

When the paint event occurs, the update region has normally been erased, so you are
painting on the widget's background.

The background can be set using
[setBackgroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setBackgroundRole)()
and [setPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#palette-prop)().

Since Qt 4.0, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) automatically
double-buffers its painting, so there is no need to write double-buffering code in
paintEvent() to avoid flicker.

**Note:** Generally, you should refrain from calling
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() or
[repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() **inside** a
paintEvent(). For example, calling
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() or
[repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() on children inside
a paintEvent() results in undefined behavior; the child may or may not get a paint
event.

**Warning:** If you are using a custom paint engine without Qt's backingstore,
[Qt::WA\_PaintOnScreen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
must be set. Otherwise,
[QWidget::paintEngine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEngine)()
will never be called; the backingstore will be used instead.

**See also** [event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)(),
[repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)(),
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)(),
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html),
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html),
[QPaintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintevent.html), and [Analog Clock
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-analogclock-example.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.palette.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### palette : [QPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html)

This property holds the widget's palette

This property describes the widget's palette. The palette is used by the widget's style
when rendering standard components, and is available as a means to ensure that custom
widgets can maintain consistency with the native platform's look and feel. It's common
that different platforms, or different styles, have different palettes.

When you assign a new palette to a widget, the color roles from this palette are
combined with the widget's default palette to form the widget's final palette. The
palette entry for the widget's background role is used to fill the widget's background
(see
[QWidget::autoFillBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#autoFillBackground-prop)),
and the foreground role initializes
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html)'s pen.

The default depends on the system environment.
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html) maintains a
system/theme palette which serves as a default for all widgets. There may also be
special palette defaults for certain types of widgets (e.g., on Windows Vista, all
classes that derive from [QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html)
have a special default palette). You can also define default palettes for widgets
yourself by passing a custom palette and the name of a widget to
[QApplication::setPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setPalette)().
Finally, the style always has the option of polishing the palette as it's assigned (see
[QStyle::polish](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#polish)()).

[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) propagates explicit palette
roles from parent to child. If you assign a brush or color to a specific role on a
palette and assign that palette to a widget, that role will propagate to all the
widget's children, overriding any system defaults for that role. Note that palettes by
default don't propagate to windows (see
[isWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#isWindow)()) unless the
[Qt::WA\_WindowPropagation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute is enabled.

[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html)'s palette propagation is
similar to its font propagation.

The current style, which is used to render the content of all standard Qt widgets, is
free to choose colors and brushes from the widget palette, or in some cases, to ignore
the palette (partially, or completely). In particular, certain styles like GTK style,
Mac style, and Windows Vista style, depend on third party APIs to render the content of
widgets, and these styles typically do not follow the palette. Because of this,
assigning roles to a widget's palette is not guaranteed to change the appearance of the
widget. Instead, you may choose to apply a
[styleSheet](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet.html).

**Warning:** Do not use this function in conjunction with [Qt Style
Sheets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet.html). When using style sheets,
the palette of a widget can be customized using the "color", "background-color",
"selection-color", "selection-background-color" and "alternate-background-color".

Style Sheets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet.html).

### pos : [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html)

This property holds the position of the widget within its parent widget

[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#geometry-prop)() inside
[moveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#moveEvent)() can lead to
infinite recursion.

Qt 5 reference:

### void QWidget::render([QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html#QPaintDevice) \**target*, const [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) \&*targetOffset* \= QPoint(), const [QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) \&*sourceRegion* \= QRegion(), [QWidget::RenderFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#RenderFlag-enum) *renderFlags* \= RenderFlags(DrawWindowBackground \| DrawChildren))

Renders the *sourceRegion* of this widget into the *target* using *renderFlags* to
determine how to render. Rendering starts at *targetOffset* in the *target*. For
example:

```
QPixmap pixmap(widget->size());
widget->render(&pixmap);
```

If *sourceRegion* is a null region, this function will use
[QWidget::rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#rect-prop)() as the
region, i.e. the entire widget.

Ensure that you call
[QPainter::end](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#end)() for the *target*
device's active painter (if any) before rendering. For example:

```
QPainter painter(this);
...
painter.end();
myWidget->render(this);
```

**Note:** To obtain the contents of a
[QOpenGLWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwidget.html), use
[QOpenGLWidget::grabFramebuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwidget.html#grabFramebuffer)()
instead.

**Note:** To obtain the contents of a QGLWidget (deprecated), use
QGLWidget::grabFrameBuffer() or QGLWidget::renderPixmap() instead.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

### void QWidget::render([QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) \**painter*, const [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) \&*targetOffset* \= QPoint(), const [QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) \&*sourceRegion* \= QRegion(), [QWidget::RenderFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#RenderFlag-enum) *renderFlags* \= RenderFlags(DrawWindowBackground \| DrawChildren))

This is an overloaded function.

Renders the widget into the *painter*'s
[QPainter::device](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#device)().

Transformations and settings applied to the *painter* will be used when rendering.

**Note:** The *painter* must be active. On macOS the widget will be rendered into a
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) and then drawn by the
*painter*.

**See also**
[QPainter::device](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#device)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.repaint.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QWidget::repaint()

Repaints the widget directly by calling
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)() immediately,
unless updates are disabled or the widget is hidden.

We suggest only using repaint() if you need an immediate repaint, for example during
animation. In almost all circumstances
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() is better, as it
permits Qt to optimize for speed and minimize flicker.

**Warning:** If you call repaint() in a function which may itself be called from
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)(), you may get
infinite recursion. The
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() function never causes
recursion.

**See also** [update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)(),
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)(), and
[setUpdatesEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#updatesEnabled-prop)().

### void QWidget::repaint(int *x*, int *y*, int *w*, int *h*)

This is an overloaded function.

This version repaints a rectangle (*x*, *y*, *w*, *h*) inside the widget.

If *w* is negative, it is replaced with `width() - x`, and if *h* is negative, it is
replaced width `height() - y`.

### void QWidget::repaint(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rect*)

This is an overloaded function.

This version repaints a rectangle *rect* inside the widget.

### void QWidget::repaint(const [QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) \&*rgn*)

This is an overloaded function.

This version repaints a region *rgn* inside the widget.

### bool QWidget::restoreGeometry(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*geometry*)

Restores the geometry and state of top-level widgets stored in the byte array
*geometry*. Returns `true` on success; otherwise returns `false`.

If the restored geometry is off-screen, it will be modified to be inside the available
screen geometry.

To restore geometry saved using
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html), you can use code like
this:

```
QSettings settings("MyCompany", "MyApp");
myWidget->restoreGeometry(settings.value("myWidget/geometry").toByteArray());
```

See the [Window
Geometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/application-windows.html#window-geometry)
documentation for an overview of geometry issues with windows.

Use
[QMainWindow::restoreState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreState)()
to restore the geometry and the state of toolbars and dock widgets.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[saveGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#saveGeometry)(),
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html),
[QMainWindow::saveState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#saveState)(),
and
[QMainWindow::restoreState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreState)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QWidget::saveGeometry() const

```

}

Qt 5 reference:

### void QWidget::scroll(int *dx*, int *dy*)

Scrolls the widget including its children *dx* pixels to the right and *dy* downward.
Both *dx* and *dy* may be negative.

After scrolling, the widgets will receive paint events for the areas that need to be
repainted. For widgets that Qt knows to be opaque, this is only the newly exposed parts.
For example, if an opaque widget is scrolled 8 pixels to the left, only an 8-pixel wide
stripe at the right edge needs updating.

Since widgets propagate the contents of their parents by default, you need to set the
[autoFillBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#autoFillBackground-prop)
property, or use
[setAttribute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setAttribute)() to set
the
[Qt::WA\_OpaquePaintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute, to make a widget opaque.

For widgets that use contents propagation, a scroll will cause an update of the entire
scroll area.

**See also** [Transparency and Double
Buffering](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#transparency-and-double-buffering).

### void QWidget::scroll(int *dx*, int *dy*, const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*r*)

This is an overloaded function.

This version only scrolls *r* and does not move the children of the widget.

If *r* is empty or invalid, the result is undefined.

**See also** [QScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html).
signatures: scroll(self, dx: int, dy: int) -> None
scroll(self, dx: int, dy: int, arg__3: PySide2.QtCore.QRect) -> None

### void QWidget::setBackgroundRole([QPalette::ColorRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorRole-enum) *role*)

Sets the background role of the widget to *role*.

The background role defines the brush from the widget's
[palette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#palette-prop) that is used to
render the background.

If *role* is
[QPalette::NoRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorRole-enum),
then the widget inherits its parent's background role.

Note that styles are free to choose any color from the palette. You can modify the
palette or set a style sheet if you don't achieve the result you want with
setBackgroundRole().

**See also**
[backgroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#backgroundRole)() and
[foregroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#foregroundRole)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.setFocus.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QWidget::setFocus()

This is an overloaded function.

Gives the keyboard input focus to this widget (or its focus proxy) if this widget or one
of its parents is the [active
window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#isActiveWindow-prop).

### void QWidget::setFocus([Qt::FocusReason](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FocusReason-enum) *reason*)

Gives the keyboard input focus to this widget (or its focus proxy) if this widget or one
of its parents is the [active
window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#isActiveWindow-prop). The
*reason* argument will be passed into any focus event sent from this function, it is
used to give an explanation of what caused the widget to get focus. If the window is not
active, the widget will be given the focus when the window becomes active.

First, a focus about to change event is sent to the focus widget (if any) to tell it
that it is about to lose the focus. Then focus is changed, a focus out event is sent to
the previous focus item and a focus in event is sent to the new item to tell it that it
just received the focus. (Nothing happens if the focus in and focus out widgets are the
same.)

**Note:** On embedded platforms, setFocus() will not cause an input panel to be opened
by the input method. If you want this to happen, you have to send a
[QEvent::RequestSoftwareInputPanel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
event to the widget yourself.

setFocus() gives focus to a widget regardless of its focus policy, but does not clear
any keyboard grab (see
[grabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabKeyboard)()).

Be aware that if the widget is hidden, it will not accept focus until it is shown.

**Warning:** If you call setFocus() in a function which may itself be called from
[focusOutEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusOutEvent)() or
[focusInEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusInEvent)(), you may
get an infinite recursion.

**See also** [hasFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focus-prop)(),
[clearFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#clearFocus)(),
[focusInEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusInEvent)(),
[focusOutEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusOutEvent)(),
[setFocusPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusPolicy-prop)(),
[focusWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusWidget)(),
[QApplication::focusWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#focusWidget)(),
[grabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabKeyboard)(),
[grabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabMouse)(), [Keyboard
Focus in Widgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/focus.html), and
[QEvent::RequestSoftwareInputPanel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).

### void QWidget::setFocusProxy([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**w*)

Sets the widget's focus proxy to widget *w*. If *w* is `nullptr`, the function resets
this widget to have no focus proxy.

Some widgets can "have focus", but create a child widget, such as
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html), to actually handle the
focus. In this case, the widget can set the line edit to be its focus proxy.

setFocusProxy() sets the widget which will actually get focus when "this widget" gets
it. If there is a focus proxy,
[setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setFocus-1)() and
[hasFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focus-prop)() operate on the
focus proxy. If "this widget" is the focus widget, then setFocusProxy() moves focus to
the new focus proxy.

The foreground role defines the color from the widget's

### void QWidget::setGraphicsEffect([QGraphicsEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html) \**effect*)

### void QWidget::setLayout([QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html) \**layout*)

Sets the layout manager for this widget to *layout*.

If there already is a layout manager installed on this widget,
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) won't let you install
another. You must first delete the existing layout manager (returned by
[layout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#layout)()) before you can call
setLayout() with the new layout.

If *layout* is the layout manager on a different widget, setLayout() will reparent the
layout and make it the layout manager for this widget.

Example:

```
    QVBoxLayout *layout = new QVBoxLayout;
    layout->addWidget(formWidget);
    setLayout(layout);
```

An alternative to calling this function is to pass this widget to the layout's
constructor.

The [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) will take ownership of
*layout*.

**See also** [layout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#layout)() and
[Layout Management](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/layout.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.setMask.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QWidget::setMask(const [QBitmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitmap.html) \&*bitmap*)

Causes only the pixels of the widget for which *bitmap* has a corresponding 1 bit to be
visible. If the region includes pixels outside the
[rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#rect-prop)() of the widget,
window system controls in that area may or may not be visible, depending on the
platform.

Note that this effect can be slow if the region is particularly complex.

The following code shows how an image with an alpha channel can be used to generate a
mask for a widget:

```
    QLabel topLevelLabel;
    QPixmap pixmap(":/images/tux.png");
    topLevelLabel.setPixmap(pixmap);
    topLevelLabel.setMask(pixmap.mask());
```

The label shown by this code is masked using the image it contains, giving the
appearance that an irregularly-shaped image is being drawn directly onto the screen.

Masked widgets receive mouse events only on their visible portions.

**See also** [mask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mask)(),
[clearMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#clearMask)(),
[windowOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowOpacity-prop)(),
and [Shaped Clock
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-shapedclock-example.html).

includes pixels outside the
[rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#rect-prop)() of the widget,
window system controls in that area may or may not be visible, depending on the
platform.

Note that this effect can be slow if the region is particularly complex.

**See also**
[windowOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowOpacity-prop).

Qt 5 reference:

### void QWidget::setParent([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**parent*)

Sets the parent of the widget to *parent*, and resets the window flags. The widget is
moved to position (0, 0\) in its new parent.

If the new parent widget is in a different window, the reparented widget and its
children are appended to the end of the [tab
chain](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusPolicy-prop) of the new
parent widget, in the same internal order as before. If one of the moved widgets had
keyboard focus, setParent() calls
[clearFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#clearFocus)() for that
widget.

If the new parent widget is in the same window as the old parent, setting the parent
doesn't change the tab order or keyboard focus.

If the "new" parent widget is the old parent widget, this function does nothing.

**Note:** The widget becomes invisible as part of changing its parent, even if it was
previously visible. You must call
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() to make the widget
visible again.

**Warning:** It is very unlikely that you will ever need this function. If you have a
widget that changes its content dynamically, it is far easier to use
[QStackedWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedwidget.html).

**See also**
[setWindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowFlags-prop)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.setTabOrder.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QWidget::setTabOrder([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**first*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**second*)

Puts the *second* widget after the *first* widget in the focus order.

It effectively removes the *second* widget from its focus chain and inserts it after the
*first* widget.

Note that since the tab order of the *second* widget is changed, you should order a
chain like this:

```
setTabOrder(a, b); // a to b
setTabOrder(b, c); // a to b to c
setTabOrder(c, d); // a to b to c to d
```

*not* like this:

```
// WRONG
setTabOrder(c, d); // c to d
setTabOrder(a, b); // a to b AND c to d
setTabOrder(b, c); // a to b to c, but not c to d
```

If *first* or *second* has a focus proxy, setTabOrder() correctly substitutes the proxy.

**Note:** Since Qt 5.10: A widget that has a child as focus proxy is understood as a
compound widget. When setting a tab order between one or two compound widgets, the local
tab order inside each will be preserved. This means that if both widgets are compound
widgets, the resulting tab order will be from the last child inside *first*, to the
first child inside *second*.

**See also**
[setFocusPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusPolicy-prop)(),
[setFocusProxy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setFocusProxy)(), and
[Keyboard Focus in Widgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/focus.html).

Qt 5 reference:

### void QWidget::setWindowState([Qt::WindowStates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum) *windowState*)

Sets the window state to *windowState*. The window state is a OR'ed combination of
[Qt::WindowState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum):
[Qt::WindowMinimized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum),
[Qt::WindowMaximized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum),
[Qt::WindowFullScreen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum), and
[Qt::WindowActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum).

If the window is not visible (i.e.
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)() returns
`false`), the window state will take effect when
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() is called. For visible
windows, the change is immediate. For example, to toggle between full-screen and normal
mode, use the following code:

```
w->setWindowState(w->windowState() ^ Qt::WindowFullScreen);
```

In order to restore and activate a minimized window (while preserving its maximized
and/or full-screen state), use the following:

```
w->setWindowState((w->windowState() & ~Qt::WindowMinimized) | Qt::WindowActive);
```

Calling this function will hide the widget. You must call
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() to make the widget
visible again.

**Note:** On some window systems
[Qt::WindowActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum) is not
immediate, and may be ignored in certain cases.

When the window state changes, the widget receives a
[changeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#changeEvent)() of type
[QEvent::WindowStateChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).

**See also**
[Qt::WindowState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum) and
[windowState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowState)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.showEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::showEvent([QShowEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshowevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive widget show events
which are passed in the *event* parameter.

Non-spontaneous show events are sent to widgets immediately before they are shown. The
spontaneous show events of windows are delivered afterwards.

Note: A widget receives spontaneous show and hide events when its mapping status is
changed by the window system, e.g. a spontaneous hide event when the user minimizes the
window, and a spontaneous show event when the window is restored again. After receiving
a spontaneous hide event, a widget is still considered visible in the sense of
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)().

**See also** [visible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop),
[event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)(), and
[QShowEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshowevent.html).

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.showFullScreen.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QWidget::showFullScreen()

Shows the widget in full-screen mode.

Calling this function only affects
[windows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#isWindow).

To return from full-screen mode, call
[showNormal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#showNormal)() or
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#close)().

**Note:** Full-screen mode works fine under Windows, but has certain problems under X.
These problems are due to limitations of the ICCCM protocol that specifies the
communication between X11 clients and the window manager. ICCCM simply does not
understand the concept of non-decorated full-screen windows. Therefore, the best we can
do is to request a borderless window and place and resize it to fill the entire screen.
Depending on the window manager, this may or may not work. The borderless window is
requested using MOTIF hints, which are at least partially supported by virtually all
modern window managers.

An alternative would be to bypass the window manager entirely and create a window with
the
[Qt::X11BypassWindowManagerHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum)
flag. This has other severe problems though, like totally broken keyboard focus and very
strange effects on desktop changes or when the user raises other windows.

X11 window managers that follow modern post-ICCCM specifications support full-screen
mode properly.

On macOS, showing a window full screen puts the entire application in full-screen mode,
providing it with a dedicated desktop. Showing another window while the application runs
in full-screen mode might automatically make that window full screen as well. To prevent
that, exit full-screen mode by calling
[showNormal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#showNormal)() or by
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#close)() on the full screen
window before showing another window.

**See also** [showNormal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#showNormal)(),
[showMaximized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#showMaximized)(),
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(),
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop)(), and
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#close)().

### size : [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html)

This property holds the size of the widget excluding any window frame

If the widget is visible when it is being resized, it receives a resize event
([resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#resizeEvent)())
immediately. If the widget is not currently visible, it is guaranteed to receive an
event before it is shown.

The size is adjusted if it lies outside the range defined by
[minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)() and
[maximumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#maximumSize-prop)().

By default, this property contains a value that depends on the user's platform and
screen geometry.

**Warning:** Calling resize() or
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#geometry-prop)() inside
[resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#resizeEvent)() can lead to
infinite recursion.

**Note:** Setting the size to `QSize(0, 0)` will cause the widget to not appear on
screen. This also applies to windows.

Qt 5 reference:

### sizeIncrement : [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html)

This property holds the size increment of the widget

When the user resizes the window, the size will move in steps of
sizeIncrement().[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#width-prop)()
pixels horizontally and
sizeIncrement.[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#height-prop)()
pixels vertically, with
[baseSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#baseSize-prop)() as the
basis. Preferred widget sizes are for non-negative integers *i* and *j*:

```
width = baseSize().width() + i * sizeIncrement().width();
height = baseSize().height() + j * sizeIncrement().height();
```

Note that while you can set the size increment for all widgets, it only affects windows.

By default, this property contains a size with zero width and height.

**Warning:** The size increment has no effect under Windows, and may be disregarded by
the window manager on X11.

**Access functions:**

| QSize | **sizeIncrement**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setSizeIncrement**(*const QSize \&*) |
| void | **[setSizeIncrement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setSizeIncrement-1)**(int *w*, int *h*) |

**See also** [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#size-prop),
[minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop), and
[maximumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#maximumSize-prop).

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.sizePolicy.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### sizePolicy : [QSizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html)

This property holds the default layout behavior of the widget

If there is a [QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html) that manages
this widget's children, the size policy specified by that layout is used. If there is no
such [QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html), the result of this
function is used.

The default policy is Preferred/Preferred, which means that the widget can be freely
resized, but prefers to be the size
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop)() returns.
Button-like widgets set the size policy to specify that they may stretch horizontally,
but are fixed vertically. The same applies to lineedit controls (such as
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html),
[QSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html) or an editable
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html)) and other horizontally
orientated widgets (such as
[QProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html)).
[QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html)'s are normally
square, so they allow growth in both directions. Widgets that support different
directions (such as [QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html),
[QScrollBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollbar.html) or QHeader) specify
stretching in the respective direction only. Widgets that can provide scroll bars
(usually subclasses of
[QScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html)) tend to specify that
they can use additional space, and that they can make do with less than
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop)().

**Access functions:**

| QSizePolicy | **sizePolicy**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setSizePolicy**(*QSizePolicy*) |
| void | **[setSizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setSizePolicy-1)**(QSizePolicy::Policy *horizontal*, QSizePolicy::Policy *vertical*) |

**See also**
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop)(),
[QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html),
[QSizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html), and
[updateGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#updateGeometry)().

### `[virtual protected]` void QWidget::tabletEvent([QTabletEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabletevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented in a subclass to receive
tablet events for the widget.

If you reimplement this handler, it is very important that you
[ignore()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html) the event if you do not
handle it, so that the widget's parent can interpret it.

The default implementation ignores the event.

If tablet tracking is switched off, tablet move events only occur if the stylus is in
contact with the tablet, or at least one stylus button is pressed, while the stylus is
being moved. If tablet tracking is switched on, tablet move events occur even while the
stylus is hovering in proximity of the tablet, with no buttons pressed.

**See also** [QEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)(),

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.update.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QWidget::update()

Updates the widget unless updates are disabled or the widget is hidden.

This function does not cause an immediate repaint; instead it schedules a paint event
for processing when Qt returns to the main event loop. This permits Qt to optimize for
more speed and less flicker than a call to
[repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() does.

Calling update() several times normally results in just one
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)() call.

Qt normally erases the widget's area before the
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)() call. If the
[Qt::WA\_OpaquePaintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
widget attribute is set, the widget is responsible for painting all its pixels with an
opaque color.

**See also** [repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)(),
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)(),
[setUpdatesEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#updatesEnabled-prop)(),
and [Analog Clock
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-analogclock-example.html).

### void QWidget::update(int *x*, int *y*, int *w*, int *h*)

This is an overloaded function.

This version updates a rectangle (*x*, *y*, *w*, *h*) inside the widget.

### void QWidget::update(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rect*)

This is an overloaded function.

This version updates a rectangle *rect* inside the widget.

### void QWidget::update(const [QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) \&*rgn*)

This is an overloaded function.

This version repaints a region *rgn* inside the widget.
signatures: update(self, x: int, y: int, w: int, h: int) -> None

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.updatesEnabled.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### updatesEnabled : bool

This property holds whether updates are enabled

An updates enabled widget receives paint events and has a system background; a disabled
widget does not. This also implies that calling
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() and
[repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() has no effect if
updates are disabled.

By default, this property is `true`.

setUpdatesEnabled() is normally used to disable updates for a short period of time, for
instance to avoid screen flicker during large changes. In Qt, widgets normally do not
generate screen flicker, but on X11 the server might erase regions on the screen when
widgets get hidden before they can be replaced by other widgets. Disabling updates
solves this.

Example:

```
setUpdatesEnabled(false);
bigVisualChanges();
setUpdatesEnabled(true);
```

Disabling a widget implicitly disables all its children. Enabling a widget enables all
child widgets *except* top-level widgets or those that have been explicitly disabled.
Re-enabling updates implicitly calls
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() on the widget.

**Access functions:**

| bool | **updatesEnabled**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setUpdatesEnabled**(bool *enable*) |

**See also** [paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)().

PythonQt.Qt.QWidget.visible.doc:

### visible : bool

This property holds whether the widget is visible

Calling setVisible(true) or
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)() sets the widget to
visible status if all its parent widgets up to the window are visible. If an ancestor is
not visible, the widget won't become visible until all its ancestors are shown. If its
size or position has changed, Qt guarantees that a widget gets move and resize events
just before it is shown. If the widget has not been resized yet, Qt will adjust the
widget's size to a useful default using
[adjustSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#adjustSize)().

Calling setVisible(false) or
[hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)() hides a widget
explicitly. An explicitly hidden widget will never become visible, even if all its
ancestors become visible, unless you show it.

A widget receives show and hide events when its visibility status changes. Between a
hide and a show event, there is no need to waste CPU cycles preparing or displaying
information to the user. A video application, for example, might simply stop generating
new frames.

A widget that happens to be obscured by other windows on the screen is considered to be
visible. The same applies to iconified windows and windows that exist on another virtual
desktop (on platforms that support this concept). A widget receives spontaneous show and
hide events when its mapping status is changed by the window system, e.g. a spontaneous
hide event when the user minimizes the window, and a spontaneous show event when the
window is restored again.

You almost never have to reimplement the setVisible() function. If you need to change
some settings before a widget is shown, use
[showEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#showEvent)() instead. If you
need to do some delayed initialization use the Polish event delivered to the
[event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)() function.

### windowModified : bool

This property holds whether the document shown in the window has unsaved changes

A modified window is a window whose content has changed but has not been saved to disk.
This flag will have different effects varied by the platform. On macOS the close button
will have a modified look; on other platforms, the window title will have an '\*'
(asterisk).

The window title must contain a "\[\*\]" placeholder, which indicates where the '\*'
should appear. Normally, it should appear right after the file name (e.g.,
"document1.txt\[\*\] \- Text Editor"). If the window isn't modified, the placeholder is
simply removed.

Note that if a widget is set as modified, all its ancestors will also be set as
modified. However, if you call `setWindowModified(false)` on a widget, this will not
propagate to its parent because other children of the parent might have been modified.

### windowOpacity : double

This property holds the level of opacity for the window.

The valid range of opacity is from 1.0 (completely opaque) to 0.0 (completely
transparent).

By default the value of this property is 1.0.

This feature is available on Embedded Linux, macOS, Windows, and X11 platforms that
support the Composite extension.

**Note:** On X11 you need to have a composite manager running, and the X11 specific
\_NET\_WM\_WINDOW\_OPACITY atom needs to be supported by the window manager you are
using.

**Warning:** Changing this property from opaque to transparent might issue a paint event
that needs to be processed before the window is displayed correctly. This affects mainly
the use of
[QScreen::grabWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#grabWindow)().
Also note that semi-transparent windows update and resize significantly slower than
opaque windows.

PythonQt.Qt.QWidgetAction.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Most actions in an application are represented as items in menus or buttons in toolbars.
However sometimes more complex widgets are necessary. For example a zoom action in a
word processor may be realized using a
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html) in a
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html), presenting a range of
different zoom levels. [QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html)
provides
[QToolBar::insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#insertWidget)()
as convenience function for inserting a single widget. However if you want to implement
an action that uses custom widgets for visualization in multiple containers then you
have to subclass QWidgetAction.

If a QWidgetAction is added for example to a
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) then
[QWidgetAction::createWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html#createWidget)()
is called. Reimplementations of that function should create a new custom widget with the
specified parent.

If the action is removed from a container widget then
[QWidgetAction::deleteWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html#deleteWidget)()
is called with the previously created custom widget as argument. The default
implementation hides the widget and deletes it using
[QObject::deleteLater](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#deleteLater)().

If you have only one single custom widget then you can set it as default widget using
[setDefaultWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html#setDefaultWidget)().
That widget will then be used if the action is added to a
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html), or in general to an action
container that supports QWidgetAction. If a QWidgetAction with only a default widget is
added to two toolbars at the same time then the default widget is shown only in the
first toolbar the action was added to. QWidgetAction takes over ownership of the default
widget.

Note that it is up to the widget to activate the action, for example by reimplementing
mouse event handlers and calling
[QAction::trigger](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#trigger)().

**macOS**: If you add a widget to a menu in the application's menu bar on macOS, the
widget will be added and it will function but with some limitations:

1. The widget is reparented away from the [QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) to the native menu view. If you show the menu in some other place (e.g. as a popup menu), the widget will not be there.
2. Focus/Keyboard handling of the widget is not possible.
3. Due to Apple's design, mouse tracking on the widget currently does not work.
4. Connecting the [triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#triggered)() signal to a slot that opens a modal dialog will cause a crash in macOS 10.4 (known bug acknowledged by Apple), a workaround is to use a QueuedConnection instead of a DirectConnection.

PythonQt.Qt.QWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A window that is supplied a parent becomes a native child window of their parent window.

An application will typically use
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) or
[QQuickView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquickview.html) for its UI, and not
QWindow directly. Still, it is possible to render directly to a QWindow with
[QBackingStore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbackingstore.html) or
[QOpenGLContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglcontext.html), when wanting
to keep dependencies to a minimum or when wanting to use OpenGL directly. The [Raster
Window Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-rasterwindow-example.html) and
[OpenGL Window
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-openglwindow-example.html) are useful
reference examples for how to render to a QWindow using either approach.

### Resource Management

Windows can potentially use a lot of memory. A usual measurement is width times height
times color depth. A window might also include multiple buffers to support double and
triple buffering, as well as depth and stencil buffers. To release a window's memory
resources, call the [destroy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#destroy)()
function.

### Content Orientation

QWindow has
[reportContentOrientationChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#contentOrientation-prop)()
that can be used to specify the layout of the window contents in relation to the screen.
The content orientation is simply a hint to the windowing system about which orientation
the window contents are in. It's useful when you wish to keep the same window size, but
rotate the contents instead, especially when doing rotation animations between different
orientations. The windowing system might use this value to determine the layout of
system popups or dialogs.

### Visibility and Windowing System Exposure

By default, the window is not visible, and you must call
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#visible-prop)(true), or
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#show)() or similar to make it
visible. To make a window hidden again, call
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#visible-prop)(false) or
[hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#hide)(). The visible property
describes the state the application wants the window to be in. Depending on the
underlying system, a visible window might still not be shown on the screen. It could,
for instance, be covered by other opaque windows or moved outside the physical area of
the screen. On windowing systems that have exposure notifications, the
[isExposed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#isExposed)() accessor
describes whether the window should be treated as directly visible on screen. The
[exposeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#exposeEvent)() function is
called whenever an area of the window is invalidated, for example due to the exposure in
the windowing system changing. On windowing systems that do not make this information
visible to the application,
[isExposed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#isExposed)() will simply
return the same value as
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#visible-prop)().

[QWindow::Visibility](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#Visibility-enum)
queried through
[visibility](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#visibility-prop)() is a
convenience API combining the functions of visible() and
[windowStates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#windowStates)().

### Rendering

There are two Qt APIs that can be used to render content into a window,
[QBackingStore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbackingstore.html) for rendering
with a [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) and flushing the
contents to a window with type
[QSurface::RasterSurface](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsurface.html#SurfaceType-enum),
and [QOpenGLContext](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglcontext.html) for
rendering with OpenGL to a window with type
[QSurface::OpenGLSurface](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsurface.html#SurfaceType-enum).

The application can start rendering as soon as
[isExposed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#isExposed)() returns `true`,
and can keep rendering until it
[isExposed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#isExposed)() returns
`false`. To find out when
[isExposed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#isExposed)() changes,
reimplement
[exposeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#exposeEvent)(). The window
will always get a resize event before the first expose event.

### Initial Geometry

If the window's width and height are left uninitialized, the window will get a
reasonable default geometry from the platform window. If the position is left
uninitialized, then the platform window will allow the windowing system to position the
window. For example on X11, the window manager usually does some kind of smart
positioning to try to avoid having new windows completely obscure existing windows.
However [setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#setGeometry)()
initializes both the position and the size, so if you want a fixed size but an automatic
position, you should call
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#resize)() or
[setWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#width-prop)() and
[setHeight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#height-prop)() instead.

Qt 5 reference:

### `[slot]` void QWindow::alert(int *msec*)

Causes an alert to be shown for *msec* miliseconds. If *msec* is `0` (the default), then
the alert is shown indefinitely until the window becomes active again. This function has
no effect on an active window.

In alert state, the window indicates that it demands attention, for example by flashing
or bouncing the taskbar entry.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.1.

### `[slot]` bool QWindow::close()

Close the window.

This closes the window, effectively calling
[destroy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#destroy)(), and potentially
quitting the application. Returns `true` on success, false if it has a parent window (in
which case the top level window should be closed instead).

**See also** [destroy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#destroy)() and
[QGuiApplication::quitOnLastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#quitOnLastWindowClosed-prop)().

Qt 5 reference:

### contentOrientation : [Qt::ScreenOrientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScreenOrientation-enum)

This property holds the orientation of the window's contents

This is a hint to the window manager in case it needs to display additional content like
popups, dialogs, status bars, or similar in relation to the window.

The recommended orientation is
[QScreen::orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#orientation-prop)()
but an application doesn't have to support all possible orientations, and thus can opt
to ignore the current screen orientation.

The difference between the window and the content orientation determines how much to
rotate the content by.
[QScreen::angleBetween](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#angleBetween)(),
[QScreen::transformBetween](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#transformBetween)(),
and [QScreen::mapBetween](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#mapBetween)()
can be used to compute the necessary transform.

The default value is
[Qt::PrimaryOrientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScreenOrientation-enum)

**Access functions:**

| --- | --- |
| void | **reportContentOrientationChange**(Qt::ScreenOrientation *orientation*) |

**Notifier signal:**

| void | **contentOrientationChanged**(Qt::ScreenOrientation *orientation*) |
| --- | --- |

### void QWindow::create()

Allocates the platform resources associated with the window.

It is at this point that the surface format set using
[setFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#setFormat)() gets resolved
into an actual native surface. However, the window remains hidden until
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#visible-prop)() is called.

Note that it is not usually necessary to call this function directly, as it will be
implicitly called by [show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#show)(),
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#visible-prop)(), and other
functions that require access to the platform resources.

Call [destroy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#destroy)() to free the
platform resources if necessary.

**See also** [destroy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#destroy)().
