## Detailed Description

QXmlSerializer translates an [XQuery
sequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractxmlreceiver.html#xquery-sequence),
usually the output of an [QXmlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html),
into XML. Consider the example:

```
QXmlQuery query;
query.setQuery("doc('index.html')/html/body/p[1]");

QXmlSerializer serializer(query, myOutputDevice);
query.evaluateTo(&serializer);
```

First it constructs a [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html) that
gets the first paragraph from document `index.html`. Then it constructs an instance of
this class with the [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html) and
[myOutputDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). Finally, it
[evaluates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html#evaluateTo) the
[query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html), producing an ordered
sequence of calls to the serializer's callback functions. The sequence of callbacks
transforms the query output to XML and writes it to
[myOutputDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

QXmlSerializer will:

- Declare namespaces when needed,
- Use appropriate escaping, when characters can't be represented in the XML,
- Handle line endings appropriately,
- Report errors, when it can't serialize the content, e.g., when asked to serialize an attribute that is a top-level node, or when more than one top-level element is encountered.

If an error occurs during serialization, result is undefined unless the serializer is
driven through a call to
[QXmlQuery::evaluateTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlquery.html#evaluateTo)().

If the generated XML should be indented and formatted for reading, use
[QXmlFormatter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qxmlformatter.html).

PythonQt.QtCore.QAbstractAnimation.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The class defines the functions for the functionality shared by all animations. By
inheriting this class, you can create custom animations that plug into the rest of the
animation framework.

The progress of an animation is given by its current time
([currentLoopTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#currentLoopTime)()),
which is measured in milliseconds from the start of the animation (0) to its end
([duration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#duration)()). The
value is updated automatically while the animation is running. It can also be set
directly with
[setCurrentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#currentTime-prop)().

At any point an animation is in one of three states:
[Running](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#State-enum),
[Stopped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#State-enum), or
[Paused](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#State-enum)--as
defined by the
[State](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#State-enum) enum. The
current state can be changed by calling
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#start)(),
[stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#stop)(),
[pause](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#pause)(), or
[resume](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#resume)(). An
animation will always reset its [current
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#currentTime-prop) when
it is started. If paused, it will continue with the same current time when resumed. When
an animation is stopped, it cannot be resumed, but will keep its current time (until
started again). QAbstractAnimation will emit
[stateChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#stateChanged)()
whenever its state changes.

An animation can loop any number of times by setting the
[loopCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#loopCount-prop)
property. When an animation's current time reaches its
[duration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#duration)(), it
will reset the current time and keep running. A loop count of 1 (the default value)
means that the animation will run one time. Note that a duration of -1 means that the
animation will run until stopped; the current time will increase indefinitely. When the
current time equals
[duration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#duration)() and
the animation is in its final loop, the
[Stopped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#State-enum) state
is entered, and the
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#finished)() signal
is emitted.

QAbstractAnimation provides pure virtual functions used by subclasses to track the
progress of the animation:
[duration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#duration)() and
[updateCurrentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#updateCurrentTime)().
The [duration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#duration)()
function lets you report a duration for the animation (as discussed above). The
animation framework calls
[updateCurrentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#updateCurrentTime)()
when current time has changed. By reimplementing this function, you can track the
animation progress. Note that neither the interval between calls nor the number of calls
to this function are defined; though, it will normally be 60 updates per second.

By reimplementing
[updateState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#updateState)(),
you can track the animation's state changes, which is particularly useful for animations
that are not driven by time.

### `[pure virtual]` int QAbstractAnimation::duration() const

This pure virtual function returns the duration of the animation, and defines for how
long [QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html)
should update the current time. This duration is local, and does not include the loop
count.

A return value of -1 indicates that the animation has no defined duration; the animation
should run forever until stopped. This is useful for animations that are not time
driven, or where you cannot easily predict its duration (e.g., event driven audio
playback in a game).

If the animation is a parallel
[QAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html), the duration
will be the longest duration of all its animations. If the animation is a sequential
[QAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html), the duration
will be the sum of the duration of all its animations.

**Note:** Getter function for property duration.

**See also**
[loopCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#loopCount-prop).

### `[slot]` void QAbstractAnimation::start([QAbstractAnimation::DeletionPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#DeletionPolicy-enum) *policy* \= KeepWhenStopped)

Starts the animation. The *policy* argument says whether or not the animation should be
deleted when it's done. When the animation starts, the
[stateChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#stateChanged)()
signal is emitted, and
[state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#state-prop)() returns
Running. When control reaches the event loop, the animation will run by itself,
periodically calling
[updateCurrentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#updateCurrentTime)()
as the animation progresses.

If the animation is currently stopped or has already reached the end, calling start()
will rewind the animation and start again from the beginning. When the animation reaches
the end, the animation will either stop, or if the loop level is more than 1, it will
rewind and continue from the beginning.

If the animation is already running, this function does nothing.

**See also** [stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#stop)()
and [state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#state-prop)().

## Detailed Description

The QAbstractItemModel class defines the standard interface that item models must use to
be able to interoperate with other components in the model/view architecture. It is not
supposed to be instantiated directly. Instead, you should subclass it to create new
models.

The QAbstractItemModel class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html). It can be
used as the underlying data model for the item view elements in QML or the item view
classes in the Qt Widgets module.

If you need a model to use with an item view such as QML's List View element or the
C\+\+ widgets [QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) or
[QTableView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html), you should consider
subclassing
[QAbstractListModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractlistmodel.html) or
[QAbstractTableModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttablemodel.html)
instead of this class.

The underlying data model is exposed to views and delegates as a hierarchy of tables. If
you do not make use of the hierarchy, then the model is a simple table of rows and
columns. Each item has a unique index specified by a
[QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html).

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/modelindex-no-parent.png)

Every item of data that can be accessed via a model has an associated model index. You
can obtain this model index using the
[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#index)() function.
Each index may have a
[sibling](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#sibling)() index;
child items have a
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#parent)() index.

Each item has a number of data elements associated with it and they can be retrieved by
specifying a role (see
[Qt::ItemDataRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum)) to the
model's [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#data)()
function. Data for all available roles can be obtained at the same time using the
[itemData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#itemData)()
function.

Data for each role is set using a particular
[Qt::ItemDataRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum). Data
for individual roles are set individually with
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setData)(), or they
can be set for all roles with
[setItemData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setItemData)().

Items can be queried with
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#flags)() (see
[Qt::ItemFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum)) to see if they
can be selected, dragged, or manipulated in other ways.

If an item has child objects,
[hasChildren](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#hasChildren)()
returns `true` for the corresponding index.

The model has a
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)() and a
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnCount)()
for each level of the hierarchy. Rows and columns can be inserted and removed with
[insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)(),
[insertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertColumns)(),
[removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRows)(),
and
[removeColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeColumns)().

The model emits signals to indicate changes. For example,
[dataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#dataChanged)()
is emitted whenever items of data made available by the model are changed. Changes to
the headers supplied by the model cause
[headerDataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#headerDataChanged)()
to be emitted. If the structure of the underlying data changes, the model can emit
[layoutChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#layoutChanged)()
to indicate to any attached views that they should redisplay any items shown, taking the
new structure into account.

The items available through the model can be searched for particular data using the
[match](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#match)() function.

To sort the model, you can use
[sort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#sort)().

### Subclassing

**Note:** Some general guidelines for subclassing models are available in the [Model
Subclassing
Reference](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-subclassing-reference).

When subclassing QAbstractItemModel, at the very least you must implement
[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#index)(),
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#parent)(),
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)(),
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnCount)(),
and [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#data)(). These
functions are used in all read-only models, and form the basis of editable models.

You can also reimplement
[hasChildren](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#hasChildren)()
to provide special behavior for models where the implementation of
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)() is
expensive. This makes it possible for models to restrict the amount of data requested by
views, and can be used as a way to implement lazy population of model data.

To enable editing in your model, you must also implement
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setData)(), and
reimplement [flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#flags)()
to ensure that `ItemIsEditable` is returned. You can also reimplement
[headerData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#headerData)()
and
[setHeaderData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setHeaderData)()
to control the way the headers for your model are presented.

The
[dataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#dataChanged)()
and
[headerDataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#headerDataChanged)()
signals must be emitted explicitly when reimplementing the
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setData)() and
[setHeaderData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setHeaderData)()
functions, respectively.

Custom models need to create model indexes for other components to use. To do this, call
[createIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#createIndex)()
with suitable row and column numbers for the item, and an identifier for it, either as a
pointer or as an integer value. The combination of these values must be unique for each
item. Custom models typically use these unique identifiers in other reimplemented
functions to retrieve item data and access information about the item's parents and
children. See the [Simple Tree Model
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-itemviews-simpletreemodel-example.html)
for more information about unique identifiers.

It is not necessary to support every role defined in
[Qt::ItemDataRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum).
Depending on the type of data contained within a model, it may only be useful to
implement the [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#data)()
function to return valid information for some of the more common roles. Most models
provide at least a textual representation of item data for the
[Qt::DisplayRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum), and
well-behaved models should also provide valid information for the
[Qt::ToolTipRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) and
[Qt::WhatsThisRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum).
Supporting these roles enables models to be used with standard Qt views. However, for
some models that handle highly-specialized data, it may be appropriate to provide data
only for user-defined roles.

Models that provide interfaces to resizable data structures can provide implementations
of
[insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)(),
[removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRows)(),
[insertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertColumns)(),and
[removeColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeColumns)().
When implementing these functions, it is important to notify any connected views about
changes to the model's dimensions both *before* and *after* they occur:

- An [insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)() implementation must call [beginInsertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginInsertRows)() *before* inserting new rows into the data structure, and [endInsertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endInsertRows)() *immediately afterwards*.
- An [insertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertColumns)() implementation must call [beginInsertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginInsertColumns)() *before* inserting new columns into the data structure, and [endInsertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endInsertColumns)() *immediately afterwards*.
- A [removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRows)() implementation must call [beginRemoveRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginRemoveRows)() *before* the rows are removed from the data structure, and [endRemoveRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endRemoveRows)() *immediately afterwards*.
- A [removeColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeColumns)() implementation must call [beginRemoveColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginRemoveColumns)() *before* the columns are removed from the data structure, and [endRemoveColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endRemoveColumns)() *immediately afterwards*.

The *private* signals that these functions emit give attached components the chance to
take action before any data becomes unavailable. The encapsulation of the insert and
remove operations with these begin and end functions also enables the model to manage
[persistent model
indexes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpersistentmodelindex.html) correctly. **If
you want selections to be handled properly, you must ensure that you call these
functions.** If you insert or remove an item with children, you do not need to call
these functions for the child items. In other words, the parent item will take care of
its child items.

To create models that populate incrementally, you can reimplement
[fetchMore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#fetchMore)() and
[canFetchMore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#canFetchMore)().
If the reimplementation of
[fetchMore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#fetchMore)() adds
rows to the model,
[beginInsertRows()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginInsertRows)
and
[endInsertRows()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endInsertRows)
must be called.

### `[protected]` void QAbstractItemModel::beginInsertColumns(const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*parent*, int *first*, int *last*)

Begins a column insertion operation.

When reimplementing
[insertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertColumns)()
in a subclass, you must call this function *before* inserting data into the model's
underlying data store.

The *parent* index corresponds to the parent into which the new columns are inserted;
*first* and *last* are the column numbers of the new columns will have after they have
been inserted.

| Inserting columns | Specify the first and last column numbers for the span of columns you want to insert into an item in a model. For example, as shown in the diagram, we insert three columns before column 4, so *first* is 4 and *last* is 6:  ``` beginInsertColumns(parent, 4, 6); ```  This inserts the three new columns as columns 4, 5, and 6\. |
| --- | --- |
| Appending columns | To append columns, insert them after the last column. For example, as shown in the diagram, we append three columns to a collection of six existing columns (ending in column 5), so *first* is 6 and *last* is 8:  ``` beginInsertColumns(parent, 6, 8); ```  This appends the two new columns as columns 6, 7, and 8\. |

**Note:** This function emits the
[columnsAboutToBeInserted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnsAboutToBeInserted)()
signal which connected views (or proxies) must handle before the data is inserted.
Otherwise, the views may end up in an invalid state.

**See also**
[endInsertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endInsertColumns)().

### `[protected]` bool QAbstractItemModel::beginMoveColumns(const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*sourceParent*, int *sourceFirst*, int *sourceLast*, const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*destinationParent*, int *destinationChild*)

Begins a column move operation.

When reimplementing a subclass, this method simplifies moving entities in your model.
This method is responsible for moving persistent indexes in the model, which you would
otherwise be required to do yourself. Using beginMoveColumns and
[endMoveColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endMoveColumns)
is an alternative to emitting
[layoutAboutToBeChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#layoutAboutToBeChanged)
and
[layoutChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#layoutChanged)
directly along with
[changePersistentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#changePersistentIndex).

The *sourceParent* index corresponds to the parent from which the columns are moved;
*sourceFirst* and *sourceLast* are the first and last column numbers of the columns to
be moved. The *destinationParent* index corresponds to the parent into which those
columns are moved. The *destinationChild* is the column to which the columns will be
moved. That is, the index at column *sourceFirst* in *sourceParent* will become column
*destinationChild* in *destinationParent*, followed by all other columns up to
*sourceLast*.

However, when moving columns down in the same parent (*sourceParent* and
*destinationParent* are equal), the columns will be placed before the *destinationChild*
index. That is, if you wish to move columns 0 and 1 so they will become columns 1 and 2,
*destinationChild* should be 3\. In this case, the new index for the source column `i`
(which is between *sourceFirst* and *sourceLast*) is equal to
`(destinationChild-sourceLast-1+i)`.

Note that if *sourceParent* and *destinationParent* are the same, you must ensure that
the *destinationChild* is not within the range of *sourceFirst* and *sourceLast* \+ 1\.
You must also ensure that you do not attempt to move a column to one of its own children
or ancestors. This method returns `false` if either condition is true, in which case you
should abort your move operation.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[endMoveColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endMoveColumns)().
signatures: beginMoveColumns(self, sourceParent: PySide2.QtCore.QModelIndex, sourceFirst: int, sourceLast: int, destinationParent: PySide2.QtCore.QModelIndex, destinationColumn: int) -> bool

*destinationParent*, followed by all other rows up to *sourceLast*.

However, when moving rows down in the same parent (*sourceParent* and
*destinationParent* are equal), the rows will be placed before the *destinationChild*
index. That is, if you wish to move rows 0 and 1 so they will become rows 1 and 2,
*destinationChild* should be 3\. In this case, the new index for the source row `i`
(which is between *sourceFirst* and *sourceLast*) is equal to
`(destinationChild-sourceLast-1+i)`.

Note that if *sourceParent* and *destinationParent* are the same, you must ensure that
the *destinationChild* is not within the range of *sourceFirst* and *sourceLast* \+ 1\.
You must also ensure that you do not attempt to move a row to one of its own children or
ancestors. This method returns `false` if either condition is true, in which case you
should abort your move operation.

| Moving rows to another parent | Specify the first and last row numbers for the span of rows in the source parent you want to move in the model. Also specify the row in the destination parent to move the span to. For example, as shown in the diagram, we move three rows from row 2 to 4 in the source, so *sourceFirst* is 2 and *sourceLast* is 4\. We move those items to above row 2 in the destination, so *destinationChild* is 2\.  ``` beginMoveRows(sourceParent, 2, 4, destinationParent, 2); ```  This moves the three rows rows 2, 3, and 4 in the source to become 2, 3 and 4 in the destination. Other affected siblings are displaced accordingly. |
| --- | --- |
| Moving rows to append to another parent | To append rows to another parent, move them to after the last row. For example, as shown in the diagram, we move three rows to a collection of 6 existing rows (ending in row 5), so *destinationChild* is 6:  ``` beginMoveRows(sourceParent, 2, 4, destinationParent, 6); ```  This moves the target rows to the end of the target parent as 6, 7 and 8\. |
| Moving rows in the same parent up | To move rows within the same parent, specify the row to move them to. For example, as shown in the diagram, we move one item from row 2 to row 0, so *sourceFirst* and *sourceLast* are 2 and *destinationChild* is 0\.  ``` beginMoveRows(parent, 2, 2, parent, 0); ```  Note that other rows may be displaced accordingly. Note also that when moving items within the same parent you should not attempt invalid or no-op moves. In the above example, item 2 is at row 2 before the move, so it cannot be moved to row 2 (where it is already) or row 3 (no-op as row 3 means above row 3, where it is already) |
| Moving rows in the same parent down | To move rows within the same parent, specify the row to move them to. For example, as shown in the diagram, we move one item from row 2 to row 4, so *sourceFirst* and *sourceLast* are 2 and *destinationChild* is 4\.  ``` beginMoveRows(parent, 2, 2, parent, 4); ```  Note that other rows may be displaced accordingly. |

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[endMoveRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endMoveRows)().
signatures: beginMoveRows(self, sourceParent: PySide2.QtCore.QModelIndex, sourceFirst: int, sourceLast: int, destinationParent: PySide2.QtCore.QModelIndex, destinationRow: int) -> bool

### `[protected]` void QAbstractItemModel::beginResetModel()

Begins a model reset operation.

A reset operation resets the model to its current state in any attached views.

**Note:** Any views attached to this model will be reset as well.

When a model is reset it means that any previous data reported from the model is now
invalid and has to be queried for again. This also means that the current item and any
selected items will become invalid.

When a model radically changes its data it can sometimes be easier to just call this
function rather than emit
[dataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#dataChanged)()
to inform other components when the underlying data source, or its structure, has
changed.

You must call this function before resetting any internal data structures in your model
or proxy model.

This function emits the signal
[modelAboutToBeReset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#modelAboutToBeReset)().

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[modelAboutToBeReset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#modelAboutToBeReset)(),
[modelReset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#modelReset)(),
and

### `[virtual]` bool QAbstractItemModel::dropMimeData(const [QMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html) \**data*, [Qt::DropAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DropAction-enum) *action*, int *row*, int *column*, const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*parent*)

Handles the *data* supplied by a drag and drop operation that ended with the given
*action*.

Returns `true` if the data and action were handled by the model; otherwise returns
`false`.

The specified *row*, *column* and *parent* indicate the location of an item in the model
where the operation ended. It is the responsibility of the model to complete the action
at the correct location.

For instance, a drop action on an item in a
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) can result in new items
either being inserted as children of the item specified by *row*, *column*, and
*parent*, or as siblings of the item.

When *row* and *column* are -1 it means that the dropped data should be considered as
dropped directly on *parent*. Usually this will mean appending the data as child items
of *parent*. If *row* and *column* are greater than or equal zero, it means that the
drop occurred just before the specified *row* and *column* in the specified *parent*.

The [mimeTypes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#mimeTypes)()
member is called to get the list of acceptable MIME types. This default implementation
assumes the default implementation of
[mimeTypes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#mimeTypes)(),
which returns a single default MIME type. If you reimplement
[mimeTypes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#mimeTypes)() in
your custom model to return multiple MIME types, you must reimplement this function to
make use of them.

**See also**
[supportedDropActions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#supportedDropActions)(),
[canDropMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#canDropMimeData)(),
and [Using drag and drop with item

### `[virtual]` bool QAbstractItemModel::insertColumns(int *column*, int *count*, const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*parent* \= QModelIndex())

On models that support this, inserts *count* new columns into the model before the given
*column*. The items in each new column will be children of the item represented by the
*parent* model index.

If *column* is 0, the columns are prepended to any existing columns.

If *column* is
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnCount)(),
the columns are appended to any existing columns.

If *parent* has no children, a single row with *count* columns is inserted.

Returns `true` if the columns were successfully inserted; otherwise returns `false`.

The base class implementation does nothing and returns `false`.

If you implement your own model, you can reimplement this function if you want to
support insertions. Alternatively, you can provide your own API for altering the data.

**See also**
[insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)(),
[removeColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeColumns)(),

### `[signal]` void QAbstractItemModel::layoutAboutToBeChanged(const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QPersistentModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpersistentmodelindex.html)\> \&*parents* \= QList\<QPersistentModelIndex\>(), [QAbstractItemModel::LayoutChangeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#LayoutChangeHint-enum) *hint* \= QAbstractItemModel::NoLayoutChangeHint)

This signal is emitted just before the layout of a model is changed. Components
connected to this signal use it to adapt to changes in the model's layout.

Subclasses should update any persistent model indexes after emitting

The optional *parents* parameter is used to give a more specific notification about what
parts of the layout of the model are changing. An empty list indicates a change to the
layout of the entire model. The order of elements in the *parents* list is not

happening while the model is relayouting.

### `[signal]` void QAbstractItemModel::layoutChanged(const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QPersistentModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpersistentmodelindex.html)\> \&*parents* \= QList\<QPersistentModelIndex\>(), [QAbstractItemModel::LayoutChangeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#LayoutChangeHint-enum) *hint* \= QAbstractItemModel::NoLayoutChangeHint)

This signal is emitted whenever the layout of items exposed by the model has changed;
for example, when the model has been sorted. When this signal is received by a view, it
should update the layout of items to reflect this change.

When subclassing
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) or
[QAbstractProxyModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractproxymodel.html),
ensure that you emit
[layoutAboutToBeChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#layoutAboutToBeChanged)()
before changing the order of items or altering the structure of the data you expose to
views, and emit layoutChanged() after changing the layout.

The optional *parents* parameter is used to give a more specific notification about what
parts of the layout of the model are changing. An empty list indicates a change to the
layout of the entire model. The order of elements in the *parents* list is not
significant. The optional *hint* parameter is used to give a hint about what is
happening while the model is relayouting.

Subclasses should update any persistent model indexes before emitting layoutChanged().
In other words, when the structure changes:

- emit [layoutAboutToBeChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#layoutAboutToBeChanged)
- Remember the [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) that will change
- Update your internal data
- Call [changePersistentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#changePersistentIndex)()
- emit layoutChanged

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also**
[layoutAboutToBeChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#layoutAboutToBeChanged)(),
[dataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#dataChanged)(),
[headerDataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#headerDataChanged)(),

and

### `[virtual]` [QModelIndexList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#QModelIndexList-typedef) QAbstractItemModel::match(const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*start*, int *role*, const [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) \&*value*, int *hits* \= 1, [Qt::MatchFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#MatchFlag-enum) *flags* \= Qt::MatchFlags(Qt::MatchStartsWith\|Qt::MatchWrap)) const

Returns a list of indexes for the items in the column of the *start* index where data
stored under the given *role* matches the specified *value*. The way the search is
performed is defined by the *flags* given. The list that is returned may be empty. Note
also that the order of results in the list may not correspond to the order in the model,
if for example a proxy model is used. The order of the results cannot be relied upon.

The search begins from the *start* index, and continues until the number of matching
data items equals *hits*, the search reaches the last row, or the search reaches *start*
again \- depending on whether `MatchWrap` is specified in *flags*. If you want to search
for all matching items, use *hits* \= -1.

By default, this function will perform a wrapping, string-based comparison on all items,
searching for items that begin with the search term specified by *value*.

**Note:** The default implementation of this function only searches columns. Reimplement
this function to include a different search behavior.

**Note:** This function can be invoked via the meta-object system and from QML. See
[Q\_INVOKABLE](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_INVOKABLE).

### `[signal]` void QAbstractItemModel::modelReset()

This signal is emitted when
[endResetModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endResetModel)()

[QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) member functions,
such as
[QModelIndex::parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#parent)(),
since indexes belonging to your model will simply call your implementation, leading to
infinite recursion.

[Q\_INVOKABLE](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_INVOKABLE).

PythonQt.QtCore.QAbstractListModel.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QAbstractListModel provides a standard interface for models that represent their data as
a simple non-hierarchical sequence of items. It is not used directly, but must be
subclassed.

Since the model provides a more specialized interface than
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html), it is
not suitable for use with tree views; you will need to subclass
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) if you
want to provide a model for that purpose. If you need to use a number of list models to
manage data, it may be more appropriate to subclass
[QAbstractTableModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttablemodel.html)
instead.

Simple models can be created by subclassing this class and implementing the minimum
number of required functions. For example, we could implement a simple read-only
[QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html)-based model that
provides a list of strings to a
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) widget. In such a case,
we only need to implement the
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)()
function to return the number of items in the list, and the
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#data)() function to
retrieve items from the list.

Since the model represents a one-dimensional structure, the
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)()
function returns the total number of items in the model. The
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnCount)()
function is implemented for interoperability with all kinds of views, but by default
informs views that the model contains only one column.

### Subclassing

When subclassing QAbstractListModel, you must provide implementations of the
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)() and
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#data)() functions.
Well behaved models also provide a
[headerData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#headerData)()
implementation.

If your model is used within QML and requires roles other than the default ones provided
by the
[roleNames](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#roleNames)()
function, you must override it.

For editable list models, you must also provide an implementation of
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setData)(), and
implement the
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractlistmodel.html#flags)() function so
that it returns a value containing
[Qt::ItemIsEditable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum).

Note that QAbstractListModel provides a default implementation of
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnCount)()
that informs views that there is only a single column of items in this model.

Models that provide interfaces to resizable list-like data structures can provide
implementations of
[insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)()
and
[removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRows)().
When implementing these functions, it is important to call the appropriate functions so
that all connected views are aware of any changes:

- An [insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)() implementation must call [beginInsertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginInsertRows)() *before* inserting new rows into the data structure, and it must call [endInsertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endInsertRows)() *immediately afterwards*.
- A [removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRows)() implementation must call [beginRemoveRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginRemoveRows)() *before* the rows are removed from the data structure, and it must call [endRemoveRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endRemoveRows)() *immediately afterwards*.

**Note:** Some general guidelines for subclassing models are available in the [Model
Subclassing
Reference](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-subclassing-reference).

PythonQt.QtCore.QAbstractProxyModel.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class defines the standard interface that proxy models must use to be able to
interoperate correctly with other model/view components. It is not supposed to be
instantiated directly.

All standard proxy models are derived from the QAbstractProxyModel class. If you need to
create a new proxy model class, it is usually better to subclass an existing class that
provides the closest behavior to the one you want to provide.

Proxy models that filter or sort items of data from a source model should be created by
using or subclassing
[QSortFilterProxyModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsortfilterproxymodel.html).

To subclass QAbstractProxyModel, you need to implement
[mapFromSource](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractproxymodel.html#mapFromSource)()
and
[mapToSource](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractproxymodel.html#mapToSource)().
The
[mapSelectionFromSource](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractproxymodel.html#mapSelectionFromSource)()
and
[mapSelectionToSource](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractproxymodel.html#mapSelectionToSource)()
functions only need to be reimplemented if you need a behavior different from the
default behavior.

**Note:** If the source model is deleted or no source model is specified, the proxy
model operates on a empty placeholder model.

## Detailed Description

The QAbstractState class is the abstract base class of states that are part of a
[QStateMachine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html). It defines the
interface that all state objects have in common. QAbstractState is part of [The State
Machine Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html).

The [entered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html#entered)() signal
is emitted when the state has been entered. The
[exited](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html#exited)() signal is
emitted when the state has been exited.

The [parentState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html#parentState)()
function returns the state's parent state. The
[machine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html#machine)() function
returns the state machine that the state is part of.

### Subclassing

The [onEntry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html#onEntry)() function
is called when the state is entered; reimplement this function to perform custom
processing when the state is entered.

The [onExit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html#onExit)() function
is called when the state is exited; reimplement this function to perform custom
processing when the state is exited.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QAbstractTransition class is the abstract base class of transitions between states
([QAbstractState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html) objects) of a
[QStateMachine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html).
QAbstractTransition is part of [The State Machine
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html).

The
[sourceState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#sourceState)()
function returns the source of the transition. The
[targetStates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#targetStates)()
function returns the targets of the transition. The
[machine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#machine)()
function returns the state machine that the transition is part of.

The [triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#triggered)()
signal is emitted when the transition has been triggered.

Transitions can cause animations to be played. Use the
[addAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#addAnimation)()
function to add an animation to the transition.

### Subclassing

The [eventTest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#eventTest)()
function is called by the state machine to determine whether an event should trigger the
transition. In your reimplementation you typically check the event type and cast the
event object to the proper type, and check that one or more properties of the event meet
your criteria.

The
[onTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#onTransition)()
function is called when the transition is triggered; reimplement this function to
perform custom processing for the transition.

### transitionType : [TransitionType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html#TransitionType-enum)

whose source state is a compound state and whose target(s) is a descendant of the
source. In such a case, an internal transition will not exit and re-enter its source
state, while an external one will.

PythonQt.QtCore.QAnimationGroup.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

An animation group is a container for animations (subclasses of
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html)). A
group is usually responsible for managing the
[state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#State-enum) of its
animations, i.e., it decides when to start, stop, resume, and pause them. Currently, Qt
provides two such groups:
[QParallelAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qparallelanimationgroup.html)
and
[QSequentialAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsequentialanimationgroup.html).
Look up their class descriptions for details.

Since QAnimationGroup inherits from
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html), you
can combine groups, and easily construct complex animation graphs. You can query
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html) for the
group it belongs to (using the
[group()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#group) function).

To start a top-level animation group, you simply use the
[start()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#start) function
from [QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html).
By a top-level animation group, we think of a group that itself is not contained within
another group. Starting sub groups directly is not supported, and may lead to unexpected
behavior.

QAnimationGroup provides methods for adding and retrieving animations. Besides that, you
can remove animations by calling
[removeAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html#removeAnimation)(),
and clear the animation group by calling
[clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html#clear)(). You may keep
track of changes in the group's animations by listening to
[QEvent::ChildAdded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[QEvent::ChildRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events.

QAnimationGroup takes ownership of the animations it manages, and ensures that they are
deleted when the animation group is deleted.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This is a fast, lightweight, and low-level class used by Qt internally. We recommend
using the higher-level [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) class
rather than this class if you want to use timers in your applications. Note that this
timer is a repeating timer that will send subsequent timer events unless the
[stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#stop)() function is called.

To use this class, create a QBasicTimer, and call its
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#start)() function with a
timeout interval and with a pointer to a
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass. When the timer
times out it will send a timer event to the
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass. The timer can be
stopped at any time using
[stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#stop)().
[isActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#isActive)() returns
`true` for a timer that is running; i.e. it has been started, has not reached the
timeout time, and has not been stopped. The timer's ID can be retrieved using
[timerId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html#timerId)().

Objects of this class cannot be copied, but can be moved, so you can maintain a list of
basic timers by holding them in container that supports move-only types, e.g.
std::vector.

The [Wiggly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-wiggly-example.html)
example uses QBasicTimer to repaint a widget at regular intervals.

PythonQt.QtCore.QBitArray.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QBitArray is an array that gives access to individual bits and provides operators
([AND](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-and),
[OR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7c),
[XOR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-5e), and
[NOT](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7e)) that work on
entire arrays of bits. It uses [implicit
sharing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) (copy-on-write) to
reduce memory usage and to avoid the needless copying of data.

The following code constructs a QBitArray containing 200 bits initialized to false (0):

```
QBitArray ba(200);
```

To initialize the bits to true, either pass `true` as second argument to the
constructor, or call [fill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#fill)()
later on.

QBitArray uses 0-based indexes, just like C\+\+ arrays. To access the bit at a
particular index position, you can use operator\[\](). On non-const bit arrays,
operator\[\]() returns a reference to a bit that can be used on the left side of an
assignment. For example:

```
QBitArray ba;
ba.resize(3);
ba[0] = true;
ba[1] = false;
ba[2] = true;
```

For technical reasons, it is more efficient to use
[testBit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#testBit)() and
[setBit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#setBit)() to access bits in
the array than operator\[\](). For example:

```
QBitArray ba(3);
ba.setBit(0, true);
ba.setBit(1, false);
ba.setBit(2, true);
```

QBitArray supports `&`
([AND](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-and)), `|`
([OR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7c)), `^`
([XOR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-5e)), `~`
([NOT](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#operator-7e)), as well as `&=`,
`|=`, and `^=`. These operators work in the same way as the built-in C\+\+ bitwise
operators of the same name. For example:

```
QBitArray x(5);
x.setBit(3, true);
// x: [ 0, 0, 0, 1, 0 ]

QBitArray y(5);
y.setBit(4, true);
// y: [ 0, 0, 0, 0, 1 ]

x |= y;
// x: [ 0, 0, 0, 1, 1 ]
```

For historical reasons, QBitArray distinguishes between a null bit array and an empty
bit array. A *null* bit array is a bit array that is initialized using QBitArray's
default constructor. An *empty* bit array is any bit array with size 0\. A null bit
array is always empty, but an empty bit array isn't necessarily null:

```
QBitArray().isNull();           // returns true
QBitArray().isEmpty();          // returns true

QBitArray(0).isNull();          // returns false
QBitArray(0).isEmpty();         // returns true

QBitArray(3).isNull();          // returns false
QBitArray(3).isEmpty();         // returns false
```

All functions except
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#isNull)() treat null bit
arrays the same as empty bit arrays; for example, QBitArray() compares equal to
QBitArray(0). We recommend that you always use
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#isEmpty)() and avoid
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#isNull)().

### bool QBitArray::fill(bool *value*, int *size* \= -1)

Sets every bit in the bit array to *value*, returning true if successful; otherwise
returns `false`. If *size* is different from -1 (the default), the bit array is resized
to *size* beforehand.

Example:

```
QBitArray ba(8);
ba.fill(true);
// ba: [ 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 ]

ba.fill(false, 2);
// ba: [ 0, 0 ]
```

**See also** [resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#resize)().

### void QBitArray::fill(bool *value*, int *begin*, int *end*)

This is an overloaded function.

Sets bits at index positions *begin* up to (but not including) *end* to *value*.

*begin* must be a valid index position in the bit array (0 \<\= *begin* \<
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#size)()).

*end* must be either a valid index position or equal to
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#size)(), in which case the fill
operation runs until the end of the array (0 \<\= *end* \<\=
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbitarray.html#size)()).

Example:

```
QBitArray ba(4);
ba.fill(true, 1, 2);            // ba: [ 0, 1, 0, 0 ]
ba.fill(true, 1, 3);            // ba: [ 0, 1, 1, 0 ]
ba.fill(true, 1, 4);            // ba: [ 0, 1, 1, 1 ]
```

PythonQt.QtCore.QBuffer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QBuffer allows you to access a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) using the
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) interface. The
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) is treated just as a
standard random-accessed file. Example:

```
    QBuffer buffer;
    char ch;

    buffer.open(QBuffer::ReadWrite);
    buffer.write("Qt rocks!");
    buffer.seek(0);
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == 'Q'
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == 't'
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == ' '
    buffer.getChar(&ch);  // ch == 'r'
```

By default, an internal [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)
buffer is created for you when you create a QBuffer. You can access this buffer directly
by calling [buffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#buffer)(). You can
also use QBuffer with an existing
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) by calling
[setBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#setBuffer)(), or by passing
your array to QBuffer's constructor.

Call [open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#open)() to open the buffer.
Then call [write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)() to write to the
buffer, and [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(),
[readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readAll)(), or
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)() to read from it.
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#size)() returns the current size
of the buffer, and you can seek to arbitrary positions in the buffer by calling
[seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#seek)(). When you are done with
accessing the buffer, call
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#close)().

The following code snippet shows how to write data to a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) using
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) and QBuffer:

```
    QByteArray byteArray;
    QBuffer buffer(&byteArray);
    buffer.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly);

    QDataStream out(&buffer);
    out << QApplication::palette();
```

Effectively, we convert the application's
[QPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html) into a byte array. Here's
how to read the data from the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html):

```
    QPalette palette;
    QBuffer buffer(&byteArray);
    buffer.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly);

    QDataStream in(&buffer);
    in >> palette;
```

[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) and
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) also provide
convenience constructors that take a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) and that create a
QBuffer behind the scenes.

QBuffer emits [readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)()
when new data has arrived in the buffer. By connecting to this signal, you can use
QBuffer to store temporary data before processing it. QBuffer also emits
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() every
time new data has been written to the buffer.

PythonQt.QtCore.QBuffer.setBuffer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QBuffer::setBuffer([QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \**byteArray*)

Makes [QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) use the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) pointed to by
*byteArray* as its internal buffer. The caller is responsible for ensuring that
*byteArray* remains valid until the
[QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) is destroyed, or until
setBuffer() is called to change the buffer.
[QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) doesn't take ownership of the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html).

Does nothing if [isOpen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isOpen)() is
true.

If you open the buffer in write-only mode or read-write mode and write something into
the [QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html), *byteArray* will be
modified.

Example:

```
    QByteArray byteArray("abc");
    QBuffer buffer;
    buffer.setBuffer(&byteArray);
    buffer.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly);
    buffer.seek(3);
    buffer.write("def", 3);
    buffer.close();
    // byteArray == "abcdef"
```

If *byteArray* is `nullptr`, the buffer creates its own internal
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) to work on. This byte
array is initially empty.

**See also** [buffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#buffer)(),
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#setData)(), and
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html#open)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QByteArray.doc: Qt 5 reference: ## Detailed Description QByteArray can be used to store both raw bytes (including '\\0's) and traditional 8-bit '\\0'-terminated strings. Using QByteArray is much more convenient than using `const char *`. Behind the scenes, it always ensures that the data is followed by a '\\0' terminator, and uses [implicit sharing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) (copy-on-write) to reduce memory usage and avoid needless copying of data. In addition to QByteArray, Qt also provides the [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) class to store string data. For most purposes, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) is the class you want to use. It stores 16-bit Unicode characters, making it easy to store non-ASCII/non-Latin-1 characters in your application. Furthermore, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) is used throughout in the Qt API. The two main cases where QByteArray is appropriate are when you need to store raw binary data, and when memory conservation is critical (e.g., with Qt for Embedded Linux). One way to initialize a QByteArray is simply to pass a `const char *` to its constructor. For example, the following code creates a byte array of size 5 containing the data "Hello": ``` QByteArray ba("Hello"); ``` Although the [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() is 5, the byte array also maintains an extra '\\0' character at the end so that if a function is used that asks for a pointer to the underlying data (e.g. a call to [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)()), the data pointed to is guaranteed to be '\\0'-terminated. QByteArray makes a deep copy of the `const char *` data, so you can modify it later without experiencing side effects. (If for performance reasons you don't want to take a deep copy of the character data, use [QByteArray::fromRawData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromRawData)() instead.) Another approach is to set the size of the array using [resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)() and to initialize the data byte per byte. QByteArray uses 0-based indexes, just like C\+\+ arrays. To access the byte at a particular index position, you can use operator\[\](). On non-const byte arrays, operator\[\]() returns a reference to a byte that can be used on the left side of an assignment. For example: ``` QByteArray ba; ba.resize(5); ba[0] = 0x3c; ba[1] = 0xb8; ba[2] = 0x64; ba[3] = 0x18; ba[4] = 0xca; ``` For read-only access, an alternative syntax is to use [at](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#at)(): ``` for (int i = 0; i < ba.size(); ++i) { if (ba.at(i) >= 'a' && ba.at(i) <= 'f') cout << "Found character in range [a-f]" << Qt::endl; } ``` [at](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#at)() can be faster than operator\[\](), because it never causes a [deep copy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html#deep-copy) to occur. To extract many bytes at a time, use [left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#left)(), [right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#right)(), or [mid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#mid)(). A QByteArray can embed '\\0' bytes. The [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() function always returns the size of the whole array, including embedded '\\0' bytes, but excluding the terminating '\\0' added by QByteArray. For example: ``` QByteArray ba1("ca\0r\0t"); ba1.size(); // Returns 2. ba1.constData(); // Returns "ca" with terminating \0. QByteArray ba2("ca\0r\0t", 3); ba2.size(); // Returns 3. ba2.constData(); // Returns "ca\0" with terminating \0. QByteArray ba3("ca\0r\0t", 4); ba3.size(); // Returns 4. ba3.constData(); // Returns "ca\0r" with terminating \0. const char cart[] = {'c', 'a', '\0', 'r', '\0', 't'}; QByteArray ba4(QByteArray::fromRawData(cart, 6)); ba4.size(); // Returns 6. ba4.constData(); // Returns "ca\0r\0t" without terminating \0. ``` If you want to obtain the length of the data up to and excluding the first '\\0' character, call [qstrlen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#qstrlen)() on the byte array. After a call to [resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)(), newly allocated bytes have undefined values. To set all the bytes to a particular value, call [fill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fill)(). To obtain a pointer to the actual character data, call [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)() or [constData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#constData)(). These functions return a pointer to the beginning of the data. The pointer is guaranteed to remain valid until a non-const function is called on the QByteArray. It is also guaranteed that the data ends with a '\\0' byte unless the QByteArray was created from a [raw data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromRawData). This '\\0' byte is automatically provided by QByteArray and is not counted in [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)(). QByteArray provides the following basic functions for modifying the byte data: [append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#append)(), [prepend](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#prepend)(), [insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#insert)(), [replace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#replace)(), and [remove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#remove)(). For example: ``` QByteArray x("and"); x.prepend("rock "); // x == "rock and" x.append(" roll"); // x == "rock and roll" x.replace(5, 3, "&"); // x == "rock & roll" ``` The [replace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#replace)() and [remove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#remove)() functions' first two arguments are the position from which to start erasing and the number of bytes that should be erased. When you [append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#append)() data to a non-empty array, the array will be reallocated and the new data copied to it. You can avoid this behavior by calling [reserve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#reserve)(), which preallocates a certain amount of memory. You can also call [capacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#capacity)() to find out how much memory QByteArray actually allocated. Data appended to an empty array is not copied. A frequent requirement is to remove whitespace characters from a byte array ('\\n', '\\t', ' ', etc.). If you want to remove whitespace from both ends of a QByteArray, use [trimmed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#trimmed)(). If you want to remove whitespace from both ends and replace multiple consecutive whitespaces with a single space character within the byte array, use [simplified](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#simplified)(). If you want to find all occurrences of a particular character or substring in a QByteArray, use [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)() or [lastIndexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#lastIndexOf)(). The former searches forward starting from a given index position, the latter searches backward. Both return the index position of the character or substring if they find it; otherwise, they return -1. For example, here's a typical loop that finds all occurrences of a particular substring: ``` QByteArray ba("We must be bold, very bold"); int j = 0; while ((j = ba.indexOf("", j)) != -1) { cout << "Found tag at index position " << j << Qt::endl; ++j; } ``` If you simply want to check whether a QByteArray contains a particular character or substring, use [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(). If you want to find out how many times a particular character or substring occurs in the byte array, use [count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#count-3)(). If you want to replace all occurrences of a particular value with another, use one of the two-parameter [replace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#replace)() overloads. [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)s can be compared using overloaded operators such as operator\<(), operator\<\=(), operator\=\=(), operator\>\=(), and so on. The comparison is based exclusively on the numeric values of the characters and is very fast, but is not what a human would expect. [QString::localeAwareCompare](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#localeAwareCompare)() is a better choice for sorting user-interface strings. For historical reasons, QByteArray distinguishes between a null byte array and an empty byte array. A *null* byte array is a byte array that is initialized using QByteArray's default constructor or by passing (const char \*)0 to the constructor. An *empty* byte array is any byte array with size 0\. A null byte array is always empty, but an empty byte array isn't necessarily null: ``` QByteArray().isNull(); // returns true QByteArray().isEmpty(); // returns true QByteArray("").isNull(); // returns false QByteArray("").isEmpty(); // returns true QByteArray("abc").isNull(); // returns false QByteArray("abc").isEmpty(); // returns false ``` All functions except [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isNull)() treat null byte arrays the same as empty byte arrays. For example, [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)() returns a valid pointer (*not* nullptr) to a '\\0' character for a byte array and QByteArray() compares equal to QByteArray(""). We recommend that you always use [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)() and avoid [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isNull)(). ### Maximum size and out-of-memory conditions The current version of QByteArray is limited to just under 2 GB (2^31 bytes) in size. The exact value is architecture-dependent, since it depends on the overhead required for managing the data block, but is no more than 32 bytes. Raw data blocks are also limited by the use of `int` type in the current version to 2 GB minus 1 byte. In case memory allocation fails, QByteArray will throw a `std::bad_alloc` exception. Out of memory conditions in the Qt containers are the only case where Qt will throw exceptions. Note that the operating system may impose further limits on applications holding a lot of allocated memory, especially large, contiguous blocks. Such considerations, the configuration of such behavior or any mitigation are outside the scope of the QByteArray API. ### Notes on Locale #### Number-String Conversions Functions that perform conversions between numeric data types and strings are performed in the C locale, irrespective of the user's locale settings. Use [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) to perform locale-aware conversions between numbers and strings. #### 8-bit Character Comparisons In QByteArray, the notion of uppercase and lowercase and of which character is greater than or less than another character is done in the Latin-1 locale. This affects functions that support a case insensitive option or that compare or lowercase or uppercase their arguments. Case insensitive operations and comparisons will be accurate if both strings contain only Latin-1 characters. Functions that this affects include [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(), [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)(), [lastIndexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#lastIndexOf)(), operator\<(), operator\<\=(), operator\>(), operator\>\=(), [isLower](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isLower)(), [isUpper](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isUpper)(), [toLower](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toLower)() and [toUpper](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toUpper)(). This issue does not apply to [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)s since they represent characters using Unicode.

PythonQt.QtCore.QByteArray.append.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*)

Appends the byte array *ba* onto the end of this byte array.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("free");
QByteArray y("dom");
x.append(y);
// x == "freedom"
```

This is the same as
insert([size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)(), *ba*).

Note: [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) is an [implicitly
shared](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) class. Consequently,
if you append to an empty byte array, then the byte array will just share the data held
in *ba*. In this case, no copying of data is done, taking [constant
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#constant-time). If a shared
instance is modified, it will be copied (copy-on-write), taking [linear
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

If the byte array being appended to is not empty, a deep copy of the data is performed,
taking [linear time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

This operation typically does not suffer from allocation overhead, because
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) preallocates extra
space at the end of the data so that it may grow without reallocating for each append
operation.

**See also**
[operator\+\=](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#operator-2b-eq)(),
[prepend](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#prepend)(), and
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#insert)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(char *ch*)

Appends the character *ch* to this byte array.

This is an overloaded function.

Appends *count* copies of character *ch* to this byte array and returns a reference to
this byte array.

If *count* is negative or zero nothing is appended to the byte array.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.7.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(const char \**str*)

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::append(const char \**str*, int *len*)

This function overloads append().

Appends the first *len* characters of the string *str* to this byte array and returns a
reference to this byte array.

If *len* is negative, the length of the string will be determined automatically using
[qstrlen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#qstrlen)(). If *len* is
zero or *str* is null, nothing is appended to the byte array. Ensure that *len* is *not*
longer than *str*.

Qt 5 reference: ### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::fromBase64(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*base64*, [QByteArray::Base64Options](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#Base64Option-enum) *options*) This is an overloaded function. Returns a decoded copy of the Base64 array *base64*, using the options defined by *options*. If *options* contains `IgnoreBase64DecodingErrors` (the default), the input is not checked for validity; invalid characters in the input are skipped, enabling the decoding process to continue with subsequent characters. If *options* contains `AbortOnBase64DecodingErrors`, then decoding will stop at the first invalid character. For example: ``` QByteArray::fromBase64("PHA+SGVsbG8/PC9wPg==", QByteArray::Base64Encoding); // returns "

Hello?

" QByteArray::fromBase64("PHA-SGVsbG8_PC9wPg==", QByteArray::Base64UrlEncoding); // returns "

Hello?

" ``` The algorithm used to decode Base64-encoded data is defined in [RFC 4648](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4648.txt). Returns the decoded data, or, if the `AbortOnBase64DecodingErrors` option was passed and the input data was invalid, an empty byte array. **Note:** The [fromBase64Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromBase64Encoding)() function is recommended in new code. This function was introduced in Qt 5.2. **See also** [toBase64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toBase64)() and [fromBase64Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromBase64Encoding)(). ### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::fromBase64(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*base64*) This is an overloaded function. Returns a decoded copy of the Base64 array *base64*. Input is not checked for validity; invalid characters in the input are skipped, enabling the decoding process to continue with subsequent characters. For example: ``` QByteArray text = QByteArray::fromBase64("UXQgaXMgZ3JlYXQh"); text.data(); // returns "Qt is great!" ``` The algorithm used to decode Base64-encoded data is defined in [RFC 4648](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4648.txt). **Note:** The [fromBase64Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromBase64Encoding)() function is recommended in new code. **See also** [toBase64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toBase64)() and [fromBase64Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromBase64Encoding)().

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::fromPercentEncoding(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*input*, char *percent* \= '%')

Returns a decoded copy of the URI/URL-style percent-encoded *input*. The *percent*
parameter allows you to replace the '%' character for another (for instance, '\_' or
'\=').

For example:

```
QByteArray text = QByteArray::fromPercentEncoding("Qt%20is%20great%33");
text.data();            // returns "Qt is great!"
```

**Note:** Given invalid input (such as a string containing the sequence "%G5", which is
not a valid hexadecimal number) the output will be invalid as well. As an example: the
sequence "%G5" could be decoded to 'W'.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

[QUrl::fromPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromPercentEncoding)().
