### int QByteArray::indexOf(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*, int *from* \= 0\) const

Returns the index position of the first occurrence of the byte array *ba* in this byte
array, searching forward from index position *from*. Returns -1 if *ba* could not be
found.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("sticky question");
QByteArray y("sti");
x.indexOf(y);               // returns 0
x.indexOf(y, 1);            // returns 10
x.indexOf(y, 10);           // returns 10
x.indexOf(y, 11);           // returns -1
```

**See also**
[lastIndexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#lastIndexOf)(),
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(), and
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#count-3)().

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the index position of the first occurrence of the character *ch* in the byte
array, searching forward from index position *from*. Returns -1 if *ch* could not be
found.

Example:

```

ba.indexOf("B");            // returns 1
ba.indexOf("B", 1);         // returns 1
ba.indexOf("B", 2);         // returns 3
ba.indexOf("X");            // returns -1

### bool QByteArray::isEmpty() const

Returns `true` if the byte array has size 0; otherwise returns `false`.

Example:

```
QByteArray().isEmpty();         // returns true
QByteArray("").isEmpty();       // returns true
QByteArray("abc").isEmpty();    // returns false
```

PythonQt.QtCore.QByteArray.isNull.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QByteArray::isNull() const

Returns `true` if this byte array is null; otherwise returns `false`.

Example:

```
QByteArray().isNull();          // returns true
QByteArray("").isNull();        // returns false
QByteArray("abc").isNull();     // returns false
```

Qt makes a distinction between null byte arrays and empty byte arrays for historical
reasons. For most applications, what matters is whether or not a byte array contains any
data, and this can be determined using
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)().

**See also** [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)().

### int QByteArray::lastIndexOf(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*, int *from* \= -1) const

Returns the index position of the last occurrence of the byte array *ba* in this byte
array, searching backward from index position *from*. If *from* is -1 (the default), the
search starts at the last byte. Returns -1 if *ba* could not be found.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("crazy azimuths");
QByteArray y("az");
x.lastIndexOf(y);           // returns 6
x.lastIndexOf(y, 6);        // returns 6
x.lastIndexOf(y, 5);        // returns 2
x.lastIndexOf(y, 1);        // returns -1
```

**See also** [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)(),
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#contains)(), and
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#count-3)().

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the index position of the last occurrence of character *ch* in the byte array,
searching backward from index position *from*. If *from* is -1 (the default), the search
starts at the last ([size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() \-
1\) byte. Returns -1 if *ch* could not be found.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("ABCBA");
ba.lastIndexOf("B");        // returns 3
ba.lastIndexOf("B", 3);     // returns 3
ba.lastIndexOf("B", 2);     // returns 1
ba.lastIndexOf("X");        // returns -1
```

**See also** [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)() and

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::leftJustified(int *width*, char *fill* \= ' ', bool *truncate* \= false) const

If *truncate* is false and the
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#size)() of the byte array is

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::number(int *n*, int *base* \= 10\)

Returns a byte array containing the string equivalent of the number *n* to base *base*
(10 by default). The *base* can be any value between 2 and 36\.

Example:

```
int n = 63;
QByteArray::number(n);              // returns "63"
QByteArray::number(n, 16);          // returns "3f"
QByteArray::number(n, 16).toUpper();  // returns "3F"
```

**Note:** The format of the number is not localized; the default C locale is used
irrespective of the user's locale.

**See also** [setNum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#setNum)() and
[toInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toInt)().

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::number(double *n*, char *f* \= 'g', int *prec* \= 6\)

This is an overloaded function.

Returns a byte array that contains the printed value of *n*, formatted in format *f*
with precision *prec*.

Argument *n* is formatted according to the *f* format specified, which is `g` by
default, and can be any of the following:

| Format | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `e` | format as \[-\]9.9e\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `E` | format as \[-\]9.9E\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `f` | format as \[-\]9.9 |
| `g` | use `e` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |
| `G` | use `E` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |

With 'e', 'E', and 'f', *prec* is the number of digits after the decimal point. With 'g'
and 'G', *prec* is the maximum number of significant digits (trailing zeroes are
omitted).

```
QByteArray ba = QByteArray::number(12.3456, 'E', 3);
// ba == 1.235E+01
```

**Note:** The format of the number is not localized; the default C locale is used
irrespective of the user's locale.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::prepend(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*ba*)

Prepends the byte array *ba* to this byte array and returns a reference to this byte
array.

Example:

```
QByteArray x("ship");
QByteArray y("air");
x.prepend(y);
// x == "airship"
```

This is the same as insert(0, *ba*).

Note: [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) is an [implicitly
shared](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) class. Consequently,
if you prepend to an empty byte array, then the byte array will just share the data held
in *ba*. In this case, no copying of data is done, taking [constant
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#constant-time). If a shared
instance is modified, it will be copied (copy-on-write), taking [linear
time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

If the byte array being prepended to is not empty, a deep copy of the data is performed,
taking [linear time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#linear-time).

**See also** [append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#append)() and
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#insert)().

### void QByteArray::reserve(int *size*)

Attempts to allocate memory for at least *size* bytes. If you know in advance how large
the byte array will be, you can call this function, and if you call
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)() often you are
likely to get better performance. If *size* is an underestimate, the worst that will
happen is that the [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) will
be a bit slower.

The sole purpose of this function is to provide a means of fine tuning
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)'s memory usage. In
general, you will rarely ever need to call this function. If you want to change the size
of the byte array, call
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)().

**See also** [squeeze](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#squeeze)() and
[capacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#capacity)().

### void QByteArray::resize(int *size*)

If *size* is less than the current size, bytes are removed from the end.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&QByteArray::setNum(double *n*, char *f* \= 'g', int *prec* \= 6\)

This is an overloaded function.

Sets the byte array to the printed value of *n*, formatted in format *f* with precision
*prec*, and returns a reference to the byte array.

The format *f* can be any of the following:

| Format | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `e` | format as \[-\]9.9e\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `E` | format as \[-\]9.9E\[\+\|-\]999 |
| `f` | format as \[-\]9.9 |
| `g` | use `e` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |
| `G` | use `E` or `f` format, whichever is the most concise |

With 'e', 'E', and 'f', *prec* is the number of digits after the decimal point. With 'g'
and 'G', *prec* is the maximum number of significant digits (trailing zeroes are
omitted).

**Note:** The format of the number is not localized; the default C locale is used
irrespective of the user's locale.

**See also** [toDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#toDouble)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::simplified() const

Returns a byte array that has whitespace removed from the start and the end, and which
has each sequence of internal whitespace replaced with a single space.

Whitespace means any character for which the standard C\+\+ `isspace()` function returns
`true` in the C locale. This includes the ASCII isspace() function returns `true` in the
C locale. This includes the ASCII characters '\\t', '\\n', '\\v', '\\f', '\\r', and ' '.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("  lots\t of\nwhitespace\r\n ");
ba = ba.simplified();
// ba == "lots of whitespace";
```

**See also** [trimmed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#trimmed)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QByteArray.size.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QByteArray::size() const

Returns the number of bytes in this byte array.

The last byte in the byte array is at position size() \- 1\. In addition,
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) ensures that the byte
at position size() is always '\\0', so that you can use the return value of
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#data)() and
[constData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#constData)() as arguments
to functions that expect '\\0'-terminated strings. If the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) object was created from
a [raw data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromRawData) that didn't
include the trailing null-termination character then
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) doesn't add it
automatically unless the [deep
copy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html#deep-copy) is created.

Example:

```
QByteArray ba("Hello");
int n = ba.size();          // n == 5
ba.data()[0];               // returns 'H'
ba.data()[4];               // returns 'o'
ba.data()[5];               // returns '\0'
```

**See also** [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#isEmpty)() and
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#resize)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QByteArray.toDouble.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### double QByteArray::toDouble(bool \**ok* \= nullptr) const

Returns the byte array converted to a `double` value.

Returns an infinity if the conversion overflows or 0.0 if the conversion fails for other
reasons (e.g. underflow).

If *ok* is not `nullptr`, failure is reported by setting \**ok* to `false`, and success
by setting \**ok* to `true`.

```
QByteArray string("1234.56");
bool ok;
double a = string.toDouble(&ok);   // a == 1234.56, ok == true

string = "1234.56 Volt";
a = str.toDouble(&ok);             // a == 0, ok == false
```

**Warning:** The [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)
content may only contain valid numerical characters which includes the plus/minus sign,
the character e used in scientific notation, and the decimal point. Including the unit
or additional characters leads to a conversion error.

**Note:** The conversion of the number is performed in the default C locale,
irrespective of the user's locale.

This function ignores leading and trailing whitespace.

**See also** [number](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#number)().

### int QByteArray::toInt(bool \**ok* \= nullptr, int *base* \= 10\) const

Returns the byte array converted to an `int` using base *base*, which is 10 by default
and must be between 2 and 36, or 0\.

If *base* is 0, the base is determined automatically using the following rules: If the
byte array begins with "0x", it is assumed to be hexadecimal; if it begins with "0", it
is assumed to be octal; otherwise it is assumed to be decimal.

Returns 0 if the conversion fails.

If *ok* is not `nullptr`, failure is reported by setting \**ok* to `false`, and success
by setting \**ok* to `true`.

```
QByteArray str("FF");
bool ok;
int hex = str.toInt(&ok, 16);     // hex == 255, ok == true
int dec = str.toInt(&ok, 10);     // dec == 0, ok == false
```

**Note:** The conversion of the number is performed in the default C locale,
irrespective of the user's locale.

**See also** [number](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#number)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::toPercentEncoding(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*exclude* \= QByteArray(), const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) \&*include* \= QByteArray(), char *percent* \= '%') const

Returns a URI/URL-style percent-encoded copy of this byte array. The *percent* parameter
allows you to override the default '%' character for another.

By default, this function will encode all characters that are not one of the following:

ALPHA ("a" to "z" and "A" to "Z") / DIGIT (0 to 9\) / "-" / "." / "\_" / "\~"

To prevent characters from being encoded pass them to *exclude*. To force characters to
be encoded pass them to *include*. The *percent* character is always encoded.

Example:

```
QByteArray text = "{a fishy string?}";
QByteArray ba = text.toPercentEncoding("{}", "s");
qDebug(ba.constData());
// prints "{a fi%73hy %73tring%3F}"
```

The hex encoding uses the numbers 0-9 and the uppercase letters A-F.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[fromPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#fromPercentEncoding)()
and

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#QByteArray) QByteArray::trimmed() const

Returns a byte array that has whitespace removed from the start and the end.

Whitespace means any character for which the standard C\+\+ `isspace()` function returns
`true` in the C locale. This includes the ASCII characters '\\t', '\\n', '\\v', '\\f',

```

trimmed() leaves internal whitespace alone.

## Detailed Description

This class is useful when you have a sequence of bytes that you want to repeatedly match
against some byte arrays (perhaps in a loop), or when you want to search for the same
sequence of bytes multiple times in the same byte array. Using a matcher object and
[indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#indexIn)() is faster
than matching a plain [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)
with [QByteArray::indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html#indexOf)()
if repeated matching takes place. This class offers no benefit if you are doing one-off
byte array matches.

Create the QByteArrayMatcher with the
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) you want to search for.
Then call [indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#indexIn)()
on the [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) that you want to
search.

### int QByteArrayMatcher::indexIn(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*ba*, int *from* \= 0\) const

Searches the byte array *ba*, from byte position *from* (default 0, i.e. from the first
byte), for the byte array
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() that was
set in the constructor or in the most recent call to
[setPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#setPattern)().
Returns the position where the
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() matched
in *ba*, or -1 if no match was found.

### int QByteArrayMatcher::indexIn(const char \**str*, int *len*, int *from* \= 0\) const

Searches the char string *str*, which has length *len*, from byte position *from*
(default 0, i.e. from the first byte), for the byte array
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() that was
set in the constructor or in the most recent call to
[setPattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#setPattern)().
Returns the position where the
[pattern](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearraymatcher.html#pattern)() matched
in *str*, or -1 if no match was found.

## Detailed Description

Child events are sent immediately to objects when children are added or removed.

In both cases you can only rely on the child being a
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) (or, if
[QObject::isWidgetType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#isWidgetType)()
returns `true`, a [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html)). This is
because in the
[QEvent::ChildAdded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) case the
child is not yet fully constructed; in the
[QEvent::ChildRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) case it
might have already been destructed.

The handler for these events is
[QObject::childEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#childEvent)().

## Detailed Description

QCollator is initialized with a
[QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) and an optional collation
strategy. It tries to initialize the collator with the specified values. The collator
can then be used to compare and sort strings in a locale dependent fashion.

A QCollator object can be used together with template based sorting algorithms such as
std::sort to sort a list of QStrings.

In addition to the locale and collation strategy, several optional flags can be set that
influence the result of the collation.

## Detailed Description

This class is used to describe an option on the command line. It allows different ways
of defining the same option with multiple aliases possible. It is also used to describe
how the option is used \- it may be a flag (e.g. `-v`) or take a value (e.g. `-o file`).

Examples:

```
QCommandLineOption verboseOption("verbose", "Verbose mode. Prints out more information.");
QCommandLineOption outputOption(QStringList() << "o" << "output", "Write generated data into <file>.", "file");
```

### void QCommandLineOption::setValueName(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*valueName*)

Sets the name of the expected value, for the documentation, to *valueName*.

Options without a value assigned have a boolean-like behavior: either the user specifies
--option or they don't.

Options with a value assigned need to set a name for the expected value, for the
documentation of the option in the help output. An option with names `o` and `output`,
and a value name of `file` will appear as `-o, --output <file>`.

Call
[QCommandLineParser::value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#value)()
if you expect the option to be present only once, and
[QCommandLineParser::values](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#values)()
if you expect that option to be present multiple times.

**See also**
[valueName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineoption.html#valueName)().

### bool QCommandLineParser::isSet(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*name*) const

Checks whether the option *name* was passed to the application.

Returns `true` if the option *name* was set, false otherwise.

The name provided can be any long or short name of any option that was added with
`addOption()`. All the options names are treated as being equivalent. If the name is not
recognized or that option was not present, false is returned.

Example:

```
bool verbose = parser.isSet("verbose");
```

### bool QCommandLineParser::isSet(const [QCommandLineOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineoption.html) \&*option*) const

This is an overloaded function.

Checks whether the *option* was passed to the application.

Returns `true` if the *option* was set, false otherwise.

This is the recommended way to check for options with no values.

Example:

```
QCoreApplication app(argc, argv);
QCommandLineParser parser;
QCommandLineOption verboseOption("verbose");
parser.addOption(verboseOption);
parser.process(app);
bool verbose = parser.isSet(verboseOption);
```

### [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) QCommandLineParser::optionNames() const

Returns a list of option names that were found.

This returns a list of all the recognized option names found by the parser, in the order
in which they were found. For any long options that were in the form {--option\=value},
the value part will have been dropped.

The names in this list do not include the preceding dash characters. Names may appear
more than once in this list if they were encountered more than once by the parser.

Any entry in the list can be used with `value()` or with `values()` to get any relevant
option values.

### bool QCommandLineParser::parse(const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*arguments*)

Parses the command line *arguments*.

Most programs don't need to call this, a simple call to
[process](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#process)() is
enough.

parse() is more low-level, and only does the parsing. The application will have to take
care of the error handling, using
[errorText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#errorText)() if
parse() returns `false`. This can be useful for instance to show a graphical error
message in graphical programs.

Calling parse() instead of
[process](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#process)() can also
be useful in order to ignore unknown options temporarily, because more option
definitions will be provided later on (depending on one of the arguments), before
calling [process](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#process)().

Don't forget that *arguments* must start with the name of the executable (ignored,
though).

Returns `false` in case of a parse error (unknown option or missing value); returns
`true` otherwise.

**See also**
[process](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#process)().

### void QCommandLineParser::process(const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*arguments*)

Processes the command line *arguments*.

In addition to parsing the options (like
[parse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#parse)()), this
function also handles the builtin options and handles errors.

The builtin options are `--version` if
[addVersionOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#addVersionOption)
was called and `--help` / `--help-all` if
[addHelpOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#addHelpOption)
was called.

When invoking one of these options, or when an error happens (for instance an unknown
option was passed), the current process will then stop, using the exit() function.

**See also**
[QCoreApplication::arguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#arguments)()
and [parse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html#parse)().

### void QCommandLineParser::process(const [QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) \&*app*)

This is an overloaded function.

The command line is obtained from the
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) instance
*app*.

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QCommandLineParser::value(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*optionName*) const

Returns the option value found for the given option name *optionName*, or an empty
string if not found.

The name provided can be any long or short name of any option that was added with
`addOption()`. All the option names are treated as being equivalent. If the name is not
recognized or that option was not present, an empty string is returned.

For options found by the parser, the last value found for that option is returned. If
the option wasn't specified on the command line, the default value is returned.

An empty string is returned if the option does not take a value.

## Detailed Description

This class is used by non-GUI applications to provide their event loop. For non-GUI
application that uses Qt, there should be exactly one QCoreApplication object. For GUI
applications, see
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html). For
applications that use the Qt Widgets module, see
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html).

QCoreApplication contains the main event loop, where all events from the operating
system (e.g., timer and network events) and other sources are processed and dispatched.
It also handles the application's initialization and finalization, as well as
system-wide and application-wide settings.

### The Event Loop and Event Handling

The event loop is started with a call to
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)(). Long-running
operations can call
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)()
to keep the application responsive.

In general, we recommend that you create a QCoreApplication,
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) or a
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html) object in your
`main()` function as early as possible.
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)() will not return
until the event loop exits; e.g., when
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)() is called.

Several static convenience functions are also provided. The QCoreApplication object is
available from
[instance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#instance)(). Events
can be sent with
[sendEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendEvent)() or
posted to an event queue with
[postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#postEvent)().
Pending events can be removed with
[removePostedEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#removePostedEvents)()
or dispatched with
[sendPostedEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendPostedEvents)().

The class provides a
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)() slot and an
[aboutToQuit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#aboutToQuit)()
signal.

### Application and Library Paths

An application has an
[applicationDirPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#applicationDirPath)()
and an
[applicationFilePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#applicationFilePath)().
Library paths (see [QLibrary](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html)) can be
retrieved with
[libraryPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#libraryPaths)()
and manipulated by
[setLibraryPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#setLibraryPaths)(),
[addLibraryPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#addLibraryPath)(),
and
[removeLibraryPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#removeLibraryPath)().

### Internationalization and Translations

Translation files can be added or removed using
[installTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#installTranslator)()
and
[removeTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#removeTranslator)().
Application strings can be translated using
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#translate)(). The
[QObject::tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)() and
QObject::trUtf8() functions are implemented in terms of
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#translate)().

### Accessing Command Line Arguments

The command line arguments which are passed to QCoreApplication's constructor should be
accessed using the
[arguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#arguments)()
function.

**Note:** QCoreApplication removes option `-qmljsdebugger="..."`. It parses the argument
of `qmljsdebugger`, and then removes this option plus its argument.

For more advanced command line option handling, create a
[QCommandLineParser](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html).

### Locale Settings

On Unix/Linux Qt is configured to use the system locale settings by default. This can
cause a conflict when using POSIX functions, for instance, when converting between data
types such as floats and strings, since the notation may differ between locales. To get
around this problem, call the POSIX function `setlocale(LC_NUMERIC,"C")` right after
initializing [QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html),
[QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html) or
QCoreApplication to reset the locale that is used for number formatting to "C"-locale.

### `[signal]` void QCoreApplication::aboutToQuit()

This signal is emitted when the application is about to quit the main event loop, e.g.
when the event loop level drops to zero. This may happen either after a call to
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)() from inside the
application or when the user shuts down the entire desktop session.

The signal is particularly useful if your application has to do some last-second
cleanup. Note that no user interaction is possible in this state.

**Note:** This is a private signal. It can be used in signal connections but cannot be

### `[static]` [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) QCoreApplication::arguments()

Returns the list of command-line arguments.

Usually arguments().at(0) is the program name, arguments().at(1) is the first argument,
and arguments().last() is the last argument. See the note below about Windows.

Calling this function is slow \- you should store the result in a variable when parsing
the command line.

**Warning:** On Unix, this list is built from the argc and argv parameters passed to the
constructor in the main() function. The string-data in argv is interpreted using
[QString::fromLocal8Bit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#fromLocal8Bit)();
hence it is not possible to pass, for example, Japanese command line arguments on a
system that runs in a Latin1 locale. Most modern Unix systems do not have this
limitation, as they are Unicode-based.

On Windows, the list is built from the argc and argv parameters only if modified
argv/argc parameters are passed to the constructor. In that case, encoding problems
might occur.

Otherwise, the arguments() are constructed from the return value of
[GetCommandLine()](http://msdn2.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms683156(VS.85).aspx). As a
result of this, the string given by arguments().at(0) might not be the program name on
Windows, depending on how the application was started.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also**
[applicationFilePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#applicationFilePath)()
and [QCommandLineParser](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommandlineparser.html).

Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` int QCoreApplication::exec()

Enters the main event loop and waits until
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() is called.
Returns the value that was passed to
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() (which is 0 if
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)() is called via
[quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)()).

It is necessary to call this function to start event handling. The main event loop
receives events from the window system and dispatches these to the application widgets.

To make your application perform idle processing (by executing a special function
whenever there are no pending events), use a
[QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) with 0 timeout. More advanced
idle processing schemes can be achieved using
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)().

We recommend that you connect clean-up code to the
[aboutToQuit()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#aboutToQuit)
signal, instead of putting it in your application's `main()` function because on some
platforms the exec() call may not return. For example, on Windows when the user logs
off, the system terminates the process after Qt closes all top-level windows. Hence,
there is no guarantee that the application will have time to exit its event loop and
execute code at the end of the `main()` function after the exec() call.

**See also** [quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)(),
[exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)(),
[processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)(),
and [QApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#exec)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QCoreApplication.exit.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QCoreApplication::exit(int *returnCode* \= 0\)

Tells the application to exit with a return code.

After this function has been called, the application leaves the main event loop and
returns from the call to
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)(). The
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)() function returns
*returnCode*. If the event loop is not running, this function does nothing.

By convention, a *returnCode* of 0 means success, and any non-zero value indicates an
error.

It's good practice to always connect signals to this slot using a
[QueuedConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ConnectionType-enum). If a
signal connected (non-queued) to this slot is emitted before control enters the main
event loop (such as before "int main" calls
[exec()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)), the slot has
no effect and the application never exits. Using a queued connection ensures that the
slot will not be invoked until after control enters the main event loop.

Note that unlike the C library function of the same name, this function *does* return to
the caller \-- it is event processing that stops.

**See also** [quit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#quit)() and
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)().

### `[static]` bool QCoreApplication::installTranslator([QTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html) \**translationFile*)

Adds the translation file *translationFile* to the list of translation files to be used
for translations.

Multiple translation files can be installed. Translations are searched for in the
reverse order in which they were installed, so the most recently installed translation
file is searched first and the first translation file installed is searched last. The
search stops as soon as a translation containing a matching string is found.

Installing or removing a
[QTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html), or changing an
installed [QTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html) generates a
[LanguageChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event for the
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) instance. A
[QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html) instance will
propagate the event to all toplevel widgets, where a reimplementation of changeEvent can
re-translate the user interface by passing user-visible strings via the
[tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)() function to the respective
property setters. User-interface classes generated by Qt Designer provide a
`retranslateUi()` function that can be called.

The function returns `true` on success and false on failure.

**Note:** [QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html)
does *not* take ownership of *translationFile*.

**See also**
[removeTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#removeTranslator)(),
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#translate)(),
[QTranslator::load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html#load)(), and
[Dynamic
Translation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/internationalization.html#dynamic-translation).

### `[static]` [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) QCoreApplication::libraryPaths()

Returns a list of paths that the application will search when dynamically loading
libraries.

The return value of this function may change when a
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) is created.
It is not recommended to call it before creating a
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html). The
directory of the application executable (**not** the working directory) is part of the
list if it is known. In order to make it known a
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) has to be
constructed as it will use `argv[0]` to find it.

Qt provides default library paths, but they can also be set using a
[qt.conf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt-conf.html) file. Paths specified in this
file will override default values. Note that if the qt.conf file is in the directory of
the application executable, it may not be found until a
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) is created.
If it is not found when calling this function, the default library paths will be used.

The list will include the installation directory for plugins if it exists (the default
installation directory for plugins is `INSTALL/plugins`, where `INSTALL` is the
directory where Qt was installed). The colon separated entries of the `QT_PLUGIN_PATH`
environment variable are always added. The plugin installation directory (and its
existence) may change when the directory of the application executable becomes known.

If you want to iterate over the list, you can use the
[foreach](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/containers.html#foreach) pseudo-keyword:

```
foreach (const QString &path, app.libraryPaths())
    do_something(path);
```

**See also**
[setLibraryPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#setLibraryPaths)(),
[addLibraryPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#addLibraryPath)(),
[removeLibraryPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#removeLibraryPath)(),
[QLibrary](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html), and [How to Create Qt
Plugins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/plugins-howto.html).

Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QCoreApplication::notify([QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**receiver*, [QEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html) \**event*)

Sends *event* to *receiver*: *receiver*-\>event(*event*). Returns the value that is
returned from the receiver's event handler. Note that this function is called for all
events sent to any object in any thread.

For certain types of events (e.g. mouse and key events), the event will be propagated to
the receiver's parent and so on up to the top-level object if the receiver is not
interested in the event (i.e., it returns `false`).

There are five different ways that events can be processed; reimplementing this virtual
function is just one of them. All five approaches are listed below:

1. Reimplementing [paintEvent()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent), [mousePressEvent()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mousePressEvent) and so on. This is the most common, easiest, and least powerful way.
2. Reimplementing this function. This is very powerful, providing complete control; but only one subclass can be active at a time.
3. Installing an event filter on [QCoreApplication::instance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#instance)(). Such an event filter is able to process all events for all widgets, so it's just as powerful as reimplementing notify(); furthermore, it's possible to have more than one application-global event filter. Global event filters even see mouse events for [disabled widgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop). Note that application event filters are only called for objects that live in the main thread.
4. Reimplementing [QObject::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#event)() (as [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) does). If you do this you get Tab key presses, and you get to see the events before any widget-specific event filters.
5. Installing an event filter on the object. Such an event filter gets all the events, including Tab and Shift\+Tab key press events, as long as they do not change the focus widget.

**Future direction:** This function will not be called for objects that live outside the
main thread in Qt 6\. Applications that need that functionality should find other
solutions for their event inspection needs in the meantime. The change may be extended
to the main thread, causing this function to be deprecated.

**Warning:** If you override this function, you must ensure all threads that process
events stop doing so before your application object begins destruction. This includes
threads started by other libraries that you may be using, but does not apply to Qt's own
threads.

**See also** [QObject::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#event)()
and
[installNativeEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#installNativeEventFilter)().

### `[static]` void QCoreApplication::postEvent([QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**receiver*, [QEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html) \**event*, int *priority* \= Qt::NormalEventPriority)

Adds the event *event*, with the object *receiver* as the receiver of the event, to an
event queue and returns immediately.

The event must be allocated on the heap since the post event queue will take ownership
of the event and delete it once it has been posted. It is *not safe* to access the event
after it has been posted.

When control returns to the main event loop, all events that are stored in the queue
will be sent using the
[notify](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#notify)() function.

Events are sorted in descending *priority* order, i.e. events with a high *priority* are
queued before events with a lower *priority*. The *priority* can be any integer value,
i.e. between INT\_MAX and INT\_MIN, inclusive; see
[Qt::EventPriority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#EventPriority-enum) for
more details. Events with equal *priority* will be processed in the order posted.

**Note:** This function is
[thread-safe](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/threads-reentrancy.html).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also**
[sendEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendEvent)(),
[notify](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#notify)(),
[sendPostedEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendPostedEvents)(),
and [Qt::EventPriority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#EventPriority-enum).

### `[static]` void QCoreApplication::processEvents([QEventLoop::ProcessEventsFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum) *flags* \= QEventLoop::AllEvents)

Processes some pending events for the calling thread according to the specified *flags*.

You can call this function occasionally when your program is busy performing a long
operation (e.g. copying a file).

In the event that you are running a local loop which calls this function continuously,
without an event loop, the
[DeferredDelete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events will
not be processed. This can affect the behaviour of widgets, e.g.
[QToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html), that rely on
[DeferredDelete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events to
function properly. An alternative would be to call
[sendPostedEvents()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendPostedEvents)
from within that local loop.

Calling this function processes events only for the calling thread, and returns after
all available events have been processed. Available events are events queued before the
function call. This means that events that are posted while the function runs will be
queued until a later round of event processing.

**Note:** This function is
[thread-safe](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/threads-reentrancy.html).

### `[static]` void QCoreApplication::processEvents([QEventLoop::ProcessEventsFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventloop.html#ProcessEventsFlag-enum) *flags*, int *ms*)

This function overloads processEvents().

Processes pending events for the calling thread for *ms* milliseconds or until there are
no more events to process, whichever is shorter.

You can call this function occasionally when your program is busy doing a long operation

### `[static slot]` void QCoreApplication::quit()

Tells the application to exit with return code 0 (success). Equivalent to calling
[QCoreApplication::exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)(0).

It's common to connect the
[QGuiApplication::lastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#lastWindowClosed)()
signal to quit(), and you also often connect e.g.
[QAbstractButton::clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#clicked)()
or signals in [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html),
[QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html), or
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html) to it.

It's good practice to always connect signals to this slot using a
[QueuedConnection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ConnectionType-enum). If a
signal connected (non-queued) to this slot is emitted before control enters the main
event loop (such as before "int main" calls
[exec()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)), the slot has
no effect and the application never exits. Using a queued connection ensures that the
slot will not be invoked until after control enters the main event loop.

Example:

```
QPushButton *quitButton = new QPushButton("Quit");
connect(quitButton, &QPushButton::clicked, &app, &QCoreApplication::quit, Qt::QueuedConnection);
```

**See also** [exit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exit)(),
[aboutToQuit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#aboutToQuit)(),
and
[QGuiApplication::lastWindowClosed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#lastWindowClosed)().

### `[static]` void QCoreApplication::removePostedEvents([QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**receiver*, int *eventType* \= 0\)

*eventType* is 0, all the events are removed for *receiver*. You should never call this
function with *eventType* of 0\.

[thread-safe](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/threads-reentrancy.html).

### `[static]` void QCoreApplication::setSetuidAllowed(bool *allow*)

Allows the application to run setuid on UNIX platforms if *allow* is true.

If *allow* is false (the default) and Qt detects the application is running with an
effective user id different than the real user id, the application will be aborted when
a [QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) instance
is created.

Qt is not an appropriate solution for setuid programs due to its large attack surface.
However some applications may be required to run in this manner for historical reasons.
This flag will prevent Qt from aborting the application when this is detected, and must
be set before a
[QCoreApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html) instance is
created.

**Note:** It is strongly recommended not to enable this option since it introduces
security risks.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.3.

**See also**
[isSetuidAllowed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#isSetuidAllowed)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QDataStream.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A data stream is a binary stream of encoded information which is 100% independent of the
host computer's operating system, CPU or byte order. For example, a data stream that is
written by a PC under Windows can be read by a Sun SPARC running Solaris.

You can also use a data stream to read/write [raw unencoded binary
data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#raw). If you want a "parsing"
input stream, see [QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html).

The QDataStream class implements the serialization of C\+\+'s basic data types, like
`char`, `short`, `int`, `char *`, etc. Serialization of more complex data is
accomplished by breaking up the data into primitive units.

A data stream cooperates closely with a
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). A
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) represents an
input/output medium one can read data from and write data to. The
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) class is an example of an I/O
device.

Example (write binary data to a stream):

```
QFile file("file.dat");
file.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly);
QDataStream out(&file);   // we will serialize the data into the file
out << QString("the answer is");   // serialize a string
out << (qint32)42;        // serialize an integer
```

Example (read binary data from a stream):

```
QFile file("file.dat");
file.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly);
QDataStream in(&file);    // read the data serialized from the file
QString str;
qint32 a;
in >> str >> a;           // extract "the answer is" and 42
```

Each item written to the stream is written in a predefined binary format that varies
depending on the item's type. Supported Qt types include
[QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html),
[QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html),
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html),
[QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html),
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html),
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html),
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) and many others. For the
complete list of all Qt types supporting data streaming see [Serializing Qt Data
Types](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/datastreamformat.html).

For integers it is best to always cast to a Qt integer type for writing, and to read
back into the same Qt integer type. This ensures that you get integers of the size you
want and insulates you from compiler and platform differences.

Enumerations can be serialized through QDataStream without the need of manually defining
streaming operators. Enum classes are serialized using the declared size.

To take one example, a `char *` string is written as a 32-bit integer equal to the
length of the string including the '\\0' byte, followed by all the characters of the
string including the '\\0' byte. When reading a `char *` string, 4 bytes are read to
create the 32-bit length value, then that many characters for the `char *` string
including the '\\0' terminator are read.

The initial I/O device is usually set in the constructor, but can be changed with
[setDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#setDevice)(). If you've
reached the end of the data (or if there is no I/O device set)
[atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#atEnd)() will return true.

### Versioning

QDataStream's binary format has evolved since Qt 1.0, and is likely to continue evolving
to reflect changes done in Qt. When inputting or outputting complex types, it's very
important to make sure that the same version of the stream
([version](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#version)()) is used for
reading and writing. If you need both forward and backward compatibility, you can
hardcode the version number in the application:

```
stream.setVersion(QDataStream::Qt_4_0);
```

If you are producing a new binary data format, such as a file format for documents
created by your application, you could use a QDataStream to write the data in a portable
format. Typically, you would write a brief header containing a magic string and a
version number to give yourself room for future expansion. For example:

```
QFile file("file.xxx");
file.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly);
QDataStream out(&file);

// Write a header with a "magic number" and a version
out << (quint32)0xA0B0C0D0;
out << (qint32)123;

out.setVersion(QDataStream::Qt_4_0);

// Write the data
out << lots_of_interesting_data;
```

Then read it in with:

```
QFile file("file.xxx");
file.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly);
QDataStream in(&file);

// Read and check the header
quint32 magic;
in >> magic;
if (magic != 0xA0B0C0D0)
    return XXX_BAD_FILE_FORMAT;

// Read the version
qint32 version;
in >> version;
if (version < 100)
    return XXX_BAD_FILE_TOO_OLD;
if (version > 123)
    return XXX_BAD_FILE_TOO_NEW;

if (version <= 110)
    in.setVersion(QDataStream::Qt_3_2);
else
    in.setVersion(QDataStream::Qt_4_0);

// Read the data
in >> lots_of_interesting_data;
if (version >= 120)
    in >> data_new_in_XXX_version_1_2;
in >> other_interesting_data;
```

You can select which byte order to use when serializing data. The default setting is
big-endian (MSB first). Changing it to little-endian breaks the portability (unless the
reader also changes to little-endian). We recommend keeping this setting unless you have
special requirements.

### Reading and Writing Raw Binary Data

You may wish to read/write your own raw binary data to/from the data stream directly.
Data may be read from the stream into a preallocated `char *` using
[readRawData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#readRawData)().
Similarly data can be written to the stream using
[writeRawData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#writeRawData)(). Note
that any encoding/decoding of the data must be done by you.

A similar pair of functions is
[readBytes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#readBytes)() and
[writeBytes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#writeBytes)(). These
differ from their *raw* counterparts as follows:
[readBytes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#readBytes)() reads a
quint32 which is taken to be the length of the data to be read, then that number of
bytes is read into the preallocated `char *`;
[writeBytes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#writeBytes)() writes a
quint32 containing the length of the data, followed by the data. Note that any
encoding/decoding of the data (apart from the length quint32) must be done by you.

### Reading and Writing Qt Collection Classes

The Qt container classes can also be serialized to a QDataStream. These include
[QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html), QLinkedList,
[QVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvector.html),
[QSet](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qset.html),
[QHash](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhash.html#qhash), and
[QMap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmap.html). The stream operators are declared
as non-members of the classes.

### Reading and Writing Other Qt Classes

In addition to the overloaded stream operators documented here, any Qt classes that you
might want to serialize to a QDataStream will have appropriate stream operators declared
as non-member of the class:

```
    QDataStream &operator<<(QDataStream &, const QXxx &);
    QDataStream &operator>>(QDataStream &, QXxx &);
```

For example, here are the stream operators declared as non-members of the
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) class:

```
    QDataStream & operator<< (QDataStream& stream, const QImage& image);
    QDataStream & operator>> (QDataStream& stream, QImage& image);
```

To see if your favorite Qt class has similar stream operators defined, check the
**Related Non-Members** section of the class's documentation page.

### Using Read Transactions

When a data stream operates on an asynchronous device, the chunks of data can arrive at
arbitrary points in time. The QDataStream class implements a transaction mechanism that
provides the ability to read the data atomically with a series of stream operators. As
an example, you can handle incomplete reads from a socket by using a transaction in a
slot connected to the readyRead() signal:

```
in.startTransaction();
QString str;
qint32 a;
in >> str >> a; // try to read packet atomically

if (!in.commitTransaction())
    return;     // wait for more data
```

If no full packet is received, this code restores the stream to the initial position,
after which you need to wait for more data to arrive.

[DoublePrecision](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#FloatingPointPrecision-enum)

[Qt\_4\_6](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#Version-enum), the

### void QDataStream::setVersion(int *v*)

[Version](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#Version-enum) enum.

You don't *have* to set a version if you are using the current version of Qt, but for
your own custom binary formats we recommend that you do; see
[Versioning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#versioning) in the
Detailed Description.

To accommodate new functionality, the datastream serialization format of some Qt classes
has changed in some versions of Qt. If you want to read data that was created by an
earlier version of Qt, or write data that can be read by a program that was compiled
with an earlier version of Qt, use this function to modify the serialization format used
by [QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html).

The [Version](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html#Version-enum) enum
provides symbolic constants for the different versions of Qt. For example:

```
QDataStream out(file);
out.setVersion(QDataStream::Qt_4_0);

## Detailed Description

A QDate object represents a particular day, regardless of calendar, locale or other
settings used when creating it or supplied by the system. It can report the year, month
and day of the month that represent the day with respect to the proleptic Gregorian
calendar or any calendar supplied as a
[QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) object.

A QDate object is typically created by giving the year, month, and day numbers
explicitly. Note that QDate interprets year numbers less than 100 as presented, i.e., as
years 1 through 99, without adding any offset. The static function
[currentDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#currentDate)() creates a
QDate object containing the date read from the system clock. An explicit date can also
be set using [setDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#setDate)(). The
[fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#fromString)() function
returns a QDate given a string and a date format which is used to interpret the date
within the string.

The [year](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#year-1)(),
[month](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#month-1)(), and
[day](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#day-1)() functions provide access to
the year, month, and day numbers. When more than one of these values is needed, it is
more efficient to call
[QCalendar::partsFromDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#partsFromDate)(),
to save repeating (potentially expensive) calendrical calculations.

Also, [dayOfWeek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#dayOfWeek-1)() and
[dayOfYear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#dayOfYear-1)() functions are
provided. The same information is provided in textual format by
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toString-1)().
[QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) can map the day numbers to
names, [QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) can map month
numbers to names.

QDate provides a full set of operators to compare two QDate objects where smaller means
earlier, and larger means later.

You can increment (or decrement) a date by a given number of days using
[addDays](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#addDays)(). Similarly you can
use [addMonths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#addMonths)() and
[addYears](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#addYears)(). The
[daysTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#daysTo)() function returns the
number of days between two dates.

The [daysInMonth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#daysInMonth-1)() and
[daysInYear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#daysInYear-1)() functions
return how many days there are in this date's month and year, respectively. The
[isLeapYear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isLeapYear)() function
indicates whether a date is in a leap year.
[QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) can also supply this
information, in some cases more conveniently.

### Remarks

#### No Year 0

In the Gregorian calendar, there is no year 0\. Dates in that year are considered
invalid. The year -1 is the year "1 before Christ" or "1 before common era." The day
before 1 January 1 CE, QDate(1, 1, 1), is 31 December 1 BCE, QDate(-1, 12, 31). Various
other calendars behave similarly; see
[QCalendar::hasYearZero](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#hasYearZero)().

#### Range of Valid Dates

Dates are stored internally as a Julian Day number, an integer count of every day in a
contiguous range, with 24 November 4714 BCE in the Gregorian calendar being Julian Day 0
(1 January 4713 BCE in the Julian calendar). As well as being an efficient and accurate
way of storing an absolute date, it is suitable for converting a date into other
calendar systems such as Hebrew, Islamic or Chinese. The Julian Day number can be
obtained using
[QDate::toJulianDay](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toJulianDay)() and
can be set using
[QDate::fromJulianDay](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#fromJulianDay)().

The range of Julian Day numbers that QDate can represent is, for technical reasons,
limited to between -784350574879 and 784354017364, which means from before 2 billion BCE
to after 2 billion CE. This is more than seven times as wide as the range of dates a
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) can represent.

Note for [Qt::TextDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum): It
is recommended that you use the English short month names (e.g. "Jan"). Although
localized month names can also be used in Qt 5, they depend on the user's locale
settings.

**Note:** Support for localized dates, including the format options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Use
[QLocale::toDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDate)() instead.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toString-1)() and
[QLocale::toDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDate)().

### `[static]` QDate QDate::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*)

This is an overloaded function.

### `[static]` QDate QDate::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*, [QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) *cal*)

Returns the [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) represented by the
*string*, using the *format* given, or an invalid date if the string cannot be parsed.

Uses *cal* as calendar if supplied, else the Gregorian calendar. Ranges of values in the
format descriptions below are for the latter; they may be different for other calendars.

These expressions may be used for the format:

| Expression | Output |
| --- | --- |
| d | The day as a number without a leading zero (1 to 31\) |
| dd | The day as a number with a leading zero (01 to 31\) |
| ddd | The abbreviated localized day name (e.g. 'Mon' to 'Sun'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| dddd | The long localized day name (e.g. 'Monday' to 'Sunday'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| M | The month as a number without a leading zero (1 to 12\) |
| MM | The month as a number with a leading zero (01 to 12\) |
| MMM | The abbreviated localized month name (e.g. 'Jan' to 'Dec'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| MMMM | The long localized month name (e.g. 'January' to 'December'). Uses the system locale to localize the name, i.e. [QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)(). |
| yy | The year as a two digit number (00 to 99\) |
| yyyy | The year as a four digit number, possibly plus a leading minus sign for negative years. |

**Note:** Unlike the other version of this function, day and month names must be given
in the user's local language. It is only possible to use the English names if the user's
language is English.

All other input characters will be treated as text. Any non-empty sequence of characters
enclosed in single quotes will also be treated (stripped of the quotes) as text and not
be interpreted as expressions. For example:

```
QDate date = QDate::fromString("1MM12car2003", "d'MM'MMcaryyyy");
// date is 1 December 2003
```

If the format is not satisfied, an invalid
[QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) is returned. The expressions that
don't expect leading zeroes (d, M) will be greedy. This means that they will use two
digits even if this will put them outside the accepted range of values and leaves too
few digits for other sections. For example, the following format string could have meant
January 30 but the M will grab two digits, resulting in an invalid date:

```
QDate date = QDate::fromString("130", "Md"); // invalid
```

For any field that is not represented in the format the following defaults are used:

| Field | Default value |
| --- | --- |
| Year | 1900 |
| Month | 1 |
| Day | 1 |

The following examples demonstrate the default values:

```
QDate::fromString("1.30", "M.d");           // January 30 1900
QDate::fromString("20000110", "yyyyMMdd");  // January 10, 2000
QDate::fromString("20000110", "yyyyMd");    // January 10, 2000
```

**Note:** If localized month and day names are used, please switch to using
[QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)().toDate() as
[QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) methods shall change to only
recognize English (C locale) names at Qt 6\.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toString-1)(),
[QDateTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)(),
[QTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#fromString)(), and
[QLocale::toDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toDate)().

### `[static]` bool QDate::isValid(int *year*, int *month*, int *day*)

This is an overloaded function.

Returns `true` if the specified date (*year*, *month*, and *day*) is valid in the
Gregorian calendar; otherwise returns `false`.

Example:

```
QDate::isValid(2002, 5, 17);  // true
QDate::isValid(2002, 2, 30);  // false (Feb 30 does not exist)
QDate::isValid(2004, 2, 29);  // true (2004 is a leap year)
QDate::isValid(2000, 2, 29);  // true (2000 is a leap year)
QDate::isValid(2006, 2, 29);  // false (2006 is not a leap year)
QDate::isValid(2100, 2, 29);  // false (2100 is not a leap year)
QDate::isValid(1202, 6, 6);   // true (even though 1202 is pre-Gregorian)
```

**See also** [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isNull)(),

and times, taking the form yyyy-MM-dd, where yyyy is the year, MM is the month of the

[QLocale::system().toString(date,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

The *format* options
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with [QLocale().toString(date,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale().toString(date,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

If the *format* is
[Qt::RFC2822Date](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the
string is formatted in an [RFC 2822](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2822.txt)
compatible way. An example of this formatting is "20 May 1995".

If the date is invalid, an empty string will be returned.

**Warning:** The
[Qt::ISODate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum) format is only
valid for years in the range 0 to 9999\.

and [QLocale::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString)().

Qt 5 reference:

### int QDate::weekNumber(int \**yearNumber* \= nullptr) const

Returns the ISO 8601 week number (1 to 53).

Returns 0 if the date is invalid. Otherwise, returns the week number for the date. If
*yearNumber* is not `nullptr` (its default), stores the year as \**yearNumber*.

In accordance with ISO 8601, each week falls in the year to which most of its days
belong, in the Gregorian calendar. As ISO 8601's week starts on Monday, this is the year
in which the week's Thursday falls. Most years have 52 weeks, but some have 53\.

**Note:** \**yearNumber* is not always the same as
[year](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#year-1)(). For example, 1 January
2000 has week number 52 in the year 1999, and 31 December 2002 has week number 1 in the
year 2003\.

**See also** [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isValid)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QDate.year.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QDate::year([QCalendar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html) *cal*) const

Returns the year of this date.

Uses *cal* as calendar, if supplied, else the Gregorian calendar.

Returns 0 if the date is invalid. For some calendars, dates before their first year may
all be invalid.

If using a calendar which has a year 0, check using
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#isValid)() if the return is 0\.
Such calendars use negative year numbers in the obvious way, with year 1 preceded by
year 0, in turn preceded by year -1 and so on.

Some calendars, despite having no year 0, have a conventional numbering of the years
before their first year, counting backwards from 1\. For example, in the proleptic
Gregorian calendar, successive years before 1 CE (the first year) are identified as 1
BCE, 2 BCE, 3 BCE and so on. For such calendars, negative year numbers are used to
indicate these years before year 1, with -1 indicating the year before 1\.

**See also** [month](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#month-1)(),
[day](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#day-1)(),

[QCalendar::isProleptic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#isProleptic)(),
and
[QCalendar::partsFromDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcalendar.html#partsFromDate)().
