Qt 5 reference:

### void QFileInfo::setFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*file*)

Sets the file that the [QFileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html)
provides information about to *file*.

The *file* can also include an absolute or relative file path. Absolute paths begin with
the directory separator (e.g. "/" under Unix) or a drive specification (under Windows).
Relative file names begin with a directory name or a file name and specify a path
relative to the current directory.

Example:

```
QFileInfo info("/usr/bin/env");

QString path = info.absolutePath(); // path = /usr/bin
QString base = info.baseName(); // base = env

info.setFile("/etc/hosts");

path = info.absolutePath(); // path = /etc
base = info.baseName(); // base = hosts
```

**See also** [isFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html#isFile)(),
[isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html#isRelative)(),
[QDir::setCurrent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#setCurrent)(), and
[QDir::isRelativePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#isRelativePath)().

Sets the file that the [QFileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html)
provides information about to *file*.

[QFileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html) will also have a relative

Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QFileInfo::suffix() const

Returns the suffix (extension) of the file.

The suffix consists of all characters in the file after (but not including) the last
'.'.

Example:

```
QFileInfo fi("/temporary/archive.tar.gz");
QString ext = fi.suffix();  // ext = "gz"
```

The suffix of a file is computed equally on all platforms, independent of file naming
conventions (e.g., ".bashrc" on Unix has an empty base name, and the suffix is
"bashrc").

**See also** [fileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html#fileName)(),
[completeSuffix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html#completeSuffix)(),
[baseName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html#baseName)(), and
[completeBaseName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html#completeBaseName)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QFileSelector.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QFileSelector is a convenience for selecting file variants based on platform or device
characteristics. This allows you to develop and deploy one codebase containing all the
different variants more easily in some circumstances, such as when the correct variant
cannot be determined during the deploy step.

### Using QFileSelector

If you always use the same file you do not need to use QFileSelector.

Consider the following example usage, where you want to use different settings files on
different locales. You might select code between locales like this:

```
    QString defaultsBasePath = "data/";
    QString defaultsPath = defaultsBasePath + "defaults.conf";
    QString localizedPath = defaultsBasePath
            + QString("%1/defaults.conf").arg(QLocale().name());
    if (QFile::exists(localizedPath))
        defaultsPath = localizedPath;
    QFile defaults(defaultsPath);
```

Similarly, if you want to pick a different data file based on target platform, your code
might look something like this:

```
    QString defaultsPath = "data/defaults.conf";
#if defined(Q_OS_ANDROID)
    defaultsPath = "data/android/defaults.conf";
#elif defined(Q_OS_IOS)
    defaultsPath = "data/ios/defaults.conf";
#endif
    QFile defaults(defaultsPath);
```

QFileSelector provides a convenient alternative to writing such boilerplate code, and in
the latter case it allows you to start using an platform-specific configuration without
a recompile. QFileSelector also allows for chaining of multiple selectors in a
convenient way, for example selecting a different file only on certain combinations of
platform and locale. For example, to select based on platform and/or locale, the code is
as follows:

```
    QFileSelector selector;
    QFile defaultsFile(selector.select("data/defaults.conf"));
```

The files to be selected are placed in directories named with a `'+'` and a selector
name. In the above example you could have the platform configurations selected by
placing them in the following locations:

```
    data/defaults.conf
    data/+android/defaults.conf
    data/+ios/+en_GB/defaults.conf
```

To find selected files, QFileSelector looks in the same directory as the base file. If
there are any directories of the form \+\<selector\> with an active selector,
QFileSelector will prefer a file with the same file name from that directory over the
base file. These directories can be nested to check against multiple selectors, for
example:

```
    images/background.png
    images/+android/+en_GB/background.png
```

With those files available, you would select a different file on the android platform,
but only if the locale was en\_GB.

For error handling in the case no valid selectors are present, it is recommended to have
a default or error-handling file in the base file location even if you expect selectors
to be present for all deployments.

In a future version, some may be marked as deploy-time static and be moved during the
deployment step as an optimization. As selectors come with a performance cost, it is
recommended to avoid their use in circumstances involving performance-critical code.

### Adding Selectors

Selectors normally available are

- platform, any of the following strings which match the platform the application is running on (list not exhaustive): android, ios, osx, darwin, mac, macos, linux, qnx, unix, windows. On Linux, if it can be determined, the name of the distribution too, like debian, fedora or opensuse.
- locale, same as QLocale().name().

Further selectors will be added from the `QT_FILE_SELECTORS` environment variable, which
when set should be a set of comma separated selectors. Note that this variable will only
be read once; selectors may not update if the variable changes while the application is
running. The initial set of selectors are evaluated only once, on first use.

You can also add extra selectors at runtime for custom behavior. These will be used in
any future calls to
[select](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileselector.html#select)(). If the extra
selectors list has been changed, calls to
[select](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileselector.html#select)() will use the
new list and may return differently.

### Conflict Resolution when Multiple Selectors Apply

When multiple selectors could be applied to the same file, the first matching selector
is chosen. The order selectors are checked in are:

1. Selectors set via [setExtraSelectors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileselector.html#setExtraSelectors)(), in the order they are in the list
2. Selectors in the `QT_FILE_SELECTORS` environment variable, from left to right
3. Locale
4. Platform

Here is an example involving multiple selectors matching at the same time. It uses
platform selectors, plus an extra selector named "admin" is set by the application based
on user credentials. The example is sorted so that the lowest matching file would be
chosen if all selectors were present:

```
    images/background.png
    images/+linux/background.png
    images/+windows/background.png
    images/+admin/background.png
    images/+admin/+linux/background.png
```

Because extra selectors are checked before platform the `+admin/background.png` will be
chosen on Windows when the admin selector is set, and `+windows/background.png` will be
chosen on Windows when the admin selector is not set. On Linux, the
`+admin/+linux/background.png` will be chosen when admin is set, and the
`+linux/background.png` when it is not.

PythonQt.QtCore.QFileSystemWatcher.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QFileSystemWatcher monitors the file system for changes to files and directories by
watching a list of specified paths.

Call [addPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#addPath)() to
watch a particular file or directory. Multiple paths can be added using the
[addPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#addPaths)()
function. Existing paths can be removed by using the
[removePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#removePath)()
and
[removePaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#removePaths)()
functions.

QFileSystemWatcher examines each path added to it. Files that have been added to the
QFileSystemWatcher can be accessed using the
[files](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#files)() function,
and directories using the
[directories](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#directories)()
function.

The
[fileChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#fileChanged)()
signal is emitted when a file has been modified, renamed or removed from disk.
Similarly, the
[directoryChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#directoryChanged)()
signal is emitted when a directory or its contents is modified or removed. Note that
QFileSystemWatcher stops monitoring files once they have been renamed or removed from
disk, and directories once they have been removed from disk.

- **Notes**:
  - On systems running a Linux kernel without inotify support, file systems that contain watched paths cannot be unmounted.
  - The act of monitoring files and directories for modifications consumes system resources. This implies there is a limit to the number of files and directories your process can monitor simultaneously. On all BSD variants, for example, an open file descriptor is required for each monitored file. Some system limits the number of open file descriptors to 256 by default. This means that [addPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#addPath)() and [addPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#addPaths)() will fail if your process tries to add more than 256 files or directories to the file system monitor. Also note that your process may have other file descriptors open in addition to the ones for files being monitored, and these other open descriptors also count in the total. macOS uses a different backend and does not suffer from this issue.

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QFileSystemWatcher::addPath(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*path*)

Adds *path* to the file system watcher if *path* exists. The path is not added if it
does not exist, or if it is already being monitored by the file system watcher.

If *path* specifies a directory, the
[directoryChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#directoryChanged)()
signal will be emitted when *path* is modified or removed from disk; otherwise the
[fileChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#fileChanged)()
signal is emitted when *path* is modified, renamed or removed.

If the watch was successful, true is returned.

Reasons for a watch failure are generally system-dependent, but may include the resource
not existing, access failures, or the total watch count limit, if the platform has one.

**Note:** There may be a system dependent limit to the number of files and directories
that can be monitored simultaneously. If this limit is been reached, *path* will not be
monitored, and false is returned.

**See also**
[addPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#addPaths)() and
[removePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#removePath)().

Qt 5 reference:

### [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) QFileSystemWatcher::addPaths(const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*paths*)

Adds each path in *paths* to the file system watcher. Paths are not added if they not
exist, or if they are already being monitored by the file system watcher.

If a path specifies a directory, the
[directoryChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#directoryChanged)()
signal will be emitted when the path is modified or removed from disk; otherwise the
[fileChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#fileChanged)()
signal is emitted when the path is modified, renamed, or removed.

The return value is a list of paths that could not be watched.

Reasons for a watch failure are generally system-dependent, but may include the resource
not existing, access failures, or the total watch count limit, if the platform has one.

**Note:** There may be a system dependent limit to the number of files and directories
that can be monitored simultaneously. If this limit has been reached, the excess *paths*
will not be monitored, and they will be added to the returned
[QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html).

**See also**
[addPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#addPath)() and
[removePaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#removePaths)().

### `[signal]` void QFileSystemWatcher::directoryChanged(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*path*)

This signal is emitted when the directory at a specified *path* is modified (e.g., when
a file is added or deleted) or removed from disk. Note that if there are several changes
during a short period of time, some of the changes might not emit this signal. However,
the last change in the sequence of changes will always generate this signal.

**Note:** This is a private signal. It can be used in signal connections but cannot be
emitted by the user.

**See also**
[fileChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#fileChanged)().

### `[signal]` void QFileSystemWatcher::fileChanged(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*path*)

This signal is emitted when the file at the specified *path* is modified, renamed or
removed from disk.

**Note:** As a safety measure, many applications save an open file by writing a new file
and then deleting the old one. In your slot function, you can check
`watcher.files().contains(path)`. If it returns `false`, check whether the file still
exists and then call `addPath()` to continue watching it.

**Note:** This is a private signal. It can be used in signal connections but cannot be
emitted by the user.

**See also**
[directoryChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#directoryChanged)().

### bool QFileSystemWatcher::removePath(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*path*)

Removes the specified *path* from the file system watcher.

If the watch is successfully removed, true is returned.

Reasons for watch removal failing are generally system-dependent, but may be due to the
path having already been deleted, for example.

**See also**
[removePaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#removePaths)()
and [addPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#addPath)().

Removes the specified *paths* from the file system watcher.

The return value is a list of paths which were not able to be unwatched successfully.

Reasons for watch removal failing are generally system-dependent, but may be due to the
path having already been deleted, for example.

[removePath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemwatcher.html#removePath)()

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QIODevice provides both a common implementation and an abstract interface for devices
that support reading and writing of blocks of data, such as
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html),
[QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) and
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html). QIODevice is abstract
and cannot be instantiated, but it is common to use the interface it defines to provide
device-independent I/O features. For example, Qt's XML classes operate on a QIODevice
pointer, allowing them to be used with various devices (such as files and buffers).

Before accessing the device,
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)() must be called to set
the correct
[OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) (such as
[ReadOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) or
[ReadWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum)). You
can then write to the device with
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)(), and read by
calling either [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), or
[readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readAll)(). Call
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#close)() when you are done
with the device.

QIODevice distinguishes between two types of devices: random-access devices and
sequential devices.

- Random-access devices support seeking to arbitrary positions using [seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)(). The current position in the file is available by calling [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#pos)(). [QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) and [QBuffer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuffer.html) are examples of random-access devices.
- Sequential devices don't support seeking to arbitrary positions. The data must be read in one pass. The functions [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#pos)() and [size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#size)() don't work for sequential devices. [QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html) and [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) are examples of sequential devices.

You can use
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)() to
determine the type of device.

QIODevice emits
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() when new data
is available for reading; for example, if new data has arrived on the network or if
additional data is appended to a file that you are reading from. You can call
[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)() to
determine the number of bytes that are currently available for reading. It's common to
use [bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)()
together with the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal when
programming with asynchronous devices such as
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html), where fragments of
data can arrive at arbitrary points in time. QIODevice emits the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal
every time a payload of data has been written to the device. Use
[bytesToWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesToWrite)() to
determine the current amount of data waiting to be written.

Certain subclasses of QIODevice, such as
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html) and
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html), are asynchronous. This
means that I/O functions such as
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)() or
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() always return
immediately, while communication with the device itself may happen when control goes
back to the event loop. QIODevice provides functions that allow you to force these
operations to be performed immediately, while blocking the calling thread and without
entering the event loop. This allows QIODevice subclasses to be used without an event
loop, or in a separate thread:

- [waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)() \- This function suspends operation in the calling thread until new data is available for reading.
- [waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)() \- This function suspends operation in the calling thread until one payload of data has been written to the device.
- waitFor....() \- Subclasses of QIODevice implement blocking functions for device-specific operations. For example, [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) has a function called [waitForStarted()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted) which suspends operation in the calling thread until the process has started.

Calling these functions from the main, GUI thread, may cause your user interface to
freeze. Example:

```
QProcess gzip;
gzip.start("gzip", QStringList() << "-c");
if (!gzip.waitForStarted())
    return false;

gzip.write("uncompressed data");

QByteArray compressed;
while (gzip.waitForReadyRead())
    compressed += gzip.readAll();
```

By subclassing QIODevice, you can provide the same interface to your own I/O devices.
Subclasses of QIODevice are only required to implement the protected
[readData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readData)() and
[writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)() functions.
QIODevice uses these functions to implement all its convenience functions, such as
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)(). QIODevice also
handles access control for you, so you can safely assume that the device is opened in
write mode if [writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)()
is called.

Some subclasses, such as [QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) and
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html), are implemented using
a memory buffer for intermediate storing of data. This reduces the number of required
device accessing calls, which are often very slow. Buffering makes functions like
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)() and
[putChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#putChar)() fast, as they can
operate on the memory buffer instead of directly on the device itself. Certain I/O
operations, however, don't work well with a buffer. For example, if several users open
the same device and read it character by character, they may end up reading the same
data when they meant to read a separate chunk each. For this reason, QIODevice allows
you to bypass any buffering by passing the Unbuffered flag to
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)(). When subclassing
QIODevice, remember to bypass any buffer you may use when the device is open in
Unbuffered mode.

Usually, the incoming data stream from an asynchronous device is fragmented, and chunks
of data can arrive at arbitrary points in time. To handle incomplete reads of data
structures, use the transaction mechanism implemented by QIODevice. See
[startTransaction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#startTransaction)()
and related functions for more details.

Some sequential devices support communicating via multiple channels. These channels
represent separate streams of data that have the property of independently sequenced
delivery. Once the device is opened, you can determine the number of channels by calling
the
[readChannelCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readChannelCount)()
and
[writeChannelCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeChannelCount)()
functions. To switch between channels, call
[setCurrentReadChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#setCurrentReadChannel)()
and
[setCurrentWriteChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#setCurrentWriteChannel)(),
respectively. QIODevice also provides additional signals to handle asynchronous
communication on a per-channel basis.

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::aboutToClose()

This signal is emitted when the device is about to close. Connect this signal if you
have operations that need to be performed before the device closes (e.g., if you have
data in a separate buffer that needs to be written to the device).

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.atEnd.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::atEnd() const

Returns `true` if the current read and write position is at the end of the device (i.e.
there is no more data available for reading on the device); otherwise returns `false`.

For some devices, atEnd() can return true even though there is more data to read. This
special case only applies to devices that generate data in direct response to you
calling [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() (e.g., `/dev`
or `/proc` files on Unix and macOS, or console input / `stdin` on all platforms).

**See also**
[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)(),
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(), and
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.bytesAvailable.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::bytesAvailable() const

Returns the number of bytes that are available for reading. This function is commonly
used with sequential devices to determine the number of bytes to allocate in a buffer
before reading.

Subclasses that reimplement this function must call the base implementation in order to
include the size of the buffer of
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). Example:

```
qint64 CustomDevice::bytesAvailable() const
{
    return buffer.size() + QIODevice::bytesAvailable();
}
```

**See also**
[bytesToWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesToWrite)(),
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)(), and
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)().

### `[virtual]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::bytesToWrite() const

For buffered devices, this function returns the number of bytes waiting to be written.
For devices with no buffer, this function returns 0\.

Subclasses that reimplement this function must call the base implementation in order to
include the size of the buffer of
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)(),

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.bytesWritten.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::bytesWritten([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *bytes*)

This signal is emitted every time a payload of data has been written to the device's
current write channel. The *bytes* argument is set to the number of bytes that were
written in this payload.

bytesWritten() is not emitted recursively; if you reenter the event loop or call
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)()
inside a slot connected to the bytesWritten() signal, the signal will not be reemitted
(although
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)()
may still return true).

**See also** [readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.canReadLine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::canReadLine() const

Returns `true` if a complete line of data can be read from the device; otherwise returns
`false`.

Note that unbuffered devices, which have no way of determining what can be read, always
return false.

This function is often called in conjunction with the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal.

Subclasses that reimplement this function must call the base implementation in order to
include the contents of the
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html)'s buffer. Example:

```
bool CustomDevice::canReadLine() const
{
    return buffer.contains('\n') || QIODevice::canReadLine();
}
```

**See also** [readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)()
and [readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)().

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::channelBytesWritten(int *channel*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *bytes*)

This signal is emitted every time a payload of data has been written to the device. The
*bytes* argument is set to the number of bytes that were written in this payload, while
*channel* is the channel they were written to. Unlike
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)(), it is
emitted regardless of the [current write
channel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#currentWriteChannel).

channelBytesWritten() can be emitted recursively \- even for the same channel.

[channelReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#channelReadyRead)().

determine how many bytes can be read.

This is a convenience function which checks if the
[OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) of the

[ReadOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) flag.

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.isSequential.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::isSequential() const

Returns `true` if this device is sequential; otherwise returns false.

Sequential devices, as opposed to a random-access devices, have no concept of a start,
an end, a size, or a current position, and they do not support seeking. You can only
read from the device when it reports that data is available. The most common example of
a sequential device is a network socket. On Unix, special files such as /dev/zero and
fifo pipes are sequential.

Regular files, on the other hand, do support random access. They have both a size and a
current position, and they also support seeking backwards and forwards in the data
stream. Regular files are non-sequential.

**See also**
[bytesAvailable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesAvailable)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.peek.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::peek(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads at most *maxSize* bytes from the device into *data*, without side effects (i.e.,
if you call [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() after
peek(), you will get the same data). Returns the number of bytes read. If an error
occurs, such as when attempting to peek a device opened in
[WriteOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) mode,
this function returns -1.

0 is returned when no more data is available for reading.

Example:

```
bool isExeFile(QFile *file)
{
    char buf[2];
    if (file->peek(buf, sizeof(buf)) == sizeof(buf))
        return (buf[0] == 'M' && buf[1] == 'Z');
    return false;
}
```

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QIODevice::peek([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

This is an overloaded function.

Peeks at most *maxSize* bytes from the device, returning the data peeked as a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html).

Example:

```
bool isExeFile(QFile *file)
{
    return file->peek(2) == "MZ";
}
```

This function has no way of reporting errors; returning an empty
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) can mean either that no
data was currently available for peeking, or that an error occurred.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.pos.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::pos() const

For random-access devices, this function returns the position that data is written to or
read from. For sequential devices or closed devices, where there is no concept of a
"current position", 0 is returned.

The current read/write position of the device is maintained internally by
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), so reimplementing this
function is not necessary. When subclassing
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), use
[QIODevice::seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)() to notify
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) about changes in the
device position.

**See also**
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)() and
[seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.read.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::read(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads at most *maxSize* bytes from the device into *data*, and returns the number of
bytes read. If an error occurs, such as when attempting to read from a device opened in
[WriteOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) mode,
this function returns -1.

0 is returned when no more data is available for reading. However, reading past the end
of the stream is considered an error, so this function returns -1 in those cases (that
is, reading on a closed socket or after a process has died).

**See also** [readData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readData)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QIODevice::read([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

This is an overloaded function.

Reads at most *maxSize* bytes from the device, and returns the data read as a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html).

This function has no way of reporting errors; returning an empty
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) can mean either that no
data was currently available for reading, or that an error occurred.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QIODevice::readAll()

This function has no way of reporting errors; returning an empty

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.readChannelFin.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::readChannelFinished()

This signal is emitted when the input (reading) stream is closed in this device. It is
emitted as soon as the closing is detected, which means that there might still be data
available for reading with
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also** [atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#atEnd)() and
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.readData.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual protected]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::readData(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads up to *maxSize* bytes from the device into *data*, and returns the number of bytes
read or -1 if an error occurred.

If there are no bytes to be read and there can never be more bytes available (examples
include socket closed, pipe closed, sub-process finished), this function returns -1.

This function is called by
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). Reimplement this
function when creating a subclass of
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

When reimplementing this function it is important that this function reads all the
required data before returning. This is required in order for
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) to be able to operate
on the class. [QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) assumes
all the requested information was read and therefore does not retry reading if there was
a problem.

This function might be called with a maxSize of 0, which can be used to perform
post-reading operations.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and
[writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)().
signatures: readData(self, data: str, maxlen: int) -> int

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.readLine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::readLine(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

This function reads a line of ASCII characters from the device, up to a maximum of
*maxSize* \- 1 bytes, stores the characters in *data*, and returns the number of bytes
read. If a line could not be read but no error occurred, this function returns 0\. If an
error occurs, this function returns the length of what could be read, or -1 if nothing
was read.

A terminating '\\0' byte is always appended to *data*, so *maxSize* must be larger than
1\.

Data is read until either of the following conditions are met:

- The first '\\n' character is read.
- *maxSize* \- 1 bytes are read.
- The end of the device data is detected.

For example, the following code reads a line of characters from a file:

```
QFile file("box.txt");
if (file.open(QFile::ReadOnly)) {
    char buf[1024];
    qint64 lineLength = file.readLine(buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (lineLength != -1) {
        // the line is available in buf
    }
}
```

The newline character ('\\n') is included in the buffer. If a newline is not encountered
before maxSize \- 1 bytes are read, a newline will not be inserted into the buffer. On
windows newline characters are replaced with '\\n'.

This function calls
[readLineData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLineData)(), which
is implemented using repeated calls to
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(). You can provide
a more efficient implementation by reimplementing
[readLineData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLineData)() in your
own subclass.

**See also** [getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(),
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(), and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QIODevice::readLine([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize* \= 0\)

This is an overloaded function.

Reads a line from the device, but no more than *maxSize* characters, and returns the
result as a byte array.

This function has no way of reporting errors; returning an empty
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) can mean either that no
data was currently available for reading, or that an error occurred.

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.readLineData.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::readLineData(char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Reads up to *maxSize* characters into *data* and returns the number of characters read.

This function is called by
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and provides
its base implementation, using
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(). Buffered devices
can improve the performance of
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() by
reimplementing this function.

[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() appends a '\\0'
byte to *data*; readLineData() does not need to do this.

If you reimplement this function, be careful to return the correct value: it should
return the number of bytes read in this line, including the terminating newline, or 0 if
there is no line to be read at this point. If an error occurs, it should return -1 if
and only if no bytes were read. Reading past EOF is considered an error.
signatures: readLineData(self, data: str, maxlen: int) -> int

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.readyRead.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QIODevice::readyRead()

This signal is emitted once every time new data is available for reading from the
device's current read channel. It will only be emitted again once new data is available,
such as when a new payload of network data has arrived on your network socket, or when a
new block of data has been appended to your device.

readyRead() is not emitted recursively; if you reenter the event loop or call
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)()
inside a slot connected to the readyRead() signal, the signal will not be reemitted
(although
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)()
may still return true).

Note for developers implementing classes derived from
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html): you should always emit
readyRead() when new data has arrived (do not emit it only because there's data still to
be read in your buffers). Do not emit readyRead() in other conditions.

**See also**
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.reset.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::reset()

Seeks to the start of input for random-access devices. Returns true on success;
otherwise returns `false` (for example, if the device is not open).

Note that when using a
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) on a
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html), calling reset() on the
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) will not have the expected result
because [QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) buffers the
file. Use the
[QTextStream::seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#seek)() function
instead.

**See also** [seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#seek)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.seek.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::seek([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *pos*)

For random-access devices, this function sets the current position to *pos*, returning
true on success, or false if an error occurred. For sequential devices, the default
behavior is to produce a warning and return false.

When subclassing [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), you
must call QIODevice::seek() at the start of your function to ensure integrity with
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html)'s built-in buffer.

**See also** [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#pos)() and
[isSequential](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isSequential)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.setErrorString.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[protected]` void QIODevice::setErrorString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*str*)

Sets the human readable description of the last device error that occurred to *str*.

**See also**
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#errorString)().

### void QIODevice::setTextModeEnabled(bool *enabled*)

If *enabled* is true, this function sets the
[Text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) flag on the
device; otherwise the
[Text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) flag is
removed. This feature is useful for classes that provide custom end-of-line handling on
a [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

The IO device should be opened before calling this function.

**See also**
[isTextModeEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#isTextModeEnabled)(),
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)(), and
[setOpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#setOpenMode)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.ungetChar.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QIODevice::ungetChar(char *c*)

Puts the character *c* back into the device, and decrements the current position unless
the position is 0\. This function is usually called to "undo" a
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)() operation, such
as when writing a backtracking parser.

If *c* was not previously read from the device, the behavior is undefined.

**Note:** This function is not available while a transaction is in progress.

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.waitForBytesWr.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::waitForBytesWritten(int *msecs*)

For buffered devices, this function waits until a payload of buffered written data has
been written to the device and the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal
has been emitted, or until *msecs* milliseconds have passed. If msecs is -1, this
function will not time out. For unbuffered devices, it returns immediately.

Returns `true` if a payload of data was written to the device; otherwise returns `false`
(i.e. if the operation timed out, or if an error occurred).

This function can operate without an event loop. It is useful when writing non-GUI
applications and when performing I/O operations in a non-GUI thread.

If called from within a slot connected to the
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() signal,
[bytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#bytesWritten)() will
not be reemitted.

Reimplement this function to provide a blocking API for a custom device. The default
implementation does nothing, and returns `false`.

**Warning:** Calling this function from the main (GUI) thread might cause your user
interface to freeze.

**See also**
[waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForReadyRead)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.waitForReadyRe.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QIODevice::waitForReadyRead(int *msecs*)

Blocks until new data is available for reading and the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal has
been emitted, or until *msecs* milliseconds have passed. If msecs is -1, this function
will not time out.

Returns `true` if new data is available for reading; otherwise returns false (if the
operation timed out or if an error occurred).

This function can operate without an event loop. It is useful when writing non-GUI
applications and when performing I/O operations in a non-GUI thread.

If called from within a slot connected to the
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() signal,
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() will not be
reemitted.

Reimplement this function to provide a blocking API for a custom device. The default
implementation does nothing, and returns `false`.

**Warning:** Calling this function from the main (GUI) thread might cause your user
interface to freeze.

**See also**
[waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#waitForBytesWritten)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::write(const char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Writes at most *maxSize* bytes of data from *data* to the device. Returns the number of
bytes that were actually written, or -1 if an error occurred.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() and

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::write(const char \**data*)

This is an overloaded function.

Writes data from a zero-terminated string of 8-bit characters to the device. Returns the
number of bytes that were actually written, or -1 if an error occurred. This is
equivalent to

```
...
QIODevice::write(data, qstrlen(data));
...
```

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() and
[writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)().

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::write(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*byteArray*)

This is an overloaded function.

Writes the content of *byteArray* to the device. Returns the number of bytes that were
actually written, or -1 if an error occurred.

[writeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#writeData)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QIODevice.writeData.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual protected]` [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QIODevice::writeData(const char \**data*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxSize*)

Writes up to *maxSize* bytes from *data* to the device. Returns the number of bytes
written, or -1 if an error occurred.

This function is called by
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html). Reimplement this
function when creating a subclass of
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html).

When reimplementing this function it is important that this function writes all the data
available before returning. This is required in order for
[QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) to be able to operate
on the class. [QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatastream.html) assumes
all the information was written and therefore does not retry writing if there was a
problem.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() and
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A JSON array is a list of values. The list can be manipulated by inserting and removing
[QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html)'s from the array.

A QJsonArray can be converted to and from a
[QVariantList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#QVariantList-typedef).
You can query the number of entries with
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#size)(),
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#insert)(), and
[removeAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#removeAt)() entries from
it and iterate over its content using the standard C\+\+ iterator pattern.

QJsonArray is an implicitly shared class and shares the data with the document it has
been created from as long as it is not being modified.

You can convert the array to and from text based JSON through
[QJsonDocument](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html).

### void QJsonArray::insert(int *i*, const [QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html) \&*value*)

Inserts *value* at index position *i* in the array. If *i* is `0`, the value is
prepended to the array. If *i* is
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#size)(), the value is appended
to the array.

**See also** [append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#append)(),
[prepend](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#prepend)(),
[replace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#replace)(), and
[removeAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#removeAt)().

Inserts *value* before the position pointed to by *before*, and returns an iterator

[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html#insert)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QJsonDocument is a class that wraps a complete JSON document and can read and write this
document both from a UTF-8 encoded text based representation as well as Qt's own binary
format.

A JSON document can be converted from its text-based representation to a QJsonDocument
using
[QJsonDocument::fromJson](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html#fromJson)().
[toJson](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html#toJson)() converts it
back to text. The parser is very fast and efficient and converts the JSON to the binary
representation used by Qt.

Validity of the parsed document can be queried with
![isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html#isNull)()

A document can be queried as to whether it contains an array or an object using
[isArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html#isArray)() and
[isObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html#isObject)(). The array
or object contained in the document can be retrieved using
[array](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html#array)() or
[object](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html#object)() and then read
or manipulated.

A document can also be created from a stored binary representation using
fromBinaryData() or fromRawData().

PythonQt.QtCore.QJsonObject.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A JSON object is a list of key value pairs, where the keys are unique strings and the
values are represented by a
[QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html).

A QJsonObject can be converted to and from a
[QVariantMap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#QVariantMap-typedef). You
can query the number of (key, value) pairs with
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonobject.html#size)(),
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonobject.html#insert)(), and
[remove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonobject.html#remove)() entries from it
and iterate over its content using the standard C\+\+ iterator pattern.

QJsonObject is an implicitly shared class, and shares the data with the document it has
been created from as long as it is not being modified.

You can convert the object to and from text based JSON through
[QJsonDocument](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsondocument.html).

## Detailed Description

A value in JSON can be one of 6 basic types:

JSON is a format to store structured data. It has 6 basic data types:

- bool [QJsonValue::Bool](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum)
- double [QJsonValue::Double](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum)
- string [QJsonValue::String](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum)
- array [QJsonValue::Array](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum)
- object [QJsonValue::Object](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum)
- null [QJsonValue::Null](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum)

A value can represent any of the above data types. In addition, QJsonValue has one
special flag to represent undefined values. This can be queried with
[isUndefined](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#isUndefined)().

The type of the value can be queried with
[type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#type)() or accessors like
[isBool](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#isBool)(),
[isString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#isString)(), and so on.
Likewise, the value can be converted to the type stored in it using the
[toBool](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#toBool)(),
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#toString)() and so on.

Values are strictly typed internally and contrary to
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) will not attempt to do any
implicit type conversions. This implies that converting to a type that is not stored in
the value will return a default constructed return value.

### QJsonValueRef

[QJsonValueRef](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#qjsonvalueref) is a
helper class for [QJsonArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html) and
[QJsonObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonobject.html). When you get an
object of type
[QJsonValueRef](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#qjsonvalueref), you
can use it as if it were a reference to a QJsonValue. If you assign to it, the
assignment will apply to the element in the
[QJsonArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html) or
[QJsonObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonobject.html) from which you got
the reference.

The following methods return
[QJsonValueRef](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#qjsonvalueref):

- [QJsonArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonarray.html)::operator\[\](int i)
- [QJsonObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonobject.html)::operator\[\](const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \& key) const

Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#QJsonValue) QJsonValue::fromVariant(const [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) \&*variant*)

Converts *variant* to a [QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html)
and returns it.

The conversion will convert [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)
types as follows:

| Source type | Destination type |
| --- | --- |
| - [QMetaType::Nullptr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::Null](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum) |
| - [QMetaType::Bool](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::Bool](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum) |
| - [QMetaType::Int](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) - [QMetaType::UInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) - [QMetaType::LongLong](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) - [QMetaType::ULongLong](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) - [QMetaType::Float](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) - [QMetaType::Double](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::Double](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum) |
| - [QMetaType::QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::String](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum) |
| - [QMetaType::QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) - [QMetaType::QVariantList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::Array](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum) |
| - [QMetaType::QVariantMap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) - [QMetaType::QVariantHash](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::Object](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum) |
| - [QMetaType::QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::String](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum). The conversion will use [QUrl::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toString)() with flag [QUrl::FullyEncoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum), so as to ensure maximum compatibility in parsing the URL |
| - [QMetaType::QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::String](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum). Since Qt 5.11, the resulting string will not include braces |
| - [QMetaType::QCborValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | Whichever type [QCborValue::toJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcborvalue.html#toJsonValue)() returns. |
| - [QMetaType::QCborArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | [QJsonValue::Array](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#Type-enum). See [QCborValue::toJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcborvalue.html#toJsonValue)() for conversion restrictions. |
| - [QMetaType::QCborMap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) | QJsonValue::Map. See [QCborValue::toJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcborvalue.html#toJsonValue)() for conversion restrictions and the "stringification" of map keys. |



##### Loss of information and other types

[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) can carry more information
than is representable in JSON. If the
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) is not one of the types
above, the conversion is not guaranteed and is subject to change in future versions of
Qt, as the UUID one did. Code should strive not to use any other types than those listed
above.

If [QVariant::isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#isNull)() returns
true, a null [QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html) is
returned or inserted into the list or object, regardless of the type carried by
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html). Note the behavior change
in Qt 6.0 affecting
[QVariant::isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#isNull)() also
affects this function.

A floating point value that is either an infinity or NaN will be converted to a null
JSON value. The values outside the range of ±2^53 may lose precision, because they are
converted to a double [QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html).

For other types not listed above, a conversion to string will be attempted, usually but
not always by calling
[QVariant::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#toString)(). If
the conversion fails the value is replaced by a null JSON value. Note that
[QVariant::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#toString)() is
also lossy for the majority of types. For example, if the passed
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) is representing raw byte
array data, it is recommended to pre-encode it to
[Base64](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4648.txt) (or another lossless encoding), otherwise
a lossy conversion using
[QString::fromUtf8](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#fromUtf8)() will be
used.

Please note that the conversions via
[QVariant::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#toString)() are
subject to change at any time. Both
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) and
[QJsonValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html) may be extended in the
future to support more types, which will result in a change in how this function
performs conversions.

**See also** [toVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qjsonvalue.html#toVariant)()
and
[QCborValue::fromVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcborvalue.html#fromVariant)().

## Detailed Description

An instance of a QLibrary object operates on a single shared object file (which we call
a "library", but is also known as a "DLL"). A QLibrary provides access to the
functionality in the library in a platform independent way. You can either pass a file
name in the constructor, or set it explicitly with
[setFileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#fileName-prop)(). When
loading the library, QLibrary searches in all the system-specific library locations
(e.g. `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` on Unix), unless the file name has an absolute path.

If the file name is an absolute path then an attempt is made to load this path first. If
the file cannot be found, QLibrary tries the name with different platform-specific file
prefixes, like "lib" on Unix and Mac, and suffixes, like ".so" on Unix, ".dylib" on the
Mac, or ".dll" on Windows.

If the file path is not absolute then QLibrary modifies the search order to try the
system-specific prefixes and suffixes first, followed by the file path specified.

This makes it possible to specify shared libraries that are only identified by their
basename (i.e. without their suffix), so the same code will work on different operating
systems yet still minimise the number of attempts to find the library.

The most important functions are
[load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#load)() to dynamically load the
library file, [isLoaded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#isLoaded)() to
check whether loading was successful, and
[resolve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#resolve)() to resolve a
symbol in the library. The
[resolve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#resolve)() function
implicitly tries to load the library if it has not been loaded yet. Multiple instances
of QLibrary can be used to access the same physical library. Once loaded, libraries
remain in memory until the application terminates. You can attempt to unload a library
using [unload](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#unload)(), but if other
instances of QLibrary are using the same library, the call will fail, and unloading will
only happen when every instance has called
[unload](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#unload)().

A typical use of QLibrary is to resolve an exported symbol in a library, and to call the
C function that this symbol represents. This is called "explicit linking" in contrast to
"implicit linking", which is done by the link step in the build process when linking an
executable against a library.

The following code snippet loads a library, resolves the symbol "mysymbol", and calls
the function if everything succeeded. If something goes wrong, e.g. the library file
does not exist or the symbol is not defined, the function pointer will be `nullptr` and
won't be called.

```
QLibrary myLib("mylib");
typedef void (*MyPrototype)();
MyPrototype myFunction = (MyPrototype) myLib.resolve("mysymbol");
if (myFunction)
    myFunction();
```

The symbol must be exported as a C function from the library for
[resolve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#resolve)() to work. This
means that the function must be wrapped in an `extern "C"` block if the library is
compiled with a C\+\+ compiler. On Windows, this also requires the use of a `dllexport`
macro; see [resolve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#resolve)() for the
details of how this is done. For convenience, there is a static
[resolve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#resolve)() function which you
can use if you just want to call a function in a library without explicitly loading the
library first:

```
typedef void (*MyPrototype)();
MyPrototype myFunction =

### fileName : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the file name of the library

We recommend omitting the file's suffix in the file name, since
[QLibrary](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html) will automatically look for
the file with the appropriate suffix (see
[isLibrary](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#isLibrary)()).

When loading the library, [QLibrary](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html)
searches in all system-specific library locations (for example, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` on
Unix), unless the file name has an absolute path. After loading the library
successfully, fileName() returns the fully-qualified file name of the library, including
the full path to the library if one was given in the constructor or passed to
setFileName().

For example, after successfully loading the "GL" library on Unix platforms, fileName()
will return "libGL.so". If the file name was originally passed as "/usr/lib/libGL",
fileName() will return "/usr/lib/libGL.so".

PythonQt.QtCore.QLibrary.loadHints.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### loadHints : [LoadHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#LoadHint-enum)

Give the [load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#load)() function some
hints on how it should behave.

You can give some hints on how the symbols are resolved. Usually, the symbols are not
resolved at load time, but resolved lazily, (that is, when
[resolve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#resolve)() is called). If you
set the loadHints to
[ResolveAllSymbolsHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#LoadHint-enum),
then all symbols will be resolved at load time if the platform supports it.

Setting
[ExportExternalSymbolsHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#LoadHint-enum)
will make the external symbols in the library available for resolution in subsequent
loaded libraries.

If
[LoadArchiveMemberHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#LoadHint-enum)
is set, the file name is composed of two components: A path which is a reference to an
archive file followed by the second component which is the reference to the archive
member. For instance, the
[fileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#fileName-prop)
`libGL.a(shr_64.o)` will refer to the library `shr_64.o` in the archive file named
`libGL.a`. This is only supported on the AIX platform.

The interpretation of the load hints is platform dependent, and if you use it you are
probably making some assumptions on which platform you are compiling for, so use them
only if you understand the consequences of them.

By default, none of these flags are set, so libraries will be loaded with lazy symbol
resolution, and will not export external symbols for resolution in other
dynamically-loaded libraries.

**Note:** Setting this property after the library has been loaded has no effect and
loadHints() will not reflect those changes.

**Note:** This property is shared among all
[QLibrary](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html) instances that refer to the
same library.

**Access functions:**

| QLibrary::LoadHints | **loadHints**() const |

### bool QLibrary::unload()

Unloads the library and returns `true` if the library could be unloaded; otherwise
returns `false`.

call this function.

instance has called unload().

[load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibrary.html#load)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QLine describes a finite length line (or a line segment) on a two-dimensional surface.
The start and end points of the line are specified using integer point accuracy for
coordinates. Use the [QLineF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html)
constructor to retrieve a floating point copy.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |

The positions of the line's start and end points can be retrieved using the
[p1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#p1)(),
[x1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#x1)(),
[y1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#y1)(),
[p2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#p2)(),
[x2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#x2)(), and
[y2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#y2)() functions. The
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#dy)() functions return the horizontal
and vertical components of the line. Use
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#isNull)() to determine whether
the QLine represents a valid line or a null line.

Finally, the line can be translated a given offset using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html#translate)() function.

PythonQt.QtCore.QLineF.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QLineF describes a finite length line (or line segment) on a two-dimensional surface.
QLineF defines the start and end points of the line using floating point accuracy for
coordinates. Use the [toLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#toLine)()
function to retrieve an integer based copy of this line.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |

The positions of the line's start and end points can be retrieved using the
[p1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#p1)(),
[x1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#x1)(),
[y1](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#y1)(),
[p2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#p2)(),
[x2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#x2)(), and
[y2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#y2)() functions. The
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#dy)() functions return the
horizontal and vertical components of the line, respectively.

The line's length can be retrieved using the
[length](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#length)() function, and altered
using the [setLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#setLength)()
function. Similarly, [angle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#angle)() and
[setAngle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#setAngle)() are respectively
used for retrieving and altering the angle of the line. Use the
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#isNull)() function to determine
whether the QLineF represents a valid line or a null line.

The [intersects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#intersects)() function
determines the
[IntersectionType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#IntersectionType-alias)
for this line and a given line, while the
[angleTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#angleTo)() function returns the
angle between the lines. In addition, the
[unitVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#unitVector)() function
returns a line that has the same starting point as this line, but with a length of only
1, while the
[normalVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#normalVector)() function
returns a line that is perpendicular to this line with the same starting point and
length.

Finally, the line can be translated a given offset using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#translate)() function, and
can be traversed using the
[pointAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlinef.html#pointAt)() function.

### Constraints

[QLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html) is limited to the minimum and
maximum values for the `int` type. Operations on a
[QLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qline.html) that could potentially result in
values outside this range will result in undefined behavior.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QLocale is initialized with a language/country pair in its constructor and offers
number-to-string and string-to-number conversion functions similar to those in
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

Example:

```
QLocale egyptian(QLocale::Arabic, QLocale::Egypt);
QString s1 = egyptian.toString(1.571429E+07, 'e');
QString s2 = egyptian.toString(10);

double d = egyptian.toDouble(s1);
int i = egyptian.toInt(s2);
```

QLocale supports the concept of a default locale, which is determined from the system's
locale settings at application startup. The default locale can be changed by calling the
static member
[setDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#setDefault)(). Setting the
default locale has the following effects:

- If a QLocale object is constructed with the default constructor, it will use the default locale's settings.
- [QString::toInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#toInt)(), [QString::toDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#toDouble)(), etc., interpret the string according to the default locale. If this fails, it falls back on the "C" locale.
- [QString::arg](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#arg)() uses the default locale to format a number when its position specifier in the format string contains an 'L', e.g. "%L1".

The following example illustrates how to use QLocale directly:

```
QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(QLocale::Hebrew, QLocale::Israel));
QLocale hebrew; // Constructs a default QLocale
QString s1 = hebrew.toString(15714.3, 'e');

bool ok;
double d;

QLocale::setDefault(QLocale::C);
d = QString("1234,56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == false, d == 0
d = QString("1234.56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == true,  d == 1234.56

QLocale::setDefault(QLocale::German);
d = QString("1234,56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == false, d == 0
d = QString("1234.56").toDouble(&ok);   // ok == true,  d == 1234.56

QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(QLocale::English, QLocale::UnitedStates));
QString str = QString("%1 %L2 %L3")
      .arg(12345).arg(12345).arg(12345, 0, 16);
// str == "12345 12,345 3039"
```

When a language/country pair is specified in the constructor, one of three things can
happen:

- If the language/country pair is found in the database, it is used.
- If the language is found but the country is not, or if the country is `AnyCountry`, the language is used with the most appropriate available country (for example, Germany for German),
- If neither the language nor the country are found, QLocale defaults to the default locale (see [setDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#setDefault)()).

Use [language](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#language)() and
[country](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#country)() to determine the
actual language and country values used.

An alternative method for constructing a QLocale object is by specifying the locale
name.

```
QLocale korean("ko");
QLocale swiss("de_CH");
```

This constructor converts the locale name to a language/country pair; it does not use
the system locale database.

**Note:** For the current keyboard input locale take a look at
[QInputMethod::locale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethod.html#locale-prop)().

QLocale's data is based on Common Locale Data Repository v39.

Returns the dash-separated language, script and country (and possibly other BCP47

Unlike the [uiLanguages](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#uiLanguages)()

PythonQt.QtCore.QLocale.c.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#QLocale) QLocale::c()

Returns a [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) object initialized
to the "C" locale.

This locale is based on en\_US but with various quirks of its own, such as simplified
number formatting and its own date formatting. It implements the POSIX standards that
describe the behavior of standard library functions of the "C" programming language.

Among other things, this means its collation order is based on the ASCII values of
letters, so that (for case-sensitive sorting) all upper-case letters sort before any
lower-case one (rather than each letter's upper- and lower-case forms sorting adjacent
to one another, before the next letter's two forms).

**See also** [system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)().
