### `[static]` void QLocale::setDefault(const [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#QLocale) \&*locale*)

Sets the global default locale to *locale*. These values are used when a
[QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) object is constructed with no
arguments. If this function is not called, the system's locale is used.

**Warning:** In a multithreaded application, the default locale should be set at
application startup, before any non-GUI threads are created.

**Warning:** This function is not
[reentrant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/threads-reentrancy.html).

[QDateTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)()

**Note:** The month and day names used must be given in the user's local language.

If the string could not be parsed, returns an invalid
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html). If the string can be
parsed and represents an invalid date-time (e.g. in a gap skipped by a time-zone
transition), an invalid [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html)
is returned, whose toMSecsSinceEpoch() represents a near-by date-time that is valid.
Passing that to fromMSecsSinceEpoch() will produce a valid date-time that isn't
faithfully represented by the string parsed.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

### double QLocale::toDouble(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*s*, bool \**ok* \= nullptr) const

Returns the double represented by the localized string *s*.

Returns an infinity if the conversion overflows or 0.0 if the conversion fails for any
other reason (e.g. underflow).

If *ok* is not `nullptr`, failure is reported by setting \**ok* to `false`, and success
by setting \**ok* to `true`.

This function does not fall back to the 'C' locale if the string cannot be interpreted
in this locale.

```
bool ok;
double d;

QLocale c(QLocale::C);
d = c.toDouble("1234.56", &ok);  // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = c.toDouble("1,234.56", &ok); // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = c.toDouble("1234,56", &ok);  // ok == false, d == 0

QLocale german(QLocale::German);
d = german.toDouble("1234,56", &ok);  // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = german.toDouble("1.234,56", &ok); // ok == true,  d == 1234.56
d = german.toDouble("1234.56", &ok);  // ok == false, d == 0

d = german.toDouble("1.234", &ok);    // ok == true,  d == 1234.0
```

Notice that the last conversion returns 1234.0, because '.' is the thousands group
separator in the German locale.

This function ignores leading and trailing whitespace.

**See also** [toFloat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toFloat)(),
[toInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toInt)(), and
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QLockFile.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A lock file can be used to prevent multiple processes from accessing concurrently the
same resource. For instance, a configuration file on disk, or a socket, a port, a region
of shared memory...

Serialization is only guaranteed if all processes that access the shared resource use
QLockFile, with the same file path.

QLockFile supports two use cases: to protect a resource for a short-term operation (e.g.
verifying if a configuration file has changed before saving new settings), and for
long-lived protection of a resource (e.g. a document opened by a user in an editor) for
an indefinite amount of time.

When protecting for a short-term operation, it is acceptable to call
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)() and wait until any
running operation finishes. When protecting a resource over a long time, however, the
application should always call
[setStaleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#setStaleLockTime)(0)
and then [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() with a
short timeout, in order to warn the user that the resource is locked.

If the process holding the lock crashes, the lock file stays on disk and can prevent any
other process from accessing the shared resource, ever. For this reason, QLockFile tries
to detect such a "stale" lock file, based on the process ID written into the file. To
cover the situation that the process ID got reused meanwhile, the current process name
is compared to the name of the process that corresponds to the process ID from the lock
file. If the process names differ, the lock file is considered stale. Additionally, the
last modification time of the lock file (30s by default, for the use case of a
short-lived operation) is taken into account. If the lock file is found to be stale, it
will be deleted.

For the use case of protecting a resource over a long time, you should therefore call
[setStaleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#setStaleLockTime)(0),
and when [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() returns
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum),
inform the user that the document is locked, possibly using
[getLockInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#getLockInfo)() for more
details.

**Note:** On Windows, this class has problems detecting a stale lock if the machine's
hostname contains characters outside the US-ASCII character set.

### bool QLockFile::getLockInfo([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) \**pid*, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \**hostname*, [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \**appname*) const

Retrieves information about the current owner of the lock file.

If [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() returns
`false`, and [error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#error)() returns
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum),
this function can be called to find out more information about the existing lock file:

- the PID of the application (returned in *pid*)
- the *hostname* it's running on (useful in case of networked filesystems),
- the name of the application which created it (returned in *appname*),

Note that [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)()
automatically deleted the file if there is no running application with this PID, so
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum) can
only happen if there is an application with this PID (it could be unrelated though).

This can be used to inform users about the existing lock file and give them the choice
to delete it. After removing the file using
[removeStaleLockFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#removeStaleLockFile)(),
the application can call
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() again.

This function returns `true` if the information could be successfully retrieved, false
if the lock file doesn't exist or doesn't contain the expected data. This can happen if
the lock file was deleted between the time where
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() failed and the
call to this function. Simply call
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() again if this
happens.

### bool QLockFile::lock()

Creates the lock file.

If another process (or another thread) has created the lock file already, this function
will block until that process (or thread) releases it.

Calling this function multiple times on the same lock from the same thread without
unlocking first is not allowed. This function will *dead-lock* when the file is locked
recursively.

Returns `true` if the lock was acquired, false if it could not be acquired due to an
unrecoverable error, such as no permissions in the parent directory.

**See also** [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#unlock)() and
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)().

### bool QLockFile::removeStaleLockFile()

Attempts to forcefully remove an existing lock file.

Calling this is not recommended when protecting a short-lived operation:
[QLockFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html) already takes care of
removing lock files after they are older than
[staleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#staleLockTime)().

This method should only be called when protecting a resource for a long time, i.e. with
[staleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#staleLockTime)(0), and
after [tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() returned
[LockFailedError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#LockError-enum), and
the user agreed on removing the lock file.

Returns `true` on success, false if the lock file couldn't be removed. This happens on
Windows, when the application owning the lock is still running.

PythonQt.QtCore.QLockFile.setStaleLockTi.doc:

### void QLockFile::setStaleLockTime(int *staleLockTime*)

Sets *staleLockTime* to be the time in milliseconds after which a lock file is
considered stale. The default value is 30000, i.e. 30 seconds. If your application
typically keeps the file locked for more than 30 seconds (for instance while saving
megabytes of data for 2 minutes), you should set a bigger value using
setStaleLockTime().

The value of *staleLockTime* is used by
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)() and
[tryLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#tryLock)() in order to
determine when an existing lock file is considered stale, i.e. left over by a crashed
process. This is useful for the case where the PID got reused meanwhile, so one way to
detect a stale lock file is by the fact that it has been around for a long time.

**See also**
[staleLockTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#staleLockTime)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QLockFile.tryLock.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QLockFile::tryLock(int *timeout* \= 0\)

Attempts to create the lock file. This function returns `true` if the lock was obtained;
otherwise it returns `false`. If another process (or another thread) has created the
lock file already, this function will wait for at most *timeout* milliseconds for the
lock file to become available.

Note: Passing a negative number as the *timeout* is equivalent to calling
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)(), i.e. this function
will wait forever until the lock file can be locked if *timeout* is negative.

If the lock was obtained, it must be released with
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#unlock)() before another
process (or thread) can successfully lock it.

Calling this function multiple times on the same lock from the same thread without
unlocking first is not allowed, this function will *always* return false when attempting
to lock the file recursively.

**See also** [lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#lock)() and
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlockfile.html#unlock)().

## Detailed Description

QMessageAuthenticationCode supports all cryptographic hashes which are supported by
[QCryptographicHash](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcryptographichash.html).

To generate message authentication code, pass hash algorithm
[QCryptographicHash::Algorithm](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcryptographichash.html#Algorithm-enum)
to constructor, then set key and message by
[setKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#setKey)()
and
[addData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#addData)()
functions. Result can be acquired by
[result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#result)()
function.

```
    QByteArray key = "key";
    QByteArray message = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    ...
    QMessageAuthenticationCode code(QCryptographicHash::Sha1);
    code.setKey(key);
    code.addData(message);
    code.result().toHex();      // returns "de7c9b85b8b78aa6bc8a7a36f70a90701c9db4d9"
```

Alternatively, this effect can be achieved by providing message, key and method to
[hash](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmessageauthenticationcode.html#hash)()
method.

```
    QMessageAuthenticationCode::hash(message, key, QCryptographicHash::Sha1).toHex();
```

## Detailed Description

Class information items are simple *name*\--*value* pairs that are specified using
[Q\_CLASSINFO](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_CLASSINFO)() in the
source code. The information can be retrieved using
[name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaclassinfo.html#name)() and
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaclassinfo.html#value)(). For example:

```
class MyClass
{
    Q_OBJECT
    Q_CLASSINFO("author", "Sabrina Schweinsteiger")
    Q_CLASSINFO("url", "http://doc.moosesoft.co.uk/1.0/")

public:
    ...
};
```

This mechanism is free for you to use in your Qt applications. Qt doesn't use it for any
of its classes.

## Detailed Description

Use [name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#name)() for the
enumerator's name. The enumerator's keys (names of each enumerated item) are returned by
[key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#key)(); use
[keyCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#keyCount)() to find the
number of keys. [isFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#isFlag)()
returns whether the enumerator is meant to be used as a flag, meaning that its values
can be combined using the OR operator.

The conversion functions
[keyToValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#keyToValue)(),
[valueToKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#valueToKey)(),
[keysToValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#keysToValue)(), and
[valueToKeys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#valueToKeys)() allow
conversion between the integer representation of an enumeration or set value and its
literal representation. The
[scope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaenum.html#scope)() function returns the
class scope this enumerator was declared in.

Qt 5 reference:

### const char \*QMetaMethod::tag() const

Returns the tag associated with this method.

Tags are special macros recognized by `moc` that make it possible to add extra
information about a method.

Tag information can be added in the following way in the function declaration:

```
    // In the class MainWindow declaration
    #ifndef Q_MOC_RUN
    // define the tag text as empty, so the compiler doesn't see it
    #  define MY_CUSTOM_TAG
    #endif
    ...
    private slots:
        MY_CUSTOM_TAG void testFunc();
```

and the information can be accessed by using:

```
    MainWindow win;
    win.show();

    int functionIndex = win.metaObject()->indexOfSlot("testFunc()");
    QMetaMethod mm = win.metaObject()->method(functionIndex);
    qDebug() << mm.tag(); // prints MY_CUSTOM_TAG
```

For the moment, `moc` will extract and record all tags, but it will not handle any of
them specially. You can use the tags to annotate your methods differently, and treat
them according to the specific needs of your application.

**Note:** Since Qt 5.0, `moc` expands preprocessor macros, so it is necessary to
surround the definition with `#ifndef` `Q_MOC_RUN`, as shown in the example above. This
was not required in Qt 4\. The code as shown above works with Qt 4 too.

PythonQt.QtCore.QMetaObject.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The Qt [Meta-Object System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/metaobjects.html) in Qt
is responsible for the signals and slots inter-object communication mechanism, runtime
type information, and the Qt property system. A single QMetaObject instance is created
for each [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass that is
used in an application, and this instance stores all the meta-information for the
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) subclass. This object is
available as
[QObject::metaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#metaObject)().

This class is not normally required for application programming, but it is useful if you
write meta-applications, such as scripting engines or GUI builders.

The functions you are most likely to find useful are these:

- [className](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#className)() returns the name of a class.
- [superClass](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#superClass)() returns the superclass's meta-object.
- [method](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#method)() and [methodCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#methodCount)() provide information about a class's meta-methods (signals, slots and other [invokable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_INVOKABLE) member functions).
- [enumerator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#enumerator)() and [enumeratorCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#enumeratorCount)() and provide information about a class's enumerators.
- [propertyCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#propertyCount)() and [property](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#property)() provide information about a class's properties.
- [constructor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#constructor)() and [constructorCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#constructorCount)() provide information about a class's meta-constructors.

The index functions
[indexOfConstructor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfConstructor)(),
[indexOfMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfMethod)(),
[indexOfEnumerator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfEnumerator)(),
and
[indexOfProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfProperty)()
map names of constructors, member functions, enumerators, or properties to indexes in
the meta-object. For example, Qt uses
[indexOfMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfMethod)()
internally when you connect a signal to a slot.

Classes can also have a list of *name*\--*value* pairs of additional class information,
stored in [QMetaClassInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaclassinfo.html)
objects. The number of pairs is returned by
[classInfoCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#classInfoCount)(),
single pairs are returned by
[classInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#classInfo)(), and you
can search for pairs with
[indexOfClassInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#indexOfClassInfo)().

**Note:** Operations that use the meta object system are generally thread- safe, as
QMetaObjects are typically static read-only instances generated at compile time.
However, if meta objects are dynamically modified by the application (for instance, when
using [QQmlPropertyMap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qqmlpropertymap.html)), then
the application has to explicitly synchronize access to the respective meta object.

### int QMetaObject::methodCount() const

Returns the number of methods in this class, including the number of methods provided by
each base class. These include signals and slots as well as normal member functions.

Use code like the following to obtain a
[QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) containing the
methods specific to a given class:

```
const QMetaObject* metaObject = obj->metaObject();
QStringList methods;
for(int i = metaObject->methodOffset(); i < metaObject->methodCount(); ++i)
    methods << QString::fromLatin1(metaObject->method(i).methodSignature());
```

## Detailed Description

Property meta-data is obtained from an object's meta-object. See
[QMetaObject::property](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#property)()
and
[QMetaObject::propertyCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#propertyCount)()
for details.

### Property Meta-Data

A property has a [name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#name)()
and a [type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#type)(), as well as
various attributes that specify its behavior:
[isReadable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isReadable)(),
[isWritable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isWritable)(),
[isDesignable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isDesignable)(),
[isScriptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isScriptable)(),
[revision](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#revision)(), and
[isStored](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isStored)().

If the property is an enumeration,
[isEnumType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isEnumType)() returns
`true`; if the property is an enumeration that is also a flag (i.e. its values can be
combined using the OR operator),
[isEnumType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isEnumType)() and
[isFlagType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#isFlagType)() both
return true. The enumerator for these types is available from
[enumerator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#enumerator)().

The property's values are set and retrieved with
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#read)(),
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#write)(), and
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaproperty.html#reset)(); they can also be
changed through [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)'s set and get
functions. See
[QObject::setProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#setProperty)()
and [QObject::property](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#property)() for
details.

### Copying and Assignment

QMetaProperty objects can be copied by value. However, each copy will refer to the same
underlying property meta-data.

PythonQt.QtCore.QMetaType.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The class is used as a helper to marshall types in
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) and in queued
signals and slots connections. It associates a type name to a type so that it can be
created and destructed dynamically at run-time. Declare new types with
[Q\_DECLARE\_METATYPE](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Q_DECLARE_METATYPE)()
to make them available to
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) and other
template-based functions. Call
[qRegisterMetaType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#qRegisterMetaType-1)()
to make types available to non-template based functions, such as the queued signal and
slot connections.

Any class or struct that has a public default constructor, a public copy constructor,
and a public destructor can be registered.

The following code allocates and destructs an instance of `MyClass`:

```
int id = QMetaType::type("MyClass");
if (id != QMetaType::UnknownType) {
    void *myClassPtr = QMetaType::create(id);
    ...
    QMetaType::destroy(id, myClassPtr);
    myClassPtr = 0;
}
```

If we want the stream operators `operator<<()` and `operator>>()` to work on
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) objects that
store custom types, the custom type must provide `operator<<()` and `operator>>()`
operators.

### `[static]` bool QMetaType::compare(const void \**lhs*, const void \**rhs*, int *typeId*, int \**result*)

Compares the objects at *lhs* and *rhs*. Both objects need to be of type *typeId*.
*result* is set to less than, equal to or greater than zero, if *lhs* is less than,
equal to or greater than *rhs*. Returns `true`, if the comparison succeeded, otherwise
`false`.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

PythonQt.QtCore.QMetaType.construct.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void \*QMetaType::construct(int *type*, void \**where*, const void \**copy*)

Constructs a value of the given *type* in the existing memory addressed by *where*, that
is a copy of *copy*, and returns *where*. If *copy* is zero, the value is default
constructed.

This is a low-level function for explicitly managing the memory used to store the type.
Consider calling [create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#create)() if
you don't need this level of control (that is, use "new" rather than "placement new").

You must ensure that *where* points to a location that can store a value of type *type*,
and that *where* is suitably aligned. The type's size can be queried by calling
[sizeOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#sizeOf-1)().

The rule of thumb for alignment is that a type is aligned to its natural boundary, which
is the smallest power of 2 that is bigger than the type, unless that alignment is larger
than the maximum useful alignment for the platform. For practical purposes, alignment
larger than 2 \* sizeof(void\*) is only necessary for special hardware instructions
(e.g., aligned SSE loads and stores on x86).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also** [destruct](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#destruct)()
and [sizeOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#sizeOf-1)().

### void \*QMetaType::construct(void \**where*, const void \**copy* \= 0\) const

Constructs a value of the type that this
[QMetaType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html) instance was constructed
for in the existing memory addressed by *where*, that is a copy of *copy*, and returns
*where*. If *copy* is zero, the value is default constructed.

This is a low-level function for explicitly managing the memory used to store the type.
Consider calling [create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#create)() if
you don't need this level of control (that is, use "new" rather than "placement new").

You must ensure that *where* points to a location where the new value can be stored and
that *where* is suitably aligned. The type's size can be queried by calling
[sizeOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#sizeOf-1)().

The rule of thumb for alignment is that a type is aligned to its natural boundary, which
is the smallest power of 2 that is bigger than the type, unless that alignment is larger
than the maximum useful alignment for the platform. For practical purposes, alignment
larger than 2 \* sizeof(void\*) is only necessary for special hardware instructions

### const [QMetaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html) \*QMetaType::metaObject() const

Returns a [QMetaObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html) relative to
this type.

If the type is a pointer type to a subclass of
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html),
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains
[QMetaType::PointerToQObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#TypeFlag-enum)

combination with
[QMetaObject::newInstance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetaobject.html#newInstance)()
to create QObjects of this type.

If the type is a [Q\_GADGET](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_GADGET),
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains
[QMetaType::IsGadget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#TypeFlag-enum).
If the type is a pointer to a
[Q\_GADGET](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#Q_GADGET),
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains
[QMetaType::PointerToGadget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#TypeFlag-enum).

pointer of this type for example, as given by QVariant::data().

If the type is an enumeration,
[flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#flags)() contains

PythonQt.QtCore.QMimeData.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QMimeData is used to describe information that can be stored in the
[clipboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qclipboard.html), and transferred via the
[drag and drop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-index.html#drag-and-drop)
mechanism. QMimeData objects associate the data that they hold with the corresponding
MIME types to ensure that information can be safely transferred between applications,
and copied around within the same application.

QMimeData objects are usually created using `new` and supplied to
[QDrag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdrag.html) or
[QClipboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qclipboard.html) objects. This is to
enable Qt to manage the memory that they use.

A single QMimeData object can store the same data using several different formats at the
same time. The [formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#formats)()
function returns a list of the available formats in order of preference. The
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#data)() function returns the
raw data associated with a MIME type, and
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#setData)() allows you to set
the data for a MIME type.

For the most common MIME types, QMimeData provides convenience functions to access the
data:

| Tester | Getter | Setter | MIME Types |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [hasText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#hasText)() | [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#text)() | [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#setText)() | `text/plain` |
| [hasHtml](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#hasHtml)() | [html](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#html)() | [setHtml](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#setHtml)() | `text/html` |
| [hasUrls](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#hasUrls)() | [urls](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#urls)() | [setUrls](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#setUrls)() | `text/uri-list` |
| [hasImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#hasImage)() | [imageData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#imageData)() | [setImageData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#setImageData)() | `image/` \* |
| [hasColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#hasColor)() | [colorData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#colorData)() | [setColorData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#setColorData)() | `application/x-color` |

For example, if your write a widget that accepts URL drags, you would end up writing
code like this:

```
void MyWidget::dragEnterEvent(QDragEnterEvent *event)
{
    if (event->mimeData()->hasUrls())
        event->acceptProposedAction();
}

void MyWidget::dropEvent(QDropEvent *event)
{
    if (event->mimeData()->hasUrls()) {
        foreach (QUrl url, event->mimeData()->urls()) {
            ...
        }
    }
}
```

There are three approaches for storing custom data in a QMimeData object:

1. Custom data can be stored directly in a QMimeData object as a [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) using [setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#setData)(). For example:

   ```
   QByteArray csvData = ...;

   QMimeData *mimeData = new QMimeData;
   mimeData->setData("text/csv", csvData);
   ```
2. We can subclass QMimeData and reimplement [hasFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#hasFormat)(), [formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#formats)(), and [retrieveData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#retrieveData)().
3. If the drag and drop operation occurs within a single application, we can subclass QMimeData and add extra data in it, and use a [qobject\_cast](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#qobject_cast)() in the receiver's drop event handler. For example:

   ```
   void MyWidget::dropEvent(QDropEvent *event)
   {
       const MyMimeData *myData =
               qobject_cast<const MyMimeData *>(event->mimeData());
       if (myData) {
           // access myData's data directly (not through QMimeData's API)
       }
   }
   ```

### Platform-Specific MIME Types

On Windows, [formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html#formats)() will
also return custom formats available in the MIME data, using the `x-qt-windows-mime`
subtype to indicate that they represent data in non-standard formats. The formats will
take the following form:

```
application/x-qt-windows-mime;value="<custom type>"
```

The following are examples of custom MIME types:

```
application/x-qt-windows-mime;value="FileGroupDescriptor"
application/x-qt-windows-mime;value="FileContents"
```

The `value` declaration of each format describes the way in which the data is encoded.

In some cases (e.g. dropping multiple email attachments), multiple data values are
available. They can be accessed by adding an `index` value:

```
application/x-qt-windows-mime;value="FileContents";index=0
application/x-qt-windows-mime;value="FileContents";index=1
```

On Windows, the MIME format does not always map directly to the clipboard formats. Qt
provides QWinMime to map clipboard formats to open-standard MIME formats. Similarly, the
QMacPasteboardMime maps MIME to Mac flavors.

### [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) QMimeData::colorData() const

Returns a color if the data stored in the object represents a color (MIME type
`application/x-color`); otherwise returns a null variant.

A [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) is used because
[QMimeData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedata.html) belongs to the Qt Core
module, whereas [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) belongs to Qt
GUI. To convert the [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) to a
[QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html), simply use
[qvariant\_cast](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html#qvariant_cast)(). For
example:

```
if (event->mimeData()->hasColor()) {
    QColor color = qvariant_cast<QColor>(event->mimeData()->colorData());
    ...

PythonQt.QtCore.QMimeDatabase.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The MIME type database is provided by the freedesktop.org shared-mime-info project. If
the MIME type database cannot be found on the system, as is the case on most Windows,
macOS, and iOS systems, Qt will use its own copy of it.

Applications which want to define custom MIME types need to install an XML file into the
locations searched for MIME definitions. These locations can be queried with

```
QStandardPaths::locateAll(QStandardPaths::GenericDataLocation, QLatin1String("mime/packages"),
                          QStandardPaths::LocateDirectory);
```

On a typical Unix system, this will be /usr/share/mime/packages/, but it is also
possible to extend the list of directories by setting the environment variable
`XDG_DATA_DIRS`. For instance adding /opt/myapp/share to `XDG_DATA_DIRS` will result in
/opt/myapp/share/mime/packages/ being searched for MIME definitions.

Here is an example of MIME XML:

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<mime-info xmlns="http://www.freedesktop.org/standards/shared-mime-info">
  <mime-type type="application/vnd.qt.qmakeprofile">
    <comment xml:lang="en">Qt qmake Profile</comment>
    <glob pattern="*.pro" weight="50"/>
  </mime-type>
</mime-info>
```

For more details about the syntax of XML MIME definitions, including defining "magic" in
order to detect MIME types based on data as well, read the Shared Mime Info
specification at
http://standards.freedesktop.org/shared-mime-info-spec/shared-mime-info-spec-latest.html

On Unix systems, a binary cache is used for more performance. This cache is generated by
the command "update-mime-database path", where path would be /opt/myapp/share/mime in
the above example. Make sure to run this command when installing the MIME type
definition file.

```
QMimeDatabase db;
QMimeType mime = db.mimeTypeForFile(fileName);
if (mime.inherits("text/plain")) {
    // The file is plain text, we can display it in a QTextEdit
}
```

### [QMimeType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html) QMimeDatabase::mimeTypeForFile(const [QFileInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileinfo.html) \&*fileInfo*, [QMimeDatabase::MatchMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html#MatchMode-enum) *mode* \= MatchDefault) const

Returns a MIME type for *fileInfo*.

A valid MIME type is always returned.

The default matching algorithm looks at both the file name and the file contents, if
necessary. The file extension has priority over the contents, but the contents will be
used if the file extension is unknown, or matches multiple MIME types. If *fileInfo* is
a Unix symbolic link, the file that it refers to will be used instead. If the file
doesn't match any known pattern or data, the default MIME type
(application/octet-stream) is returned.

When *mode* is set to
[MatchExtension](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html#MatchMode-enum),
only the file name is used, not the file contents. The file doesn't even have to exist.
If the file name doesn't match any known pattern, the default MIME type
(application/octet-stream) is returned. If multiple MIME types match this file, the
first one (alphabetically) is returned.

When *mode* is set to
[MatchContent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html#MatchMode-enum),
and the file is readable, only the file contents are used to determine the MIME type.
This is equivalent to calling
[mimeTypeForData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html#mimeTypeForData)
with a [QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) as input device.

*fileInfo* may refer to an absolute or relative path.

**See also**
[QMimeType::isDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html#isDefault-prop)()
and
[mimeTypeForData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html#mimeTypeForData)().

### [QMimeType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html) QMimeDatabase::mimeTypeForFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*, [QMimeDatabase::MatchMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html#MatchMode-enum) *mode* \= MatchDefault) const

Returns a MIME type for the file named *fileName* using *mode*.

This is an overloaded function.

### [QMimeType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html) QMimeDatabase::mimeTypeForFileNameAndData(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*, [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) \**device*) const

Returns a MIME type for the given *fileName* and *device* data.

This overload can be useful when the file is remote, and we started to download some of
its data in a device. This allows to do full MIME type matching for remote files as
well.

If the device is not open, it will be opened by this function, and closed after the MIME
type detection is completed.

A valid MIME type is always returned. If *device* data doesn't match any known MIME type
data, the default MIME type (application/octet-stream) is returned.

This method looks at both the file name and the file contents, if necessary. The file
extension has priority over the contents, but the contents will be used if the file
extension is unknown, or matches multiple MIME types.

## Detailed Description

For instance a file named "readme.txt" has the MIME type "text/plain". The MIME type can
be determined from the file name, or from the file contents, or from both. MIME type
determination can also be done on buffers of data not coming from files.

Determining the MIME type of a file can be useful to make sure your application supports
it. It is also useful in file-manager-like applications or widgets, in order to display
an appropriate [icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html#iconName-prop)
for the file, or even the descriptive
[comment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html#comment-prop) in detailed
views.

To check if a file has the expected MIME type, you should use
[inherits](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html#inherits)() rather than a
simple string comparison based on the
[name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimetype.html#name-prop)(). This is because
MIME types can inherit from each other: for instance a C source file is a specific type
of plain text file, so text/x-csrc inherits text/plain.

### parentMimeTypes : const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html)

This property holds the names of parent MIME types

A type is a subclass of another type if any instance of the first type is also an
instance of the second. For example, all image/svg\+xml files are also text/xml,
text/plain and application/octet-stream files. Subclassing is about the format, rather
than the category of the data (for example, there is no 'generic spreadsheet' class that
all spreadsheets inherit from). Conversely, the parent mimetype of image/svg\+xml is
text/xml.

A mimetype can have multiple parents. For instance application/x-perl has two parents:
application/x-executable and text/plain. This makes it possible to both execute perl
scripts, and to open them in text editors.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class is used as an index into item models derived from
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html). The
index is used by item views, delegates, and selection models to locate an item in the
model.

New QModelIndex objects are created by the model using the
[QAbstractItemModel::createIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#createIndex)()
function. An *invalid* model index can be constructed with the QModelIndex constructor.
Invalid indexes are often used as parent indexes when referring to top-level items in a
model.

Model indexes refer to items in models, and contain all the information required to
specify their locations in those models. Each index is located in a given row and
column, and may have a parent index; use
[row](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#row)(),
[column](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#column)(), and
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#parent)() to obtain this
information. Each top-level item in a model is represented by a model index that does
not have a parent index \- in this case,
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#parent)() will return an
invalid model index, equivalent to an index constructed with the zero argument form of
the QModelIndex() constructor.

To obtain a model index that refers to an existing item in a model, call
[QAbstractItemModel::index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#index)()
with the required row and column values, and the model index of the parent. When
referring to top-level items in a model, supply QModelIndex() as the parent index.

The [model](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#model)() function
returns the model that the index references as a
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html). The
child() function is used to examine items held under the index in the model. The
[sibling](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#sibling)() function allows
you to traverse items in the model on the same level as the index.

**Note:** Model indexes should be used immediately and then discarded. You should not
rely on indexes to remain valid after calling model functions that change the structure
of the model or delete items. If you need to keep a model index over time use a
[QPersistentModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpersistentmodelindex.html).

signatures: child(self, row: int, column: int) -> PySide2.QtCore.QModelIndex

Qt 5 reference:

### void QMutex::lock()

Locks the mutex. If another thread has locked the mutex then this call will block until
that thread has unlocked it.

Calling this function multiple times on the same mutex from the same thread is allowed
if this mutex is a [recursive
mutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrecursivemutex.html). If this mutex is a
[non-recursive mutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html), this function
will *dead-lock* when the mutex is locked recursively.

**See also** [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html#unlock)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QMutex.tryLock.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QMutex::tryLock(int *timeout* \= 0\)

Attempts to lock the mutex. This function returns `true` if the lock was obtained;
otherwise it returns `false`. If another thread has locked the mutex, this function will
wait for at most *timeout* milliseconds for the mutex to become available.

Note: Passing a negative number as the *timeout* is equivalent to calling
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html#lock)(), i.e. this function will
wait forever until mutex can be locked if *timeout* is negative.

If the lock was obtained, the mutex must be unlocked with
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html#unlock)() before another thread
can successfully lock it.

Calling this function multiple times on the same mutex from the same thread is allowed
if this mutex is a [recursive
mutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrecursivemutex.html). If this mutex is a
[non-recursive mutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html), this function
will *always* return false when attempting to lock the mutex recursively.

**See also** [lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html#lock)() and
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html#unlock)().

## Detailed Description

QParallelAnimationGroup--a [container for
animations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html)--starts all its
animations when it is
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#start) itself,
i.e., runs all animations in parallel. The animation group finishes when the longest
lasting animation has finished.

You can treat QParallelAnimationGroup as any other
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html), e.g.,
pause, resume, or add it to other animation groups.

```
    QParallelAnimationGroup *group = new QParallelAnimationGroup;
    group->addAnimation(anim1);
    group->addAnimation(anim2);

    group->start();
```

In this example, `anim1` and `anim2` are two
[QPropertyAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpropertyanimation.html)s that
have already been set up.

## Detailed Description

If you wish to introduce a delay between animations in a
[QSequentialAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsequentialanimationgroup.html),

## Detailed Description

A point is specified by a x coordinate and an y coordinate which can be accessed using
the [x](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#x)() and
[y](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#y)() functions. The
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#isNull)() function returns
`true` if both x and y are set to 0\. The coordinates can be set (or altered) using the
[setX](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#setX)() and
[setY](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#setY)() functions, or
alternatively the [rx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#rx)() and
[ry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#ry)() functions which return
references to the coordinates (allowing direct manipulation).

Given a point *p*, the following statements are all equivalent:

```
QPoint p;

p.setX(p.x() + 1);
p += QPoint(1, 0);
p.rx()++;
```

A QPoint object can also be used as a vector: Addition and subtraction are defined as
for vectors (each component is added separately). A QPoint object can also be divided or
multiplied by an `int` or a `qreal`.

In addition, the QPoint class provides the
[manhattanLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html#manhattanLength)()
function which gives an inexpensive approximation of the length of the QPoint object
interpreted as a vector. Finally, QPoint objects can be streamed as well as compared.

```

QPoint q(-1, 4);
int lengthSquared = QPoint::dotProduct(p, q);   // lengthSquared becomes 25

## Detailed Description

A point is specified by a x coordinate and an y coordinate which can be accessed using
the [x](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html#x)() and
[y](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html#y)() functions. The coordinates of
the point are specified using floating point numbers for accuracy. The
[isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html#isNull)() function returns
`true` if both x and y are set to 0.0. The coordinates can be set (or altered) using the
[setX](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html#setX)() and
[setY](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html#setY)() functions, or

[ry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html#ry)() functions which return
references to the coordinates (allowing direct manipulation).

Given a point *p*, the following statements are all equivalent:

```
QPointF p;

p.setX(p.x() + 1.0);
p += QPointF(1.0, 0.0);
p.rx()++;
```

A QPointF object can also be used as a vector: Addition and subtraction are defined as
for vectors (each component is added separately). A QPointF object can also be divided
or multiplied by an `int` or a `qreal`.

[QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) object into a QPointF object,

function which returns a [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) copy
of *this* point. Finally, QPointF objects can be streamed as well as compared.

PythonQt.QtCore.QProcess.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

### Running a Process

To start a process, pass the name and command line arguments of the program you want to
run as arguments to [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)().
Arguments are supplied as individual strings in a
[QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html).

Alternatively, you can set the program to run with
[setProgram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProgram)() and
[setArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setArguments)(), and
then call [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() or
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#open)().

For example, the following code snippet runs the analog clock example in the Fusion
style on X11 platforms by passing strings containing "-style" and "fusion" as two items
in the list of arguments:

```
    QObject *parent;
    ...
    QString program = "./path/to/Qt/examples/widgets/analogclock";
    QStringList arguments;
    arguments << "-style" << "fusion";

    QProcess *myProcess = new QProcess(parent);
    myProcess->start(program, arguments);
```

QProcess then enters the
[Starting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessState-enum) state,
and when the program has started, QProcess enters the
[Running](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessState-enum) state and
emits [started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)().

QProcess allows you to treat a process as a sequential I/O device. You can write to and
read from the process just as you would access a network connection using
[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html). You can then write to
the process's standard input by calling
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#write)(), and read the
standard output by calling
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), and
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(). Because it
inherits [QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), QProcess can
also be used as an input source for QXmlReader, or for generating data to be uploaded
using
[QNetworkAccessManager](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qnetworkaccessmanager.html).

When the process exits, QProcess reenters the
[NotRunning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessState-enum) state
(the initial state), and emits
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#finished)().

The [finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#finished)() signal
provides the exit code and exit status of the process as arguments, and you can also
call [exitCode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#exitCode)() to obtain
the exit code of the last process that finished, and
[exitStatus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#exitStatus)() to obtain
its exit status. If an error occurs at any point in time, QProcess will emit the
[errorOccurred](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#errorOccurred)()
signal. You can also call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#error)() to find the type of
error that occurred last, and
[state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#state)() to find the current
process state.

**Note:** QProcess is not supported on
[VxWorks](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/vxworks.html), iOS, tvOS, watchOS, or the
Universal Windows Platform.

### Communicating via Channels

Processes have two predefined output channels: The standard output channel (`stdout`)
supplies regular console output, and the standard error channel (`stderr`) usually
supplies the errors that are printed by the process. These channels represent two
separate streams of data. You can toggle between them by calling
[setReadChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setReadChannel)().
QProcess emits
[readyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readyRead)() when data is
available on the current read channel. It also emits
[readyReadStandardOutput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readyReadStandardOutput)()
when new standard output data is available, and when new standard error data is
available,
[readyReadStandardError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readyReadStandardError)()
is emitted. Instead of calling
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)(),
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)(), or
[getChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#getChar)(), you can
explicitly read all data from either of the two channels by calling
[readAllStandardOutput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readAllStandardOutput)()
or
[readAllStandardError](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readAllStandardError)().

The terminology for the channels can be misleading. Be aware that the process's output
channels correspond to QProcess's *read* channels, whereas the process's input channels
correspond to QProcess's *write* channels. This is because what we read using QProcess
is the process's output, and what we write becomes the process's input.

QProcess can merge the two output channels, so that standard output and standard error
data from the running process both use the standard output channel. Call
[setProcessChannelMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProcessChannelMode)()
with
[MergedChannels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum)
before starting the process to activate this feature. You also have the option of
forwarding the output of the running process to the calling, main process, by passing
[ForwardedChannels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum)
as the argument. It is also possible to forward only one of the output channels \-
typically one would use
[ForwardedErrorChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum),
but
[ForwardedOutputChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannelMode-enum)
also exists. Note that using channel forwarding is typically a bad idea in GUI
applications \- you should present errors graphically instead.

Certain processes need special environment settings in order to operate. You can set
environment variables for your process by calling
[setProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProcessEnvironment)().
To set a working directory, call
[setWorkingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setWorkingDirectory)().
By default, processes are run in the current working directory of the calling process.

The positioning and the screen Z-order of windows belonging to GUI applications started
with QProcess are controlled by the underlying windowing system. For Qt 5 applications,
the positioning can be specified using the `-qwindowgeometry` command line option; X11
applications generally accept a `-geometry` command line option.

### Synchronous Process API

QProcess provides a set of functions which allow it to be used without an event loop, by
suspending the calling thread until certain signals are emitted:

- [waitForStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted)() blocks until the process has started.
- [waitForReadyRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForReadyRead)() blocks until new data is available for reading on the current read channel.
- [waitForBytesWritten](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForBytesWritten)() blocks until one payload of data has been written to the process.
- [waitForFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForFinished)() blocks until the process has finished.

Calling these functions from the main thread (the thread that calls
[QApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#exec)()) may
cause your user interface to freeze.

The following example runs `gzip` to compress the string "Qt rocks!", without an event
loop:

```
    QProcess gzip;
    gzip.start("gzip", QStringList() << "-c");
    if (!gzip.waitForStarted())
        return false;

    gzip.write("Qt rocks!");
    gzip.closeWriteChannel();

    if (!gzip.waitForFinished())
        return false;

    QByteArray result = gzip.readAll();
```

### Notes for Windows Users

Some Windows commands (for example, `dir`) are not provided by separate applications,
but by the command interpreter itself. If you attempt to use QProcess to execute these
commands directly, it won't work. One possible solution is to execute the command
interpreter itself (`cmd.exe` on some Windows systems), and ask the interpreter to
execute the desired command.

### void QProcess::closeReadChannel([QProcess::ProcessChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ProcessChannel-enum) *channel*)

PythonQt.QtCore.QProcess.closeWriteChann.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QProcess::closeWriteChannel()

Schedules the write channel of
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) to be closed. The channel
will close once all data has been written to the process. After calling this function,
any attempts to write to the process will fail.

Closing the write channel is necessary for programs that read input data until the
channel has been closed. For example, the program "more" is used to display text data in
a console on both Unix and Windows. But it will not display the text data until
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html)'s write channel has been
closed. Example:

```
QProcess more;
more.start("more");
more.write("Text to display");
more.closeWriteChannel();
// QProcess will emit readyRead() once "more" starts printing
```

The write channel is implicitly opened when
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() is called.

**See also**
[closeReadChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#closeReadChannel)().

### `[signal]` void QProcess::finished(int *exitCode*, [QProcess::ExitStatus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#ExitStatus-enum) *exitStatus*)

This signal is emitted when the process finishes. *exitCode* is the exit code of the
process (only valid for normal exits), and *exitStatus* is the exit status. After the
process has finished, the buffers in
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) are still intact. You can
still read any data that the process may have written before it finished.

**Note:** Signal *finished* is overloaded in this class. To connect to this signal by
using the function pointer syntax, Qt provides a convenient helper for obtaining the
function pointer as shown in this example:

```
connect(process, QOverload<int, QProcess::ExitStatus>::of(&QProcess::finished),
    [=](int exitCode, QProcess::ExitStatus exitStatus){ /* ... */ });
```

[exitStatus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#exitStatus)().

### void QProcess::setProcessEnvironment(const [QProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html) \&*environment*)

will pass to the child process.

For example, the following code adds the environment variable `TMPDIR`:

QProcess process;
QProcessEnvironment env = QProcessEnvironment::systemEnvironment();
env.insert("TMPDIR", "C:\\MyApp\\temp"); // Add an environment variable

process.start("myapp");
```

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) object will be in read-only

result in error).

To make the process read EOF right away, pass
[nullDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#nullDevice)() here. This
is cleaner than using
[closeWriteChannel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#closeWriteChannel)()
before writing any data, because it can be set up prior to starting the process.

If the file *fileName* does not exist at the moment
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() is called or is not
readable, starting the process will fail.

Calling setStandardInputFile() after the process has started has no effect.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[setStandardOutputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardOutputFile)(),
[setStandardErrorFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardErrorFile)(),
and
[setStandardOutputProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardOutputProcess)().

### void QProcess::setStandardOutputFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*, [QIODevice::OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) *mode* \= Truncate)

Redirects the process' standard output to the file *fileName*. When the redirection is
in place, the standard output read channel is closed: reading from it using
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#read)() will always fail, as
will
[readAllStandardOutput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#readAllStandardOutput)().

To discard all standard output from the process, pass
[nullDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#nullDevice)() here. This
is more efficient than simply never reading the standard output, as no
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) buffers are filled.

If the file *fileName* doesn't exist at the moment
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() is called, it will be
created. If it cannot be created, the starting will fail.

If the file exists and *mode* is
[QIODevice::Truncate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum),
the file will be truncated. Otherwise (if *mode* is
[QIODevice::Append](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum)),
the file will be appended to.

Calling setStandardOutputFile() after the process has started has no effect.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

[setStandardInputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardInputFile)(),
[setStandardErrorFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardErrorFile)(),

### void QProcess::start(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*program*, const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*arguments*, [QIODevice::OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) *mode* \= ReadWrite)

Starts the given *program* in a new process, passing the command line arguments in
*arguments*.

The [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) object will immediately
enter the Starting state. If the process starts successfully,
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) will emit
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)(); otherwise,
[errorOccurred](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#errorOccurred)() will
be emitted.

**Note:** Processes are started asynchronously, which means the
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)() and
[errorOccurred](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#errorOccurred)()
signals may be delayed. Call
[waitForStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted)() to
make sure the process has started (or has failed to start) and those signals have been
emitted.

**Note:** No further splitting of the arguments is performed.

**Windows:** The arguments are quoted and joined into a command line that is compatible
with the `CommandLineToArgvW()` Windows function. For programs that have different
command line quoting requirements, you need to use
[setNativeArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setNativeArguments)().
One notable program that does not follow the `CommandLineToArgvW()` rules is cmd.exe
and, by consequence, all batch scripts.

The [OpenMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#OpenModeFlag-enum) is
set to *mode*.

If the [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html) object is already
running a process, a warning may be printed at the console, and the existing process
will continue running unaffected.

**See also** [processId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#processId)(),
[started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#started)(),
[waitForStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#waitForStarted)(), and
[setNativeArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setNativeArguments)().

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QProcess::startDetached([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) \**pid* \= nullptr)

Starts the program set by
[setProgram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProgram)() with
arguments set by
[setArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setArguments)() in a new
process, and detaches from it. Returns `true` on success; otherwise returns `false`. If
the calling process exits, the detached process will continue to run unaffected.

**Unix:** The started process will run in its own session and act like a daemon.

The process will be started in the directory set by
[setWorkingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setWorkingDirectory)().
If
[workingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#workingDirectory)()
is empty, the working directory is inherited from the calling process.

If the function is successful then \**pid* is set to the process identifier of the
started process. Note that the child process may exit and the PID may become invalid
without notice. Furthermore, after the child process exits, the same PID may be recycled
and used by a completely different process. User code should be careful when using this
variable, especially if one intends to forcibly terminate the process by operating
system means.

Only the following property setters are supported by startDetached():

- [setArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setArguments)()
- [setCreateProcessArgumentsModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setCreateProcessArgumentsModifier)()
- [setNativeArguments](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setNativeArguments)()
- [setProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProcessEnvironment)()
- [setProgram](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setProgram)()
- [setStandardErrorFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardErrorFile)()
- [setStandardInputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardInputFile)()
- [setStandardOutputFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setStandardOutputFile)()
- [setWorkingDirectory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#setWorkingDirectory)()

All other properties of the [QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html)
object are ignored.

**Note:** The called process inherits the console window of the calling process. To
suppress console output, redirect standard/error output to
[QProcess::nullDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#nullDevice)().

This function was introduced in Qt 5.10.

**See also** [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)(),
[startDetached](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#startDetached-1)(const
QString \&program, const QStringList \&arguments, const QString \&workingDirectory,
qint64 \*pid), and
[startDetached](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess-obsolete.html#startDetached-2)(const
QString \&command).

### `[static]` bool QProcess::startDetached(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*program*, const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*arguments*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*workingDirectory* \= QString(), [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) \**pid* \= nullptr)

This function overloads startDetached().

Starts the program *program* with the arguments *arguments* in a new process, and
detaches from it. Returns `true` on success; otherwise returns `false`. If the calling
process exits, the detached process will continue to run unaffected.

Argument handling is identical to the respective
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)() overload.

The process will be started in the directory *workingDirectory*. If *workingDirectory*
is empty, the working directory is inherited from the calling process.

If the function is successful then \**pid* is set to the process identifier of the
started process.

**See also** [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#start)().

### `[static]` [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) QProcess::systemEnvironment()

Returns the environment of the calling process as a list of key\=value pairs. Example:

```
QStringList environment = QProcess::systemEnvironment();
// environment = {"PATH=/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin",
//                "USER=greg", "HOME=/home/greg"}
```

This function does not cache the system environment. Therefore, it's possible to obtain
an updated version of the environment if low-level C library functions like `setenv` or
`putenv` have been called.

However, note that repeated calls to this function will recreate the list of environment
variables, which is a non-trivial operation.

**Note:** For new code, it is recommended to use
[QProcessEnvironment::systemEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html#systemEnvironment)()

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

### `[slot]` void QProcess::terminate()

Attempts to terminate the process.

The process may not exit as a result of calling this function (it is given the chance to
prompt the user for any unsaved files, etc).

On Windows, terminate() posts a WM\_CLOSE message to all top-level windows of the
process and then to the main thread of the process itself. On Unix and macOS the
`SIGTERM` signal is sent.

Console applications on Windows that do not run an event loop, or whose event loop does
not handle the WM\_CLOSE message, can only be terminated by calling
[kill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#kill)().

**See also** [kill](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#kill)().

### bool QProcess::waitForFinished(int *msecs* \= 30000\)

Blocks until the process has finished and the
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#finished)() signal has been
emitted, or until *msecs* milliseconds have passed.

timed out, if an error occurred, or if this

applications and when performing I/O operations in a non-GUI thread.

PythonQt.QtCore.QProcessEnvironment.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A process's environment is composed of a set of key\=value pairs known as environment
variables. The QProcessEnvironment class wraps that concept and allows easy manipulation
of those variables. It's meant to be used along with
[QProcess](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html), to set the environment for
child processes. It cannot be used to change the current process's environment.

The environment of the calling process can be obtained using
[QProcessEnvironment::systemEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html#systemEnvironment)().

On Unix systems, the variable names are case-sensitive. Note that the Unix environment
allows both variable names and contents to contain arbitrary binary data (except for the
NUL character). QProcessEnvironment will preserve such variables, but does not support
manipulating variables whose names or values cannot be encoded by the current locale
settings (see
[QTextCodec::codecForLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#codecForLocale)).

On Windows, the variable names are case-insensitive, but case-preserving.
QProcessEnvironment behaves accordingly.

### `[static]` [QProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html#QProcessEnvironment) QProcessEnvironment::systemEnvironment()

The systemEnvironment function returns the environment of the calling process.

It is returned as a
[QProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html). This
function does not cache the system environment. Therefore, it's possible to obtain an
updated version of the environment if low-level C library functions like `setenv` or
`putenv` have been called.

However, note that repeated calls to this function will recreate the
[QProcessEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocessenvironment.html)
object, which is a non-trivial operation.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[QProcess::systemEnvironment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html#systemEnvironment)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QPropertyAnimation interpolates over [Qt
properties](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/properties.html). As property values are
stored in [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)s, the class
inherits [QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html),
and supports animation of the same [meta
types](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum) as its super class.

A class declaring properties must be a
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html). To make it possible to
animate a property, it must provide a setter (so that QPropertyAnimation can set the
property's value). Note that this makes it possible to animate many of Qt's widgets.
Let's look at an example:

```
    QPropertyAnimation *animation = new QPropertyAnimation(myWidget, "geometry");
    animation->setDuration(10000);
    animation->setStartValue(QRect(0, 0, 100, 30));
    animation->setEndValue(QRect(250, 250, 100, 30));

    animation->start();
```

The property name and the [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)
instance of which property should be animated are passed to the constructor. You can
then specify the start and end value of the property. The procedure is equal for
properties in classes you have implemented yourself--just check with
[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) that your
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) type is supported.

The [QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) class
description explains how to set up the animation in detail. Note, however, that if a
start value is not set, the property will start at the value it had when the
QPropertyAnimation instance was created.

QPropertyAnimation works like a charm on its own. For complex animations that, for
instance, contain several objects,
[QAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qanimationgroup.html) is provided.
An animation group is an animation that can contain other animations, and that can
manage when its animations are played. Look at
[QParallelAnimationGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qparallelanimationgroup.html)
for an example.

PythonQt.QtCore.QReadWriteLock.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A read-write lock is a synchronization tool for protecting resources that can be
accessed for reading and writing. This type of lock is useful if you want to allow
multiple threads to have simultaneous read-only access, but as soon as one thread wants
to write to the resource, all other threads must be blocked until the writing is
complete.

In many cases, QReadWriteLock is a direct competitor to
[QMutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html). QReadWriteLock is a good
choice if there are many concurrent reads and writing occurs infrequently.

Example:

```
QReadWriteLock lock;

void ReaderThread::run()
{
    ...
    lock.lockForRead();
    read_file();
    lock.unlock();
    ...
}

void WriterThread::run()
{
    ...
    lock.lockForWrite();
    write_file();
    lock.unlock();
    ...
}
```

To ensure that writers aren't blocked forever by readers, readers attempting to obtain a
lock will not succeed if there is a blocked writer waiting for access, even if the lock
is currently only accessed by other readers. Also, if the lock is accessed by a writer
and another writer comes in, that writer will have priority over any readers that might
also be waiting.

Like [QMutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html), a QReadWriteLock can be
recursively locked by the same thread when constructed with
[QReadWriteLock::Recursive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#RecursionMode-enum)
as
[QReadWriteLock::RecursionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#RecursionMode-enum).
In such cases, [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#unlock)()
must be called the same number of times
[lockForWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#lockForWrite)() or
[lockForRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html#lockForRead)() was
called. Note that the lock type cannot be changed when trying to lock recursively, i.e.
it is not possible to lock for reading in a thread that already has locked for writing
(and vice versa).
