Qt 5 reference:

### void QSettings::beginGroup(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*prefix*)

Appends *prefix* to the current group.

The current group is automatically prepended to all keys specified to
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html). In addition, query
functions such as
[childGroups](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#childGroups)(),
[childKeys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#childKeys)(), and
[allKeys](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#allKeys)() are based on the
group. By default, no group is set.

Groups are useful to avoid typing in the same setting paths over and over. For example:

```
settings.beginGroup("mainwindow");
settings.setValue("size", win->size());
settings.setValue("fullScreen", win->isFullScreen());
settings.endGroup();

settings.beginGroup("outputpanel");
settings.setValue("visible", panel->isVisible());
settings.endGroup();
```

This will set the value of three settings:

- `mainwindow/size`
- `mainwindow/fullScreen`
- `outputpanel/visible`

Call [endGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#endGroup)() to reset
the current group to what it was before the corresponding beginGroup() call. Groups can
be nested.

**See also** [endGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#endGroup)()
and [group](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#group)().

### void QSettings::setIniCodec([QTextCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html) \**codec*)

Sets the codec for accessing INI files (including `.conf` files on Unix) to *codec*. The
codec is used for decoding any data that is read from the INI file, and for encoding any
data that is written to the file. By default, no codec is used, and non-ASCII characters
are encoded using standard INI escape sequences.

**Warning:** The codec must be set immediately after creating the
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html) object, before accessing
any data.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also** [iniCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#iniCodec)().

### void QSettings::setIniCodec(const char \**codecName*)

This is an overloaded function.

Sets the codec for accessing INI files (including `.conf` files on Unix) to the
[QTextCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html) for the encoding
specified by *codecName*. Common values for `codecName` include "ISO 8859-1", "UTF-8",
and "UTF-16". If the encoding isn't recognized, nothing happens.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also**
[QTextCodec::codecForName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#codecForName)().

Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QSettings::setPath([QSettings::Format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Format-enum) *format*, [QSettings::Scope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) *scope*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*path*)

Sets the path used for storing settings for the given *format* and *scope*, to *path*.
The *format* can be a custom format.

The table below summarizes the default values:

| Platform | Format | Scope | Path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Windows | [IniFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Format-enum) | [UserScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) | `FOLDERID_RoamingAppData` |
| [SystemScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) | `FOLDERID_ProgramData` |
| Unix | [NativeFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Format-enum), [IniFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Format-enum) | [UserScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) | `$HOME/.config` |
| [SystemScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) | `/etc/xdg` |
| macOS and iOS | [IniFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Format-enum) | [UserScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) | `$HOME/.config` |
| [SystemScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) | `/etc/xdg` |

The default [UserScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum)
paths on Unix, macOS, and iOS (`$HOME/.config` or $HOME/Settings) can be overridden by
the user by setting the `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` environment variable. The default
[SystemScope](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Scope-enum) paths on
Unix, macOS, and iOS (`/etc/xdg`) can be overridden when building the Qt library using
the `configure` script's `-sysconfdir` flag (see
[QLibraryInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlibraryinfo.html) for details).

Setting the
[NativeFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#Format-enum) paths on
Windows, macOS, and iOS has no effect.

**Warning:** This function doesn't affect existing
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html) objects.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also**
[registerFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#registerFormat)().

### void QSettings::setValue(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*key*, const [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) \&*value*)

Sets the value of setting *key* to *value*. If the *key* already exists, the previous

### void QSettings::sync()

changed in the meantime by another application.

This function is called automatically from
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html)'s destructor and by the
event loop at regular intervals, so you normally don't need to call it yourself.

### [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) QSettings::value(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*key*, const [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) \&*defaultValue* \= QVariant()) const

Returns the value for setting *key*. If the setting doesn't exist, returns

[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) is returned.

Note that the Windows registry and INI files use case-insensitive keys, whereas the
CFPreferences API on macOS and iOS uses case-sensitive keys. To avoid portability
problems, see the [Section and Key

settings.setValue("animal/snake", 58);
settings.value("animal/snake", 1024).toInt();   // returns 58
settings.value("animal/zebra", 1024).toInt();   // returns 1024
settings.value("animal/zebra").toInt();         // returns 0
```

[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html#contains)(), and

PythonQt.QtCore.QSharedMemory.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QSharedMemory provides access to a shared memory segment by multiple threads and
processes. It also provides a way for a single thread or process to lock the memory for
exclusive access.

When using this class, be aware of the following platform differences:

- Windows: QSharedMemory does not "own" the shared memory segment. When all threads or processes that have an instance of QSharedMemory attached to a particular shared memory segment have either destroyed their instance of QSharedMemory or exited, the Windows kernel releases the shared memory segment automatically.
- Unix: QSharedMemory "owns" the shared memory segment. When the last thread or process that has an instance of QSharedMemory attached to a particular shared memory segment detaches from the segment by destroying its instance of QSharedMemory, the Unix kernel release the shared memory segment. But if that last thread or process crashes without running the QSharedMemory destructor, the shared memory segment survives the crash.
- HP-UX: Only one attach to a shared memory segment is allowed per process. This means that QSharedMemory should not be used across multiple threads in the same process in HP-UX.

Remember to lock the shared memory with
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#lock)() before reading from
or writing to the shared memory, and remember to release the lock with
[unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#unlock)() after you are
done.

QSharedMemory automatically destroys the shared memory segment when the last instance of
QSharedMemory is detached from the segment, and no references to the segment remain.

**Warning:** QSharedMemory changes the key in a Qt-specific way, unless otherwise
specified. Interoperation with non-Qt applications is achieved by first creating a
default shared memory with QSharedMemory() and then setting a native key with
[setNativeKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#setNativeKey)().
When using native keys, shared memory is not protected against multiple accesses on it
(for example, unable to
[lock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#lock)()) and a user-defined
mechanism should be used to achieve such protection.

### bool QSharedMemory::attach([QSharedMemory::AccessMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#AccessMode-enum) *mode* \= ReadWrite)

Attempts to attach the process to the shared memory segment identified by the key that
was passed to the constructor or to a call to
[setKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#setKey)() or
[setNativeKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#setNativeKey)().
The access *mode* is
[ReadWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#AccessMode-enum) by
default. It can also be
[ReadOnly](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#AccessMode-enum).
Returns `true` if the attach operation is successful. If false is returned, call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#error)() to determine
which error occurred. After attaching the shared memory segment, a pointer to the shared
memory can be obtained by calling
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#data)().

**See also**
[isAttached](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#isAttached)(),
[detach](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#detach)(), and
[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#create)().

### bool QSharedMemory::lock()

This is a semaphore that locks the shared memory segment for access by this process and
returns `true`. If another process has locked the segment, this function blocks until
the lock is released. Then it acquires the lock and returns `true`. If this function
returns `false`, it means that you have ignored a false return from
[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#create)() or
[attach](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#attach)(), that you have
set the key with
[setNativeKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#setNativeKey)() or
that
[QSystemSemaphore::acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)()
failed due to an unknown system error.

**See also** [unlock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#unlock)(),
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#data)(), and
[QSystemSemaphore::acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)().

You can use the native key to access shared memory segments that have not been created

Qt 5 reference:

### void QSharedMemory::setKey(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*key*)

Sets the platform independent *key* for this shared memory object. If *key* is the same
as the current key, the function returns without doing anything.

You can call [key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#key)() to
retrieve the platform independent key. Internally,
[QSharedMemory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html) converts this key
into a platform specific key. If you instead call
[nativeKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#nativeKey)(), you will
get the platform specific, converted key.

If the shared memory object is attached to an underlying shared memory segment, it will
[detach](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#detach) from it before
setting the new key. This function does not do an
[attach](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#attach)().

**See also** [key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#key)(),
[nativeKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#nativeKey)(), and
[isAttached](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#isAttached)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QSharedMemory.setNativeK.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QSharedMemory::setNativeKey(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*key*)

Sets the native, platform specific, *key* for this shared memory object. If *key* is the
same as the current native key, the function returns without doing anything. If all you
want is to assign a key to a segment, you should call
[setKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#setKey)() instead.

You can call
[nativeKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#nativeKey)() to
retrieve the native key. If a native key has been assigned, calling
[key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#key)() will return a null
string.

If the shared memory object is attached to an underlying shared memory segment, it will
[detach](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#detach) from it before
setting the new key. This function does not do an
[attach](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#attach)().

The application will not be portable if you set a native key.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

**See also**
[nativeKey](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#nativeKey)(),
[key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#key)(), and
[isAttached](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsharedmemory.html#isAttached)().

## Detailed Description

A size is specified by a [width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#width)()
and a [height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#height)(). It can be set in
the constructor and changed using the
[setWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#setWidth)(),
[setHeight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#setHeight)(), or
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#scale)() functions, or using
arithmetic operators. A size can also be manipulated directly by retrieving references
to the width and height using the
[rwidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#rwidth)() and
[rheight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#rheight)() functions. Finally,
the width and height can be swapped using the
[transpose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#transpose)() function.

The [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#isValid)() function
determines if a size is valid (a valid size has both width and height greater than or
equal to zero). The [isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#isEmpty)()
function returns `true` if either of the width and height is less than, or equal to,
zero, while the [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#isNull)()
function returns `true` only if both the width and the height is zero.

Use the [expandedTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#expandedTo)()
function to retrieve a size which holds the maximum height and width of *this* size and
a given size. Similarly, the
[boundedTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html#boundedTo)() function returns
a size which holds the minimum height and width of *this* size and a given size.

QSize objects can be streamed as well as compared.

PythonQt.QtCore.QSocketNotifier.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QSocketNotifier makes it possible to integrate Qt's event loop with other event
loops based on file descriptors. File descriptor action is detected in Qt's main event
loop
([QCoreApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)()).

Once you have opened a device using a low-level (usually platform-specific) API, you can
create a socket notifier to monitor the file descriptor. The socket notifier is enabled
by default, i.e. it emits the
[activated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#activated)() signal
whenever a socket event corresponding to its type occurs. Connect the
[activated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#activated)() signal
to the slot you want to be called when an event corresponding to your socket notifier's
type occurs.

There are three types of socket notifiers: read, write, and exception. The type is
described by the
[Type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#Type-enum) enum, and must
be specified when constructing the socket notifier. After construction it can be
determined using the
[type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#type)() function. Note
that if you need to monitor both reads and writes for the same file descriptor, you must
create two socket notifiers. Note also that it is not possible to install two socket
notifiers of the same type
([Read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#Type-enum),
[Write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#Type-enum),
[Exception](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#Type-enum)) on the
same socket.

The [setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#setEnabled)()
function allows you to disable as well as enable the socket notifier. It is generally
advisable to explicitly enable or disable the socket notifier, especially for write
notifiers. A disabled notifier ignores socket events (the same effect as not creating
the socket notifier). Use the
[isEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#isEnabled)()
function to determine the notifier's current status.

Finally, you can use the
[socket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html#socket)() function to
retrieve the socket identifier. Although the class is called QSocketNotifier, it is

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QStandardPaths::findExecutable(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*executableName*, const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*paths* \= QStringList())

Finds the executable named *executableName* in the specified *paths*, or the system
paths if paths is empty.

On most operating systems the system path is determined by the `PATH` environment
variable. The directories where to search for the executable can be set in the paths
argument. To search in both your own paths and the system paths, call findExecutable
twice, once with paths set and once with paths empty. Symlinks are not resolved in order
to preserve behavior for the case of executables whose behavior depends on the name they
are invoked with .

**Note:** On Windows, the usual executable extensions (from the PATHEXT environment
variable) are automatically appended. For example, the findExecutable("foo") call finds
`foo.exe` or `foo.bat` if present.

Returns the absolute file path to the executable, or an empty string if not found.

If the given \\n executableName is an absolute path pointing to an executable its clean
path is returned.

PythonQt.QtCore.QStandardPaths.setTestMo.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QStandardPaths::setTestModeEnabled(bool *testMode*)

If *testMode* is `true`, this enables a special "test mode" in
[QStandardPaths](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandardpaths.html), which changes
writable locations to point to test directories. This prevents auto tests from reading
or writing to the current user's configuration.

It affects the locations into which test programs might write files:
`GenericDataLocation`, `DataLocation`, `ConfigLocation`, `GenericConfigLocation`,
`AppConfigLocation`, `GenericCacheLocation`, and `CacheLocation`. Other locations are
not affected.

On Unix, `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set to `~/.qttest/share`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set to
`~/.qttest/config`, and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is set to `~/.qttest/cache`.

On macOS, data goes to `~/.qttest/Application Support`, cache goes to `~/.qttest/Cache`,
and config goes to `~/.qttest/Preferences`.

On Windows, everything goes to a "qttest" directory under `%APPDATA%`.

PythonQt.QtCore.QState.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QState objects can have child states, and can have transitions to other states. QState
is part of [The State Machine
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html).

The [addTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#addTransition)()
function adds a transition. The
[removeTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#removeTransition)()
function removes a transition. The
[transitions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#transitions)() function
returns the state's outgoing transitions.

The [assignProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#assignProperty)()
function is used for defining property assignments that should be performed when a state
is entered.

Top-level states must be passed a
[QStateMachine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html) object as their
parent state, or added to a state machine using
[QStateMachine::addState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#addState)().

### States with Child States

The [childMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#childMode) property
determines how child states are treated. For non-parallel state groups, the
[setInitialState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#setInitialState)()
function must be called to set the initial state. The child states are mutually
exclusive states, and the state machine needs to know which child state to enter when
the parent state is the target of a transition.

The state emits the
[QState::finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#finished)() signal
when a final child state
([QFinalState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfinalstate.html)) is entered.

The [setErrorState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#setErrorState)() sets
the state's error state. The error state is the state that the state machine will
transition to if an error is detected when attempting to enter the state (e.g. because
no initial state has been set).

## Detailed Description

QStateMachine is based on the concepts and notation of
[Statecharts](http://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~dharel/SCANNED.PAPERS/Statecharts.pdf).
QStateMachine is part of [The State Machine
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html).

A state machine manages a set of states (classes that inherit from
[QAbstractState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html)) and
transitions (descendants of
[QAbstractTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttransition.html))
between those states; these states and transitions define a state graph. Once a state
graph has been built, the state machine can execute it. QStateMachine's execution
algorithm is based on the [State Chart XML (SCXML)](http://www.w3.org/TR/scxml/)
algorithm. The framework's
[overview](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/statemachine-api.html) gives several state
graphs and the code to build them.

Use the [addState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#addState)()
function to add a top-level state to the state machine. States are removed with the
[removeState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#removeState)()
function. Removing states while the machine is running is discouraged.

Before the machine can be started, the [initial
state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#initialState) must be set. The
initial state is the state that the machine enters when started. You can then
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#start)() the state
machine. The [started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#started)()
signal is emitted when the initial state is entered.

The machine is event driven and keeps its own event loop. Events are posted to the
machine through
[postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#postEvent)(). Note
that this means that it executes asynchronously, and that it will not progress without a
running event loop. You will normally not have to post events to the machine directly as
Qt's transitions, e.g.,
[QEventTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeventtransition.html) and its
subclasses, handle this. But for custom transitions triggered by events,
[postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#postEvent)() is
useful.

The state machine processes events and takes transitions until a top-level final state
is entered; the state machine then emits the
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#finished)() signal. You can
also [stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#stop)() the state
machine explicitly. The
[stopped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#stopped)() signal is
emitted in this case.

The following snippet shows a state machine that will finish when a button is clicked:

```
QPushButton button;

QStateMachine machine;
QState *s1 = new QState();
s1->assignProperty(&button, "text", "Click me");

QFinalState *s2 = new QFinalState();
s1->addTransition(&button, &QPushButton::clicked, s2);

machine.addState(s1);
machine.addState(s2);
machine.setInitialState(s1);
machine.start();
```

This code example uses [QState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html), which
inherits [QAbstractState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractstate.html). The
[QState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html) class provides a state that you
can use to set properties and invoke methods on
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)s when the state is entered or
exited. It also contains convenience functions for adding transitions, e.g.,
[QSignalTransition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsignaltransition.html)s as in
this example. See the [QState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html) class
description for further details.

If an error is encountered, the machine will look for an [error
state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#errorState), and if one is
available, it will enter this state. The types of errors possible are described by the
[Error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#Error-enum) enum. After
the error state is entered, the type of the error can be retrieved with
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#error)(). The execution of
the state graph will not stop when the error state is entered. If no error state applies
to the erroneous state, the machine will stop executing and an error message will be
printed to the console.

**Note:** Important: setting the
[ChildMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#ChildMode-enum) of a state
machine to parallel
([ParallelStates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#ChildMode-enum))
results in an invalid state machine. It can only be set to (or kept as)
[ExclusiveStates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#ChildMode-enum).

### int QStateMachine::postDelayedEvent([QEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html) \**event*, int *delay*)

This is an overloaded function.

Posts the given *event* for processing by this state machine, with the given *delay* in
milliseconds. Returns an identifier associated with the delayed event, or -1 if the
event could not be posted.

This function returns immediately. When the delay has expired, the event will be added
to the state machine's event queue for processing. The state machine takes ownership of
the event and deletes it once it has been processed.

You can only post events when the state machine is running.

**Note:** This function is
[thread-safe](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/threads-reentrancy.html).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.15.

**See also**
[cancelDelayedEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#cancelDelayedEvent)()
and [postEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#postEvent)().
signatures: postDelayedEvent(self, event: PySide2.QtCore.QEvent, delay: int) -> int

Posts the given *event* of the given *priority* for processing by this state machine.

This function returns immediately. The event is added to the state machine's event

the event and deletes it once it has been processed.

[postDelayedEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#postDelayedEvent)().

### `[slot]` void QStateMachine::start()

Starts this state machine. The machine will reset its configuration and transition to
the initial state. When a final top-level state
([QFinalState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfinalstate.html)) is entered, the
machine will emit the
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#finished)() signal.

**Note:** A state machine will not run without a running event loop, such as the main
application event loop started with
[QCoreApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#exec)()
or [QApplication::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#exec)().

**See also** [started](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#started)(),
[finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#finished)(),
[stop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#stop)(),
[initialState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstate.html#initialState)(), and
[setRunning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatemachine.html#running-prop)().

## Detailed Description

This class is useful when you have a sequence of
[QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html)s that you want to repeatedly
match against some strings (perhaps in a loop), or when you want to search for the same
sequence of characters multiple times in the same string. Using a matcher object and
[indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringmatcher.html#indexIn)() is faster
than matching a plain [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) with
[QString::indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#indexOf)() if
repeated matching takes place. This class offers no benefit if you are doing one-off
string matches.

Create the QStringMatcher with the
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) you want to search for. Then
call [indexIn](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringmatcher.html#indexIn)() on the
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) that you want to search.

Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::buildAbi()

Returns the full architecture string that Qt was compiled for. This string is useful for
identifying different, incompatible builds. For example, it can be used as an identifier
to request an upgrade package from a server.

The values returned from this function are kept stable as follows: the mandatory
components of the result will not change in future versions of Qt, but optional suffixes
may be added.

The returned value is composed of three or more parts, separated by dashes ("-"). They
are:

| Component | Value |
| --- | --- |
| CPU Architecture | The same as [QSysInfo::buildCpuArchitecture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#buildCpuArchitecture)(), such as "arm", "i386", "mips" or "x86\_64" |
| Endianness | "little\_endian" or "big\_endian" |
| Word size | Whether it's a 32- or 64-bit application. Possible values are: "llp64" (Windows 64-bit), "lp64" (Unix 64-bit), "ilp32" (32-bit) |
| (Optional) ABI | Zero or more components identifying different ABIs possible in this architecture. Currently, Qt has optional ABI components for ARM and MIPS processors: one component is the main ABI (such as "eabi", "o32", "n32", "o64"); another is whether the calling convention is using hardware floating point registers ("hardfloat" is present). Additionally, if Qt was configured with `-qreal float`, the ABI option tag "qreal\_float" will be present. If Qt was configured with another type as qreal, that type is present after "qreal\_", with all characters other than letters and digits escaped by an underscore, followed by two hex digits. For example, `-qreal long double` becomes "qreal\_long\_20double". |

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also**
[QSysInfo::buildCpuArchitecture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#buildCpuArchitecture)().

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::buildCpuArchitecture()

Returns the architecture of the CPU that Qt was compiled for, in text format. Note that
this may not match the actual CPU that the application is running on if there's an
emulation layer or if the CPU supports multiple architectures (like x86-64 processors
supporting i386 applications). To detect that, use

may be added over time.

- "arm"

- "i386"
- "ia64"
- "mips"
- "mips64"
- "power"
- "power64"
- "sparc"
- "sparcv9"
- "x86\_64"

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::currentCpuArchitecture()

Note that this function depends on what the OS will report and may not detect the actual
CPU architecture if the OS hides that information or is unable to provide it. For
example, a 32-bit OS running on a 64-bit CPU is usually unable to determine the CPU is

functions being used, there may be discrepancies.

Typical returned values are (note: list not exhaustive):

- "mips"
- "mips64"
- "power"
- "power64"

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::kernelType()

Returns the type of the operating system kernel Qt was compiled for. It's also the
kernel the application is running on, unless the host operating system is running a form
of compatibility or virtualization layer.

Values returned by this function are stable and will not change over time, so
applications can rely on the returned value as an identifier, except that new OS kernel
types may be added over time.

On Windows, this function returns the type of Windows kernel, like "winnt". On Unix
systems, it returns the same as the output of `uname -s` (lowercased).

**Note:** This function may return surprising values: it returns "linux" for all
operating systems running Linux (including Android), "qnx" for all operating systems
running QNX, "freebsd" for Debian/kFreeBSD, and "darwin" for macOS and iOS. For
information on the type of product the application is running on, see
[productType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#productType)().

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also** [QFileSelector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileselector.html),
[kernelVersion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#kernelVersion)(),

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::productType()

Returns the product name of the operating system this application is running in. If the
application is running on some sort of emulation or virtualization layer (such as WINE
on a Unix system), this function will inspect the emulation / virtualization layer.

Values returned by this function are stable and will not change over time, so
applications can rely on the returned value as an identifier, except that new OS types
may be added over time.

**Linux and Android note**: this function returns "android" for Linux systems running
Android userspace, notably when using the Bionic library. For all other Linux systems,
regardless of C library being used, it tries to determine the distribution name and
returns that. If determining the distribution name failed, it returns "unknown".

**macOS note**: this function returns "osx" for all macOS systems, regardless of Apple
naming convention. The returned string will be updated for Qt 6\. Note that this
function erroneously returned "macos" for macOS 10.12 in Qt versions 5.6.2, 5.7.1, and
5.8.0.

**Darwin, iOS, tvOS, and watchOS note**: this function returns "ios" for iOS systems,
"tvos" for tvOS systems, "watchos" for watchOS systems, and "darwin" in case the system
could not be determined.

**[FreeBSD](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcore-attribution-freebsd.html#freebsd)
note**: this function returns "debian" for Debian/kFreeBSD and "unknown" otherwise.

**Windows note**: this function "winrt" for WinRT builds, and "windows" for normal
desktop builds.

For other Unix-type systems, this function usually returns "unknown".

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also** [QFileSelector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfileselector.html),
[kernelType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#kernelType)(),

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QSysInfo::productVersion()

Returns the product version of the operating system in string form. If the version could
not be determined, this function returns "unknown".

It will return the Android, iOS, macOS, Windows full-product versions on those systems.

Typical returned values are (note: list not exhaustive):

- "2016.09" (Amazon Linux AMI 2016.09)
- "7.1" (Android Nougat)
- "25" (Fedora 25\)
- "10.1" (iOS 10.1)
- "10.12" (macOS Sierra)
- "10.0" (tvOS 10\)
- "16.10" (Ubuntu 16.10)
- "3.1" (watchOS 3.1)
- "7 SP 1" (Windows 7 Service Pack 1\)
- "8.1" (Windows 8.1)
- "10" (Windows 10\)
- "Server 2016" (Windows Server 2016\)

On Linux systems, it will try to determine the distribution version and will return
that. This is also done on Debian/kFreeBSD, so this function will return Debian version
in that case.

In all other Unix-type systems, this function always returns "unknown".

**Note:** The version string returned from this function is not guaranteed to be
orderable. On Linux, the version of the distribution may jump unexpectedly, please refer
to the distribution's documentation for versioning practices.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also**
[kernelType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#kernelType)(),
[kernelVersion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsysinfo.html#kernelVersion)(),

PythonQt.QtCore.QSystemSemaphore.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A semaphore is a generalization of a mutex. While a mutex can be locked only once, a
semaphore can be acquired multiple times. Typically, a semaphore is used to protect a
certain number of identical resources.

Like its lighter counterpart
[QSemaphore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsemaphore.html), a QSystemSemaphore can
be accessed from multiple [threads](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html).
Unlike [QSemaphore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsemaphore.html), a
QSystemSemaphore can also be accessed from multiple
[processes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprocess.html). This means
QSystemSemaphore is a much heavier class, so if your application doesn't need to access
your semaphores across multiple processes, you will probably want to use
[QSemaphore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsemaphore.html).

Semaphores support two fundamental operations,
[acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)() and
[release](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#release)():

[acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)() tries to
acquire one resource. If there isn't a resource available, the call blocks until a
resource becomes available. Then the resource is acquired and the call returns.

[release](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#release)() releases
one resource so it can be acquired by another process. The function can also be called
with a parameter n \> 1, which releases n resources.

A system semaphore is created with a string key that other processes can use to use the
same semaphore.

Example: Create a system semaphore

```
QSystemSemaphore sem("market", 3, QSystemSemaphore::Create);
                             // resources available == 3
sem.acquire();               // resources available == 2
sem.acquire();               // resources available == 1
sem.acquire();               // resources available == 0
sem.release();               // resources available == 1
sem.release(2);              // resources available == 3
```

A typical application of system semaphores is for controlling access to a circular
buffer shared by a producer process and a consumer processes.

### Platform-Specific Behavior

When using this class, be aware of the following platform differences:

**Windows:** QSystemSemaphore does not own its underlying system semaphore. Windows owns
it. This means that when all instances of QSystemSemaphore for a particular key have
been destroyed, either by having their destructors called, or because one or more
processes crash, Windows removes the underlying system semaphore.

**Unix:**

- QSystemSemaphore owns the underlying system semaphore in Unix systems. This means that the last process having an instance of QSystemSemaphore for a particular key must remove the underlying system semaphore in its destructor. If the last process crashes without running the QSystemSemaphore destructor, Unix does not automatically remove the underlying system semaphore, and the semaphore survives the crash. A subsequent process that constructs a QSystemSemaphore with the same key will then be given the existing system semaphore. In that case, if the QSystemSemaphore constructor has specified its [access mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum) as [Open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum), its initial resource count will not be reset to the one provided but remain set to the value it received in the crashed process. To protect against this, the first process to create a semaphore for a particular key (usually a server), must pass its [access mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum) as [Create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#AccessMode-enum), which will force Unix to reset the resource count in the underlying system semaphore.
- When a process using QSystemSemaphore terminates for any reason, Unix automatically reverses the effect of all acquire operations that were not released. Thus if the process acquires a resource and then exits without releasing it, Unix will release that resource.

### bool QSystemSemaphore::release(int *n* \= 1\)

Releases *n* resources guarded by the semaphore. Returns `true` unless there is a system
error.

Example: Create a system semaphore having five resources; acquire them all and then
release them all.

```
QSystemSemaphore sem("market", 5, QSystemSemaphore::Create);
for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i)  // acquire all 5 resources
    sem.acquire();
sem.release(5);              // release the 5 resources
```

This function can also "create" resources. For example, immediately following the
sequence of statements above, suppose we add the statement:

```
sem.release(10);          // "create" 10 new resources
```

Ten new resources are now guarded by the semaphore, in addition to the five that already
existed. You would not normally use this function to create more resources.

**See also**
[acquire](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsystemsemaphore.html#acquire)().

## Detailed Description

QTemporaryDir is used to create unique temporary directories safely. The directory
itself is created by the constructor. The name of the temporary directory is guaranteed
to be unique (i.e., you are guaranteed to not overwrite an existing directory), and the
directory will subsequently be removed upon destruction of the QTemporaryDir object. The
directory name is either auto-generated, or created based on a template, which is passed
to QTemporaryDir's constructor.

Example:

```
    // Within a function/method...

    QTemporaryDir dir;
    if (dir.isValid()) {
        // dir.path() returns the unique directory path
    }

    // The QTemporaryDir destructor removes the temporary directory
    // as it goes out of scope.
```

It is very important to test that the temporary directory could be created, using
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporarydir.html#isValid)(). Do not use
[exists()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#exists-1), since a
default-constructed [QDir](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html) represents the
current directory, which exists.

The path to the temporary directory can be found by calling
[path](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporarydir.html#path)().

A temporary directory will have some static part of the name and some part that is
calculated to be unique. The default path will be determined from
[QCoreApplication::applicationName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#applicationName-prop)()
(otherwise `qt_temp`) and will be placed into the temporary path as returned by
[QDir::tempPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#tempPath)(). If you
specify your own path, a relative path will not be placed in the temporary directory by
default, but be relative to the current working directory. In all cases, a random string
will be appended to the path in order to make it unique.

## Detailed Description

QTemporaryFile is used to create unique temporary files safely. The file itself is
created by calling
[open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html#open)(). The name of the
temporary file is guaranteed to be unique (i.e., you are guaranteed to not overwrite an
existing file), and the file will subsequently be removed upon destruction of the
QTemporaryFile object. This is an important technique that avoids data corruption for
applications that store data in temporary files. The file name is either auto-generated,
or created based on a template, which is passed to QTemporaryFile's constructor.

Example:

```
    // Within a function/method...

    QTemporaryFile file;
    if (file.open()) {
        // file.fileName() returns the unique file name
    }

    // The QTemporaryFile destructor removes the temporary file
    // as it goes out of scope.
```

Reopening a QTemporaryFile after calling
[close](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledevice.html#close)() is safe. For as
long as the QTemporaryFile object itself is not destroyed, the unique temporary file
will exist and be kept open internally by QTemporaryFile.

The file name of the temporary file can be found by calling
[fileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html#fileName)(). Note that
this is only defined after the file is first opened; the function returns an empty
string before this.

A temporary file will have some static part of the name and some part that is calculated
to be unique. The default filename will be determined from
[QCoreApplication::applicationName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#applicationName-prop)()
(otherwise `qt_temp`) and will be placed into the temporary path as returned by
[QDir::tempPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#tempPath)(). If you
specify your own filename, a relative file path will not be placed in the temporary
directory by default, but be relative to the current working directory. It is important
to specify the correct directory if the
[rename](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html#rename)() function will
be called, as QTemporaryFile can only rename files within the same volume / filesystem
as the temporary file itself was created on.

Specified filenames can contain the following template `XXXXXX` (six upper case "X"
characters), which will be replaced by the auto-generated portion of the filename. Note
that the template is case sensitive. If the template is not present in the filename,
QTemporaryFile appends the generated part to the filename given. Only the last
occurrence of `"XXXXXX"` will be considered.

**Note:** On Linux, QTemporaryFile will attempt to create unnamed temporary files. If
that succeeds, [open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html#open)()
will return true but exists() will be false. If you call
[fileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html#fileName)() or any
function that calls it, QTemporaryFile will give the file a name, so most applications
will not see a difference.

### bool QTemporaryFile::rename(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*newName*)

Renames the current temporary file to *newName* and returns true if it succeeded.

This function has an important difference compared to QFile::rename(): it will not
perform a copy\+delete if the low-level system call to rename the file fails, something
that could happen if *newName* specifies a file in a different volume or filesystem than
the temporary file was created on. In other words,
[QTemporaryFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtemporaryfile.html) only supports
atomic file renaming.

This functionality is intended to support materializing the destination file with all
contents already present, so another process cannot see an incomplete file in the
process of being written. The
[QSaveFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsavefile.html) class can be used for a
similar purpose too, particularly if the destination file is not temporary.

**See also** [QSaveFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsavefile.html),
[QSaveFile::commit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsavefile.html#commit)(), and
QFile::rename().

## Detailed Description

QTextBoundaryFinder allows to find Unicode text boundaries in a string, accordingly to
the Unicode text boundary specification (see [Unicode Standard Annex
#14](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr14/) and [Unicode Standard Annex
#29](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/)).

QTextBoundaryFinder can operate on a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) in four possible modes
depending on the value of *BoundaryType*.

Units of Unicode characters that make up what the user thinks of as a character or basic
unit of the language are here called Grapheme clusters. The two unicode characters 'A'
\+ diaeresis do for example form one grapheme cluster as the user thinks of them as one
character, yet it is in this case represented by two unicode code points (see
<https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/#Grapheme_Cluster_Boundaries>).

Word boundaries are there to locate the start and end of what a language considers to be
a word (see <https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/#Word_Boundaries>).

Line break boundaries give possible places where a line break might happen and sentence
boundaries will show the beginning and end of whole sentences (see
<https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/#Sentence_Boundaries> and
<https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr14/>).

The first position in a string is always a valid boundary and refers to the position
before the first character. The last position at the length of the string is also valid
and refers to the position after the last character.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt uses Unicode to store, draw and manipulate strings. In many situations you may wish
to deal with data that uses a different encoding. For example, most Japanese documents
are still stored in Shift-JIS or ISO 2022-JP, while Russian users often have their
documents in KOI8-R or Windows-1251.

Qt provides a set of QTextCodec classes to help with converting non-Unicode formats to
and from Unicode. You can also create your own codec classes.

The supported encodings are:

- [Big5](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codec-big5.html)
- [Big5-HKSCS](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codec-big5hkscs.html)
- CP949
- [EUC-JP](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codec-eucjp.html)
- [EUC-KR](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codec-euckr.html)
- [GB18030](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codec-gbk.html)
- HP-ROMAN8
- IBM 850
- IBM 866
- IBM 874
- [ISO 2022-JP](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codecs-jis.html)
- ISO 8859-1 to 10
- ISO 8859-13 to 16
- Iscii-Bng, Dev, Gjr, Knd, Mlm, Ori, Pnj, Tlg, and Tml
- KOI8-R
- KOI8-U
- Macintosh
- [Shift-JIS](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codec-sjis.html)
- TIS-620
- [TSCII](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/codec-tscii.html)
- UTF-8
- UTF-16
- UTF-16BE
- UTF-16LE
- UTF-32
- UTF-32BE
- UTF-32LE
- Windows-1250 to 1258

If Qt is compiled with ICU support enabled, most codecs supported by ICU will also be
available to the application.

[QTextCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html)s can be used as follows
to convert some locally encoded string to Unicode. Suppose you have some string encoded
in Russian KOI8-R encoding, and want to convert it to Unicode. The simple way to do it
is like this:

```
QByteArray encodedString = "...";
QTextCodec *codec = QTextCodec::codecForName("KOI8-R");
QString string = codec->toUnicode(encodedString);
```

After this, `string` holds the text converted to Unicode. Converting a string from
Unicode to the local encoding is just as easy:

```
QString string = "...";
QTextCodec *codec = QTextCodec::codecForName("KOI8-R");
QByteArray encodedString = codec->fromUnicode(string);
```

To read or write files in various encodings, use
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) and its
[setCodec()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setCodec) function. See
the [Codecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-tools-codecs-example.html)
example for an application of QTextCodec to file I/O.

Some care must be taken when trying to convert the data in chunks, for example, when
receiving it over a network. In such cases it is possible that a multi-byte character
will be split over two chunks. At best this might result in the loss of a character and
at worst cause the entire conversion to fail.

The approach to use in these situations is to create a
[QTextDecoder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextdecoder.html) object for the
codec and use this [QTextDecoder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextdecoder.html)
for the whole decoding process, as shown below:

```
QTextCodec *codec = QTextCodec::codecForName("Shift-JIS");
QTextDecoder *decoder = codec->makeDecoder();

QString string;
while (new_data_available()) {
    QByteArray chunk = get_new_data();
    string += decoder->toUnicode(chunk);
}
delete decoder;
```

The [QTextDecoder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextdecoder.html) object
maintains state between chunks and therefore works correctly even if a multi-byte
character is split between chunks.

### Creating Your Own Codec Class

Support for new text encodings can be added to Qt by creating QTextCodec subclasses.

The pure virtual functions describe the encoder to the system and the coder is used as
required in the different text file formats supported by
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html), and under X11, for
the locale-specific character input and output.

To add support for another encoding to Qt, make a subclass of QTextCodec and implement
the functions listed in the table below.

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#name)() | Returns the official name for the encoding. If the encoding is listed in the [IANA character-sets encoding file](http://www.iana.org/assignments/character-sets/character-sets.xml), the name should be the preferred MIME name for the encoding. |
| [aliases](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#aliases)() | Returns a list of alternative names for the encoding. QTextCodec provides a default implementation that returns an empty list. For example, "ISO-8859-1" has "latin1", "CP819", "IBM819", and "iso-ir-100" as aliases. |
| [mibEnum()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#mibEnum) | Return the MIB enum for the encoding if it is listed in the [IANA character-sets encoding file](http://www.iana.org/assignments/character-sets/character-sets.xml). |
| [convertToUnicode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#convertToUnicode)() | Converts an 8-bit character string to Unicode. |
| [convertFromUnicode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#convertFromUnicode)() | Converts a Unicode string to an 8-bit character string. |

PythonQt.QtCore.QTextStream.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QTextStream can operate on a
[QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html), a
[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) or a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). Using QTextStream's
streaming operators, you can conveniently read and write words, lines and numbers. For
generating text, QTextStream supports formatting options for field padding and
alignment, and formatting of numbers. Example:

```
QFile data("output.txt");
if (data.open(QFile::WriteOnly | QFile::Truncate)) {
    QTextStream out(&data);
    out << "Result: " << qSetFieldWidth(10) << left << 3.14 << 2.7;
    // writes "Result: 3.14      2.7       "
}
```

It's also common to use QTextStream to read console input and write console output.
QTextStream is locale aware, and will automatically decode standard input using the
correct codec. Example:

```
QTextStream stream(stdin);
QString line;
while (stream.readLineInto(&line)) {
    ...
}
```

Besides using QTextStream's constructors, you can also set the device or string
QTextStream operates on by calling
[setDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setDevice)() or
[setString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setString)(). You can
seek to a position by calling
[seek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#seek)(), and
[atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#atEnd)() will return true
when there is no data left to be read. If you call
[flush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#flush)(), QTextStream will
empty all data from its write buffer into the device and call
[flush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#flush)() on the device.

Internally, QTextStream uses a Unicode based buffer, and
[QTextCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html) is used by QTextStream
to automatically support different character sets. By default,
[QTextCodec::codecForLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#codecForLocale)()
is used for reading and writing, but you can also set the codec by calling
[setCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setCodec)(). Automatic
Unicode detection is also supported. When this feature is enabled (the default
behavior), QTextStream will detect the UTF-16 or the UTF-32 BOM (Byte Order Mark) and
switch to the appropriate UTF codec when reading. QTextStream does not write a BOM by
default, but you can enable this by calling
[setGenerateByteOrderMark](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setGenerateByteOrderMark)(true).
When QTextStream operates on a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) directly, the codec is
disabled.

There are three general ways to use QTextStream when reading text files:

- Chunk by chunk, by calling [readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#readLine)() or [readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#readAll)().
- Word by word. QTextStream supports streaming into [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)s, [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)s and char\* buffers. Words are delimited by space, and leading white space is automatically skipped.
- Character by character, by streaming into [QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html) or char types. This method is often used for convenient input handling when parsing files, independent of character encoding and end-of-line semantics. To skip white space, call [skipWhiteSpace](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#skipWhiteSpace)().

Since the text stream uses a buffer, you should not read from the stream using the
implementation of a superclass. For instance, if you have a
[QFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfile.html) and read from it directly using
[QFile::readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)() instead
of using the stream, the text stream's internal position will be out of sync with the
file's position.

By default, when reading numbers from a stream of text, QTextStream will automatically
detect the number's base representation. For example, if the number starts with "0x", it
is assumed to be in hexadecimal form. If it starts with the digits 1-9, it is assumed to
be in decimal form, and so on. You can set the integer base, thereby disabling the
automatic detection, by calling
[setIntegerBase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setIntegerBase)().
Example:

```
QTextStream in("0x50 0x20");
int firstNumber, secondNumber;

in >> firstNumber;             // firstNumber == 80
in >> dec >> secondNumber;     // secondNumber == 0

char ch;
in >> ch;                      // ch == 'x'
```

QTextStream supports many formatting options for generating text. You can set the field
width and pad character by calling
[setFieldWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setFieldWidth)() and
[setPadChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setPadChar)(). Use
[setFieldAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setFieldAlignment)()
to set the alignment within each field. For real numbers, call
[setRealNumberNotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setRealNumberNotation)()
and
[setRealNumberPrecision](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setRealNumberPrecision)()
to set the notation
([SmartNotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#RealNumberNotation-enum),
[ScientificNotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#RealNumberNotation-enum),
[FixedNotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#RealNumberNotation-enum))
and precision in digits of the generated number. Some extra number formatting options
are also available through
[setNumberFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setNumberFlags)().

Like `<iostream>` in the standard C\+\+ library, QTextStream also defines several global

| [Qt::oct](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#oct) | Same as [setIntegerBase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setIntegerBase)(8). |

### [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) QTextStream::pos() const

if an error occurs (e.g., if there is no device or string, or if there's a device
error).

this function may have to seek the device to reconstruct a valid device position. This
operation can be expensive, so you may want to avoid calling this function in a tight
loop.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). Avoid this function when
working on large files, as it will consume a significant amount of memory.

Calling [readLine()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#readLine) is

PythonQt.QtCore.QTextStream.readLine.doc:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QTextStream::readLine([qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxlen* \= 0\)

Reads one line of text from the stream, and returns it as a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). The maximum allowed line
length is set to *maxlen*. If the stream contains lines longer than this, then the lines
will be split after *maxlen* characters and returned in parts.

If *maxlen* is 0, the lines can be of any length.

The returned line has no trailing end-of-line characters ("\\n" or "\\r\\n"), so calling
[QString::trimmed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#trimmed)() can be
unnecessary.

If the stream has read to the end of the file, readLine() will return a null
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). For strings, or for devices
that support it, you can explicitly test for the end of the stream using
[atEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#atEnd)().

**See also** [readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#readAll)()
and [QIODevice::readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)().

### bool QTextStream::readLineInto([QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \**line*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *maxlen* \= 0\)

Reads one line of text from the stream into *line*. If *line* is `nullptr`, the read
line is not stored.

The maximum allowed line length is set to *maxlen*. If the stream contains lines longer
than this, then the lines will be split after *maxlen* characters and returned in parts.

If *maxlen* is 0, the lines can be of any length.

The resulting line has no trailing end-of-line characters ("\\n" or "\\r\\n"), so
calling [QString::trimmed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#trimmed)()
can be unnecessary.

If *line* has sufficient capacity for the data that is about to be read, this function
may not need to allocate new memory. Because of this, it can be faster than
[readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#readLine)().

Returns `false` if the stream has read to the end of the file or an error has occurred;
otherwise returns `true`. The contents in *line* before the call are discarded in any
case.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.5.

**See also** [readAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#readAll)()
and [QIODevice::readLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#readLine)().

### void QTextStream::setAutoDetectUnicode(bool *enabled*)

If *enabled* is true, [QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html)
will attempt to detect Unicode encoding by peeking into the stream data to see if it can
find the UTF-8, UTF-16, or UTF-32 Byte Order Mark (BOM). If this mark is found,
[QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) will replace the
current codec with the UTF codec.

This function can be used together with
[setCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setCodec)(). It is common
to set the codec to UTF-8, and then enable UTF-16 detection.

[autoDetectUnicode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#autoDetectUnicode)(),
[setCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setCodec)(), and

### void QTextStream::setCodec([QTextCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html) \**codec*)

Sets the codec for this stream to *codec*. The codec is used for decoding any data that
is read from the assigned device, and for encoding any data that is written. By default,
[QTextCodec::codecForLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#codecForLocale)()
is used, and automatic unicode detection is enabled.

If [QTextStream](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html) operates on a
string, this function does nothing.

**Warning:** If you call this function while the text stream is reading from an open
sequential socket, the internal buffer may still contain text decoded using the old
codec.

**See also** [codec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#codec)(),
[setAutoDetectUnicode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setAutoDetectUnicode)(),
and [setLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextstream.html#setLocale)().

### void QTextStream::setCodec(const char \**codecName*)

Sets the codec for this stream to the
[QTextCodec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html) for the encoding
specified by *codecName*. Common values for `codecName` include "ISO 8859-1", "UTF-8",
and "UTF-16". If the encoding isn't recognized, nothing happens.

Example:

```
QTextStream out(&file);
out.setCodec("UTF-8");
```

[QTextCodec::codecForName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcodec.html#codecForName)()

PythonQt.QtCore.QThreadPool.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QThreadPool manages and recycles individual
[QThread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html) objects to help reduce thread
creation costs in programs that use threads. Each Qt application has one global
QThreadPool object, which can be accessed by calling
[globalInstance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#globalInstance)().

To use one of the QThreadPool threads, subclass
[QRunnable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html) and implement the run()
virtual function. Then create an object of that class and pass it to
[QThreadPool::start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#start)().

```
class HelloWorldTask : public QRunnable
{
    void run() override
    {
        qDebug() << "Hello world from thread" << QThread::currentThread();
    }
};

HelloWorldTask *hello = new HelloWorldTask();
// QThreadPool takes ownership and deletes 'hello' automatically
QThreadPool::globalInstance()->start(hello);
```

QThreadPool deletes the [QRunnable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html)
automatically by default. Use
[QRunnable::setAutoDelete](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html#setAutoDelete)()
to change the auto-deletion flag.

QThreadPool supports executing the same
[QRunnable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html) more than once by calling
tryStart(this) from within
[QRunnable::run](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html#run)(). If autoDelete
is enabled the [QRunnable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html) will be
deleted when the last thread exits the run function. Calling
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#start)() multiple times with
the same [QRunnable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html) when autoDelete
is enabled creates a race condition and is not recommended.

Threads that are unused for a certain amount of time will expire. The default expiry
timeout is 30000 milliseconds (30 seconds). This can be changed using
[setExpiryTimeout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#expiryTimeout-prop)().
Setting a negative expiry timeout disables the expiry mechanism.

Call
[maxThreadCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#maxThreadCount-prop)()
to query the maximum number of threads to be used. If needed, you can change the limit
with
[setMaxThreadCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#maxThreadCount-prop)().
The default
[maxThreadCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#maxThreadCount-prop)()
is
[QThread::idealThreadCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html#idealThreadCount)().
The
[activeThreadCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#activeThreadCount-prop)()
function returns the number of threads currently doing work.

The reserveThread() function reserves a thread for external use. Use releaseThread()
when your are done with the thread, so that it may be reused. Essentially, these
functions temporarily increase or reduce the active thread count and are useful when
implementing time-consuming operations that are not visible to the QThreadPool.

Note that QThreadPool is a low-level class for managing threads, see the Qt Concurrent
module for higher level alternatives.

PythonQt.QtCore.QThreadPool.expiryTimeou.doc:

### expiryTimeout : int

Threads that are unused for *expiryTimeout* milliseconds are considered to have expired
and will exit. Such threads will be restarted as needed. The default *expiryTimeout* is
30000 milliseconds (30 seconds). If *expiryTimeout* is negative, newly created threads
will not expire, e.g., they will not exit until the thread pool is destroyed.

Note that setting *expiryTimeout* has no effect on already running threads. Only newly
created threads will use the new *expiryTimeout*. We recommend setting the
*expiryTimeout* immediately after creating the thread pool, but before calling
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#start)().

**Access functions:**

| --- | --- |
| void | **setExpiryTimeout**(int *expiryTimeout*) |

### void QThreadPool::start([QRunnable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html) \**runnable*, int *priority* \= 0\)

Reserves a thread and uses it to run *runnable*, unless this thread will make the
current thread count exceed
[maxThreadCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthreadpool.html#maxThreadCount-prop)().
In that case, *runnable* is added to a run queue instead. The *priority* argument can be
used to control the run queue's order of execution.

Note that the thread pool takes ownership of the *runnable* if
[runnable-\>autoDelete()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html#autoDelete)
returns `true`, and the *runnable* will be deleted automatically by the thread pool
after the [runnable-\>run()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html#run)
returns. If
[runnable-\>autoDelete()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrunnable.html#autoDelete)
returns `false`, ownership of *runnable* remains with the caller. Note that changing the
auto-deletion on *runnable* after calling this functions results in undefined behavior.

PythonQt.QtCore.QTime.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QTime object contains a clock time, which it can express as the numbers of hours,
minutes, seconds, and milliseconds since midnight. It provides functions for comparing
times and for manipulating a time by adding a number of milliseconds.

QTime uses the 24-hour clock format; it has no concept of AM/PM. Unlike
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html), QTime knows nothing
about time zones or daylight-saving time (DST).

A QTime object is typically created either by giving the number of hours, minutes,
seconds, and milliseconds explicitly, or by using the static function
[currentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#currentTime)(), which
creates a QTime object that represents the system's local time.

The [hour](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#hour)(),
[minute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#minute)(),
[second](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#second)(), and
[msec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#msec)() functions provide access to
the number of hours, minutes, seconds, and milliseconds of the time. The same
information is provided in textual format by the
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#toString)() function.

The [addSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#addSecs)() and
[addMSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#addMSecs)() functions provide
the time a given number of seconds or milliseconds later than a given time.
Correspondingly, the number of seconds or milliseconds between two times can be found
using [secsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#secsTo)() or
[msecsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#msecsTo)().

QTime provides a full set of operators to compare two QTime objects; an earlier time is
considered smaller than a later one; if
A.[msecsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#msecsTo)(B) is positive, then
A \< B.

### QTime QTime::addMSecs(int *ms*) const

Returns a [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) object containing a
time *ms* milliseconds later than the time of this object (or earlier if *ms* is
negative).

Note that the time will wrap if it passes midnight. See

Returns a null time if this time is invalid.

**See also** [addSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#addSecs)(),
[msecsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#msecsTo)(), and

PythonQt.QtCore.QTime.addSecs.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### QTime QTime::addSecs(int *s*) const

Returns a [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) object containing a
time *s* seconds later than the time of this object (or earlier if *s* is negative).

Note that the time will wrap if it passes midnight.

Returns a null time if this time is invalid.

Example:

```
QTime n(14, 0, 0);                // n == 14:00:00
QTime t;
t = n.addSecs(70);                // t == 14:01:10
t = n.addSecs(-70);               // t == 13:58:50
t = n.addSecs(10 * 60 * 60 + 5);  // t == 00:00:05
t = n.addSecs(-15 * 60 * 60);     // t == 23:00:00
```

**See also** [addMSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#addMSecs)(),
[secsTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#secsTo)(), and
[QDateTime::addSecs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#addSecs)().

### `[static]` QTime QTime::currentTime()

Returns the current time as reported by the system clock.

Note that the accuracy depends on the accuracy of the underlying operating system; not
all systems provide 1-millisecond accuracy.

Furthermore, currentTime() only increases within each day; it shall drop by 24 hours
each time midnight passes; and, beside this, changes in it may not correspond to elapsed
time, if a daylight-saving transition intervenes.

PythonQt.QtCore.QTime.fromString.doc:
