### `[static]` QTime QTime::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, [Qt::DateFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum) *format* \= Qt::TextDate)

Returns the time represented in the *string* as a
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) using the *format* given, or an
invalid time if this is not possible.

Note that fromString() uses a "C" locale encoded string to convert milliseconds to a
float value. If the default locale is not "C", this may result in two conversion
attempts (if the conversion fails for the default locale). This should be considered an
implementation detail.

**Note:** Support for localized dates, including the format options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Use
[QLocale::toTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toTime)() instead.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#toString)() and
[QLocale::toTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toTime)().

### `[static]` QTime QTime::fromString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*string*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*format*)

Returns the [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) represented by the
*string*, using the *format* given, or an invalid time if the string cannot be parsed.

These expressions may be used for the format:

| Expression | Output |
| --- | --- |
| h | The hour without a leading zero (0 to 23 or 1 to 12 if AM/PM display) |
| hh | The hour with a leading zero (00 to 23 or 01 to 12 if AM/PM display) |
| H | The hour without a leading zero (0 to 23, even with AM/PM display) |
| HH | The hour with a leading zero (00 to 23, even with AM/PM display) |
| m | The minute without a leading zero (0 to 59\) |
| mm | The minute with a leading zero (00 to 59\) |
| s | The whole second, without any leading zero (0 to 59\) |
| ss | The whole second, with a leading zero where applicable (00 to 59\) |
| z | The fractional part of the second, to go after a decimal point, without trailing zeroes (0 to 999). Thus "`s.z`" reports the seconds to full available (millisecond) precision without trailing zeroes. |
| zzz | The fractional part of the second, to millisecond precision, including trailing zeroes where applicable (000 to 999). |
| AP or A | Interpret as an AM/PM time. *A/AP* will match an upper-case version of either [QLocale::amText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#amText)() or [QLocale::pmText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#pmText)(). |
| ap or a | Interpret as an am/pm time. *a/ap* will match a lower-case version of either [QLocale::amText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#amText)() or [QLocale::pmText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#pmText)(). |

All other input characters will be treated as text. Any non-empty sequence of characters
enclosed in single quotes will also be treated (stripped of the quotes) as text and not
be interpreted as expressions.

```
QTime time = QTime::fromString("1mm12car00", "m'mm'hcarss");
// time is 12:01.00
```

If the format is not satisfied, an invalid
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) is returned. Expressions that do
not expect leading zeroes to be given (h, m, s and z) are greedy. This means that they
will use two digits even if this puts them outside the range of accepted values and
leaves too few digits for other sections. For example, the following string could have
meant 00:07:10, but the m will grab two digits, resulting in an invalid time:

```
QTime time = QTime::fromString("00:710", "hh:ms"); // invalid
```

Any field that is not represented in the format will be set to zero. For example:

```
QTime time = QTime::fromString("1.30", "m.s");
// time is 00:01:30.000
```

**Note:** If localized forms of am or pm (the AP, ap, A or a formats) are used, please
switch to using
[QLocale::system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#system)().toTime() as
[QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) methods shall change to only
recognize English (C locale) at Qt 6\.

**See also** [toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#toString)(),
[QDateTime::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#fromString)(),
[QDate::fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#fromString)(), and
[QLocale::toTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toTime)().

### int QTime::msecsTo(const QTime \&*t*) const

Returns the number of milliseconds from this time to *t*. If *t* is earlier than this
time, the number of milliseconds returned is negative.

Because [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) measures time within a

### int QTime::restart()

Sets this time to the current time and returns the number of milliseconds that have
elapsed since the last time start() or restart() was called.

This function is guaranteed to be atomic and is thus very handy for repeated
measurements. Call start() to start the first measurement, and restart() for each later
measurement.

Note that the counter wraps to zero 24 hours after the last call to start() or
restart().

**Warning:** If the system's clock setting has been changed since the last time start()
or restart() was called, the result is undefined. This can happen when daylight-saving
time is turned on or off.

**See also** [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime-obsolete.html#start)(),
[elapsed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime-obsolete.html#elapsed)(), and
[currentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#currentTime)().

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the time as a string. The *format* parameter determines the format of the
string.

If *format* is
[Qt::TextDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
format is HH:mm:ss; e.g. 1 second before midnight would be "23:59:59".

If *format* is
[Qt::ISODate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the string
format corresponds to the ISO 8601 extended specification for representations of dates,
represented by HH:mm:ss. To include milliseconds in the ISO 8601 date, use the *format*
[Qt::ISODateWithMs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), which
corresponds to HH:mm:ss.zzz.

The *format* options
[Qt::SystemLocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum):,
[Qt::SystemLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::SystemLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with:
[QLocale::system().toString(time,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale::system().toString(time,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

The *format* options
[Qt::LocaleDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum),
[Qt::DefaultLocaleShortDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
and
[Qt::DefaultLocaleLongDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum)
shall be removed in Qt 6\. Their use should be replaced with: [QLocale().toString(time,
QLocale::ShortFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString) or
[QLocale().toString(time,
QLocale::LongFormat)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toString).

If the *format* is
[Qt::RFC2822Date](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DateFormat-enum), the
string is formatted in an [RFC 2822](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2822.txt)
compatible way. An example of this formatting is "23:59:20".

If the time is invalid, an empty string will be returned.

**See also** [fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html#fromString)(),
[QDate::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html#toString-1)(),
[QDateTime::toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html#toString)(), and

PythonQt.QtCore.QTimeLine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It's most commonly used to animate a GUI control by calling a slot periodically. You can
construct a timeline by passing its duration in milliseconds to QTimeLine's constructor.
The timeline's duration describes for how long the animation will run. Then you set a
suitable frame range by calling
[setFrameRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#setFrameRange)().
Finally connect the
[frameChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#frameChanged)() signal
to a suitable slot in the widget you wish to animate (for example,
[setValue()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#value-prop) in
[QProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html)). When you proceed
to calling [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#start)(), QTimeLine
will enter Running state, and start emitting
[frameChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#frameChanged)() at
regular intervals, causing your widget's connected property's value to grow from the
lower end to the upper and of your frame range, at a steady rate. You can specify the
update interval by calling
[setUpdateInterval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#updateInterval-prop)().
When done, QTimeLine enters
[NotRunning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#State-enum) state, and
emits [finished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#finished)().

Example:

```
...
progressBar = new QProgressBar(this);
progressBar->setRange(0, 100);

// Construct a 1-second timeline with a frame range of 0 - 100
QTimeLine *timeLine = new QTimeLine(1000, this);
timeLine->setFrameRange(0, 100);
connect(timeLine, &QTimeLine::frameChanged, progressBar, &QProgressBar::setValue);

// Clicking the push button will start the progress bar animation
pushButton = new QPushButton(tr("Start animation"), this);
connect(pushButton, &QPushButton::clicked, timeLine, &QTimeLine::start);
...
```

By default the timeline runs once, from its beginning to its end, upon which you must
call [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#start)() again to restart
from the beginning. To make the timeline loop, you can call
[setLoopCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#loopCount-prop)(),
passing the number of times the timeline should run before finishing. The direction can
also be changed, causing the timeline to run backward, by calling
[setDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#direction-prop)(). You
can also pause and unpause the timeline while it's running by calling
[setPaused](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#setPaused)(). For
interactive control, the
[setCurrentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#currentTime-prop)()
function is provided, which sets the time position of the time line directly. Although
most useful in
[NotRunning](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#State-enum) state (e.g.,
connected to a
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueChanged)() signal
in a [QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html)), this function can be
called at any time.

The frame interface is useful for standard widgets, but QTimeLine can be used to control
any type of animation. The heart of QTimeLine lies in the
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)()
function, which generates a *value* between 0 and 1 for a given time. This value is
typically used to describe the steps of an animation, where 0 is the first step of an
animation, and 1 is the last step. When running, QTimeLine generates values between 0
and 1 by calling
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)() and
emitting
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueChanged)(). By
default,
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)() applies
an interpolation algorithm to generate these value. You can choose from a set of
predefined timeline algorithms by calling
[setEasingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#easingCurve-prop)().

Note that, by default, QTimeLine uses
[QEasingCurve::InOutSine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum),
which provides a value that grows slowly, then grows steadily, and finally grows slowly.
For a custom timeline, you can reimplement
[valueForTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#valueForTime)(), in
which case QTimeLine's
[easingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#easingCurve-prop)
property is ignored.

### `[slot]` void QTimeLine::start()

Starts the timeline. [QTimeLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html) will
enter Running state, and once it enters the event loop, it will update its current time,

resume a stopped timeline without restarting, you can call
[resume](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#resume)() instead.

**See also** [resume](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html#resume)(),

PythonQt.QtCore.QTimeZone.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class provides a stateless calculator for time zone conversions between UTC and the
local time in a specific time zone. By default it uses the host system time zone data to
perform these conversions.

This class is primarily designed for use in
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html); most applications will
not need to access this class directly and should instead use
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) with a
[Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) of
[Qt::TimeZone](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

**Note:** For consistency with
[QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html), QTimeZone does not
account for leap seconds.

### Remarks

#### IANA Time Zone IDs

QTimeZone uses the IANA time zone IDs as defined in the IANA Time Zone Database
(http://www.iana.org/time-zones). This is to ensure a standard ID across all supported
platforms. Most platforms support the IANA IDs and the IANA Database natively, but for
Windows a mapping is required to the native IDs. See below for more details.

The IANA IDs can and do change on a regular basis, and can vary depending on how
recently the host system data was updated. As such you cannot rely on any given ID
existing on any host system. You must use
[availableTimeZoneIds](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#availableTimeZoneIds)()
to determine what IANA IDs are available.

The IANA IDs and database are also know as the Olson IDs and database, named after their
creator.

#### UTC Offset Time Zones

A default UTC time zone backend is provided which is always guaranteed to be available.
This provides a set of generic Offset From UTC time zones in the range UTC-14:00 to
UTC\+14:00. These time zones can be created using either the standard ISO format names
"UTC\+00:00" as listed by
[availableTimeZoneIds](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#availableTimeZoneIds)(),
or using the number of offset seconds.

#### Windows Time Zones

Windows native time zone support is severely limited compared to the standard IANA TZ
Database. Windows time zones cover larger geographic areas and are thus less accurate in
their conversions. They also do not support as much historic conversion data and so may
only be accurate for the current year.

QTimeZone uses a conversion table derived form the Unicode CLDR data to map between IANA
IDs and Windows IDs. Depending on your version of Windows and Qt, this table may not be
able to provide a valid conversion, in which "UTC" will be returned.

QTimeZone provides a public API to use this conversion table. The Windows ID used is the
Windows Registry Key for the time zone which is also the MS Exchange EWS ID as well, but
is different to the Time Zone Name (TZID) and COD code used by MS Exchange in versions
before 2007\.

#### System Time Zone

QTimeZone does not support any concept of a system or default time zone. If you require
a [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) that uses the current
system time zone at any given moment then you should use a
[Qt::TimeSpec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum) of
[Qt::LocalTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimeSpec-enum).

The method
[systemTimeZoneId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#systemTimeZoneId)()
returns the current system IANA time zone ID which on Unix-like systems will always be
correct. On Windows this ID is translated from the Windows system ID using an internal
translation table and the user's selected country. As a consequence there is a small
chance any Windows install may have IDs not known by Qt, in which case "UTC" will be
returned.

Creating a new QTimeZone instance using the system time zone ID will only produce a
fixed named copy of the time zone, it will not change if the system time zone changes.

#### Time Zone Offsets

The difference between UTC and the local time in a time zone is expressed as an offset
in seconds from UTC, i.e. the number of seconds to add to UTC to obtain the local time.
The total offset is comprised of two component parts, the standard time offset and the
daylight-saving time offset. The standard time offset is the number of seconds to add to
UTC to obtain standard time in the time zone. The daylight-saving time offset is the
number of seconds to add to the standard time offset to obtain daylight-saving time
(abbreviated DST and sometimes called "daylight time" or "summer time") in the time
zone.

Note that the standard and DST offsets for a time zone may change over time as countries
have changed DST laws or even their standard time offset.

(CLDR)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcore-attribution-unicode-cldr.html#unicode-cldr)
for details.

### int QTimeZone::offsetFromUtc(const [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) \&*atDateTime*) const

Returns the total effective offset at the given *atDateTime*, i.e. the number of seconds
to add to UTC to obtain the local time. This includes any DST offset that may be in
effect, i.e. it is the sum of
[standardTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#standardTimeOffset)()
and
[daylightTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#daylightTimeOffset)()
for the given datetime.

For example, for the time zone "Europe/Berlin" the standard time offset is \+3600
seconds and the DST offset is \+3600 seconds. During standard time offsetFromUtc() will
return \+3600 (UTC\+01:00), and during DST it will return \+7200 (UTC\+02:00).

**See also**
[standardTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#standardTimeOffset)()
and
[daylightTimeOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimezone.html#daylightTimeOffset)().

seconds. During both standard and DST

PythonQt.QtCore.QTimer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QTimer class provides a high-level programming interface for timers. To use it,
create a QTimer, connect its
[timeout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout)() signal to the
appropriate slots, and call
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#start-1)(). From then on, it will
emit the [timeout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout)() signal at
constant intervals.

Example for a one second (1000 millisecond) timer (from the [Analog
Clock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-analogclock-example.html)
example):

```
    QTimer *timer = new QTimer(this);
    connect(timer, &QTimer::timeout, this, QOverload<>::of(&AnalogClock::update));
    timer->start(1000);
```

From then on, the `update()` slot is called every second.

You can set a timer to time out only once by calling
[setSingleShot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#singleShot-prop)(true).
You can also use the static
[QTimer::singleShot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#singleShot)()
function to call a slot after a specified interval:

```
    QTimer::singleShot(200, this, &Foo::updateCaption);
```

In multithreaded applications, you can use QTimer in any thread that has an event loop.
To start an event loop from a non-GUI thread, use
[QThread::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html#exec)(). Qt uses the
timer's [thread affinity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#thread) to
determine which thread will emit the
[timeout()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout) signal. Because of
this, you must start and stop the timer in its thread; it is not possible to start a
timer from another thread.

As a special case, a QTimer with a timeout of 0 will time out as soon as possible,
though the ordering between zero timers and other sources of events is unspecified. Zero
timers can be used to do some work while still providing a snappy user interface:

```
    QTimer *timer = new QTimer(this);
    connect(timer, &QTimer::timeout, this, &Foo::processOneThing);
    timer->start();
```

From then on, `processOneThing()` will be called repeatedly. It should be written in
such a way that it always returns quickly (typically after processing one data item) so
that Qt can deliver events to the user interface and stop the timer as soon as it has
done all its work. This is the traditional way of implementing heavy work in GUI
applications, but as multithreading is nowadays becoming available on more and more
platforms, we expect that zero-millisecond QTimer objects will gradually be replaced by
[QThread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qthread.html)s.

### Accuracy and Timer Resolution

The accuracy of timers depends on the underlying operating system and hardware. Most
platforms support a resolution of 1 millisecond, though the accuracy of the timer will
not equal this resolution in many real-world situations.

The accuracy also depends on the [timer
type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum). For
[Qt::PreciseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum), QTimer
will try to keep the accuracy at 1 millisecond. Precise timers will also never time out
earlier than expected.

For [Qt::CoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum) and
[Qt::VeryCoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum) types,
QTimer may wake up earlier than expected, within the margins for those types: 5% of the
interval for
[Qt::CoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum) and 500 ms
for [Qt::VeryCoarseTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum).

All timer types may time out later than expected if the system is busy or unable to
provide the requested accuracy. In such a case of timeout overrun, Qt will emit
[timeout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timeout)() only once, even if
multiple timeouts have expired, and then will resume the original interval.

### Alternatives to QTimer

An alternative to using QTimer is to call
[QObject::startTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#startTimer)() for
your object and reimplement the
[QObject::timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent)()
event handler in your class (which must inherit
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)). The disadvantage is that
[timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#timerEvent)() does not
support such high-level features as single-shot timers or signals.

Another alternative is
[QBasicTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbasictimer.html). It is typically less
cumbersome than using
[QObject::startTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#startTimer)()
directly. See [Timers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/timers.html) for an overview
of all three approaches.

Some operating systems limit the number of timers that may be used; Qt tries to work
around these limitations.

### `[static]` void QTimer::singleShot(int *msec*, const [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**receiver*, const char \**member*)

This is an overloaded function.

This static function calls a slot after a given time interval.

It is very convenient to use this function because you do not need to bother with a
[timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent) or create a
local [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) object.

The *receiver* is the receiving object and the *member* is the slot. The time interval
is given in the duration object *msec*.

**Note:** This function is
[reentrant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/threads-reentrancy.html).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.8.

**See also**
[setSingleShot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#singleShot-prop)() and
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#start-1)().

### `[static]` void QTimer::singleShot(int *msec*, [Qt::TimerType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TimerType-enum) *timerType*, const [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**receiver*, const char \**member*)

This is an overloaded function.

This static function calls a slot after a given time interval.

It is very convenient to use this function because you do not need to bother with a
[timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent) or create a
local [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) object.

The *receiver* is the receiving object and the *member* is the slot. The time interval
is given in the duration object *msec*. The *timerType* affects the accuracy of the
timer.

**Note:** This function is
[reentrant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/threads-reentrancy.html).

This function was introduced in Qt 5.8.

**See also** [start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html#start-1)().

### `[static]` template \<typename PointerToMemberFunction\> void QTimer::singleShot(int *msec*, const [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**receiver*, PointerToMemberFunction *method*)

This is an overloaded function.

This static function calls a member function of a
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) after a given time interval.

It is very convenient to use this function because you do not need to bother with a
[timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent) or create a
local [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) object.

## Detailed Description

Timer events are sent at regular intervals to objects that have started one or more
timers. Each timer has a unique identifier. A timer is started with
[QObject::startTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#startTimer)().

The [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) class provides a high-level
programming interface that uses signals instead of events. It also provides single-shot
timers.

The event handler
[QObject::timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent)()
receives timer events.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

An object of this class contains a set of translations from a source language to a
target language. QTranslator provides functions to look up translations in a translation
file. Translation files are created using [Qt
Linguist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtlinguist-index.html).

The most common use of QTranslator is to: load a translation file, and install it using
[QCoreApplication::installTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#installTranslator)().

Here's an example `main()` function using the QTranslator:

```
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    QApplication app(argc, argv);

    QTranslator translator;
    // look up e.g. :/i18n/myapp_de.qm
    if (translator.load(QLocale(), QLatin1String("myapp"), QLatin1String("_"), QLatin1String(":/i18n")))
        QCoreApplication::installTranslator(&translator);

    QPushButton hello(QCoreApplication::translate("main", "Hello world!"));
    hello.resize(100, 30);

    hello.show();
    return app.exec();
}
```

Note that the translator must be created *before* the application's widgets.

Most applications will never need to do anything else with this class. The other
functions provided by this class are useful for applications that work on translator
files.

### Looking up Translations

It is possible to look up a translation using
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html#translate)() (as
[tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)() and
[QCoreApplication::translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#translate)()
do). The [translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html#translate)()
function takes up to three parameters:

- The *context* \- usually the class name for the [tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)() caller.
- The *source text* \- usually the argument to [tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)().
- The *disambiguation* \- an optional string that helps disambiguate different uses of the same text in the same context.

For example, the "Cancel" in a dialog might have "Anuluj" when the program runs in
Polish (in this case the source text would be "Cancel"). The context would (normally) be
the dialog's class name; there would normally be no comment, and the translated text
would be "Anuluj".

But it's not always so simple. The Spanish version of a printer dialog with settings for
two-sided printing and binding would probably require both "Activado" and "Activada" as
translations for "Enabled". In this case the source text would be "Enabled" in both
cases, and the context would be the dialog's class name, but the two items would have
disambiguations such as "two-sided printing" for one and "binding" for the other. The
disambiguation enables the translator to choose the appropriate gender for the Spanish
version, and enables Qt to distinguish between translations.

### Using Multiple Translations

Multiple translation files can be installed in an application. Translations are searched
for in the reverse order in which they were installed, so the most recently installed
translation file is searched for translations first and the earliest translation file is
searched last. The search stops as soon as a translation containing a matching string is
found.

This mechanism makes it possible for a specific translation to be "selected" or given
priority over the others; simply uninstall the translator from the application by
passing it to the
[QCoreApplication::removeTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#removeTranslator)()
function and reinstall it with
[QCoreApplication::installTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#installTranslator)().
It will then be the first translation to be searched for matching strings.

### bool QTranslator::load(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*filename*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*directory* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*search\_delimiters* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*suffix* \= QString())

Loads *filename* \+ *suffix* (".qm" if the *suffix* is not specified), which may be an
absolute file name or relative to *directory*. Returns `true` if the translation is
successfully loaded; otherwise returns `false`.

If *directory* is not specified, the current directory is used (i.e., as
[currentPath()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#currentPath)).

The previous contents of this translator object are discarded.

If the file name does not exist, other file names are tried in the following order:

1. File name without *suffix* appended.
2. File name with text after a character in *search\_delimiters* stripped ("\_." is the default for *search\_delimiters* if it is an empty string) and *suffix*.
3. File name stripped without *suffix* appended.
4. File name stripped further, etc.

For example, an application running in the fr\_CA locale (French-speaking Canada) might
call load("foo.fr\_ca", "/opt/foolib"). load() would then try to open the first existing
readable file from this list:

1. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_ca.qm`
2. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_ca`
3. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr.qm`
4. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr`
5. `/opt/foolib/foo.qm`
6. `/opt/foolib/foo`

Usually, it is better to use the QTranslator::load(const
[QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&, const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&) function instead, because
it uses
[QLocale::uiLanguages](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#uiLanguages)()
and not simply the locale name, which refers to the formatting of dates and numbers and
not necessarily the UI language.

### bool QTranslator::load(const [QLocale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html) \&*locale*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*filename*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*prefix* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*directory* \= QString(), const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*suffix* \= QString())

Loads *filename* \+ *prefix* \+ [ui language
name](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#uiLanguages) \+ *suffix* (".qm" if
the *suffix* is not specified), which may be an absolute file name or relative to
*directory*. Returns `true` if the translation is successfully loaded; otherwise returns
`false`.

The previous contents of this translator object are discarded.

If the file name does not exist, other file names are tried in the following order:

1. File name without *suffix* appended.
2. File name with ui language part after a "\_" character stripped and *suffix*.
3. File name with ui language part stripped without *suffix* appended.
4. File name with ui language part stripped further, etc.

For example, an application running in the *locale* with the following [ui
languages](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#uiLanguages) \- "es",
"fr-CA", "de" might call load(QLocale(), "foo", ".", "/opt/foolib", ".qm"). load() would
replace '-' (dash) with '\_' (underscore) in the ui language and then try to open the
first existing readable file from this list:

1. `/opt/foolib/foo.es.qm`
2. `/opt/foolib/foo.es`
3. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_CA.qm`
4. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr_CA`
5. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr.qm`
6. `/opt/foolib/foo.fr`
7. `/opt/foolib/foo.de.qm`
8. `/opt/foolib/foo.de`
9. `/opt/foolib/foo.qm`
10. `/opt/foolib/foo`.
11. `/opt/foolib/foo`

On operating systems where file system is case sensitive,
[QTranslator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtranslator.html) also tries to load a
lower-cased version of the locale name.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It can parse and construct URLs in both encoded and unencoded form. QUrl also has
support for internationalized domain names (IDNs).

The most common way to use QUrl is to initialize it via the constructor by passing a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html). Otherwise,
[setUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUrl)() can also be used.

URLs can be represented in two forms: encoded or unencoded. The unencoded representation
is suitable for showing to users, but the encoded representation is typically what you
would send to a web server. For example, the unencoded URL
"http://bühler.example.com/List of applicants.xml" would be sent to the server as
"http://xn--bhler-kva.example.com/List%20of%20applicants.xml".

A URL can also be constructed piece by piece by calling
[setScheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setScheme)(),
[setUserName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserName)(),
[setPassword](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPassword)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)(),
[setPort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPort)(),
[setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPath)(),
[setQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setQuery)() and
[setFragment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setFragment)(). Some
convenience functions are also available:
[setAuthority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setAuthority)() sets the
user name, password, host and port.
[setUserInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserInfo)() sets the user
name and password at once.

Call [isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() to check if the
URL is valid. This can be done at any point during the constructing of a URL. If
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() returns `false`, you
should [clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#clear)() the URL before
proceeding, or start over by parsing a new URL with
[setUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUrl)().

Constructing a query is particularly convenient through the use of the
[QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) class and its methods
[QUrlQuery::setQueryItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQueryItems)(),
[QUrlQuery::addQueryItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#addQueryItem)()
and
[QUrlQuery::removeQueryItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#removeQueryItem)().
Use
[QUrlQuery::setQueryDelimiters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQueryDelimiters)()
to customize the delimiters used for generating the query string.

For the convenience of generating encoded URL strings or query strings, there are two
static functions called
[fromPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromPercentEncoding)()
and
[toPercentEncoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toPercentEncoding)()
which deal with percent encoding and decoding of
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) objects.

[fromLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromLocalFile)() constructs
a QUrl by parsing a local file path.
[toLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toLocalFile)() converts a URL
to a local file path.

The human readable representation of the URL is fetched with
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toString)(). This representation
is appropriate for displaying a URL to a user in unencoded form. The encoded form
however, as returned by
[toEncoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toEncoded)(), is for internal
use, passing to web servers, mail clients and so on. Both forms are technically correct
and represent the same URL unambiguously \-- in fact, passing either form to QUrl's
constructor or to [setUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUrl)() will
yield the same QUrl object.

QUrl conforms to the URI specification from [RFC
3986](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.txt) (Uniform Resource Identifier: Generic
Syntax), and includes scheme extensions from [RFC
1738](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1738.txt) (Uniform Resource Locators). Case
folding rules in QUrl conform to [RFC 3491](http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3491.txt)
(Nameprep: A Stringprep Profile for Internationalized Domain Names (IDN)). It is also
compatible with the [file URI
specification](http://freedesktop.org/wiki/Specifications/file-uri-spec/) from
freedesktop.org, provided that the locale encodes file names using UTF-8 (required by
IDN).

#### Relative URLs vs Relative Paths

Calling [isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isRelative)() will
return whether or not the URL is relative. A relative URL has no
[scheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#scheme). For example:

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("main.qml").isRelative();          // true: no scheme
    qDebug() << QUrl("qml/main.qml").isRelative();      // true: no scheme
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:main.qml").isRelative();     // false: has "file" scheme
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:qml/main.qml").isRelative(); // false: has "file" scheme
```

Notice that a URL can be absolute while containing a relative path, and vice versa:

```
    // Absolute URL, relative path
    QUrl url("file:file.txt");
    qDebug() << url.isRelative();                 // false: has "file" scheme
    qDebug() << QDir::isAbsolutePath(url.path()); // false: relative path

    // Relative URL, absolute path
    url = QUrl("/home/user/file.txt");
    qDebug() << url.isRelative();                 // true: has no scheme
    qDebug() << QDir::isAbsolutePath(url.path()); // true: absolute path
```

A relative URL can be resolved by passing it as an argument to
[resolved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#resolved)(), which returns an
absolute URL. [isParentOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isParentOf)() is
used for determining whether one URL is a parent of another.

#### Error checking

QUrl is capable of detecting many errors in URLs while parsing it or when components of
the URL are set with individual setter methods (like
[setScheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setScheme)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)() or
[setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPath)()). If the parsing or
setter function is successful, any previously recorded error conditions will be
discarded.

By default, QUrl setter methods operate in
[QUrl::TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum),
which means they accept some common mistakes and mis-representation of data. An
alternate method of parsing is
[QUrl::StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), which
applies further checks. See
[QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) for a
description of the difference of the parsing modes.

QUrl only checks for conformance with the URL specification. It does not try to verify
that high-level protocol URLs are in the format they are expected to be by handlers
elsewhere. For example, the following URIs are all considered valid by QUrl, even if
they do not make sense when used:

- "http:/filename.html"
- "mailto://example.com"

When the parser encounters an error, it signals the event by making
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() return false and
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toString)() /
[toEncoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toEncoded)() return an empty
string. If it is necessary to show the user the reason why the URL failed to parse, the
error condition can be obtained from QUrl by calling
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#errorString)(). Note that
this message is highly technical and may not make sense to end-users.

QUrl is capable of recording only one error condition. If more than one error is found,
it is undefined which error is reported.

#### Character Conversions

Follow these rules to avoid erroneous character conversion when dealing with URLs and
strings:

- When creating a [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) to contain a URL from a [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) or a char\*, always use [QString::fromUtf8](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html#fromUtf8)().

### `[static]` [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::fromAce(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*domain*)

Returns the Unicode form of the given domain name *domain*, which is encoded in the
ASCII Compatible Encoding (ACE). The result of this function is considered equivalent to
*domain*.

If the value in *domain* cannot be encoded, it will be converted to
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) and returned.

The ASCII Compatible Encoding (ACE) is defined by RFC 3490, RFC 3491 and RFC 3492\. It
is part of the Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) specification,
which allows for domain names (like `"example.com"`) to be written using international
characters.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.fromLocalFile.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::fromLocalFile(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*localFile*)

Returns a [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) representation of
*localFile*, interpreted as a local file. This function accepts paths separated by
slashes as well as the native separator for this platform.

This function also accepts paths with a doubled leading slash (or backslash) to indicate
a remote file, as in "//servername/path/to/file.txt". Note that only certain platforms
can actually open this file using
[QFile::open](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#open)().

An empty *localFile* leads to an empty URL (since Qt 5.4).

```
    qDebug() << QUrl::fromLocalFile("file.txt");            // QUrl("file:file.txt")
    qDebug() << QUrl::fromLocalFile("/home/user/file.txt"); // QUrl("file:///home/user/file.txt")
    qDebug() << QUrl::fromLocalFile("file:file.txt");       // doesn't make sense; expects path, not url with scheme
```

In the first line in snippet above, a file URL is constructed from a local, relative
path. A file URL with a relative path only makes sense if there is a base URL to resolve
it against. For example:

```
    QUrl url = QUrl::fromLocalFile("file.txt");
    QUrl baseUrl = QUrl("file:/home/user/");
    // wrong: prints QUrl("file:file.txt"), as url already has a scheme
    qDebug() << baseUrl.resolved(url);
```

To resolve such a URL, it's necessary to remove the scheme beforehand:

```
    // correct: prints QUrl("file:///home/user/file.txt")
    url.setScheme(QString());
    qDebug() << baseUrl.resolved(url);
```

For this reason, it is better to use a relative URL (that is, no scheme) for relative
file paths:

```
    QUrl url = QUrl("file.txt");
    QUrl baseUrl = QUrl("file:/home/user/");
    // prints QUrl("file:///home/user/file.txt")
    qDebug() << baseUrl.resolved(url);
```

**See also** [toLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toLocalFile)(),
[isLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isLocalFile)(), and
[QDir::toNativeSeparators](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdir.html#toNativeSeparators)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.fromUserInput.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::fromUserInput(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*userInput*)

Returns a valid URL from a user supplied *userInput* string if one can be deducted. In
the case that is not possible, an invalid
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl)() is returned.

Most applications that can browse the web, allow the user to input a URL in the form of
a plain string. This string can be manually typed into a location bar, obtained from the
clipboard, or passed in via command line arguments.

When the string is not already a valid URL, a best guess is performed, making various
web related assumptions.

In the case the string corresponds to a valid file path on the system, a file:// URL is
constructed, using
[QUrl::fromLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromLocalFile)().

If that is not the case, an attempt is made to turn the string into a http:// or ftp://
URL. The latter in the case the string starts with 'ftp'. The result is then passed
through [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html)'s tolerant parser, and in
the case or success, a valid [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) is
returned, or else a [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl)().



#### Examples:

- qt-project.org becomes http://qt-project.org
- ftp.qt-project.org becomes ftp://ftp.qt-project.org
- hostname becomes http://hostname
- /home/user/test.html becomes file:///home/user/test.html

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

### `[static]` [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::fromUserInput(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*userInput*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*workingDirectory*, [QUrl::UserInputResolutionOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#UserInputResolutionOption-enum) *options* \= DefaultResolution)

Returns a valid URL from a user supplied *userInput* string if one can be deduced. In
the case that is not possible, an invalid
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl)() is returned.

This overload takes a *workingDirectory* path, in order to be able to handle relative
paths. This is especially useful when handling command line arguments. If
*workingDirectory* is empty, no handling of relative paths will be done, so this method
will behave like its one argument overload.

By default, an input string that looks like a relative path will only be treated as such
if the file actually exists in the given working directory.

If the application can handle files that don't exist yet, it should pass the flag
[AssumeLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#UserInputResolutionOption-enum)
in *options*.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.
signatures: fromUserInput(userInput: str, workingDirectory: str, options: PySide2.QtCore.QUrl.UserInputResolutionOptions=...) -> PySide2.QtCore.QUrl

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::host([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= FullyDecoded) const

Returns the host of the URL if it is defined; otherwise an empty string is returned.

The *options* argument controls how the hostname will be formatted. The
[QUrl::EncodeUnicode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
option will cause this function to return the hostname in the ASCII-Compatible Encoding

Unicode form, according to the list of permissible top-level domains (see
[idnWhitelist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#idnWhitelist)()).

All other flags are ignored. Host names cannot contain control or percent characters, so
the returned value can be considered fully decoded.

**See also** [setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)(),
[idnWhitelist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#idnWhitelist)(),
[setIdnWhitelist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setIdnWhitelist)(), and
[authority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#authority)().

### bool QUrl::matches(const [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) \&*url*, [QUrl::FormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#UrlFormattingOption-enum) *options*) const

Returns `true` if this URL and the given *url* are equal after applying *options* to
both; otherwise returns `false`.

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.password.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::password([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= FullyDecoded) const

Returns the password of the URL if it is defined; otherwise an empty string is returned.

The *options* argument controls how to format the user name component. All values
produce an unambiguous result. With
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
all percent-encoded sequences are decoded; otherwise, the returned value may contain
some percent-encoded sequences for some control sequences not representable in decoded
form in [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

Note that
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
may cause data loss if those non-representable sequences are present. It is recommended
to use that value when the result will be used in a non-URL context, such as setting in
[QAuthenticator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qauthenticator.html) or negotiating
a login.

**See also** [setPassword](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPassword)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.path.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::path([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= FullyDecoded) const

Returns the path of the URL.

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:file.txt").path();                   // "file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("/home/user/file.txt").path();             // "/home/user/file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("http://www.example.com/test/123").path(); // "/test/123"
```

The *options* argument controls how to format the path component. All values produce an
unambiguous result. With
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
all percent-encoded sequences are decoded; otherwise, the returned value may contain
some percent-encoded sequences for some control sequences not representable in decoded
form in [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

Note that
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
may cause data loss if those non-representable sequences are present. It is recommended
to use that value when the result will be used in a non-URL context, such as sending to
an FTP server.

An example of data loss is when you have non-Unicode percent-encoded sequences and use
[FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
(the default):

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("/foo%FFbar").path();
```

In this example, there will be some level of data loss because the `%FF` cannot be
converted.

Data loss can also occur when the path contains sub-delimiters (such as `+`):

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("/foo+bar%2B").path(); // "/foo+bar+"
```

Other decoding examples:

```
    const QUrl url("/temporary/Mambo %235%3F.mp3");
    qDebug() << url.path(QUrl::FullyDecoded);  // "/temporary/Mambo #5?.mp3"
    qDebug() << url.path(QUrl::PrettyDecoded); // "/temporary/Mambo #5?.mp3"
    qDebug() << url.path(QUrl::FullyEncoded);  // "/temporary/Mambo%20%235%3F.mp3"
```

**See also** [setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPath)().

### int QUrl::port(int *defaultPort* \= -1) const

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::query([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *options* \= PrettyDecoded) const

Returns the query string of the URL if there's a query string, or an empty result if
not. To determine if the parsed URL contained a query string, use
[hasQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasQuery)().

The *options* argument controls how to format the query component. All values produce an
unambiguous result. With
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
all percent-encoded sequences are decoded; otherwise, the returned value may contain
some percent-encoded sequences for some control sequences not representable in decoded
form in [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

Note that use of
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
in queries is discouraged, as queries often contain data that is supposed to remain
percent-encoded, including the use of the "%2B" sequence to represent a plus character
('\+').

**See also** [setQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setQuery)() and
[hasQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasQuery)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.resolved.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) QUrl::resolved(const [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#QUrl) \&*relative*) const

Returns the result of the merge of this URL with *relative*. This URL is used as a base
to convert *relative* to an absolute URL.

If *relative* is not a relative URL, this function will return *relative* directly.
Otherwise, the paths of the two URLs are merged, and the new URL returned has the scheme
and authority of the base URL, but with the merged path, as in the following example:

```
QUrl baseUrl("http://qt.digia.com/Support/");
QUrl relativeUrl("../Product/Library/");
qDebug(baseUrl.resolved(relativeUrl).toString());
// prints "http://qt.digia.com/Product/Library/"
```

Calling resolved() with ".." returns a
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) whose directory is one level higher
than the original. Similarly, calling resolved() with "../.." removes two levels from
the path. If *relative* is "/", the path becomes "/".

**See also** [isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isRelative)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.scheme.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::scheme() const

Returns the scheme of the URL. If an empty string is returned, this means the scheme is
undefined and the URL is then relative.

The scheme can only contain US-ASCII letters or digits, which means it cannot contain
any character that would otherwise require encoding. Additionally, schemes are always
returned in lowercase form.

**See also** [setScheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setScheme)() and
[isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isRelative)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.setAuthority.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrl::setAuthority(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*authority*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *mode* \= TolerantMode)

Sets the authority of the URL to *authority*.

The authority of a URL is the combination of user info, a host name and a port. All of
these elements are optional; an empty authority is therefore valid.

The user info and host are separated by a '@', and the host and port are separated by a
':'. If the user info is empty, the '@' must be omitted; although a stray ':' is
permitted if the port is empty.

The following example shows a valid authority string:

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-authority.png)

The *authority* data is interpreted according to *mode*: in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), any '%'
characters must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal characters and some characters
(including space) are not allowed in undecoded form. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) (the
default), all characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will
correct stray '%' not followed by two hex characters.

This function does not allow *mode* to be
[QUrl::DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum). To
set fully decoded data, call
[setUserName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserName)(),
[setPassword](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPassword)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)() and
[setPort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPort)() individually.

**See also** [authority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#authority)(),
[setUserInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserInfo)(),
[setHost](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setHost)(), and
[setPort](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPort)().
signatures: setAuthority(self, authority: str, mode: PySide2.QtCore.QUrl.ParsingMode=...) -> None

### void QUrl::setFragment(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fragment*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *mode* \= TolerantMode)

Sets the fragment of the URL to *fragment*. The fragment is the last part of the URL,
represented by a '#' followed by a string of characters. It is typically used in HTTP
for referring to a certain link or point on a page:

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-fragment.png)

The fragment is sometimes also referred to as the URL "reference".

Passing an argument of QString() (a null
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)) will unset the fragment.
Passing an argument of [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)("")
(an empty but not null [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)) will
set the fragment to an empty string (as if the original URL had a lone "#").

The *fragment* data is interpreted according to *mode*: in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), any '%'
characters must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal characters and some characters
(including space) are not allowed in undecoded form. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), all
characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will correct stray '%'
not followed by two hex characters. In
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), '%' stand
for themselves and encoded characters are not possible.

[QUrl::DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum)
should be used when setting the fragment from a data source which is not a URL or with a
fragment obtained by calling
[fragment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fragment)() with the
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
formatting option.

**See also** [fragment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fragment)() and
[hasFragment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasFragment)().
signatures: setFragment(self, fragment: str, mode: PySide2.QtCore.QUrl.ParsingMode=...) -> None

Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrl::setHost(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*host*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *mode* \= DecodedMode)

Sets the host of the URL to *host*. The host is part of the authority.

The *host* data is interpreted according to *mode*: in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), any '%'
characters must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal characters and some characters
(including space) are not allowed in undecoded form. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), all
characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will correct stray '%'
not followed by two hex characters. In
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), '%' stand
for themselves and encoded characters are not possible.

Note that, in all cases, the result of the parsing must be a valid hostname according to
STD 3 rules, as modified by the Internationalized Resource Identifiers specification
(RFC 3987). Invalid hostnames are not permitted and will cause
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() to become false.

**See also** [host](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#host)() and
[setAuthority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setAuthority)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.setIdnWhitelist.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QUrl::setIdnWhitelist(const [QStringList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstringlist.html) \&*list*)

Sets the whitelist of Top-Level Domains (TLDs) that are allowed to have non-ASCII
characters in domains to the value of *list*.

Note that if you call this function, you need to do so *before* you start any threads
that might access
[idnWhitelist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#idnWhitelist)().

Qt comes with a default list that contains the Internet top-level domains that have
published support for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and rules to guarantee that
no deception can happen between similarly-looking characters (such as the Latin
lowercase letter `'a'` and the Cyrillic equivalent, which in most fonts are visually
identical).

This list is periodically maintained, as registrars publish new rules.

This function is provided for those who need to manipulate the list, in order to add or
remove a TLD. It is not recommended to change its value for purposes other than testing,
as it may expose users to security risks.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[idnWhitelist](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#idnWhitelist)().

[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), all
characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will correct stray '%'
not followed by two hex characters. In
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), '%' stand
for themselves and encoded characters are not possible.

[QUrl::DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum)

### void QUrl::setPort(int *port*)

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.setQuery.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrl::setQuery(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*query*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *mode* \= TolerantMode)

Sets the query string of the URL to *query*.

This function is useful if you need to pass a query string that does not fit into the
key-value pattern, or that uses a different scheme for encoding special characters than
what is suggested by [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html).

Passing a value of QString() to *query* (a null
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)) unsets the query completely.
However, passing a value of
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)("") will set the query to an
empty value, as if the original URL had a lone "?".

The *query* data is interpreted according to *mode*: in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), any '%'
characters must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal characters and some characters
(including space) are not allowed in undecoded form. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), all
characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will correct stray '%'
not followed by two hex characters. In
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), '%' stand
for themselves and encoded characters are not possible.

Query strings often contain percent-encoded sequences, so use of
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) is
discouraged. One special sequence to be aware of is that of the plus character ('\+').
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) does not convert spaces to plus
characters, even though HTML forms posted by web browsers do. In order to represent an
actual plus character in a query, the sequence "%2B" is usually used. This function will
leave "%2B" sequences untouched in
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) or
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum).

**See also** [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#query)() and
[hasQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasQuery)().

### void QUrl::setQuery(const [QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) \&*query*)

This is an overloaded function.

Sets the query string of the URL to *query*.

This function reconstructs the query string from the
[QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) object and sets on this
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) object. This function does not have
parsing parameters because the
[QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) contains data that is
already parsed.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also** [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#query)() and
[hasQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#hasQuery)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.setScheme.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrl::setScheme(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*scheme*)

Sets the scheme of the URL to *scheme*. As a scheme can only contain ASCII characters,
no conversion or decoding is done on the input. It must also start with an ASCII letter.

The scheme describes the type (or protocol) of the URL. It's represented by one or more
ASCII characters at the start the URL.

A scheme is strictly [RFC 3986](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc3986.txt)-compliant: `scheme
= ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "-" / "." )`

The following example shows a URL where the scheme is "ftp":

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-authority2.png)

To set the scheme, the following call is used:

```
    QUrl url;
    url.setScheme("ftp");
```

The scheme can also be empty, in which case the URL is interpreted as relative.

**See also** [scheme](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#scheme)() and
[isRelative](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isRelative)().

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrl.setUrl.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrl::setUrl(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*url*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *parsingMode* \= TolerantMode)

Parses *url* and sets this object to that value.
[QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) will automatically percent encode
all characters that are not allowed in a URL and decode the percent-encoded sequences
that represent an unreserved character (letters, digits, hyphens, undercores, dots and
tildes). All other characters are left in their original forms.

Parses the *url* using the parser mode *parsingMode*. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) (the
default), [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html) will correct certain
mistakes, notably the presence of a percent character ('%') not followed by two
hexadecimal digits, and it will accept any character in any position. In
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), encoding
mistakes will not be tolerated and [QUrl](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html)
will also check that certain forbidden characters are not present in unencoded form. If
an error is detected in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum),
[isValid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isValid)() will return false. The
parsing mode
[DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) is not
permitted in this context and will produce a run-time warning.

**See also** [url](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#url)() and
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#toString)().

### void QUrl::setUserInfo(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*userInfo*, [QUrl::ParsingMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) *mode* \= TolerantMode)

Sets the user info of the URL to *userInfo*. The user info is an optional part of the
authority of the URL, as described in
[setAuthority](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setAuthority)().

The user info consists of a user name and optionally a password, separated by a ':'. If
the password is empty, the colon must be omitted. The following example shows a valid
user info string:

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-authority3.png)

The *userInfo* data is interpreted according to *mode*: in
[StrictMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum), any '%'
characters must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal characters and some characters
(including space) are not allowed in undecoded form. In
[TolerantMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum) (the
default), all characters are accepted in undecoded form and the tolerant parser will
correct stray '%' not followed by two hex characters.

This function does not allow *mode* to be
[QUrl::DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum). To
set fully decoded data, call
[setUserName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setUserName)() and
[setPassword](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPassword)() individually.

[setPassword](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setPassword)(), and

### `[static]` [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QUrl::toAce(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*domain*)

Returns the ASCII Compatible Encoding of the given domain name *domain*. The result of
this function is considered equivalent to *domain*.

The ASCII-Compatible Encoding (ACE) is defined by RFC 3490, RFC 3491 and RFC 3492\. It
is part of the Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) specification,
which allows for domain names (like `"example.com"`) to be written using international
characters.

Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrl::toLocalFile() const

Returns the path of this URL formatted as a local file path. The path returned will use
forward slashes, even if it was originally created from one with backslashes.

If this URL contains a non-empty hostname, it will be encoded in the returned value in
the form found on SMB networks (for example, "//servername/path/to/file.txt").

```
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:file.txt").toLocalFile();            // "file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("file:/home/user/file.txt").toLocalFile(); // "/home/user/file.txt"
    qDebug() << QUrl("file.txt").toLocalFile();                 // ""; wasn't a local file as it had no scheme
```

Note: if the path component of this URL contains a non-UTF-8 binary sequence (such as
%80), the behaviour of this function is undefined.

**See also**
[fromLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fromLocalFile)() and
[isLocalFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#isLocalFile)().
