PythonQt.QtCore.QUrlQuery.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It is used to parse the query strings found in URLs like the following:

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-querystring.png)

Query strings like the above are used to transmit options in the URL and are usually
decoded into multiple key-value pairs. The one above would contain two entries in its
list, with keys "type" and "color". QUrlQuery can also be used to create a query string
suitable for use in
[QUrl::setQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setQuery)() from the
individual components of the query.

The most common way of parsing a query string is to initialize it in the constructor by
passing it the query string. Otherwise, the
[setQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQuery)() method can be
used to set the query to be parsed. That method can also be used to parse a query with
non-standard delimiters, after having set them using the
[setQueryDelimiters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQueryDelimiters)()
function.

The encoded query string can be obtained again using
[query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#query)(). This will take all
the internally-stored items and encode the string using the delimiters.

### Encoding

All of the getter methods in QUrlQuery support an optional parameter of type
[QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
including [query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#query)(), which
dictate how to encode the data in question. Except for
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum),
the returned value must still be considered a percent-encoded string, as there are
certain values which cannot be expressed in decoded form (like control characters, byte
sequences not decodable to UTF-8). For that reason, the percent character is always
represented by the string "%25".

#### Handling of spaces and plus ("\+")

Web browsers usually encode spaces found in HTML FORM elements to a plus sign ("\+") and
plus signs to its percent-encoded form (%2B). However, the Internet specifications
governing URLs do not consider spaces and the plus character equivalent.

For that reason, QUrlQuery never encodes the space character to "\+" and will never
decode "\+" to a space character. Instead, space characters will be rendered "%20" in
encoded form.

To support encoding like that of HTML forms, QUrlQuery also never decodes the "%2B"
sequence to a plus sign nor encode a plus sign. In fact, any "%2B" or "\+" sequences
found in the keys, values, or query string are left exactly like written (except for the
uppercasing of "%2b" to "%2B").

#### Full decoding

With
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
formatting, all percent-encoded sequences will be decoded fully and the '%' character is
used to represent itself.
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
should be used with care, since it may cause data loss. See the documentation of
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
for information on what data may be lost.

This formatting mode should be used only when dealing with text presented to the user in
contexts where percent-encoding is not desired. Note that QUrlQuery setters and query
methods do not support the counterpart
[QUrl::DecodedMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ParsingMode-enum)
parsing, so using
[QUrl::FullyDecoded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum)
to obtain a listing of keys may result in keys not found in the object.

### Non-standard delimiters

By default, QUrlQuery uses an equal sign ("\=") to separate a key from its value, and an
ampersand ("\&") to separate key-value pairs from each other. It is possible to change
the delimiters that QUrlQuery uses for parsing and for reconstructing the query by
calling
[setQueryDelimiters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQueryDelimiters)().

Non-standard delimiters should be chosen from among what RFC 3986 calls
"sub-delimiters". They are:

```
sub-delims    = "!" / "$" / "&" / "'" / "(" / ")"
              / "*" / "+" / "," / ";" / "="
```

Use of other characters is not supported and may result in unexpected behaviour.
QUrlQuery does not verify that you passed a valid delimiter.

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrlQuery::query([QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *encoding* \= QUrl::PrettyDecoded) const

Returns the reconstructed query string, formed from the key-value pairs currently stored
in this [QUrlQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html) object and
separated by the query delimiters chosen for this object. The keys and values are
encoded using the options given by the *encoding* parameter.

For this function, the only ambiguous delimiter is the hash ("#"), as in URLs it is used
to separate the query string from the fragment that may follow.

The order of the key-value pairs in the returned string is exactly the same as in the
original query.

**See also** [setQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#setQuery)(),
[QUrl::setQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#setQuery)(),
[QUrl::fragment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#fragment)(), and
[Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#encoding).

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QUrlQuery::queryItemValue(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*key*, [QUrl::ComponentFormattingOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurl.html#ComponentFormattingOption-enum) *encoding* \= QUrl::PrettyDecoded) const

Returns the query value associated with key *key* from the URL, using the options
specified in *encoding* to encode the return value. If the key *key* is not found, this
function returns an empty string. If you need to distinguish between an empty value and
a non-existent key, you should check for the key's presence first using
[hasQueryItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#hasQueryItem)().

If the key *key* is multiply defined, this function will return the first one found, in
the order they were present in the query string or added using
[addQueryItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#addQueryItem)().

**See also**
[addQueryItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#addQueryItem)(),
[allQueryItemValues](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#allQueryItemValues)(),
and [Encoding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#encoding).

PythonQt.QtCore.QUrlQuery.setQueryDelimi.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QUrlQuery::setQueryDelimiters([QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html) *valueDelimiter*, [QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html) *pairDelimiter*)

Sets the characters used for delimiting between keys and values, and between key-value
pairs in the URL's query string. The default value delimiter is '\=' and the default
pair delimiter is '\&'.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qurl-querystring.png)

*valueDelimiter* will be used for separating keys from values, and *pairDelimiter* will
be used to separate key-value pairs. Any occurrences of these delimiting characters in
the encoded representation of the keys and values of the query string are percent
encoded when returned in
[query](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#query)().

If *valueDelimiter* is set to '(' and *pairDelimiter* is ')', the above query string
would instead be represented like this:

```
http://www.example.com/cgi-bin/drawgraph.cgi?type(pie)color(green)
```

**Note:** Non-standard delimiters should be chosen from among what RFC 3986 calls
"sub-delimiters". They are:

```
sub-delims    = "!" / "$" / "&" / "'" / "(" / ")"
              / "*" / "+" / "," / ";" / "="
```

Use of other characters is not supported and may result in unexpected behaviour. This
method does not verify that you passed a valid delimiter.

**See also**
[queryValueDelimiter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#queryValueDelimiter)()
and
[queryPairDelimiter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qurlquery.html#queryPairDelimiter)().
signatures: setQueryDelimiters(self, valueDelimiter: str, pairDelimiter: str) -> None

PythonQt.QtCore.QUuid.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Using *U*niversally *U*nique *ID*entifiers (UUID) is a standard way to uniquely identify
entities in a distributed computing environment. A UUID is a 16-byte (128-bit) number
generated by some algorithm that is meant to guarantee that the UUID will be unique in
the distributed computing environment where it is used. The acronym GUID is often used
instead, *G*lobally *U*nique *ID*entifiers, but it refers to the same thing.

Actually, the GUID is one *variant* of UUID. Multiple variants are in use. Each UUID
contains a bit field that specifies which type (variant) of UUID it is. Call
[variant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#variant)() to discover which
type of UUID an instance of QUuid contains. It extracts the three most significant bits
of byte 8 of the 16 bytes. In QUuid, byte 8 is `QUuid::data4[0]`. If you create
instances of QUuid using the constructor that accepts all the numeric values as
parameters, use the following table to set the three most significant bits of parameter
`b1`, which becomes `QUuid::data4[0]` and contains the variant field in its three most
significant bits. In the table, 'x' means *don't care*.

| msb0 | msb1 | msb2 | Variant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | x | x | NCS (Network Computing System) |
| 1 | 0 | x | DCE (Distributed Computing Environment) |
| 1 | 1 | 0 | Microsoft (GUID) |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | Reserved for future expansion |

If [variant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#variant)() returns
[QUuid::DCE](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#Variant-enum), the UUID also
contains a *version* field in the four most significant bits of `QUuid::data3`, and you
can call [version](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#version)() to discover
which version your QUuid contains. If you create instances of QUuid using the
constructor that accepts all the numeric values as parameters, use the following table
to set the four most significant bits of parameter `w2`, which becomes `QUuid::data3`
and contains the version field in its four most significant bits.

| msb0 | msb1 | msb2 | msb3 | Version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | Time |
| 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | Embedded POSIX |
| 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | Md5(Name) |
| 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | Random |
| 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | Sha1 |

The field layouts for the DCE versions listed in the table above are specified in the
[Network Working Group UUID Specification](http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4122.txt).

Most platforms provide a tool for generating new UUIDs, e.g. `uuidgen` and `guidgen`.
You can also use
[createUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#createUuid)(). UUIDs
generated by [createUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#createUuid)()
are of the random type. Their
[QUuid::Version](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#Version-enum) bits are
set to [QUuid::Random](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#Version-enum), and
their [QUuid::Variant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#Variant-enum) bits
are set to [QUuid::DCE](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#Variant-enum). The
rest of the UUID is composed of random numbers. Theoretically, this means there is a
small chance that a UUID generated by
[createUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#createUuid)() will not be
unique. But it is [a *very* small
chance](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_Unique_Identifier#Random_UUID_probability_of_duplicates).

UUIDs can be constructed from numeric values or from strings, or using the static
[createUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#createUuid)() function. They
can be converted to a string with
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#toString)(). UUIDs have a
[variant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#variant)() and a
[version](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#version)(), and null UUIDs
return true from [isNull](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#isNull)().

### `[static]` QUuid QUuid::createUuid()

On any platform other than Windows, this function returns a new UUID with variant
[QUuid::DCE](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#Variant-enum) and version
[QUuid::Random](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#Version-enum). On Windows,
a GUID is generated using the Windows API and will be of the type that the API decides
to create.

**See also** [variant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#variant)() and
[version](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#version)().

### `[static]` QUuid QUuid::fromRfc4122(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*bytes*)

Creates a [QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html) object from the binary
representation of the UUID, as specified by RFC 4122 section 4.1.2. See
[toRfc4122](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#toRfc4122)() for a further
explanation of the order of *bytes* required.

The byte array accepted is NOT a human readable format.

If the conversion fails, a null UUID is created.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

**See also** [toRfc4122](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#toRfc4122)() and
[QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#QUuid-1)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QUuid::toByteArray() const

Returns the binary representation of this
[QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html). The byte array is formatted as
five hex fields separated by '-' and enclosed in curly braces, i.e.,
"{xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx}" where 'x' is a hex digit. From left to right,
the five hex fields are obtained from the four public data members in
[QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html) as follows:

| Field \# | Source |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | data1 |
| 2 | data2 |
| 3 | data3 |
| 4 | data4\[0\] .. data4\[1\] |
| 5 | data4\[2\] .. data4\[7\] |

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QUuid::toByteArray([QUuid::StringFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html#StringFormat-enum) *mode*) const

Returns the string representation of this
[QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html), with the formattiong controlled
by the *mode* parameter. From left to right, the five hex fields are obtained from the
four public data members in [QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html) as
follows:

| Field \# | Source |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | data1 |
| 2 | data2 |
| 3 | data3 |
| 4 | data4\[0\] .. data4\[1\] |
| 5 | data4\[2\] .. data4\[7\] |

This function was introduced in Qt 5.11.

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QUuid::toRfc4122() const

Returns the binary representation of this
[QUuid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/quuid.html). The byte array is in big endian

PythonQt.QtCore.QVariantAnimation.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class is part of [The Animation
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/animation-overview.html). It serves as a
base class for property and item animations, with functions for shared functionality.

The class performs interpolation over
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)s, but leaves using the
interpolated values to its subclasses. Currently, Qt provides
[QPropertyAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpropertyanimation.html), which
animates Qt [properties](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/properties.html). See the
[QPropertyAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpropertyanimation.html) class
description if you wish to animate such properties.

You can then set start and end values for the property by calling
[setStartValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#startValue-prop)()
and
[setEndValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#endValue-prop)(),
and finally call
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#start)() to start the
animation. QVariantAnimation will interpolate the property of the target object and emit
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#valueChanged)().
To react to a change in the current value you have to reimplement the
updateCurrentValue() virtual function or connect to said signal.

It is also possible to set values at specified steps situated between the start and end
value. The interpolation will then touch these points at the specified steps. Note that
the start and end values are defined as the key values at 0.0 and 1.0.

There are two ways to affect how QVariantAnimation interpolates the values. You can set
an easing curve by calling
[setEasingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#easingCurve-prop)(),
and configure the duration by calling
[setDuration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#duration-prop)().
You can change how the [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)s are
interpolated by creating a subclass of QVariantAnimation, and reimplementing the virtual
[interpolated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#interpolated)()
function.

Subclassing QVariantAnimation can be an alternative if you have
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)s that you do not wish to
declare as Qt properties. Note, however, that you in most cases will be better off
declaring your [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) as a
property.

Not all [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) types are
supported. Below is a list of currently supported
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) types:

- [Int](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [UInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [Double](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [Float](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QLineF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)
- [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmetatype.html#Type-enum)

If you need to interpolate other variant types, including custom types, you have to
implement interpolation for these yourself. To do this, you can register an interpolator
function for a given type. This function takes 3 parameters: the start value, the end
value, and the current progress.

Example:

```
    QVariant myColorInterpolator(const QColor &start, const QColor &end, qreal progress)
    {
        ...
        return QColor(...);
    }
    ...
    qRegisterAnimationInterpolator<QColor>(myColorInterpolator);
```

Another option is to reimplement
[interpolated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#interpolated)(),
which returns interpolation values for the value being interpolated.

### currentValue : const [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)

This property holds the current value of the animation.

This property describes the current value; an interpolated value between the [start
value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#startValue-prop) and
the [end
value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#endValue-prop), using
the current time for progress. The value itself is obtained from
[interpolated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#interpolated)(),
which is called repeatedly as the animation is running.

[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) calls the
virtual updateCurrentValue() function when the current value changes. This is
particularly useful for subclasses that need to track updates. For example,
[QPropertyAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpropertyanimation.html) uses
this function to animate Qt
[properties](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/properties.html).

**Notifier signal:**

| --- | --- |

**See also**
[startValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#startValue-prop)

### easingCurve : [QEasingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html)

This property holds the easing curve of the animation

This property defines the easing curve of the animation. By default, a linear easing
curve is used, resulting in linear interpolation. Other curves are provided, for
instance,
[QEasingCurve::InCirc](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum),
which provides a circular entry curve. Another example is
[QEasingCurve::InOutElastic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum),
which provides an elastic effect on the values of the interpolated variant.

[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) will use
the
[QEasingCurve::valueForProgress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#valueForProgress)()
to transform the "normalized progress"
([currentTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#currentTime-prop)
/
[totalDuration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html#totalDuration))
of the animation into the effective progress actually used by the animation. It is this
effective progress that will be the progress when
[interpolated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#interpolated)()
is called. Also, the steps in the
[keyValues](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#keyValues) are
referring to this effective progress.

The easing curve is used with the interpolator, the
[interpolated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html#interpolated)()
virtual function, and the animation's duration to control how the current value changes
as the animation progresses.

**Access functions:**

| QEasingCurve | **easingCurve**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setEasingCurve**(const QEasingCurve \&*easing*) |

PythonQt.QtCore.QVariantAnimation.interp.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) QVariantAnimation::interpolated(const [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) \&*from*, const [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) \&*to*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *progress*) const

This virtual function returns the linear interpolation between variants *from* and *to*,
at *progress*, usually a value between 0 and 1\. You can reimplement this function in a
subclass of
[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html) to
provide your own interpolation algorithm.

Note that in order for the interpolation to work with a
[QEasingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html) that return a value
smaller than 0 or larger than 1 (such as
[QEasingCurve::InBack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html#Type-enum))
you should make sure that it can extrapolate. If the semantic of the datatype does not
allow extrapolation this function should handle that gracefully.

You should call the
[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html)
implementation of this function if you want your class to handle the types already
supported by Qt (see class
[QVariantAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariantanimation.html)
description for a list of supported types).

**See also** [QEasingCurve](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qeasingcurve.html).
signatures: interpolated(self, from_: typing.Any, to: typing.Any, progress: float) -> typing.Any

Qt 5 reference:

### bool QWaitCondition::wait([QMutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html) \**lockedMutex*, [QDeadlineTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdeadlinetimer.html) *deadline* \= QDeadlineTimer(QDeadlineTimer::Forever))

Releases the *lockedMutex* and waits on the wait condition. The *lockedMutex* must be
initially locked by the calling thread. If *lockedMutex* is not in a locked state, the
behavior is undefined. If *lockedMutex* is a recursive mutex, this function returns
immediately. The *lockedMutex* will be unlocked, and the calling thread will block until
either of these conditions is met:

- Another thread signals it using [wakeOne](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeOne)() or [wakeAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeAll)(). This function will return true in this case.
- the deadline given by *deadline* is reached. If *deadline* is `QDeadlineTimer::Forever` (the default), then the wait will never timeout (the event must be signalled). This function will return false if the wait timed out.

The *lockedMutex* will be returned to the same locked state. This function is provided
to allow the atomic transition from the locked state to the wait state.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.12.

**See also** [wakeOne](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeOne)()
and [wakeAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeAll)().

### bool QWaitCondition::wait([QMutex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmutex.html) \**lockedMutex*, unsigned long *time*)

This is an overloaded function.

### bool QWaitCondition::wait([QReadWriteLock](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qreadwritelock.html) \**lockedReadWriteLock*, [QDeadlineTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdeadlinetimer.html) *deadline* \= QDeadlineTimer(QDeadlineTimer::Forever))

Releases the *lockedReadWriteLock* and waits on the wait condition. The
*lockedReadWriteLock* must be initially locked by the calling thread. If
*lockedReadWriteLock* is not in a locked state, this function returns immediately. The
*lockedReadWriteLock* must not be locked recursively, otherwise this function will not
release the lock properly. The *lockedReadWriteLock* will be unlocked, and the calling
thread will block until either of these conditions is met:

- Another thread signals it using [wakeOne](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeOne)() or [wakeAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeAll)(). This function will return true in this case.
- the deadline given by *deadline* is reached. If *deadline* is `QDeadlineTimer::Forever` (the default), then the wait will never timeout (the event must be signalled). This function will return false if the wait timed out.

The *lockedReadWriteLock* will be returned to the same locked state. This function is
provided to allow the atomic transition from the locked state to the wait state.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.12.

**See also** [wakeOne](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeOne)()
and [wakeAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeAll)().

Wakes all threads waiting on the wait condition. The order in which the threads are

PythonQt.QtCore.QWaitCondition.wakeOne.doc:

### void QWaitCondition::wakeOne()

Wakes one thread waiting on the wait condition. The thread that is woken up depends on
the operating system's scheduling policies, and cannot be controlled or predicted.

If you want to wake up a specific thread, the solution is typically to use different
wait conditions and have different threads wait on different conditions.

**See also**
[wakeAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwaitcondition.html#wakeAll)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QAbstractButton.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This class implements an *abstract* button. Subclasses of this class handle user
actions, and specify how the button is drawn.

QAbstractButton provides support for both push buttons and checkable (toggle) buttons.
Checkable buttons are implemented in the
[QRadioButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradiobutton.html) and
[QCheckBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html) classes. Push buttons are
implemented in the [QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html)
and [QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html) classes; these
also provide toggle behavior if required.

Any button can display a label containing text and an icon.
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)() sets the
text; [setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)()
sets the icon. If a button is disabled, its label is changed to give the button a
"disabled" appearance.

If the button is a text button with a string containing an ampersand ('\&'),
QAbstractButton automatically creates a shortcut key. For example:

```
QPushButton *button = new QPushButton(tr("Ro&ck && Roll"), this);
```

The **Alt\+C** shortcut is assigned to the button, i.e., when the user presses
**Alt\+C** the button will call
[animateClick](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#animateClick)().
See the [QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html#mnemonic)
documentation for details. To display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&'.

You can also set a custom shortcut key using the
[setShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#shortcut-prop)()
function. This is useful mostly for buttons that do not have any text, and therefore
can't have any automatic shortcut.

```
button->setIcon(QIcon(":/images/print.png"));
button->setShortcut(tr("Alt+F7"));
```

All the buttons provided by Qt
([QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html),
[QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html),
[QCheckBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html), and
[QRadioButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradiobutton.html)) can display both
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop) and
[icons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet-reference.html#icon).

A button can be made the default button in a dialog by means of
[QPushButton::setDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#default-prop)()
and
[QPushButton::setAutoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)().

QAbstractButton provides most of the states used for buttons:

- [isDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#down-prop)() indicates whether the button is *pressed* down.
- [isChecked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)() indicates whether the button is *checked*. Only checkable buttons can be checked and unchecked (see below).
- [isEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop)() indicates whether the button can be pressed by the user.

  **Note:** As opposed to other widgets, buttons derived from QAbstractButton accept mouse
  and context menu events when disabled.
- [setAutoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop)() sets whether the button will auto-repeat if the user holds it down. [autoRepeatDelay](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeatDelay-prop) and [autoRepeatInterval](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeatInterval-prop) define how auto-repetition is done.
- [setCheckable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkable-prop)() sets whether the button is a toggle button or not.

The difference between
[isDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#down-prop)() and
[isChecked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)() is
as follows. When the user clicks a toggle button to check it, the button is first
*pressed* then released into the *checked* state. When the user clicks it again (to
uncheck it), the button moves first to the *pressed* state, then to the *unchecked*
state
([isChecked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)() and
[isDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#down-prop)() are both
false).

QAbstractButton provides four signals:

1. [pressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#pressed)() is emitted when the left mouse button is pressed while the mouse cursor is inside the button.
2. [released](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#released)() is emitted when the left mouse button is released.
3. [clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#clicked)() is emitted when the button is first pressed and then released, when the shortcut key is typed, or when [click](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#click)() or [animateClick](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#animateClick)() is called.
4. [toggled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#toggled)() is emitted when the state of a toggle button changes.

To subclass QAbstractButton, you must reimplement at least
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#paintEvent)() to
draw the button's outline and its text or pixmap. It is generally advisable to
reimplement [sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop)()
as well, and sometimes
[hitButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#hitButton)() (to
determine whether a button press is within the button). For buttons with more than two
states (like tri-state buttons), you will also have to reimplement
[checkStateSet](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkStateSet)()
and
[nextCheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#nextCheckState)().

### autoExclusive : bool

This property holds whether auto-exclusivity is enabled

If auto-exclusivity is enabled, checkable buttons that belong to the same parent widget
behave as if they were part of the same exclusive button group. In an exclusive button
group, only one button can be checked at any time; checking another button automatically
unchecks the previously checked one.

The property has no effect on buttons that belong to a button group.

autoExclusive is off by default, except for radio buttons.

Qt 5 reference:

### `[signal]` void QAbstractButton::toggled(bool *checked*)

This signal is emitted whenever a checkable button changes its state. *checked* is true
if the button is checked, or false if the button is unchecked.

This may be the result of a user action,
[click](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#click)() slot
activation, or because
[setChecked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)() is
called.

The states of buttons in exclusive button groups are updated before this signal is
emitted. This means that slots can act on either the "off" signal or the "on" signal
emitted by the buttons in the group whose states have changed.

For example, a slot that reacts to signals emitted by newly checked buttons but which
ignores signals from buttons that have been unchecked can be implemented using the
following pattern:

```
void MyWidget::reactToToggle(bool checked)
{
   if (checked) {
      // Examine the new button states.
      ...
   }
}
```

Button groups can be created using the
[QButtonGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html) class, and updates
to the button states monitored with the
[QButtonGroup::buttonClicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html#buttonClicked)()
signal.

**Note:** Notifier signal for property
[checked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop).

**See also**
[checked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop) and
[clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#clicked)().

## Detailed Description

A QAbstractItemDelegate provides the interface and common functionality for delegates in
the model/view architecture. Delegates display individual items in views, and handle the
editing of model data.

The QAbstractItemDelegate class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

To render an item in a custom way, you must implement
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#paint)() and
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#sizeHint)().
The [QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html)
class provides default implementations for these functions; if you do not need custom
rendering, subclass that class instead.

We give an example of drawing a progress bar in items; in our case for a package
management program.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/widgetdelegate.png)

We create the `WidgetDelegate` class, which inherits from
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html). We
do the drawing in the
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#paint)() function:

```
void WidgetDelegate::paint(QPainter *painter, const QStyleOptionViewItem &option,
                           const QModelIndex &index) const
{
    if (index.column() == 1) {
        int progress = index.data().toInt();

        QStyleOptionProgressBar progressBarOption;
        progressBarOption.rect = option.rect;
        progressBarOption.minimum = 0;
        progressBarOption.maximum = 100;
        progressBarOption.progress = progress;
        progressBarOption.text = QString::number(progress) + "%";
        progressBarOption.textVisible = true;

        QApplication::style()->drawControl(QStyle::CE_ProgressBar,
                                           &progressBarOption, painter);
    } else
        QStyledItemDelegate::paint(painter, option, index);
```

Notice that we use a
[QStyleOptionProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoptionprogressbar.html)
and initialize its members. We can then use the current
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html) to draw it.

To provide custom editing, there are two approaches that can be used. The first approach
is to create an editor widget and display it directly on top of the item. To do this you
must reimplement
[createEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#createEditor)()
to provide an editor widget,
[setEditorData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#setEditorData)()
to populate the editor with the data from the model, and
[setModelData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#setModelData)()
so that the delegate can update the model with data from the editor.

The second approach is to handle user events directly by reimplementing
[editorEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#editorEvent)().

## Detailed Description

QAbstractItemView class is the base class for every standard view that uses a
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html).
QAbstractItemView is an abstract class and cannot itself be instantiated. It provides a
standard interface for interoperating with models through the signals and slots
mechanism, enabling subclasses to be kept up-to-date with changes to their models. This
class provides standard support for keyboard and mouse navigation, viewport scrolling,
item editing, and selections. The keyboard navigation implements this functionality:

| Keys | Functionality |
| --- | --- |
| Arrow keys | Changes the current item and selects it. |
| Ctrl\+Arrow keys | Changes the current item but does not select it. |
| Shift\+Arrow keys | Changes the current item and selects it. The previously selected item(s) is not deselected. |
| Ctr\+Space | Toggles selection of the current item. |
| Tab/Backtab | Changes the current item to the next/previous item. |
| Home/End | Selects the first/last item in the model. |
| Page up/Page down | Scrolls the rows shown up/down by the number of visible rows in the view. |
| Ctrl\+A | Selects all items in the model. |

Note that the above table assumes that the [selection
mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionMode-prop)
allows the operations. For instance, you cannot select items if the selection mode is
[QAbstractItemView::NoSelection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#SelectionMode-enum).

The QAbstractItemView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

The view classes that inherit QAbstractItemView only need to implement their own
view-specific functionality, such as drawing items, returning the geometry of items,
finding items, etc.

QAbstractItemView provides common slots such as
[edit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#edit)() and
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setCurrentIndex)().
Many protected slots are also provided, including
[dataChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#dataChanged)(),
[rowsInserted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#rowsInserted)(),
[rowsAboutToBeRemoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#rowsAboutToBeRemoved)(),
[selectionChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionChanged)(),
and
[currentChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#currentChanged)().

The root item is returned by
[rootIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#rootIndex)(), and
the current item by
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#currentIndex)().
To make sure that an item is visible use
[scrollTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#scrollTo)().

Some of QAbstractItemView's functions are concerned with scrolling, for example
[setHorizontalScrollMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#horizontalScrollMode-prop)()
and
[setVerticalScrollMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#verticalScrollMode-prop)().
To set the range of the scroll bars, you can, for example, reimplement the view's
[resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#resizeEvent)()
function:

```
void MyView::resizeEvent(QResizeEvent *event) {
    horizontalScrollBar()->setRange(0, realWidth - width());
    ...
}
```

Note that the range is not updated until the widget is shown.

Several other functions are concerned with selection control; for example
[setSelectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionMode-prop)(),
and
[setSelectionBehavior](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionBehavior-prop)().
This class provides a default selection model to work with
([selectionModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionModel)()),
but this can be replaced by using
[setSelectionModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setSelectionModel)()
with an instance of
[QItemSelectionModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html).

For complete control over the display and editing of items you can specify a delegate
with
[setItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setItemDelegate)().

QAbstractItemView provides a lot of protected functions. Some are concerned with
editing, for example,
[edit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#edit)(), and
[commitData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#commitData)(),
whilst others are keyboard and mouse event handlers.

**Note:** If you inherit QAbstractItemView and intend to update the contents of the
viewport, you should use
viewport-\>[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#update)()
instead of [update()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update) as all
painting operations take place on the viewport.

### autoScroll : bool

This property holds whether autoscrolling in drag move events is enabled

If this property is set to true (the default), the
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html)
automatically scrolls the contents of the view if the user drags within 16 pixels of the
viewport edge. If the current item changes, then the view will scroll automatically to
ensure that the current item is fully visible.

This property only works if the viewport accepts drops. Autoscroll is switched off by
setting this property to false.

### dragDropOverwriteMode : bool

This property holds the view's drag and drop behavior

If its value is `true`, the selected data will overwrite the existing item data when
dropped, while moving the data will clear the item. If its value is `false`, the
selected data will be inserted as a new item when the data is dropped. When the data is
moved, the item is removed as well.

The default value is `false`, as in the
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) and
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) subclasses. In the
[QTableView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtableview.html) subclass, on the other
hand, the property has been set to `true`.

Note: This is not intended to prevent overwriting of items. The model's implementation
of flags() should do that by not returning
[Qt::ItemIsDropEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum).

This property was introduced in Qt 4.2.

### `[slot]` void QAbstractItemView::edit(const [QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) \&*index*)

Starts editing the item corresponding to the given *index* if it is editable.

Note that this function does not change the current index. Since the current index
defines the next and previous items to edit, users may find that keyboard navigation
does not work as expected. To provide consistent navigation behavior, call
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setCurrentIndex)()
before this function with the same model index.

**See also**
[QModelIndex::flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html#flags)().

Starts editing the item at *index*, creating an editor if necessary, and returns `true`
if the view's
[State](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#State-enum) is now
[EditingState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#State-enum);
otherwise returns `false`.

The action that caused the editing process is described by *trigger*, and the associated
event is specified by *event*.

Editing can be forced by specifying the *trigger* to be
[QAbstractItemView::AllEditTriggers](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#EditTrigger-enum).

[closeEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#closeEditor)().

This function should only be used to display static content within the visible area
corresponding to an item of data. If you want to display custom dynamic content or

### void QAbstractItemView::setItemDelegate([QAbstractItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html) \**delegate*)

Sets the item delegate for this view and its model to *delegate*. This is useful if you
want complete control over the editing and display of items.

Any existing delegate will be removed, but not deleted.
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) does not
take ownership of *delegate*.

**Warning:** You should not share the same instance of a delegate between views. Doing
so can cause incorrect or unintuitive editing behavior since each view connected to a
given delegate may receive the
[closeEditor()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#closeEditor)
signal, and attempt to access, modify or close an editor that has already been closed.

[itemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#itemDelegate)().

### void QAbstractItemView::setItemDelegateForColumn(int *column*, [QAbstractItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html) \**delegate*)

items on *column* will be drawn and managed by *delegate* instead of using the default
delegate (i.e.,
[itemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#itemDelegate)()).

Any existing column delegate for *column* will be removed, but not deleted.
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) does not

will take precedence and manage the intersecting cell index.

**Warning:** You should not share the same instance of a delegate between views. Doing

given delegate may receive the
[closeEditor()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#closeEditor)

### `[virtual]` void QAbstractItemView::setModel([QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) \**model*)

Sets the *model* for the view to present.

This function will create and set a new selection model, replacing any model that was
previously set with
[setSelectionModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setSelectionModel)().
However, the old selection model will not be deleted as it may be shared between several
views. We recommend that you delete the old selection model if it is no longer required.
This is done with the following code:

```
QItemSelectionModel *m = view->selectionModel();
view->setModel(new model);
delete m;
```

If both the old model and the old selection model do not have parents, or if their
parents are long-lived objects, it may be preferable to call their
[deleteLater](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#deleteLater)() functions
to explicitly delete them.

The view *does not* take ownership of the model unless it is the model's parent object
because the model may be shared between many different views.

**See also** [model](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#model)(),
[selectionModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionModel)(),
and
[setSelectionModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#setSelectionModel)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QAbstractScrollArea.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QAbstractScrollArea is a low-level abstraction of a scrolling area. The area provides a
central widget called the viewport, in which the contents of the area is to be scrolled
(i.e, the visible parts of the contents are rendered in the viewport).

Next to the viewport is a vertical scroll bar, and below is a horizontal scroll bar.
When all of the area contents fits in the viewport, each scroll bar can be either
visible or hidden depending on the scroll bar's
[Qt::ScrollBarPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScrollBarPolicy-enum).
When a scroll bar is hidden, the viewport expands in order to cover all available space.
When a scroll bar becomes visible again, the viewport shrinks in order to make room for
the scroll bar.

It is possible to reserve a margin area around the viewport, see
[setViewportMargins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#setViewportMargins)().
The feature is mostly used to place a
[QHeaderView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html) widget above or
beside the scrolling area. Subclasses of QAbstractScrollArea should implement margins.

When inheriting QAbstractScrollArea, you need to do the following:

- Control the scroll bars by setting their range, value, page step, and tracking their movements.
- Draw the contents of the area in the viewport according to the values of the scroll bars.
- Handle events received by the viewport in [viewportEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#viewportEvent)() \- notably resize events.
- Use `viewport->update()` to update the contents of the viewport instead of [update()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update) as all painting operations take place on the viewport.

With a scroll bar policy of
[Qt::ScrollBarAsNeeded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScrollBarPolicy-enum)
(the default), QAbstractScrollArea shows scroll bars when they provide a non-zero
scrolling range, and hides them otherwise.

The scroll bars and viewport should be updated whenever the viewport receives a resize
event or the size of the contents changes. The viewport also needs to be updated when
the scroll bars values change. The initial values of the scroll bars are often set when
the area receives new contents.

We give a simple example, in which we have implemented a scroll area that can scroll any
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html). We make the widget a child
of the viewport; this way, we do not have to calculate which part of the widget to draw
but can simply move the widget with
[QWidget::move](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#pos-prop)(). When the
area contents or the viewport size changes, we do the following:

```
    QSize areaSize = viewport()->size();
    QSize  widgetSize = widget->size();

    verticalScrollBar()->setPageStep(areaSize.height());
    horizontalScrollBar()->setPageStep(areaSize.width());
    verticalScrollBar()->setRange(0, widgetSize.height() - areaSize.height());
    horizontalScrollBar()->setRange(0, widgetSize.width() - areaSize.width());
    updateWidgetPosition();
```

When the scroll bars change value, we need to update the widget position, i.e., find the
part of the widget that is to be drawn in the viewport:

```
    int hvalue = horizontalScrollBar()->value();
    int vvalue = verticalScrollBar()->value();
    QPoint topLeft = viewport()->rect().topLeft();

    widget->move(topLeft.x() - hvalue, topLeft.y() - vvalue);
```

In order to track scroll bar movements, reimplement the virtual function
[scrollContentsBy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#scrollContentsBy)().
In order to fine-tune scrolling behavior, connect to a scroll bar's
[QAbstractSlider::actionTriggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#actionTriggered)()
signal and adjust the
[QAbstractSlider::sliderPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderPosition-prop)
as you wish.

For convenience, QAbstractScrollArea makes all viewport events available in the virtual
[viewportEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#viewportEvent)()
handler. [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html)'s specialized
handlers are remapped to viewport events in the cases where this makes sense. The
remapped specialized handlers are:
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#paintEvent)(),
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#mousePressEvent)(),
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(),
[mouseDoubleClickEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#mouseDoubleClickEvent)(),
[mouseMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#mouseMoveEvent)(),
[wheelEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#wheelEvent)(),
[dragEnterEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#dragEnterEvent)(),
[dragMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#dragMoveEvent)(),
[dragLeaveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#dragLeaveEvent)(),
[dropEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#dropEvent)(),
[contextMenuEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#contextMenuEvent)(),
and
[resizeEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#resizeEvent)().

[QScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html), which inherits
QAbstractScrollArea, provides smooth scrolling for any
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) (i.e., the widget is scrolled
pixel by pixel). You only need to subclass QAbstractScrollArea if you need more
specialized behavior. This is, for instance, true if the entire contents of the area is
not suitable for being drawn on a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) or if you do not want smooth
scrolling.

### void QAbstractScrollArea::addScrollBarWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*, [Qt::Alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) *alignment*)

Adds *widget* as a scroll bar widget in the location specified by *alignment*.

Scroll bar widgets are shown next to the horizontal or vertical scroll bar, and can be
placed on either side of it. If you want the scroll bar widgets to be always visible,
set the scrollBarPolicy for the corresponding scroll bar to `AlwaysOn`.

*alignment* must be one of Qt::Alignleft and
[Qt::AlignRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum), which
maps to the horizontal scroll bar, or
[Qt::AlignTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) and
[Qt::AlignBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum), which
maps to the vertical scroll bar.

A scroll bar widget can be removed by either re-parenting the widget or deleting it.
It's also possible to hide a widget with
[QWidget::hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)()

The scroll bar widget will be resized to fit the scroll bar geometry for the current
style. The following describes the case for scroll bar widgets on the horizontal scroll
bar:

The height of the widget will be set to match the height of the scroll bar. To control
the width of the widget, use
[QWidget::setMinimumWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumWidth-prop)
and
[QWidget::setMaximumWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#maximumWidth-prop),
or implement
[QWidget::sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop)() and
set a horizontal size policy. If you want a square widget, call
[QStyle::pixelMetric](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#pixelMetric)([QStyle::PM\_ScrollBarExtent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PixelMetric-enum))
and set the width to this value.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also**
[scrollBarWidgets](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#scrollBarWidgets)().
signatures: addScrollBarWidget(self, widget: PySide2.QtWidgets.QWidget, alignment: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.Alignment) -> None

### `[virtual protected]` void QAbstractScrollArea::scrollContentsBy(int *dx*, int *dy*)

This virtual handler is called when the scroll bars are moved by *dx*, *dy*, and
consequently the viewport's contents should be scrolled accordingly.

The default implementation simply calls
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#update)() on the entire
[viewport](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#viewport)(),
subclasses can reimplement this handler for optimization purposes, or \- like
[QScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html) \- to move a contents
widget. The parameters *dx* and *dy* are there for convenience, so that the class knows
how much should be scrolled (useful e.g. when doing pixel-shifts). You may just as well
ignore these values and scroll directly to the position the scroll bars indicate.

Calling this function in order to scroll programmatically is an error, use the scroll
bars instead (e.g. by calling
[QScrollBar::setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop)()
directly).
signatures: scrollContentsBy(self, dx: int, dy: int) -> None

### void QAbstractScrollArea::setCornerWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*)

Sets the widget in the corner between the two scroll bars to be *widget*.

You will probably also want to set at least one of the scroll bar modes to `AlwaysOn`.

Passing `nullptr` shows no widget in the corner.

Any previous corner widget is hidden.

You may call setCornerWidget() with the same widget at different times.

All widgets set here will be deleted by the scroll area when it is destroyed unless you
separately reparent the widget after setting some other corner widget (or `nullptr`).

Any *newly* set widget should have no current parent.

By default, no corner widget is present.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

[cornerWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#cornerWidget)(),

## Detailed Description

The class is designed as a common super class for widgets like
[QScrollBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollbar.html),
[QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html) and
[QDial](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdial.html).

Here are the main properties of the class:

1. [value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop): The bounded integer that QAbstractSlider maintains.
2. [minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#minimum-prop): The lowest possible value.
3. [maximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#maximum-prop): The highest possible value.
4. [singleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#singleStep-prop): The smaller of two natural steps that an abstract sliders provides and typically corresponds to the user pressing an arrow key.
5. [pageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#pageStep-prop): The larger of two natural steps that an abstract slider provides and typically corresponds to the user pressing PageUp or PageDown.
6. [tracking](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#tracking-prop): Whether slider tracking is enabled.
7. [sliderPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderPosition-prop): The current position of the slider. If [tracking](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#tracking-prop) is enabled (the default), this is identical to [value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop).

Unity (1) may be viewed as a third step size.
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop)() lets
you set the current value to any integer in the allowed range, not just
[minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#minimum-prop)() \+ *n*
\*
[singleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#singleStep-prop)()
for integer values of *n*. Some widgets may allow the user to set any value at all;
others may just provide multiples of
[singleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#singleStep-prop)()
or [pageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#pageStep-prop)().

QAbstractSlider emits a comprehensive set of signals:

| Signal | Emitted when |
| --- | --- |
| [valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#valueChanged)() | the value has changed. The [tracking](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#tracking-prop) determines whether this signal is emitted during user interaction. |
| [sliderPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderPressed)() | the user starts to drag the slider. |
| [sliderMoved](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderMoved)() | the user drags the slider. |
| [sliderReleased](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderReleased)() | the user releases the slider. |
| [actionTriggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#actionTriggered)() | a slider action was triggered. |
| [rangeChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#rangeChanged)() | a the range has changed. |

QAbstractSlider provides a virtual
[sliderChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderChange)()
function that is well suited for updating the on-screen representation of sliders. By
calling
[triggerAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#triggerAction)(),
subclasses trigger slider actions. Two helper functions
[QStyle::sliderPositionFromValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#sliderPositionFromValue)()
and
[QStyle::sliderValueFromPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#sliderValueFromPosition)()
help subclasses and styles to map screen coordinates to logical range values.

### `[signal]` void QAbstractSlider::actionTriggered(int *action*)

This signal is emitted when the slider action *action* is triggered. Actions are
[SliderSingleStepAdd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#SliderAction-enum),
[SliderSingleStepSub](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#SliderAction-enum),
[SliderPageStepAdd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#SliderAction-enum),
[SliderPageStepSub](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#SliderAction-enum),
[SliderToMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#SliderAction-enum),
[SliderToMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#SliderAction-enum),
and
[SliderMove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#SliderAction-enum).

When the signal is emitted, the
[sliderPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderPosition-prop)
has been adjusted according to the action, but the
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop) has not yet
been propagated (meaning the
[valueChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#valueChanged)()
signal was not yet emitted), and the visual display has not been updated. In slots
connected to this signal you can thus safely adjust any action by calling
[setSliderPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderPosition-prop)()
yourself, based on both the action and the slider's value.

**See also**
[triggerAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#triggerAction)().

### invertedAppearance : bool

This property holds whether or not a slider shows its values inverted.

If this property is `false` (the default), the minimum and maximum will be shown in its
classic position for the inherited widget. If the value is true, the minimum and maximum
appear at their opposite location.

Note: This property makes most sense for sliders and dials. For scroll bars, the visual
effect of the scroll bar subcontrols depends on whether or not the styles understand
inverted appearance; most styles ignore this property for scroll bars.

**Access functions:**

| bool | **invertedAppearance**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setInvertedAppearance**(*bool*) |

### invertedControls : bool

This property holds whether or not the slider inverts its wheel and key events.

If this property is `false`, scrolling the mouse wheel "up" and using keys like page up
will increase the slider's value towards its maximum. Otherwise pressing page up will
move value towards the slider's minimum.

PythonQt.QtGui.QAbstractSpinBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The class is designed as a common super class for widgets like
[QSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html),
[QDoubleSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html) and
[QDateTimeEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html)

Here are the main properties of the class:

1. [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#text-prop): The text that is displayed in the QAbstractSpinBox.
2. [alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet-reference.html#alignment): The alignment of the text in the QAbstractSpinBox.
3. [wrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#wrapping-prop): Whether the QAbstractSpinBox wraps from the minimum value to the maximum value and vice versa.

QAbstractSpinBox provides a virtual
[stepBy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#stepBy)() function
that is called whenever the user triggers a step. This function takes an integer value
to signify how many steps were taken. E.g. Pressing
[Qt::Key\_Down](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum) will trigger a call
to [stepBy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#stepBy)(-1).

When the user triggers a step whilst holding the
[Qt::ControlModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#KeyboardModifier-enum),
QAbstractSpinBox steps by 10 instead of making a single step. This step modifier affects
wheel events, key events and interaction with the spinbox buttons. Note that on macOS,
Control corresponds to the Command key.

Since Qt 5.12,
[QStyle::SH\_SpinBox\_StepModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#StyleHint-enum)
can be used to select which
[Qt::KeyboardModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#KeyboardModifier-enum)
increases the step rate.
[Qt::NoModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#KeyboardModifier-enum)
disables this feature.

QAbstractSpinBox also provide a virtual function
[stepEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#stepEnabled)() to
determine whether stepping up/down is allowed at any point. This function returns a
bitset of
[StepEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#StepEnabledFlag-enum).

Qt 5 reference:

### keyboardTracking : bool

This property holds whether keyboard tracking is enabled for the spinbox.

If keyboard tracking is enabled (the default), the spinbox emits the valueChanged() and
textChanged() signals while the new value is being entered from the keyboard.

E.g. when the user enters the value 600 by typing 6, 0, and 0, the spinbox emits 3
signals with the values 6, 60, and 600 respectively.

If keyboard tracking is disabled, the spinbox doesn't emit the valueChanged() and
textChanged() signals while typing. It emits the signals later, when the return key is
pressed, when keyboard focus is lost, or when other spinbox functionality is used, e.g.
pressing an arrow key.

This property was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**Access functions:**

| --- | --- |
| void | **setKeyboardTracking**(bool *kt*) |

### specialValueText : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the special-value text

If set, the spin box will display this text instead of a numeric value whenever the
current value is equal to minimum(). Typical use is to indicate that this choice has a
special (default) meaning.

For example, if your spin box allows the user to choose a scale factor (or zoom level)
for displaying an image, and your application is able to automatically choose one that
will enable the image to fit completely within the display window, you can set up the
spin box like this:

```
    QSpinBox *zoomSpinBox = new QSpinBox;
    zoomSpinBox->setRange(0, 1000);
    zoomSpinBox->setSingleStep(10);
    zoomSpinBox->setSuffix("%");
    zoomSpinBox->setSpecialValueText(tr("Automatic"));
    zoomSpinBox->setValue(100);
```

The user will then be able to choose a scale from 1% to 1000% or select "Auto" to leave
it up to the application to choose. Your code must then interpret the spin box value of
0 as a request from the user to scale the image to fit inside the window.

All values are displayed with the prefix and suffix (if set), *except* for the special
value, which only shows the special value text. This special text is passed in the
[QSpinBox::textChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html#textChanged)()
signal that passes a [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html).

To turn off the special-value text display, call this function with an empty string. The
default is no special-value text, i.e. the numeric value is shown as usual.

If no special-value text is set, specialValueText() returns an empty string.

**Access functions:**

| QString | **specialValueText**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setSpecialValueText**(const QString \&*txt*) |

PythonQt.QtGui.QAbstractSpinBox.stepBy.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` void QAbstractSpinBox::stepBy(int *steps*)

Virtual function that is called whenever the user triggers a step. The *steps* parameter
indicates how many steps were taken. For example, pressing `Qt::Key_Down` will trigger a
call to `stepBy(-1)`, whereas pressing `Qt::Key_PageUp` will trigger a call to
`stepBy(10)`.

If you subclass `QAbstractSpinBox` you must reimplement this function. Note that this
function is called even if the resulting value will be outside the bounds of minimum and
maximum. It's this function's job to handle these situations.

**See also**
[stepUp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#stepUp)(),
[stepDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#stepDown)(), and
[keyPressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#keyPressEvent)().

The up arrow will be painted as disabled unless (stepEnabled() \&

[StepUpEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html#StepEnabledFlag-enum)
if value \< maximum().

If you subclass
[QAbstractSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractspinbox.html) you will

[QSpinBox::minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html#minimum-prop)(),

### wrapping : bool

This property holds whether the spin box is circular.

If wrapping is true stepping up from maximum() value will take you to the minimum()
value and vice versa. Wrapping only make sense if you have minimum() and maximum()
values set.

```
QSpinBox *spinBox = new QSpinBox(this);
spinBox->setRange(0, 100);
spinBox->setWrapping(true);
spinBox->setValue(100);
spinBox->stepBy(1);
// value is 0
```

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QAbstractTableModel provides a standard interface for models that represent their data
as a two-dimensional array of items. It is not used directly, but must be subclassed.

Since the model provides a more specialized interface than
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html), it is
not suitable for use with tree views, although it can be used to provide data to a
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html). If you need to represent
a simple list of items, and only need a model to contain a single column of data,
subclassing the
[QAbstractListModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractlistmodel.html) may be
more appropriate.

The [rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)()
and
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnCount)()
functions return the dimensions of the table. To retrieve a model index corresponding to
an item in the model, use
[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttablemodel.html#index)() and provide
only the row and column numbers.

### Subclassing

When subclassing QAbstractTableModel, you must implement
[rowCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#rowCount)(),
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#columnCount)(),
and [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#data)(). Default
implementations of the
[index](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttablemodel.html#index)() and
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#parent)() functions
are provided by QAbstractTableModel. Well behaved models will also implement
[headerData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#headerData)().

Editable models need to implement
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#setData)(), and
implement [flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstracttablemodel.html#flags)()
to return a value containing
[Qt::ItemIsEditable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum).

Models that provide interfaces to resizable data structures can provide implementations
of
[insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)(),
[removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRows)(),
[insertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertColumns)(),
and
[removeColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeColumns)().
When implementing these functions, it is important to call the appropriate functions so
that all connected views are aware of any changes:

- An [insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertRows)() implementation must call [beginInsertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginInsertRows)() *before* inserting new rows into the data structure, and it must call [endInsertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endInsertRows)() *immediately afterwards*.
- An [insertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#insertColumns)() implementation must call [beginInsertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginInsertColumns)() *before* inserting new columns into the data structure, and it must call [endInsertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endInsertColumns)() *immediately afterwards*.
- A [removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeRows)() implementation must call [beginRemoveRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginRemoveRows)() *before* the rows are removed from the data structure, and it must call [endRemoveRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endRemoveRows)() *immediately afterwards*.
- A [removeColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#removeColumns)() implementation must call [beginRemoveColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#beginRemoveColumns)() *before* the columns are removed from the data structure, and it must call [endRemoveColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html#endRemoveColumns)() *immediately afterwards*.

**Note:** Some general guidelines for subclassing models are available in the [Model
Subclassing
Reference](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-subclassing-reference).
