PythonQt.QtGui.QFontComboBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The combobox is populated with an alphabetized list of font family names, such as Arial,
Helvetica, and Times New Roman. Family names are displayed using the actual font when
possible. For fonts such as Symbol, where the name is not representable in the font
itself, a sample of the font is displayed next to the family name.

QFontComboBox is often used in toolbars, in conjunction with a
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html) for controlling the font
size and two [QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html)s for
bold and italic.

When the user selects a new font, the
[currentFontChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontcombobox.html#currentFontChanged)()
signal is emitted in addition to
[currentIndexChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html#currentIndexChanged)().

Call
[setWritingSystem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontcombobox.html#writingSystem-prop)()
to tell QFontComboBox to show only fonts that support a given writing system, and
[setFontFilters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontcombobox.html#fontFilters-prop)()
to filter out certain types of fonts as e.g. non scalable fonts or monospaced fonts.

![Screenshot of QFontComboBox on Windows
Vista](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windowsvista-fontcombobox.png)

## Detailed Description

The QFontInfo class provides the same access functions as
[QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html), e.g.
[family](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontinfo.html#family)(),
[pointSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontinfo.html#pointSize)(),
[italic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontinfo.html#italic)(),
[weight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontinfo.html#weight)(),
[fixedPitch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontinfo.html#fixedPitch)(),
[styleHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontinfo.html#styleHint)() etc. But
whilst the [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) access functions
return the values that were set, a QFontInfo object returns the values that apply to the
font that will actually be used to draw the text.

For example, when the program asks for a 25pt Courier font on a machine that has a
non-scalable 24pt Courier font, [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html)
will (normally) use the 24pt Courier for rendering. In this case,
[QFont::pointSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html#pointSize)() returns 25
and
[QFontInfo::pointSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontinfo.html#pointSize)()
returns 24\.

There are three ways to create a QFontInfo object.

1. Calling the QFontInfo constructor with a [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) creates a font info object for a screen-compatible font, i.e. the font cannot be a printer font. If the font is changed later, the font info object is *not* updated.

   (Note: If you use a printer font the values returned may be inaccurate. Printer fonts
   are not always accessible so the nearest screen font is used if a printer font is
   supplied.)
2. [QWidget::fontInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#fontInfo)() returns the font info for a widget's font. This is equivalent to calling QFontInfo(widget-\>[font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet-reference.html#font)()). If the widget's font is changed later, the font info object is *not* updated.
3. [QPainter::fontInfo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#fontInfo)() returns the font info for a painter's current font. If the painter's font is changed later, the font info object is *not* updated.

PythonQt.QtGui.QFontMetrics.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QFontMetrics functions calculate the size of characters and strings for a given font.
There are three ways you can create a QFontMetrics object:

1. Calling the QFontMetrics constructor with a [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) creates a font metrics object for a screen-compatible font, i.e. the font cannot be a printer font. If the font is changed later, the font metrics object is *not* updated.

   (Note: If you use a printer font the values returned may be inaccurate. Printer fonts
   are not always accessible so the nearest screen font is used if a printer font is
   supplied.)
2. [QWidget::fontMetrics](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#fontMetrics)() returns the font metrics for a widget's font. This is equivalent to QFontMetrics(widget-\>[font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet-reference.html#font)()). If the widget's font is changed later, the font metrics object is *not* updated.
3. [QPainter::fontMetrics](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#fontMetrics)() returns the font metrics for a painter's current font. If the painter's font is changed later, the font metrics object is *not* updated.

Once created, the object provides functions to access the individual metrics of the
font, its characters, and for strings rendered in the font.

There are several functions that operate on the font:
[ascent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#ascent)(),
[descent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#descent)(),
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#height)(),
[leading](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#leading)() and
[lineSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#lineSpacing)() return
the basic size properties of the font. The
[underlinePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#underlinePos)(),
[overlinePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#overlinePos)(),
[strikeOutPos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#strikeOutPos)() and
[lineWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#lineWidth)() functions,
return the properties of the line that underlines, overlines or strikes out the
characters. These functions are all fast.

There are also some functions that operate on the set of glyphs in the font:
[minLeftBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#minLeftBearing)(),
[minRightBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#minRightBearing)()
and [maxWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#maxWidth)(). These
are by necessity slow, and we recommend avoiding them if possible.

For each character, you can get its
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
[leftBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#leftBearing)(), and
[rightBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#rightBearing)(), and
find out whether it is in the font using
[inFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#inFont)(). You can also
treat the character as a string, and use the string functions on it.

The string functions include
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
to return the width of a string in pixels (or points, for a printer),
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#boundingRect)(), to
return a rectangle large enough to contain the rendered string, and
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#size)(), to return the size
of that rectangle.

Example:

```
QFont font("times", 24);
QFontMetrics fm(font);
int pixelsWide = fm.horizontalAdvance("What's the width of this text?");
int pixelsHigh = fm.height();
```

PythonQt.QtGui.QFontMetrics.ascent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### int QFontMetrics::ascent() const

Returns the ascent of the font.

The ascent of a font is the distance from the baseline to the highest position
characters extend to. In practice, some font designers break this rule, e.g. when they
put more than one accent on top of a character, or to accommodate a certain character,
so it is possible (though rare) that this value will be too small.

**See also** [descent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#descent)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QFontMetrics.boundingRect.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) QFontMetrics::boundingRect([QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html) *ch*) const

Returns the rectangle that is covered by ink if character *ch* were to be drawn at the
origin of the coordinate system.

Note that the bounding rectangle may extend to the left of (0, 0\) (e.g., for italicized
fonts), and that the text output may cover *all* pixels in the bounding rectangle. For a
space character the rectangle will usually be empty.

Note that the rectangle usually extends both above and below the base line.

**Warning:** The width of the returned rectangle is not the advance width of the
character. Use boundingRect(const
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&) or
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)()
instead.

**See also**
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)().

### [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) QFontMetrics::boundingRect(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*) const

Returns the bounding rectangle of the characters in the string specified by *text*. The
bounding rectangle always covers at least the set of pixels the text would cover if
drawn at (0, 0).

Note that the bounding rectangle may extend to the left of (0, 0), e.g. for italicized
fonts, and that the width of the returned rectangle might be different than what the
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)()
method returns.

If you want to know the advance width of the string (to lay out a set of strings next to
each other), use
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)()
instead.

Newline characters are processed as normal characters, *not* as linebreaks.

The height of the bounding rectangle is at least as large as the value returned by
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#height)().

**See also**
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#height)(),
[QPainter::boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#boundingRect)(),
and
[tightBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#tightBoundingRect)().

### [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) QFontMetrics::boundingRect(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rect*, int *flags*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, int *tabStops* \= 0, int \**tabArray* \= nullptr) const

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the bounding rectangle of the characters in the string specified by *text*,
which is the set of pixels the text would cover if drawn at (0, 0). The drawing, and
hence the bounding rectangle, is constrained to the rectangle *rect*.

The *flags* argument is the bitwise OR of the following flags:

- [Qt::AlignLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the left border, except for Arabic and Hebrew where it aligns to the right.
- [Qt::AlignRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the right border, except for Arabic and Hebrew where it aligns to the left.
- [Qt::AlignJustify](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) produces justified text.
- [Qt::AlignHCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns horizontally centered.
- [Qt::AlignTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the top border.
- [Qt::AlignBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the bottom border.
- [Qt::AlignVCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns vertically centered
- [Qt::AlignCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) (\=\= `Qt::AlignHCenter | Qt::AlignVCenter`)
- [Qt::TextSingleLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) ignores newline characters in the text.
- [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) expands tabs (see below)
- [Qt::TextShowMnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) interprets "\&x" as x; i.e., underlined.
- [Qt::TextWordWrap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) breaks the text to fit the rectangle.

[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) alignment
defaults to
[Qt::AlignLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) and
vertical alignment defaults to
[Qt::AlignTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum).

If several of the horizontal or several of the vertical alignment flags are set, the
resulting alignment is undefined.

If [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) is set
in *flags*, then: if *tabArray* is non-null, it specifies a 0-terminated sequence of
pixel-positions for tabs; otherwise if *tabStops* is non-zero, it is used as the tab
spacing (in pixels).

Note that the bounding rectangle may extend to the left of (0, 0), e.g. for italicized
fonts, and that the text output may cover *all* pixels in the bounding rectangle.

Newline characters are processed as linebreaks.

Despite the different actual character heights, the heights of the bounding rectangles
of "Yes" and "yes" are the same.

The bounding rectangle returned by this function is somewhat larger than that calculated
by the simpler boundingRect() function. This function uses the [maximum
left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#minLeftBearing) and
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#minRightBearing) font
bearings as is necessary for multi-line text to align correctly. Also, fontHeight() and
[lineSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#lineSpacing)() are
used to calculate the height, rather than individual character heights.

**See also**
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
[QPainter::boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#boundingRect)(),
and [Qt::Alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum).

### [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) QFontMetrics::boundingRect(int *x*, int *y*, int *width*, int *height*, int *flags*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, int *tabStops* \= 0, int \**tabArray* \= nullptr) const

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the bounding rectangle for the given *text* within the rectangle specified by
the *x* and *y* coordinates, *width*, and *height*.

If [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) is set
in *flags* and *tabArray* is non-null, it specifies a 0-terminated sequence of
pixel-positions for tabs; otherwise, if *tabStops* is non-zero, it is used as the tab
spacing (in pixels).

Qt 5 reference:

### int QFontMetrics::descent() const

Returns the descent of the font.

The descent is the distance from the base line to the lowest point characters extend to.
In practice, some font designers break this rule, e.g. to accommodate a certain
character, so it is possible (though rare) that this value will be too small.

**See also** [ascent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#ascent)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QFontMetrics.elidedText.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QFontMetrics::elidedText(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, [Qt::TextElideMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextElideMode-enum) *mode*, int *width*, int *flags* \= 0\) const

If the string *text* is wider than *width*, returns an elided version of the string
(i.e., a string with "..." in it). Otherwise, returns the original string.

The *mode* parameter specifies whether the text is elided on the left (e.g., "...tech"),
in the middle (e.g., "Tr...ch"), or on the right (e.g., "Trol...").

The *width* is specified in pixels, not characters.

The *flags* argument is optional and currently only supports
[Qt::TextShowMnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) as
value.

The elide mark follows the
[layoutdirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#LayoutDirection-enum). For
example, it will be on the right side of the text for right-to-left layouts if the
*mode* is `Qt::ElideLeft`, and on the left side of the text if the *mode* is
`Qt::ElideRight`.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.
signatures: elidedText(self, text: str, mode: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.TextElideMode, width: int, flags: int=...) -> str

### [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html) QFontMetrics::size(int *flags*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, int *tabStops* \= 0, int \**tabArray* \= nullptr) const

Returns the size in pixels of *text*.

The *flags* argument is the bitwise OR of the following flags:

- [Qt::TextSingleLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) ignores newline characters.
- [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) expands tabs (see below)
- [Qt::TextShowMnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) interprets "\&x" as x; i.e., underlined.
- [Qt::TextWordWrap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) breaks the text to fit the rectangle.

If [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) is set
in *flags*, then: if *tabArray* is non-null, it specifies a 0-terminated sequence of
pixel-positions for tabs; otherwise if *tabStops* is non-zero, it is used as the tab
spacing (in pixels).

Newline characters are processed as linebreaks.

Despite the different actual character heights, the heights of the bounding rectangles
of "Yes" and "yes" are the same.

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetrics.html#boundingRect)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QFontMetricsF.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QFontMetricsF functions calculate the size of characters and strings for a given font.
You can construct a QFontMetricsF object with an existing
[QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) to obtain metrics for that font.
If the font is changed later, the font metrics object is *not* updated.

Once created, the object provides functions to access the individual metrics of the
font, its characters, and for strings rendered in the font.

There are several functions that operate on the font:
[ascent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#ascent)(),
[descent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#descent)(),
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#height)(),
[leading](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#leading)() and
[lineSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#lineSpacing)()
return the basic size properties of the font. The
[underlinePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#underlinePos)(),
[overlinePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#overlinePos)(),
[strikeOutPos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#strikeOutPos)() and
[lineWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#lineWidth)()
functions, return the properties of the line that underlines, overlines or strikes out
the characters. These functions are all fast.

There are also some functions that operate on the set of glyphs in the font:
[minLeftBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#minLeftBearing)(),
[minRightBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#minRightBearing)()
and [maxWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#maxWidth)(). These
are by necessity slow, and we recommend avoiding them if possible.

For each character, you can get its
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
[leftBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#leftBearing)(), and
[rightBearing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#rightBearing)(),
and find out whether it is in the font using
[inFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#inFont)(). You can also
treat the character as a string, and use the string functions on it.

The string functions include
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
to return the width of a string in pixels (or points, for a printer),
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#boundingRect)(), to
return a rectangle large enough to contain the rendered string, and
[size](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#size)(), to return the size
of that rectangle.

Example:

```
QFont font("times", 24);
QFontMetricsF fm(font);
qreal pixelsWide = fm.horizontalAdvance("What's the width of this text?");
qreal pixelsHigh = fm.height();
```

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QFontMetricsF::ascent() const

Returns the ascent of the font.

The ascent of a font is the distance from the baseline to the highest position
characters extend to. In practice, some font designers break this rule, e.g. when they
put more than one accent on top of a character, or to accommodate a certain character,
so it is possible (though rare) that this value will be too small.

**See also** [descent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#descent)().

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QFontMetricsF::boundingRect(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*) const

Returns the bounding rectangle of the characters in the string specified by *text*. The
bounding rectangle always covers at least the set of pixels the text would cover if
drawn at (0, 0).

Note that the bounding rectangle may extend to the left of (0, 0), e.g. for italicized
fonts, and that the width of the returned rectangle might be different than what the
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)()
method returns.

If you want to know the advance width of the string (to lay out a set of strings next to
each other), use
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)()
instead.

Newline characters are processed as normal characters, *not* as linebreaks.

The height of the bounding rectangle is at least as large as the value returned
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#height)().

**See also**
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#height)(), and
[QPainter::boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#boundingRect)().

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QFontMetricsF::boundingRect([QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html) *ch*) const

Returns the bounding rectangle of the character *ch* relative to the left-most point on
the base line.

Note that the bounding rectangle may extend to the left of (0, 0), e.g. for italicized
fonts, and that the text output may cover *all* pixels in the bounding rectangle.

Note that the rectangle usually extends both above and below the base line.

**See also**
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)().

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QFontMetricsF::boundingRect(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rect*, int *flags*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, int *tabStops* \= 0, int \**tabArray* \= nullptr) const

This is an overloaded function.

Returns the bounding rectangle of the characters in the given *text*. This is the set of
pixels the text would cover if drawn when constrained to the bounding rectangle
specified by *rect*. If *rect* is a reference to a `nullptr` object, e.g. when passing a
default constructed [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html), the
bounding rectangle will not constrain itself to the size.

The *flags* argument is the bitwise OR of the following flags:

- [Qt::AlignLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the left border, except for Arabic and Hebrew where it aligns to the right.
- [Qt::AlignRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the right border, except for Arabic and Hebrew where it aligns to the left.
- [Qt::AlignJustify](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) produces justified text.
- [Qt::AlignHCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns horizontally centered.
- [Qt::AlignTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the top border.
- [Qt::AlignBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns to the bottom border.
- [Qt::AlignVCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) aligns vertically centered
- [Qt::AlignCenter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) (\=\= `Qt::AlignHCenter | Qt::AlignVCenter`)
- [Qt::TextSingleLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) ignores newline characters in the text.
- [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) expands tabs (see below)
- [Qt::TextShowMnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) interprets "\&x" as x; i.e., underlined.
- [Qt::TextWordWrap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) breaks the text to fit the rectangle.

[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) alignment
defaults to
[Qt::AlignLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) and
vertical alignment defaults to
[Qt::AlignTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum).

If several of the horizontal or several of the vertical alignment flags are set, the
resulting alignment is undefined.

These flags are defined in
[Qt::AlignmentFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum).

If [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) is set
in *flags*, the following behavior is used to interpret tab characters in the text:

- If *tabArray* is non-null, it specifies a 0-terminated sequence of pixel-positions for tabs in the text.
- If *tabStops* is non-zero, it is used as the tab spacing (in pixels).

Note that the bounding rectangle may extend to the left of (0, 0), e.g. for italicized
fonts.

Newline characters are processed as line breaks.

Despite the different actual character heights, the heights of the bounding rectangles
of "Yes" and "yes" are the same.

The bounding rectangle returned by this function is somewhat larger than that calculated
by the simpler boundingRect() function. This function uses the [maximum
left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#minLeftBearing) and
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#minRightBearing) font
bearings as is necessary for multi-line text to align correctly. Also, fontHeight() and
[lineSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#lineSpacing)() are
used to calculate the height, rather than individual character heights.

**See also**
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
[QPainter::boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#boundingRect)(),
and [Qt::Alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum).
signatures: boundingRect(self, r: PySide2.QtCore.QRectF, flags: int, string: str, tabstops: int=..., tabarray: typing.Optional[typing.Sequence[int]]=...) -> PySide2.QtCore.QRectF

Returns the descent of the font.

The descent is the distance from the base line to the lowest point characters extend to.
(Note that this is different from X, which adds 1 pixel.) In practice, some font
designers break this rule, e.g. to accommodate a certain character, so it is possible

Qt 5 reference:

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QFontMetricsF::elidedText(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, [Qt::TextElideMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextElideMode-enum) *mode*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *width*, int *flags* \= 0\) const

If the string *text* is wider than *width*, returns an elided version of the string
(i.e., a string with "..." in it). Otherwise, returns the original string.

The *mode* parameter specifies whether the text is elided on the left (for example,
"...tech"), in the middle (for example, "Tr...ch"), or on the right (for example,
"Trol...").

The *width* is specified in pixels, not characters.

The *flags* argument is optional and currently only supports
[Qt::TextShowMnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) as
value.

The elide mark follows the
[layoutdirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#LayoutDirection-enum). For
example, it will be on the right side of the text for right-to-left layouts if the
*mode* is `Qt::ElideLeft`, and on the left side of the text if the *mode* is
`Qt::ElideRight`.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

Qt 5 reference:

### [QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizef.html) QFontMetricsF::size(int *flags*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, int *tabStops* \= 0, int \**tabArray* \= nullptr) const

Returns the size in pixels of the characters in the given *text*.

The *flags* argument is the bitwise OR of the following flags:

- [Qt::TextSingleLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) ignores newline characters.
- [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) expands tabs (see below)
- [Qt::TextShowMnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) interprets "\&x" as x; i.e., underlined.
- [Qt::TextWordWrap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) breaks the text to fit the rectangle.

These flags are defined in the
[Qt::TextFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) enum.

If [Qt::TextExpandTabs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum) is set
in *flags*, the following behavior is used to interpret tab characters in the text:

- If *tabArray* is non-null, it specifies a 0-terminated sequence of pixel-positions for tabs in the text.
- If *tabStops* is non-zero, it is used as the tab spacing (in pixels).

Newline characters are processed as line breaks.

Note: Despite the different actual character heights, the heights of the bounding
rectangles of "Yes" and "yes" are the same.

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#boundingRect)().
signatures: size(self, flags: int, str: str, tabstops: int=..., tabarray: typing.Optional[typing.Sequence[int]]=...) -> PySide2.QtCore.QSizeF

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QFontMetricsF::tightBoundingRect(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*) const

Returns a tight bounding rectangle around the characters in the string specified by
*text*. The bounding rectangle always covers at least the set of pixels the text would
cover if drawn at (0, 0).

Note that the bounding rectangle may extend to the left of (0, 0), e.g. for italicized
fonts, and that the width of the returned rectangle might be different than what the
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)()
method returns.

If you want to know the advance width of the string (to lay out a set of strings next to
each other), use
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)()
instead.

Newline characters are processed as normal characters, *not* as linebreaks.

**Warning:** Calling this method is very slow on Windows.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also**
[horizontalAdvance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#horizontalAdvance)(),
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#height)(), and
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#boundingRect)().

### fieldGrowthPolicy : [FieldGrowthPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qformlayout.html#FieldGrowthPolicy-enum)

This property holds the way in which the form's fields grow

The default value depends on the widget or application style. For QMacStyle, the default
is
[FieldsStayAtSizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qformlayout.html#FieldGrowthPolicy-enum);
for [QCommonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcommonstyle.html) derived styles
(like Plastique and Windows), the default is
[ExpandingFieldsGrow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qformlayout.html#FieldGrowthPolicy-enum);
for Qt Extended styles, the default is
[AllNonFixedFieldsGrow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qformlayout.html#FieldGrowthPolicy-enum).

If none of the fields can grow and the form is resized, extra space is distributed
according to the current [form
alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qformlayout.html#formAlignment-prop).

PythonQt.QtGui.QFrame.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

[QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) uses this to "raise" the menu
above the surrounding screen.
[QProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html) has a "sunken"
look. [QLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html) has a flat look. The
frames of widgets like these can be changed.

```
QLabel label(...);
label.setFrameStyle(QFrame::Panel | QFrame::Raised);
label.setLineWidth(2);

QProgressBar pbar(...);
label.setFrameStyle(QFrame::NoFrame);
```

The QFrame class can also be used directly for creating simple placeholder frames
without any contents.

The frame style is specified by a [frame
shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum) and a [shadow
style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shadow-enum) that is used to
visually separate the frame from surrounding widgets. These properties can be set
together using the
[setFrameStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#setFrameStyle)() function
and read with [frameStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#frameStyle)().

The frame shapes are
[NoFrame](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum),
[Box](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum),
[Panel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum),
[StyledPanel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum),
[HLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum) and
[VLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum); the shadow styles
are [Plain](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shadow-enum),
[Raised](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shadow-enum) and
[Sunken](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shadow-enum).

A frame widget has three attributes that describe the thickness of the border:
[lineWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#lineWidth-prop),
[midLineWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#midLineWidth-prop), and
[frameWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#frameWidth-prop).

- The line width is the width of the frame border. It can be modified to customize the frame's appearance.
- The mid-line width specifies the width of an extra line in the middle of the frame, which uses a third color to obtain a special 3D effect. Notice that a mid-line is only drawn for [Box](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum), [HLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum) and [VLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum) frames that are raised or sunken.
- The frame width is determined by the frame style, and the [frameWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#frameWidth-prop)() function is used to obtain the value defined for the style used.

The margin between the frame and the contents of the frame can be customized with the
[QWidget::setContentsMargins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setContentsMargins)()
function.

This table shows some of the combinations of styles and line widths:

![Table of frame styles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/frames.png)

### void QFrame::setFrameStyle(int *style*)

Sets the frame style to *style*.

The *style* is the bitwise OR between a frame shape and a frame shadow style. See the
picture of the frames in the main class documentation.

The frame shapes are given in
[QFrame::Shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum) and the

[QFrame::Shadow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shadow-enum).

If a mid-line width greater than 0 is specified, an additional line is drawn for
[Raised](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shadow-enum) or
[Sunken](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shadow-enum)
[Box](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum),
[HLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum), and
[VLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#Shape-enum) frames. The mid-color
of the current color group is used for drawing middle lines.

**See also** [frameStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#frameStyle)().

## Detailed Description

Gesture objects are not constructed directly by developers. They are created by the
[QGestureRecognizer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html) object
that is registered with the application; see
[QGestureRecognizer::registerRecognizer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#registerRecognizer)().

For an overview of gesture handling in Qt and information on using gestures in your
applications, see the [Gestures in Widgets and Graphics
View](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/gestures-overview.html) document.

### Gesture Properties

The class has a list of properties that can be queried by the user to get some
gesture-specific arguments. For example, the pinch gesture has a scale factor that is
exposed as a property.

Developers of custom gesture recognizers can add additional properties in order to
provide additional information about a gesture. This can be done by adding new dynamic
properties to a QGesture object, or by subclassing the QGesture class (or one of its
subclasses).

### Lifecycle of a Gesture Object

A QGesture instance is implicitly created when needed and is owned by Qt. Developers
should never destroy them or store them for later use as Qt may destroy particular
instances of them and create new ones to replace them.

The registered gesture recognizer monitors the input events for the target object via
its [recognize()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)
function, updating the properties of the gesture object as required.

The gesture object may be delivered to the target object in a
[QGestureEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html) if the
corresponding gesture is active or has just been canceled. Each event that is delivered
contains a list of gesture objects, since support for more than one gesture may be
enabled for the target object. Due to the way events are handled in Qt, gesture events
may be filtered by other objects.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGestureEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The QGestureEvent class contains a list of gestures, which can be obtained using the
[gestures](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#gestures)() function.

The gestures are either active or canceled. A list of those that are currently being
executed can be obtained using the
[activeGestures](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#activeGestures)()
function. A list of those which were previously active and have been canceled can be
accessed using the
[canceledGestures](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#canceledGestures)()
function. A gesture might be canceled if the current window loses focus, for example, or
because of a timeout, or for other reasons.

If the event handler does not accept the event by calling the generic
[QEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)() function, all
individual [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object that were
not accepted and in the
[Qt::GestureStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GestureState-enum) state
will be propagated up the parent widget chain until a widget accepts them individually,
by calling
[QGestureEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#accept)()
for each of them, or an event filter consumes the event.

### Further Reading

For an overview of gesture handling in Qt and information on using gestures in your
applications, see the [Gestures in Widgets and Graphics
View](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/gestures-overview.html) document.

### void QGestureEvent::accept([QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) \**gesture*)

Sets the accept flag of the given *gesture* object, the equivalent of calling
[setAccepted(gesture,
true)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#setAccepted).

Setting the accept flag indicates that the event receiver wants the gesture. Unwanted
gestures may be propagated to the parent widget.

**See also**
[QGestureEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#ignore)().

### void QGestureEvent::accept([Qt::GestureType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GestureType-enum) *gestureType*)

Sets the accept flag of the given *gestureType*, the equivalent of calling
[setAccepted(gestureType,
true)](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#setAccepted).

Setting the accept flag indicates that the event receiver wants the gesture. Unwanted
gestures may be propagated to the parent widget.

**See also**
[QGestureEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#ignore)().

Qt 5 reference:

### void QGestureEvent::setAccepted([QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) \**gesture*, bool *value*)

Sets the accept flag of the given *gesture* object to the specified *value*.

Setting the accept flag indicates that the event receiver wants the *gesture*. Unwanted
gestures may be propagated to the parent widget.

By default, gestures in events of type
[QEvent::Gesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) are
accepted, and gestures in
[QEvent::GestureOverride](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
events are ignored.

For convenience, the accept flag can also be set with
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#accept)(gesture), and
cleared with
[ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#ignore)(gesture).

**See also**
[isAccepted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#isAccepted)().

### void QGestureEvent::setAccepted([Qt::GestureType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GestureType-enum) *gestureType*, bool *value*)

Sets the accept flag of the given *gestureType* object to the specified *value*.

Setting the accept flag indicates that the event receiver wants to receive gestures of
the specified type, *gestureType*. Unwanted gestures may be propagated to the parent
widget.

By default, gestures in events of type
[QEvent::Gesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) are
accepted, and gestures in
[QEvent::GestureOverride](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
events are ignored.

For convenience, the accept flag can also be set with
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#accept)(gestureType), and
cleared with
[ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgestureevent.html#ignore)(gestureType).
signatures: setAccepted(self, arg__1: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.GestureType, arg__2: bool) -> None
setAccepted(self, arg__1: PySide2.QtWidgets.QGesture, arg__2: bool) -> None

PythonQt.QtGui.QGestureRecognizer.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Gesture recognizers are responsible for creating and managing
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) objects and monitoring
input events sent to [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html) subclasses.
QGestureRecognizer is the base class for implementing custom gestures.

Developers that only need to provide gesture recognition for standard gestures do not
need to use this class directly. Instances will be created behind the scenes by the
framework.

For an overview of gesture handling in Qt and information on using gestures in your
applications, see the [Gestures in Widgets and Graphics
View](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/gestures-overview.html) document.

### Recognizing Gestures

The process of recognizing gestures involves filtering input events sent to specific
objects, and modifying the associated
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) objects to include relevant
information about the user's input.

Gestures are created when the framework calls
[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#create)() to handle
user input for a particular instance of a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) or
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html) subclass. A
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object is created for each
widget or item that is configured to use gestures.

Once a [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) has been created for
a target object, the gesture recognizer will receive events for it in its
[recognize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)()
handler function.

When a gesture is canceled, the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#reset)() function is
called, giving the recognizer the chance to update the appropriate properties in the
corresponding [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object.

### Supporting New Gestures

To add support for new gestures, you need to derive from QGestureRecognizer to create a
custom recognizer class, construct an instance of this class, and register it with the
application by calling
[QGestureRecognizer::registerRecognizer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#registerRecognizer)().
You can also subclass [QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) to
create a custom gesture class, or rely on dynamic properties to express specific details
of the gesture you want to handle.

Your custom QGestureRecognizer subclass needs to reimplement the
[recognize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)()
function to handle and filter the incoming input events for
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html) subclasses.
Although the logic for gesture recognition is implemented in this function, you can
store persistent information about the state of the recognition process in the
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) object supplied. The
[recognize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#recognize)()
function must return a value of
[QGestureRecognizer::Result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#ResultFlag-enum)
that indicates the state of recognition for a given gesture and target object. This
determines whether or not a gesture event will be delivered to a target object.

If you choose to represent a gesture by a custom
[QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) subclass, you will need to
reimplement the
[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#create)() function
to construct instances of your gesture class. Similarly, you may need to reimplement the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#reset)() function if
your custom gesture objects need to be specially handled when a gesture is canceled.

### `[pure virtual]` [QGestureRecognizer::Result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#ResultFlag-enum) QGestureRecognizer::recognize([QGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesture.html) \**gesture*, [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) \**watched*, [QEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html) \**event*)

Handles the given *event* for the *watched* object, updating the state of the *gesture*
object as required, and returns a suitable result for the current recognition step.

This function is called by the framework to allow the recognizer to filter input events
dispatched to [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) or
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html) instances
that it is monitoring.

The result reflects how much of the gesture has been recognized. The state of the
*gesture* object is set depending on the result.

**See also**
[QGestureRecognizer::Result](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgesturerecognizer.html#ResultFlag-enum).

[Qt::CustomGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GestureType-enum) flag

PythonQt.QtGui.QGlyphRun.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

When Qt displays a string of text encoded in Unicode, it will first convert the Unicode
points into a list of glyph indexes and a list of positions based on one or more fonts.
The Unicode representation of the text and the
[QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) object will in this case serve as
a convenient abstraction that hides the details of what actually takes place when
displaying the text on-screen. For instance, by the time the text actually reaches the
screen, it may be represented by a set of fonts in addition to the one specified by the
user, e.g. in case the originally selected font did not support all the writing systems
contained in the text.

Under certain circumstances, it can be useful as an application developer to have more
low-level control over which glyphs in a specific font are drawn to the screen. This
could for instance be the case in applications that use an external font engine and text
shaper together with Qt. QGlyphRun provides an interface to the raw data needed to get
text on the screen. It contains a list of glyph indexes, a position for each glyph and a
font.

It is the user's responsibility to ensure that the selected font actually contains the
provided glyph indexes.

[QTextLayout::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#glyphRuns)()
or
[QTextFragment::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextfragment.html#glyphRuns)()
can be used to convert unicode encoded text into a list of QGlyphRun objects, and
[QPainter::drawGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawGlyphRun)()
can be used to draw the glyphs.

**Note:** Please note that [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html)
is considered local to the thread in which it is constructed. This in turn means that a
new [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) will have to be created
and set on the QGlyphRun if it is moved to a different thread. If the QGlyphRun contains
a reference to a [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) from a
different thread than the current, it will not be possible to draw the glyphs using a
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html), as the
[QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) is considered invalid and
inaccessible in this case.

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QGlyphRun::boundingRect() const

Returns the smallest rectangle that contains all glyphs in this
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html). If a bounding rect has
been set using
[setBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#setBoundingRect)(),
then this will be returned. Otherwise the bounding rect will be calculated based on the
font metrics of the glyphs in the glyph run.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also**
[setBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#setBoundingRect)().

[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html) to be *boundingRect*.
This rectangle will be returned by
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#boundingRect)() unless
it is empty, in which case the bounding rectangle of the glyphs in the glyph run will be
returned instead.

**Note:** Unless you are implementing text shaping, you should not have to use this
function. It is used specifically when the
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html) should represent an area
which is smaller than the area of the glyphs it contains. This could happen e.g. if the
glyph run is retrieved by calling
[QTextLayout::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#glyphRuns)()
and the specified range only includes part of a ligature (where two or more characters
are combined to a single glyph.) When this is the case, the bounding rect should only
include the appropriate part of the ligature glyph, based on a calculation of the
average width of the characters in the ligature.

In order to support such a case (an example is selections which should be drawn with a
different color than the main text color), it is necessary to clip the painting
mechanism to the rectangle returned from
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#boundingRect)() to
avoid drawing the entire ligature glyph.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.0.

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html#boundingRect)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt currently supports three types of gradient fills:

- *Linear* gradients interpolate colors between start and end points.
- *Simple* radial gradients interpolate colors between a focal point and end points on a circle surrounding it.
- *Extended* radial gradients interpolate colors between a center and a focal circle.
- *Conical* gradients interpolate colors around a center point.

A gradient's type can be retrieved using the
[type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#type)() function. Each of the
types is represented by a subclass of QGradient:

| [QLinearGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineargradient.html) | [QRadialGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html) | [QConicalGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qconicalgradient.html) |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |

The colors in a gradient are defined using stop points of the
[QGradientStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#QGradientStop-typedef)
type; i.e., a position and a color. Use the
[setColorAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setColorAt)() function to
define a single stop point. Alternatively, use the
[setStops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setStops)() function to
define several stop points in one go. Note that the latter function *replaces* the
current set of stop points.

It is the gradient's complete set of stop points (accessible through the
[stops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#stops)() function) that
describes how the gradient area should be filled. If no stop points have been specified,
a gradient of black at 0 to white at 1 is used.

A diagonal linear gradient from black at (100, 100\) to white at (200, 200\) could be
specified like this:

```
    QLinearGradient linearGrad(QPointF(100, 100), QPointF(200, 200));
    linearGrad.setColorAt(0, Qt::black);
    linearGrad.setColorAt(1, Qt::white);
```

A gradient can have an arbitrary number of stop points. The following would create a
radial gradient starting with red in the center, blue and then green on the edges:

```
    QRadialGradient radialGrad(QPointF(100, 100), 100);
    radialGrad.setColorAt(0, Qt::red);
    radialGrad.setColorAt(0.5, Qt::blue);
    radialGrad.setColorAt(1, Qt::green);
```

It is possible to repeat or reflect the gradient outside its area by specifiying the
[spread method](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) using the
[setSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setSpread)() function. The
default is to pad the outside area with the color at the closest stop point. The
currently set [spread
method](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) can be retrieved
using the [spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#spread)() function.
The [QGradient::Spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum)
enum defines three different methods:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [PadSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) | [RepeatSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) | [ReflectSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) |

Note that the [setSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setSpread)()
function only has effect for linear and radial gradients. The reason is that the conical
gradient is closed by definition, i.e. the *conical* gradient fills the entire circle
from 0 \- 360 degrees, while the boundary of a radial or a linear gradient can be
specified through its radius or final stop points, respectively.

The gradient coordinates can be specified in logical coordinates, relative to device
coordinates, or relative to object bounding box coordinates. The [coordinate
mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#CoordinateMode-enum) can be set
using the
[setCoordinateMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setCoordinateMode)()
function. The default is
[LogicalMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#CoordinateMode-enum),
where the gradient coordinates are specified in the same way as the object coordinates.
To retrieve the currently set [coordinate
mode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#CoordinateMode-enum) use
[coordinateMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#coordinateMode)().

## Detailed Description

The graphics anchor provides an API that enables you to query and manipulate the
properties an anchor has. When an anchor is added to the layout with
[QGraphicsAnchorLayout::addAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchor)(),
a QGraphicsAnchor instance is returned where the properties are initialized to their
default values. The properties can then be further changed, and they will be picked up
the next time the layout is activated.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsAnchor.sizePolic.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### sizePolicy : [QSizePolicy::Policy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum)

This property holds the size policy for the
[QGraphicsAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html).

By setting the size policy on an anchor you can configure how the anchor can resize
itself from its preferred spacing. For instance, if the anchor has the size policy
[QSizePolicy::Minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum),
the spacing is the minimum size of the anchor. However, its size can grow up to the
anchors maximum size. If the default size policy is
[QSizePolicy::Fixed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum),
the anchor can neither grow or shrink, which means that the only size the anchor can
have is the spacing.
[QSizePolicy::Fixed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#Policy-enum) is
the default size policy.
[QGraphicsAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html) always has a
minimum spacing of 0 and a very large maximum spacing.

**Access functions:**

| QSizePolicy::Policy | **sizePolicy**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setSizePolicy**(QSizePolicy::Policy *policy*) |

**See also**
[QGraphicsAnchor::spacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html#spacing-prop).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsAnchorLayout.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The anchor layout allows developers to specify how widgets should be placed relative to
each other, and to the layout itself. The specification is made by adding anchors to the
layout by calling
[addAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchor)(),
[addAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchors)()
or
[addCornerAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addCornerAnchors)().

Existing anchors in the layout can be accessed with the
[anchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#anchor)()
function. Items that are anchored are automatically added to the layout, and if items
are removed, all their anchors will be automatically removed.

![Using an anchor layout to align simple colored
widgets.](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/simpleanchorlayout-example.png)

Anchors are always set up between edges of an item, where the "center" is also
considered to be an edge. Consider the following example:

```
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorLeft, a, Qt::AnchorRight);
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorTop, a, Qt::AnchorBottom);
```

Here, the right edge of item `a` is anchored to the left edge of item `b` and the bottom
edge of item `a` is anchored to the top edge of item `b`, with the result that item `b`
will be placed diagonally to the right and below item `b`.

The
[addCornerAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addCornerAnchors)()
function provides a simpler way of anchoring the corners of two widgets than the two
individual calls to
[addAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchor)()
shown in the code above. Here, we see how a widget can be anchored to the top-left
corner of the enclosing layout:

```
layout->addCornerAnchors(a, Qt::TopLeftCorner, layout, Qt::TopLeftCorner);
```

In cases where anchors are used to match the widths or heights of widgets, it is
convenient to use the
[addAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchors)()
function. As with the other functions for specifying anchors, it can also be used to
anchor a widget to a layout.

### Size Hints and Size Policies in an Anchor Layout

QGraphicsAnchorLayout respects each item's size hints and size policies. Note that there
are some properties of
[QSizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html) that are [not
respected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#known-issues).

### Spacing within an Anchor Layout

The layout may distribute some space between the items. If the spacing has not been
explicitly specified, the actual amount of space will usually be 0\.

However, if the first edge is the *opposite* of the second edge (e.g., the right edge of
the first widget is anchored to the left edge of the second widget), the size of the
anchor will be queried from the style through a pixel metric:
[PM\_LayoutHorizontalSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PixelMetric-enum)
for horizontal anchors and
[PM\_LayoutVerticalSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#PixelMetric-enum)
for vertical anchors.

If the spacing is negative, the items will overlap to some extent.

### Known Issues

There are some features that QGraphicsAnchorLayout currently does not support. This
might change in the future, so avoid using these features if you want to avoid any
future regressions in behaviour:

- Stretch factors are not respected.
- [QSizePolicy::ExpandFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizepolicy.html#PolicyFlag-enum) is not respected.
- Height for width is not respected.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsAnchorLayout.add.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QGraphicsAnchor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html) \*QGraphicsAnchorLayout::addAnchor([QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**firstItem*, [Qt::AnchorPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AnchorPoint-enum) *firstEdge*, [QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#QGraphicsLayoutItem) \**secondItem*, [Qt::AnchorPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AnchorPoint-enum) *secondEdge*)

Creates an anchor between the edge *firstEdge* of item *firstItem* and the edge
*secondEdge* of item *secondItem*. The spacing of the anchor is picked up from the
style. Anchors between a layout edge and an item edge will have a size of 0\. If there
is already an anchor between the edges, the new anchor will replace the old one.

*firstItem* and *secondItem* are automatically added to the layout if they are not part
of the layout. This means that
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#count)() can
increase by up to 2\.

The spacing an anchor will get depends on the type of anchor. For instance, anchors from
the Right edge of one item to the Left edge of another (or vice versa) will use the
default horizontal spacing. The same behaviour applies to Bottom to Top anchors, (but
they will use the default vertical spacing). For all other anchor combinations, the
spacing will be 0\. All anchoring functions will follow this rule.

The spacing can also be set manually by using
[QGraphicsAnchor::setSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchor.html#spacing-prop)()
method.

Calling this function where *firstItem* or *secondItem* are ancestors of the layout have
undefined behaviour.

**See also**
[addAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addAnchors)()
and
[addCornerAnchors](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#addCornerAnchors)().

Anchors two or four edges of *firstItem* with the corresponding edges of *secondItem*,
so that *firstItem* has the same size as *secondItem* in the dimensions specified by
*orientations*.

For example, the following example anchors the left and right edges of two items to
match their widths:

```
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorLeft, c, Qt::AnchorLeft);
layout->addAnchor(b, Qt::AnchorRight, c, Qt::AnchorRight);
```

This can also be achieved using the following line of code:

```
layout->addAnchors(b, c, Qt::Horizontal);
```

Creates two anchors between *firstItem* and *secondItem* specified by the corners,
*firstCorner* and *secondCorner*, where one is for the horizontal edge and another one
for the vertical edge.

This is a convenience function, since anchoring corners can be expressed as anchoring
two edges. For instance:

```
layout->addAnchor(a, Qt::AnchorTop, layout, Qt::AnchorTop);
layout->addAnchor(a, Qt::AnchorLeft, layout, Qt::AnchorLeft);
```

This can also be achieved with the following line of code:

```
layout->addCornerAnchors(a, Qt::TopLeftCorner, layout, Qt::TopLeftCorner);
```

If there is already an anchor between the edge pairs, it will be replaced by the anchors
that this function specifies.

*firstItem* and *secondItem* are automatically added to the layout if they are not part
of the layout. This means that
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsanchorlayout.html#count)() can
increase by up to 2\.

## Detailed Description

A blur effect blurs the source. This effect is useful for reducing details, such as when
the source loses focus and you want to draw attention to other elements. The level of
detail can be modified using the
[setBlurRadius](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#blurRadius-prop)()
function. Use
[setBlurHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#blurHints-prop)()
to choose the blur hints.

By default, the blur radius is 5 pixels. The blur radius is specified in device
coordinates.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicseffect-blur.png)

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsBlurEffect.blurH.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### blurHints : [BlurHints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#BlurHint-enum)

This property holds the blur hint of the effect.

Use the
[PerformanceHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#BlurHint-enum)
hint to say that you want a faster blur, the
[QualityHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#BlurHint-enum)
hint to say that you prefer a higher quality blur, or the
[AnimationHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#BlurHint-enum)
when you want to animate the blur radius.

By default, the blur hint is
[PerformanceHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html#BlurHint-enum).

## Detailed Description

A drop shadow effect renders the source with a drop shadow. The color of the drop shadow
can be modified using the
[setColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html#color-prop)()
function. The drop shadow offset can be modified using the
[setOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html#offset-prop)()
function and the blur radius of the drop shadow can be changed with the
[setBlurRadius](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html#blurRadius-prop)()
function.

By default, the drop shadow is a semi-transparent dark gray
([QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html)(63, 63, 63, 180)) shadow,
blurred with a radius of 1 at an offset of 8 pixels towards the lower right. The drop
shadow offset is specified in device coordinates.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsEffect.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Effects alter the appearance of elements by hooking into the rendering pipeline and
operating between the source (e.g., a
[QGraphicsPixmapItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html)) and
the destination device (e.g.,
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html)'s viewport).
Effects can be disabled by calling
[setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#enabled-prop)(false).
If effects are disabled, the source is rendered directly.

To add a visual effect to a
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html), for example, you
can use one of the standard effects, or alternately, create your own effect by creating
a subclass of QGraphicsEffect. The effect can then be installed on the item using
[QGraphicsItem::setGraphicsEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setGraphicsEffect)().

Qt provides the following standard effects:

- [QGraphicsBlurEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsblureffect.html) \- blurs the item by a given radius
- [QGraphicsDropShadowEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsdropshadoweffect.html) \- renders a dropshadow behind the item
- [QGraphicsColorizeEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicscolorizeeffect.html) \- renders the item in shades of any given color
- [QGraphicsOpacityEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsopacityeffect.html) \- renders the item with an opacity

|  | |
| --- | --- |
|  |  |
|  |  |

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicseffect-widget.png)

For more information on how to use each effect, refer to the specific effect's
documentation.

To create your own custom effect, create a subclass of QGraphicsEffect (or any other
existing effects) and reimplement the virtual function
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)(). This function is
called whenever the effect needs to redraw. The
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)() function takes
the painter with which to draw as an argument. For more information, refer to the
documentation for
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)(). In the
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#draw)() function you can
call
[sourcePixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#sourcePixmap)()
to get a pixmap of the graphics effect source which you can then process.

If your effect changes, use
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#update)() to request
for a redraw. If your custom effect changes the bounding rectangle of the source, e.g.,
a radial glow effect may need to apply an extra margin, you can reimplement the virtual
[boundingRectFor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#boundingRectFor)()
function, and call
[updateBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#updateBoundingRect)()
to notify the framework whenever this rectangle changes. The virtual
[sourceChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html#sourceChanged)()
function is called to notify the effects that the source has changed in some way \-
e.g., if the source is a
[QGraphicsRectItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html) and its
rectangle parameters have changed.

### `[protected]` bool QGraphicsEffect::sourceIsPixmap() const

Returns `true` if the source effectively is a pixmap, e.g., a
[QGraphicsPixmapItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html).

## Detailed Description

QGraphicsEllipseItem respresents an ellipse with a fill and an outline, and you can also
use it for ellipse segments (see
[startAngle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#startAngle)(),
[spanAngle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#spanAngle)()).

|  |  |
| --- | --- |

To set the item's ellipse, pass a
[QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) to QGraphicsEllipseItem's
constructor, or call
[setRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#setRect)(). The
[rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#rect)() function
returns the current ellipse geometry.

QGraphicsEllipseItem uses the rect and the pen width to provide a reasonable
implementation of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#boundingRect)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#shape)(), and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#contains)(). The
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html#paint)() function
draws the ellipse using the item's associated pen and brush, which you can set by
calling
[setPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setPen)()
and
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setBrush)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The most common way to use QGraphicsGridLayout is to construct an object on the heap
with no parent, add widgets and layouts by calling
[addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#addItem)(), and
finally assign the layout to a widget by calling
[QGraphicsWidget::setLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#setLayout)().
QGraphicsGridLayout automatically computes the dimensions of the grid as you add items.

```
QGraphicsScene scene;
QGraphicsWidget *textEdit = scene.addWidget(new QTextEdit);
QGraphicsWidget *pushButton = scene.addWidget(new QPushButton);

QGraphicsGridLayout *layout = new QGraphicsGridLayout;
layout->addItem(textEdit, 0, 0);
layout->addItem(pushButton, 0, 1);

QGraphicsWidget *form = new QGraphicsWidget;
form->setLayout(layout);
scene.addItem(form);
```

The layout takes ownership of the items. In some cases when the layout item also
inherits from [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html)
(such as
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget))
there will be a ambiguity in ownership because the layout item belongs to two ownership
hierarchies. See the documentation of
[QGraphicsLayoutItem::setOwnedByLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setOwnedByLayout)()
how to handle this. You can access each item in the layout by calling
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#count)() and
[itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#itemAt)(). Calling
[removeAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#removeAt)() will
remove an item from the layout, without destroying it.

### Size Hints and Size Policies in QGraphicsGridLayout

QGraphicsGridLayout respects each item's size hints and size policies, and when a cell
in the grid has more space than the items can fill, each item is arranged according to
the layout's alignment for that item. You can set an alignment for each item by calling
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#setAlignment)(),
and check the alignment for any item by calling
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#alignment)().
You can also set the alignment for an entire row or column by calling
[setRowAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#setRowAlignment)()
and
[setColumnAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html#setColumnAlignment)()
respectively. By default, items are aligned to the top left.
