Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It provides a light-weight foundation for writing your own custom items. This includes
defining the item's geometry, collision detection, its painting implementation and item
interaction through its event handlers. QGraphicsItem is part of the [Graphics View
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html)

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-items.png)

For convenience, Qt provides a set of standard graphics items for the most common
shapes. These are:

- [QGraphicsEllipseItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsellipseitem.html) provides an ellipse item
- [QGraphicsLineItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslineitem.html) provides a line item
- [QGraphicsPathItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspathitem.html) provides an arbitrary path item
- [QGraphicsPixmapItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html) provides a pixmap item
- [QGraphicsPolygonItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html) provides a polygon item
- [QGraphicsRectItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html) provides a rectangular item
- [QGraphicsSimpleTextItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicssimpletextitem.html) provides a simple text label item
- [QGraphicsTextItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicstextitem.html) provides an advanced text browser item

All of an item's geometric information is based on its local coordinate system. The
item's position, [pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#pos)(), is
the only function that does not operate in local coordinates, as it returns a position
in parent coordinates. [The Graphics View Coordinate
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#the-graphics-view-coordinate-system)
describes the coordinate system in detail.

You can set whether an item should be visible (i.e., drawn, and accepting events), by
calling
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setVisible)(). Hiding
an item will also hide its children. Similarly, you can enable or disable an item by
calling
[setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setEnabled)(). If you
disable an item, all its children will also be disabled. By default, items are both
visible and enabled. To toggle whether an item is selected or not, first enable
selection by setting the
[ItemIsSelectable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flag, and then call
[setSelected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setSelected)().
Normally, selection is toggled by the scene, as a result of user interaction.

To write your own graphics item, you first create a subclass of QGraphicsItem, and then
start by implementing its two pure virtual public functions:
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)(),
which returns an estimate of the area painted by the item, and
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)(), which implements
the actual painting. For example:

```
class SimpleItem : public QGraphicsItem
{
public:
    QRectF boundingRect() const override
    {
        qreal penWidth = 1;
        return QRectF(-10 - penWidth / 2, -10 - penWidth / 2,
                      20 + penWidth, 20 + penWidth);
    }

    void paint(QPainter *painter, const QStyleOptionGraphicsItem *option,
               QWidget *widget) override
    {
        painter->drawRoundedRect(-10, -10, 20, 20, 5, 5);
    }
};
```

The [boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)()
function has many different purposes.
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) bases its item
index on
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)(),
and [QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) uses it both
for culling invisible items, and for determining the area that needs to be recomposed
when drawing overlapping items. In addition, QGraphicsItem's collision detection
mechanisms use
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() to
provide an efficient cut-off. The fine grained collision algorithm in
[collidesWithItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#collidesWithItem)()
is based on calling
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)(), which returns an
accurate outline of the item's shape as a
[QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html).

[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) expects all
items
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() and
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)() to remain
unchanged unless it is notified. If you want to change an item's geometry in any way,
you must first call
[prepareGeometryChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#prepareGeometryChange)()
to allow [QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) to
update its bookkeeping.

Collision detection can be done in two ways:

1. Reimplement [shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)() to return an accurate shape for your item, and rely on the default implementation of [collidesWithItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#collidesWithItem)() to do shape-shape intersection. This can be rather expensive if the shapes are complex.
2. Reimplement [collidesWithItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#collidesWithItem)() to provide your own custom item and shape collision algorithm.

The [contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)()
function can be called to determine whether the item *contains* a point or not. This
function can also be reimplemented by the item. The default behavior of
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)() is based on
calling [shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)().

Items can contain other items, and also be contained by other items. All items can have
a parent item and a list of children. Unless the item has no parent, its position is in
*parent* coordinates (i.e., the parent's local coordinates). Parent items propagate both
their position and their transformation to all children.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-parentchild.png)

### Transformations

QGraphicsItem supports projective transformations in addition to its base position,
[pos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#pos)(). There are several
ways to change an item's transformation. For simple transformations, you can call either
of the convenience functions
[setRotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setRotation)() or
[setScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setScale)(), or you can
pass any transformation matrix to
[setTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransform)().
For advanced transformation control you also have the option of setting several combined
transformations by calling
[setTransformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransformations)().

Item transformations accumulate from parent to child, so if both a parent and child item
are rotated 90 degrees, the child's total transformation will be 180 degrees. Similarly,
if the item's parent is scaled to 2x its original size, its children will also be twice
as large. An item's transformation does not affect its own local geometry; all geometry
functions (e.g.,
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)(),
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)(), and all the
mapping functions) still operate in local coordinates. For convenience, QGraphicsItem
provides the functions
[sceneTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneTransform)(),
which returns the item's total transformation matrix (including its position and all
parents' positions and transformations), and
[scenePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scenePos)(), which
returns its position in scene coordinates. To reset an item's matrix, call
[resetTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#resetTransform)().

Certain transformation operations produce a different outcome depending on the order in
which they are applied. For example, if you scale an transform, and then rotate it, you
may get a different result than if the transform was rotated first. However, the order
you set the transformation properties on QGraphicsItem does not affect the resulting
transformation; QGraphicsItem always applies the properties in a fixed, defined order:

- The item's base transform is applied ([transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)())
- The item's transformations list is applied in order ([transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations)())
- The item is rotated relative to its transform origin point ([rotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#rotation)(), [transformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformOriginPoint)())
- The item is scaled relative to its transform origin point ([scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scale-1)(), [transformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformOriginPoint)())

### Painting

The [paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() function is
called by [QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) to
paint the item's contents. The item has no background or default fill of its own;
whatever is behind the item will shine through all areas that are not explicitly painted
in this function. You can call
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)() to schedule a
repaint, optionally passing the rectangle that needs a repaint. Depending on whether or
not the item is visible in a view, the item may or may not be repainted; there is no
equivalent to
[QWidget::repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() in
QGraphicsItem.

Items are painted by the view, starting with the parent items and then drawing children,
in ascending stacking order. You can set an item's stacking order by calling
[setZValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setZValue)(), and test
it by calling [zValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#zValue)(),
where items with low z-values are painted before items with high z-values. Stacking
order applies to sibling items; parents are always drawn before their children.

### Sorting

All items are drawn in a defined, stable order, and this same order decides which items
will receive mouse input first when you click on the scene. Normally you don't have to
worry about sorting, as the items follow a "natural order", following the logical
structure of the scene.

An item's children are stacked on top of the parent, and sibling items are stacked by
insertion order (i.e., in the same order that they were either added to the scene, or
added to the same parent). If you add item A, and then B, then B will be on top of A. If
you then add C, the items' stacking order will be A, then B, then C.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-zorder.png)

This example shows the stacking order of all limbs of the robot from the [Drag and Drop
Robot](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-graphicsview-dragdroprobot-example.html)
example. The torso is the root item (all other items are children or descendants of the
torso), so it is drawn first. Next, the head is drawn, as it is the first item in the
torso's list of children. Then the upper left arm is drawn. As the lower arm is a child
of the upper arm, the lower arm is then drawn, followed by the upper arm's next sibling,
which is the upper right arm, and so on.

For advanced users, there are ways to alter how your items are sorted:

- You can call [setZValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setZValue)() on an item to explicitly stack it on top of, or under, other sibling items. The default Z value for an item is 0\. Items with the same Z value are stacked by insertion order.
- You can call [stackBefore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#stackBefore)() to reorder the list of children. This will directly modify the insertion order.
- You can set the [ItemStacksBehindParent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum) flag to stack a child item behind its parent.

The stacking order of two sibling items also counts for each item's children and
descendant items. So if one item is on top of another, then all its children will also
be on top of all the other item's children as well.

### Events

QGraphicsItem receives events from
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) through the
virtual function
[sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)(). This
function distributes the most common events to a set of convenience event handlers:

- [contextMenuEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contextMenuEvent)() handles context menu events
- [focusInEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusInEvent)() and [focusOutEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusOutEvent)() handle focus in and out events
- [hoverEnterEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverEnterEvent)(), [hoverMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverMoveEvent)(), and [hoverLeaveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverLeaveEvent)() handles hover enter, move and leave events
- [inputMethodEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#inputMethodEvent)() handles input events, for accessibility support
- [keyPressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#keyPressEvent)() and [keyReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#keyReleaseEvent)() handle key press and release events
- [mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)(), [mouseMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseMoveEvent)(), [mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(), and [mouseDoubleClickEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseDoubleClickEvent)() handles mouse press, move, release, click and double-click events

You can filter events for any other item by installing event filters. This functionality
is separate from Qt's regular event filters (see
[QObject::installEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#installEventFilter)()),
which only work on subclasses of
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html). After installing your item
as an event filter for another item by calling
[installSceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#installSceneEventFilter)(),
the filtered events will be received by the virtual function
[sceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEventFilter)().
You can remove item event filters by calling
[removeSceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#removeSceneEventFilter)().

### Custom Data

Sometimes it's useful to register custom data with an item, be it a custom item, or a
standard item. You can call
[setData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setData)() on any item
to store data in it using a key-value pair (the key being an integer, and the value is a
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)). To get custom data from
an item, call [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#data)(). This
functionality is completely untouched by Qt itself; it is provided for the user's
convenience.

### `[virtual]` void QGraphicsItem::advance(int *phase*)

This virtual function is called twice for all items by the
[QGraphicsScene::advance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#advance)()
slot. In the first phase, all items are called with *phase* \=\= 0, indicating that
items on the scene are about to advance, and then all items are called with *phase* \=\=
1\. Reimplement this function to update your item if you need simple scene-controlled
animation.

The default implementation does nothing.

This function is intended for animations. An alternative is to multiple-inherit from
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) and
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) and use the
[Animation Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/animation-overview.html).

**See also**
[QGraphicsScene::advance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#advance)()
and [QTimeLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.boundingRec.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual]` [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QGraphicsItem::boundingRect() const

This pure virtual function defines the outer bounds of the item as a rectangle; all
painting must be restricted to inside an item's bounding rect.
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) uses this to
determine whether the item requires redrawing.

Although the item's shape can be arbitrary, the bounding rect is always rectangular, and
it is unaffected by the items' transformation.

If you want to change the item's bounding rectangle, you must first call
[prepareGeometryChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#prepareGeometryChange)().
This notifies the scene of the imminent change, so that it can update its item geometry
index; otherwise, the scene will be unaware of the item's new geometry, and the results
are undefined (typically, rendering artifacts are left within the view).

Reimplement this function to let
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) determine what
parts of the widget, if any, need to be redrawn.

Note: For shapes that paint an outline / stroke, it is important to include half the pen
width in the bounding rect. It is not necessary to compensate for antialiasing, though.

Example:

```
QRectF CircleItem::boundingRect() const
{
    qreal penWidth = 1;
    return QRectF(-radius - penWidth / 2, -radius - penWidth / 2,
                  diameter + penWidth, diameter + penWidth);
}
```

**See also**
[boundingRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRegion)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)(),
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)(), [The
Graphics View Coordinate
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#the-graphics-view-coordinate-system),
and
[prepareGeometryChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#prepareGeometryChange)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.boundingReg.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) QGraphicsItem::boundingRegion(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*itemToDeviceTransform*) const

Returns the bounding region for this item. The coordinate space of the returned region
depends on *itemToDeviceTransform*. If you pass an identity
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) as a parameter, this
function will return a local coordinate region.

The bounding region describes a coarse outline of the item's visual contents. Although
it's expensive to calculate, it's also more precise than
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)(),
and it can help to avoid unnecessary repainting when an item is updated. This is
particularly efficient for thin items (e.g., lines or simple polygons). You can tune the
granularity for the bounding region by calling
[setBoundingRegionGranularity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setBoundingRegionGranularity)().
The default granularity is 0; in which the item's bounding region is the same as its
bounding rect.

*itemToDeviceTransform* is the transformation from item coordinates to device
coordinates. If you want this function to return a
[QRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html) in scene coordinates, you can
pass
[sceneTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneTransform)()
as an argument.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[boundingRegionGranularity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRegionGranularity)().

Qt 5 reference:

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QGraphicsItem::boundingRegionGranularity() const

Returns the item's bounding region granularity; a value between and including 0 and 1\.
The default value is 0 (i.e., the lowest granularity, where the bounding region
corresponds to the item's bounding rectangle).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[setBoundingRegionGranularity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setBoundingRegionGranularity)().

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QGraphicsItem::childrenBoundingRect() const

Returns the bounding rect of this item's descendants (i.e., its children, their
children, etc.) in local coordinates. The rectangle will contain all descendants after
they have been mapped to local coordinates. If the item has no children, this function
returns an empty [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html).

This does not include this item's own bounding rect; it only returns its descendants'
accumulated bounding rect. If you need to include this item's bounding rect, you can add
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() to
childrenBoundingRect() using QRectF::operator\|().

This function is linear in complexity; it determines the size of the returned bounding
rect by iterating through all descendants.

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() and
[sceneBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneBoundingRect)().

Qt 5 reference:

### [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) QGraphicsItem::clipPath() const

Returns this item's clip path, or an empty
[QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) if this item is not
clipped. The clip path constrains the item's appearance and interaction (i.e., restricts
the area the item can draw within and receive events for).

You can enable clipping by setting the
[ItemClipsToShape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
or
[ItemClipsChildrenToShape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flags. The item's clip path is calculated by intersecting all clipping ancestors'
shapes. If the item sets
[ItemClipsToShape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum),
the final clip is intersected with the item's own shape.

**Note:** Clipping introduces a performance penalty for all items involved; you should
generally avoid using clipping if you can (e.g., if your items always draw inside
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() or
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)() boundaries,
clipping is not necessary).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also**
[isClipped](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isClipped)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)(), and
[setFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setFlags)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.collidesWit.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QGraphicsItem::collidesWithItem(const [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#QGraphicsItem) \**other*, [Qt::ItemSelectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemSelectionMode-enum) *mode* \= Qt::IntersectsItemShape) const

Returns `true` if this item collides with *other*; otherwise returns `false`.

The *mode* is applied to *other*, and the resulting shape or bounding rectangle is then
compared to this item's shape. The default value for *mode* is
[Qt::IntersectsItemShape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemSelectionMode-enum);
*other* collides with this item if it either intersects, contains, or is contained by
this item's shape (see
[Qt::ItemSelectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemSelectionMode-enum)
for details).

The default implementation is based on shape intersection, and it calls
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)() on both items.
Because the complexity of arbitrary shape-shape intersection grows with an order of
magnitude when the shapes are complex, this operation can be noticeably time-consuming.
You have the option of reimplementing this function in a subclass of
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) to provide a
custom algorithm. This allows you to make use of natural constraints in the shapes of
your own items, in order to improve the performance of the collision detection. For
instance, two untransformed perfectly circular items' collision can be determined very
efficiently by comparing their positions and radii.

Keep in mind that when reimplementing this function and calling
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)() or
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() on
*other*, the returned coordinates must be mapped to this item's coordinate system before
any intersection can take place.

**See also**
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)() and
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#shape)().
signatures: collidesWithItem(self, other: PySide2.QtWidgets.QGraphicsItem, mode: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.ItemSelectionMode=...) -> bool

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.collidesWit.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QGraphicsItem::collidesWithPath(const [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) \&*path*, [Qt::ItemSelectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemSelectionMode-enum) *mode* \= Qt::IntersectsItemShape) const

Returns `true` if this item collides with *path*.

The collision is determined by *mode*. The default value for *mode* is
[Qt::IntersectsItemShape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemSelectionMode-enum);
*path* collides with this item if it either intersects, contains, or is contained by
this item's shape.

Note that this function checks whether the item's shape or bounding rectangle (depending
on *mode*) is contained within *path*, and not whether *path* is contained within the

### [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) QGraphicsItem::deviceTransform(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*viewportTransform*) const

Returns this item's device transformation matrix, using *viewportTransform* to map from
scene to device coordinates. This matrix can be used to map coordinates and geometrical
shapes from this item's local coordinate system to the viewport's (or any device's)
coordinate system. To map coordinates from the viewport, you must first invert the
returned matrix.

Example:

```
QGraphicsRectItem rect;
rect.setPos(100, 100);

rect.deviceTransform(view->viewportTransform()).map(QPointF(0, 0));
// returns the item's (0, 0) point in view's viewport coordinates

rect.deviceTransform(view->viewportTransform()).inverted().map(QPointF(100, 100));
// returns view's viewport's (100, 100) coordinate in item coordinates
```

This function is the same as combining this item's scene transform with the view's
viewport transform, but it also understands the
[ItemIgnoresTransformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flag. The device transform can be used to do accurate coordinate mapping (and collision
detection) for untransformable items.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also**
[transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)(),
[setTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransform)(),
[scenePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scenePos)(), [The
Graphics View Coordinate
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#the-graphics-view-coordinate-system),
and
[itemTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#itemTransform)().

Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual protected]` void QGraphicsItem::dragEnterEvent([QGraphicsSceneDragDropEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscenedragdropevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented to receive drag enter events
for this item. Drag enter events are generated as the cursor enters the item's area.

By accepting the event (i.e., by calling
[QEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)()), the item
will accept drop events, in addition to receiving drag move and drag leave. Otherwise,
the event will be ignored and propagate to the item beneath. If the event is accepted,
the item will receive a drag move event before control goes back to the event loop.

A common implementation of dragEnterEvent accepts or ignores *event* depending on the
associated mime data in *event*. Example:

```
CustomItem::CustomItem()
{
    setAcceptDrops(true);
    ...
}

void CustomItem::dragEnterEvent(QGraphicsSceneDragDropEvent *event)
{
    event->setAccepted(event->mimeData()->hasFormat("text/plain"));
}
```

Items do not receive drag and drop events by default; to enable this feature, call
`setAcceptDrops(true)`.

The default implementation does nothing.

**See also**
[dropEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#dropEvent)(),
[dragMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#dragMoveEvent)(),
and
[dragLeaveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#dragLeaveEvent)().

### `[virtual protected]` void QGraphicsItem::dragMoveEvent([QGraphicsSceneDragDropEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscenedragdropevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented to receive drag move events
for this item. Drag move events are generated as the cursor moves around inside the
item's area. Most often you will not need to reimplement this function; it is used to
indicate that only parts of the item can accept drops.

toggles whether or not the item will accept drops at the position from the event. By
default, *event* is accepted, indicating that the item allows drops at the specified
position.

Items do not receive drag and drop events by default; to enable this feature, call
`setAcceptDrops(true)`.

The default implementation does nothing.

### void QGraphicsItem::grabKeyboard()

Grabs the keyboard input.

The item will receive all keyboard input to the scene until one of the following events
occur:

- The item becomes invisible
- The item is removed from the scene
- The item is deleted
- The item calls [ungrabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#ungrabKeyboard)()
- Another item calls grabKeyboard(); the item will regain the keyboard grab when the other item calls [ungrabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#ungrabKeyboard)().

When an item gains the keyboard grab, it receives a
[QEvent::GrabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event.
When it loses the keyboard grab, it receives a
[QEvent::UngrabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
event. These events can be used to detect when your item gains or loses the keyboard
grab through other means than gaining input focus.

It is almost never necessary to explicitly grab the keyboard in Qt, as Qt grabs and
releases it sensibly. In particular, Qt grabs the keyboard when your item gains input
focus, and releases it when your item loses input focus, or when the item is hidden.

Note that only visible items can grab keyboard input. Calling grabKeyboard() on an
invisible item has no effect.

Keyboard events are not affected.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[ungrabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#ungrabKeyboard)(),
[grabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#grabMouse)(), and
[setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setFocus)().

### void QGraphicsItem::grabMouse()

Grabs the mouse input.

This item will receive all mouse events for the scene until any of the following events
occurs:

- The item becomes invisible
- The item is removed from the scene
- The item is deleted
- The item call [ungrabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#ungrabMouse)()
- Another item calls grabMouse(); the item will regain the mouse grab when the other item calls [ungrabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#ungrabMouse)().

When an item gains the mouse grab, it receives a
[QEvent::GrabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event.
When it loses the mouse grab, it receives a
[QEvent::UngrabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event.
These events can be used to detect when your item gains or loses the mouse grab through
other means than receiving mouse button events.

It is almost never necessary to explicitly grab the mouse in Qt, as Qt grabs and
releases it sensibly. In particular, Qt grabs the mouse when you press a mouse button,
and keeps the mouse grabbed until you release the last mouse button. Also,
[Qt::Popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum) widgets
implicitly call grabMouse() when shown, and
[ungrabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#ungrabMouse)() when
hidden.

Note that only visible items can grab mouse input. Calling grabMouse() on an invisible
item has no effect.

Keyboard events are not affected.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[QGraphicsScene::mouseGrabberItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#mouseGrabberItem)(),
[ungrabMouse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#ungrabMouse)(), and
[grabKeyboard](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#grabKeyboard)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.installScen.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::installSceneEventFilter([QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#QGraphicsItem) \**filterItem*)

Installs an event filter for this item on *filterItem*, causing all events for this item
to first pass through *filterItem*'s
[sceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEventFilter)()
function.

To filter another item's events, install this item as an event filter for the other
item. Example:

```
QGraphicsScene scene;
QGraphicsEllipseItem *ellipse = scene.addEllipse(QRectF(-10, -10, 20, 20));
QGraphicsLineItem *line = scene.addLine(QLineF(-10, -10, 20, 20));

line->installSceneEventFilter(ellipse);
// line's events are filtered by ellipse's sceneEventFilter() function.

ellipse->installSceneEventFilter(line);
// ellipse's events are filtered by line's sceneEventFilter() function.
```

An item can only filter events for other items in the same scene. Also, an item cannot
filter its own events; instead, you can reimplement
[sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)()
directly.

Items must belong to a scene for scene event filters to be installed and used.

**See also**
[removeSceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#removeSceneEventFilter)(),
[sceneEventFilter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEventFilter)(),
and [sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)().

### `[virtual]` bool QGraphicsItem::isObscuredBy(const [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#QGraphicsItem) \**item*) const

Returns `true` if this item's bounding rect is completely obscured by the opaque shape
of *item*.

The base implementation maps *item*'s
[opaqueArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#opaqueArea)() to this

[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() is

this item is obscured by *item*.

Returns a [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) that maps
coordinates from this item to *other*. If *ok* is not null, and if there is no such
transform, the boolean pointed to by *ok* will be set to false; otherwise it will be set
to true.

This transform provides an alternative to the
[mapToItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mapToItem)() or
[mapFromItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mapFromItem)()
functions, by returning the appropriate transform so that you can map shapes and
coordinates yourself. It also helps you write more efficient code when repeatedly
mapping between the same two items.

**Note:** In rare circumstances, there is no transform that maps between two items.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also**
[mapToItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mapToItem)(),
[mapFromItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mapFromItem)(), and
[deviceTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#deviceTransform)().

### `[virtual protected]` void QGraphicsItem::mouseDoubleClickEvent([QGraphicsSceneMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscenemouseevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented to receive mouse
double-click events for this item.

When doubleclicking an item, the item will first receive a mouse press event, followed
by a release event (i.e., a click), then a double-click event, and finally a release
event.

Calling [QEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() or
[QEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)() on *event* has
no effect.

The default implementation calls
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)().
If you want to keep the base implementation when reimplementing this function, call
QGraphicsItem::mouseDoubleClickEvent() in your reimplementation.

Note that an item will not receive double click events if it is neither
[selectable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
nor
[movable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
(single mouse clicks are ignored in this case, and that stops the generation of double
clicks).

**See also**
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)(),
[mouseMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseMoveEvent)(),
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(),
and [sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)().

### `[virtual protected]` void QGraphicsItem::mouseMoveEvent([QGraphicsSceneMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscenemouseevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented to receive mouse move events
for this item. If you do receive this event, you can be certain that this item also
received a mouse press event, and that this item is the current mouse grabber.

Calling [QEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() or
[QEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)() on *event* has
no effect.

The default implementation handles basic item interaction, such as selection and moving.
If you want to keep the base implementation when reimplementing this function, call
QGraphicsItem::mouseMoveEvent() in your reimplementation.

Please note that
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)()
decides which graphics item it is that receives mouse events. See the
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)()
description for details.

**See also**
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)(),
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(),
[mouseDoubleClickEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseDoubleClickEvent)(),
and [sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)().

### `[virtual protected]` void QGraphicsItem::mousePressEvent([QGraphicsSceneMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscenemouseevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented to receive mouse press
events for this item. Mouse press events are only delivered to items that accept the
mouse button that is pressed. By default, an item accepts all mouse buttons, but you can
change this by calling
[setAcceptedMouseButtons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setAcceptedMouseButtons)().

The mouse press event decides which item should become the mouse grabber (see
[QGraphicsScene::mouseGrabberItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#mouseGrabberItem)()).
If you do not reimplement this function, the press event will propagate to any topmost
item beneath this item, and no other mouse events will be delivered to this item.

If you do reimplement this function, *event* will by default be accepted (see
[QEvent::accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)()), and this
item is then the mouse grabber. This allows the item to receive future move, release and
double-click events. If you call
[QEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() on *event*,
this item will lose the mouse grab, and *event* will propagate to any topmost item
beneath. No further mouse events will be delivered to this item unless a new mouse press
event is received.

The default implementation handles basic item interaction, such as selection and moving.
If you want to keep the base implementation when reimplementing this function, call
QGraphicsItem::mousePressEvent() in your reimplementation.

The event is [QEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)()d
for items that are neither
[movable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
nor
[selectable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum).

**See also**
[mouseMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseMoveEvent)(),
[mouseReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseReleaseEvent)(),
[mouseDoubleClickEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mouseDoubleClickEvent)(),
and [sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)().

Qt 5 reference:

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QGraphicsItem::opacity() const

Returns this item's local opacity, which is between 0.0 (transparent) and 1.0 (opaque).
This value is combined with parent and ancestor values into the
[effectiveOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#effectiveOpacity)().
The effective opacity decides how the item is rendered and also affects its visibility
when queried by functions such as
[QGraphicsView::items](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html#items)().

The opacity property decides the state of the painter passed to the
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() function. If the
item is cached, i.e.,
[ItemCoordinateCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum)
or
[DeviceCoordinateCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum),
the effective property will be applied to the item's cache as it is rendered.

The default opacity is 1.0; fully opaque.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also**
[setOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setOpacity)(),
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)(),
[ItemIgnoresParentOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum),
and
[ItemDoesntPropagateOpacityToChildren](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum).

### `[virtual]` [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) QGraphicsItem::opaqueArea() const

This virtual function returns a shape representing the area where this item is opaque.
An area is opaque if it is filled using an opaque brush or color (i.e., not

This function is used by

The default implementation returns an empty
[QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html), indicating that

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.paint.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual]` void QGraphicsItem::paint([QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) \**painter*, const [QStyleOptionGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleoptiongraphicsitem.html) \**option*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**widget* \= 0\)

This function, which is usually called by
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html), paints the
contents of an item in local coordinates.

Reimplement this function in a
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) subclass to
provide the item's painting implementation, using *painter*. The *option* parameter
provides style options for the item, such as its state, exposed area and its
level-of-detail hints. The *widget* argument is optional. If provided, it points to the
widget that is being painted on; otherwise, it is 0\. For cached painting, *widget* is
always 0\.

```
void RoundRectItem::paint(QPainter *painter,
                          const QStyleOptionGraphicsItem *option,
                          QWidget *widget)
{
    painter->drawRoundedRect(-10, -10, 20, 20, 5, 5);
}
```

The painter's pen is 0-width by default, and its pen is initialized to the
[QPalette::Text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorRole-enum) brush
from the paint device's palette. The brush is initialized to
[QPalette::Window](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorRole-enum).

Make sure to constrain all painting inside the boundaries of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() to
avoid rendering artifacts (as
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) does not clip the
painter for you). In particular, when
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) renders the outline of a
shape using an assigned [QPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpen.html), half of
the outline will be drawn outside, and half inside, the shape you're rendering (e.g.,
with a pen width of 2 units, you must draw outlines 1 unit inside
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)()).
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) does not support
use of cosmetic pens with a non-zero width.

All painting is done in local coordinates.

**Note:** It is mandatory that an item will always redraw itself in the exact same way,
unless [update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)() was
called; otherwise visual artifacts may occur. In other words, two subsequent calls to
paint() must always produce the same output, unless
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)() was called
between them.

**Note:** Enabling caching for an item does not guarantee that paint() will be invoked
only once by the Graphics View framework, even without any explicit call to
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)(). See the
documentation of
[setCacheMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setCacheMode)() for
more details.

**See also**
[setCacheMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setCacheMode)(),
[QPen::width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpen.html#width)(), [Item
Coordinates](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#item-coordinates), and
[ItemUsesExtendedStyleOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum).
signatures: paint(self, painter: PySide2.QtGui.QPainter, option: PySide2.QtWidgets.QStyleOptionGraphicsItem, widget: typing.Optional[PySide2.QtWidgets.QWidget]=...) -> None

### `[virtual protected]` bool QGraphicsItem::sceneEventFilter([QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#QGraphicsItem) \**watched*, [QEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html) \**event*)

### [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) QGraphicsItem::sceneTransform() const

Returns this item's scene transformation matrix. This matrix can be used to map
coordinates and geometrical shapes from this item's local coordinate system to the
scene's coordinate system. To map coordinates from the scene, you must first invert the
returned matrix.

Example:

```
QGraphicsRectItem rect;
rect.setPos(100, 100);

rect.sceneTransform().map(QPointF(0, 0));
// returns QPointF(100, 100);

rect.sceneTransform().inverted().map(QPointF(100, 100));
// returns QPointF(0, 0);
```

Unlike [transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)(),
which returns only an item's local transformation, this function includes the item's
(and any parents') position, and all the transformation properties.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also**
[transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)(),
[setTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransform)(),
[scenePos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scenePos)(), [The
Graphics View Coordinate

and
[Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.scroll.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::scroll([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *dx*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *dy*, const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rect* \= QRectF())

Scrolls the contents of *rect* by *dx*, *dy*. If *rect* is a null rect (the default),
the item's bounding rect is scrolled.

Scrolling provides a fast alternative to simply redrawing when the contents of the item
(or parts of the item) are shifted vertically or horizontally. Depending on the current
transformation and the capabilities of the paint device (i.e., the viewport), this
operation may consist of simply moving pixels from one location to another using
memmove(). In most cases this is faster than rerendering the entire area.

After scrolling, the item will issue an update for the newly exposed areas. If scrolling
is not supported (e.g., you are rendering to an OpenGL viewport, which does not benefit
from scroll optimizations), this function is equivalent to calling update(*rect*).

**Note:** Scrolling is only supported when
[QGraphicsItem::ItemCoordinateCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum)
is enabled; in all other cases calling this function is equivalent to calling
update(*rect*). If you for sure know that the item is opaque and not overlapped by other
items, you can map the *rect* to viewport coordinates and scroll the viewport.

```
QTransform xform = item->deviceTransform(view->viewportTransform());
QRect deviceRect = xform.mapRect(rect).toAlignedRect();
view->viewport()->scroll(dx, dy, deviceRect);
```

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)().
signatures: scroll(self, dx: float, dy: float, rect: PySide2.QtCore.QRectF=...) -> None

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setAcceptHo.doc:

### void QGraphicsItem::setAcceptHoverEvents(bool *enabled*)

If *enabled* is true, this item will accept hover events; otherwise, it will ignore
them. By default, items do not accept hover events.

Hover events are delivered when there is no current mouse grabber item. They are sent
when the mouse cursor enters an item, when it moves around inside the item, and when the
cursor leaves an item. Hover events are commonly used to highlight an item when it's
entered, and for tracking the mouse cursor as it hovers over the item (equivalent to
[QWidget::mouseTracking](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#mouseTracking-prop)).

Parent items receive hover enter events before their children, and leave events after
their children. The parent does not receive a hover leave event if the cursor enters a
child, though; the parent stays "hovered" until the cursor leaves its area, including
its children's areas.

If a parent item handles child events, it will receive hover move, drag move, and drop
events as the cursor passes through its children, but it does not receive hover enter
and hover leave, nor drag enter and drag leave events on behalf of its children.

A
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
with window decorations will accept hover events regardless of the value of
[acceptHoverEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#acceptHoverEvents)().

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[acceptHoverEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#acceptHoverEvents)(),
[hoverEnterEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverEnterEvent)(),
[hoverMoveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverMoveEvent)(),
and
[hoverLeaveEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hoverLeaveEvent)().

### void QGraphicsItem::setAcceptedMouseButtons([Qt::MouseButtons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#MouseButton-enum) *buttons*)

Sets the mouse *buttons* that this item accepts mouse events for.

By default, all mouse buttons are accepted. If an item accepts a mouse button, it will
become the mouse grabber item when a mouse press event is delivered for that button.
However, if the item does not accept the mouse button,
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) will forward
the mouse events to the first item beneath it that does.

To disable mouse events for an item (i.e., make it transparent for mouse events), call
setAcceptedMouseButtons(0).

**See also**
[acceptedMouseButtons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#acceptedMouseButtons)()
and
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mousePressEvent)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setActive.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setActive(bool *active*)

If *active* is true, and the scene is active, this item's panel will be activated.
Otherwise, the panel is deactivated.

If the item is not part of an active scene, *active* will decide what happens to the
panel when the scene becomes active or the item is added to the scene. If true, the
item's panel will be activated when the item is either added to the scene or the scene
is activated. Otherwise, the item will stay inactive independent of the scene's
activated state.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also** [isPanel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isPanel)(),
[QGraphicsScene::setActivePanel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#setActivePanel)(),
and
[QGraphicsScene::isActive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#isActive)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setBounding.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setBoundingRegionGranularity([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *granularity*)

Sets the bounding region granularity to *granularity*; a value between and including 0
and 1\. The default value is 0 (i.e., the lowest granularity, where the bounding region
corresponds to the item's bounding rectangle).

The granularity is used by
[boundingRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRegion)()
to calculate how fine the bounding region of the item should be. The highest achievable
granularity is 1, where
[boundingRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRegion)()
will return the finest outline possible for the respective device (e.g., for a
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) viewport, this
gives you a pixel-perfect bounding region). The lowest possible granularity is 0\. The
value of *granularity* describes the ratio between device resolution and the resolution
of the bounding region (e.g., a value of 0.25 will provide a region where each chunk
corresponds to 4x4 device units / pixels).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[boundingRegionGranularity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRegionGranularity)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setCacheMod.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setCacheMode([QGraphicsItem::CacheMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum) *mode*, const [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html) \&*logicalCacheSize* \= QSize())

Sets the item's cache mode to *mode*.

The optional *logicalCacheSize* argument is used only by
[ItemCoordinateCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum)
mode, and describes the resolution of the cache buffer; if *logicalCacheSize* is (100,
100), [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) will fit
the item into 100x100 pixels in graphics memory, regardless of the logical size of the
item itself. By default
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) uses the size of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)().
For all other cache modes than
[ItemCoordinateCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum),
*logicalCacheSize* is ignored.

Caching can speed up rendering if your item spends a significant time redrawing itself.
In some cases the cache can also slow down rendering, in particular when the item spends
less time redrawing than
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) spends redrawing
from the cache.

When caching is enabled, an item's
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() function will
generally draw into an offscreen pixmap cache; for any subsequent repaint requests, the
Graphics View framework will redraw from the cache. This approach works particularly
well with QGLWidget, which stores all the cache as OpenGL textures.

Be aware that [QPixmapCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmapcache.html)'s
cache limit may need to be changed to obtain optimal performance.

You can read more about the different cache modes in the
[CacheMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum)
documentation.

**Note:** Enabling caching does not imply that the item's
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() function will be
called only in response to an explicit
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)() call. For
instance, under memory pressure, Qt may decide to drop some of the cache information; in
such cases an item's
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() function will be
called even if there was no
[update](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#update)() call (that is,
exactly as if there were no caching enabled).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**See also**
[cacheMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#cacheMode)(),
[CacheMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum), and
[QPixmapCache::setCacheLimit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmapcache.html#setCacheLimit)().

### void QGraphicsItem::setCursor(const [QCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcursor.html) \&*cursor*)

Sets the current cursor shape for the item to *cursor*. The mouse cursor will assume
this shape when it's over this item. See the [list of predefined cursor
objects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#CursorShape-enum) for a range of
useful shapes.

An editor item might want to use an I-beam cursor:

```
item->setCursor(Qt::IBeamCursor);
```

If no cursor has been set, the cursor of the item beneath is used.

**See also** [cursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#cursor)(),
[hasCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hasCursor)(),
[unsetCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#unsetCursor)(),
[QWidget::cursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#cursor-prop), and
[QGuiApplication::overrideCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#overrideCursor)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setEnabled.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setEnabled(bool *enabled*)

If *enabled* is true, the item is enabled; otherwise, it is disabled.

Disabled items are visible, but they do not receive any events, and cannot take focus
nor be selected. Mouse events are discarded; they are not propagated unless the item is
also invisible, or if it does not accept mouse events (see
[acceptedMouseButtons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#acceptedMouseButtons)()).
A disabled item cannot become the mouse grabber, and as a result of this, an item loses
the grab if it becomes disabled when grabbing the mouse, just like it loses focus if it
had focus when it was disabled.

Disabled items are traditionally drawn using grayed-out colors (see
[QPalette::Disabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html#ColorGroup-enum)).

If you disable a parent item, all its children will also be disabled. If you enable a
parent item, all children will be enabled, unless they have been explicitly disabled
(i.e., if you call setEnabled(false) on a child, it will not be re-enabled if its parent
is disabled, and then enabled again).

Items are enabled by default.

**Note:** If you install an event filter, you can still intercept events before they are
delivered to items; this mechanism disregards the item's enabled state.

**See also**
[isEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isEnabled)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setFiltersC.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setFiltersChildEvents(bool *enabled*)

If *enabled* is true, this item is set to filter all events for all its children (i.e.,
all events intented for any of its children are instead sent to this item); otherwise,
if *enabled* is false, this item will only handle its own events. The default value is
false.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[filtersChildEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#filtersChildEvents)().

### void QGraphicsItem::setFlag([QGraphicsItem::GraphicsItemFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum) *flag*, bool *enabled* \= true)

**See also** [flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#flags)() and

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setFlags.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setFlags([QGraphicsItem::GraphicsItemFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum) *flags*)

Sets the item flags to *flags*. All flags in *flags* are enabled; all flags not in
*flags* are disabled.

If the item had focus and *flags* does not enable
[ItemIsFocusable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum),
the item loses focus as a result of calling this function. Similarly, if the item was
selected, and *flags* does not enabled
[ItemIsSelectable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum),
the item is automatically unselected.

By default, no flags are enabled.
([QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
enables the
[ItemSendsGeometryChanges](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flag by default in order to track position changes.)

**See also** [flags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#flags)() and
[setFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setFlag)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setFocus.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setFocus([Qt::FocusReason](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FocusReason-enum) *focusReason* \= Qt::OtherFocusReason)

Gives keyboard input focus to this item. The *focusReason* argument will be passed into
any [focus event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfocusevent.html) generated by this
function; it is used to give an explanation of what caused the item to get focus.

Only enabled items that set the
[ItemIsFocusable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flag can accept keyboard focus.

If this item is not visible, not active, or not associated with a scene, it will not
gain immediate input focus. However, it will be registered as the preferred focus item
for its subtree of items, should it later become visible.

As a result of calling this function, this item will receive a [focus in
event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusInEvent) with
*focusReason*. If another item already has focus, that item will first receive a [focus
out event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusOutEvent)
indicating that it has lost input focus.

**See also**
[clearFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#clearFocus)(),
[hasFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hasFocus)(),
[focusItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusItem)(), and
[focusProxy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusProxy)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setFocusPro.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setFocusProxy([QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#QGraphicsItem) \**item*)

Sets the item's focus proxy to *item*.

If an item has a focus proxy, the focus proxy will receive input focus when the item
gains input focus. The item itself will still have focus (i.e.,
[hasFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hasFocus)() will return
true), but only the focus proxy will receive the keyboard input.

A focus proxy can itself have a focus proxy, and so on. In such case, keyboard input
will be handled by the outermost focus proxy.

The focus proxy *item* must belong to the same scene as this item.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[focusProxy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#focusProxy)(),
[setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setFocus)(), and
[hasFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hasFocus)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setGraphics.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setGraphicsEffect([QGraphicsEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicseffect.html) \**effect*)

Sets *effect* as the item's effect. If there already is an effect installed on this
item, [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) will delete
the existing effect before installing the new *effect*. You can delete an existing
effect by calling setGraphicsEffect(`nullptr`).

If *effect* is the installed effect on a different item, setGraphicsEffect() will remove
the effect from the item and install it on this item.

[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) takes ownership
of *effect*.

**Note:** This function will apply the effect on itself and all its children.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[graphicsEffect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#graphicsEffect)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setOpacity.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setOpacity([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *opacity*)

Sets this item's local *opacity*, between 0.0 (transparent) and 1.0 (opaque). The item's
local opacity is combined with parent and ancestor opacities into the
[effectiveOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#effectiveOpacity)().

By default, opacity propagates from parent to child, so if a parent's opacity is 0.5 and
the child is also 0.5, the child's effective opacity will be 0.25.

The opacity property decides the state of the painter passed to the
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() function. If the
item is cached, i.e.,
[ItemCoordinateCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum)
or
[DeviceCoordinateCache](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#CacheMode-enum),
the effective property will be applied to the item's cache as it is rendered.

There are two item flags that affect how the item's opacity is combined with the parent:
[ItemIgnoresParentOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
and
[ItemDoesntPropagateOpacityToChildren](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum).

**Note:** Setting the opacity of an item to 0 will not make the item invisible
(according to
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isVisible)()), but the
item will be treated like an invisible one. See the documentation of
[setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setVisible)() for
more information.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.5.

**See also** [opacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#opacity)(),
[effectiveOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#effectiveOpacity)(),
and [setVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setVisible)().

### void QGraphicsItem::setParentItem([QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#QGraphicsItem) \**newParent*)

Sets this item's parent item to *newParent*. If this item already has a parent, it is
first removed from the previous parent. If *newParent* is 0, this item will become a
top-level item.

Note that this implicitly adds this graphics item to the scene of the parent. You should
not [add](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addItem) the item to
the scene yourself.

The behavior when calling this function on an item that is an ancestor of *newParent* is
undefined.

**See also**
[parentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#parentItem)() and
[childItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#childItems)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setRotation.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setRotation([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *angle*)

Sets the clockwise rotation *angle*, in degrees, around the Z axis. The default value is
0 (i.e., the item is not rotated). Assigning a negative value will rotate the item
counter-clockwise. Normally the rotation angle is in the range (-360, 360), but it's
also possible to assign values outside of this range (e.g., a rotation of 370 degrees is
the same as a rotation of 10 degrees).

The item is rotated around its transform origin point, which by default is (0, 0). You
can select a different transformation origin by calling
[setTransformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransformOriginPoint)().

The rotation is combined with the item's
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scale-1)(),
[transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)() and
[transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations)()
to map the item's coordinate system to the parent item.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[rotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#rotation)(),
[setTransformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransformOriginPoint)(),
and
[Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setScale.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setScale([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *factor*)

Sets the scale *factor* of the item. The default scale factor is 1.0 (i.e., the item is
not scaled). A scale factor of 0.0 will collapse the item to a single point. If you
provide a negative scale factor, the item will be flipped and mirrored (i.e., rotated
180 degrees).

The item is scaled around its transform origin point, which by default is (0, 0). You
can select a different transformation origin by calling
[setTransformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransformOriginPoint)().

The scale is combined with the item's
[rotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#rotation)(),
[transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)() and
[transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations)()
to map the item's coordinate system to the parent item.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also** [scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scale-1)(),
[setTransformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransformOriginPoint)(),
and [Transformations
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-painting-transformations-example.html).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setSelected.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setSelected(bool *selected*)

If *selected* is true and this item is selectable, this item is selected; otherwise, it
is unselected.

If the item is in a group, the whole group's selected state is toggled by this function.
If the group is selected, all items in the group are also selected, and if the group is
not selected, no item in the group is selected.

Only visible, enabled, selectable items can be selected. If *selected* is true and this
item is either invisible or disabled or unselectable, this function does nothing.

By default, items cannot be selected. To enable selection, set the
[ItemIsSelectable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flag.

This function is provided for convenience, allowing individual toggling of the selected
state of an item. However, a more common way of selecting items is to call
[QGraphicsScene::setSelectionArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#setSelectionArea)(),
which will call this function for all visible, enabled, and selectable items within a
specified area on the scene.

**See also**
[isSelected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isSelected)() and
[QGraphicsScene::selectedItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#selectedItems)().

### void QGraphicsItem::setTransform(const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*matrix*, bool *combine* \= false)

Sets the item's current transformation matrix to *matrix*.

If *combine* is true, then *matrix* is combined with the current matrix; otherwise,
*matrix* *replaces* the current matrix. *combine* is false by default.

To simplify interaction with items using a transformed view,
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) provides mapTo...
and mapFrom... functions that can translate between items' and the scene's coordinates.
For example, you can call
[mapToScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mapToScene)() to map
an item coordinate to a scene coordinate, or
[mapFromScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#mapFromScene)() to
map from scene coordinates to item coordinates.

The transformation matrix is combined with the item's
[rotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#rotation)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scale-1)() and
[transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations)()
into a combined transformation that maps the item's coordinate system to its parent.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**See also**
[transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)(),
[setRotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setRotation)(),
[setScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setScale)(),
[setTransformOriginPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransformOriginPoint)(),
[The Graphics View Coordinate
System](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#the-graphics-view-coordinate-system),
and
[Transformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transformations).
signatures: setTransform(self, matrix: PySide2.QtGui.QTransform, combine: bool=...) -> None

### void QGraphicsItem::setTransformations(const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QGraphicsTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicstransform.html) \*\> \&*transformations*)

Sets a list of graphics *transformations*
([QGraphicsTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicstransform.html)) that
currently apply to this item.

If all you want is to rotate or scale an item, you should call
[setRotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setRotation)() or
[setScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setScale)() instead. If
you want to set an arbitrary transformation on an item, you can call
[setTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setTransform)().

[QGraphicsTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicstransform.html) is for
applying and controlling a chain of individual transformation operations on an item.
It's particularly useful in animations, where each transform operation needs to be
interpolated independently, or differently.

The transformations are combined with the item's
[rotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#rotation)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#scale-1)() and
[transform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#transform)() to map
the item's coordinate system to the parent item.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.
