PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.setVisible.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::setVisible(bool *visible*)

If *visible* is true, the item is made visible. Otherwise, the item is made invisible.
Invisible items are not painted, nor do they receive any events. In particular, mouse
events pass right through invisible items, and are delivered to any item that may be
behind. Invisible items are also unselectable, they cannot take input focus, and are not
detected by [QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html)'s
item location functions.

If an item becomes invisible while grabbing the mouse, (i.e., while it is receiving
mouse events,) it will automatically lose the mouse grab, and the grab is not regained
by making the item visible again; it must receive a new mouse press to regain the mouse
grab.

Similarly, an invisible item cannot have focus, so if the item has focus when it becomes
invisible, it will lose focus, and the focus is not regained by simply making the item
visible again.

If you hide a parent item, all its children will also be hidden. If you show a parent
item, all children will be shown, unless they have been explicitly hidden (i.e., if you
call setVisible(false) on a child, it will not be reshown even if its parent is hidden,
and then shown again).

Items are visible by default; it is unnecessary to call setVisible() on a new item.

**Note:** An item with opacity set to 0 will still be considered visible, although it
will be treated like an invisible item: mouse events will pass through it, it will not
be included in the items returned by
[QGraphicsView::items](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html#items)(),
and so on. However, the item will retain the focus.

**See also**
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isVisible)(),
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#show)(),
[hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#hide)(), and
[setOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setOpacity)().

### void QGraphicsItem::setZValue([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *z*)

Sets the Z-value of the item to *z*. The Z value decides the stacking order of sibling
(neighboring) items. A sibling item of high Z value will always be drawn on top of
another sibling item with a lower Z value.

If you restore the Z value, the item's insertion order will decide its stacking order.

The Z-value does not affect the item's size in any way.

The default Z-value is 0\.

**See also** [zValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#zValue)(),
[Sorting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sorting),
[stackBefore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#stackBefore)(), and
[ItemStacksBehindParent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum).

Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) QGraphicsItem::shape() const

Returns the shape of this item as a
[QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) in local
coordinates. The shape is used for many things, including collision detection, hit
tests, and for the
[QGraphicsScene::items](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#items)()
functions.

The default implementation calls
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)() to
return a simple rectangular shape, but subclasses can reimplement this function to
return a more accurate shape for non-rectangular items. For example, a round item may
choose to return an elliptic shape for better collision detection. For example:

```
QPainterPath RoundItem::shape() const
{
    QPainterPath path;
    path.addEllipse(boundingRect());
    return path;
}
```

The outline of a shape can vary depending on the width and style of the pen used when
drawing. If you want to include this outline in the item's shape, you can create a shape
from the stroke using
[QPainterPathStroker](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html).

This function is called by the default implementations of
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)() and
[collidesWithPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#collidesWithPath)().

**See also**
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)(),
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#contains)(),
[prepareGeometryChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#prepareGeometryChange)(),
and [QPainterPathStroker](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpathstroker.html).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsItem.stackBefore.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QGraphicsItem::stackBefore(const [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#QGraphicsItem) \**sibling*)

Stacks this item before *sibling*, which must be a sibling item (i.e., the two items
must share the same parent item, or must both be toplevel items). The *sibling* must
have the same Z value as this item, otherwise calling this function will have no effect.

By default, all sibling items are stacked by insertion order (i.e., the first item you
add is drawn before the next item you add). If two items' Z values are different, then
the item with the highest Z value is drawn on top. When the Z values are the same, the
insertion order will decide the stacking order.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[setZValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setZValue)(),
[ItemStacksBehindParent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum),
and [Sorting](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sorting).

### `[virtual]` int QGraphicsItem::type() const

Returns the type of an item as an int. All standard graphicsitem classes are associated
with a unique value; see
[QGraphicsItem::Type](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#anonymous-enum).
This type information is used by
[qgraphicsitem\_cast](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#qgraphicsitem_cast)()
to distinguish between types.

The default implementation (in
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html)) returns
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#anonymous-enum).

To enable use of
[qgraphicsitem\_cast](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#qgraphicsitem_cast)()
with a custom item, reimplement this function and declare a Type enum value equal to
your custom item's type. Custom items must return a value larger than or equal to
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#anonymous-enum)
(65536).

For example:

```
class CustomItem : public QGraphicsItem
{
public:
   enum { Type = UserType + 1 };

   int type() const override
   {
       // Enable the use of qgraphicsitem_cast with this item.
       return Type;
   }
   ...
};
```

**See also**
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#anonymous-enum).

### void QGraphicsItem::update(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rect* \= QRectF())

Schedules a redraw of the area covered by *rect* in this item. You can call this
function whenever your item needs to be redrawn, such as if it changes appearance or
size.

This function does not cause an immediate paint; instead it schedules a paint request
that is processed by
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) after control
reaches the event loop. The item will only be redrawn if it is visible in any associated
view.

As a side effect of the item being repainted, other items that overlap the area *rect*
may also be repainted.

If the item is invisible (i.e.,
[isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isVisible)() returns
`false`), this function does nothing.

**See also** [paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#paint)() and
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#boundingRect)().

### `[virtual protected]` void QGraphicsItem::wheelEvent([QGraphicsSceneWheelEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscenewheelevent.html) \**event*)

This event handler, for event *event*, can be reimplemented to receive wheel events for
this item. If you reimplement this function, *event* will be accepted by default.

If you ignore the event, (i.e., by calling
[QEvent::ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)(),) it will
propagate to any item beneath this item. If no items accept the event, it will be
ignored by the scene, and propagate to the view (e.g., the view's vertical scroll bar).

The default implementation ignores the event.

**See also**
[sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)().

## Detailed Description

A QGraphicsItemGroup is a special type of compound item that treats itself and all its
children as one item (i.e., all events and geometries for all children are merged
together). It's common to use item groups in presentation tools, when the user wants to
group several smaller items into one big item in order to simplify moving and copying of
items.

If all you want is to store items inside other items, you can use any
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) directly by
passing a suitable parent to
[setParentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setParentItem)().

The
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitemgroup.html#boundingRect)()
function of QGraphicsItemGroup returns the bounding rectangle of all items in the item
group. QGraphicsItemGroup ignores the
[ItemIgnoresTransformations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#GraphicsItemFlag-enum)
flag on its children (i.e., with respect to the geometry of the group item, the children
are treated as if they were transformable).

There are two ways to construct an item group. The easiest and most common approach is
to pass a list of items (e.g., all selected items) to
[QGraphicsScene::createItemGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#createItemGroup)(),
which returns a new QGraphicsItemGroup item. The other approach is to manually construct
a QGraphicsItemGroup item, add it to the scene calling
[QGraphicsScene::addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addItem)(),
and then add items to the group manually, one at a time by calling
[addToGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitemgroup.html#addToGroup)().
To dismantle ("ungroup") an item group, you can either call
[QGraphicsScene::destroyItemGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#destroyItemGroup)(),
or you can manually remove all items from the group by calling
[removeFromGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitemgroup.html#removeFromGroup)().

```
// Group all selected items together
QGraphicsItemGroup *group = scene->createItemGroup(scene->selecteditems());

// Destroy the group, and delete the group item
scene->destroyItemGroup(group);
```

The operation of adding and removing items preserves the items' scene-relative position
and transformation, as opposed to calling
[setParentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setParentItem)(),
where only the child item's parent-relative position and transformation are kept.

The addtoGroup() function reparents the target item to this item group, keeping the
item's position and transformation intact relative to the scene. Visually, this means
that items added via
[addToGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitemgroup.html#addToGroup)()
will remain completely unchanged as a result of this operation, regardless of the item
or the group's current position or transformation; although the item's position and
matrix are likely to change.

The
[removeFromGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitemgroup.html#removeFromGroup)()
function has similar semantics to
[setParentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setParentItem)();
it reparents the item to the parent item of the item group. As with
[addToGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitemgroup.html#addToGroup)(),
the item's scene-relative position and transformation remain intact.

## Detailed Description

QGraphicsLayout is an abstract class that defines a virtual API for arranging
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
children and other
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html)
objects for a
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget).
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
assigns responsibility to a QGraphicsLayout through
[QGraphicsWidget::setLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#setLayout)().
As the widget is resized, the layout will automatically arrange the widget's children.
QGraphicsLayout inherits
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html), so,
it can be managed by any layout, including its own subclasses.

### Writing a Custom Layout

You can use QGraphicsLayout as a base to write your own custom layout (e.g., a
flowlayout), but it is more common to use one of its subclasses instead \-
[QGraphicsLinearLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html)
or [QGraphicsGridLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html).
When creating a custom layout, the following functions must be reimplemented as a bare
minimum:

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [QGraphicsLayoutItem::setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setGeometry)() | Notifies you when the geometry of the layout is set. You can store the geometry in your own layout class in a reimplementation of this function. |
| [QGraphicsLayoutItem::sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#sizeHint)() | Returns the layout's size hints. |
| [QGraphicsLayout::count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#count)() | Returns the number of items in your layout. |
| [QGraphicsLayout::itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#itemAt)() | Returns a pointer to an item in your layout. |
| [QGraphicsLayout::removeAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#removeAt)() | Removes an item from your layout without destroying it. |

For more details on how to implement each function, refer to the individual function
documentation.

Each layout defines its own API for arranging widgets and layout items. For example,
with a grid layout, you require a row and a column index with optional row and column
spans, alignment, spacing, and more. A linear layout, however, requires a single row or
column index to position its items. For a grid layout, the order of insertion does not
affect the layout in any way, but for a linear layout, the order is essential. When
writing your own layout subclass, you are free to choose the API that best suits your
layout.

QGraphicsLayout provides the
[addChildLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#addChildLayoutItem)()
convenience function to add layout items to a custom layout. The function will
automatically reparent graphics items, if required.

### Activating the Layout

When the layout's geometry changes, QGraphicsLayout immediately rearranges all of its
managed items by calling
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setGeometry)()
on each item. This rearrangement is called *activating* the layout.

QGraphicsLayout updates its own geometry to match the
[contentsRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#contentsRect)()
of the
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html) it is
managing. Thus, it will automatically rearrange all its items when the widget is
resized. QGraphicsLayout caches the sizes of all its managed items to avoid calling
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setGeometry)()
too often.

**Note:** A QGraphicsLayout will have the same geometry as the
[contentsRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#contentsRect)()
of the widget (not the layout) it is assigned to.

#### Activating the Layout Implicitly

The layout can be activated implicitly using one of two ways: by calling
[activate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#activate)() or by
calling
[invalidate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#invalidate)().
Calling [activate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#activate)()
activates the layout immediately. In contrast, calling
[invalidate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#invalidate)() is
delayed, as it posts a
[LayoutRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event to the
managed widget. Due to event compression, the
[activate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#activate)() will only
be called once after control has returned to the event loop. This is referred to as
*invalidating* the layout. Invalidating the layout also invalidates any cached
information. Also, the
[invalidate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#invalidate)()
function is a virtual function. So, you can invalidate your own cache in a subclass of
QGraphicsLayout by reimplementing this function.

### Event Handling

QGraphicsLayout listens to events for the widget it manages through the virtual
[widgetEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#widgetEvent)()
event handler. When the layout is assigned to a widget, all events delivered to the
widget are first processed by
[widgetEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#widgetEvent)().
This allows the layout to be aware of any relevant state changes on the widget such as
visibility changes or layout direction changes.

### Margin Handling

The margins of a QGraphicsLayout can be modified by reimplementing
[setContentsMargins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#setContentsMargins)()
and
[getContentsMargins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#getContentsMargins)().

### void QGraphicsLayout::activate()

Activates the layout, causing all items in the layout to be immediately rearranged. This
function is based on calling
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#count)() and
[itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#itemAt)(), and then
calling
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setGeometry)()
on all items sequentially. When activated, the layout will adjust its geometry to its
parent's
[contentsRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#contentsRect)().
The parent will then invalidate any layout of its own.

If called in sequence or recursively, e.g., by one of the arranged items in response to
being resized, this function will do nothing.

Note that the layout is free to use geometry caching to optimize this process. To
forcefully invalidate any such cache, you can call
[invalidate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#invalidate)()
before calling activate().

**See also**
[invalidate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#invalidate)().

### `[pure virtual]` void QGraphicsLayout::removeAt(int *index*)

This pure virtual function must be reimplemented in a subclass of
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout)
to remove the item at *index*. The reimplementation can assume that *index* is valid
(i.e., it respects the value of
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#count)()).

The implementation must ensure that the
[parentLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#parentLayoutItem)()
of the removed item does not point to this layout, since the item is considered to be
removed from the layout hierarchy.

If the layout is to be reused between applications, we recommend that the layout deletes
the item, but the graphics view framework does not depend on this.

The subclass is free to decide how to store the items.

**See also** [itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#itemAt)()
and [count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayout.html#count)().

## Detailed Description

QGraphicsLayoutItem is an abstract class that defines a set of virtual functions
describing sizes, size policies, and size hints for any object arranged by
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout).
The API contains functions relevant for both the item itself and for the user of the
item as most of QGraphicsLayoutItem's functions are also part of the subclass' public
API.

In most cases, existing layout-aware classes such as
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
and
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout)
already provide the functionality you require. However, subclassing these classes will
enable you to create both graphical elements that work well with layouts
([QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget))
or custom layouts
([QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout)).

### Subclassing QGraphicsLayoutItem

If you create a subclass of QGraphicsLayoutItem and reimplement its virtual functions,
you will enable the layout to resize and position your item along with other
QGraphicsLayoutItems including
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
and
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout).

You can start by reimplementing important functions: the protected
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#sizeHint)()
function, as well as the public
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setGeometry)()
function. If you want your items to be aware of immediate geometry changes, you can also
reimplement
[updateGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#updateGeometry)().

The geometry, size hint, and size policy affect the item's size and position. Calling
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setGeometry)()
will always resize and reposition the item immediately. Normally, this function is
called by
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout)
after the layout has been activated, but it can also be called by the item's user at any
time.

The [sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#sizeHint)()
function returns the item' minimum, preferred and maximum size hints. You can override
these properties by calling
[setMinimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setMinimumSize)(),
[setPreferredSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setPreferredSize)()
or
[setMaximumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setMaximumSize)().
You can also use functions such as
[setMinimumWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setMinimumWidth)()
or
[setMaximumHeight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setMaximumHeight)()
to set only the width or height component if desired.

The
[effectiveSizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#effectiveSizeHint)()
function, on the other hand, returns a size hint for any given
[Qt::SizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#SizeHint-enum), and guarantees
that the returned size is bound to the minimum and maximum sizes and size hints. You can
set the item's vertical and horizontal size policy by calling
[setSizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setSizePolicy)().
The [sizePolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#sizePolicy)
property is used by the layout system to describe how this item prefers to grow or
shrink.

### Nesting QGraphicsLayoutItems

QGraphicsLayoutItems can be nested within other QGraphicsLayoutItems, similar to layouts
that can contain sublayouts. This is done either by passing a QGraphicsLayoutItem
pointer to QGraphicsLayoutItem's protected constructor, or by calling
[setParentLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setParentLayoutItem)().
The
[parentLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#parentLayoutItem)()
function returns a pointer to the item's layoutItem parent. If the item's parent is
`nullptr` or if the parent does not inherit from
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html), the
[parentLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#parentLayoutItem)()
function then returns `nullptr`.
[isLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#isLayout)()
returns `true` if the QGraphicsLayoutItem subclass is itself a layout, or false
otherwise.

Qt uses QGraphicsLayoutItem to provide layout functionality in the [Graphics View
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html), but in the future its
use may spread throughout Qt itself.

### [QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizef.html) QGraphicsLayoutItem::effectiveSizeHint([Qt::SizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#SizeHint-enum) *which*, const [QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizef.html) \&*constraint* \= QSizeF()) const

Returns the effective size hint for this
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html).

*which* is the size hint in question. *constraint* is an optional argument that defines
a special constrain when calculating the effective size hint. By default, *constraint*
is [QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizef.html)(-1, -1), which means there
is no constraint to the size hint.

If you want to specify the widget's size hint for a given width or height, you can
provide the fixed dimension in *constraint*. This is useful for widgets that can grow
only either vertically or horizontally, and need to set either their width or their
height to a special value.

For example, a text paragraph item fit into a column width of 200 may grow vertically.
You can pass [QSizeF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsizef.html)(200, -1) as a
constraint to get a suitable minimum, preferred and maximum height).

You can adjust the effective size hint by reimplementing
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#sizeHint)() in a
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html)
subclass, or by calling one of the following functions:
[setMinimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setMinimumSize)(),
[setPreferredSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setPreferredSize),
or
[setMaximumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setMaximumSize)()
(or a combination of both).

This function caches each of the size hints and guarantees that
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#sizeHint)() will
be called only once for each value of *which* \- unless *constraint* is not specified
and
[updateGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#updateGeometry)()
has been called.

**See also**
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#sizeHint)().

### bool QGraphicsLayoutItem::ownedByLayout() const

Returns whether a layout should delete this item in its destructor. If its true, then
the layout will delete it. If its false, then it is assumed that another object has the
ownership of it, and the layout won't delete this item.

If the item inherits both
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) and
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html) (such
as
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
does) the item is really part of two ownership hierarchies. This property informs what
the layout should do with its child items when it is destructed. In the case of
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget),
it is preferred that when the layout is deleted it won't delete its children (since they
are also part of the graphics item hierarchy).

By default this value is initialized to false in
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html), but
it is overridden by
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout)
to return true. This is because
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout)
is not normally part of the
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) hierarchy, so the
parent layout should delete it. Subclasses might override this default behaviour by
calling
[setOwnedByLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setOwnedByLayout)(true).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.6.

**See also**
[setOwnedByLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setOwnedByLayout)().

### `[virtual]` void QGraphicsLayoutItem::setGeometry(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rect*)

This virtual function sets the geometry of the
[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html) to
*rect*, which is in parent coordinates (e.g., the top-left corner of *rect* is
equivalent to the item's position in parent coordinates).

[QGraphicsLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html) to
receive geometry updates. The layout will call this function when it does a
rearrangement.

[minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#minimumSize)
and
[maximumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#maximumSize),
it will be adjusted to its closest size so that it is within the legal bounds.

[geometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#geometry)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The default orientation for a linear layout is
[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum). You can
choose a vertical orientation either by calling
[setOrientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#setOrientation)(),
or by passing
[Qt::Vertical](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) to
QGraphicsLinearLayout's constructor.

The most common way to use QGraphicsLinearLayout is to construct an object on the heap
with no parent, add widgets and layouts by calling
[addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#addItem)(), and
finally assign the layout to a widget by calling
[QGraphicsWidget::setLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#setLayout)().

```
QGraphicsScene scene;
QGraphicsWidget *textEdit = scene.addWidget(new QTextEdit);
QGraphicsWidget *pushButton = scene.addWidget(new QPushButton);

QGraphicsLinearLayout *layout = new QGraphicsLinearLayout;
layout->addItem(textEdit);
layout->addItem(pushButton);

QGraphicsWidget *form = new QGraphicsWidget;
form->setLayout(layout);
scene.addItem(form);
```

You can add widgets, layouts, stretches
([addStretch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#addStretch)(),
[insertStretch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#insertStretch)()
or
[setStretchFactor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#setStretchFactor)()),
and spacings
([setItemSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#setItemSpacing)())
to a linear layout. The layout takes ownership of the items. In some cases when the
layout item also inherits from
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) (such as
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget))
there will be a ambiguity in ownership because the layout item belongs to two ownership
hierarchies. See the documentation of
[QGraphicsLayoutItem::setOwnedByLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslayoutitem.html#setOwnedByLayout)()
how to handle this. You can access each item in the layout by calling
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#count)() and
[itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#itemAt)().
Calling
[removeAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#removeAt)() or
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#removeItem)()
will remove an item from the layout, without destroying it.

### Size Hints and Size Policies in QGraphicsLinearLayout

QGraphicsLinearLayout respects each item's size hints and size policies, and when the
layout contains more space than the items can fill, each item is arranged according to
the layout's alignment for that item. You can set an alignment for each item by calling
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#setAlignment)(),
and check the alignment for any item by calling
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#alignment)().
By default, items are aligned to the top left.

### Spacing within QGraphicsLinearLayout

Between the items, the layout distributes some space. The actual amount of space depends
on the managed widget's current style, but the common spacing is 4\. You can also set
your own spacing by calling
[setSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#setSpacing)(),
and get the current spacing value by calling
[spacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#spacing)(). If
you want to configure individual spacing for your items, you can call
[setItemSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicslinearlayout.html#setItemSpacing)().

### Stretch Factor in QGraphicsLinearLayout

You can assign a stretch factor to each item to control how much space it will get
compared to the other items. By default, two identical widgets arranged in a linear
layout will have the same size, but if the first widget has a stretch factor of 1 and
the second widget has a stretch factor of 2, the first widget will get 1/3 of the
available space, and the second will get 2/3.

QGraphicsLinearLayout calculates the distribution of sizes by adding up the stretch
factors of all items, and then dividing the available space accordingly. The default
stretch factor is 0 for all items; a factor of 0 means the item does not have any
defined stretch factor; effectively this is the same as setting the stretch factor to
1\. The stretch factor only applies to the available space in the lengthwise direction
of the layout (following its orientation). If you want to control both the item's
horizontal and vertical stretch, you can use
[QGraphicsGridLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsgridlayout.html)
instead.

### QGraphicsLinearLayout Compared to Other Layouts

QGraphicsLinearLayout is very similar to
[QVBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvboxlayout.html) and
[QHBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhboxlayout.html), but in contrast to
these classes, it is used to manage
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
and
[QGraphicsLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicslayout)
instead of [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and
[QLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html).

## Detailed Description

The class extends a
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) with
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html)'s signal/slot and property
mechanisms. It maps many of
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html)'s basic setters
and getters to properties and adds notification signals for many of them.

### Parents and Children

Each graphics object can be constructed with a parent item. This ensures that the item
will be destroyed when its parent item is destroyed. Although QGraphicsObject inherits
from both [QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html) and
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html), you should use
the functions provided by
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html), *not*
[QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html), to manage the relationships
between parent and child items.

The relationships between items can be explored using the
[parentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#parentItem)() and
[childItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#childItems)()
functions. In the hierarchy of items in a scene, the
[parentObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#parentObject)() and
[parentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#parentWidget)()
functions are the equivalent of the
[QWidget::parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#parent)() and
[QWidget::parentWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#parentWidget)()
functions for [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) subclasses.

## Detailed Description

An opacity effect renders the source with an opacity. This effect is useful for making
the source semi-transparent, similar to a fade-in/fade-out sequence. The opacity can be
modified using the
[setOpacity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsopacityeffect.html#opacity-prop)()
function.

By default, the opacity is 0.7.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicseffect-opacity.png)

Qt 5 reference:

### opacityMask : [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html)

This property holds the opacity mask of the effect.

An opacity mask allows you apply opacity to portions of an element.

For example:

```
...
QLinearGradient alphaGradient(rect.topLeft(), rect.bottomLeft());
alphaGradient.setColorAt(0.0, Qt::transparent);
alphaGradient.setColorAt(0.5, Qt::black);
alphaGradient.setColorAt(1.0, Qt::transparent);
QGraphicsOpacityEffect *effect = new QGraphicsOpacityEffect;
effect->setOpacityMask(alphaGradient);
...
```

There is no opacity mask by default.

## Detailed Description

To set the item's path, pass a
[QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) to

[setPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspathitem.html#setPath)() function.

returns the current path.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-pathitem.png)

QGraphicsPathItem uses the path to provide a reasonable implementation of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspathitem.html#boundingRect)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspathitem.html#shape)(), and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspathitem.html#contains)(). The
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspathitem.html#paint)() function
draws the path using the item's associated pen and brush, which you can set by calling
the
[setPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setPen)()
and
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setBrush)()

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsPixmapItem.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

To set the item's pixmap, pass a
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) to QGraphicsPixmapItem's
constructor, or call the
[setPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#setPixmap)()
function. The
[pixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#pixmap)() function
returns the current pixmap.

QGraphicsPixmapItem uses pixmap's optional alpha mask to provide a reasonable
implementation of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#boundingRect)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#shape)(), and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#contains)().

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-pixmapitem.png)

The pixmap is drawn at the item's (0, 0\) coordinate, as returned by
[offset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#offset)(). You can
change the drawing offset by calling
[setOffset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#setOffset)().

You can set the pixmap's transformation mode by calling
[setTransformationMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#setTransformationMode)().
By default,
[Qt::FastTransformation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TransformationMode-enum)
is used, which provides fast, non-smooth scaling.
[Qt::SmoothTransformation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TransformationMode-enum)
enables
[QPainter::SmoothPixmapTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#RenderHint-enum)
on the painter, and the quality depends on the platform and viewport. The result is
usually not as good as calling QPixmap::scale() directly. Call
[transformationMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspixmapitem.html#transformationMode)()
to get the current transformation mode for the item.

## Detailed Description

To set the item's polygon, pass a
[QPolygonF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpolygonf.html) to QGraphicsPolygonItem's
constructor, or call the
[setPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html#setPolygon)()
function. The
[polygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html#polygon)()
function returns the current polygon.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-polygonitem.png)

QGraphicsPolygonItem uses the polygon and the pen width to provide a reasonable
implementation of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html#boundingRect)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html#shape)(), and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html#contains)(). The
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicspolygonitem.html#paint)() function
draws the polygon using the item's associated pen and brush, which you can set by
calling the
[setPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setPen)()
and
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setBrush)()
functions.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsProxyWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QGraphicsProxyWidget embeds
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html)-based widgets, for example, a
[QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html),
[QFontComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontcombobox.html), or even
[QFileDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html), into
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html). It forwards
events between the two objects and translates between
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html)'s integer-based geometry and
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)'s
qreal-based geometry. QGraphicsProxyWidget supports all core features of
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), including tab focus,
keyboard input, Drag \& Drop, and popups. You can also embed complex widgets, e.g.,
widgets with subwidgets.

Example:

```
int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    QApplication app(argc, argv);

    QTabWidget *tabWidget = new QTabWidget;

    QGraphicsScene scene;
    QGraphicsProxyWidget *proxy = scene.addWidget(tabWidget);

    QGraphicsView view(&scene);
    view.show();

    return app.exec();
}
```

QGraphicsProxyWidget takes care of automatically embedding popup children of embedded
widgets through creating a child proxy for each popup. This means that when an embedded
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html) shows its popup list, a
new QGraphicsProxyWidget is created automatically, embedding the popup, and positioning
it correctly. This only works if the popup is child of the embedded widget (for example
[QToolButton::setMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#setMenu)()
requires the [QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) instance to be child
of the [QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html)).

### Embedding a Widget with QGraphicsProxyWidget

There are two ways to embed a widget using QGraphicsProxyWidget. The most common way is
to pass a widget pointer to
[QGraphicsScene::addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addWidget)()
together with any relevant
[Qt::WindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum). This
function returns a pointer to a QGraphicsProxyWidget. You can then choose to reparent or
position either the proxy, or the embedded widget itself.

For example, in the code snippet below, we embed a group box into the proxy:

```
QGroupBox *groupBox = new QGroupBox("Contact Details");
QLabel *numberLabel = new QLabel("Telephone number");
QLineEdit *numberEdit = new QLineEdit;

QFormLayout *layout = new QFormLayout;
layout->addRow(numberLabel, numberEdit);
groupBox->setLayout(layout);

QGraphicsScene scene;
QGraphicsProxyWidget *proxy = scene.addWidget(groupBox);

QGraphicsView view(&scene);
view.show();
```

The image below is the output obtained with its contents margin and contents rect
labeled.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qgraphicsproxywidget-embed.png)

Alternatively, you can start by creating a new QGraphicsProxyWidget item, and then call
[setWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html#setWidget)() to
embed a [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) later. The
[widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html#widget)() function
returns a pointer to the embedded widget. QGraphicsProxyWidget shares ownership with
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), so if either of the two
widgets are destroyed, the other widget will be automatically destroyed as well.

### Synchronizing Widget States

QGraphicsProxyWidget keeps its state in sync with the embedded widget. For example, if
the proxy is hidden or disabled, the embedded widget will be hidden or disabled as well,
and vice versa. When the widget is embedded by calling addWidget(), QGraphicsProxyWidget
copies the state from the widget into the proxy, and after that, the two will stay
synchronized where possible. By default, when you embed a widget into a proxy, both the
widget and the proxy will be visible because a
[QGraphicsWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html#qgraphicswidget)
is visible when created (you do not have to call
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#show)()). If you explicitly
hide the embedded widget, the proxy will also become invisible.

Example:

```
QGraphicsScene scene;

QLineEdit *edit = new QLineEdit;
QGraphicsProxyWidget *proxy = scene.addWidget(edit);

edit->isVisible();  // returns true
proxy->isVisible(); // also returns true

edit->hide();

edit->isVisible();  // returns false
proxy->isVisible(); // also returns false
```

QGraphicsProxyWidget maintains symmetry for the following states:

| [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) state | QGraphicsProxyWidget state | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [QWidget::enabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::enabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html#enabled-prop) |  |
| [QWidget::visible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#visible-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::visible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html#visible-prop) | The explicit state is also symmetric. |
| [QWidget::geometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#geometry-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::geometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#geometry-prop) | Geometry is only guaranteed to be symmetric while the embedded widget is visible. |
| [QWidget::layoutDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#layoutDirection-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::layoutDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#layoutDirection-prop) |  |
| [QWidget::style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#style) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#style) |  |
| [QWidget::palette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#palette-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::palette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#palette-prop) |  |
| [QWidget::font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#font-prop) |  |
| [QWidget::cursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#cursor-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::cursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#cursor) | The embedded widget overrides the proxy widget cursor. The proxy cursor changes depending on which embedded subwidget is currently under the mouse. |
| [QWidget::sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop)() | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html#sizeHint)() | All size hint functionality from the embedded widget is forwarded by the proxy. |
| QWidget::getContentsMargins() | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::getContentsMargins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#getContentsMargins)() | Updated once by [setWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html#setWidget)(). |
| [QWidget::windowTitle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowTitle-prop) | [QGraphicsProxyWidget::windowTitle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicswidget.html#windowTitle-prop) | Updated once by [setWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html#setWidget)(). |

**Note:** [QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) keeps
the embedded widget in a special state that prevents it from disturbing other widgets
(both embedded and not embedded) while the widget is embedded. In this state, the widget
may differ slightly in behavior from when it is not embedded.

**Warning:** This class is provided for convenience when bridging QWidgets and
QGraphicsItems, it should not be used for high-performance scenarios. In particular,
embedding widgets into a scene that is then displayed through a
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) that uses an
OpenGL viewport will not work for all combinations.

### void QGraphicsProxyWidget::setWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**widget*)

Embeds *widget* into this proxy widget. The embedded widget must reside exclusively
either inside or outside of Graphics View. You cannot embed a widget as long as it is is
visible elsewhere in the UI, at the same time.

*widget* must be a top-level widget whose parent is `nullptr`.

When the widget is embedded, its state (e.g., visible, enabled, geometry, size hints) is
copied into the proxy widget. If the embedded widget is explicitly hidden or disabled,
the proxy widget will become explicitly hidden or disabled after embedding is complete.
The class documentation has a full overview over the shared state.

[QGraphicsProxyWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html)'s
window flags determine whether the widget, after embedding, will be given window
decorations or not.

After this function returns,
[QGraphicsProxyWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html)
will keep its state synchronized with that of *widget* whenever possible.

If a widget is already embedded by this proxy when this function is called, that widget
will first be automatically unembedded. Passing `nullptr` for the *widget* argument will
only unembed the widget, and the ownership of the currently embedded widget will be
passed on to the caller. Every child widget that are embedded will also be embedded and
their proxy widget destroyed.

Note that widgets with the
[Qt::WA\_PaintOnScreen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
widget attribute set and widgets that wrap an external application or controller cannot
be embedded. Examples are
[QOpenGLWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwidget.html) and QAxWidget.

**See also**
[widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsproxywidget.html#widget)().

## Detailed Description

To set the item's rectangle, pass a
[QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) to QGraphicsRectItem's
constructor, or call the
[setRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html#setRect)() function.
The [rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html#rect)() function
returns the current rectangle.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/graphicsview-rectitem.png)

QGraphicsRectItem uses the rectangle and the pen width to provide a reasonable
implementation of
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html#boundingRect)(),
[shape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html#shape)(), and
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html#contains)(). The
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrectitem.html#paint)() function
draws the rectangle using the item's associated pen and brush, which you can set by
calling the
[setPen](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setPen)()
and
[setBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractgraphicsshapeitem.html#setBrush)()
functions.

**Note:** The rendering of invalid rectangles, such as those with negative widths or
heights, is undefined. If you cannot be sure that you are using valid rectangles (for
example, if you are creating rectangles using data from an unreliable source) then you
should use
[QRectF::normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html#normalized)() to
create normalized rectangles, and use those instead.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsRotation.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

You can provide the desired axis by assigning a
[QVector3D](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvector3d.html) to the axis property or
by passing a member if [Qt::Axis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Axis-enum)
to the [setAxis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrotation.html#axis-prop)
convenience function. By default the axis is (0, 0, 1\) i.e., rotation around the Z
axis.

The angle property, which is provided by QGraphicsRotation, now describes the number of
degrees to rotate around this axis.

QGraphicsRotation provides certain parameters to help control how the rotation should be
applied.

The origin is the point that the item is rotated around (i.e., it stays fixed relative
to the parent as the rest of the item is rotated). By default the origin is
[QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html)(0, 0).

The angle property provides the number of degrees to rotate the item clockwise around
the origin. This value also be negative, indicating a counter-clockwise rotation. For
animation purposes it may also be useful to provide rotation angles exceeding (-360,
360\) degrees, for instance to animate how an item rotates several times.

Note: the final rotation is the combined effect of a rotation in 3D space followed by a
projection back to 2D. If several rotations are performed in succession, they will not
behave as expected unless they were all around the Z axis.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsRotation.angle.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### angle : [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef)

This property holds the angle for clockwise rotation, in degrees.

The angle can be any real number; the default value is 0.0. A value of 180 will rotate
180 degrees, clockwise. If you provide a negative number, the item will be rotated
counter-clockwise. Normally the rotation angle will be in the range (-360, 360), but you
can also provide numbers outside of this range (e.g., a angle of 370 degrees gives the
same result as 10 degrees). Setting the angle to NaN results in no rotation.

This property holds a rotation axis, specified by a vector in 3D space.

### void QGraphicsRotation::setAxis([Qt::Axis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Axis-enum) *axis*)

Convenience function to set the axis to *axis*.

Note: the [Qt::YAxis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Axis-enum) rotation for
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) is inverted from the
correct mathematical rotation in 3D space. The
[QGraphicsRotation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsrotation.html) class
implements a correct mathematical rotation. The following two sequences of code will
perform the same transformation:

```
QTransform t;

QGraphicsRotation r;
r.setAxis(Qt::YAxis);
r.setAngle(-45);
```

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsScale.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) provides
certain parameters to help control how the scale should be applied.

The origin is the point that the item is scaled from (i.e., it stays fixed relative to
the parent as the rest of the item grows). By default the origin is
[QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html)(0, 0).

The parameters
[xScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscale.html#xScale-prop),
[yScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscale.html#yScale-prop), and
[zScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscale.html#zScale-prop) describe
the scale factors to apply in horizontal, vertical, and depth directions. They can take
on any value, including 0 (to collapse the item to a point) or negative value. A
negative [xScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscale.html#xScale-prop)
value will mirror the item horizontally. A negative
[yScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscale.html#yScale-prop) value will
flip the item vertically. A negative
[zScale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscale.html#zScale-prop) will flip
the item end for end.

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsScene.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The class serves as a container for QGraphicsItems. It is used together with
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) for visualizing
graphical items, such as lines, rectangles, text, or even custom items, on a 2D surface.
QGraphicsScene is part of the [Graphics View
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/graphicsview.html).

QGraphicsScene also provides functionality that lets you efficiently determine both the
location of items, and for determining what items are visible within an arbitrary area
on the scene. With the
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) widget, you can
either visualize the whole scene, or zoom in and view only parts of the scene.

Example:

```
QGraphicsScene scene;
scene.addText("Hello, world!");

QGraphicsView view(&scene);
view.show();
```

Note that QGraphicsScene has no visual appearance of its own; it only manages the items.
You need to create a
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html) widget to
visualize the scene.

To add items to a scene, you start off by constructing a QGraphicsScene object. Then,
you have two options: either add your existing
[QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) objects by
calling [addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addItem)(), or
you can call one of the convenience functions
[addEllipse](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addEllipse)(),
[addLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addLine)(),
[addPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addPath)(),
[addPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addPixmap)(),
[addPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addPolygon)(),
[addRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addRect)(), or
[addText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#addText)(), which all
return a pointer to the newly added item. The dimensions of the items added with these
functions are relative to the item's coordinate system, and the items position is
initialized to (0, 0\) in the scene.

You can then visualize the scene using
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html). When the scene
changes, (e.g., when an item moves or is transformed) QGraphicsScene emits the
[changed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#changed)() signal. To
remove an item, call
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#removeItem)().

QGraphicsScene uses an indexing algorithm to manage the location of items efficiently.
By default, a BSP (Binary Space Partitioning) tree is used; an algorithm suitable for
large scenes where most items remain static (i.e., do not move around). You can choose
to disable this index by calling
[setItemIndexMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#itemIndexMethod-prop)().
For more information about the available indexing algorithms, see the
[itemIndexMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#itemIndexMethod-prop)
property.

The scene's bounding rect is set by calling
[setSceneRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#sceneRect-prop)().
Items can be placed at any position on the scene, and the size of the scene is by
default unlimited. The scene rect is used only for internal bookkeeping, maintaining the
scene's item index. If the scene rect is unset, QGraphicsScene will use the bounding
area of all items, as returned by
[itemsBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#itemsBoundingRect)(),
as the scene rect. However,
[itemsBoundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#itemsBoundingRect)()
is a relatively time consuming function, as it operates by collecting positional
information for every item on the scene. Because of this, you should always set the
scene rect when operating on large scenes.

One of QGraphicsScene's greatest strengths is its ability to efficiently determine the
location of items. Even with millions of items on the scene, the
[items](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#items)() functions can
determine the location of an item within a few milliseconds. There are several overloads
to [items](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#items)(): one that
finds items at a certain position, one that finds items inside or intersecting with a
polygon or a rectangle, and more. The list of returned items is sorted by stacking
order, with the topmost item being the first item in the list. For convenience, there is
also an [itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#itemAt)()
function that returns the topmost item at a given position.

QGraphicsScene maintains selection information for the scene. To select items, call
[setSelectionArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#setSelectionArea)(),
and to clear the current selection, call
[clearSelection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#clearSelection)().
Call
[selectedItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#selectedItems)()
to get the list of all selected items.

### Event Handling and Propagation

Another responsibility that QGraphicsScene has, is to propagate events from
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html). To send an event
to a scene, you construct an event that inherits
[QEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html), and then send it using, for
example,
[QCoreApplication::sendEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#sendEvent)().
[event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#event)() is responsible
for dispatching the event to the individual items. Some common events are handled by
convenience event handlers. For example, key press events are handled by
[keyPressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#keyPressEvent)(),
and mouse press events are handled by
[mousePressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#mousePressEvent)().

Key events are delivered to the *focus item*. To set the focus item, you can either call
[setFocusItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#setFocusItem)(),
passing an item that accepts focus, or the item itself can call
[QGraphicsItem::setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setFocus)().
Call [focusItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#focusItem)() to
get the current focus item. For compatibility with widgets, the scene also maintains its
own focus information. By default, the scene does not have focus, and all key events are
discarded. If
[setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#setFocus)() is called,
or if an item on the scene gains focus, the scene automatically gains focus. If the
scene has focus,
[hasFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#hasFocus)() will
return true, and key events will be forwarded to the focus item, if any. If the scene
loses focus, (i.e., someone calls
[clearFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#clearFocus)()) while
an item has focus, the scene will maintain its item focus information, and once the
scene regains focus, it will make sure the last focus item regains focus.

For mouse-over effects, QGraphicsScene dispatches *hover events*. If an item accepts
hover events (see
[QGraphicsItem::acceptHoverEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#acceptHoverEvents)()),
it will receive a
[GraphicsSceneHoverEnter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
event when the mouse enters its area. As the mouse continues moving inside the item's
area, QGraphicsScene will send it
[GraphicsSceneHoverMove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
events. When the mouse leaves the item's area, the item will receive a
[GraphicsSceneHoverLeave](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
event.

All mouse events are delivered to the current *mouse grabber* item. An item becomes the
scene's mouse grabber if it accepts mouse events (see
[QGraphicsItem::acceptedMouseButtons](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#acceptedMouseButtons)())
and it receives a mouse press. It stays the mouse grabber until it receives a mouse
release when no other mouse buttons are pressed. You can call
[mouseGrabberItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#mouseGrabberItem)()
to determine what item is currently grabbing the mouse.

### void QGraphicsScene::addItem([QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) \**item*)

Adds or moves the *item* and all its children to this scene. This scene takes ownership
of the *item*.

If the item is visible (i.e.,
[QGraphicsItem::isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#isVisible)()
returns true), [QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html)
will emit [changed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#changed)()
once control goes back to the event loop.

If the item is already in a different scene, it will first be removed from its old
scene, and then added to this scene as a top-level.

[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) will send
ItemSceneChange notifications to *item* while it is added to the scene. If item does not
currently belong to a scene, only one notification is sent. If it does belong to scene
already (i.e., it is moved to this scene),
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) will send an
addition notification as the item is removed from its previous scene.

If the item is a panel, the scene is active, and there is no active panel in the scene,

### `[slot]` void QGraphicsScene::advance()

This slot *advances* the scene by one step, by calling
[QGraphicsItem::advance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#advance)()
for all items on the scene. This is done in two phases: in the first phase, all items
are notified that the scene is about to change, and in the second phase all items are
notified that they can move. In the first phase,
[QGraphicsItem::advance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#advance)()
is called passing a value of 0 as an argument, and 1 is passed in the second phase.

Note that you can also use the [Animation
Framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/animation-overview.html) for animations.

**See also**
[QGraphicsItem::advance](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#advance)()
and [QTimeLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeline.html).

### backgroundBrush : [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html)

This property holds the background brush of the scene.

Set this property to changes the scene's background to a different color, gradient or
texture. The default background brush is
[Qt::NoBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum). The
background is drawn before (behind) the items.

Example:

```
QGraphicsScene scene;
QGraphicsView view(&scene);
view.show();

// a blue background
scene.setBackgroundBrush(Qt::blue);

// a gradient background
QRadialGradient gradient(0, 0, 10);
gradient.setSpread(QGradient::RepeatSpread);
scene.setBackgroundBrush(gradient);
```

[QGraphicsScene::render](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#render)()
calls
[drawBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#drawBackground)()
to draw the scene background. For more detailed control over how the background is
drawn, you can reimplement
[drawBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#drawBackground)()
in a subclass of
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsScene.bspTreeDep.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bspTreeDepth : int

This property holds the depth of
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html)'s BSP index
tree

This property has no effect when
[NoIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#ItemIndexMethod-enum)
is used.

This value determines the depth of
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html)'s BSP tree. The
depth directly affects
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html)'s performance
and memory usage; the latter growing exponentially with the depth of the tree. With an
optimal tree depth,
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) can instantly
determine the locality of items, even for scenes with thousands or millions of items.
This also greatly improves rendering performance.

By default, the value is 0, in which case Qt will guess a reasonable default depth based
on the size, location and number of items in the scene. If these parameters change
frequently, however, you may experience slowdowns as
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) retunes the
depth internally. You can avoid potential slowdowns by fixating the tree depth through
setting this property.

The depth of the tree and the size of the scene rectangle decide the granularity of the
scene's partitioning. The size of each scene segment is determined by the following
algorithm:

```
QSizeF segmentSize = sceneRect().size() / pow(2, depth - 1);
```

The BSP tree has an optimal size when each segment contains between 0 and 10 items.

This property was introduced in Qt 4.3.

**Access functions:**

| int | **bspTreeDepth**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setBspTreeDepth**(int *depth*) |

**See also**
[itemIndexMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#itemIndexMethod-prop).

### `[signal]` void QGraphicsScene::focusItemChanged([QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) \**newFocusItem*, [QGraphicsItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html) \**oldFocusItem*, [Qt::FocusReason](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FocusReason-enum) *reason*)

This signal is emitted by
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) whenever focus
changes in the scene (i.e., when an item gains or loses input focus, or when focus
passes from one item to another). You can connect to this signal if you need to keep
track of when other items gain input focus. It is particularly useful for implementing
virtual keyboards, input methods, and cursor items.

*oldFocusItem* is a pointer to the item that previously had focus, or 0 if no item had
focus before the signal was emitted. *newFocusItem* is a pointer to the item that gained
input focus, or `nullptr` if focus was lost. *reason* is the reason for the focus change
(e.g., if the scene was deactivated while an input field had focus, *oldFocusItem* would
point to the input field item, *newFocusItem* would be `nullptr`, and *reason* would be
[Qt::ActiveWindowFocusReason](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FocusReason-enum).

PythonQt.QtGui.QGraphicsScene.focusOnTou.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### focusOnTouch : bool

This property holds whether items gain focus when receiving a *touch begin* event.

The usual behavior is to transfer focus only when an item is clicked. Often a tap on a
touchpad is interpreted as equivalent to a mouse click by the operating system,
generating a synthesized click event in response. However, at least on macOS you can
configure this behavior.

By default, [QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html)
also transfers focus when you touch on a trackpad or similar. If the operating system is
configured to not generate a synthetic mouse click on tapping the trackpad, this is
surprising. If the operating system does generate synthetic mouse clicks on tapping the
trackpad, the focus transfer on starting a touch gesture is unnecessary.

With focusOnTouch switched off,
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) behaves as one
would expect on macOS.

The default value is `true`, ensuring that the default behavior is just as in Qt
versions prior to 5.12. Set to `false` to prevent touch events from triggering focus
changes.

This property was introduced in Qt 5.12.

**Access functions:**

| bool | **focusOnTouch**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setFocusOnTouch**(bool *enabled*) |

### font : [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html)

This property holds the scene's default font

This property provides the scene's font. The scene font defaults to, and resolves all
its entries from,
[QApplication::font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#font).

If the scene's font changes, either directly through setFont() or indirectly when the
application font changes,
[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) first sends
itself a [FontChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event,
and it then sends [FontChange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
events to all top-level widget items in the scene. These items respond by resolving
their own fonts to the scene, and they then notify their children, who again notify
their children, and so on, until all widget items have updated their fonts.

Changing the scene font, (directly or indirectly through
[QApplication::setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setFont)(),)
automatically schedules a redraw the entire scene.

This property was introduced in Qt 4.4.

**Access functions:**

| QFont | **font**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setFont**(const QFont \&*font*) |

**See also** [QWidget::font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop),
[QApplication::setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#setFont)(),
[palette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#palette-prop), and
[style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#style)().

### foregroundBrush : [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html)

This property holds the foreground brush of the scene.

Change this property to set the scene's foreground to a different color, gradient or
texture.

The foreground is drawn after (on top of) the items. The default foreground brush is
[Qt::NoBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#BrushStyle-enum) ( i.e. the
foreground is not drawn).

Example:

```
QGraphicsScene scene;
QGraphicsView view(&scene);
view.show();

// a white semi-transparent foreground
scene.setForegroundBrush(QColor(255, 255, 255, 127));

// a grid foreground
scene.setForegroundBrush(QBrush(Qt::lightGray, Qt::CrossPattern));
```

[QGraphicsScene::render](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#render)()
calls
[drawForeground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#drawForeground)()
to draw the scene foreground. For more detailed control over how the foreground is
drawn, you can reimplement the
[drawForeground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#drawForeground)()
function in a [QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html)
subclass.

**Access functions:**

| QBrush | **foregroundBrush**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setForegroundBrush**(const QBrush \&*brush*) |

### itemIndexMethod : [ItemIndexMethod](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#ItemIndexMethod-enum)

This property holds the item indexing method.

[QGraphicsScene](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html) applies an
indexing algorithm to the scene, to speed up item discovery functions like
[items](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#items)() and
[itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#itemAt)(). Indexing is
most efficient for static scenes (i.e., where items don't move around). For dynamic
scenes, or scenes with many animated items, the index bookkeeping can outweigh the fast
lookup speeds.

For the common case, the default index method
[BspTreeIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsscene.html#ItemIndexMethod-enum)
works fine. If your scene uses many animations and you are experiencing slowness, you
can disable indexing by calling `setItemIndexMethod(NoIndex)`.
