Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QImageIOPlugin is a factory for creating
[QImageIOHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html) objects,
which are used internally by
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) and
[QImageWriter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html) to add support for
different image formats to Qt.

Writing an image I/O plugin is achieved by subclassing this base class, reimplementing
the pure virtual functions
[capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)()
and [create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#create)(), and
exporting the class with the
[Q\_PLUGIN\_METADATA](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtplugin.html#Q_PLUGIN_METADATA)()
macro. See [How to Create Qt
Plugins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/plugins-howto.html) for details.

An image format plugin can support three capabilities: reading
([CanRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum)),
writing
([CanWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum)) and
*incremental* reading
([CanReadIncremental](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum)).
Reimplement
[capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)() in
you subclass to expose the capabilities of your image format.

[create](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#create)() should create
an instance of your
[QImageIOHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html) subclass,
with the provided device and format properly set, and return this handler.

The json metadata file for the plugin needs to contain information about the image
formats the plugins supports, together with the corresponding MIME types (one for each
format). For a jpeg plugin, this could, for example, look as follows:

```
{
  "Keys": [ "jpg", "jpeg" ],
  "MimeTypes": [ "image/jpeg", "image/jpeg" ]
}
```

Different plugins can support different capabilities. For example, you may have one
plugin that supports reading the GIF format, and another that supports writing. Qt will
select the correct plugin for the job, depending on the return value of
[capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)().
If several plugins support the same capability, Qt will select one arbitrarily.

PythonQt.QtGui.QImageIOPlugin.capabiliti.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual]` [QImageIOPlugin::Capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum) QImageIOPlugin::capabilities([QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) \**device*, const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*format*) const

Returns the capabilities of the plugin, based on the data in *device* and the format
*format*. If *device* is `0`, it should simply report whether the format can be read or
written. Otherwise, it should attempt to determine whether the given format (or any
format supported by the plugin if *format* is empty) can be read from or written to
*device*. It should do this without changing the state of *device* (typically by using
[QIODevice::peek](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html#peek)()).

For example, if the
[QImageIOPlugin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html) supports the
BMP format, *format* is either empty or `"bmp"`, and the data in the device starts with
the characters `"BM"`, this function should return
[CanRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum). If
*format* is `"bmp"`, *device* is `0` and the handler supports both reading and writing,
this function should return
[CanRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum) \|
[CanWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#Capability-enum).

Format names are always given in lower case.

PythonQt.QtGui.QImageIOPlugin.create.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual]` [QImageIOHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html) \*QImageIOPlugin::create([QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) \**device*, const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*format* \= QByteArray()) const

Creates and returns a
[QImageIOHandler](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html) subclass,
with *device* and *format* set. The *format* must come from the values listed in the
`"Keys"` entry in the plugin metadata, or be empty. If it is empty, the data in *device*
must have been recognized by the
[capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)()
method (with a likewise empty format).

Format names are always given in lower case.

PythonQt.QtGui.QImageReader.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The most common way to read images is through
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) and
[QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html)'s constructors, or by calling
[QImage::load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#load)() and
[QPixmap::load](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#load)(). QImageReader is
a specialized class which gives you more control when reading images. For example, you
can read an image into a specific size by calling
[setScaledSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setScaledSize)(),
and you can select a clip rect, effectively loading only parts of an image, by calling
[setClipRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setClipRect)().
Depending on the underlying support in the image format, this can save memory and speed
up loading of images.

To read an image, you start by constructing a QImageReader object. Pass either a file
name or a device pointer, and the image format to QImageReader's constructor. You can
then set several options, such as the clip rect (by calling
[setClipRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setClipRect)()) and
scaled size (by calling
[setScaledSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setScaledSize)()).
[canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#canRead)() returns the
image if the QImageReader can read the image (i.e., the image format is supported and
the device is open for reading). Call
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)() to read the image.

If any error occurs when reading the image,
[read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)() will return a null
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html). You can then call
[error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#error)() to find the type
of error that occurred, or
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#errorString)() to get
a human readable description of what went wrong.

**Note:** QImageReader assumes exclusive control over the file or device that is
assigned. Any attempts to modify the assigned file or device during the lifetime of the
QImageReader object will yield undefined results.

### Formats

Call
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)()
for a list of formats that QImageReader can read. QImageReader supports all built-in
image formats, in addition to any image format plugins that support reading. Call
[supportedMimeTypes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedMimeTypes)()
to obtain a list of supported MIME types, which for example can be passed to
[QFileDialog::setMimeTypeFilters](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html#setMimeTypeFilters)().

QImageReader autodetects the image format by default, by looking at the provided
(optional) format string, the file name suffix, and the data stream contents. You can
enable or disable this feature, by calling
[setAutoDetectImageFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setAutoDetectImageFormat)().

### High Resolution Versions of Images

It is possible to provide high resolution versions of images should a scaling between
*device pixels* and *device independent pixels* be in effect.

The high resolution version is marked by the suffix `@2x` on the base name. The image
read will have its *device pixel ratio* set to a value of 2\.

This can be disabled by setting the environment variable
`QT_HIGHDPI_DISABLE_2X_IMAGE_LOADING`.

### bool QImageReader::canRead() const

Returns `true` if an image can be read for the device (i.e., the image format is
supported, and the device seems to contain valid data); otherwise returns `false`.

canRead() is a lightweight function that only does a quick test to see if the image data
is valid. [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)() may still
return false after canRead() returns `true`, if the image data is corrupt.

**Note:** A [QMimeDatabase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html)
lookup is normally a better approach than this function for identifying potentially
non-image files or data.

For images that support animation, canRead() returns `false` when all frames have been
read.

**See also** [read](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#read)(),
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)(),
and [QMimeDatabase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmimedatabase.html).

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) QImageReader::read()

Reads an image from the device. On success, the image that was read is returned;
otherwise, a null [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) is returned.
You can then call [error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#error)()
to find the type of error that occurred, or
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#errorString)() to get
a human readable description of the error.

For image formats that support animation, calling read() repeatedly will return the next
frame. When all frames have been read, a null image will be returned.

**See also** [canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#canRead)(),
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)(),
[supportsAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportsAnimation)(),
and [QMovie](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmovie.html).

### bool QImageReader::read([QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) \**image*)

This is an overloaded function.

Reads an image from the device into *image*, which must point to a
[QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html). Returns `true` on success;
otherwise, returns `false`.

If *image* has same format and size as the image data that is about to be read, this
function may not need to allocate a new image before reading. Because of this, it can be
faster than the other read() overload, which always constructs a new image; especially
when reading several images with the same format and size.

```
QImage icon(64, 64, QImage::Format_RGB32);
QImageReader reader("icon_64x64.bmp");
if (reader.read(&icon)) {
    // Display icon
}
```

For image formats that support animation, calling read() repeatedly will return the next
frame. When all frames have been read, a null image will be returned.

**See also** [canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#canRead)(),
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportedImageFormats)(),
[supportsAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#supportsAnimation)(),
and [QMovie](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmovie.html).

### void QImageReader::setAutoDetectImageFormat(bool *enabled*)

If *enabled* is true, image format autodetection is enabled; otherwise, it is disabled.
By default, autodetection is enabled.

[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) uses an extensive
approach to detecting the image format; firstly, if you pass a file name to
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html), it will attempt to
detect the file extension if the given file name does not point to an existing file, by
appending supported default extensions to the given file name, one at a time. It then
uses the following approach to detect the image format:

- Image plugins are queried first, based on either the optional format string, or the file name suffix (if the source device is a file). No content detection is done at this stage. [QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) will choose the first plugin that supports reading for this format.
- If no plugin supports the image format, Qt's built-in handlers are checked based on either the optional format string, or the file name suffix.
- If no capable plugins or built-in handlers are found, each plugin is tested by inspecting the content of the data stream.
- If no plugins could detect the image format based on data contents, each built-in image handler is tested by inspecting the contents.
- Finally, if all above approaches fail, [QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) will report failure when trying to read the image.

By disabling image format autodetection,
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html) will only query the
plugins and built-in handlers based on the format string (i.e., no file name extensions
are tested).

**See also**
[autoDetectImageFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#autoDetectImageFormat)(),
[QImageIOHandler::canRead](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageiohandler.html#canRead)(),
and
[QImageIOPlugin::capabilities](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimageioplugin.html#capabilities)().

### void QImageReader::setQuality(int *quality*)

Sets the quality setting of the image format to *quality*.

Some image formats, in particular lossy ones, entail a tradeoff between a) visual
quality of the resulting image, and b) decoding execution time. This function sets the
level of that tradeoff for image formats that support it.

In case of scaled image reading, the quality setting may also influence the tradeoff
level between visual quality and execution speed of the scaling algorithm.

The value range of *quality* depends on the image format. For example, the "jpeg" format
supports a quality range from 0 (low visual quality) to 100 (high visual quality).

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also** [quality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#quality)()
and
[setScaledSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html#setScaledSize)().

### `[static]` QList\<[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)\> QImageReader::supportedImageFormats()

Returns the list of image formats supported by
[QImageReader](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagereader.html).

By default, Qt can read the following formats:

| Format | MIME type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMP | image/bmp | Windows Bitmap |
| GIF | image/gif | Graphic Interchange Format (optional) |
| JPG | image/jpeg | Joint Photographic Experts Group |
| PNG | image/png | Portable Network Graphics |
| PBM | image/x-portable-bitmap | Portable Bitmap |
| PGM | image/x-portable-graymap | Portable Graymap |
| PPM | image/x-portable-pixmap | Portable Pixmap |
| XBM | image/x-xbitmap | X11 Bitmap |
| XPM | image/x-xpixmap | X11 Pixmap |
| SVG | image/svg\+xml | Scalable Vector Graphics |

Reading and writing SVG files is supported through the [Qt
SVG](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtsvg-index.html) module. The [Qt Image
Formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimageformats-index.html) module provides
support for additional image formats.

Note that the [QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html)
instance must be created before this function is called.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QImageWriter supports setting format specific options, such as compression level and
quality, prior to storing the image. If you do not need such options, you can use
[QImage::save](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#save)() or
[QPixmap::save](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#save)() instead.

To store an image, you start by constructing a QImageWriter object. Pass either a file
name or a device pointer, and the image format to QImageWriter's constructor. You can
then set several options, such as quality (by calling
[setQuality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#setQuality)()).
[canWrite](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#canWrite)() returns
`true` if QImageWriter can write the image (i.e., the image format is supported and the
device is open for writing). Call
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#write)() to write the image
to the device.

If any error occurs when writing the image,
[write](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#write)() will return false.
You can then call [error](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#error)()
to find the type of error that occurred, or
[errorString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#errorString)() to get
a human readable description of what went wrong.

Call
[supportedImageFormats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#supportedImageFormats)()
for a list of formats that QImageWriter can write. QImageWriter supports all built-in
image formats, in addition to any image format plugins that support writing.

**Note:** QImageWriter assumes exclusive control over the file or device that is
assigned. Any attempts to modify the assigned file or device during the lifetime of the
QImageWriter object will yield undefined results. If immediate access to a resource is
desired, the use of a scope is the recommended method.

For example:

```
    QString imagePath(QStringLiteral("path/image.jpeg"));
    QImage image(64, 64, QImage::Format_RGB32);
    image.fill(Qt::red);
    {
        QImageWriter writer(imagePath);
        writer.write(image);
    }

    QFile::rename(imagePath,
                  QStringLiteral("path/other_image.jpeg"));
```

### void QImageWriter::setDevice([QIODevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qiodevice.html) \**device*)

Sets [QImageWriter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html)'s device to

[QTcpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtcpsocket.html) and
[QUdpSocket](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qudpsocket.html), where more logic is
required to open the device.

[setFileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#setFileName)().

### void QImageWriter::setQuality(int *quality*)

Sets the quality setting of the image format to *quality*.

Some image formats, in particular lossy ones, entail a tradeoff between a) visual
quality of the resulting image, and b) encoding execution time and compression level.
This function sets the level of that tradeoff for image formats that support it. For
other formats, this value is ignored.

The value range of *quality* depends on the image format. For example, the "jpeg" format
supports a quality range from 0 (low visual quality, high compression) to 100 (high
visual quality, low compression).

**See also** [quality](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#quality)().

### void QImageWriter::setSubType(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*type*)

This is an image format specific function that sets the subtype of the image to *type*.
Subtype can be used by a handler to determine which format it should use while saving
the image.

For example, saving an image in DDS format with A8R8G8R8 subtype:

```
QImageWriter writer("some/image.dds");
if (writer.supportsOption(QImageIOHandler::SubType))
    writer.setSubType("A8R8G8B8");
writer.write(image);
```

This function was introduced in Qt 5.4.

**See also** [subType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimagewriter.html#subType)().

### void QImageWriter::setText(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*key*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*)

Sets the image text associated with the key *key* to *text*. This is useful for storing
copyright information or other information about the image. Example:

```

### `[static]` QList\<[QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html)\> QImageWriter::supportedImageFormats()

Returns the list of image formats supported by

By default, Qt can write the following formats:

| Format | MIME type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |

| XBM | image/x-xbitmap | X11 Bitmap |
| XPM | image/x-xpixmap | X11 Pixmap |

SVG](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtsvg-index.html) module. The [Qt Image
Formats](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimageformats-index.html) module provides
support for additional image formats.

## Detailed Description

The input value can be a string, a number or an item from a list. A label must be set to
tell the user what they should enter.

Five static convenience functions are provided:
[getText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getText)(),
[getMultiLineText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getMultiLineText)(),
[getInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getInt)(),
[getDouble](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getDouble)(), and
[getItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputdialog.html#getItem)(). All the
functions can be used in a similar way, for example:

```
    bool ok;
    QString text = QInputDialog::getText(this, tr("QInputDialog::getText()"),
                                         tr("User name:"), QLineEdit::Normal,
                                         QDir::home().dirName(), &ok);
    if (ok && !text.isEmpty())
        textLabel->setText(text);
```

The `ok` variable is set to true if the user clicks **OK**; otherwise, it is set to
false.

![Input Dialogs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/inputdialogs.png)

The [Standard
Dialogs](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-dialogs-standarddialogs-example.html)
example shows how to use QInputDialog as well as other built-in Qt dialogs.

Static convenience function to get a floating point number from the user.

*title* is the text which is displayed in the title bar of the dialog. *label* is the
text which is shown to the user (it should say what should be entered). *value* is the
default floating point number that the line edit will be set to. *min* and *max* are the
minimum and maximum values the user may choose. *decimals* is the maximum number of
decimal places the number may have. *step* is the amount by which the values change as
the user presses the arrow buttons to increment or decrement the value.

If *ok* is nonnull, \**ok* will be set to true if the user pressed **OK** and to false
if the user pressed **Cancel**. The dialog's parent is *parent*. The dialog will be
modal and uses the widget *flags*.

This function returns the floating point number which has been entered by the user.

Use this static function like this:

```
    bool ok;
    double d = QInputDialog::getDouble(this, tr("QInputDialog::getDouble()"),
                                       tr("Amount:"), 37.56, -10000, 10000, 2, &ok,
                                       Qt::WindowFlags(), 1);
    if (ok)
        doubleLabel->setText(QString("$%1").arg(d));
```

text which is shown to the user (it should say what should be entered). *items* is the
string list which is inserted into the combo box. *current* is the number of the item

current text of the combo box.

    bool ok;
    QString item = QInputDialog::getItem(this, tr("QInputDialog::getItem()"),
                                         tr("Season:"), items, 0, false, &ok);
    if (ok && !item.isEmpty())
        itemLabel->setText(item);

- [accepted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#accepted)() if *member* has NO arguments.

The signal will be disconnected from the slot when the dialog is closed.

property.

PythonQt.QtGui.QInputMethodEvent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Input method events are sent to widgets when an input method is used to enter text into
a widget. Input methods are widely used to enter text for languages with non-Latin
alphabets.

Note that when creating custom text editing widgets, the
[Qt::WA\_InputMethodEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
window attribute must be set explicitly (using the
[QWidget::setAttribute](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setAttribute)()
function) in order to receive input method events.

The events are of interest to authors of keyboard entry widgets who want to be able to
correctly handle languages with complex character input. Text input in such languages is
usually a three step process:

1. **Starting to Compose**

   When the user presses the first key on a keyboard, an input context is created. This
   input context will contain a string of the typed characters.
2. **Composing**

   With every new key pressed, the input method will try to create a matching string for
   the text typed so far called preedit string. While the input context is active, the user
   can only move the cursor inside the string belonging to this input context.
3. **Completing**

   At some point, the user will activate a user interface component (perhaps using a
   particular key) where they can choose from a number of strings matching the text they
   have typed so far. The user can either confirm their choice cancel the input; in either
   case the input context will be closed.

QInputMethodEvent models these three stages, and transfers the information needed to
correctly render the intermediate result. A QInputMethodEvent has two main parameters:
[preeditString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#preeditString)()
and
[commitString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#commitString)().
The
[preeditString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#preeditString)()
parameter gives the currently active preedit string. The
[commitString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#commitString)()
parameter gives a text that should get added to (or replace parts of) the text of the
editor widget. It usually is a result of the input operations and has to be inserted to
the widgets text directly before the preedit string.

If the
[commitString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#commitString)()
should replace parts of the of the text in the editor,
[replacementLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#replacementLength)()
will contain the number of characters to be replaced.
[replacementStart](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#replacementStart)()
contains the position at which characters are to be replaced relative from the start of
the preedit string.

A number of attributes control the visual appearance of the preedit string (the visual
appearance of text outside the preedit string is controlled by the widget only). The
[AttributeType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#AttributeType-enum)
enum describes the different attributes that can be set.

A class implementing
[QWidget::inputMethodEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#inputMethodEvent)()
or
[QGraphicsItem::inputMethodEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#inputMethodEvent)()
should at least understand and honor the
[TextFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#AttributeType-enum)
and
[Cursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#AttributeType-enum)
attributes.

Since input methods need to be able to query certain properties from the widget or
graphics item, subclasses must also implement
[QWidget::inputMethodQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#inputMethodQuery)()
and
[QGraphicsItem::inputMethodQuery](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#inputMethodQuery)(),
respectively.

When receiving an input method event, the text widget has to performs the following
steps:

1. If the widget has selected text, the selected text should get removed.
2. Remove the text starting at [replacementStart](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#replacementStart)() with length [replacementLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#replacementLength)() and replace it by the [commitString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#commitString)(). If [replacementLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#replacementLength)() is 0, [replacementStart](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#replacementStart)() gives the insertion position for the [commitString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#commitString)().

   When doing replacement the area of the preedit string is ignored, thus a replacement
   starting at -1 with a length of 2 will remove the last character before the preedit
   string and the first character afterwards, and insert the commit string directly before
   the preedit string.

   If the widget implements undo/redo, this operation gets added to the undo stack.
3. If there is no current preedit string, insert the [preeditString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#preeditString)() at the current cursor position; otherwise replace the previous [preeditString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#preeditString) with the one received from this event.

   If the widget implements undo/redo, the
   [preeditString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#preeditString)()
   should not influence the undo/redo stack in any way.

   The widget should examine the list of attributes to apply to the preedit string. It has
   to understand at least the
   [TextFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodevent.html#AttributeType-enum)
   and Cursor attributes and render them as specified.

## Detailed Description

It is used by the input method to query a set of properties of the object to be able to
support complex input method operations as support for surrounding text and
reconversions.

[queries](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodqueryevent.html#queries)()
specifies which properties are queried.

The object should call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qinputmethodqueryevent.html#setValue)() on
the event to fill in the requested data before calling
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QIntValidator.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Example of use:

```
QValidator *validator = new QIntValidator(100, 999, this);
QLineEdit *edit = new QLineEdit(this);

// the edit lineedit will only accept integers between 100 and 999
edit->setValidator(validator);
```

Below we present some examples of validators. In practice they would normally be
associated with a widget as in the example above.

```
QString str;
int pos = 0;
QIntValidator v(100, 900, this);

str = "1";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Intermediate
str = "012";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Intermediate

str = "123";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Acceptable
str = "678";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Acceptable

str = "999";
v.validate(str, pos);    // returns Intermediate

str = "1234";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Invalid
str = "-123";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Invalid
str = "abc";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Invalid
str = "12cm";
v.validate(str, pos);     // returns Invalid
```

Notice that the value `999` returns Intermediate. Values consisting of a number of
digits equal to or less than the max value are considered intermediate. This is intended
because the digit that prevents a number from being in range is not necessarily the last
digit typed. This also means that an intermediate number can have leading zeros.

The minimum and maximum values are set in one call with
[setRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qintvalidator.html#setRange)(), or
individually with
[setBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qintvalidator.html#bottom-prop)() and
[setTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qintvalidator.html#top-prop)().

QIntValidator uses its
[locale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#locale)() to interpret the
number. For example, in Arabic locales, QIntValidator will accept Arabic digits.

**Note:** The
[QLocale::NumberOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#NumberOption-enum)
set on the [locale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#locale)() also
affect the way the number is interpreted. For example, since
[QLocale::RejectGroupSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#NumberOption-enum)
is not set by default, the validator will accept group separators. It is thus
recommended to use
[QLocale::toInt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlocale.html#toInt)() to obtain the
numeric value.

Qt 5 reference:

### `[override virtual]` [QValidator::State](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) QIntValidator::validate([QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*input*, int \&*pos*) const

Reimplements:
[QValidator::validate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#validate)(QString
\&input, int \&pos) const.

Returns [Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if
the *input* is an integer within the valid range. If *input* has at most as many digits
as the top of the range, or is a prefix of an integer in the valid range, returns
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).
Otherwise, returns
[Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).

If the valid range consists of just positive integers (e.g., 32 to 100\) and *input* is
a negative integer, then Invalid is returned. (On the other hand, if the range consists
of negative integers (e.g., -100 to -32) and *input* is a positive integer, then
Intermediate is returned, because the user might be just about to type the minus
(especially for right-to-left languages).

Similarly, if the valid range is between 46 and 53, then 41 and 59 will be evaluated as
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum), as
otherwise the user wouldn't be able to change a value from 49 to 51\.

```
int pos = 0;

s = "abc";
v.validate(s, pos);    // returns Invalid

s = "5";
v.validate(s, pos);    // returns Intermediate

s = "50";
v.validate(s, pos);    // returns Acceptable
```

By default, the *pos* parameter is not used by this validator.
signatures: validate(self, arg__1: str, arg__2: int) -> PySide2.QtGui.QValidator.State

PythonQt.QtGui.QItemDelegate.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QItemDelegate can be used to provide custom display features and editor widgets for item
views based on
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html)
subclasses. Using a delegate for this purpose allows the display and editing mechanisms
to be customized and developed independently from the model and view.

The QItemDelegate class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html). Note that
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html) has
taken over the job of drawing Qt's item views. We recommend the use of
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html) when
creating new delegates.

When displaying items from a custom model in a standard view, it is often sufficient to
simply ensure that the model returns appropriate data for each of the
[roles](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) that determine the
appearance of items in views. The default delegate used by Qt's standard views uses this
role information to display items in most of the common forms expected by users.
However, it is sometimes necessary to have even more control over the appearance of
items than the default delegate can provide.

This class provides default implementations of the functions for painting item data in a
view and editing data from item models. Default implementations of the
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#paint)() and
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#sizeHint)() virtual
functions, defined in
[QAbstractItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html),
are provided to ensure that the delegate implements the correct basic behavior expected
by views. You can reimplement these functions in subclasses to customize the appearance
of items.

When editing data in an item view, QItemDelegate provides an editor widget, which is a
widget that is placed on top of the view while editing takes place. Editors are created
with a [QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html);
a default static instance provided by
[QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html) is
installed on all item delegates. You can set a custom factory using
[setItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#setItemEditorFactory)()
or set a new default factory with
[QItemEditorFactory::setDefaultFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html#setDefaultFactory)().
It is the data stored in the item model with the
[Qt::EditRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) that is
edited.

Only the standard editing functions for widget-based delegates are reimplemented here:

- [createEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#createEditor)() returns the widget used to change data from the model and can be reimplemented to customize editing behavior.
- [setEditorData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#setEditorData)() provides the widget with data to manipulate.
- [updateEditorGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#updateEditorGeometry)() ensures that the editor is displayed correctly with respect to the item view.
- [setModelData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#setModelData)() returns updated data to the model.

The
[closeEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#closeEditor)()
signal indicates that the user has completed editing the data, and that the editor
widget can be destroyed.

### Standard Roles and Data Types

The default delegate used by the standard views supplied with Qt associates each
standard role (defined by
[Qt::ItemDataRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum)) with
certain data types. Models that return data in these types can influence the appearance
of the delegate as described in the following table.

| Role | Accepted Types |
| --- | --- |
| [Qt::BackgroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html) ( |
| [Qt::BackgroundColorRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) (obsolete; use [Qt::BackgroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) instead) |
| [Qt::CheckStateRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [Qt::CheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#CheckState-enum) |
| [Qt::DecorationRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html), [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) and [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) |
| [Qt::DisplayRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) and types with a string representation |
| [Qt::EditRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | See [QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html) for details |
| [Qt::FontRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) |
| [Qt::SizeHintRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsize.html) |
| [Qt::TextAlignmentRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [Qt::Alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum) |
| [Qt::ForegroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QBrush](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbrush.html) ( |
| [Qt::TextColorRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) | [QColor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html) (obsolete; use [Qt::ForegroundRole](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemDataRole-enum) instead) |

If the default delegate does not allow the level of customization that you need, either
for display purposes or for editing data, it is possible to subclass QItemDelegate to
implement the desired behavior.

### Subclassing

When subclassing QItemDelegate to create a delegate that displays items using a custom
renderer, it is important to ensure that the delegate can render items suitably for all
the required states; e.g. selected, disabled, checked. The documentation for the
[paint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#paint)() function contains
some hints to show how this can be achieved.

You can provide custom editors by using a
[QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html). The
[Color Editor Factory
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-itemviews-coloreditorfactory-example.html)
shows how a custom editor can be made available to delegates with the default item
editor factory. This way, there is no need to subclass QItemDelegate. An alternative is
to reimplement
[createEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#createEditor)(),
[setEditorData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#setEditorData)(),
[setModelData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#setModelData)(),
and
[updateEditorGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemdelegate.html#updateEditorGeometry)().
This process is described in the [Spin Box Delegate
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-itemviews-spinboxdelegate-example.html).

### QStyledItemDelegate vs. QItemDelegate

Since Qt 4.4, there are two delegate classes: QItemDelegate and
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html).
However, the default delegate is
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html).
These two classes are independent alternatives to painting and providing editors for
items in views. The difference between them is that
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html) uses
the current style to paint its items. We therefore recommend using
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html) as
the base class when implementing custom delegates or when working with Qt style sheets.
The code required for either class should be equal unless the custom delegate needs to
use the style for drawing.

Returns `true` if the given *editor* is a valid
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) and the given *event* is
handled; otherwise returns `false`. The following key press events are handled by
default:

- **Tab**
- **Backtab**
- **Enter**
- **Return**
- **Esc**

In the case of **Tab**, **Backtab**, **Enter** and **Return** key press events, the
*editor*'s data is committed to the model and the editor is closed. If the *event* is a
**Tab** key press the view will open an editor on the next item in the view. Likewise,
if the *event* is a **Backtab** key press the view will open an editor on the *previous*
item in the view.

If the event is a **Esc** key press event, the *editor* is closed *without* committing
its data.

**See also**
[commitData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#commitData)()
and
[closeEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html#closeEditor)().

## Detailed Description

QItemEditorCreatorBase objects are specialized widget factories that provide editor
widgets for one particular [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)
data type. They are used by
[QItemEditorFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html) to
create editors for
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html)s.
Creator bases must be registered with
[QItemEditorFactory::registerEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html#registerEditor)().

An editor should provide a user property for the data it edits. QItemDelagates can then
access the property using Qt's [meta-object
system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/metaobjects.html) to set and retrieve the
editing data. A property is set as the user property with the USER keyword:

```
Q_PROPERTY(QColor color READ color WRITE setColor USER true)
```

If the editor does not provide a user property, it must return the name of the property
from
[valuePropertyName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorcreatorbase.html#valuePropertyName)();
delegates will then use the name to access the property. If a user property exists, item
delegates will not call
[valuePropertyName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorcreatorbase.html#valuePropertyName)().

[QStandardItemEditorCreator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstandarditemeditorcreator.html)
is a convenience template class that can be used to register widgets without the need to
subclass QItemEditorCreatorBase.

## Detailed Description

When editing data in an item view, editors are created and displayed by a delegate.
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html),
which is the delegate by default installed on Qt's item views, uses a QItemEditorFactory
to create editors for it. A default unique instance provided by QItemEditorFactory is
used by all item delegates. If you set a new default factory with
[setDefaultFactory](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html#setDefaultFactory)(),
the new factory will be used by existing and new delegates.

A factory keeps a collection of
[QItemEditorCreatorBase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorcreatorbase.html)
instances, which are specialized editors that produce editors for one particular
[QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html) data type (All Qt models
store their data in [QVariant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvariant.html)s).

### Standard Editing Widgets

The standard factory implementation provides editors for a variety of data types. These
are created whenever a delegate needs to provide an editor for data supplied by a model.
The following table shows the relationship between types and the standard editors
provided.

| Type | Editor Widget |
| --- | --- |
| bool | [QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html) |
| double | [QDoubleSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html) |
| int | [QSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html) |
| unsigned int |
| [QDate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdate.html) | [QDateEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdateedit.html) |
| [QDateTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetime.html) | [QDateTimeEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html) |
| [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) | [QLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html) |
| [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) | [QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html) |
| [QTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtime.html) | [QTimeEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimeedit.html) |

Additional editors can be registered with the
[registerEditor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemeditorfactory.html#registerEditor)()
function.

## Detailed Description

A QItemSelection describes the items in a model that have been selected by the user. A
QItemSelection is basically a list of selection ranges, see
[QItemSelectionRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html). It
provides functions for creating and manipulating selections, and selecting a range of
items from a model.

The QItemSelection class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

An item selection can be constructed and initialized to contain a range of items from an
existing model. The following example constructs a selection that contains a range of
items from the given `model`, beginning at the `topLeft`, and ending at the
`bottomRight`.

```
QItemSelection *selection = new QItemSelection(topLeft, bottomRight);
```

An empty item selection can be constructed, and later populated as required. So, if the
model is going to be unavailable when we construct the item selection, we can rewrite
the above code in the following way:

```
QItemSelection *selection = new QItemSelection();
...
selection->select(topLeft, bottomRight);
```

QItemSelection saves memory, and avoids unnecessary work, by working with selection
ranges rather than recording the model item index for each item in the selection.
Generally, an instance of this class will contain a list of non-overlapping selection
ranges.

Use [merge](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselection.html#merge)() to merge one
item selection into another without making overlapping ranges. Use
[split](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselection.html#split)() to split one
selection range into smaller ranges based on a another selection range.

## Detailed Description

A QItemSelectionModel keeps track of the selected items in a view, or in several views
onto the same model. It also keeps track of the currently selected item in a view.

The QItemSelectionModel class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

The selected items are stored using ranges. Whenever you want to modify the selected
items use [select](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#select)()
and provide either a
[QItemSelection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselection.html), or a
[QModelIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmodelindex.html) and a
[QItemSelectionModel::SelectionFlag](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#SelectionFlag-enum).

The QItemSelectionModel takes a two layer approach to selection management, dealing with
both selected items that have been committed and items that are part of the current
selection. The current selected items are part of the current interactive selection (for
example with rubber-band selection or keyboard-shift selections).

To update the currently selected items, use the bitwise OR of
[QItemSelectionModel::Current](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#SelectionFlag-enum)
and any of the other
[SelectionFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#SelectionFlag-enum).
If you omit the
[QItemSelectionModel::Current](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#SelectionFlag-enum)
command, a new current selection will be created, and the previous one added to the
whole selection. All functions operate on both layers; for example,
[selecteditems()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtablewidget.html#selectedItems)
will return items from both layers.

**Note:** Since 5.5,
[model](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#model),
[hasSelection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#hasSelection),
and
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#currentIndex)
are meta-object properties.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QItemSelectionRange contains information about a range of selected items in a model. A
range of items is a contiguous array of model items, extending to cover a number of
adjacent rows and columns with a common parent item; this can be visualized as a
two-dimensional block of cells in a table. A selection range has a
[top](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#top)(),
[left](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#left)() a
[bottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#bottom)(),
[right](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#right)() and a
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#parent)().

The QItemSelectionRange class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

The model items contained in the selection range can be obtained using the
[indexes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#indexes)()
function. Use
[QItemSelectionModel::selectedIndexes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionmodel.html#selectedIndexes)()
to get a list of all selected items for a view.

You can determine whether a given model item lies within a particular range by using the
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#contains)()
function. Ranges can also be compared using the overloaded operators for equality and
inequality, and the
[intersects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qitemselectionrange.html#intersects)()
function allows you to determine whether two ranges overlap.

## Detailed Description

Key events are sent to the widget with keyboard input focus when keys are pressed or
released.

A key event contains a special accept flag that indicates whether the receiver will
handle the key event. This flag is set by default for
[QEvent::KeyPress](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[QEvent::KeyRelease](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum), so there
is no need to call [accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)()
when acting on a key event. For
[QEvent::ShortcutOverride](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) the
receiver needs to explicitly accept the event to trigger the override. Calling
[ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() on a key event will
propagate it to the parent widget. The event is propagated up the parent widget chain
until a widget accepts it or an event filter consumes it.

The
[QWidget::setEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop)()
function can be used to enable or disable mouse and keyboard events for a widget.

The event handlers
[QWidget::keyPressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#keyPressEvent)(),
[QWidget::keyReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#keyReleaseEvent)(),
[QGraphicsItem::keyPressEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#keyPressEvent)()
and
[QGraphicsItem::keyReleaseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#keyReleaseEvent)()
receive key events.

### int QKeyEvent::key() const

Returns the code of the key that was pressed or released.

See [Qt::Key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum) for the list of
keyboard codes. These codes are independent of the underlying window system. Note that
this function does not distinguish between capital and non-capital letters, use the
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeyevent.html#text)() function (returning the
Unicode text the key generated) for this purpose.

A value of either 0 or
[Qt::Key\_unknown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum) means that the
event is not the result of a known key; for example, it may be the result of a compose
sequence, a keyboard macro, or due to key event compression.

**See also**
[Qt::WA\_KeyCompression](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum).

## Detailed Description

In its most common form, a key sequence describes a combination of keys that must be
used together to perform some action. Key sequences are used with
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) objects to specify which
keyboard shortcuts can be used to trigger actions.

Key sequences can be constructed for use as keyboard shortcuts in three different ways:

- For standard shortcuts, a [standard key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#StandardKey-enum) can be used to request the platform-specific key sequence associated with each shortcut.
- For custom shortcuts, human-readable strings such as "Ctrl\+X" can be used, and these can be translated into the appropriate shortcuts for users of different languages. Translations are made in the "[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html)" context.
- For hard-coded shortcuts, integer key codes can be specified with a combination of values defined by the [Qt::Key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum) and [Qt::Modifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum) enum values. Each key code consists of a single [Qt::Key](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum) value and zero or more modifiers, such as [Qt::SHIFT](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum), [Qt::CTRL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum), [Qt::ALT](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum) and [Qt::META](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum).

For example, **Ctrl P** might be a sequence used as a shortcut for printing a document,
and can be specified in any of the following ways:

```
QKeySequence(QKeySequence::Print);
QKeySequence(tr("Ctrl+P"));
QKeySequence(tr("Ctrl+p"));
QKeySequence(Qt::CTRL + Qt::Key_P);
```

Note that, for letters, the case used in the specification string does not matter. In
the above examples, the user does not need to hold down the **Shift** key to activate a
shortcut specified with "Ctrl\+P". However, for other keys, the use of **Shift** as an
unspecified extra modifier key can lead to confusion for users of an application whose
keyboards have different layouts to those used by the developers. See the [Keyboard
Layout
Issues](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#keyboard-layout-issues)
section below for more details.

It is preferable to use standard shortcuts where possible. When creating key sequences
for non-standard shortcuts, you should use human-readable strings in preference to
hard-coded integer values.

QKeySequence objects can be cast to a
[QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) to obtain a human-readable
translated version of the sequence. Similarly, the
[toString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#toString)() function
produces human-readable strings for use in menus. On macOS, the appropriate symbols are
used to describe keyboard shortcuts using special keys on the Macintosh keyboard.

An alternative way to specify hard-coded key codes is to use the Unicode code point of
the character; for example, 'A' gives the same key sequence as
[Qt::Key\_A](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum).

**Note:** On macOS, references to "Ctrl",
[Qt::CTRL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum),
[Qt::Key\_Control](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum) and
[Qt::ControlModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#KeyboardModifier-enum)
correspond to the **Command** keys on the Macintosh keyboard, and references to "Meta",
[Qt::META](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum),
[Qt::Key\_Meta](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum) and
[Qt::MetaModifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#KeyboardModifier-enum)
correspond to the **Control** keys. Developers on macOS can use the same shortcut
descriptions across all platforms, and their applications will automatically work as
expected on macOS.

### Keyboard Layout Issues

Many key sequence specifications are chosen by developers based on the layout of certain
types of keyboard, rather than choosing keys that represent the first letter of an
action's name, such as **Ctrl S** ("Ctrl\+S") or **Ctrl C** ("Ctrl\+C"). Additionally,
because certain symbols can only be entered with the help of modifier keys on certain
keyboard layouts, key sequences intended for use with one keyboard layout may map to a
different key, map to no keys at all, or require an additional modifier key to be used
on different keyboard layouts.

For example, the shortcuts, **Ctrl plus** and **Ctrl minus**, are often used as
shortcuts for zoom operations in graphics applications, and these may be specified as
"Ctrl\+\+" and "Ctrl\+-" respectively. However, the way these shortcuts are specified
and interpreted depends on the keyboard layout. Users of Norwegian keyboards will note
that the **\+** and **\-** keys are not adjacent on the keyboard, but will still be able
to activate both shortcuts without needing to press the **Shift** key. However, users
with British keyboards will need to hold down the **Shift** key to enter the **\+**
symbol, making the shortcut effectively the same as "Ctrl\+Shift\+\=".

Although some developers might resort to fully specifying all the modifiers they use on
their keyboards to activate a shortcut, this will also result in unexpected behavior for
users of different keyboard layouts.

For example, a developer using a British keyboard may decide to specify
"Ctrl\+Shift\+\=" as the key sequence in order to create a shortcut that coincidentally
behaves in the same way as **Ctrl plus**. However, the **\=** key needs to be accessed
using the **Shift** key on Norwegian keyboard, making the required shortcut effectively
**Ctrl Shift Shift \=** (an impossible key combination).

As a result, both human-readable strings and hard-coded key codes can both be
problematic to use when specifying a key sequence that can be used on a variety of
different keyboard layouts. Only the use of [standard
shortcuts](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#StandardKey-enum)
guarantees that the user will be able to use the shortcuts that the developer intended.

Despite this, we can address this issue by ensuring that human-readable strings are
used, making it possible for translations of key sequences to be made for users of
different languages. This approach will be successful for users whose keyboards have the
most typical layout for the language they are using.

### GNU Emacs Style Key Sequences

Key sequences similar to those used in [GNU Emacs](http://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/),
allowing up to four key codes, can be created by using the multiple argument
constructor, or by passing a human-readable string of comma-separated key sequences.

For example, the key sequence, **Ctrl X** followed by **Ctrl C**, can be specified using
either of the following ways:

```
QKeySequence(tr("Ctrl+X, Ctrl+C"));
QKeySequence(Qt::CTRL + Qt::Key_X, Qt::CTRL + Qt::Key_C);
```

**Warning:** A [QApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html)
instance must have been constructed before a QKeySequence is created; otherwise, your
application may crash.

### `[static]` [QKeySequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#QKeySequence) QKeySequence::mnemonic(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*)

Returns the shortcut key sequence for the mnemonic in *text*, or an empty key sequence
if no mnemonics are found.

For example, mnemonic("E\&xit") returns `Qt::ALT+Qt::Key_X`, mnemonic("\&Quit") returns
`ALT+Key_Q`, and mnemonic("Quit") returns an empty
[QKeySequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html).

We provide a [list of common
mnemonics](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/accelerators.html) in English. At the time

### [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) QKeySequence::toString([QKeySequence::SequenceFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#SequenceFormat-enum) *format* \= PortableText) const

Return a string representation of the key sequence, based on *format*.

For example, the value
[Qt::CTRL](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Modifier-enum)\+[Qt::Key\_O](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Key-enum)
results in "Ctrl\+O". If the key sequence has multiple key codes, each is separated by
commas in the string returned, such as "Alt\+X, Ctrl\+Y, Z". The strings, "Ctrl",
"Shift", etc. are translated using
[QObject::tr](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#tr)() in the
"[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html)" context.

If the key sequence has no keys, an empty string is returned.

On macOS, the string returned resembles the sequence that is shown in the menu bar if
*format* is
[QKeySequence::NativeText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#SequenceFormat-enum);
otherwise, the string uses the "portable" format, suitable for writing to a file.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also**
[fromString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#fromString)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QLCDNumber.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-lcdnumber.png)

It can display a number in just about any size. It can display decimal, hexadecimal,
octal or binary numbers. It is easy to connect to data sources using the
[display](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#display)() slot, which is
overloaded to take any of five argument types.

There are also slots to change the base with
[setMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#mode-prop)() and the
decimal point with
[setSmallDecimalPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#smallDecimalPoint-prop)().

QLCDNumber emits the
[overflow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#overflow)() signal when it
is asked to display something beyond its range. The range is set by
[setDigitCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#setDigitCount)(), but
[setSmallDecimalPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#smallDecimalPoint-prop)()
also influences it. If the display is set to hexadecimal, octal or binary, the integer
equivalent of the value is displayed.

These digits and other symbols can be shown: 0/O, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5/S, 6, 7, 8, 9/g, minus,
decimal point, A, B, C, D, E, F, h, H, L, o, P, r, u, U, Y, colon, degree sign (which is
specified as single quote in the string) and space. QLCDNumber substitutes spaces for
illegal characters.

It is not possible to retrieve the contents of a QLCDNumber object, although you can
retrieve the numeric value with
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#value-prop)(). If you really
need the text, we recommend that you connect the signals that feed the
[display](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlcdnumber.html#display)() slot to another
slot as well and store the value there.

Incidentally, QLCDNumber is the very oldest part of Qt, tracing its roots back to a
BASIC program on the [Sinclair
Spectrum](http://www.nvg.ntnu.no/sinclair/computers/zxspectrum/zxspectrum.htm).

PythonQt.QtGui.QLabel.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-label.png)

QLabel is used for displaying text or an image. No user interaction functionality is
provided. The visual appearance of the label can be configured in various ways, and it
can be used for specifying a focus mnemonic key for another widget.

A QLabel can contain any of the following content types:

| Content | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| Plain text | Pass a [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) to [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#text-prop)(). |
| Rich text | Pass a [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) that contains rich text to [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#text-prop)(). |
| A pixmap | Pass a [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) to [setPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#pixmap-prop)(). |
| A movie | Pass a [QMovie](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmovie.html) to [setMovie](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#setMovie)(). |
| A number | Pass an *int* or a *double* to [setNum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#setNum)(), which converts the number to plain text. |
| Nothing | The same as an empty plain text. This is the default. Set by [clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#clear)(). |

**Warning:** When passing a [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)
to the constructor or calling
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#text-prop)(), make sure to
sanitize your input, as QLabel tries to guess whether it displays the text as plain text
or as rich text, a subset of HTML 4 markup. You may want to call
[setTextFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#textFormat-prop)()
explicitly, e.g. in case you expect the text to be in plain format but cannot control
the text source (for instance when displaying data loaded from the Web).

When the content is changed using any of these functions, any previous content is
cleared.

By default, labels display [left-aligned,
vertically-centered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet-reference.html#alignment)
text and images, where any tabs in the text to be displayed are [automatically
expanded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFlag-enum). However, the look
of a QLabel can be adjusted and fine-tuned in several ways.

The positioning of the content within the QLabel widget area can be tuned with
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#alignment-prop)() and
[setIndent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#indent-prop)(). Text content
can also wrap lines along word boundaries with
[setWordWrap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#wordWrap-prop)(). For
example, this code sets up a sunken panel with a two-line text in the bottom right
corner (both lines being flush with the right side of the label):

```
QLabel *label = new QLabel(this);
label->setFrameStyle(QFrame::Panel | QFrame::Sunken);
label->setText("first line\nsecond line");
label->setAlignment(Qt::AlignBottom | Qt::AlignRight);
```

The properties and functions QLabel inherits from
[QFrame](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html) can also be used to specify the
widget frame to be used for any given label.

A QLabel is often used as a label for an interactive widget. For this use QLabel
provides a useful mechanism for adding an mnemonic (see
[QKeySequence](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html)) that will set the
keyboard focus to the other widget (called the QLabel's "buddy"). For example:

```
QLineEdit *phoneEdit = new QLineEdit(this);
QLabel *phoneLabel = new QLabel("&Phone:", this);
phoneLabel->setBuddy(phoneEdit);
```

In this example, keyboard focus is transferred to the label's buddy (the
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html)) when the user presses
Alt\+P. If the buddy was a button (inheriting from
[QAbstractButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html)), triggering
the mnemonic would emulate a button click.

PythonQt.QtGui.QLabel.indent.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### indent : int

This property holds the label's text indent in pixels

If a label displays text, the indent applies to the left edge if
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#alignment-prop)() is
[Qt::AlignLeft](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum), to the
right edge if
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#alignment-prop)() is
[Qt::AlignRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum), to the
top edge if [alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#alignment-prop)()
is [Qt::AlignTop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum), and to
the bottom edge if
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#alignment-prop)() is
[Qt::AlignBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#AlignmentFlag-enum).

If indent is negative, or if no indent has been set, the label computes the effective
indent as follows: If
[frameWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#frameWidth-prop)() is 0, the
effective indent becomes 0\. If
[frameWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#frameWidth-prop)() is
greater than 0, the effective indent becomes half the width of the "x" character of the
widget's current [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop)().

By default, the indent is -1, meaning that an effective indent is calculating in the
manner described above.

**Access functions:**

| int | **indent**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setIndent**(*int*) |

**See also**
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/stylesheet-reference.html#alignment),
[margin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#margin-prop),
[frameWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qframe.html#frameWidth-prop)(), and
[font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop)().

Qt 5 reference:

### void QLabel::setBuddy([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**buddy*)

Sets this label's buddy to *buddy*.

When the user presses the shortcut key indicated by this label, the keyboard focus is
transferred to the label's buddy widget.

The buddy mechanism is only available for QLabels that contain text in which one
character is prefixed with an ampersand, '\&'. This character is set as the shortcut
key. See the
[QKeySequence::mnemonic](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qkeysequence.html#mnemonic)()
documentation for details (to display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&').

In a dialog, you might create two data entry widgets and a label for each, and set up
the geometry layout so each label is just to the left of its data entry widget (its
"buddy"), for example:

```
QLineEdit *nameEdit  = new QLineEdit(this);
QLabel    *nameLabel = new QLabel("&Name:", this);
nameLabel->setBuddy(nameEdit);
QLineEdit *phoneEdit  = new QLineEdit(this);
QLabel    *phoneLabel = new QLabel("&Phone:", this);
phoneLabel->setBuddy(phoneEdit);
// (layout setup not shown)
```

With the code above, the focus jumps to the Name field when the user presses Alt\+N, and
to the Phone field when the user presses Alt\+P.

To unset a previously set buddy, call this function with *buddy* set to nullptr.

**See also** [buddy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#buddy)(),
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#text-prop)(),
[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html), and
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#alignment-prop)().

### text : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the label's text

If no text has been set this will return an empty string. Setting the text clears any
previous content.

The text will be interpreted either as plain text or as rich text, depending on the text
format setting; see
[setTextFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html#textFormat-prop)(). The
default setting is
[Qt::AutoText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TextFormat-enum); i.e.
[QLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html) will try to auto-detect the
format of the text set. See [Supported HTML
Subset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/richtext-html-subset.html) for the definition
of rich text.

If a buddy has been set, the buddy mnemonic key is updated from the new text.

Note that [QLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html) is well-suited to
display small rich text documents, such as small documents that get their document
specific settings (font, text color, link color) from the label's palette and font
properties. For large documents, use
[QTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) in read-only mode
instead. [QTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) can also provide
a scroll bar when necessary.

**Note:** This function enables mouse tracking if *text* contains rich text.

PythonQt.QtGui.QLayout.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This is an abstract base class inherited by the concrete classes
[QBoxLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qboxlayout.html),
[QGridLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgridlayout.html),
[QFormLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qformlayout.html), and
[QStackedLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstackedlayout.html).

For users of QLayout subclasses or of
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) there is seldom any
need to use the basic functions provided by QLayout, such as
[setSizeConstraint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#sizeConstraint-prop)()
or [setMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#setMenuBar)(). See
[Layout Management](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/layout.html) for more
information.

To make your own layout manager, implement the functions
[addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#addItem)(),
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#sizeHint)(),
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#setGeometry)(),
[itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#itemAt)() and
[takeAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#takeAt)(). You should also
implement [minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#minimumSize)()

support children whose heights depend on their widths, implement

Layout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-layouts-borderlayout-example.html)

Layout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-layouts-flowlayout-example.html)
