PythonQt.QtGui.QLayout.replaceWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#QLayoutItem) \*QLayout::replaceWidget([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**from*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**to*, [Qt::FindChildOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FindChildOption-enum) *options* \= Qt::FindChildrenRecursively)

Searches for widget *from* and replaces it with widget *to* if found. Returns the layout
item that contains the widget *from* on success. Otherwise `nullptr` is returned. If
*options* contains `Qt::FindChildrenRecursively` (the default), sub-layouts are searched
for doing the replacement. Any other flag in *options* is ignored.

Notice that the returned item therefore might not belong to this layout, but to a
sub-layout.

The returned layout item is no longer owned by the layout and should be either deleted
or inserted to another layout. The widget *from* is no longer managed by the layout and
may need to be deleted or hidden. The parent of widget *from* is left unchanged.

This function works for the built-in Qt layouts, but might not work for custom layouts.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.2.

**See also** [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#indexOf)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QLayout.takeAt.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[pure virtual]` [QLayoutItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#QLayoutItem) \*QLayout::takeAt(int *index*)

Must be implemented in subclasses to remove the layout item at *index* from the layout,
and return the item. If there is no such item, the function must do nothing and return
0\. Items are numbered consecutively from 0\. If an item is removed, other items will be
renumbered.

The following code fragment shows a safe way to remove all items from a layout:

```
QLayoutItem *child;
while ((child = layout->takeAt(0)) != nullptr) {
    ...
    delete child->widget(); // delete the widget
    delete child;   // delete the layout item
}
```

**See also** [itemAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#itemAt)() and
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#count)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QLayoutItem.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

This is used by custom layouts.

Pure virtual functions are provided to return information about the layout, including,
[sizeHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#sizeHint)(),
[minimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#minimumSize)(),
[maximumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#maximumSize)() and
expanding().

The layout's geometry can be set and retrieved with
[setGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#setGeometry)() and
[geometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#geometry)(), and its
alignment with
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#setAlignment)() and
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#alignment)().

[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#isEmpty)() returns whether
the layout item is empty. If the concrete item is a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), it can be retrieved using
[widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#widget)(). Similarly for
[layout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#layout)() and
[spacerItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#spacerItem)().

Some layouts have width and height interdependencies. These can be expressed using
[hasHeightForWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#hasHeightForWidth)(),
[heightForWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#heightForWidth)(),
and
[minimumHeightForWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayoutitem.html#minimumHeightForWidth)().
For more explanation see the *Qt Quarterly* article [Trading Height for
Width](http://doc.qt.io/archives/qq/qq04-height-for-width.html).

PythonQt.QtGui.QLineEdit.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-lineedit.png)

A line edit allows the user to enter and edit a single line of plain text with a useful
collection of editing functions, including undo and redo, cut and paste, and drag and
drop (see
[setDragEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#dragEnabled-prop)()).

By changing the
[echoMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#echoMode-prop)() of a line
edit, it can also be used as a "write-only" field, for inputs such as passwords.

The length of the text can be constrained to
[maxLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#maxLength-prop)(). The
text can be arbitrarily constrained using a
[validator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#validator)() or an
[inputMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#inputMask-prop)(), or
both. When switching between a validator and an input mask on the same line edit, it is
best to clear the validator or input mask to prevent undefined behavior.

A related class is [QTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) which
allows multi-line, rich text editing.

You can change the text with
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() or
[insert](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#insert)(). The text is
retrieved with [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)();
the displayed text (which may be different, see
[EchoMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum)) is
retrieved with
[displayText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#displayText-prop)().
Text can be selected with
[setSelection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#setSelection)() or
[selectAll](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#selectAll)(), and the
selection can be [cut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#cut)(),
[copy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#copy)()ied and
[paste](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#paste)()d. The text can be
aligned with
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#alignment-prop)().

When the text changes the
[textChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#textChanged)() signal is
emitted; when the text changes other than by calling
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() the
[textEdited](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#textEdited)() signal is
emitted; when the cursor is moved the
[cursorPositionChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#cursorPositionChanged)()
signal is emitted; and when the Return or Enter key is pressed the
[returnPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#returnPressed)()
signal is emitted.

When editing is finished, either because the line edit lost focus or Return/Enter is
pressed the
[editingFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#editingFinished)()
signal is emitted.

Note that if there is a validator set on the line edit, the
[returnPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#returnPressed)()/[editingFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#editingFinished)()
signals will only be emitted if the validator returns
[QValidator::Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).

By default, QLineEdits have a frame as specified by platform style guides; you can turn
it off by calling
[setFrame](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#frame-prop)(false).

The default key bindings are described below. The line edit also provides a context menu
(usually invoked by a right mouse click) that presents some of these editing options.

| Keypress | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Left Arrow | Moves the cursor one character to the left. |
| Shift\+Left Arrow | Moves and selects text one character to the left. |
| Right Arrow | Moves the cursor one character to the right. |
| Shift\+Right Arrow | Moves and selects text one character to the right. |
| Home | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the line. |
| End | Moves the cursor to the end of the line. |
| Backspace | Deletes the character to the left of the cursor. |
| Ctrl\+Backspace | Deletes the word to the left of the cursor. |
| Delete | Deletes the character to the right of the cursor. |
| Ctrl\+Delete | Deletes the word to the right of the cursor. |
| Ctrl\+A | Select all. |
| Ctrl\+C | Copies the selected text to the clipboard. |
| Ctrl\+Insert | Copies the selected text to the clipboard. |
| Ctrl\+K | Deletes to the end of the line. |
| Ctrl\+V | Pastes the clipboard text into line edit. |
| Shift\+Insert | Pastes the clipboard text into line edit. |
| Ctrl\+X | Deletes the selected text and copies it to the clipboard. |
| Shift\+Delete | Deletes the selected text and copies it to the clipboard. |
| Ctrl\+Z | Undoes the last operation. |
| Ctrl\+Y | Redoes the last undone operation. |

Any other key sequence that represents a valid character, will cause the character to be
inserted into the line edit.

### `[override virtual protected]` void QLineEdit::contextMenuEvent([QContextMenuEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcontextmenuevent.html) \**event*)

Reimplements:
[QWidget::contextMenuEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#contextMenuEvent)(QContextMenuEvent
\*event).

Shows the standard context menu created with
[createStandardContextMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#createStandardContextMenu)().

If you do not want the line edit to have a context menu, you can set its
[contextMenuPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#contextMenuPolicy-prop)
to
[Qt::NoContextMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ContextMenuPolicy-enum).
If you want to customize the context menu, reimplement this function. If you want to
extend the standard context menu, reimplement this function, call
[createStandardContextMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#createStandardContextMenu)()
and extend the menu returned.

```
void LineEdit::contextMenuEvent(QContextMenuEvent *event)
{
    QMenu *menu = createStandardContextMenu();
    menu->addAction(tr("My Menu Item"));
    //...
    menu->exec(event->globalPos());
    delete menu;
}
```

The *event* parameter is used to obtain the position where the mouse cursor was when the
event was generated.

**See also**
[setContextMenuPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#contextMenuPolicy-prop)().

### cursorMoveStyle : [Qt::CursorMoveStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#CursorMoveStyle-enum)

This property holds the movement style of cursor in this line edit.

When this property is set to
[Qt::VisualMoveStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#CursorMoveStyle-enum),
the line edit will use visual movement style. Pressing the left arrow key will always
cause the cursor to move left, regardless of the text's writing direction. The same
behavior applies to right arrow key.

[Qt::LogicalMoveStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#CursorMoveStyle-enum)
(the default), within a LTR text block, increase cursor position when pressing left
arrow key, decrease cursor position when pressing the right arrow key. If the text block
is right to left, the opposite behavior applies.

This property was introduced in Qt 4.8.

### echoMode : [EchoMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum)

This property holds the line edit's echo mode.

The echo mode determines how the text entered in the line edit is displayed (or echoed)
to the user.

The most common setting is
[Normal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum), in which the
text entered by the user is displayed verbatim, but
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html) also supports modes that
allow the entered text to be suppressed or obscured: these include
[NoEcho](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum),
[Password](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum) and
[PasswordEchoOnEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum).

The widget's display and the ability to copy or drag the text is affected by this
setting.

By default, this property is set to
[Normal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#EchoMode-enum).

**Access functions:**

| --- | --- |

PythonQt.QtGui.QLineEdit.inputMask.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### inputMask : [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html)

This property holds the validation input mask.

If no mask is set, inputMask() returns an empty string.

Sets the [QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html)'s validation
mask. Validators can be used instead of, or in conjunction with masks; see
[setValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#setValidator)().

Unset the mask and return to normal
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html) operation by passing an
empty string ("").

The input mask is an input template string. It can contain the following elements:

| Mask Characters | Defines the [Category](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#Category-enum) of input characters that are considered valid in this position |
| --- | --- |
| Meta Characters | Various special meanings |
| Separators | All other characters are regarded as immutable separators |

The following table shows the mask and meta characters that can be used in an input
mask.

| Mask Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `A` | character of the Letter category required, such as A-Z, a-z. |
| `a` | character of the Letter category permitted but not required. |
| `N` | character of the Letter or Number category required, such as A-Z, a-z, 0-9. |
| `n` | character of the Letter or Number category permitted but not required. |
| `X` | Any non-blank character required. |
| `x` | Any non-blank character permitted but not required. |
| `9` | character of the Number category required, e.g 0-9. |
| `0` | character of the Number category permitted but not required. |
| `D` | character of the Number category and larger than zero required, such as 1-9 |
| `d` | character of the Number category and larger than zero permitted but not required, such as 1-9. |
| `#` | character of the Number category, or plus/minus sign permitted but not required. |
| `H` | Hexadecimal character required. A-F, a-f, 0-9. |
| `h` | Hexadecimal character permitted but not required. |
| `B` | Binary character required. 0-1. |
| `b` | Binary character permitted but not required. |
| Meta Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `>` | All following alphabetic characters are uppercased. |
| `<` | All following alphabetic characters are lowercased. |
| `!` | Switch off case conversion. |
| `;c` | Terminates the input mask and sets the *blank* character to *c*. |
| `[ ] { }` | Reserved. |
| `\` | Use `\` to escape the special characters listed above to use them as separators. |

When created or cleared, the line edit will be filled with a copy of the input mask
string where the meta characters have been removed, and the mask characters have been
replaced with the *blank* character (by default, a `space`).

When an input mask is set, the
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() method returns a
modified copy of the line edit content where all the *blank* characters have been
removed. The unmodified content can be read using
[displayText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#displayText-prop)().

The
[hasAcceptableInput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#acceptableInput-prop)()
method returns false if the current content of the line edit does not fulfil the
requirements of the input mask.

Examples:

| Mask | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `000.000.000.000;_` | IP address; blanks are `_`. |
| `HH:HH:HH:HH:HH:HH;_` | MAC address |
| `0000-00-00` | ISO Date; blanks are `space` |
| `>AAAAA-AAAAA-AAAAA-AAAAA-AAAAA;#` | License number; blanks are `#` and all (alphabetic) characters are converted to uppercase. |

To get range control (e.g., for an IP address) use masks together with
[validators](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#setValidator).

**Access functions:**

| QString | **inputMask**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setInputMask**(const QString \&*inputMask*) |

**See also**
[maxLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#maxLength-prop),
[QChar::isLetter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#isLetter)(),
[QChar::isNumber](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#isNumber)(), and
[QChar::digitValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html#digitValue)().

### `[signal]` void QLineEdit::inputRejected()

This signal is emitted when the user presses a key that is not considered to be
acceptable input. For example, if a key press results in a validator's validate() call
to return Invalid. Another case is when trying to enter in more characters beyond the
maximum length of the line edit.

not all of it is. For example, if there is a maximum length set and the clipboard text
is longer than the maximum length when it is pasted.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.12.

### modified : bool

This property holds whether the line edit's contents has been modified by the user.

The modified flag is never read by
[QLineEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html); it has a default value
of false and is changed to true whenever the user changes the line edit's contents.

This is useful for things that need to provide a default value but do not start out
knowing what the default should be (perhaps it depends on other fields on the form).
Start the line edit without the best default, and when the default is known, if
modified() returns `false` (the user hasn't entered any text), insert the default value.

Calling [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#text-prop)() resets
the modified flag to false.

Setting this property makes the line edit display a grayed-out placeholder text as long

Normally, an empty line edit shows the placeholder text even when it has focus. However,

### void QLineEdit::setValidator(const [QValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html) \**v*)

Sets the validator for values of line edit to *v*.

The line edit's
[returnPressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#returnPressed)() and
[editingFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#editingFinished)()
signals will only be emitted if *v* validates the line edit's content as
[Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum). The user
may change the content to any
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) value
during editing, but will be prevented from editing the text to a value that *v*
validates as [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).

This allows you to constrain the text that shall finally be entered when editing is
done, while leaving users with enough freedom to edit the text from one valid state to
another.

If *v* \=\= 0, setValidator() removes the current input validator. The initial setting
is to have no input validator (i.e. any input is accepted up to
[maxLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#maxLength-prop)()).

**See also** [validator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#validator)(),
[hasAcceptableInput](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineedit.html#acceptableInput-prop)(),
[QIntValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qintvalidator.html),
[QDoubleValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublevalidator.html), and
[QRegExpValidator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregexpvalidator.html).

## Detailed Description

Linear gradients interpolate colors between start and end points. Outside these points
the gradient is either padded, reflected or repeated depending on the currently set
[spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) method:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [PadSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) (default) | [ReflectSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) | [RepeatSpread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) |

The colors in a gradient is defined using stop points of the
[QGradientStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#QGradientStop-typedef)
type, i.e. a position and a color. Use the
[QGradient::setColorAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setColorAt)()
or the
[QGradient::setStops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setStops)()
function to define the stop points. It is the gradient's complete set of stop points
that describes how the gradient area should be filled. If no stop points have been
specified, a gradient of black at 0 to white at 1 is used.

In addition to the functions inherited from
[QGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html), the QLinearGradient
class provides the
[finalStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineargradient.html#finalStop)()
function which returns the final stop point of the gradient, and the
[start](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlineargradient.html#start)() function
returning the start point of the gradient.

PythonQt.QtGui.QListView.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-listview.png)

A QListView presents items stored in a model, either as a simple non-hierarchical list,
or as a collection of icons. This class is used to provide lists and icon views that
were previously provided by the `QListBox` and `QIconView` classes, but using the more
flexible approach provided by Qt's model/view architecture.

The QListView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

This view does not display horizontal or vertical headers; to display a list of items
with a horizontal header, use
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) instead.

QListView implements the interfaces defined by the
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) class to
allow it to display data provided by models derived from the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) class.

Items in a list view can be displayed using one of two view modes: In
[ListMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#ViewMode-enum), the items
are displayed in the form of a simple list; in
[IconMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#ViewMode-enum), the list
view takes the form of an *icon view* in which the items are displayed with icons like
files in a file manager. By default, the list view is in
[ListMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#ViewMode-enum). To change
the view mode, use the
[setViewMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#viewMode-prop)()
function, and to determine the current view mode, use
[viewMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#viewMode-prop)().

Items in these views are laid out in the direction specified by the
[flow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#flow-prop)() of the list view.
The items may be fixed in place, or allowed to move, depending on the view's
[movement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#movement-prop)() state.

If the items in the model cannot be completely laid out in the direction of flow, they
can be wrapped at the boundary of the view widget; this depends on
[isWrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#isWrapping-prop)(). This
property is useful when the items are being represented by an icon view.

The [resizeMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#resizeMode-prop)()
and [layoutMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#layoutMode-prop)()
govern how and when the items are laid out. Items are spaced according to their
[spacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#spacing-prop)(), and can
exist within a notional grid of size specified by
[gridSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#gridSize-prop)(). The items
can be rendered as large or small icons depending on their
[iconSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#iconSize-prop)().

### Improving Performance

It is possible to give the view hints about the data it is handling in order to improve
its performance when displaying large numbers of items. One approach that can be taken
for views that are intended to display items with equal sizes is to set the
[uniformItemSizes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#uniformItemSizes-prop)
property to true.

### flow : [Flow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum)

This property holds which direction the items layout should flow.

If this property is
[LeftToRight](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum), the items
will be laid out left to right. If the
[isWrapping](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#isWrapping-prop) property
is `true`, the layout will wrap when it reaches the right side of the visible area. If
this property is
[TopToBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum), the items
will be laid out from the top of the visible area, wrapping when it reaches the bottom.

Setting this property when the view is visible will cause the items to be laid out
again.

By default, this property is set to
[TopToBottom](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Flow-enum).

### layoutMode : [LayoutMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#LayoutMode-enum)

determines whether the layout of items should happen immediately or be delayed.

This property holds the layout mode for the items. When the mode is
[SinglePass](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#LayoutMode-enum) (the
default), the items are laid out all in one go. When the mode is
[Batched](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#LayoutMode-enum), the items
are laid out in batches of
[batchSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#batchSize-prop) items,
while processing events. This makes it possible to instantly view and interact with the
visible items while the rest are being laid out.

### movement : [Movement](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Movement-enum)

This property holds whether the items can be moved freely, are snapped to a grid, or
cannot be moved at all.

This property determines how the user can move the items in the view.
[Static](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Movement-enum) means that the
items can't be moved the user.
[Free](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Movement-enum) means that the
user can drag and drop the items to any position in the view.
[Snap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Movement-enum) means that the
user can drag and drop the items, but only to the positions in a notional grid signified
by the [gridSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#gridSize-prop)
property.

Setting this property when the view is visible will cause the items to be laid out
again.

By default, this property is set to
[Static](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#Movement-enum).

**Access functions:**

| QListView::Movement | **movement**() const |
| --- | --- |
| void | **setMovement**(QListView::Movement *movement*) |

**See also**
[gridSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#gridSize-prop),
[resizeMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html#resizeMode-prop), and

This property holds the item text word-wrapping policy

PythonQt.QtGui.QListWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-listview.png)

QListWidget is a convenience class that provides a list view similar to the one supplied
by [QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html), but with a classic
item-based interface for adding and removing items. QListWidget uses an internal model
to manage each
[QListWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html) in the list.

For a more flexible list view widget, use the
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) class with a standard
model.

List widgets are constructed in the same way as other widgets:

```
    QListWidget *listWidget = new QListWidget(this);
```

The
[selectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionMode-prop)()
of a list widget determines how many of the items in the list can be selected at the
same time, and whether complex selections of items can be created. This can be set with
the
[setSelectionMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#selectionMode-prop)()
function.

There are two ways to add items to the list: they can be constructed with the list
widget as their parent widget, or they can be constructed with no parent widget and
added to the list later. If a list widget already exists when the items are constructed,
the first method is easier to use:

```
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Oak"), listWidget);
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Fir"), listWidget);
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Pine"), listWidget);
```

If you need to insert a new item into the list at a particular position, then it should
be constructed without a parent widget. The
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#insertItem)() function
should then be used to place it within the list. The list widget will take ownership of
the item.

```
    QListWidgetItem *newItem = new QListWidgetItem;
    newItem->setText(itemText);
    listWidget->insertItem(row, newItem);
```

For multiple items,
[insertItems](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#insertItems)() can be
used instead. The number of items in the list is found with the
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#count-prop)() function. To
remove items from the list, use
[takeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#takeItem)().

The current item in the list can be found with
[currentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#currentItem)(), and
changed with
[setCurrentItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#setCurrentItem)().
The user can also change the current item by navigating with the keyboard or clicking on
a different item. When the current item changes, the
[currentItemChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#currentItemChanged)()
signal is emitted with the new current item and the item that was previously current.

PythonQt.QtGui.QListWidgetItem.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A QListWidgetItem represents a single item in a
[QListWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html). Each item can hold
several pieces of information, and will display them appropriately.

The item view convenience classes use a classic item-based interface rather than a pure
model/view approach. For a more flexible list view widget, consider using the
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) class with a standard
model.

List items can be inserted automatically into a list, when they are constructed, by
specifying the list widget:

```
    new QListWidgetItem(tr("Hazel"), listWidget);
```

Alternatively, list items can also be created without a parent widget, and later
inserted into a list using
[QListWidget::insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidget.html#insertItem)().

List items are typically used to display
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#text)() and an
[icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#icon)(). These are set
with the [setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setText)()
and [setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setIcon)()
functions. The appearance of the text can be customized with
[setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setFont)(),
[setForeground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setForeground)(),
and
[setBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setBackground)().
Text in list items can be aligned using the
[setTextAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setTextAlignment)()
function. Tooltips, status tips and "What's This?" help can be added to list items with
[setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setToolTip)(),
[setStatusTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setStatusTip)(),
and
[setWhatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setWhatsThis)().

By default, items are enabled, selectable, checkable, and can be the source of drag and
drop operations.

Each item's flags can be changed by calling
[setFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setFlags)() with the
appropriate value (see
[Qt::ItemFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum)). Checkable
items can be checked, unchecked and partially checked with the
[setCheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setCheckState)()
function. The corresponding
[checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#checkState)()
function indicates the item's current check state.

The [isHidden](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#isHidden)()
function can be used to determine whether the item is hidden. To hide an item, use
[setHidden](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#setHidden)().

### Subclassing

When subclassing QListWidgetItem to provide custom items, it is possible to define new
types for them enabling them to be distinguished from standard items. For subclasses
that require this feature, ensure that you call the base class constructor with a new
type value equal to or greater than
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistwidgetitem.html#ItemType-enum),
within *your* constructor.

## Detailed Description

### Qt Main Window Framework

A main window provides a framework for building an application's user interface. Qt has
QMainWindow and its [related
classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/widget-classes.html#main-window-and-related-classes)
for main window management. QMainWindow has its own layout to which you can add
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html)s,
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html)s, a
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html), and a
[QStatusBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html). The layout has a
center area that can be occupied by any kind of widget. You can see an image of the
layout below.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/mainwindowlayout.png)

**Note:** Creating a main window without a central widget is not supported. You must
have a central widget even if it is just a placeholder.

### Creating Main Window Components

A central widget will typically be a standard Qt widget such as a
[QTextEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) or a
[QGraphicsView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsview.html). Custom widgets
can also be used for advanced applications. You set the central widget with
`setCentralWidget()`.

Main windows have either a single (SDI) or multiple (MDI) document interface. You create
MDI applications in Qt by using a
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html) as the central widget.

We will now examine each of the other widgets that can be added to a main window. We
give examples on how to create and add them.

#### Creating Menus

Qt implements menus in [QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) and
QMainWindow keeps them in a
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html).
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html)s are added to the menus,
which display them as menu items.

You can add new menus to the main window's menu bar by calling `menuBar()`, which
returns the [QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html) for the window,
and then add a menu with
[QMenuBar::addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html#addMenu)().

QMainWindow comes with a default menu bar, but you can also set one yourself with
`setMenuBar()`. If you wish to implement a custom menu bar (i.e., not use the
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html) widget), you can set it
with `setMenuWidget()`.

An example of how to create menus follows:

```
    void MainWindow::createMenus()
    {
        fileMenu = menuBar()->addMenu(tr("&File"));
        fileMenu->addAction(newAct);
        fileMenu->addAction(openAct);
        fileMenu->addAction(saveAct);
```

The `createPopupMenu()` function creates popup menus when the main window receives
context menu events. The default implementation generates a menu with the checkable
actions from the dock widgets and toolbars. You can reimplement `createPopupMenu()` for
a custom menu.

#### Creating Toolbars

Toolbars are implemented in the
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) class. You add a toolbar to
a main window with `addToolBar()`.

You control the initial position of toolbars by assigning them to a specific
[Qt::ToolBarArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ToolBarArea-enum). You can
split an area by inserting a toolbar break \- think of this as a line break in text
editing \- with `addToolBarBreak()` or `insertToolBarBreak()`. You can also restrict
placement by the user with
[QToolBar::setAllowedAreas](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#allowedAreas-prop)()
and
[QToolBar::setMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#movable-prop)().

The size of toolbar icons can be retrieved with `iconSize()`. The sizes are platform
dependent; you can set a fixed size with `setIconSize()`. You can alter the appearance
of all tool buttons in the toolbars with `setToolButtonStyle()`.

An example of toolbar creation follows:

```
    void MainWindow::createToolBars()
    {
        fileToolBar = addToolBar(tr("File"));
        fileToolBar->addAction(newAct);
```

#### Creating Dock Widgets

Dock widgets are implemented in the
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) class. A dock widget
is a window that can be docked into the main window. You add dock widgets to a main
window with `addDockWidget()`.

There are four dock widget areas as given by the
[Qt::DockWidgetArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#DockWidgetArea-enum)
enum: left, right, top, and bottom. You can specify which dock widget area that should
occupy the corners where the areas overlap with `setCorner()`. By default each area can
only contain one row (vertical or horizontal) of dock widgets, but if you enable nesting
with `setDockNestingEnabled()`, dock widgets can be added in either direction.

Two dock widgets may also be stacked on top of each other. A
[QTabBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtabbar.html) is then used to select which
of the widgets should be displayed.

We give an example of how to create and add dock widgets to a main window:

```
    QDockWidget *dockWidget = new QDockWidget(tr("Dock Widget"), this);
    dockWidget->setAllowedAreas(Qt::LeftDockWidgetArea |
                                Qt::RightDockWidgetArea);
    dockWidget->setWidget(dockWidgetContents);
    addDockWidget(Qt::LeftDockWidgetArea, dockWidget);
```

#### The Status Bar

You can set a status bar with `setStatusBar()`, but one is created the first time
`statusBar()` (which returns the main window's status bar) is called. See
[QStatusBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatusbar.html) for information on how
to use it.

### Storing State

QMainWindow can store the state of its layout with `saveState()`; it can later be
retrieved with `restoreState()`. It is the position and size (relative to the size of
the main window) of the toolbars and dock widgets that are stored.

### animated : bool

This property holds whether manipulating dock widgets and tool bars is animated

When a dock widget or tool bar is dragged over the main window, the main window adjusts
its contents to indicate where the dock widget or tool bar will be docked if it is
dropped. Setting this property causes
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) to move its contents
in a smooth animation. Clearing this property causes the contents to snap into their new
positions.

By default, this property is set. It may be cleared if the main window contains widgets
which are slow at resizing or repainting themselves.

Setting this property is identical to setting the
[AnimatedDocks](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#DockOption-enum)
option using
[setDockOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#dockOptions-prop)().

This property was introduced in Qt 4.2.

### dockNestingEnabled : bool

This property holds whether docks can be nested

If this property is `false`, dock areas can only contain a single row (horizontal or
vertical) of dock widgets. If this property is `true`, the area occupied by a dock
widget can be split in either direction to contain more dock widgets.

Dock nesting is only necessary in applications that contain a lot of dock widgets. It
gives the user greater freedom in organizing their main window. However, dock nesting
leads to more complex (and less intuitive) behavior when a dock widget is dragged over
the main window, since there are more ways in which a dropped dock widget may be placed
in the dock area.

Setting this property is identical to setting the
[AllowNestedDocks](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#DockOption-enum)
option using
[setDockOptions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#dockOptions-prop)().

This property was introduced in Qt 4.2.

Qt 5 reference:

### void QMainWindow::resizeDocks(const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) \*\> \&*docks*, const [QList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlist.html)\<int\> \&*sizes*, [Qt::Orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) *orientation*)

Resizes the dock widgets in the list *docks* to the corresponding size in pixels from
the list *sizes*. If *orientation* is
[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum), adjusts
the width, otherwise adjusts the height of the dock widgets. The sizes will be adjusted
such that the maximum and the minimum sizes are respected and the
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) itself will not be
resized. Any additional/missing space is distributed amongst the widgets according to
the relative weight of the sizes.

Example:

```
    resizeDocks({blueWidget, yellowWidget}, {20 , 40}, Qt::Horizontal);
```

If the blue and the yellow widget are nested on the same level they will be resized such
that the yellowWidget is twice as big as the blueWidget

If some widgets are grouped in tabs, only one widget per group should be specified.
Widgets not in the list might be changed to respect the constraints.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.6.
signatures: resizeDocks(self, docks: typing.Sequence[PySide2.QtWidgets.QDockWidget], sizes: shibokensupport.typing27.Sequence, orientation: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.Orientation) -> None

### bool QMainWindow::restoreState(const [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) \&*state*, int *version* \= 0\)

Restores the *state* of this mainwindow's toolbars and dockwidgets. Also restores the
corner settings too. The *version* number is compared with that stored in *state*. If
they do not match, the mainwindow's state is left unchanged, and this function returns
`false`; otherwise, the state is restored, and this function returns `true`.

To restore geometry saved using
[QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html), you can use code like
this:

```
void MainWindow::readSettings()
{
    QSettings settings("MyCompany", "MyApp");
    restoreGeometry(settings.value("myWidget/geometry").toByteArray());
    restoreState(settings.value("myWidget/windowState").toByteArray());
}
```

**See also**
[saveState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#saveState)(),
[QWidget::saveGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#saveGeometry)(),
[QWidget::restoreGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#restoreGeometry)(),
and
[restoreDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreDockWidget)().
signatures: restoreState(self, state: PySide2.QtCore.QByteArray, version: int=...) -> bool

PythonQt.QtGui.QMainWindow.saveState.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QMainWindow::saveState(int *version* \= 0\) const

Saves the current state of this mainwindow's toolbars and dockwidgets. This includes the
corner settings which can be set with
[setCorner](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#setCorner)(). The
*version* number is stored as part of the data.

The [objectName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#objectName-prop)
property is used to identify each
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) and
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html). You should make sure
that this property is unique for each
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) and
[QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) you add to the
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html)

To restore the saved state, pass the return value and *version* number to
[restoreState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreState)().

To save the geometry when the window closes, you can implement a close event like this:

```
void MyMainWindow::closeEvent(QCloseEvent *event)
{
    QSettings settings("MyCompany", "MyApp");
    settings.setValue("geometry", saveGeometry());
    settings.setValue("windowState", saveState());
    QMainWindow::closeEvent(event);
}
```

**See also**
[restoreState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#restoreState)(),
[QWidget::saveGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#saveGeometry)(),
and
[QWidget::restoreGeometry](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#restoreGeometry)().

### void QMainWindow::splitDockWidget([QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) \**first*, [QDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdockwidget.html) \**second*, [Qt::Orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) *orientation*)

Splits the space covered by the *first* dock widget into two parts, moves the *first*
dock widget into the first part, and moves the *second* dock widget into the second
part.

The *orientation* specifies how the space is divided: A
[Qt::Horizontal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) split
places the second dock widget to the right of the first; a
[Qt::Vertical](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#Orientation-enum) split places
the second dock widget below the first.

*Note*: if *first* is currently in a tabbed docked area, *second* will be added as a new
tab, not as a neighbor of *first*. This is because a single tab can contain only one
dock widget.

*Note*: The
[Qt::LayoutDirection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#LayoutDirection-enum)
influences the order of the dock widgets in the two parts of the divided area. When
right-to-left layout direction is enabled, the placing of the dock widgets will be
reversed.

**See also**
[tabifyDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#tabifyDockWidget)(),
[addDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#addDockWidget)(),
and
[removeDockWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#removeDockWidget)().
signatures: splitDockWidget(self, after: PySide2.QtWidgets.QDockWidget, dockwidget: PySide2.QtWidgets.QDockWidget, orientation: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.Orientation) -> None

PythonQt.QtGui.QMatrix.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A matrix specifies how to translate, scale, shear or rotate the coordinate system, and
is typically used when rendering graphics. QMatrix, in contrast to
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html), does not allow
perspective transformations.
[QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) is the recommended
transformation class in Qt.

A QMatrix object can be built using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#setMatrix)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#scale)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#rotate)(),
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#translate)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#shear)() functions.
Alternatively, it can be built by applying [basic matrix
operations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#basic-matrix-operations).
The matrix can also be defined when constructed, and it can be reset to the identity
matrix (the default) using the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#reset)() function.

The QMatrix class supports mapping of graphic primitives: A given point, line, polygon,
region, or painter path can be mapped to the coordinate system defined by *this* matrix
using the [map](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#map)() function. In case
of a rectangle, its coordinates can be transformed using the
[mapRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#mapRect)() function. A
rectangle can also be transformed into a *polygon* (mapped to the coordinate system
defined by *this* matrix), using the
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#mapToPolygon)() function.

QMatrix provides the
[isIdentity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#isIdentity)() function
which returns `true` if the matrix is the identity matrix, and the
[isInvertible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#isInvertible)() function
which returns `true` if the matrix is non-singular (i.e. AB \= BA \= I). The
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#inverted)() function returns
an inverted copy of *this* matrix if it is invertible (otherwise it returns the identity
matrix). In addition, QMatrix provides the
[determinant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#determinant)() function
returning the matrix's determinant.

Finally, the QMatrix class supports matrix multiplication, and objects of the class can
be streamed as well as compared.

### Rendering Graphics

When rendering graphics, the matrix defines the transformations but the actual
transformation is performed by the drawing routines in
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html).

By default, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) operates on the
associated device's own coordinate system. The standard coordinate system of a
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) has its origin
located at the top-left position. The *x* values increase to the right; *y* values
increase downward. For a complete description, see the [coordinate
system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html) documentation.

[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) has functions to translate,
scale, shear and rotate the coordinate system without using a QMatrix. For example:

|  | ``` void SimpleTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.rotate(45);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QMatrix"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

Although these functions are very convenient, it can be more efficient to build a
QMatrix and call
[QPainter::setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter-obsolete.html#setMatrix)()
if you want to perform more than a single transform operation. For example:

|  | ``` void CombinedTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      QMatrix matrix;     matrix.translate(50, 50);     matrix.rotate(45);     matrix.scale(0.5, 1.0);     painter.setMatrix(matrix);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QMatrix"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

### Basic Matrix Operations

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qmatrix-representation.png)

A QMatrix object contains a 3 x 3 matrix. The `dx` and `dy` elements specify horizontal
and vertical translation. The `m11` and `m22` elements specify horizontal and vertical
scaling. And finally, the `m21` and `m12` elements specify horizontal and vertical
*shearing*.

QMatrix transforms a point in the plane to another point using the following formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
```

The point *(x, y)* is the original point, and *(x', y')* is the transformed point. *(x',
y')* can be transformed back to *(x, y)* by performing the same operation on the
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#inverted)() matrix.

The various matrix elements can be set when constructing the matrix, or by using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#setMatrix)() function later
on. They can also be manipulated using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#translate)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#rotate)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#scale)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#shear)() convenience functions,
The currently set values can be retrieved using the
[m11](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m11)(),
[m12](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m12)(),
[m21](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m21)(),
[m22](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#m22)(),
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#dy)() functions.

Translation is the simplest transformation. Setting `dx` and `dy` will move the
coordinate system `dx` units along the X axis and `dy` units along the Y axis. Scaling
can be done by setting `m11` and `m22`. For example, setting `m11` to 2 and `m22` to 1.5
will double the height and increase the width by 50%. The identity matrix has `m11` and
`m22` set to 1 (all others are set to 0\) mapping a point to itself. Shearing is
controlled by `m12` and `m21`. Setting these elements to values different from zero will
twist the coordinate system. Rotation is achieved by carefully setting both the shearing
factors and the scaling factors.

Here's the combined transformations example using basic matrix operations:

|  | ``` void BasicOperations::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     double pi = 3.14;      double a    = pi/180 * 45.0;     double sina = sin(a);     double cosa = cos(a);      QMatrix translationMatrix(1, 0, 0, 1, 50.0, 50.0);     QMatrix rotationMatrix(cosa, sina, -sina, cosa, 0, 0);     QMatrix scalingMatrix(0.5, 0, 0, 1.0, 0, 0);      QMatrix matrix;     matrix =  scalingMatrix * rotationMatrix * translationMatrix;      QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.setMatrix(matrix);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QMatrix"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

```

The point (x, y) is the original point, and (x', y') is the transformed point.

The rectangle's coordinates are transformed using the following formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
```

If rotation or shearing has been specified, this function returns the *bounding*
rectangle. To retrieve the exact region the given *rectangle* maps to, use the
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#mapToPolygon)() function
instead.

**See also**
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#mapToPolygon)() and
[Basic Matrix
Operations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix.html#basic-matrix-operations).

### [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) QMatrix::mapRect(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rectangle*) const

This is an overloaded function.

Creates and returns a [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) object that
is a copy of the given *rectangle*, mapped into the coordinate system defined by this
matrix. Note that the transformed coordinates are rounded to the nearest integer.

### [QPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpolygon.html) QMatrix::mapToPolygon(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rectangle*) const

Creates and returns a [QPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpolygon.html)

## Detailed Description

The QMatrix4x4 class in general is treated as a row-major matrix, in that the
constructors and
[operator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#operator-28-29)()
functions take data in row-major format, as is familiar in C-style usage.

Internally the data is stored as column-major format, so as to be optimal for passing to
OpenGL functions, which expect column-major data.

When using these functions be aware that they return data in **column-major** format:

- [data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#data)()
- [constData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#constData)()

Qt 5 reference:

### void QMatrix4x4::optimize()

Optimize the usage of this matrix from its current elements.

Some operations such as
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#translate)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#scale)(), and
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#rotate)() can be performed
more efficiently if the matrix being modified is already known to be the identity, a
previous [translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#translate)(), a
previous [scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#scale)(), etc.

Normally the [QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html) class
keeps track of this special type internally as operations are performed. However, if the
matrix is modified directly with operator()() or
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#data)(), then
[QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html) will lose track of the
special type and will revert to the safest but least efficient operations thereafter.

By calling optimize() after directly modifying the matrix, the programmer can force
[QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html) to recover the special
type if the elements appear to conform to one of the known optimized types.

**See also** operator()(),
[data](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#data)(), and
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html#translate)().

the z co-ordinate. The value of 1024 corresponds to the projection factor used by

dropping the third row and third column of the
[QMatrix4x4](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmatrix4x4.html). This is suitable for

### void QMatrix4x4::viewport(float *left*, float *bottom*, float *width*, float *height*, float *nearPlane* \= 0.0f, float *farPlane* \= 1.0f)

Multiplies this matrix by another that performs the scale and bias transformation used
by OpenGL to transform from normalized device coordinates (NDC) to viewport (window)

dimension to the viewport with it's near-lower-left corner at (*left*, *bottom*,

controlled by the functions glViewport() and glDepthRange().

PythonQt.QtGui.QMdiArea.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QMdiArea functions, essentially, like a window manager for MDI windows. For instance, it
draws the windows it manages on itself and arranges them in a cascading or tile pattern.
QMdiArea is commonly used as the center widget in a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html) to create MDI
applications, but can also be placed in any layout. The following code adds an area to a
main window:

```
    QMainWindow *mainWindow = new QMainWindow;
    mainWindow->setCentralWidget(mdiArea);
```

Unlike the window managers for top-level windows, all window flags
([Qt::WindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum)) are
supported by QMdiArea as long as the flags are supported by the current widget style. If
a specific flag is not supported by the style (e.g., the
[WindowShadeButtonHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum)),
you can still shade the window with showShaded().

Subwindows in QMdiArea are instances of
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html). They are added
to an MDI area with
[addSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#addSubWindow)(). It is
common to pass a [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), which is
set as the internal widget, to this function, but it is also possible to pass a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) directly.The
class inherits [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), and you can
use the same API as with a normal top-level window when programming.
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) also has behavior
that is specific to MDI windows. See the
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) class description
for more details.

A subwindow becomes active when it gets the keyboard focus, or when
[setFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#setFocus-1)() is called. The
user activates a window by moving focus in the usual ways. The MDI area emits the
[subWindowActivated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#subWindowActivated)()
signal when the active window changes, and the
[activeSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activeSubWindow)()
function returns the active subwindow.

The convenience function
[subWindowList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#subWindowList)()
returns a list of all subwindows. This information could be used in a popup menu
containing a list of windows, for example.

The subwindows are sorted by the current
[WindowOrder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#WindowOrder-enum). This
is used for the
[subWindowList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#subWindowList)() and
for
[activateNextSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activateNextSubWindow)()
and
[activatePreviousSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activatePreviousSubWindow)().
Also, it is used when cascading or tiling the windows with
[cascadeSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#cascadeSubWindows)()
and [tileSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#tileSubWindows)().

QMdiArea provides two built-in layout strategies for subwindows:
[cascadeSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#cascadeSubWindows)()
and [tileSubWindows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#tileSubWindows)().
Both are slots and are easily connected to menu entries.

| --- | --- |

**Note:** The default scroll bar property for QMdiArea is
[Qt::ScrollBarAlwaysOff](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScrollBarPolicy-enum).

PythonQt.QtGui.QMdiArea.activeSubWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) \*QMdiArea::activeSubWindow() const

Returns a pointer to the current active subwindow. If no window is currently active,
`nullptr` is returned.

Subwindows are treated as top-level windows with respect to window state, i.e., if a
widget outside the MDI area is the active window, no subwindow will be active. Note that
if a widget in the window in which the MDI area lives gains focus, the window will be
activated.

**See also**
[setActiveSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#setActiveSubWindow)()
and [Qt::WindowState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowState-enum).

PythonQt.QtGui.QMdiArea.addSubWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) \*QMdiArea::addSubWindow([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*, [Qt::WindowFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WindowType-enum) *windowFlags* \= Qt::WindowFlags())

Adds *widget* as a new subwindow to the MDI area. If *windowFlags* are non-zero, they
will override the flags set on the widget.

The *widget* can be either a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) or another
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) (in which case the MDI area
will create a subwindow and set the *widget* as the internal widget).

**Note:** Once the subwindow has been added, its parent will be the *viewport widget* of
the [QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html).

```
    QMdiArea mdiArea;
    QMdiSubWindow *subWindow1 = new QMdiSubWindow;
    subWindow1->setWidget(internalWidget1);
    subWindow1->setAttribute(Qt::WA_DeleteOnClose);
    mdiArea.addSubWindow(subWindow1);

    QMdiSubWindow *subWindow2 =
        mdiArea.addSubWindow(internalWidget2);
```

When you create your own subwindow, you must set the
[Qt::WA\_DeleteOnClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
widget attribute if you want the window to be deleted when closed in the MDI area. If
not, the window will be hidden and the MDI area will not activate the next subwindow.

Returns the [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) that
is added to the MDI area.

**See also**
[removeSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#removeSubWindow)().
signatures: addSubWindow(self, widget: PySide2.QtWidgets.QWidget, flags: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.WindowFlags=...) -> PySide2.QtWidgets.QMdiSubWindow

### void QMdiArea::removeSubWindow([QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*)

Removes *widget* from the MDI area. The *widget* must be either a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) or a widget that
is the internal widget of a subwindow. Note *widget* is never actually deleted by
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html). If a
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) is passed in, its
parent is set to `nullptr` and it is removed; but if an internal widget is passed in,
the child widget is set to `nullptr` and the
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) is *not* removed.

**See also**
[addSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#addSubWindow)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QMdiSubWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QMdiSubWindow represents a top-level window in a
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html), and consists of a title
bar with window decorations, an internal widget, and (depending on the current style) a
window frame and a size grip. QMdiSubWindow has its own layout, which consists of the
title bar and a center area for the internal widget.

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qmdisubwindowlayout.png)

The most common way to construct a QMdiSubWindow is to call
[QMdiArea::addSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#addSubWindow)()
with the internal widget as the argument. You can also create a subwindow yourself, and
set an internal widget by calling
[setWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#setWidget)().

You use the same API when programming with subwindows as with regular top-level windows
(e.g., you can call functions such as
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)(),
[hide](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#hide)(),
[showMaximized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#showMaximized)(), and
[setWindowTitle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#windowTitle-prop)()).

### Subwindow Handling

QMdiSubWindow also supports behavior specific to subwindows in an MDI area.

By default, each QMdiSubWindow is visible inside the MDI area viewport when moved
around, but it is also possible to specify transparent window movement and resizing
behavior, where only the outline of a subwindow is updated during these operations. The
[setOption](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#setOption)() function
is used to enable this behavior.

The [isShaded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#isShaded)()
function detects whether the subwindow is currently shaded (i.e., the window is
collapsed so that only the title bar is visible). To enter shaded mode, call
[showShaded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#showShaded)().
QMdiSubWindow emits the
[windowStateChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#windowStateChanged)()
signal whenever the window state has changed (e.g., when the window becomes minimized,
or is restored). It also emits
[aboutToActivate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#aboutToActivate)()
before it is activated.

In keyboard-interactive mode, the windows are moved and resized with the keyboard. You
can enter this mode through the system menu of the window. The
[keyboardSingleStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#keyboardSingleStep-prop)
and
[keyboardPageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#keyboardPageStep-prop)
properties control the distance the widget is moved or resized for each keypress event.
When shift is pressed down page step is used; otherwise single step is used.

You can also change the active window with the keyboard. By pressing the control and tab
keys at the same time, the next (using the current
[WindowOrder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#WindowOrder-enum))
subwindow will be activated. By pressing control, shift, and tab, you will activate the
previous window. This is equivalent to calling
[activateNextSubWindow()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activateNextSubWindow)
and
[activatePreviousSubWindow()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html#activatePreviousSubWindow).
Note that these shortcuts overrides global shortcuts, but not the
[QMdiArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdiarea.html)s shortcuts.

### void QMdiSubWindow::setSystemMenu([QMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html) \**systemMenu*)

Sets *systemMenu* as the current system menu for this subwindow.

By default, each [QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html)
has a standard system menu.

QActions for the system menu created by
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) will
automatically be updated depending on the current window state; e.g., the minimize
action will be disabled after the window is minimized.

QActions added by the user are not updated by
[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html).

[QMdiSubWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html) takes ownership
of *systemMenu*; you do not have to delete it. Any existing menus will be deleted.

**See also**
[systemMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#systemMenu)() and
[showSystemMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmdisubwindow.html#showSystemMenu)().

### `[slot]` void QMdiSubWindow::showShaded()

Calling this function makes the subwindow enter the shaded mode. When the subwindow is
shaded, only the title bar is visible.

PythonQt.QtGui.QMenu.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/fusion-menu.png)

A menu widget is a selection menu. It can be either a pull-down menu in a menu bar or a
standalone context menu. Pull-down menus are shown by the menu bar when the user clicks
on the respective item or presses the specified shortcut key. Use
[QMenuBar::addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html#addMenu)() to
insert a menu into a menu bar. Context menus are usually invoked by some special
keyboard key or by right-clicking. They can be executed either asynchronously with
[popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#popup)() or synchronously with
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#exec)(). Menus can also be invoked
in response to button presses; these are just like context menus except for how they are
invoked.

### Actions

A menu consists of a list of action items. Actions are added with the
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addAction)(),
[addActions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#addActions)() and
[insertAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#insertAction)()
functions. An action is represented vertically and rendered by
[QStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html). In addition, actions can have
a text label, an optional icon drawn on the very left side, and shortcut key sequence
such as "Ctrl\+X".

The existing actions held by a menu can be found with
[actions](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#actions)().

There are four kinds of action items: separators, actions that show a submenu, widgets,
and actions that perform an action. Separators are inserted with
[addSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addSeparator)(), submenus
with [addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addMenu)(), and all other
items are considered action items.

When inserting action items you usually specify a receiver and a slot. The receiver will
be notified whenever the item is
[triggered()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html#triggered). In addition,
QMenu provides two signals,
[triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#triggered)() and
[hovered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#hovered)(), which signal the
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) that was triggered from the
menu.

You clear a menu with [clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#clear)() and
remove individual action items with
[removeAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#removeAction)().

A QMenu can also provide a tear-off menu. A tear-off menu is a top-level window that
contains a copy of the menu. This makes it possible for the user to "tear off"
frequently used menus and position them in a convenient place on the screen. If you want
this functionality for a particular menu, insert a tear-off handle with
[setTearOffEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#tearOffEnabled-prop)().
When using tear-off menus, bear in mind that the concept isn't typically used on
Microsoft Windows so some users may not be familiar with it. Consider using a
[QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) instead.

Widgets can be inserted into menus with the
[QWidgetAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html) class. Instances
of this class are used to hold widgets, and are inserted into menus with the
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addAction)() overload that
takes a [QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html). If the
[QWidgetAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html) fires the
[triggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#triggered)() signal, the menu
will close.

**Warning:** To make QMenu visible on the screen,
[exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#exec)() or
[popup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#popup)() should be used instead of
[show](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)().

### QMenu on macOS with Qt Build Against Cocoa

QMenu can be inserted only once in a menu/menubar. Subsequent insertions will have no
effect or will result in a disabled menu item.

See the
[Menus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-mainwindows-menus-example.html)
example for an example of how to use
[QMenuBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenubar.html) and QMenu in your
application.

**Important inherited functions:**
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addAction)(),
[removeAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#removeAction)(),
[clear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#clear)(),
[addSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addSeparator)(), and
[addMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#addMenu)().
