PythonQt.QtGui.QPrinter.setFullPage.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QPrinter::setFullPage(bool *fp*)

If *fp* is true, enables support for painting over the entire page; otherwise restricts
painting to the printable area reported by the device.

By default, full page printing is disabled. In this case, the origin of the
[QPrinter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html)'s coordinate system
coincides with the top-left corner of the printable area.

If full page printing is enabled, the origin of the
[QPrinter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html)'s coordinate system
coincides with the top-left corner of the paper itself. In this case, the [device
metrics](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html#PaintDeviceMetric-enum)
will report the exact same dimensions as indicated by
[PaperSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#PaperSize-typedef). It may
not be possible to print on the entire physical page because of the printer's margins,
so the application must account for the margins itself.

**See also** [fullPage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#fullPage)(),
[pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)(),
[setPageSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPageSize)(),
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html#width)(), and
[height](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html#height)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QPrinter.setOutputFileNam.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QPrinter::setOutputFileName(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*fileName*)

Sets the name of the output file to *fileName*.

Setting a null or empty name (0 or "") disables printing to a file. Setting a non-empty
name enables printing to a file.

This can change the value of
[outputFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#outputFormat)(). If the
file name has the ".pdf" suffix PDF is generated. If the file name has a suffix other
than ".pdf", the output format used is the one set with
[setOutputFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setOutputFormat)().

[QPrinter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html) uses Qt's cross-platform
PDF print engines respectively. If you can produce this format natively, for example
macOS can generate PDF's from its print engine, set the output format back to
[NativeFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#OutputFormat-enum).

**See also**
[outputFileName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#outputFileName)() and
[setOutputFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setOutputFormat)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QPrinter.setOutputFormat.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### void QPrinter::setOutputFormat([QPrinter::OutputFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#OutputFormat-enum) *format*)

Sets the output format for this printer to *format*.

If *format* is the same value as currently set then no change will be made.

If *format* is
[NativeFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#OutputFormat-enum) then
the [printerName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#printerName) will be
set to the default printer. If there are no valid printers configured then no change
will be made. If you want to set
[NativeFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#OutputFormat-enum) with
a specific [printerName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#printerName)
then use
[setPrinterName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPrinterName)().

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also**
[outputFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#outputFormat)() and
[setPrinterName](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPrinterName)().

### bool QPrinter::setPageLayout(const [QPageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html) \&*newLayout*)

Sets the page layout to *newLayout*.

If the *newLayout* is not valid for the current printer then the page layout will not be
changed. For example, if the page size is not supported by the printer, or if the
margins fall outside the printable area.

Returns true if the page layout was successfully set to *newLayout*.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.3.

**See also**
[pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)(),
[setPageSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPageSize)(),
[setPageOrientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPageOrientation)(),
and [setPageMargins](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPageMargins)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QPrinter.setPageMargins.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QPrinter::setPageMargins(const [QMarginsF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmarginsf.html) \&*margins*)

Set the page margins to *margins* using the current units. Returns `true` if the page
margins were set successfully.

**See also** [pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)()
and [setPageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPageLayout)().

### bool QPrinter::setPageMargins(const [QMarginsF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmarginsf.html) \&*margins*, [QPageLayout::Unit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Unit-enum) *units*)

Set the page margins to *margins* in the given *units*. If *units* are not provided then
the current units are used.

If in Full Page mode then no check is performed on the *margins* set, otherwise the
*margins* must fall within the printable area for the page size on the current printer.

To obtain the current page margins use
[pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)().margins().

Returns `true` if the page margins was successfully set to *margins*.

This function was introduced in Qt 5.3.

**See also** [pageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageLayout)()
and [setPageLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#setPageLayout)().
signatures: setPageMargins(self, left: float, top: float, right: float, bottom: float, unit: PySide2.QtPrintSupport.QPrinter.Unit) -> None

PythonQt.QtGui.QPrinter.setPageOrder.doc:

### void QPrinter::setPageOrder([QPrinter::PageOrder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#PageOrder-enum) *pageOrder*)

Sets the page order to *pageOrder*.

The page order can be
[QPrinter::FirstPageFirst](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#PageOrder-enum)
or
[QPrinter::LastPageFirst](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#PageOrder-enum).
The application is responsible for reading the page order and printing accordingly.

This function is mostly useful for setting a default value that the user can override in
the print dialog.

This function is only supported under X11.

**See also** [pageOrder](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprinter.html#pageOrder)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QPrinter.setPageOrientati.doc:

### bool QPrinter::setPageOrientation([QPageLayout::Orientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Orientation-enum) *orientation*)

Sets the page *orientation* to
[QPageLayout::Portrait](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Orientation-enum)
or
[QPageLayout::Landscape](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpagelayout.html#Orientation-enum).

The printer driver reads this setting and prints the page using the specified
orientation.

### int QPrinter::toPage() const

PythonQt.QtGui.QProgressBar.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-progressbar.png)

A progress bar is used to give the user an indication of the progress of an operation
and to reassure them that the application is still running.

The progress bar uses the concept of *steps*. You set it up by specifying the minimum
and maximum possible step values, and it will display the percentage of steps that have
been completed when you later give it the current step value. The percentage is
calculated by dividing the progress
([value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#value-prop)() \-
[minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#minimum-prop)()) divided
by [maximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#maximum-prop)() \-
[minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#minimum-prop)().

You can specify the minimum and maximum number of steps with
[setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#minimum-prop)() and
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#maximum-prop). The
current number of steps is set with
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#value-prop)(). The
progress bar can be rewound to the beginning with
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html#reset)().

If minimum and maximum both are set to 0, the bar shows a busy indicator instead of a
percentage of steps. This is useful, for example, when using QNetworkAccessManager to
download items when they are unable to determine the size of the item being downloaded.

PythonQt.QtGui.QProgressDialog.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A progress dialog is used to give the user an indication of how long an operation is
going to take, and to demonstrate that the application has not frozen. It can also give
the user an opportunity to abort the operation.

A common problem with progress dialogs is that it is difficult to know when to use them;
operations take different amounts of time on different hardware. QProgressDialog offers
a solution to this problem: it estimates the time the operation will take (based on time
for steps), and only shows itself if that estimate is beyond
[minimumDuration](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#minimumDuration-prop)()
(4 seconds by default).

Use [setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#minimum-prop)()
and [setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#maximum-prop)()
or the constructor to set the number of "steps" in the operation and call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() as the
operation progresses. The number of steps can be chosen arbitrarily. It can be the
number of files copied, the number of bytes received, the number of iterations through
the main loop of your algorithm, or some other suitable unit. Progress starts at the
value set by
[setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#minimum-prop)(),
and the progress dialog shows that the operation has finished when you call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() with
the value set by
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#maximum-prop)() as
its argument.

The dialog automatically resets and hides itself at the end of the operation. Use
[setAutoReset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#autoReset-prop)()
and
[setAutoClose](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#autoClose-prop)()
to change this behavior. Note that if you set a new maximum (using
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#maximum-prop)() or
[setRange](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setRange)()) that
equals your current
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)(), the
dialog will not close regardless.

There are two ways of using QProgressDialog: modal and modeless.

Compared to a modeless QProgressDialog, a modal QProgressDialog is simpler to use for
the programmer. Do the operation in a loop, call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() at
intervals, and check for cancellation with
[wasCanceled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#wasCanceled-prop)().
For example:

```
    QProgressDialog progress("Copying files...", "Abort Copy", 0, numFiles, this);
    progress.setWindowModality(Qt::WindowModal);

    for (int i = 0; i < numFiles; i++) {
        progress.setValue(i);

        if (progress.wasCanceled())
            break;
        //... copy one file
    }
    progress.setValue(numFiles);
```

A modeless progress dialog is suitable for operations that take place in the background,
where the user is able to interact with the application. Such operations are typically
based on [QTimer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtimer.html) (or
[QObject::timerEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#timerEvent)()) or
[QSocketNotifier](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsocketnotifier.html); or performed
in a separate thread. A
[QProgressBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressbar.html) in the status bar
of your main window is often an alternative to a modeless progress dialog.

You need to have an event loop to be running, connect the
[canceled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#canceled)() signal to
a slot that stops the operation, and call
[setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#value-prop)() at
intervals. For example:

```
// Operation constructor
Operation::Operation(QObject *parent)
    : QObject(parent), steps(0)
{
    pd = new QProgressDialog("Operation in progress.", "Cancel", 0, 100);
    connect(pd, &QProgressDialog::canceled, this, &Operation::cancel);
    t = new QTimer(this);
    connect(t, &QTimer::timeout, this, &Operation::perform);
    t->start(0);
}

void Operation::perform()
{
    pd->setValue(steps);
    //... perform one percent of the operation
    steps++;
    if (steps > pd->maximum())
        t->stop();
}

void Operation::cancel()
{
    t->stop();
    //... cleanup
}
```

In both modes the progress dialog may be customized by replacing the child widgets with
custom widgets by using
[setLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setLabel)(),
[setBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setBar)(), and
[setCancelButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setCancelButton)().
The functions
[setLabelText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#labelText-prop)()
and
[setCancelButtonText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#setCancelButtonText)()
set the texts shown.

style.](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/fusion-progressdialog.png)

### minimumDuration : int

This property holds the time that must pass before the dialog appears

If the expected duration of the task is less than the minimumDuration, the dialog will
not appear at all. This prevents the dialog popping up for tasks that are quickly over.
For tasks that are expected to exceed the minimumDuration, the dialog will pop up after
the minimumDuration time or as soon as any progress is set.

If set to 0, the dialog is always shown as soon as any progress is set. The default is
4000 milliseconds.

### value : int

This property holds the current amount of progress made.

For the progress dialog to work as expected, you should initially set this property to
[QProgressDialog::minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#minimum-prop)()
and finally set it to
[QProgressDialog::maximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#maximum-prop)();
you can call setValue() any number of times in-between.

**Warning:** If the progress dialog is modal (see
[QProgressDialog::QProgressDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html#QProgressDialog)()),
setValue() calls
[QCoreApplication::processEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcoreapplication.html#processEvents)(),
so take care that this does not cause undesirable re-entrancy in your code. For example,
don't use a [QProgressDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qprogressdialog.html)
inside a [paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#paintEvent)()!

PythonQt.QtGui.QPushButton.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-pushbutton.png)

The push button, or command button, is perhaps the most commonly used widget in any
graphical user interface. Push (click) a button to command the computer to perform some
action, or to answer a question. Typical buttons are OK, Apply, Cancel, Close, Yes, No
and Help.

A command button is rectangular and typically displays a text label describing its
action. A shortcut key can be specified by preceding the preferred character with an
ampersand in the text. For example:

```
QPushButton *button = new QPushButton("&Download", this);
```

In this example the shortcut is *Alt\+D*. See the
[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html#mnemonic) documentation
for details (to display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&').

Push buttons display a textual label, and optionally a small icon. These can be set
using the constructors and changed later using
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)() and
[setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)(). If the
button is disabled, the appearance of the text and icon will be manipulated with respect
to the GUI style to make the button look "disabled".

A push button emits the signal
[clicked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#clicked)() when it is
activated by the mouse, the Spacebar or by a keyboard shortcut. Connect to this signal
to perform the button's action. Push buttons also provide less commonly used signals,
for example [pressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#pressed)()
and [released](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#released)().

Command buttons in dialogs are by default auto-default buttons, i.e., they become the
default push button automatically when they receive the keyboard input focus. A default
button is a push button that is activated when the user presses the Enter or Return key
in a dialog. You can change this with
[setAutoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)().
Note that auto-default buttons reserve a little extra space which is necessary to draw a
default-button indicator. If you do not want this space around your buttons, call
[setAutoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)(false).

Being so central, the button widget has grown to accommodate a great many variations in
the past decade. The Microsoft style guide now shows about ten different states of
Windows push buttons and the text implies that there are dozens more when all the
combinations of features are taken into consideration.

The most important modes or states are:

- Available or not (grayed out, disabled).
- Standard push button, toggling push button or menu button.
- On or off (only for toggling push buttons).
- Default or normal. The default button in a dialog can generally be "clicked" using the Enter or Return key.
- Auto-repeat or not.
- Pressed down or not.

As a general rule, use a push button when the application or dialog window performs an
action when the user clicks on it (such as Apply, Cancel, Close and Help) *and* when the
widget is supposed to have a wide, rectangular shape with a text label. Small, typically
square buttons that change the state of the window rather than performing an action
(such as the buttons in the top-right corner of the
[QFileDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfiledialog.html)) are not command
buttons, but tool buttons. Qt provides a special class
([QToolButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html)) for these buttons.

If you need toggle behavior (see
[setCheckable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkable-prop)())
or a button that auto-repeats the activation signal when being pushed down like the
arrows in a scroll bar (see
[setAutoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop)()),
a command button is probably not what you want. When in doubt, use a tool button.

**Note:** On macOS when a push button's width becomes smaller than 50 or its height
becomes smaller than 30, the button's corners are changed from round to square. Use the
[setMinimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)()
function to prevent this behavior.

A variation of a command button is a menu button. These provide not just one command,
but several, since when they are clicked they pop up a menu of options. Use the method
[setMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#setMenu)() to associate a
popup menu with a push button.

Other classes of buttons are option buttons (see
[QRadioButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradiobutton.html)) and check boxes
(see [QCheckBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcheckbox.html)).

In Qt, the [QAbstractButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html)
base class provides most of the modes and other API, and QPushButton provides GUI logic.
See [QAbstractButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html) for more
information about the API.

### autoDefault : bool

This property holds whether the push button is an auto default button

If this property is set to true then the push button is an auto default button.

In some GUI styles a default button is drawn with an extra frame around it, up to 3
pixels or more. Qt automatically keeps this space free around auto-default buttons,
i.e., auto-default buttons may have a slightly larger size hint.

This property's default is true for buttons that have a
[QDialog](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html) parent; otherwise it defaults
to false.

See the [default](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#default) property for
details of how [default](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#default) and
auto-default interact.

PythonQt.QtGui.QPushButton.default.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### default : bool

This property holds whether the push button is the default button

Default and autodefault buttons decide what happens when the user presses enter in a
dialog.

A button with this property set to true (i.e., the dialog's *default* button,) will
automatically be pressed when the user presses enter, with one exception: if an
*autoDefault* button currently has focus, the
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
button is pressed. When the dialog has
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
buttons but no default button, pressing enter will press either the
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
button that currently has focus, or if no button has focus, the next
[autoDefault](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html#autoDefault-prop)
button in the focus chain.

In a dialog, only one push button at a time can be the default button. This button is
then displayed with an additional frame (depending on the GUI style).

The default button behavior is provided only in dialogs. Buttons can always be clicked
from the keyboard by pressing Spacebar when the button has focus.

If the default property is set to false on the current default button while the dialog
is visible, a new default will automatically be assigned the next time a push button in
the dialog receives focus.

This property's default is false.

| --- | --- |
| void | **setDefault**(*bool*) |

## Detailed Description

Quaternions are used to represent rotations in 3D space, and consist of a 3D rotation
axis specified by the x, y, and z coordinates, and a scalar representing the rotation
angle.

PythonQt.QtGui.QQuaternion.nlerp.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [QQuaternion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#QQuaternion) QQuaternion::nlerp(const [QQuaternion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#QQuaternion) \&*q1*, const [QQuaternion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#QQuaternion) \&*q2*, float *t*)

Interpolates along the shortest linear path between the rotational positions *q1* and
*q2*. The value *t* should be between 0 and 1, indicating the distance to travel between
*q1* and *q2*. The result will be
[normalized](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#normalized)().

If *t* is less than or equal to 0, then *q1* will be returned. If *t* is greater than or
equal to 1, then *q2* will be returned.

The nlerp() function is typically faster than
[slerp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#slerp)() and will give
approximate results to spherical interpolation that are good enough for some
applications.

**See also** [slerp](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qquaternion.html#slerp)().
signatures: nlerp(q1: PySide2.QtGui.QQuaternion, q2: PySide2.QtGui.QQuaternion, t: float) -> PySide2.QtGui.QQuaternion

Rotates *vector* with this quaternion to produce a new vector in 3D space. The following
code:

```
    QVector3D result = q.rotatedVector(vector);
```

is equivalent to the following:

```
    QVector3D result = (q * QQuaternion(0, vector) * q.conjugated()).vector();
```

PythonQt.QtGui.QRadialGradient.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Qt supports both simple and extended radial gradients.

Simple radial gradients interpolate colors between a focal point and end points on a
circle surrounding it. Extended radial gradients interpolate colors between a focal
circle and a center circle. Points outside the cone defined by the two circles will be
transparent. For simple radial gradients the focal point is adjusted to lie inside the
center circle, whereas the focal point can have any position in an extended radial
gradient.

Outside the end points the gradient is either padded, reflected or repeated depending on
the currently set
[spread](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#Spread-enum) method:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |

The colors in a gradient is defined using stop points of the
[QGradientStop](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#QGradientStop-typedef)
type, i.e. a position and a color. Use the
[QGradient::setColorAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setColorAt)()
or the
[QGradient::setStops](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html#setStops)()
function to define the stop points. It is the gradient's complete set of stop points
that describes how the gradient area should be filled. If no stop points have been
specified, a gradient of black at 0 to white at 1 is used.

In addition to the functions inherited from
[QGradient](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgradient.html), the QRadialGradient
class provides the
[center](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html#center)(),
[focalPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html#focalPoint)() and
[radius](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qradialgradient.html#radius)() functions
returning the gradient's center, focal point and radius respectively.

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-radiobutton.png)

A QRadioButton is an option button that can be switched on (checked) or off (unchecked).
Radio buttons typically present the user with a "one of many" choice. In a group of
radio buttons, only one radio button at a time can be checked; if the user selects
another button, the previously selected button is switched off.

Radio buttons are
[autoExclusive](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoExclusive-prop)
by default. If auto-exclusive is enabled, radio buttons that belong to the same parent
widget behave as if they were part of the same exclusive button group. If you need
multiple exclusive button groups for radio buttons that belong to the same parent
widget, put them into a
[QButtonGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbuttongroup.html).

Whenever a button is switched on or off, it emits the
[toggled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#toggled)() signal.
Connect to this signal if you want to trigger an action each time the button changes
state. Use
[isChecked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)() to
see if a particular button is selected.

Just like [QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html), a radio
button displays text, and optionally a small icon. The icon is set with
[setIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)(). The text
can be set in the constructor or with
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(). A
shortcut key can be specified by preceding the preferred character with an ampersand in
the text. For example:

```
QRadioButton *button = new QRadioButton("Search from the &cursor", this);
```

In this example the shortcut is *Alt\+c*. See the
[QShortcut](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qshortcut.html#mnemonic) documentation
for details. To display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&'.

Important inherited members:
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)(),
[setDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#down-prop)(),
[isDown](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#down-prop)(),
[autoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop)(),
[group](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#group)(),
[setAutoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop)(),
[toggle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#toggle)(),
[pressed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#pressed)(),

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QRasterWindow is a [QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html) with a
raster-based, non-OpenGL surface. On top of the functionality offered by
[QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html), QRasterWindow adds a virtual
[paintEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevicewindow.html#paintEvent)()
function and the possibility to open a
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) on itself. The underlying
paint engine will be the raster one, meaning that all drawing will happen on the CPU.
For performing accelerated, OpenGL-based drawing, use
[QOpenGLWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qopenglwindow.html) instead.

Internally the class is thin wrapper for
[QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html) and
[QBackingStore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbackingstore.html) and is very
similar to the [Raster Window
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-rasterwindow-example.html) that uses
these classes directly.

PythonQt.QtGui.QRawFont.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

**Note:** QRawFont is a low level class. For most purposes
[QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) is a more appropriate class.

Most commonly, when presenting text in a user interface, the exact fonts used to render
the characters is to some extent unknown. This can be the case for several reasons: For
instance, the actual, physical fonts present on the target system could be unexpected to
the developers, or the text could contain user selected styles, sizes or writing systems
that are not supported by font chosen in the code.

Therefore, Qt's [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) class really
represents a query for fonts. When text is interpreted, Qt will do its best to match the
text to the query, but depending on the support, different fonts can be used behind the
scenes.

For most use cases, this is both expected and necessary, as it minimizes the possibility
of text in the user interface being undisplayable. In some cases, however, more direct
control over the process might be useful. It is for these use cases the QRawFont class
exists.

A QRawFont object represents a single, physical instance of a given font in a given
pixel size. I.e. in the typical case it represents a set of TrueType or OpenType font
tables and uses a user specified pixel size to convert metrics into logical pixel units.
It can be used in combination with the
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html) class to draw specific
glyph indexes at specific positions, and also have accessors to some relevant data in
the physical font.

QRawFont only provides support for the main font technologies: GDI and DirectWrite on
Windows platforms,
[FreeType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtgui-attribution-freetype.html#freetype)
on Linux platforms and CoreText on macOS. For other font back-ends, the APIs will be
disabled.

QRawFont can be constructed in a number of ways:

- It can be constructed by calling QTextLayout::glyphs() or QTextFragment::glyphs(). The returned QGlyphs objects will contain QRawFont objects which represent the actual fonts used to render each portion of the text.
- It can be constructed by passing a [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) object to [QRawFont::fromFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#fromFont)(). The function will return a QRawFont object representing the font that will be selected as response to the [QFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfont.html) query and the selected writing system.
- It can be constructed by passing a file name or [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) directly to the QRawFont constructor, or by calling [loadFromFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromFile)() or [loadFromData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromData)(). In this case, the font will not be registered in [QFontDatabase](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontdatabase.html), and it will not be available as part of regular font selection.

QRawFont is considered local to the thread in which it is constructed (either using a
constructor, or by calling
[loadFromData](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromData)() or
[loadFromFile](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#loadFromFile)()). The
QRawFont cannot be moved to a different thread, but will have to be recreated in the
thread in question.

**Note:** For the requirement of caching glyph indexes and font selections for static
text to avoid reshaping and relayouting in the inner loop of an application, a better
choice is the [QStaticText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstatictext.html) class,
since it optimizes the memory cost of the cache and also provides the possibility of
paint engine specific caches for an additional speed-up.

Qt 5 reference:

### [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html) QRawFont::alphaMapForGlyph([quint32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint32-typedef) *glyphIndex*, [QRawFont::AntialiasingType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#AntialiasingType-enum) *antialiasingType* \= SubPixelAntialiasing, const [QTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html) \&*transform* \= QTransform()) const

This function returns a rasterized image of the glyph at the given *glyphIndex* in the
underlying font, using the *transform* specified. If the
[QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) is not valid, this function
will return an invalid [QImage](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html).

If the font is a color font, then the resulting image will contain the rendered glyph at
the current pixel size. In this case, the *antialiasingType* will be ignored.

Otherwise, if *antialiasingType* is set to
[QRawFont::SubPixelAntialiasing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#AntialiasingType-enum),
then the resulting image will be in
[QImage::Format\_RGB32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum) and
the RGB values of each pixel will represent the subpixel opacities of the pixel in the
rasterization of the glyph. Otherwise, the image will be in the format of
[QImage::Format\_Indexed8](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qimage.html#Format-enum)
and each pixel will contain the opacity of the pixel in the rasterization.

**See also**
[pathForGlyph](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#pathForGlyph)() and
[QPainter::drawGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawGlyphRun)().

### [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) QRawFont::ascent() const

Returns the ascent of this [QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html)
in pixel units.

The ascent of a font is the distance from the baseline to the highest position
characters extend to. In practice, some font designers break this rule, e.g. when they
put more than one accent on top of a character, or to accommodate an unusual character
in an exotic language, so it is possible (though rare) that this value will be too
small.

**See also**
[QFontMetricsF::ascent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfontmetricsf.html#ascent)().

### [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qbytearray.html) QRawFont::fontTable(const char \**tagName*) const

Retrieves the sfnt table named *tagName* from the underlying physical font, or an empty
byte array if no such table was found. The returned font table's byte order is Big
Endian, like the sfnt format specifies. The *tagName* must be four characters long and
should be formatted in the default endianness of the current platform.

### bool QRawFont::glyphIndexesForChars(const [QChar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qchar.html) \**chars*, int *numChars*, [quint32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint32-typedef) \**glyphIndexes*, int \**numGlyphs*) const

Converts a string of unicode points to glyph indexes using the CMAP table in the
underlying font. The function works like
[glyphIndexesForString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#glyphIndexesForString)()
except it take an array (*chars*), the results will be returned though *glyphIndexes*
array and number of glyphs will be set in *numGlyphs*. The size of *glyphIndexes* array
must be at least *numChars*, if that's still not enough, this function will return
false, then you can resize *glyphIndexes* from the size returned in *numGlyphs*.

**See also**
[glyphIndexesForString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#glyphIndexesForString)(),
[advancesForGlyphIndexes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#advancesForGlyphIndexes)(),
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html),
[QTextLayout::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#glyphRuns)(),
and
[QTextFragment::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextfragment.html#glyphRuns)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QRawFont.glyphIndexesForS.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QVector](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvector.html)\<[quint32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#quint32-typedef)\> QRawFont::glyphIndexesForString(const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*) const

Converts the string of unicode points given by *text* to glyph indexes using the CMAP
table in the underlying font, and returns a vector containing the result.

Note that, in cases where there are other tables in the font that affect the shaping of
the text, the returned glyph indexes will not correctly represent the rendering of the
text. To get the correctly shaped text, you can use
[QTextLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html) to lay out and shape
the text, then call QTextLayout::glyphs() to get the set of glyph index list and
[QRawFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html) pairs.

**See also**
[advancesForGlyphIndexes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#advancesForGlyphIndexes)(),
[glyphIndexesForChars](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrawfont.html#glyphIndexesForChars)(),
[QGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qglyphrun.html),
[QTextLayout::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#glyphRuns)(),
and
[QTextFragment::glyphRuns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextfragment.html#glyphRuns)().

### `[override virtual]` [QValidator::State](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) QRegExpValidator::validate([QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*input*, int \&*pos*) const

Reimplements:
[QValidator::validate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#validate)(QString
\&input, int \&pos) const.

Returns [Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if
*input* is matched by the regular expression for this validator,
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if it has
matched partially (i.e. could be a valid match if additional valid characters are
added), and [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if
*input* is not matched.

Additionally, if *input* is not matched, the *pos* parameter is set to the length of the
*input* parameter.

For example, if the regular expression is **\\w\\d\\d** (word-character, digit, digit)
then "A57" is
[Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum), "E5" is
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum), and "\+9"
is [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).

**See also**
[QRegExp::exactMatch](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregexp.html#exactMatch)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QRegion.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

QRegion is used with
[QPainter::setClipRegion](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setClipRegion)()
to limit the paint area to what needs to be painted. There is also a
[QWidget::repaint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#repaint)() function
that takes a QRegion parameter. QRegion is the best tool for minimizing the amount of
screen area to be updated by a repaint.

This class is not suitable for constructing shapes for rendering, especially as
outlines. Use [QPainterPath](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainterpath.html) to
create paths and shapes for use with
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html).

QRegion is an [implicitly
shared](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/implicit-sharing.html) class.

### Creating and Using Regions

A region can be created from a rectangle, an ellipse, a polygon or a bitmap. Complex
regions may be created by combining simple regions using
[united](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#united)(),
[intersected](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#intersected)(),
[subtracted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#subtracted)(), or
[xored](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#xored)() (exclusive or). You can
move a region using
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#translate)().

You can test whether a region
[isEmpty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#isEmpty)() or if it
[contains](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#contains)() a
[QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) or
[QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html). The bounding rectangle can be
found with
[boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#boundingRect)().

Iteration over the region (with
[begin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#begin)(),
[end](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion.html#end)(), or ranged-for loops) gives
a decomposition of the region into rectangles.

Example of using complex regions:

```
void MyWidget::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *)
{
    QRegion r1(QRect(100, 100, 200, 80),    // r1: elliptic region
               QRegion::Ellipse);
    QRegion r2(QRect(100, 120, 90, 30));    // r2: rectangular region
    QRegion r3 = r1.intersected(r2);        // r3: intersection

    QPainter painter(this);
    painter.setClipRegion(r3);
    ...                                     // paint clipped graphics
}
```

PythonQt.QtGui.QRegion.isEmpty.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QRegion::isEmpty() const

Returns `true` if the region is empty; otherwise returns `false`. An empty region is a
region that contains no points.

Example:

```
QRegion r1(10, 10, 20, 20);
r1.isEmpty();               // false

QRegion r3;
r3.isEmpty();               // true

QRegion r2(40, 40, 20, 20);
r3 = r1.intersected(r2);    // r3: intersection of r1 and r2
r3.isEmpty();               // true

r3 = r1.united(r2);         // r3: union of r1 and r2
r3.isEmpty();               // false
```

Qt 5 reference:

### void QRegion::setRects(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \**rects*, int *number*)

Sets the region using the array of rectangles specified by *rects* and *number*. The
rectangles *must* be optimally Y-X sorted and follow these restrictions:

- The rectangles must not intersect.
- All rectangles with a given top coordinate must have the same height.
- No two rectangles may abut horizontally (they should be combined into a single wider rectangle in that case).
- The rectangles must be sorted in ascending order, with Y as the major sort key and X as the minor sort key.

**See also** [rects](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregion-obsolete.html#rects)().

### `[override virtual]` [QValidator::State](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) QRegularExpressionValidator::validate([QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*input*, int \&*pos*) const

Reimplements:
[QValidator::validate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#validate)(QString
\&input, int \&pos) const.

Returns [Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if
*input* is matched by the regular expression for this validator,
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if it has
matched partially (i.e. could be a valid match if additional valid characters are
added), and [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum) if
*input* is not matched.

In case the *input* is not matched, the *pos* parameter is set to the length of the
*input* parameter; otherwise, it is not modified.

For example, if the regular expression is **\\w\\d\\d** (word-character, digit, digit)
then "A57" is
[Acceptable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum), "E5" is
[Intermediate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum), and "\+9"
is [Invalid](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qvalidator.html#State-enum).

**See also**
[QRegularExpression::match](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qregularexpression.html#match)().
signatures: validate(self, input: str, pos: int) -> PySide2.QtGui.QValidator.State

## Detailed Description

QRgba64 is a 64-bit data-structure containing four 16-bit color channels: Red, green,
blue and alpha.

QRgba64 can be used as a replacement for
[QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef) when higher
precision is needed. In particular a premultiplied QRgba64 can operate on
unpremultiplied [QRgb](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcolor.html#QRgb-typedef)
without loss of precision except for alpha 0\.

A note on logical vs physical dots per inch: physical DPI is based on the actual
physical pixel sizes when available, and is useful for print preview and other cases
where it's desirable to know the exact physical dimensions of screen displayed contents.

Logical dots per inch are used to convert font and user interface elements from point
sizes to pixel sizes, and might be different from the physical dots per inch. The
logical dots per inch are sometimes user-settable in the desktop environment's settings
panel, to let the user globally control UI and font sizes in different applications.

PythonQt.QtGui.QScreen.grabWindow.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QPixmap](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html) QScreen::grabWindow(WId *window*, int *x* \= 0, int *y* \= 0, int *width* \= -1, int *height* \= -1)

Creates and returns a pixmap constructed by grabbing the contents of the given *window*
restricted by [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html)(*x*, *y*, *width*,
*height*).

The arguments (*x*, *y*) specify the offset in the window, whereas (*width*, *height*)
specify the area to be copied. If *width* is negative, the function copies everything to
the right border of the window. If *height* is negative, the function copies everything
to the bottom of the window.

The offset and size arguments are specified in device independent pixels. The returned
pixmap may be larger than the requested size when grabbing from a high-DPI screen. Call
[QPixmap::devicePixelRatio](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpixmap.html#devicePixelRatio)()
to determine if this is the case.

The window system identifier (`WId`) can be retrieved using the
[QWidget::winId](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#winId)() function. The
rationale for using a window identifier and not a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html), is to enable grabbing of
windows that are not part of the application, window system frames, and so on.

**Warning:** Grabbing windows that are not part of the application is not supported on
systems such as iOS, where sandboxing/security prevents reading pixels of windows not
owned by the application.

The grabWindow() function grabs pixels from the screen, not from the window, i.e. if
there is another window partially or entirely over the one you grab, you get pixels from
the overlying window, too. The mouse cursor is generally not grabbed.

Note on X11 that if the given *window* doesn't have the same depth as the root window,
and another window partially or entirely obscures the one you grab, you will *not* get
pixels from the overlying window. The contents of the obscured areas in the pixmap will
be undefined and uninitialized.

On Windows Vista and above grabbing a layered window, which is created by setting the
[Qt::WA\_TranslucentBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute, will not work. Instead grabbing the desktop widget should work.

**Warning:** In general, grabbing an area outside the screen is not safe. This depends
on the underlying window system.
signatures: grabWindow(self, window: int, x: int=..., y: int=..., w: int=..., h: int=...) -> PySide2.QtGui.QPixmap

This property holds the screen orientation

The screen orientation represents the physical orientation of the display. For example,
the screen orientation of a mobile device will change based on how it is being held. A
change to the orientation might or might not trigger a change to the primary orientation

[orientationUpdateMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#orientationUpdateMask)(),

[setOrientationUpdateMask](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#setOrientationUpdateMask)()
with a mask of the orientations it wants to receive.

[Qt::PrimaryOrientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScreenOrientation-enum)
is never returned.

dimensions *target*.

Example, *a* is Qt::Landscape, *b* is Qt::Portrait, and *target* is
[QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html)(0, 0, w, h) the resulting
transform will be such that the point
[QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html)(0, 0\) is mapped to
[QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html)(0, w), and
[QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html)(h, w) is mapped to
[QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html)(0, h). Thus, the landscape
coordinate system [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html)(0, 0, h, w) is
mapped (with a 90 degree rotation) into the portrait coordinate system
[QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html)(0, 0, w, h).

[Qt::PrimaryOrientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScreenOrientation-enum)
is interpreted as the screen's
[primaryOrientation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscreen.html#primaryOrientation-prop)().
signatures: transformBetween(self, a: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.ScreenOrientation, b: PySide2.QtCore.Qt.ScreenOrientation, target: PySide2.QtCore.QRect) -> PySide2.QtGui.QTransform

PythonQt.QtGui.QScrollArea.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A scroll area is used to display the contents of a child widget within a frame. If the
widget exceeds the size of the frame, the view can provide scroll bars so that the
entire area of the child widget can be viewed. The child widget must be specified with
[setWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html#setWidget)(). For
example:

```
QLabel *imageLabel = new QLabel;
QImage image("happyguy.png");
imageLabel->setPixmap(QPixmap::fromImage(image));

scrollArea = new QScrollArea;
scrollArea->setBackgroundRole(QPalette::Dark);
scrollArea->setWidget(imageLabel);
```

The code above creates a scroll area (shown in the images below) containing an image
label. When scaling the image, the scroll area can provide the necessary scroll bars:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |

The scroll bars appearance depends on the currently set [scroll bar
policies](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ScrollBarPolicy-enum). You can
control the appearance of the scroll bars using the inherited functionality from
[QAbstractScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html).

For example, you can set the
[QAbstractScrollArea::horizontalScrollBarPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#horizontalScrollBarPolicy-prop)
and
[QAbstractScrollArea::verticalScrollBarPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#verticalScrollBarPolicy-prop)
properties. Or if you want the scroll bars to adjust dynamically when the contents of
the scroll area changes, you can use the
[horizontalScrollBar()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#horizontalScrollBar)
and
[verticalScrollBar()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#verticalScrollBar)
functions (which enable you to access the scroll bars) and set the scroll bars' values
whenever the scroll area's contents change, using the
[QScrollBar::setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop)()
function.

You can retrieve the child widget using the
[widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html#widget)() function. The
view can be made to be resizable with the
[setWidgetResizable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html#widgetResizable-prop)()
function. The alignment of the widget can be specified with
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html#alignment-prop)().

Two convenience functions
[ensureVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html#ensureVisible)() and
[ensureWidgetVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html#ensureWidgetVisible)()
ensure a certain region of the contents is visible inside the viewport, by scrolling the
contents if necessary.

### Size Hints and Layouts

When using a scroll area to display the contents of a custom widget, it is important to
ensure that the [size
hint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#sizeHint-prop) of the child widget
is set to a suitable value. If a standard
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) is used for the child widget,
it may be necessary to call
[QWidget::setMinimumSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#minimumSize-prop)()
to ensure that the contents of the widget are shown correctly within the scroll area.

If a scroll area is used to display the contents of a widget that contains child widgets
arranged in a layout, it is important to realize that the size policy of the layout will
also determine the size of the widget. This is especially useful to know if you intend
to dynamically change the contents of the layout. In such cases, setting the layout's
[size constraint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#sizeConstraint-prop)
property to one which provides constraints on the minimum and/or maximum size of the
layout (e.g.,
[QLayout::SetMinAndMaxSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlayout.html#SizeConstraint-enum))
will cause the size of the scroll area to be updated whenever the contents of the layout
changes.

For a complete example using the QScrollArea class, see the [Image
Viewer](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-imageviewer-example.html)
example. The example shows how to combine
[QLabel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlabel.html) and QScrollArea to display an
image.

[autoFillBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#autoFillBackground-prop)

it later, the *widget* will not be visible \- regardless of when you
[show()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show) the scroll area. In this
case, you can also not [show()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#show)

PythonQt.QtGui.QScrollBar.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A scroll bar is a control that enables the user to access parts of a document that is
larger than the widget used to display it. It provides a visual indication of the user's
current position within the document and the amount of the document that is visible.
Scroll bars are usually equipped with other controls that enable more accurate
navigation. Qt displays scroll bars in a way that is appropriate for each platform.

If you need to provide a scrolling view onto another widget, it may be more convenient
to use the [QScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollarea.html) class
because this provides a viewport widget and scroll bars. QScrollBar is useful if you
need to implement similar functionality for specialized widgets using
[QAbstractScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html); for
example, if you decide to subclass
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html). For most
other situations where a slider control is used to obtain a value within a given range,
the [QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html) class may be more
appropriate for your needs.

|  | Scroll bars typically include four separate controls: a slider, scroll arrows, and a page control.  - a. The slider provides a way to quickly go to any part of the document, but does not support accurate navigation within large documents. - b. The scroll arrows are push buttons which can be used to accurately navigate to a particular place in a document. For a vertical scroll bar connected to a text editor, these typically move the current position one "line" up or down, and adjust the position of the slider by a small amount. In editors and list boxes a "line" might mean one line of text; in an image viewer it might mean 20 pixels. - c. The page control is the area over which the slider is dragged (the scroll bar's background). Clicking here moves the scroll bar towards the click by one "page". This value is usually the same as the length of the slider. |
| --- | --- |

Each scroll bar has a value that indicates how far the slider is from the start of the
scroll bar; this is obtained with
[value](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop)() and set
with [setValue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#value-prop)().
This value always lies within the range of values defined for the scroll bar, from
[minimum()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#minimum-prop) to
[maximum()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#minimum-prop)
inclusive. The range of acceptable values can be set with
[setMinimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#minimum-prop)() and
[setMaximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#maximum-prop)(). At
the minimum value, the top edge of the slider (for a vertical scroll bar) or left edge
(for a horizontal scroll bar) will be at the top (or left) end of the scroll bar. At the
maximum value, the bottom (or right) edge of the slider will be at the bottom (or right)
end of the scroll bar.

The length of the slider is usually related to the value of the page step, and typically
represents the proportion of the document area shown in a scrolling view. The page step
is the amount that the value changes by when the user presses the **Page Up** and **Page
Down** keys, and is set with
[setPageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#pageStep-prop)().
Smaller changes to the value defined by the line step are made using the cursor keys,
and this quantity is set with
[setSingleStep()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#singleStep-prop).

Note that the range of values used is independent of the actual size of the scroll bar
widget. You do not need to take this into account when you choose values for the range
and the page step.

The range of values specified for the scroll bar are often determined differently to
those for a [QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html) because the
length of the slider needs to be taken into account. If we have a document with 100
lines, and we can only show 20 lines in a widget, we may wish to construct a scroll bar
with a page step of 20, a minimum value of 0, and a maximum value of 80\. This would
give us a scroll bar with five "pages".

|  | The relationship between a document length, the range of values used in a scroll bar, and the page step is simple in many common situations. The scroll bar's range of values is determined by subtracting a chosen page step from some value representing the length of the document. In such cases, the following equation is useful: *document length* \= [maximum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#maximum-prop)() \- [minimum](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#minimum-prop)() \+ [pageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#pageStep-prop)(). |
| --- | --- |

QScrollBar only provides integer ranges. Note that although QScrollBar handles very
large numbers, scroll bars on current screens cannot usefully represent ranges above
about 100,000 pixels. Beyond that, it becomes difficult for the user to control the
slider using either the keyboard or the mouse, and the scroll arrows will have limited
use.

ScrollBar inherits a comprehensive set of signals from
[QAbstractSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html):

- [valueChanged()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#valueChanged) is emitted when the scroll bar's value has changed. The tracking() determines whether this signal is emitted during user interaction.
- [rangeChanged()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#rangeChanged) is emitted when the scroll bar's range of values has changed.
- [sliderPressed()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderPressed) is emitted when the user starts to drag the slider.
- [sliderMoved()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderMoved) is emitted when the user drags the slider.
- [sliderReleased()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#sliderReleased) is emitted when the user releases the slider.
- [actionTriggered()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#actionTriggered) is emitted when the scroll bar is changed by user interaction or via the [triggerAction()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#triggerAction) function.

A scroll bar can be controlled by the keyboard, but it has a default
[focusPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusPolicy-prop)() of
[Qt::NoFocus](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#FocusPolicy-enum). Use
[setFocusPolicy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#focusPolicy-prop)() to
enable keyboard interaction with the scroll bar:

- Left/Right move a horizontal scroll bar by one single step.
- Up/Down move a vertical scroll bar by one single step.
- PageUp moves up one page.
- PageDown moves down one page.
- Home moves to the start (minimum).
- End moves to the end (maximum).

The slider itself can be controlled by using the
[triggerAction()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#triggerAction)
function to simulate user interaction with the scroll bar controls. This is useful if
you have many different widgets that use a common range of values.

Most GUI styles use the
[pageStep](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractslider.html#pageStep-prop)()
value to calculate the size of the slider.

## Detailed Description

The scroll event is sent to indicate that the receiver should be scrolled. Usually the
receiver should be something visual like
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) or
[QGraphicsObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsobject.html).

Some care should be taken that no conflicting QScrollEvents are sent from two sources.
Using [QScroller::scrollTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#scrollTo)
is save however.

### [QScrollEvent::ScrollState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollevent.html#ScrollState-enum) QScrollEvent::scrollState() const

Returns the current scroll state as a combination of ScrollStateFlag values.
[ScrollStarted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollevent.html#ScrollState-enum)
(or
[ScrollFinished](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollevent.html#ScrollState-enum))
will be set, if this scroll event is the first (or last) event in a scrolling activity.
Please note that both values can be set at the same time, if the activity consists of a
single [QScrollEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollevent.html). All other
scroll events in between will have their state set to
[ScrollUpdated](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollevent.html#ScrollState-enum).

A widget could for example revert selections when scrolling is started and stopped.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The scroll prepare event is sent before scrolling (usually by
[QScroller](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html)) is started. The object
receiving this event should set
[viewportSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollprepareevent.html#viewportSize),
maxContentPos and
[contentPos](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollprepareevent.html#contentPos). It
also should accept this event to indicate that scrolling should be started.

It is not guaranteed that a
[QScrollEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollevent.html) will be sent after
an acceepted QScrollPrepareEvent, e.g. in a case where the maximum content position is
(0,0).

PythonQt.QtGui.QScroller.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

With kinetic scrolling, the user can push the widget in a given direction and it will
continue to scroll in this direction until it is stopped either by the user or by
friction. Aspects of inertia, friction and other physical concepts can be changed in
order to fine-tune an intuitive user experience.

The QScroller object is the object that stores the current position and scrolling speed
and takes care of updates. QScroller can be triggered by a flick gesture

```
    QWidget *w = ...;
    QScroller::grabGesture(w, QScroller::LeftMouseButtonGesture);
```

or directly like this:

```
    QWidget *w = ...;
    QScroller *scroller = QScroller::scroller(w);
    scroller->scrollTo(QPointF(100, 100));
```

The scrolled QObjects receive a
[QScrollPrepareEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollprepareevent.html)
whenever the scroller needs to update its geometry information and a
[QScrollEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollevent.html) whenever the
content of the object should actually be scrolled.

The scroller uses the global
[QAbstractAnimation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html) timer
to generate its QScrollEvents. This can be changed with
[QScrollerProperties::FrameRate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollerproperties.html#ScrollMetric-enum)
on a per-QScroller basis.

The [Dir View
Example](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-itemviews-dirview-example.html)
shows one way to use a QScroller with a
[QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html). An example in the
`scroller` examples directory also demonstrates QScroller.

Even though this kinetic scroller has a large number of settings available via
[QScrollerProperties](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollerproperties.html), we
recommend that you leave them all at their default, platform optimized values. Before
changing them you can experiment with the `plot` example in the `scroller` examples
directory.

### `[slot]` void QScroller::ensureVisible(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rect*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *xmargin*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *ymargin*)

Starts scrolling so that the rectangle *rect* is visible inside the viewport with
additional margins specified in pixels by *xmargin* and *ymargin* around the rect.

In cases where it is not possible to fit the rect plus margins inside the viewport the
contents are scrolled so that as much as possible is visible from *rect*.

The scrolling speed is calculated so that the given position is reached after a
platform-defined time span.

This function performs the actual scrolling by calling
[scrollTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#scrollTo)().

**See also** [scrollTo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#scrollTo)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QScroller.grabGesture.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` [Qt::GestureType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GestureType-enum) QScroller::grabGesture([QObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#QObject) \**target*, [QScroller::ScrollerGestureType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#ScrollerGestureType-enum) *scrollGestureType* \= TouchGesture)

Registers a custom scroll gesture recognizer, grabs it for the *target* and returns the
resulting gesture type. If *scrollGestureType* is set to
[TouchGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#ScrollerGestureType-enum)
the gesture triggers on touch events. If it is set to one of
[LeftMouseButtonGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#ScrollerGestureType-enum),
[RightMouseButtonGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#ScrollerGestureType-enum)
or
[MiddleMouseButtonGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#ScrollerGestureType-enum)
it triggers on mouse events of the corresponding button.

Only one scroll gesture can be active on a single object at the same time. If you call
this function twice on the same object, it will ungrab the existing gesture before
grabbing the new one.

**Note:** To avoid unwanted side-effects, mouse events are consumed while the gesture is
triggered. Since the initial mouse press event is not consumed, the gesture sends a fake
mouse release event at the global position `(INT_MIN, INT_MIN)`. This ensures that
internal states of the widget that received the original mouse press are consistent.

**See also**
[ungrabGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#ungrabGesture)() and
[grabbedGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#grabbedGesture)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QScroller.handleInput.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QScroller::handleInput([QScroller::Input](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#Input-enum) *input*, const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \&*position*, [qint64](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qint64-typedef) *timestamp* \= 0\)

This function is used by gesture recognizers to inform the scroller about a new input
event. The scroller changes its internal
[state](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#state-prop)() according to the
input event and its attached scroller properties. The scroller doesn't distinguish
between the kind of input device the event came from. Therefore the event needs to be
split into the *input* type, a *position* and a milli-second *timestamp*. The *position*
needs to be in the target's coordinate system.

The return value is `true` if the event should be consumed by the calling filter or
`false` if the event should be forwarded to the control.

**Note:** Using
[grabGesture](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#grabGesture)() should be
sufficient for most use cases.
signatures: handleInput(self, input: PySide2.QtWidgets.QScroller.Input, position: PySide2.QtCore.QPointF, timestamp: int=...) -> bool

### `[slot]` void QScroller::resendPrepareEvent()

This function resends the
[QScrollPrepareEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollprepareevent.html).
Calling resendPrepareEvent triggers a
[QScrollPrepareEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscrollprepareevent.html) from

### `[slot]` void QScroller::scrollTo(const [QPointF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpointf.html) \&*pos*)

Starts scrolling the widget so that point *pos* is at the top-left position in the
viewport.

The behaviour when scrolling outside the valid scroll area is undefined. In this case
the scroller might or might not overshoot.

The scrolling speed will be calculated so that the given position will be reached after
a platform-defined time span.

*pos* is given in viewport coordinates.

**See also**
[ensureVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html#ensureVisible)().

## Detailed Description

The QScrollerProperties class stores the parameters used by
[QScroller](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html).

The default settings are platform dependent so that Qt emulates the platform behaviour
for kinetic scrolling.

As a convention the QScrollerProperties are in physical units (meter, seconds) and are
converted by [QScroller](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qscroller.html) using the
current DPI.

PythonQt.QtGui.QSessionManager.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A session manager in a desktop environment (in which Qt GUI applications live) keeps
track of a session, which is a group of running applications, each of which has a
particular state. The state of an application contains (most notably) the documents the
application has open and the position and size of its windows.

The session manager is used to save the session, e.g., when the machine is shut down,
and to restore a session, e.g., when the machine is started up. We recommend that you
use [QSettings](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsettings.html) to save an
application's settings, for example, window positions, recently used files, etc. When
the application is restarted by the session manager, you can restore the settings.

QSessionManager provides an interface between the application and the platform's session
manager. In Qt, session management requests for action are handled by the two signals
[QGuiApplication::commitDataRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#commitDataRequest)()
and
[QGuiApplication::saveStateRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#saveStateRequest)().
Both provide a reference to a QSessionManager object as argument. The session manager
can only be accessed in slots invoked by these signals.

**Warning:** If you use QSessionManager, you should disable fallback session management:
[QGuiApplication::setFallbackSessionManagementEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#setFallbackSessionManagementEnabled)().

No user interaction is possible *unless* the application gets explicit permission from
the session manager. You ask for permission by calling
[allowsInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsInteraction)()
or, if it is really urgent,
[allowsErrorInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsErrorInteraction)().
Qt does not enforce this, but the session manager may.

You can try to abort the shutdown process by calling
[cancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#cancel)().

For sophisticated session managers provided on Unix/X11, QSessionManager offers further
possibilities to fine-tune an application's session management behavior:
[setRestartCommand](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#setRestartCommand)(),
[setDiscardCommand](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#setDiscardCommand)(),
[setRestartHint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#setRestartHint)(),
[setProperty](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qobject.html#setProperty)(),
[requestPhase2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#requestPhase2)().
See the respective function descriptions for further details.

### bool QSessionManager::allowsErrorInteraction()

Returns `true` if error interaction is permitted; otherwise returns `false`.

This is similar to
[allowsInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsInteraction)(),
but also enables the application to tell the user about any errors that occur. Session
managers may give error interaction requests higher priority, which means that it is
more likely that an error interaction is permitted. However, you are still not
guaranteed that the session manager will allow interaction.

**See also**
[allowsInteraction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#allowsInteraction)(),
[release](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#release)(), and

### void QSessionManager::requestPhase2()

Requests a second session management phase for the application. The application may then
return immediately from the
[QGuiApplication::commitDataRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#commitDataRequest)()
or
[QApplication::saveStateRequest](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html#saveStateRequest)()
function, and they will be called again once most or all other applications have
finished their session management.

The two phases are useful for applications such as the X11 window manager that need to
store information about another application's windows and therefore have to wait until
these applications have completed their respective session management tasks.

**Note:** If another application has requested a second phase it may get called before,
simultaneously with, or after your application's second phase.

**See also**
[isPhase2](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qsessionmanager.html#isPhase2)().
