PythonQt.QtGui.QTextLayout.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

It offers many features expected from a modern text layout engine, including Unicode
compliant rendering, line breaking and handling of cursor positioning. It can also
produce and render device independent layout, something that is important for WYSIWYG
applications.

The class has a rather low level API and unless you intend to implement your own text
rendering for some specialized widget, you probably won't need to use it directly.

QTextLayout can be used with both plain and rich text.

QTextLayout can be used to create a sequence of
[QTextLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html) instances with given
widths and can position them independently on the screen. Once the layout is done, these
lines can be drawn on a paint device.

The text to be laid out can be provided in the constructor or set with
[setText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#setText)().

The layout can be seen as a sequence of
[QTextLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html) objects; use
[createLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#createLine)() to create
a [QTextLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html) instance, and
[lineAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#lineAt)() or
[lineForTextPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#lineForTextPosition)()
to retrieve created lines.

Here is a code snippet that demonstrates the layout phase:

```
int leading = fontMetrics.leading();
qreal height = 0;
textLayout.setCacheEnabled(true);
textLayout.beginLayout();
while (1) {
    QTextLine line = textLayout.createLine();
    if (!line.isValid())
        break;

    line.setLineWidth(lineWidth);
    height += leading;
    line.setPosition(QPointF(0, height));
    height += line.height();
}
textLayout.endLayout();
```

The text can then be rendered by calling the layout's
[draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#draw)() function:

```
QPainter painter(this);
textLayout.draw(&painter, QPoint(0, 0));
```

For a given position in the text you can find a valid cursor position with
[isValidCursorPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#isValidCursorPosition)(),
[nextCursorPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#nextCursorPosition)(),
and
[previousCursorPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#previousCursorPosition)().

The QTextLayout itself can be positioned with
[setPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#setPosition)(); it has
a [boundingRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#boundingRect)(),
and a [minimumWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#minimumWidth)()
and a
[maximumWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#maximumWidth)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextLayout.createLine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### [QTextLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html) QTextLayout::createLine()

Returns a new text line to be laid out if there is text to be inserted into the layout;
otherwise returns an invalid text line.

The text layout creates a new line object that starts after the last line in the layout,
or at the beginning if the layout is empty. The layout maintains an internal cursor, and
each line is filled with text from the cursor position onwards when the
[QTextLine::setLineWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#setLineWidth)()
function is called.

Once
[QTextLine::setLineWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#setLineWidth)()
is called, a new line can be created and filled with text. Repeating this process will
lay out the whole block of text contained in the
[QTextLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html). If there is no text
left to be inserted into the layout, the
[QTextLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html) returned will not be
valid (isValid() will return false).

[QTextLayout](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html). This is an expensive
function, and should not be called in a time sensitive context.

If *from* is less than zero, then the glyph run will begin at the first character in the
layout. If *length* is less than zero, it will span the entire string from the start
position.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.8.

**See also** [draw](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#draw)() and
[QPainter::drawGlyphRun](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#drawGlyphRun)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextLayout.isValidCursor.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### bool QTextLayout::isValidCursorPosition(int *pos*) const

/ Returns `true` if position *pos* is a valid cursor position.

In a Unicode context some positions in the text are not valid cursor positions, because
the position is inside a Unicode surrogate or a grapheme cluster.

A grapheme cluster is a sequence of two or more Unicode characters that form one
indivisible entity on the screen. For example the latin character \`Ä' can be
represented in Unicode by two characters, \`A' (0x41), and the combining diaresis
(0x308). A text cursor can only validly be positioned before or after these two
characters, never between them since that wouldn't make sense. In indic languages every
syllable forms a grapheme cluster.

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextLength.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

When we specify a value for the length of an element in a text document, we often need
to provide some other information so that the length is used in the way we expect. For
example, when we specify a table width, the value can represent a fixed number of
pixels, or it can be a percentage value. This information changes both the meaning of
the value and the way it is used.

Generally, this class is used to specify table widths. These can be specified either as
a fixed amount of pixels, as a percentage of the containing frame's width, or by a
variable width that allows it to take up just the space it requires.

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextLine.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A text line is usually created by
[QTextLayout::createLine](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlayout.html#createLine)().

After being created, the line can be filled using the
[setLineWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#setLineWidth)() or
[setNumColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#setNumColumns)()
functions. A line has a number of attributes including the rectangle it occupies,
[rect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#rect)(), its coordinates,
[x](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#x)() and
[y](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#y)(), its
[textLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#textLength)(),
[width](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#width)() and
[naturalTextWidth](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#naturalTextWidth)(),
and its [ascent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#ascent)() and
[descent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#descent)() relative to the
text. The position of the cursor in terms of the line is available from
[cursorToX](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#cursorToX)() and its
inverse from [xToCursor](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#xToCursor)().
A line can be moved with
[setPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#setPosition)().

[textStart](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#textStart)(), and if

[textLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextline.html#textLength)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A list contains a sequence of text blocks, each of which is marked with a bullet point
or other symbol. Multiple levels of lists can be used, and the automatic numbering
feature provides support for ordered numeric and alphabetical lists.

Lists are created by using a text cursor to insert an empty list at the current position
or by moving existing text into a new list. The
[QTextCursor::insertList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcursor.html#insertList)()
function inserts an empty block into the document at the cursor position, and makes it
the first item in a list.

```
    QTextListFormat listFormat;
    if (list) {
        listFormat = list->format();
        listFormat.setIndent(listFormat.indent() + 1);
    }

    listFormat.setStyle(QTextListFormat::ListDisc);
    cursor.insertList(listFormat);
```

The
[QTextCursor::createList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcursor.html#createList)()
function takes the contents of the cursor's current block and turns it into the first
item of a new list.

The cursor's current list is found with
[QTextCursor::currentList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcursor.html#currentList)().

The number of items in a list is given by
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#count)(). Each item can be
obtained by its index in the list with the
[item](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#item)() function. Similarly,
the index of a given item can be found with
[itemNumber](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#itemNumber)(). The text
of each item can be found with the
[itemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#itemText)() function.

Note that the items in the list may not be adjacent elements in the document. For
example, the top-level items in a multi-level list will be separated by the items in
lower levels of the list.

List items can be deleted by index with the
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#removeItem)() function.
[remove](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#remove)() deletes the
specified item in the list.

The list's format is set with
[setFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#setFormat)() and read with
[format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html#format)(). The format
describes the decoration of the list itself, and not the individual items.

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextListFormat.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A list is composed of one or more items, represented as text blocks. The list's format
specifies the appearance of items in the list. In particular, it determines the
indentation and the style of each item.

The indentation of the items is an integer value that causes each item to be offset from
the left margin by a certain amount. This value is read with
[indent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlistformat.html#indent)() and set with
[setIndent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlistformat.html#setIndent)().

The style used to decorate each item is set with
[setStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlistformat.html#setStyle)() and can
be read with the
[style](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlistformat.html#style)() function. The
style controls the type of bullet points and numbering scheme used for items in the
list. Note that lists that use the decimal numbering scheme begin counting at 1 rather
than 0\.

Style properties can be set to further configure the appearance of list items; for
example, the
[ListNumberPrefix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextformat.html#Property-enum)
and
[ListNumberSuffix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextformat.html#Property-enum)
properties can be used to customize the numbers used in an ordered list so that they
appear as (1), (2), (3), etc.:

```
QTextListFormat listFormat;

listFormat.setStyle(QTextListFormat::ListDecimal);
listFormat.setNumberPrefix("(");
listFormat.setNumberSuffix(")");

cursor.insertList(listFormat);
```

## Detailed Description

The common grouping text objects are lists
([QTextList](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlist.html)), frames
([QTextFrame](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextframe.html)), and tables
([QTextTable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html)). A text object has an
associated [format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextobject.html#format)() and
[document](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextobject.html#document)().

There are essentially two kinds of text objects: those that are used with blocks (block
formats), and those that are used with characters (character formats). The first kind
are derived from
[QTextBlockGroup](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextblockgroup.html), and the
second kind from [QTextFrame](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextframe.html).

You rarely need to use this class directly. When creating custom text objects, you will
also need to reimplement
[QTextDocument::createObject](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextdocument.html#createObject)()
which acts as a factory method for creating text objects.

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextTable.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A table is a group of cells ordered into rows and columns. Each table contains at least
one row and one column. Each cell contains a block, and is surrounded by a frame.

Tables are usually created and inserted into a document with the
[QTextCursor::insertTable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcursor.html#insertTable)()
function. For example, we can insert a table with three rows and two columns at the
current cursor position in an editor using the following lines of code:

```
    QTextCursor cursor(editor->textCursor());
    cursor.movePosition(QTextCursor::Start);

    QTextTable *table = cursor.insertTable(rows, columns, tableFormat);
```

The table format is either defined when the table is created or changed later with
[setFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#setFormat)().

The table currently being edited by the cursor is found with
[QTextCursor::currentTable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcursor.html#currentTable)().
This allows its format or dimensions to be changed after it has been inserted into a
document.

A table's size can be changed with
[resize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#resize)(), or by using
[insertRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#insertRows)(),
[insertColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#insertColumns)(),
[removeRows](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#removeRows)(), or
[removeColumns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#removeColumns)(). Use
[cellAt](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#cellAt)() to retrieve table
cells.

The starting and ending positions of table rows can be found by moving a cursor within a
table, and using the
[rowStart](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#rowStart)() and
[rowEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#rowEnd)() functions to
obtain cursors at the start and end of each row.

Rows and columns within a QTextTable can be merged and split using the
[mergeCells](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#mergeCells)() and
[splitCell](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#splitCell)() functions.
However, only cells that span multiple rows or columns can be split. (Merging or
splitting does not increase or decrease the number of rows and columns.)

Note that if you have merged multiple columns and rows into one cell, you will not be
able to split the merged cell into new cells spanning over more than one row or column.
To be able to split cells spanning over several rows and columns you need to do this
over several iterations.

| Original Table | Suppose we have a 2x3 table of names and addresses. To merge both columns in the first row we invoke [mergeCells](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#mergeCells)() with *row* \= 0, *column* \= 0, *numRows* \= 1 and *numColumns* \= 2\. ```     table->mergeCells(0, 0, 1, 2); ``` |
| --- | --- |
|  | This gives us the following table. To split the first row of the table back into two cells, we invoke the [splitCell](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#splitCell)() function with *numRows* and *numCols* \= 1\. ```     table->splitCell(0, 0, 1, 1); ``` |
| Split Table | This results in the original table. |

### void QTextTable::mergeCells(int *row*, int *column*, int *numRows*, int *numCols*)

Merges the cell at the specified *row* and *column* with the adjacent cells into one
cell. The new cell will span *numRows* rows and *numCols* columns. This method does
nothing if *numRows* or *numCols* is less than the current number of rows or columns
spanned by the cell.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also**
[splitCell](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#splitCell)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextTableCell.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Table cells are pieces of document structure that belong to a table. The table orders
cells into particular rows and columns; cells can also span multiple columns and rows.

Cells are usually created when a table is inserted into a document with
[QTextCursor::insertTable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcursor.html#insertTable)(),
but they are also created and destroyed when a table is resized.

Cells contain information about their location in a table; you can obtain the
[row](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#row)() and
[column](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#column)() numbers of a
cell, and its
[rowSpan](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#rowSpan)() and
[columnSpan](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#columnSpan)().

The [format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#format)() of a cell
describes the default character format of its contents. The
[firstCursorPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#firstCursorPosition)()
and
[lastCursorPosition](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#lastCursorPosition)()
functions are used to obtain the extent of the cell in the document.

### void QTextTableCell::setFormat(const [QTextCharFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcharformat.html) \&*format*)

Sets the cell's character format to *format*. This can for example be used to change the
background color of the entire cell:

[QTextTableCell](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html) cell \=
table-\>cellAt(2, 3);
[QTextCharFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextcharformat.html) format \=
cell.[format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#format)();
format.setBackground([Qt::blue](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#GlobalColor-enum));
cell.setFormat(format);

Note that the cell's row or column span cannot be changed through this function. You
have to use
[QTextTable::mergeCells](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#mergeCells)
and
[QTextTable::splitCell](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttable.html#splitCell)
instead.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.2.

**See also** [format](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecell.html#format)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QTextTableCellFormat.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

The table cell format of a table cell in a document specifies the visual properties of
the table cell.

The padding properties of a table cell are controlled by
[setLeftPadding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecellformat.html#setLeftPadding)(),
[setRightPadding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecellformat.html#setRightPadding)(),
[setTopPadding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecellformat.html#setTopPadding)(),
and
[setBottomPadding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecellformat.html#setBottomPadding)().
All the paddings can be set at once using
[setPadding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttablecellformat.html#setPadding)().

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A table is a group of cells ordered into rows and columns. Each table contains at least
one row and one column. Each cell contains a block. Tables in rich text documents are
formatted using the properties defined in this class.

Tables are horizontally justified within their parent frame according to the table's
alignment. This can be read with the
[alignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#alignment)()
function and set with
[setAlignment](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#setAlignment)().

Cells within the table are separated by cell spacing. The number of pixels between cells
is set with
[setCellSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#setCellSpacing)()
and read with
[cellSpacing](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#cellSpacing)().
The contents of each cell is surrounded by cell padding. The number of pixels between
each cell edge and its contents is set with
[setCellPadding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#setCellPadding)()
and read with
[cellPadding](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#cellPadding)().

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qtexttableformat-cell.png)

The table's background color can be read with the
[background](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextformat.html#background)() function,
and can be specified with
[setBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextformat.html#setBackground)().
The background color of each cell can be set independently, and will control the color
of the cell within the padded area.

The table format also provides a way to constrain the widths of the columns in the
table. Columns can be assigned a fixed width, a variable width, or a percentage of the
available width (see
[QTextLength](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextlength.html)). The
[columns](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#columns)() function
returns the number of columns with constraints, and the
[columnWidthConstraints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#columnWidthConstraints)()
function returns the constraints defined for the table. These quantities can also be set
by calling
[setColumnWidthConstraints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#setColumnWidthConstraints)()
with a vector containing new constraints. If no constraints are required,
[clearColumnWidthConstraints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtexttableformat.html#clearColumnWidthConstraints)()
can be used to remove them.

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-timeedit.png)

Many of the properties and functions provided by QTimeEdit are implemented in
[QDateTimeEdit](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html). These are the
relevant properties of this class:

- [time](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#time) holds the time displayed by the widget.
- [minimumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#minimumTime-prop) defines the minimum (earliest) time that can be set by the user.
- [maximumTime](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#maximumTime-prop) defines the maximum (latest) time that can be set by the user.
- [displayFormat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdatetimeedit.html#displayFormat-prop) contains a string that is used to format the time displayed in the widget.

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Toolbar buttons are added by adding *actions*, using
[addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addAction)() or
[insertAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#insertAction)(). Groups
of buttons can be separated using
[addSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addSeparator)() or
[insertSeparator](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#insertSeparator)().
If a toolbar button is not appropriate, a widget can be inserted instead using
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addWidget)() or
[insertWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#insertWidget)().
Examples of suitable widgets are
[QSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qspinbox.html),
[QDoubleSpinBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdoublespinbox.html), and
[QComboBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qcombobox.html). When a toolbar button is
pressed, it emits the
[actionTriggered](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#actionTriggered)()
signal.

A toolbar can be fixed in place in a particular area (e.g., at the top of the window),
or it can be movable between toolbar areas; see
[setMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#movable-prop)(),
[isMovable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#movable-prop)(),
[allowedAreas](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#allowedAreas-prop)() and
[isAreaAllowed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#isAreaAllowed)().

When a toolbar is resized in such a way that it is too small to show all the items it
contains, an extension button will appear as the last item in the toolbar. Pressing the
extension button will pop up a menu containing the items that do not currently fit in
the toolbar.

When a QToolBar is not a child of a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html), it loses the ability
to populate the extension pop up with widgets added to the toolbar using
[addWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addWidget)(). Please use
widget actions created by inheriting
[QWidgetAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html) and implementing
[QWidgetAction::createWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidgetaction.html#createWidget)()
instead.

PythonQt.QtGui.QToolBox.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A toolbox is a widget that displays a column of tabs one above the other, with the
current item displayed below the current tab. Every tab has an index position within the
column of tabs. A tab's item is a
[QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html).

Each item has an
[itemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#itemText)(), an optional
[itemIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#itemIcon)(), an optional
[itemToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#itemToolTip)(), and a
[widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#widget)(). The item's
attributes can be changed with
[setItemText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemText)(),
[setItemIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemIcon)(), and
[setItemToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemToolTip)().
Each item can be enabled or disabled individually with
[setItemEnabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#setItemEnabled)().

Items are added using
[addItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#addItem)(), or inserted at
particular positions using
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#insertItem)(). The total
number of items is given by
[count](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#count-prop)(). Items can be
deleted with delete, or removed from the toolbox with
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#removeItem)(). Combining
[removeItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#removeItem)() and
[insertItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#insertItem)() allows you
to move items to different positions.

The index of the current item widget is returned by
[currentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#currentIndex-prop)(),
and set with
[setCurrentIndex](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#currentIndex-prop)().
The index of a particular item can be found using
[indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#indexOf)(), and the item at a
given index is returned by item().

The [currentChanged](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbox.html#currentChanged)()
signal is emitted when the current item is changed.

PythonQt.QtGui.QToolButton.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

A tool button is a special button that provides quick-access to specific commands or
options. As opposed to a normal command button, a tool button usually doesn't show a
text label, but shows an icon instead.

Tool buttons are normally created when new
[QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) instances are created with
[QToolBar::addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addAction)() or
existing actions are added to a toolbar with
[QToolBar::addAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html#addAction)(). It
is also possible to construct tool buttons in the same way as any other widget, and
arrange them alongside other widgets in layouts.

One classic use of a tool button is to select tools; for example, the "pen" tool in a
drawing program. This would be implemented by using a QToolButton as a toggle button
(see
[setCheckable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkable-prop)()).

QToolButton supports auto-raising. In auto-raise mode, the button draws a 3D frame only
when the mouse points at it. The feature is automatically turned on when a button is
used inside a [QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html). Change it
with
[setAutoRaise](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#autoRaise-prop)().

A tool button's icon is set as [QIcon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qicon.html).
This makes it possible to specify different pixmaps for the disabled and active state.
The disabled pixmap is used when the button's functionality is not available. The active
pixmap is displayed when the button is auto-raised because the mouse pointer is hovering
over it.

The button's look and dimension is adjustable with
[setToolButtonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#toolButtonStyle-prop)()
and
[setIconSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#iconSize-prop)().
When used inside a [QToolBar](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbar.html) in a
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html), the button
automatically adjusts to
[QMainWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html)'s settings (see
[QMainWindow::setToolButtonStyle](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#toolButtonStyle-prop)()
and
[QMainWindow::setIconSize](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmainwindow.html#iconSize-prop)()).
Instead of an icon, a tool button can also display an arrow symbol, specified with
[arrowType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#arrowType-prop).

A tool button can offer additional choices in a popup menu. The popup menu can be set
using [setMenu](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#setMenu)(). Use
[setPopupMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#popupMode-prop)() to
configure the different modes available for tool buttons with a menu set. The default
mode is DelayedPopupMode which is sometimes used with the "Back" button in a web
browser. After pressing and holding the button down for a while, a menu pops up showing
a list of possible pages to jump to. The timeout is style dependent, see
[QStyle::SH\_ToolButton\_PopupDelay](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyle.html#StyleHint-enum).

### `[slot]` void QToolButton::setDefaultAction([QAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qaction.html) \**action*)

Sets the default action to *action*.

If a tool button has a default action, the action defines the following properties of
the button:

- [checkable](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checkable-prop)
- [checked](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#checked-prop)
- [enabled](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#enabled-prop)
- [font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#font-prop)
- [icon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#icon-prop)
- [popupMode](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#popupMode-prop) (assuming the action has a menu)
- [statusTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#statusTip-prop)
- [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#text-prop)
- [toolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#toolTip-prop)
- [whatsThis](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#whatsThis-prop)

Other properties, such as
[autoRepeat](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html#autoRepeat-prop),
are not affected by actions.

**See also**
[defaultAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtoolbutton.html#defaultAction)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QToolTip.doc:
Qt 5 reference: ## Detailed Description The tip is a short piece of text reminding the user of the widget's function. It is drawn immediately below the given position in a distinctive black-on-yellow color combination. The tip can be any [rich text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtextedit.html) formatted string. Rich text displayed in a tool tip is implicitly word-wrapped unless specified differently with `

`. The simplest and most common way to set a widget's tool tip is by calling its [QWidget::setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#toolTip-prop)() function. It is also possible to show different tool tips for different regions of a widget, by using a [QHelpEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qhelpevent.html) of type [QEvent::ToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum). Intercept the help event in your widget's [event()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event) function and call [QToolTip::showText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#showText)() with the text you want to display. The [Tooltips](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtwidgets-widgets-tooltips-example.html) example illustrates this technique. If you are calling [QToolTip::hideText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#hideText)(), or [QToolTip::showText](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#showText)() with an empty string, as a result of a [ToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)-event you should also call [ignore()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore) on the event, to signal that you don't want to start any tooltip specific modes. Note that, if you want to show tooltips in an item view, the model/view architecture provides functionality to set an item's tool tip; e.g., the [QTableWidgetItem::setToolTip](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtablewidgetitem.html#setToolTip)() function. However, if you want to provide custom tool tips in an item view, you must intercept the help event in the [QAbstractItemView::viewportEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html#viewportEvent)() function and handle it yourself. The default tool tip color and font can be customized with [setPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#setPalette)() and [setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#setFont)(). When a tooltip is currently on display, [isVisible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#isVisible)() returns `true` and [text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtooltip.html#text)() the currently visible text. **Note:** Tool tips use the inactive color group of [QPalette](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpalette.html), because tool tips are not active windows.

PythonQt.QtGui.QToolTip.showText.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[static]` void QToolTip::showText(const [QPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpoint.html) \&*pos*, const [QString](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstring.html) \&*text*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html) \**w*, const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rect*)

Shows *text* as a tool tip, with the global position *pos* as the point of interest. The
tool tip will be shown with a platform specific offset from this point of interest.

If you specify a non-empty rect the tip will be hidden as soon as you move your cursor
out of this area.

The *rect* is in the coordinates of the widget you specify with *w*. If the *rect* is
not empty you must specify a widget. Otherwise this argument can be `nullptr` but it is
used to determine the appropriate screen on multi-head systems.

If *text* is empty the tool tip is hidden. If the text is the same as the currently
shown tooltip, the tip will *not* move. You can force moving by first hiding the tip
with an empty text, and then showing the new tip at the new position.

PythonQt.QtGui.QTouchDevice.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Each [QTouchEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html) contains a
QTouchDevice pointer to allow accessing device-specific properties like type and
capabilities. It is the responsibility of the platform or generic plug-ins to register
the available touch devices via QWindowSystemInterface before generating any touch
events. Applications do not need to instantiate this class, they should just access the
global instances pointed to by
[QTouchEvent::device](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#device)().

## Detailed Description

### Enabling Touch Events

Touch events occur when pressing, releasing, or moving one or more touch points on a
touch device (such as a touch-screen or track-pad). To receive touch events, widgets
have to have the
[Qt::WA\_AcceptTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute set and graphics items need to have the
[acceptTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#setAcceptTouchEvents)
attribute set to true.

When using
[QAbstractScrollArea](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html) based
widgets, you should enable the
[Qt::WA\_AcceptTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#WidgetAttribute-enum)
attribute on the scroll area's
[viewport](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#viewport).

Similarly to [QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html), Qt
automatically grabs each touch point on the first press inside a widget, and the widget
will receive all updates for the touch point until it is released. Note that it is
possible for a widget to receive events for numerous touch points, and that multiple
widgets may be receiving touch events at the same time.

### Event Handling

All touch events are of type
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum),
[QEvent::TouchUpdate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum),
[QEvent::TouchEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) or
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).
Reimplement [QWidget::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)() or
[QAbstractScrollArea::viewportEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractscrollarea.html#viewportEvent)()
for widgets and
[QGraphicsItem::sceneEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgraphicsitem.html#sceneEvent)()
for items in a graphics view to receive touch events.

Unlike widgets, QWindows receive touch events always, there is no need to opt in. When
working directly with a [QWindow](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html), it
is enough to reimplement
[QWindow::touchEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwindow.html#touchEvent)().

The [QEvent::TouchUpdate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) and
[QEvent::TouchEnd](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events are
sent to the widget or item that accepted the
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event. If
the [QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event
is not accepted and not filtered by an event filter, then no further touch events are
sent until the next
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum).

Some systems may send an event of type
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum). Upon
receiving this event applications are requested to ignore the entire active touch
sequence. For example in a composited system the compositor may decide to treat certain
gestures as system-wide gestures. Whenever such a decision is made (the gesture is
recognized), the clients will be notified with a
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event so
they can update their state accordingly.

The [touchPoints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#touchPoints)()
function returns a list of all touch points contained in the event. Note that this list
may be empty, for example in case of a
[QEvent::TouchCancel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event.
Information about each touch point can be retrieved using the
[QTouchEvent::TouchPoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent-touchpoint.html)
class. The
[Qt::TouchPointState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#TouchPointState-enum)
enum describes the different states that a touch point may have.

**Note:** The list of
[touchPoints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#touchPoints)() will
never be partial: A touch event will always contain a touch point for each existing
physical touch contacts targetting the window or widget to which the event is sent. For
instance, assuming that all touches target the same window or widget, an event with a
condition of
[touchPoints](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtouchevent.html#touchPoints)().count()\=\=2
is guaranteed to imply that the number of fingers touching the touchscreen or touchpad
is exactly two.

### Event Delivery and Propagation

By default, [QGuiApplication](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qguiapplication.html)
translates the first touch point in a QTouchEvent into a
[QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html). This makes it
possible to enable touch events on existing widgets that do not normally handle
QTouchEvent. See below for information on some special considerations needed when doing
this.

[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) is the
first touch event sent to a widget. The
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event
contains a special accept flag that indicates whether the receiver wants the event. By
default, the event is accepted. You should call
[ignore](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#ignore)() if the touch event is
not handled by your widget. The
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event is
propagated up the parent widget chain until a widget accepts it with
[accept](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#accept)(), or an event filter
consumes it. For QGraphicsItems, the
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) event is
propagated to items under the mouse (similar to mouse event propagation for
QGraphicsItems).

### Touch Point Grouping

As mentioned above, it is possible that several widgets can be receiving QTouchEvents at
the same time. However, Qt makes sure to never send duplicate
[QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum) events to
the same widget, which could theoretically happen during propagation if, for example,
the user touched 2 separate widgets in a
[QGroupBox](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qgroupbox.html) and both widgets ignored
the [QEvent::TouchBegin](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qevent.html#Type-enum)
event.

To avoid this, Qt will group new touch points together using the following rules:

- When the first touch point is detected, the destination widget is determined firstly by the location on screen and secondly by the propagation rules.
- When additional touch points are detected, Qt first looks to see if there are any active touch points on any ancestor or descendent of the widget under the new touch point. If there are, the new touch point is grouped with the first, and the new touch point will be sent in a single QTouchEvent to the widget that handled the first touch point. (The widget under the new touch point will not receive an event).

This makes it possible for sibling widgets to handle touch events independently while
making sure that the sequence of QTouchEvents is always correct.

### Mouse Events and Touch Event Synthesizing

QTouchEvent delivery is independent from that of
[QMouseEvent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmouseevent.html). The application
flags
[Qt::AA\_SynthesizeTouchForUnhandledMouseEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ApplicationAttribute-enum)
and
[Qt::AA\_SynthesizeMouseForUnhandledTouchEvents](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ApplicationAttribute-enum)
can be used to enable or disable automatic synthesizing of touch events to mouse events
and mouse events to touch events.

### Caveats

- As mentioned above, enabling touch events means multiple widgets can be receiving touch events simultaneously. Combined with the default [QWidget::event](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#event)() handling for QTouchEvents, this gives you great flexibility in designing touch user interfaces. Be aware of the implications. For example, it is possible that the user is moving a [QSlider](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qslider.html) with one finger and pressing a [QPushButton](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpushbutton.html) with another. The signals emitted by these widgets will be interleaved.
- Recursion into the event loop using one of the exec() methods (e.g., [QDialog::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qdialog.html#exec)() or [QMenu::exec](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qmenu.html#exec)()) in a QTouchEvent event handler is not supported. Since there are multiple event recipients, recursion may cause problems, including but not limited to lost events and unexpected infinite recursion.
- QTouchEvents are not affected by a [mouse grab](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#grabMouse) or an [active pop-up widget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qapplication.html#activePopupWidget). The behavior of QTouchEvents is undefined when opening a pop-up or grabbing the mouse while there are more than one active touch points.

## Detailed Description

A transformation specifies how to translate, scale, shear, rotate or project the
coordinate system, and is typically used when rendering graphics.

QTransform differs from QMatrix in that it is a true 3x3 matrix, allowing perspective
transformations. QTransform's toAffine() method allows casting QTransform to QMatrix. If
a perspective transformation has been specified on the matrix, then the conversion will
cause loss of data.

QTransform is the recommended transformation class in Qt.

A QTransform object can be built using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#setMatrix)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#scale)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#rotate)(),
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#translate)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#shear)() functions.
Alternatively, it can be built by applying [basic matrix
operations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#basic-matrix-operations).
The matrix can also be defined when constructed, and it can be reset to the identity
matrix (the default) using the
[reset](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#reset)() function.

The QTransform class supports mapping of graphic primitives: A given point, line,
polygon, region, or painter path can be mapped to the coordinate system defined by
*this* matrix using the [map](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#map)()
function. In case of a rectangle, its coordinates can be transformed using the
[mapRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#mapRect)() function. A
rectangle can also be transformed into a *polygon* (mapped to the coordinate system
defined by *this* matrix), using the
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#mapToPolygon)()
function.

QTransform provides the
[isIdentity](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#isIdentity)() function
which returns `true` if the matrix is the identity matrix, and the
[isInvertible](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#isInvertible)()
function which returns `true` if the matrix is non-singular (i.e. AB \= BA \= I). The
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#inverted)() function
returns an inverted copy of *this* matrix if it is invertible (otherwise it returns the
identity matrix), and
[adjoint](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#adjoint)() returns the
matrix's classical adjoint. In addition, QTransform provides the
[determinant](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#determinant)() function
which returns the matrix's determinant.

Finally, the QTransform class supports matrix multiplication, addition and subtraction,
and objects of the class can be streamed as well as compared.

### Rendering Graphics

When rendering graphics, the matrix defines the transformations but the actual
transformation is performed by the drawing routines in
[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html).

By default, [QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) operates on the
associated device's own coordinate system. The standard coordinate system of a
[QPaintDevice](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpaintdevice.html) has its origin
located at the top-left position. The *x* values increase to the right; *y* values
increase downward. For a complete description, see the [coordinate
system](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/coordsys.html) documentation.

[QPainter](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html) has functions to translate,
scale, shear and rotate the coordinate system without using a QTransform. For example:

|  | ``` void SimpleTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.rotate(45);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QTransform"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

Although these functions are very convenient, it can be more efficient to build a
QTransform and call
[QPainter::setTransform](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpainter.html#setTransform)()
if you want to perform more than a single transform operation. For example:

|  | ``` void CombinedTransformation::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      QTransform transform;     transform.translate(50, 50);     transform.rotate(45);     transform.scale(0.5, 1.0);     painter.setTransform(transform);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QTransform"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

### Basic Matrix Operations

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/qtransform-representation.png)

A QTransform object contains a 3 x 3 matrix. The `m31` (`dx`) and `m32` (`dy`) elements
specify horizontal and vertical translation. The `m11` and `m22` elements specify
horizontal and vertical scaling. The `m21` and `m12` elements specify horizontal and
vertical *shearing*. And finally, the `m13` and `m23` elements specify horizontal and
vertical projection, with `m33` as an additional projection factor.

QTransform transforms a point in the plane to another point using the following
formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
if (!isAffine()) {
    w' = m13*x + m23*y + m33
    x' /= w'
    y' /= w'
}
```

The point *(x, y)* is the original point, and *(x', y')* is the transformed point. *(x',
y')* can be transformed back to *(x, y)* by performing the same operation on the
[inverted](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#inverted)() matrix.

The various matrix elements can be set when constructing the matrix, or by using the
[setMatrix](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#setMatrix)() function
later on. They can also be manipulated using the
[translate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#translate)(),
[rotate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#rotate)(),
[scale](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#scale)() and
[shear](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#shear)() convenience
functions. The currently set values can be retrieved using the
[m11](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m11)(),
[m12](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m12)(),
[m13](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m13)(),
[m21](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m21)(),
[m22](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m22)(),
[m23](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m23)(),
[m31](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m31)(),
[m32](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m32)(),
[m33](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#m33)(),
[dx](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#dx)() and
[dy](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#dy)() functions.

Translation is the simplest transformation. Setting `dx` and `dy` will move the
coordinate system `dx` units along the X axis and `dy` units along the Y axis. Scaling
can be done by setting `m11` and `m22`. For example, setting `m11` to 2 and `m22` to 1.5
will double the height and increase the width by 50%. The identity matrix has `m11`,
`m22`, and `m33` set to 1 (all others are set to 0\) mapping a point to itself. Shearing
is controlled by `m12` and `m21`. Setting these elements to values different from zero
will twist the coordinate system. Rotation is achieved by setting both the shearing
factors and the scaling factors. Perspective transformation is achieved by setting both
the projection factors and the scaling factors.

#### Combining Transforms

Here's the combined transformations example using basic matrix operations:

|  | ``` void BasicOperations::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *) {     const double a = qDegreesToRadians(45.0);     double sina = sin(a);     double cosa = cos(a);      QTransform scale(0.5, 0, 0, 1.0, 0, 0);     QTransform rotate(cosa, sina, -sina, cosa, 0, 0);     QTransform translate(1, 0, 0, 1, 50.0, 50.0);      QTransform transform = scale * rotate * translate;      QPainter painter(this);     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::blue, 1, Qt::DashLine));     painter.drawRect(0, 0, 100, 100);      painter.setTransform(transform);      painter.setFont(QFont("Helvetica", 24));     painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::black, 1));     painter.drawText(20, 10, "QTransform"); } ``` |
| --- | --- |

The combined transform first scales each operand, then rotates it, and finally
translates it, just as in the order in which the product of its factors is written. This
means the point to which the transforms are applied is implicitly multiplied on the left
with the transform to its right.

#### Relation to Matrix Notation

The matrix notation in QTransform is the transpose of a commonly-taught convention which
represents transforms and points as matrices and vectors. That convention multiplies its
matrix on the left and column vector to the right. In other words, when several
transforms are applied to a point, the right-most matrix acts directly on the vector
first. Then the next matrix to the left acts on the result of the first operation \- and
so on. As a result, that convention multiplies the matrices that make up a composite
transform in the reverse of the order in QTransform, as you can see in [Combining
Transforms](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#combining-transforms).
Transposing the matrices, and combining them to the right of a row vector that
represents the point, lets the matrices of transforms appear, in their product, in the
order in which we think of the transforms being applied to the point.

### void QTransform::map([qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *x*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) *y*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) \**tx*, [qreal](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtglobal.html#qreal-typedef) \**ty*) const

Maps the given coordinates *x* and *y* into the coordinate system defined by this
matrix. The resulting values are put in \**tx* and \**ty*, respectively.

The coordinates are transformed using the following formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
if (!isAffine()) {
    w' = m13*x + m23*y + m33
    x' /= w'
    y' /= w'
}
```

The point (x, y) is the original point, and (x', y') is the transformed point.

**See also** [Basic Matrix
Operations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#basic-matrix-operations).

PythonQt.QtGui.QTransform.mapRect.doc:

### [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) QTransform::mapRect(const [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) \&*rectangle*) const

Creates and returns a [QRectF](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrectf.html) object
that is a copy of the given *rectangle*, mapped into the coordinate system defined by
this matrix.

The rectangle's coordinates are transformed using the following formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx
y' = m22*y + m12*x + dy
if (!isAffine()) {
    w' = m13*x + m23*y + m33
    x' /= w'
    y' /= w'
}
```

If rotation or shearing has been specified, this function returns the *bounding*
rectangle. To retrieve the exact region the given *rectangle* maps to, use the
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#mapToPolygon)()
function instead.

**See also**
[mapToPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#mapToPolygon)() and
[Basic Matrix
Operations](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtransform.html#basic-matrix-operations).

### [QPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpolygon.html) QTransform::mapToPolygon(const [QRect](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qrect.html) \&*rectangle*) const

Creates and returns a [QPolygon](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qpolygon.html)
representation of the given *rectangle*, mapped into the coordinate system defined by

The rectangle's coordinates are transformed using the following formulas:

```
x' = m11*x + m21*y + dx

if (!isAffine()) {

rounding), so `matrix.map(QPolygon(rectangle))` is not always the same as
`matrix.mapToPolygon(rectangle)`.

transformations. For example, if the matrix both scales and shears, the type would be
`TxShear`, because `TxShear` has a higher enumeration value than `TxScale`.

Knowing the transformation type of a matrix is useful for optimization: you can often
handle specific types more optimally than handling the generic case.

PythonQt.QtGui.QTreeView.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-treeview.png)

A QTreeView implements a tree representation of items from a model. This class is used
to provide standard hierarchical lists that were previously provided by the `QListView`
class, but using the more flexible approach provided by Qt's model/view architecture.

The QTreeView class is one of the [Model/View
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#model-view-classes)
and is part of Qt's [model/view
framework](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html).

QTreeView implements the interfaces defined by the
[QAbstractItemView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html) class to
allow it to display data provided by models derived from the
[QAbstractItemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html) class.

It is simple to construct a tree view displaying data from a model. In the following
example, the contents of a directory are supplied by a
[QFileSystemModel](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qfilesystemmodel.html) and
displayed as a tree:

```
    QFileSystemModel *model = new QFileSystemModel;
    model->setRootPath(QDir::currentPath());
    QTreeView *tree = new QTreeView(splitter);
    tree->setModel(model);
```

The model/view architecture ensures that the contents of the tree view are updated as
the model changes.

Items that have children can be in an expanded (children are visible) or collapsed
(children are hidden) state. When this state changes a
[collapsed](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#collapsed)() or
[expanded](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#expanded)() signal is
emitted with the model index of the relevant item.

The amount of indentation used to indicate levels of hierarchy is controlled by the
[indentation](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#indentation-prop)
property.

Headers in tree views are constructed using the
[QHeaderView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html) class and can be
hidden using `header()->hide()`. Note that each header is configured with its
[stretchLastSection](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#stretchLastSection-prop)
property set to true, ensuring that the view does not waste any of the space assigned to
it for its header. If this value is set to true, this property will override the resize
mode set on the last section in the header.

By default, all columns in a tree view are movable except the first. To disable movement
of these columns, use
[QHeaderView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html)'s
[setSectionsMovable()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#setSectionsMovable)
function. For more information about rearranging sections, see [Moving Header
Sections](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qheaderview.html#moving-header-sections).

### Key Bindings

QTreeView supports a set of key bindings that enable the user to navigate in the view
and interact with the contents of items:

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Up | Moves the cursor to the item in the same column on the previous row. If the parent of the current item has no more rows to navigate to, the cursor moves to the relevant item in the last row of the sibling that precedes the parent. |
| Down | Moves the cursor to the item in the same column on the next row. If the parent of the current item has no more rows to navigate to, the cursor moves to the relevant item in the first row of the sibling that follows the parent. |
| Left | Hides the children of the current item (if present) by collapsing a branch. |
| Minus | Same as Left. |
| Right | Reveals the children of the current item (if present) by expanding a branch. |
| Plus | Same as Right. |
| Asterisk | Expands the current item and all its children (if present). |
| PageUp | Moves the cursor up one page. |
| PageDown | Moves the cursor down one page. |
| Home | Moves the cursor to an item in the same column of the first row of the first top-level item in the model. |
| End | Moves the cursor to an item in the same column of the last row of the last top-level item in the model. |
| F2 | In editable models, this opens the current item for editing. The Escape key can be used to cancel the editing process and revert any changes to the data displayed. |

### Improving Performance

It is possible to give the view hints about the data it is handling in order to improve
its performance when displaying large numbers of items. One approach that can be taken
for views that are intended to display items with equal heights is to set the
[uniformRowHeights](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#uniformRowHeights-prop)
property to true.

indentation of the items in the tree view.

PythonQt.QtGui.QTreeWidget.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

![](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/images/windows-treeview.png)

The QTreeWidget class is a convenience class that provides a standard tree widget with a
classic item-based interface similar to that used by the
[QListView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qlistview.html) class in Qt 3\. This
class is based on Qt's Model/View architecture and uses a default model to hold items,
each of which is a
[QTreeWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html).

Developers who do not need the flexibility of the Model/View framework can use this
class to create simple hierarchical lists very easily. A more flexible approach involves
combining a [QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) with a
standard item model. This allows the storage of data to be separated from its
representation.

In its simplest form, a tree widget can be constructed in the following way:

```
QTreeWidget *treeWidget = new QTreeWidget();
treeWidget->setColumnCount(1);
QList<QTreeWidgetItem *> items;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i)
    items.append(new QTreeWidgetItem(static_cast<QTreeWidget *>(nullptr), QStringList(QString("item: %1").arg(i))));
treeWidget->insertTopLevelItems(0, items);
```

Before items can be added to the tree widget, the number of columns must be set with
[setColumnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#columnCount-prop)().
This allows each item to have one or more labels or other decorations. The number of
columns in use can be found with the
[columnCount](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#columnCount-prop)()
function.

The tree can have a header that contains a section for each column in the widget. It is
easiest to set up the labels for each section by supplying a list of strings with
[setHeaderLabels](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#setHeaderLabels)(),
but a custom header can be constructed with a
[QTreeWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html) and inserted
into the tree with the
[setHeaderItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#setHeaderItem)()
function.

The items in the tree can be sorted by column according to a predefined sort order. If
sorting is enabled, the user can sort the items by clicking on a column header. Sorting
can be enabled or disabled by calling
[setSortingEnabled()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#sortingEnabled-prop).
The
[isSortingEnabled()](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html#sortingEnabled-prop)
function indicates whether sorting is enabled.

### void QTreeWidget::setItemWidget([QTreeWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html) \**item*, int *column*, [QWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#QWidget) \**widget*)

Sets the given *widget* to be displayed in the cell specified by the given *item* and
*column*.

The given *widget*'s
[autoFillBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qwidget.html#autoFillBackground-prop)
property must be set to true, otherwise the widget's background will be transparent,
showing both the model data and the tree widget item.

This function should only be used to display static content in the place of a tree
widget item. If you want to display custom dynamic content or implement a custom editor
widget, use [QTreeView](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreeview.html) and subclass
[QStyledItemDelegate](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qstyleditemdelegate.html)
instead.

This function cannot be called before the item hierarchy has been set up, i.e., the
[QTreeWidgetItem](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html) that will
hold *widget* must have been added to the view before *widget* is set.

**Note:** The tree takes ownership of the widget.

This function was introduced in Qt 4.1.

**See also**
[itemWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html#itemWidget)() and
[Delegate
Classes](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/model-view-programming.html#delegate-classes).

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

Tree widget items are used to hold rows of information for tree widgets. Rows usually
contain several columns of data, each of which can contain a text label and an icon.

The QTreeWidgetItem class is a convenience class that replaces the QListViewItem class
in Qt 3\. It provides an item for use with the
[QTreeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html) class.

Items are usually constructed with a parent that is either a
[QTreeWidget](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidget.html) (for top-level items)
or a QTreeWidgetItem (for items on lower levels of the tree). For example, the following
code constructs a top-level item to represent cities of the world, and adds a entry for
Oslo as a child item:

```
    QTreeWidgetItem *cities = new QTreeWidgetItem(treeWidget);
    cities->setText(0, tr("Cities"));
    QTreeWidgetItem *osloItem = new QTreeWidgetItem(cities);
    osloItem->setText(0, tr("Oslo"));
    osloItem->setText(1, tr("Yes"));
```

Items can be added in a particular order by specifying the item they follow when they
are constructed:

```
    QTreeWidgetItem *planets = new QTreeWidgetItem(treeWidget, cities);
    planets->setText(0, tr("Planets"));
```

Each column in an item can have its own background brush which is set with the
[setBackground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setBackground)()
function. The current background brush can be found with
[background](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#background)(). The
text label for each column can be rendered with its own font and brush. These are
specified with the
[setFont](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setFont)() and
[setForeground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setForeground)()
functions, and read with
[font](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#font)() and
[foreground](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#foreground)().

The main difference between top-level items and those in lower levels of the tree is
that a top-level item has no
[parent](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#parent)(). This
information can be used to tell the difference between items, and is useful to know when
inserting and removing items from the tree. Children of an item can be removed with
[takeChild](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#takeChild)() and
inserted at a given index in the list of children with the
[insertChild](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#insertChild)()
function.

By default, items are enabled, selectable, checkable, and can be the source of a drag
and drop operation. Each item's flags can be changed by calling
[setFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setFlags)() with the
appropriate value (see
[Qt::ItemFlags](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qt.html#ItemFlag-enum)). Checkable
items can be checked and unchecked with the
[setCheckState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#setCheckState)()
function. The corresponding
[checkState](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#checkState)()
function indicates whether the item is currently checked.

### Subclassing

When subclassing QTreeWidgetItem to provide custom items, it is possible to define new
types for them so that they can be distinguished from standard items. The constructors
for subclasses that require this feature need to call the base class constructor with a
new type value equal to or greater than
[UserType](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qtreewidgetitem.html#ItemType-enum).

Qt 5 reference:

## Detailed Description

For an overview of Qt's Undo Framework, see the [overview
document](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundo.html).

A QUndoCommand represents a single editing action on a document; for example, inserting
or deleting a block of text in a text editor. QUndoCommand can apply a change to the
document with [redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() and
undo the change with
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)(). The implementations
for these functions must be provided in a derived class.

```
class AppendText : public QUndoCommand
{
public:
    AppendText(QString *doc, const QString &text)
        : m_document(doc), m_text(text) { setText("append text"); }
    void undo() override
        { m_document->chop(m_text.length()); }
    void redo() override
        { m_document->append(m_text); }
private:
    QString *m_document;
    QString m_text;
};
```

A QUndoCommand has an associated
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#text)(). This is a short
string describing what the command does. It is used to update the text properties of the
stack's undo and redo actions; see
[QUndoStack::createUndoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createUndoAction)()
and
[QUndoStack::createRedoAction](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#createRedoAction)().

QUndoCommand objects are owned by the stack they were pushed on.
[QUndoStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html) deletes a command if it
has been undone and a new command is pushed. For example:

```
MyCommand *command1 = new MyCommand();
stack->push(command1);
MyCommand *command2 = new MyCommand();
stack->push(command2);

stack->undo();

MyCommand *command3 = new MyCommand();
stack->push(command3); // command2 gets deleted
```

In effect, when a command is pushed, it becomes the top-most command on the stack.

To support command compression, QUndoCommand has an
[id](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#id)() and the virtual function
[mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)(). These
functions are used by
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)().

To support command macros, a QUndoCommand object can have any number of child commands.
Undoing or redoing the parent command will cause the child commands to be undone or
redone. A command can be assigned to a parent explicitly in the constructor. In this
case, the command will be owned by the parent.

The parent in this case is usually an empty command, in that it doesn't provide its own
implementation of [undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)()
and [redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)(). Instead, it
uses the base implementations of these functions, which simply call
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)() or
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() on all its children.
The parent should, however, have a meaningful
[text](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#text)().

```
QUndoCommand *insertRed = new QUndoCommand(); // an empty command
insertRed->setText("insert red text");

new InsertText(document, idx, text, insertRed); // becomes child of insertRed
new SetColor(document, idx, text.length(), Qt::red, insertRed);

stack.push(insertRed);
```

Another way to create macros is to use the convenience functions
[QUndoStack::beginMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#beginMacro)()
and
[QUndoStack::endMacro](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#endMacro)().

### `[virtual]` int QUndoCommand::id() const

Returns the ID of this command.

A command ID is used in command compression. It must be an integer unique to this
command's class, or -1 if the command doesn't support compression.

If the command supports compression this function must be overridden in the derived
class to return the correct ID. The base implementation returns -1.

[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)() will only
try to merge two commands if they have the same ID, and the ID is not -1.

**See also**
[mergeWith](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#mergeWith)() and
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)().

PythonQt.QtGui.QUndoCommand.mergeWith.doc:
Qt 5 reference:

### `[virtual]` bool QUndoCommand::mergeWith(const [QUndoCommand](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#QUndoCommand) \**command*)

Attempts to merge this command with *command*. Returns `true` on success; otherwise
returns `false`.

If this function returns `true`, calling this command's
[redo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#redo)() must have the same
effect as redoing both this command and *command*. Similarly, calling this command's
[undo](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#undo)() must have the same
effect as undoing *command* and this command.

[QUndoStack](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html) will only try to merge
two commands if they have the same id, and the id is not -1.

The default implementation returns `false`.

```
bool AppendText::mergeWith(const QUndoCommand *other)
{
    if (other->id() != id()) // make sure other is also an AppendText command
        return false;
    m_text += static_cast<const AppendText*>(other)->m_text;
    return true;
}
```

**See also** [id](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundocommand.html#id)() and
[QUndoStack::push](https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qundostack.html#push)().
